## [2.416.6] — 2026-10-01

_The one-time bill demo stays in September 2026, so its bills can be sent whatever today's date is._

### Fixed
- **Demo data: September bills in the one-time bill demo can be sent again**
  (DEF-BIL-8334). The main demo closes the month before today, so a demo built
  on 1 October closed September, where every one-time bill demo date sits, and
  Send refused them. The one-time bill demo is kept in September 2026 on
  purpose — its worked figures depend on the month's length — and its seed now
  reopens September when the main demo has closed it. The main demo is
  unchanged. Re-checked on a demo built today: Maria's first bill $393.15 and
  the Unit D final bill $93.47 both send, and the eight end-to-end one-time
  bill cases all pass.

## [2.416.5] — 2026-10-01

_The demo now prorates first and final bills, because its billing cycle has a start date._

### Fixed
- **Demo data: the one-time bill's demo cycle has a first run date**
  (DEF-BIL-8333). Without it the product could not tell how long the cycle is,
  so every demo first and final bill charged whole monthly base charges.
  Re-running the demo seed repairs an existing demo database. Figures that
  move: Maria Alvarez's first bill (Unit C, Sep 12–30) $397.82 → $393.15; her
  final bill (Unit D, Sep 1–18) $103.67 → $93.47, so the deposit refund goes
  from $46.33 to $56.53. The interim bill stays $185.13.

### Known
- **On a demo seeded from 1 October, September bills cannot be sent**
  (DEF-BIL-8334): the demo closes the month before today, and the one-time
  bill demo's dates are in September.
## [2.416.4] — 2026-10-01

_One-time bills: catch-up and penalty bills priced month by month, and three things a clerk could not do or could not check._

### Fixed
- **A catch-up or penalty bill over several months no longer overcharges sewer**
  (DEF-BIL-8560). Sewer is 40% of each month's own water. Before, each month
  was charged on all the months' water together. Maria Alvarez's July–September
  catch-up comes down from $710.06 to $649.49. Her penalty bill comes down from
  $1,268.62 to $1,167.85.
- **A catch-up or penalty bill keeps its months** (DEF-BIL-8561). Review shows
  one group per month, each with its subtotal. Each saved line carries its month,
  and every water line names its meter.
- **The bill's footer adds up** (DEF-BIL-8565). A first bill's deposit and
  connection charge, and a penalty's tamper charge, now have their own line,
  "One-time charges". Maria Alvarez's first bill reads $194.26 + tax $3.89 +
  one-time charges $195.00 = $393.15 (with the base prorated from her move-in
  day, 2.416.3).
- **A catch-up saves its own estimates in Meter Reads only where no reading
  covered the stretch** (DEF-BIL-8564). A share of a real reading is not saved
  again, so the next bill does not count the same water twice.

### Added
- **An interim bill can estimate a meter that has no reading** (DEF-BIL-8562).
  On step 2 the clerk presses Estimate. The meter is billed on Meter Reads' own
  estimate and marked Estimated. When the bill is sent, the estimate is saved in
  Meter Reads, as the bulk run does.

### Not fixed
- **A month cut at a price change charges a whole month's per-cart trash charge
  in each part** (DEF-BIL-8566). No rule says whether it should be prorated;
  this needs a ruling.

## [2.416.3] — 2026-09-30

_A first bill now charges the base only for the days from move-in, as the signed rule says._

### Fixed
- **One-time bill, First bill: the base charge is prorated from the move-in
  day** (DEF-BIL-8331). It used to charge the whole month's base however few
  days the bill covered. The signed worked example now holds through the
  one-time bill: moving in on day 16 of a 30-day cycle with a $30.50 base
  charges $15.25 (15 of 30 days). The cycle's length is read the same way the
  final bill reads it. Maria Alvarez's first bill from 09/12 (19 of 30 days) goes
  from $397.82 to $393.15 once her cycle's calendar can be read. Interim and
  final bills are unchanged.

### Known
- **The demo cycle has no first run date, so its calendar cannot be read and
  no demo bill prorates** (DEF-BIL-8333). With the demo as seeded, Maria's
  first bill still shows $397.82; the final bill for Unit D would become $93.47
  (not $103.67) once the cycle has a first run date.


## [2.416.1] — 2026-09-30

_A first bill for an account with no billing cycle now waits for a cycle instead of charging a whole month._

### Fixed
- **One-time bill, First bill: an account with no billing cycle is stopped at
  step 1** (DEF-BIL-8330, PO ruling 2026-09-30, option A). As soon as the
  account is picked, its card shows Cycle *None* and the problem list and the
  account field both say *"No billing cycle. Assign one on the account."*
  Continue waits until a cycle is assigned. The server refuses the same bill
  with the same sentence, before anything is priced, so it can no longer be
  created another way. Before this, a one-day first bill for such an account
  (John Mauli) cost $418.00, the same as a whole month. Interim, final,
  catch-up, penalty and fee bills are unchanged.
- **One-time bill: the account card's Cycle no longer says *None* for an
  account on a cycle that has no name** (DEF-BIL-8332). It shows the cycle's
  code instead, and such an account's first bill is not stopped.
- **One-time bill, First bill: a bill from the account's own move-in date now
  starts from the reading taken that day** (DEF-BIL-8563). Before, the move-in
  reading was treated as the closing reading, so step 2 said no move-in
  reading was on file, nothing was priced and there was no deposit or
  connection charge. The move-in day is still a billed day. Found by the J74
  end-to-end walk: Maria Alvarez, Unit C, moved in 09/12, now bills $397.82
  from 09/12 ($150.00 deposit, $45.00 connection charge, plus usage).

### Known
- **A first bill still charges the whole month's base charge even when the
  account IS on a cycle** (DEF-BIL-8331, found while fixing the above; not
  fixed here). A 16-day first bill charges the $8.00 monthly base where 16 of
  31 days is $4.13.


## [2.416.0] — 2026-09-30

_The bill run's Check reads each batch of 500 accounts once, instead of once per account._

### Changed
- **Bill run, Check: about fourteen times faster** (plan B27). Each batch of
  500 accounts now reads its taxes, rates, charge codes, meters, readings,
  service points, agreements and previous bills in a few queries for the whole
  batch, instead of asking the same questions for every account: about 0.05
  seconds an account instead of 0.69, so 40,000 accounts take about half an
  hour on one worker instead of about 7.7 hours. What the Check finds is
  unchanged — a test compares the two ways account by account. Figures are in
  `04-docs/05-modules/07-billing/19-check-cost-measured.md`.

### Fixed
- **A payment recorded while the Check was running could be missed and never
  flagged** (DEF-BIL-8491). An account's result now records when its facts were
  read, so a payment (or reading, meter or plan change) made after that is
  always picked up by the automatic re-check.
- **Meter-reading lookups for a bill period searched every month of stored
  readings** (DEF-BIL-8490); they now look only in the months the period
  covers.

## [2.415.0] — 2026-09-30

_Three bulk-run Check fixes: a new price rechecks its accounts, a swapped meter bills both parts, and the default-plan answer waits on a question._

### Fixed
- **Bill run, Check: publishing a new price rechecks the accounts on that plan**
  (DEF-BIL-8245). Before, only saving the plan itself did. Now a new dated price
  version on any of the plan's rate schedules rechecks exactly that plan's
  accounts, within a minute or on the next look. A draft price does not.
- **Bill run, Check: a meter swapped during the month bills both parts**
  (DEF-BIL-8244). Where the old meter's last reading and the new meter's first
  are both recorded, the account shows under *Meter swapped* with both parts —
  e.g. old meter 13,500 → 13,620 (120 kWh) and new meter 0 → 85 (85 kWh),
  suggest 205 kWh. Accepted, the bill charges 205 kWh on one line with one
  base charge and lists each meter's readings, and both readings are locked as
  billed when the bill is sent. ⚠ The pricing is built; the clerk's *Accept*
  on the Check screen still holds the account until the Check's answer list
  takes it (the next bulk-run change). If either reading is missing the choice
  stays *Estimate the missing part* or *Hold*.

### Open
- **"Use the customer type's default plan" is not offered for real yet**
  (DEF-BIL-8246). The product has no place that says what a customer type's
  default plan is; that is a question for the Product Owner (OQ-RAT-12782).
  Choosing it still holds the account.

## [2.414.0] — 2026-09-30

_Two more payment checks on the bulk bill run's Check._

### Added
- **Bill run, Check: a payment the utility received but could not match to an
  account is flagged as "Unmatched payment" on the account it was tied to**
  (DEF-BIL-8240). A $120.00 bank transfer with no account number, tied to
  Maria's account by the payer's name and not yet posted, is flagged; the clerk
  holds the account or bills it without the payment. A credit balance is never
  flagged — Maria's $80.00 June credit simply comes off her next bill (Product
  Owner ruling, option B).
- **Bill run, Check: a level-pay account more than 20% off its level is flagged
  as "Level pay off track"** (DEF-BIL-8241) — the same threshold the automatic
  re-level uses. Level $242 against a trailing average of $300 is +23.97% and is
  flagged; $260 (+7.44%) is not. It is a warning: the account still bills and
  nothing is re-levelled.

- **Bill run, Check: "Add to bill" on a payment-plan instalment now bills the
  account and prints the instalment on the bill as its own line** (DEF-BIL-8243)
  — "Instalment 2: 45.00 USD due 2026-09-15." — instead of holding the account.
  It is not an extra charge: the instalment is part of the balance already
  carried forward, so the bill's total and amount due do not change.

### Not built
- **"Bounced payment not reversed" is still shown as not checked**
  (DEF-BIL-8500): nothing in the product records a bank return against one of
  our payments before its reversal is written.

## [2.413.0] — 2026-09-30

_The rest of the bulk bill run: the Check split into categories, fixes on the row, leave out, the sign-off summary, Not in this run and the Check report._

### Added
- **Bill run, Check: a blocked row is fixed on the row** (DEF-BIL-8218). A unit
  with no plan, a connection with no size, or premises with no city-limits
  answer is set right there — the owning screen's own rules and audit apply —
  and that account is checked again at once.
- **Bill run, Check: leave a ready account out, put it back** (DEF-BIL-8217).
  A left-out account is not billed and waits in Pending billing as "left out by
  clerk".
- **Bill run, Sign off: every figure is now shown** (DEF-BIL-8220): accounts
  regular and master, units on their own account and through a master, usage
  and base charges per service, taxes, fees, credits, previous balance,
  payments applied, amount due and how it will be paid — each section says so
  if it does not add up. Waived standing charges are listed with their amount.
- **Bill run, after Send: Not in this run lists every account not billed with
  how long it has waited; a selection can be left for the next cycle**
  (DEF-BIL-8223), and a **Check report** tab shows the Check as it stood at Send.
- **The next bill after a skipped instalment says the plan now ends a month
  later** (DEF-BIL-8248).

### Changed
- **Bill run, Check: the screen reads the server's grouped findings a page at a
  time** (DEF-BIL-8216) and shows "n of N" while checking (DEF-BIL-8224). A
  change re-checks only the part of the Check it touched (DEF-BIL-8286).

### Fixed
- **Every account the run does not bill now reaches Pending billing at Send**
  (DEF-BIL-8410); a held month billed by the next bill is no longer billed again
  by a catch-up run (DEF-BIL-8413).
- **Paid after cut-off → "Apply to this bill" bills the account, counting the
  payment once** (DEF-BIL-8243, that one choice).
- **A standing-charges-only account with no reading is no longer blocked by the
  missing-multiplier check** (DEF-BIL-8247).
- **Estimate the reading can be recorded on the Check** (DEF-BIL-8551,
  DEF-BIL-8415): the row asks how much, starting from the account's usual month.
- **Waive saves with its reason** (DEF-BIL-8552); a waived account is listed as
  Waived and never counted as Failed to draft (DEF-BIL-8416).
- **Price N is the number of bills Calculate will make** (DEF-BIL-8554).
- **The Check report shows who answered what, and when** (DEF-BIL-8555).
- **Blocked and unanswered accounts reach Pending billing at Send**
  (DEF-BIL-8553, DEF-BIL-8474); a skipped instalment extends the plan
  (DEF-BIL-8556).
- **An account already billed for the whole period is not billed again**
  (DEF-BIL-8473); a gap row and an overlap row each offer only their own answers
  (DEF-BIL-8472); a master account's bill prices (DEF-BIL-8470); Sign off lists
  the bills an account's credit covers (DEF-BIL-8242).
- **Checking and Sending show n of N, and the Check never shows 0 while it is
  still running** (DEF-BIL-8417, DEF-BIL-8422, DEF-BIL-8419).

## [2.412.6] — 2026-09-30

### Fixed
- **Bank import and the report editor could crash instead of showing a refusal**
  that arrived after the page first drew; they now show the refusal
  (DEF-GOV-8540).
- Record-keeping checks: 9 of 58 failing repository checks are green again, each
  failure dated to the change that caused it; the rest are filed with owners.

## [2.412.5] — 2026-09-30

### Fixed
- **One-time bill: a refusal now says what is actually wrong and where to fix
  it.** "Water can't be priced. Check its rates." and "This one-time bill can't
  be created as asked" are gone. Each of the 40 reasons the pricing can stop has
  its own sentence, naming the service, the date or the meter size — for
  example "No Water rate on Aug 31, 2026. Add one in Plans & Rates." or "Water
  size W-58 has no price. Add it to the rate schedule." Where no sentence is
  written yet, the engine's own plain sentence is shown instead (DEF-BIL-8287,
  DEF-BIL-8288).
- **One-time bill: no failure is shown while step 1 is still being filled
  in.** The side panel says "Finish step 1 to see figures." and a refusal is
  shown only when Continue is pressed (DEF-BIL-8289).
- **One-time bill: Continue pressed straight after typing no longer leaves
  "This step isn't finished" on its own.** Continue waits for the account's
  days to pay and for the newest check (DEF-BIL-8327).
- **One-time bill: a first bill whose To is the move-in day is stopped on the
  To field** with "To must be after move-in." (DEF-BIL-8288).
- **One-time bill: the account card's Cycle shows the cycle,** or "None" —
  it showed the days to pay (DEF-BIL-8329).
- **One-time catch-up: each period and reading row says Waiting, Estimated or
  Actual truthfully,** and shows the share of a reading that period is priced
  on — no longer "Actual 700 kWh" on a half-month priced at 361.3 (DEF-BIL-8328).

## [2.412.4] — 2026-09-30

### Fixed
- **A queued printed letter or text message told the clerk to connect a provider
  that cannot be connected.** Print and text providers "cannot be connected yet",
  so the reason now says the platform cannot deliver that channel yet; email,
  which a utility can connect, still says "not connected" (DEF-NOT-8451).
- 8 more tests left behind by the 4 September sending change pass again, and the
  supplier-invoice attachment test now proves the door its closed question opened.

## [2.412.3] — 2026-09-30

### Fixed
- **Twelve kinds of customer message would never have been delivered** once a
  utility connected its own mail or text provider: the clerk's account message,
  the five service-request messages, the new-connection quote and confirmation,
  the two property-sale letters, the meter-visit text and the scheduled-report
  email waited in the queue for ever. Each is now kept and sent like every other
  customer document, and a check fails if a new message type is ever added
  without a place in the kept list (DEF-NOT-8450, under the PO's 2026-08-30
  "keep all of them" ruling).
- 30 notification tests that had failed since 4 September (a test set-up gap,
  not a product fault) pass again.

## [2.412.2] — 2026-09-30

### Changed
- **One-time bill: a closing customer's leftover deposit is refunded** (PO ruling,
  OQ-248 closed, option A). A $150.00 deposit against a $103.67 final balance now
  sends: the bill is settled and $46.33 is recorded as owed back to the customer
  (customer credit), until the refund is paid out. The final bill used to be
  refused at Send.
- **One-time bill: the Send card asks the same five confirmations a bill run
  does** (PO ruling, option B) — compliance, email, texts, autopay and ready to
  send. Send stays off until all five are ticked, and each is recorded as ticked,
  with who and when. The single "I checked the amounts" tick is gone.

### Fixed
- **One-time bill: a catch-up with a stretch nobody read could not be priced**
  (DEF-BIL-8324, PO ruling option A). A reading taken after the empty stretch —
  including one the clerk types on step 2 — is shared across the months it
  measured; what no reading covers is the meter's own estimate from its history.
  Either way the line is marked estimated.

## [2.412.0] — 2026-09-30

### Changed
- **A bill run's check now looks at every account completely and never stops
  at the first problem.** An account with no plan, a disputed reading and a
  payment question now shows all three, each under its own heading, and one
  broken account no longer stops the others — a reading stored with no unit
  used to stop the whole run; now only that account waits (DEF-BIL-8205,
  8206, 8207).
- **The check is saved and re-checks itself.** Results are kept with the time
  each account was checked; when an account's plan, reading, meter or payment
  changes, just that account is checked again (six accounts on a plan that is
  then published turn ready in about half a second, without re-running the
  whole run).
- **Nothing is fixed without a clerk's say-so.** Where the product can suggest
  an answer — the meter's own unit, a register rollover the dial proves
  (99,950 → 00,120 = 170), billing the other services — it is shown as a
  suggestion and used only once accepted, per account or for all.
- **A bulk run now prices at the rate in force on the last day of the
  period**, like a one-time bill: $3.25 until Sep 30 and $3.50 from Oct 1,
  period ending Sep 30, billed Oct 1 → $3.25 (DEF-BIL-8214).
- Payment checks at the check step (paid after the cut-off, plan instalment
  due, in collections, deposit not paid, autopay card expiring) (DEF-BIL-8211);
  warnings such as a $0.00 base now appear at the check, not only on drafts
  (DEF-BIL-8210); every problem has a label in all eleven languages
  (DEF-BIL-8209).
- **A clerk's estimate is saved in Meter Reads when the bill is sent**, so the
  next reading is trued up against it: Aug 1,000 · Sep estimated 5 · Oct 1,012
  → October bills 7, not 12 (DEF-BIL-8280).
- **Standing charges, the five rulings of 2026-09-30.** *Bill without it* bills
  the service's base now and its usage next bill ("usage: no reading, billed
  next bill"). *Standing charges only* offers **Waive** with a required reason:
  not billed, nothing carried forward, and Sign off is served the amount waived
  ($26). A held account's next bill runs from the day after its last bill
  (Sep 1 – Oct 31) with ONE base. An overlap bills from the day after the last
  bill with the base prorated ($8 × 14/30 = $3.73), and "Bill as is" is refused
  for an overlap. Skipping a plan instalment extends the plan one month through
  the payments module ($45 a month, $270 unchanged, never $90 in a month).
- **A sent run's check record is locked and kept as long as the bills**:
  decisions, answers-for-all, the account checks and each account's final
  findings refuse any change after Send (in the database as well as the app);
  automatic re-check stops; a catch-up run checks its accounts afresh; a
  read-only Check report is served. Re-check on the Check screen now re-checks
  only the named accounts (DEF-BIL-8219).

## [2.411.2] — 2026-09-30

### Fixed
- **Posting a large file of meter readings no longer ends in "Internal Server
  Error"** (DEF-MET-8106). A file of more than 200 readings now posts in the

  after a post** (DEF-MET-8108). It used to be rebuilt inside the post and could

## [2.410.21] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **The guard added in 2.410.19 could not run on a system that had already got
  past that point in the upgrade.** An upgrade step is only ever run once, so a
  system whose earlier step had already completed — before the guard existed —
  went straight on to the step that installs the safeguard and failed there with
  a database error naming nothing, exactly as before. The same check is now in
  that later step too, where it fires on any system that has got this far. It
  names every offending version and points at the command that repairs them,
  including the "this one has no end date" option.
- **And the same was true of the overlap check.** The earlier step also looks for
  two prices charging on the same day, and on a system already past that step the
  look never happens either — so an overlap appearing later would have failed the
  safeguard step with a raw database error naming one row and no decision. That
  check now runs in the later step too, listing every pair.

## [2.410.20] — 2026-09-29

### Added
- **Fixing a rate version that has no end date no longer means inventing one.**
  A version whose dates were typed backwards is usually the newest one on its
  schedule, and the newest version's honest end is *no end* — it runs until
  further notice. Until now the repair command only accepted a date, so putting
  such a row right meant typing some far-future date nobody had decided onto the
  field that decides which price applies. It now accepts "this one has no end"
  instead, and still refuses if that would make the version swallow a later one.

## [2.410.19] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **An upgrade could still stop, this time with a message naming nothing at
  all.** The upgrade checks that no two rate-schedule versions charge on the
  same day. It never checked something simpler: that a version's end date comes
  *after* its start. A version whose window runs backwards cannot be turned into
  a date range at all, so the step that installs the safeguard failed with a
  database error naming no utility, no schedule and no row — after the previous
  step had reported everything in order. The report meant to help had the same
  blind spot and listed nothing.
  Now the upgrade stops on those rows first and names every one of them, the
  report lists them as their own problem with the bills counted, and the command
  will take the end date you give it. As before, it will not invent a date for
  you.

## [2.410.18] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **The command that unsticks an interrupted upgrade could tell you there was
  nothing to fix.** It read the rate schedules without first telling the
  database which utility it was asking about. Every one of our tables is set up
  so that a query which does not say who it is for sees **no rows at all** —
  that is deliberate, and it is what keeps one utility's data away from
  another's. So the command came back with "no overlapping rate-schedule
  window" while the upgrade went on stopping on exactly such a window. Worse,
  the same blindness applied to the question *has this price already been used
  on a bill* — it would have answered "no bills" without being able to see any.
  It now asks about each utility in turn, by name, and says how many it looked
  at. The check that refuses to move a price a sent bill was based on works
  again.

## [2.410.17] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **An upgrade could stop halfway and tell you to do something impossible.**
  The upgrade checks that no rate schedule has two versions charging on the same
  day, because on such a day the system cannot tell which price to use. That
  check is right and it should stop the upgrade. What it then told you to do
  could not be done. It offered two ways out: record a correction, or give the
  earlier version the end date it should have had. **Recording a correction does
  not help** — a correction deliberately covers the same dates as the version it
  corrects, so both versions still charge on that day, and you end up looking at
  exactly the same message. **And nothing in the product would let you change an
  end date** on a version that is already in use. It also pointed at a tool that
  is not installed on the server. So an upgrade could stop, permanently, on one
  overlapping day on one schedule.
  There is now a command on the server that does it, and it will not guess for
  you: it shows you the schedule, the days that two versions both charge for,
  and whether either version has already been used on a bill, and then it asks
  you which of the two dates is wrong. You run it, answer, and finish the
  upgrade. It refuses to change anything that a bill already sent out was priced
  from, and it records every change in the audit trail.
- **The report that counts these overlaps disagreed with the upgrade about which
  ones it could fix by itself.** It described an overlap as one it would repair
  automatically when in fact the upgrade would stop on it — so you were sent
  back and forth between the two, being told different things. They now use the
  same word for the same thing.

## [2.410.15] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **Putting up a tax rate used to make the tax vanish from the bill.** A
  utility raises its state tax from 6.25% to 7.00% on 1 January and records it
  the way the product asks — end the old rate on 31 December, add the new one
  from 1 January. The January bills then carried **no tax at all**: not the old
  rate, not the new one. The product was choosing the tax by which row had been
  typed in first, and only then asking whether it was still in force. On a
  $196.00 bill that is **$13.72 a month not collected**, on a bill that looks
  completely normal. It now charges $13.72 in January and the old $12.25 on a
  December bill. **No bill already issued changes**: every tax on every
  database we can see carries no dates at all, and a tax with no dates applies
  on every day, so the old way of choosing and the new way pick the same row —
  measured, not assumed.
- **Two tax rates live on the same day now stop the bill instead of one of
  them being charged.** It is the same answer the product already gives for two
  rate schedules and two discount versions: charging one of them would mean the
  figure on a customer's bill was decided by which row came back first. The
  clerk is told how many there are, whose they are and on what date, and asked
  to retire one. Nothing in any database we can see is in that state.

## [2.410.14] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **A discount can no longer be worth two different things on the same day.**
  A discount is priced by a series of dated versions, one in force at a time.
  Nothing in the database stopped two of them being in force on one date, and
  when that happened the product did not stop and ask — it quietly used one of
  them, so the reduction on a customer's bill depended on which row came back
  first. The database now refuses the second one, the screens refuse to guess,
  and putting a new version in force closes off every older one instead of
  just the most recent. This is the same fault that stopped one utility's
  one-time and final bills on their sewer rates this week, found and closed on
  discounts before it reached anybody. On the databases we can see there were
  **no** overlapping discounts to clean up; on a real utility's database the
  count is whatever `10-scripts/rat_schedule_overlap_census.py --discounts`
  reports, and it must be run before upgrading.
- **Typing an end date before the start date is refused where it is typed.**
  It used to save, and only the database would have complained, in language
  nobody could act on.

### Changed
- The signed database design now states the discount rule, so the check that
  asks *"was every rule we signed actually built?"* covers discounts. It
  covered 32 rules; it now covers 33, and it could not read rules written in
  that form at all until today.

### Known, filed, not fixed
- **Two tax rows for one authority can hold any dates at all, and the product
  picks between them without looking at the date.** A tax rate filed as a new
  row for a new period therefore produces no tax line rather than the new
  rate. It has never bitten because every tax on every database we hold is
  undated (2 rows, 0 of them dated). `DEF-RAT-8051`.

## [2.410.13] — 2026-09-29

### Changed
- **A corrected rate schedule version now records the day it stopped being
  used.** When a clerk fixes a typo in a live rate — the board approved
  `$3.20` and somebody typed `$32.00` — the product keeps both rows: the wrong
  one for the record and the right one for the bills. The wrong one used to
  carry **no end date at all**, so the schedule's own Versions & filings table
  showed it as `02/01/2026 →` — *still running* — for ever, on a row that had
  not priced anything since the day it was corrected. It now reads
  `02/01/2026 – 03/01/2026`. **Product Owner ruling 2026-09-29**, choosing one
  of three options put to them, verbatim: *"i will take this and use
  superseded_by in filter - so that it is always unique and even if we see in
  audit it is clear"*.
  **The edge case, and it is the reason this is not one line.** A version can
  be switched on today for a date in the FUTURE. Correct it before that date
  arrives and the plain rule would end it before it started — a version
  running from 1 February, corrected on 15 January, ending 17 days before it
  began — which the product already refuses by name, so the whole correction
  would fail and the clerk could not fix their typo at all. Such a row now
  reads *replaced the day it would have started*: 1 February.
  **Nothing about which price is charged changes.** A corrected row has never
  priced anything once it is corrected, and both of the places that decide
  which version prices a date drop it before they look at a date at all. No
  issued bill's basis moves.
  **It applies from today forward and nothing already in the database is
  changed.** Whether the rows corrected before today should be given an end
  date too is a separate decision for the Product Owner; the count that
  decision needs is `10-scripts/rat_schedule_overlap_census.py
  --corrected-open`, which reports **0** on this container's demo database —
  and this container holds no production data.

## [2.410.12] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **The One-time bill stops telling a clerk it cannot send a bill it can.**
  Step 3 carried a panel headed *"Sending the bill"* saying a one-time bill
  *"can be drafted but not sent yet"*. That stopped being true on **23 August**,
  when the Product Owner settled where the due date comes from, and the server
  dropped its own matching refusal on **2 September**. Only the screen's copy
  went on refusing — in all eleven languages, for twenty-seven days. The panel
  and its words are gone. **It does not follow that a bill can be issued from
  this screen yet: that button has never been built**, and it is tracked
  separately rather than implied.
- **Step 2 names the customer, the way step 1 does.** Step 1 read
  *"AC-2026-00058 — Rostan Chase"* and step 2, about the same account, read
  *"Account with no name on file"*. The preview was never sent the customer's
  name, and the sentence it fell back to was about the wrong thing entirely —
  it appeared whenever the account could not be billed, which says nothing
  about whether anyone is on file. Step 2 now reads
  *"AC-2026-00032 — Hugo Faulkner"*.

### Removed
- **321 words of engineering notes, and a 39-word explanation, come off the
  screen.** A clerk previewing a one-time bill was offered *"3 thing(s) this
  part of the product cannot do yet"*, which opened onto three paragraphs
  citing five internal reference codes, and step 3 explained at length why
  charge lines cannot be typed by hand. Both are reasons rather than
  instructions, and the Product Owner has already asked for exactly this kind
  of note to be moved off a sibling screen and into the design document. The
  notes are kept where they are read by the people who need them.
  **Nothing about what the product charges has changed**, including the one of
  those notes that describes real money: a short bill still carries a whole
  period's base charge, which the Product Owner ruled on in August.

## [2.410.11] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **`DEF-RAT-8000` — a rate schedule could hold several prices for the same
  day, and the database now refuses it.** The design has always said two
  versions of one rate schedule must never both be in force on one date, and
  the database was meant to enforce it. It never did: one missing PostgreSQL
  extension meant the rule was written down and never switched on, and the
  note saying so sat in the code for six weeks. One utility reached **four
  versions of one sewer schedule in force on 29 October 2026**, which is why
  its one-time bills and move-out final bills were refusing to produce a bill.
  Upgrading closes any window that was simply left open, leaves corrections
  exactly as they are, and **stops with a report rather than guessing** when
  two versions start on the same day and there is no way to tell which the
  utility meant. Correcting a live price still works unchanged.
- **`DEF-RAT-8001` — filing a rate change now closes every old price, not just
  the newest one.** A schedule that had somehow ended up with two open prices
  kept one of them for ever, because each new rate change only ever closed the
  most recent. Nothing a clerk sees has changed; the schedule simply comes back
  to one price in force.
- **`DEF-RAT-8002` — a move-out final bill no longer refuses on a schedule
  whose price was corrected.** The ordinary nightly run and the one-time bill
  read the same table two different ways: the nightly run knew to ignore a
  price that had been corrected, and the one-time path did not, so it saw two
  prices where there was one and refused. Both read it the same way now.
- **`DEF-RAT-8003` — a comment in the rate-change code claimed a database
  guarantee that did not exist.** Corrected, and the guarantee it described is
  now real.

## [2.410.10] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **Two register rows now say what a browser saw.** `DEF-CUS-7910` and
  `DEF-CUS-7911` — the Review step drawing its Messages panel twice, and its
  charges table dropping *Each* and *Amount* — were fixed in `2.410.6` and are
  re-verified here by pressing through the wizard in a real browser at 1440px.
  No product code changed.

### Found
- **The New Connect wizard's Create button has never worked, and nobody had
  pressed it.** Every walkthrough of this wizard filled its five steps and
  stopped. Pressed for the first time, it answers **422** every single time: the
  screen sends four billing preferences — autopay, tax exempt, the certificate
  number and its expiry — that the master-account door does not accept, so the
  whole build is refused and nothing is written. A clerk sees *"This app sent a
  field an account doesn't have. Nothing was saved."* `DEF-CUS-8020`.
- **Pressing Create twice makes two of everything.** With the parcel-number box
  left empty — the ordinary case — the same build committed twice produced two
  connections, two accounts, two customers, two properties at one address and
  two payments of $250.00, each posting its own ledger pair. A build that names
  a parcel number is saved only by a uniqueness check on that number, which is
  not the same thing as being safe to press twice. `DEF-CUS-8021`.
- **A parked build reopens two steps early.** A draft parked on *Charges*
  reopens on *Units*, every time. Nothing typed is lost. `DEF-CUS-8022`.
- Four smaller findings: parked drafts list as identical unlabelled rows
  (`DEF-CUS-8023`), *Who is billed* is marked required and does not hold
  (`DEF-CUS-8024`), the done screen prints internal codes at the clerk
  (`DEF-CUS-8025`), *Your counter* renders a literal `{{when}}`
  (`DEF-PAY-8026`), and New Connect never offers *raise a move-in instead* for
  an address that already takes the service (`DEF-CUS-8027`).

### Verified
- **What Create writes, read back with SQL.** On an isolated clone: the account,
  customer, property, 3 units, 6 service points, 6 meters, 5 work orders, the
  $225.00 charge and the $250.00 payment all exist; money is stored to four
  decimals and shown to two; a cleared payment posts a balanced ledger pair
  ($250.00 debit against $25.00 + $225.00 credit) written by the posting
  service; `audit_log` carries six rows for it; every row carries the right
  tenant; and a second tenant, probed as the non-superuser role `sbh_rls_probe`,
  sees none of it while the owning tenant sees all of it.
- **The ten facts `DEF-CUS-7863` names were each typed on screen and none of
  them reached the database** — the unit line, latitude, longitude, the verified
  tick, the customer category, the date of birth, the paperless and SMS
  preferences, the co-applicant, the mailing address and the document number.
  Ten out of ten absent; the eleventh, account custom data, could not be typed
  because this utility has defined no such fields.

## [2.410.9] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **Database ids no longer reach a clerk when a bill cannot be priced.** On the
  One-time bill screen a clerk was shown, word for word: *"R2: 4 versions of
  schedule '01a0b366-61fa-7f50-8cc4-25fa070287cc' are in force for 'sewer' on
  2026-10-29 (01a0b366-…, 01a0b388-…, 01a0b424-…, 01a0e712-…)"* — four database
  ids in one sentence. The same sentence reached the bill-run screen, the
  move-in and move-out final-bill previews and six other lists. It now reads
  **"4 schedules price Sewer on 29 Oct 2026. Ask an administrator to retire
  one."**, in the clerk's own language, and the long version goes on being
  written to the log and the audit record where an engineer needs it. Nine
  places in the pricing engine wrote a sentence like that; all nine were
  changed, and the ten new sentences are in all eleven languages.

### Added
- **A check that stops it coming back.** The old protection read the source
  code, and the id was not in the source — it was put into the sentence while
  the bill was being priced. The new check **runs the pricing engine**, asks it
  to refuse in each of the nine ways, and reads what a screen would be given.
  It also prints, every single run, how much it is NOT looking at: 28 of the
  engine's 37 refusals and 4 screens, so nobody reads a green tick as a clean
  bill of health for the whole product.

## [2.410.8] — 2026-09-29

### Added
- **A check that a database rule the signed schema promises was actually
  built.** The schema document says two price versions of one rate schedule
  may never be in force on overlapping dates, and the database was never told
  to enforce it — so four versions of one sewer schedule are in force from the
  same date at a live utility, one-time and move-out final bills refuse, and
  the ordinary monthly run quietly picks one of the four. Nothing in the
  repository had ever asked whether a line of the signed schema exists in the
  database. `G137` now asks, on every merge: it reads the schema document's own
  SQL and compares 32 of its 34 table-level rules against a real PostgreSQL,
  says out loud which ones it cannot check, and — with no database to hand —
  still answers the question for this kind of rule from the migrations alone.
  It is red today on the one that is missing. The missing rule itself is
  another lane's to build; this is the check.
- **The review that was deferred in August is back on the agenda**, written out
  in plain words with what it has since cost, in the human-review ledger
  (`DEF-RAT-7980`).

## [2.410.0] — 2026-09-29

### Changed
- **The New Request wizard's Service step asks for the services in ONE table**,
  with `+ Service` under it. Picking a service and saying when it is wanted is
  one act now, in one row, instead of a list of chips and a separate table of
  dates. Each row also says whether that service is new at the property or
  already there, so a clerk can see it before promising a date.

  message, how it goes, to whom and when. **A message that will NOT be sent gets

  otherwise look the same. Where the product cannot answer yet, the card says
  that rather than showing an empty list.

## [2.401.0] — 2026-09-29

### Changed
- **New Connect: Charges and Review are the approved five-step drawings now,
  and the Communication step disappears into Review.** Step 4 gains a strip
  across the top naming the build a clerk is pricing — the customer, the
  address, the scope, the units, the services, the counts and the plan — so
  pricing the wrong build is visible before the money is decided rather than on
  the last screen. *Who is billed* becomes one dropdown instead of three cards,
  and **all three choices stay on it**: the two the server will not honour are
  present and greyed rather than hidden, because a clerk who cannot see a
  choice never learns it exists. Taking payment is one *Payment option* list
  instead of a yes/no and a separate tender, and the reference box renames
  itself after the tender — **Check number** for a check.
- **Step 4 also asks the owner's billing preferences for the first time:**
  autopay, tax exempt, the certificate number and when the exemption lapses.
  The accounts side has accepted all four since it was built and New Connect
  never sent any of them, so a utility opening a tax-exempt developer's account
  through this wizard had to go and set it afterwards. They now travel with the
  build and land on the account the commit creates.
- **Step 5 is *What will be created*.** A nine-cell strip across the top, then
  four collapsible groups — Customer, Premise, Units and work, Charges and
  payment — each with its own **Edit**, which is the Product Owner's report
  that *"the information architecture is not grouped in logical section and
  text is so much"*. The charge lines are repeated there, read-only. **The step
  numbers behind those four Edit links are looked up rather than typed**, so
  they follow the steps the next time these move.
- **Everything the Communication step held is on Review, and one thing more.**
  The contact card, the three messages with their channel, template, timing and
  state, and the whole template picker with its search — all present. What is
  new is that a message can be taken off the list and a template chosen per
  message, **and both now reach the server**: the door has accepted them all
  along and nothing was sending them, so a clerk's choice used to stop at the
  browser. **Nothing goes out yet either way** — every row still says so, for
  the reason it always has.

### Fixed
- **The last screen before Create now tells the truth about what Create
  makes.** The table names each record and where it will show, and five of its
  rows had to be corrected against what the code actually does: the address is
  created earlier and not by this press; a meter's record is created here and
  the meter is *fitted* on the work order; **no message is queued today**, where
  the design said three; the audit trail gets more than one entry, so no count
  is claimed; and — the important one — **the invoice and the payment DO happen
  now**. The design still carried a note saying they did not, written before
  the work that made them, and a warning about money that is no longer true is
  worse than no warning.

### Not built, deliberately
- **The quantity on a charge line is still counted from the units and cannot be
  typed.** The design draws a box you could type into; which numbers a clerk
  reported entering — 1, 2 and 15 — has not been settled, and it multiplies a
  price on a real invoice. Nothing here guesses, and a test now fails if
  somebody builds the box before it is settled.
- **The *Remaining* figure on the charges footer is not shown.** The line is
  there and says when it is due; the amount is the total less what was taken,
  and this product never does money arithmetic in the browser — that is where
  two of our worst money defects came from. The figure is on the build's own
  Charges tab the moment the build exists.
- **The third *Take payment* choice, *"No, the developer pays per unit"*, is
  not offered.** It asks the same question as *Who is billed* one panel above,
  and the answer it offers is one the server refuses.

- **New Request now has four steps instead of six, and the server half of that
  moved with it.** When something you typed is refused, the wizard takes you
  back to the step that holds the field — and every one of those steps has a
  new number. Documents were step 4 and are now part of step 1, the address
  search was step 3 and is now step 2, the services were step 2 and are now
  step 3, and the fees and the payment were step 5 and are now step 3 as well.
  Each door on the server names its own step, so a refusal cannot send you to
  a screen the field is not on. The one place it stays silent is the door that
  saves several steps' fields in one go: no single step is true of it, and
  leaving you where you are is better than moving you somewhere wrong
  (`DEF-CUS-7860`).
- **The tender is spelled `check` and no longer `cheque`.** This was not only
  a label: it was the value stored against a request, and it was the last
  British spelling of a tender in the product — payments has said `check` all
  along. Requests already recorded are corrected by the upgrade. A caller
  still sending the old word keeps working and gets the new one stored.

### Added
- **The review step can now show what the customer will be told.** For the
  request in front of you: the message, the channel, the address it goes to,
  and when. **A message that will NOT be sent still gets a row saying so** —
  an absent row and a withheld one look identical on a screen, and the
  difference is the point of the card.
  ⚠ **Two of its three rows cannot be sent by this product yet**, and the card
  says which: *Request received* has wording and really is queued when you
  submit; *Documents needed* and *Fee due* have no wording written for them
  anywhere, so whatever is ticked, nothing leaves. Writing those two letters is
  notifications work and is not in this change.
- **A fee table's total is now worked out on the server** and printed by the
  browser rather than added up there, with the currency beside it. It is not
  the sum of the amounts you can see: a waived line keeps its own amount on
  screen and is not part of what is owed, which is exactly why the number comes
  from one place.

### Fixed
- **Nothing a clerk can see.** Three findings this work measured are filed and
  not fixed here: a service centre still cannot say it takes a *check*, because
  the portal's own list of what a counter accepts spells it the British way and
  refuses the American one by name (`DEF-TEN-7861`, tenancy's to fix); a fee
  row's **Charged per** is whatever the screen sent and is blank when it sends
  nothing, while the unit price beside it comes from the price list
  (`DEF-CUS-7862`); and the one mixed save door carries no step (`DEF-CUS-7860`).

## [2.396.0] — 2026-09-29

### Changed
- **Settings → Security is the screen the Product Owner approved on 2026-09-29.**
  It had five cards in a ragged three-then-two grid: an empty column in the top
  row, a whole card whose only content was a *View audit log* button, and the
  Save button below the fold. It is now three cards side by side — **Passwords**,
  **Sessions** and **Signing in** — then Save, then the audit log full width
  underneath it.
  The grouping is the argument rather than the tidying. *Stay signed in* left the
  card of its own because "how long may a clerk stay signed in" is the same
  question as the idle timeout and the hard limit, and having its own card made it
  look like a different one. The lockout pair joined the allowed-address list
  because both answer *who gets in*; before, they sat in different rows.
  Units now live inside the value a person picks — `12 hours`, `5 tries`,
  `8 characters` — which is what let every *"Between 4 and 12 hours."* caption go
  and every label shrink to a name. The sentence explaining that the product keeps
  an audit log was removed from the page head: the audit log is on the page now,
  which says it better than a sentence about it.

### Added
- **The last five changes made on this tab, on the tab** — who changed what, and
  from what to what, with the old value struck through. It can honestly show
  fewer than five, or none at all, because the audit log is pruned on a schedule;
  it says so by showing nothing rather than by explaining itself. Values read the
  way the controls above them read: `8 hours → 1 hour`, never a raw number.

### Known
- On a phone the left-hand menu does not fold away, so screens are pushed off the
  side. That is the app frame and affects every screen, not this one.
- Two sentences on this screen are longer than our own limit for a plain fact.
  They are the wording the drawing was approved with, so they were built as
  drawn rather than quietly shortened afterwards.

## [2.394.1] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **The script that decides which security values a utility may pick had stopped
  running**, an hour after the values it measures changed shape. It read the
  settings table expecting a floor and a ceiling; four settings had just become
  lists of allowed values, so it stopped with an error on all four.
  It now reads the shape off each setting the same way the server's own
  validator does, so the two cannot disagree. The wording follows: it no longer
  says a value is "outside the range" but that it is **not on today's list, and
  that utility keeps it** — which is what actually happens now.
  Proved both ways: it runs clean on the demo data, and on a throwaway copy
  planted with 23 minutes and 11 days it names both and names the utility.

## [2.394.0] — 2026-09-29

### Changed
- **Settings → Security: the four typed numbers are now choice lists, on the
  server.** *Hard limit*, *Wrong passwords*, *Lockout length* and *Stay signed
  in for* were boxes you typed a number into; the approved redesign makes each
  one a short dropdown, so all eight settings on that tab are lists now and no
  range is left. The server refuses anything off the list **by name**, which is
  what stops the screen offering one set of values and the server accepting
  another.
  **Nobody is moved off a value they already hold.** Two of the four lists are
  narrower than the range they replace, so a utility can be sitting on a value
  the screen no longer offers — 23 minutes, say. **Their dropdown carries 23,
  in its place on the list, and nobody else's does.** The sign-in still obeys
  it and a save leaves it alone, so the tab goes on working for them; what they
  cannot do is pick a different unlisted value, and once they move off 23 it is
  gone from their list for good. This is the lesson of
  2026-09-28, when a withdrawal moved utilities from 480 minutes to 60 and
  signed their staff out seven hours earlier.
  **Two of the lists are provisional.** *Hard limit* offers every hour from 4 to
  12 and *Wrong passwords* every value from 3 to 10 — the whole of the old
  range, so those two withdraw nothing and are settled. *Lockout length* and
  *Stay signed in for* carry the lists on the approved drawing until the value
  census has been run against the production database; every utility on this
  container holds the seeded default, so the count here proves the counter
  works and nothing else.

### Added
- **The Security tab's own change history, as a server read.** The last five
  changes made on that tab — when, who, which setting, and the old value and
  the new one, which the screen prints the way the control above prints it
  (`480 minutes → 60 minutes`, `Never → Every 90 days`, `Off → On`) — the same
  wording function that labels the dropdowns, so the history and the control
  can never disagree, in any of the eleven languages. It is this tab's history,
  not the platform-wide log, and it reads through the audit module's own
  selectors rather than querying the trail a second time.
  **A change the product made during an upgrade is attributed to *Product
  upgrade*** rather than left blank, so a clerk asking why they are being signed
  out earlier finds the answer on the screen it happened on.
  **Fewer than five rows, or none, is a true answer** — the audit trail is
  pruned on a retention schedule — and the read says so in a field, so the
  screen can state it without inventing a row.
  Nothing renders any of this yet; the Security tab itself is a separate piece
  of work.

## [2.393.10] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **One table answered "something went wrong" where it should have answered
  "nothing here", and that difference matters.** Every table holding a
  utility's data is guarded by a rule saying *only show a row to the utility it
  belongs to*. On the table recording what class, type and status each customer
  account had, that rule was written so that if the system had not yet been
  told **which** utility was asking, the database raised an error instead of
  simply showing nothing. **No customer data ever crossed between utilities** —
  what went wrong is subtler and still worth fixing: an error is an answer. A
  screen that fails tells whoever is asking that they touched something real,
  where an empty list tells them nothing at all. It now shows nothing. Asking
  as the row's own utility, and being refused as a different one, are both
  unchanged. (`DEF-GOV-7821`)
- **The written template new tables are copied from had the faulty wording in
  it**, while a later page of the same document said the corrected wording was
  required — so whoever built that table followed the instructions exactly and
  still got it wrong. The template is corrected, or the next table repeats it.
  Every other table in the product — **305 of them** — already had the right
  form; this was the last one.

## [2.393.9] — 2026-09-29

### Fixed
- **Six of our own automated checks had never actually run on this machine, and
  one of them is the check that the product keeps each utility's data private
  from every other.** They were not broken and they were not lying — each one
  needs a particular set-up to run, could not find it, and said so honestly and
  then stopped. The trouble is that "did not run" looks almost identical to
  "nothing to check" in a list of a hundred and thirty-seven results, so nobody
  noticed. **The private-data check is the one that matters**, because keeping
  one utility from seeing another's customers is the first rule this product
  has. All six can now find what they need. (`DEF-GOV-7813`)
- **Two people picking the next free record number could both be told the same
  number was free, even when one of them had already claimed a block of them
  and written it down.** The tool that hands out numbers only looked at numbers
  already USED, so a block that had been reserved and published was invisible
  to it — which punished exactly the person who had done the careful thing. It
  now reads the reservations too, and refuses **every** number in someone
  else's block rather than only the first, because otherwise the clash simply
  moves to the second number. This is what caused four clashes in one day.
  (`DEF-GOV-7814`)
- **Two pairs of records were sharing one pair of numbers**, filed minutes
  apart by two people. The numbers are unique across the whole product, so a
  reference to one of them pointed at two different things. Moved, and the move
  is written down. (`DEF-MET-7811`, `DEF-MET-7812`)

## [2.393.5] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Two builds were missing from this changelog, so anyone told to look in one
  of them found nothing.** Builds `2.385.0` and `2.385.1` went out on 27 and 28
  September and neither was written up — between the entry for `2.384.2` and
  the one for `2.386.0` there was simply a gap. Both are now written up from
  what they actually shipped. (`DEF-GOV-6813`, `DEF-GOV-6930`)
- **The check that is meant to notice a missing entry was only ever looking at
  a fraction of the builds, and reported that it had looked at all of them.**
  It reads the project's own history to learn what has been released, but the
  copy of that history on a working machine is deliberately shortened — so it
  could see the **16** most recent builds while the changelog records **772**,
  and it still said *every* build had been written up. It now states how far
  back it could actually see, when it passes and when it fails, so the part it
  could not check is a number somebody can act on instead of being invisible.
  It still checks what it can see; that is how the two builds above were found.
  (`DEF-GOV-7807`)
- **The defect register's own check could not see two teams using the same
  number.** Our numbering rule says a defect number is unique across the whole
  product, and the three letters in the middle only say which part of the
  product it came from. The check compared the whole code instead, so two
  records numbered 7700 from different areas both passed as fine — which
  happened four times on 28 September. It now counts them and reports how many
  there are: **28 numbers are currently shared by more than one record.** The
  decision to block a merge stays with the check that already owns it, on
  purpose — a check that can never be satisfied is one people stop reading.
  (`DEF-GOV-7808`)

## [2.393.3] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Every local browser check of the product was silently testing against the
  live deployed system instead of the one on the machine, and sign-in failed
  with *"That email or password is incorrect."* on a correct password.** When
  the product is built for a developer's machine, the command that builds it
  was not told which environment it was building for — and with nothing said,
  it assumes **production**. So it wrote the address of the real, deployed
  service into the page, and the browser then refused to call it, because the
  local server hands the page a rule saying *only talk to yourself*. The two
  rules are each correct on their own; it is the pair that breaks, which is why
  neither file looked wrong. The build is now told which environment it is for,
  in both places that start a local stack. (`DEF-INF-7802`)
- **It stayed hidden because the local stack only rebuilt the page when it was
  missing entirely**, so every run after the deployment change quietly reused
  pages built before it and kept working. The stack now checks what it is about
  to serve and rebuilds it if it names a deployed address, and refuses outright
  if it still does afterwards — so the next change of this kind cannot hide the
  same way. **Proved by booting the stack from a deleted build and signing in:
  the page carries no deployed address at all, and sign-in returns a session
  for Dana Whitfield.**
