## [2.392.2] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Setting the product up on a brand-new machine could not finish, for about
  an hour, and this is the fix.** The previous build taught the server to stop
  rather than serve when the place its information is kept has not been brought
  up to date — which on a brand-new, completely empty setup is *always* true at
  the very first start. The one command that sets everything up started the
  server first and then reached the update step *through* that server, so the
  server was refusing to start and the update it was waiting for could never be
  run. **The update step is now a separate, short-lived job that does not go
  through the server at all**, so it works on an empty setup, during an outage,
  and while the server is refusing — and setup now runs in the order a real
  deployment uses: build, update, then start.

## [2.392.1] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Two defect numbers were listed twice in our own records, each copy saying
  something different — one said the problem was fixed, the other said it was
  still open.** Nobody reading the list could tell which was true, and the
  count of outstanding problems was two higher than the real number. The stale
  copy of each has been removed and the correct one kept. (`DEF-GOV-7650`)
- **The tool that stops two people accidentally using the same defect number
  had stopped working because of it.** That tool refuses to do anything at all
  while a number appears twice, so for several days it was switched off for
  everyone working on this branch — on days when three people did pick the same
  number. It works again.
- **A new check now refuses a save that would list a number twice**, and says
  which number, so this cannot come back silently. Removing a duplicate still
  goes through without complaint, because that is the repair.

## [2.391.1] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Nobody could sign in, and the server now refuses to start rather than
  pretend it can.** Sign-in failed for everyone: the program had been updated
  to use five new pieces of information about how long a session lasts and how
  many wrong passwords lock an account, and the place those are kept had not
  been updated to hold them yet. So every attempt to sign in asked for
  something that was not there and failed — **while the automatic check that
  tells the network which servers are working kept saying this one was fine**,
  so it stayed in service, failing every request.
- **What changed: a server now looks, before it accepts a single visitor, at
  whether the place the information is kept has been brought up to date for the
  version it is running.** If it has not, it **stops, will not take traffic,
  and prints the one command that fixes it** along with a list of exactly what
  is missing. The previous version keeps serving customers while that is sorted
  out, instead of a broken one taking over silently.
- **Three answers, not two, and the middle one matters.** If the server simply
  cannot reach where the information is kept — a brief network problem, a
  planned failover — it says so loudly and **starts anyway**, because a server
  that refused would be gone by the time the connection came back. "We could
  not check" is never reported as "everything is fine", and never as "something
  is wrong" either.
- **The working check that reports a server as healthy is deliberately
  unchanged.** Making it ask the database a question would mean a slow database
  takes every server out of service at once — the monitoring would create the
  outage instead of reporting it. The server simply never gets as far as saying
  it is healthy when it cannot do its job.
- **And the step that was skipped is now hard to skip quietly.** A new check
  fails the build if the update step is ever moved back into the wrong place,
  if the new look-before-you-serve check is removed, or if the instructions
  stop naming the recovery command. **What is still done by hand is said
  plainly in the operations guide**: bringing the stored information up to date
  is a separate command a person runs, and no automated pipeline exists to run
  it.

## [2.391.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **A new connection's one-time charges now become a real bill the moment the
  connection is created, and the money the clerk takes is recorded with it.**
  Pressing **Create connection** writes three things in one act: the
  connection, an **invoice on the owner's account** for the charges, due after
  the payment terms the clerk typed, and the **payment**, if one was taken at
  the counter. It is one act — all of it, or none of it.
- **A build whose charges cannot be billed is no longer created at all, and
  this is the visible change.** Until today it was created anyway and the money
  was remembered as a number on the build with no bill behind it: nothing
  reached Billing, nothing reached Finance, and nobody was ever asked for it.
  On a build the size of the worked example that is **$1,035.00 that existed on
  one screen and in no ledger.** The clerk is now stopped and told — a worse
  moment and a better outcome. They fix the charges and press Create again;
  nothing they typed is lost.
- **A build with no charge on it is untouched** and is created exactly as
  before. The rule bites only where there IS a bill to write and it fails.
- **The figure on the bill is worked out on the server and never taken from the
  screen.** If the two disagree — because somebody edited a price between the
  clerk reading the total and pressing the button — the connection is refused
  and both figures are named, rather than a different amount being billed
  quietly.

### Added
- **Payment at the counter, when a connection is created.** How it was paid,
  how much, the date, the date it clears and its own reference. Every field is
  optional and *no payment now* is the ordinary case.
- **Cash, cheques and money orders need an open till here too**, exactly as the
  Record-a-payment screen already requires. Card, bank transfer and wire do
  not, because that money never reaches a drawer.
- **A payment with no clearing date says so.** It is recorded as still on its
  way: it does not come off the bill and it does not reach the books — which is
  right, because a cheque handed over is not a cheque that cleared. The
  connection now reports that plainly instead of leaving it to be noticed.
- **Paying more than the bill is kept, not lost.** The remainder is held on the
  account as a credit and the connection says so.
- **A payment this utility cannot take is answered, not crashed.** A tender
  that is not on the utility's own list — or one it has retired — used to reach
  the clerk as *"Something went wrong on our side"* after they had filled in
  the whole wizard. They are now told which step to go back to, and the
  connection is not half-made.

### Known
- **This is the engine, and the screen has not caught up.** The five-step
  wizard's payment fields are not built yet, so a clerk cannot type a clearing
  date or a tender on that screen today. What a clerk CAN already see is the
  refusal: a build whose charges cannot be billed is not created.
- **Pressing Create twice still makes one bill and one payment.** A build can
  only be created once, and a retried request finds the payment it already made
  instead of making a second.
- **The disconnect wizard refused on its last step and would not say why, and
  now it says why.** A clerk filled all four steps, pressed *Schedule the
  disconnection*, and read *"This disconnect step can't be done as asked.
  Check the case."* — which is true of eighteen completely different
  situations and useless in every one of them. The server had already worked
  out the exact reason and sent it; the screen was throwing it away. **The
  screen now shows the real reason in one short sentence**, in all eleven
  languages: *"No case is open."* · *"This supply is already cut."* ·
  *"This account is closed."* · *"The final notice is not sent. Advance the
  ladder first."* and the rest. A reason we have no sentence for still shows
  the old general line rather than a blank, so nothing can end up silent.
- **And the clerk is no longer made to fill four steps for a disconnection
  that could never have gone through.** Four of those reasons are settled the
  moment the account is picked — there is no case open, the supply is already
  cut, the account is closed, or the final notice has not gone out yet. The
  first step now says so straight away, in the same words the last step would
  have used, and *Continue* stops there. **The server still checks everything
  again when the button is pressed**, because days can pass in between and a
  screen must not be the thing that decides.


## [2.392.4] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **On Plans & Rates, editing a charge code that is priced per connection
  size, the Amount box sat empty and turned red the moment you clicked it —
  and said nothing.** The box is deliberately not typeable there: a code that
  charges a different amount for each size has no single amount, and the
  server refuses one that states both. But an empty box labelled *Amount*,
  ringed in red, reads as something you have failed to fill in. **The red was
  never an error** — it is the ordinary red outline every box in the product
  gets while it has the cursor in it, and there was no message under it
  because nothing was wrong. The box now shows what is actually true: the
  range of prices the size table holds and how many sizes are priced, for
  example `12.00–60.00 · 6 sizes`. It is still not typeable, and the line
  underneath still says why. The figures come from the server exactly as it
  sends them — nothing is added up or rounded in the browser — and if a price
  in the table below has been changed and not yet saved, the box shows the
  number of sizes on its own rather than a range that might be out of date.
- **A field anywhere in the product can no longer be marked wrong with
  nothing to read.** Every box in the shared form kit used to treat a blank
  message as a real complaint, so it would draw the red border and then have
  nothing to put under it. A blank message now counts as no complaint at all.
- **And a box you cannot type in is never marked wrong.** There is nothing a
  person can do about an error on a field they cannot edit; the server's own
  sentence still appears at the top of the form, where it belongs.


## [2.392.3] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **A meter can now be given its connection size while it is being fitted.**
  On a unit, **Assets → + Assign from inventory** asked which service the meter
  would serve and never asked what size the connection is — so a spare that
  came off the shelf without one was installed without one, and the unit's
  **Size** column read *no size recorded*. On water, electric, gas, trash and
  fire that is the very thing the base charge is priced on, so the bill could
  not be worked out at all; the failure only showed up weeks later, in the
  middle of a bill run, where nobody was looking. The form now offers the size,
  and it is **required on the services whose price depends on it** and left
  optional on the ones where a blank is the right answer — solar, battery,
  storm water, broadband and sewer. Which services those are comes from the
  utility's own ratified rate bands, not from a list typed into the screen.
  Reported by the Product Owner on build 2.390.1.
- If a size is somehow still missing when the meter is saved, the server says
  *Choose this meter's connection size.* and the meter does not move — it is
  not quietly installed and left unbillable.

### Known, and deliberately not changed in this build
- **Two other screens that install a meter still do not ask for a size:** the
  full-page **Reassign** screen reached from the asset register, and the
  bulk **Assign** on the asset list. Neither asks which service the meter will
  serve either, so neither is affected by the new rule, and widening it to them
  would have stopped a clerk assigning a meter from those screens at all. Both
  are written down and will be fixed together.
- **Meters already installed without a size are untouched.** They have been
  counted, not repaired: the count goes to the Product Owner first and the
  repair is a separate decision.

## [2.392.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **The Accounts list's row of figures is now four boxes, one per kind of
  account, and pressing one narrows the list to it.** They read **Active ·
  Pending · Disconnecting · Suspended**, with a short line under each saying
  what it means for billing: *billing normally*, *no bill can be raised*,
  *still consuming*, *base charges only*. Press a box and the list shows only
  those accounts, with the same chip in the filter bar you would get by
  choosing the status by hand; press it again and the list goes back to
  everything and returns to page one.
- ⚠ **THE BIG NUMBER AT THE TOP LEFT GETS SMALLER, AND NOTHING IS BROKEN.**
  The box that used to read **Accounts 79** counted every account a utility has
  ever had, open and closed together. The box in its place reads **Active**,
  and it counts only the accounts being billed normally — so on our demo
  utility it reads **71** rather than 79. The eight it no longer counts are
  closed, pending, being disconnected or suspended, and three of those four now
  have a box of their own. **If a number you knew has dropped this morning,
  this is why.**
- **"Disconnecting", not "Disconnects".** *Disconnects* is already a tab on
  this screen and it lists the disconnection REQUESTS. The box counts the
  ACCOUNTS on their way out, which is a different thing, so it gets a different
  word.

### Removed
- **Two boxes that never counted anything are gone.** *Past-due 60+* and
  *Closed this year* had both read **"Not counted yet"** since the day they
  were added — honestly, and for weeks — because neither figure can be worked
  out from what the product stores today. They told a clerk nothing and they
  are not replaced.
- ⚠ **AND ONE THAT DID WORK IS GONE WITH THEM: *Outstanding*.** It really did
  add up what every customer owes, and it is not one of the four the Product
  Owner asked for. **After this release the Accounts screen shows no total of
  what the utility is owed anywhere** — the BALANCE column still shows what one
  customer owes, and the whole-utility figure lives on the Finance screen
  (Revenue & AR), which is the number it was always checked against. Worth
  saying out loud to anyone who read it here every morning.
- **The fifth box, *Accounts*, goes too** — its number is the one explained
  above.

### Fixed
- **The list stopped asking the server twice.** Counting the pending accounts
  used to cost a second, whole extra request whose rows were thrown away. All
  four counts now arrive with the list itself, in one go.

## [2.390.2] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **`+ Build your own` on Reports → Catalogue does something now.** Pressing it
  did nothing: it went to the Custom sub-tab of the catalogue you were already
  looking at, so from Custom nothing happened at all and from the main list it
  just switched tabs to an empty page. It now opens the report editor on a
  blank report, and **Save as** creates it. Reported by the Product Owner on
  build 2.388.0.
- What the blank editor does: you choose what the report is about, tick the
  columns you want, say where it should live and who may see it, then press
  **Save as** and name it. Until you have chosen a subject and at least one
  column, **Save as** says which of the two is still missing rather than
  failing at the server. The saved report appears under **Custom**.
- **One honest limit, stated rather than hidden:** a report that has never been
  saved cannot be previewed, because the preview runs a saved report. The
  editor shows the columns you have chosen and says *Nothing to show yet.* in
  place of rows, until the first save.
- The run-history dialog now carries a screen id like every other screen. It
  had been routed since 27 September without one.

## [2.390.1] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **Nothing on the dev site could reach the server at all, and now it can.**
  Before a browser sends a request carrying an unusual header, it asks the
  server's permission. Our app puts a support reference on *every single*
  request, and the server was only granting permission for the six ordinary
  headers its library grants by default — so permission was refused every
  time, the request was never sent, and every screen failed at once. The
  server now grants the two headers our own app sends. **Nothing has to be
  changed on any machine**: it is a code fix and it ships with this build.
- **Six pieces of information the server sends back with an answer were
  invisible to the app, with nothing anywhere to show that anything was
  wrong.** A browser hides an unusual *reply* header from a page served on a
  different address unless the server says otherwise, and ours said nothing.
  So the app could not see the tag that lets it skip re-downloading a list it
  already has, the wait-and-try-again time after the server asks it to slow
  down, the filename the server chose for a download, or the two facts the
  audit log's banner is written from — which is how that banner could state
  the wrong date range. All six are now visible to the app.
- **And the thing that will break it next time is named.** Both lists are
  derived by hand from the app's own code, so they go stale the day somebody
  adds a header and does not think of the server. Two new checks read the
  app's code and fail if it starts sending, or reading, a header the server
  has not granted.

## [2.390.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **Starting a new connection becomes five screens instead of eight**, each
  named in one word: **Customer · Premise · Units · Charges · Review.** Nothing
  a clerk used to be asked disappears — every field, table and check on the old
  eight appears on one of the five. What is removed is the explaining: sentences
  telling the clerk why the product works the way it does, which belong in the
  code and not on a screen.
- **A build parked halfway through reopens where it belongs**, on the step its
  old one became, and an old link to a numbered step still works. **Nobody
  loses a keystroke.**
- **The question of what is being built moves to where it can be answered.**
  It used to be asked before the address was searched, which is the thing that
  decides it; it now sits under the address search, already filled in from what
  was found, and can still be changed.
- **An address that is already served is refused with a message, and only when
  the exact unit already has that service.** A building with service and units
  without it is still a new connection — which is the ordinary case at an
  apartment block.
- **The units and everything attached to them become one table**, grouped by
  unit, with rows added at the bottom. Who occupies a unit is chosen on the
  unit's own row rather than at the end, and a bulk choice applied to every row
  is now required — with every row still editable afterwards.
- **A shared area takes the same plan as the rest of the property.** Until now
  it was asked for nowhere and took none.
- **Who the bill goes to keeps all three choices on screen.** Only the owner's
  account can be chosen today, and the other two are greyed out by a real check
  rather than by a decision typed into the code.

### Added
- **A new connection now asks for the customer the way a move-in does** — full
  name, category and sub-category, government ID, date of birth, a
  co-applicant, and a mailing address in the standard US form. An existing
  customer is found by **customer number**, searched on what was just typed.
- **A property can carry its latitude, longitude and a *location verified*
  tick**, all optional. The point belongs to the building, and every screen
  showing one says which it is showing.
- **How the customer wants to be contacted is captured while the connection is
  made** — language, paperless billing and text reminders with their details,
  and autopay and tax exemption with the money.
- **A payment taken at the counter is recorded here**, with the fields that
  payment type needs: amount, date and its own reference. **Payment terms still
  have no default**, deliberately: a guessed due date starts a late-fee clock on
  a real invoice.
- **Documents show the document number**, last four digits only.

### Fixed
- **Fourteen findings reported from the running product** on 28 September, one
  record each. The largest of them: two columns on the documents table that
  could never show anything are hidden until there is something to show; three
  separate controls for picking services become one; and the plan is shown in
  full rather than summarised.

### Known
- **What is being built here is the record and the drawings, not the screens.**
  The five-step wizard is specified, its rules are written down and its
  findings are filed; the screens themselves and the entry in the books at
  creation are not in this version. **A clerk driving the product today still
  sees eight steps.**
- **One question is deliberately unanswered**, and it is about money: when a
  clerk enters quantities on an early step, the charges are priced on the
  number of units rather than on those quantities. Whether that is wrong
  depends on what those numbers were, and nobody has guessed — the charge
  quantity is unchanged until it is settled.

## [2.389.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **Six sign-in and lockout rules stop being the same for everybody and become
  settings each utility chooses for itself**, inside limits we set: how long a
  quiet screen waits before signing someone out, how long a working day's
  sign-in lasts at most, whether *"Keep me signed in"* is offered at all, how
  long it lasts, how many wrong passwords lock an account, and how long that
  lock holds. **Every default is exactly what the product does today**, so on
  the day this ships nothing changes for almost every utility.
- **The exception, and it is the only visible part of this release.** The two
  longest quiet-screen settings — **four hours and eight hours** — are
  withdrawn, because a screen left signed in all afternoon in a public office
  is the risk this setting exists to manage. **A utility on either is moved to
  one hour.** Their staff will be signed out up to seven hours earlier than
  before, and this is the one thing worth telling those utilities in advance.
  The upgrade records the move against each utility it touches, so the list of
  who was affected is a fact somebody can look up rather than a guess.
- **The customer portal keeps following the staff setting** and gets no setting
  of its own — one setting is one thing less for an administrator to get wrong.

### Added
- **Finished sign-ins are now cleared away every night**, at 03:20. Until now
  nothing ever removed one, so every sign-in anybody had ever made was still
  stored. Only sign-ins that have already run out or been signed out are
  removed; a sign-in that is still open, even one left idle, is never touched.
  It runs on the existing background scheduler, which must be deployed for it
  to run at all.

### Release note
- **Sessions opened before the deploy keep their old cookie until they expire;
  nobody is forced to sign out.** And, published with that sentence rather than
  instead of it: **utilities that were on a four- or eight-hour inactivity
  timeout now sign their staff out after one hour**, so a person who steps away
  for longer than an hour will be asked to sign in again where yesterday they
  were not. Those utilities are told before the release ships.

### Fixed
- **"Keep me signed in" now actually keeps you signed in.** Ticking it was
  supposed to let you close the browser and come back without signing in again,
  and it never did: the part of it that remembers you on your own machine was
  being thrown away the moment the browser closed, so the box did the one thing
  it exists to prevent. It now lasts as long as the utility says it should.
  **It starts working at each person's next sign-in**, not at the moment of the
  upgrade.

## [2.388.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **The product is being moved onto a load-balanced setup, and the first thing a
  load balancer does is ask each copy of the app "are you alive?".** It asks
  using the copy's own private network address rather than the public name, and
  the app — which only answers to names it has been told about — replied
  **"I do not know that name"**. Every copy would have been declared dead and
  replaced, for ever, and nothing would ever have served a customer. **The app
  now answers that question before it checks who asked.** It says `ok`, and it
  deliberately does not look at the database while doing so: if it did, a slow
  database would make every copy look dead, and a slow product would become no
  product at all.
- **The database upgrade no longer runs inside every copy of the app.** With one
  copy that was fine. With two it is a race — both start the same upgrade, one
  loses and stops, and the machine restarts it straight back into the same race —
  and while it runs, nothing answers the "are you alive?" question, so the copy
  is killed **partway through the upgrade it is waiting for**. The upgrade now
  runs once, as its own job, before a new version is released.
- **The screens and the API will live at two different addresses**, so the
  browser now asks permission before every call. Permission is granted to
  **exactly one address per environment** — never to "anyone", which would not
  even work, because a browser refuses "anyone" together with "send the sign-in
  cookie" and the sign-in cookie is the whole point.
- **The screens are now built once per environment, and each build knows which
  API to talk to.** There are three commands — one for dev, one for sandbox, one
  for live — and each writes the right address into what the browser downloads.
  ⚠ **The address is written in at build time, so changing the setting on its own
  changes nothing that is already published**: it takes a rebuild and a fresh
  upload. **A build with no address set now stops with an error instead of
  producing something that would look fine and fail on every screen at once.**
- **Seventeen links that open a file — a route sheet, a reading sheet, a bill
  PDF, a period pack, a remittance receipt, a plan agreement, a year of
  documents — now go to the API's address like everything else.** They were
  written by hand, one at a time, and were the only part of the product that
  would have kept pointing at the screens' own address. **Nothing in our testing
  could have caught it**: a browser is never asked to follow one of those links
  by any test we have, so all seventeen would have opened a new tab containing
  the application itself, with no error anywhere.
- **The rule that says what a page is allowed to load now travels inside the
  page.** It used to be added by the small web server that served the screens,
  and there is no longer one — so it is written into the page itself, per
  environment. ⚠ **One thing it can no longer do**: a utility that has connected
  its own map service had that map's address added to the rule as the page was
  served, and a page written once for everybody cannot carry a different address
  per utility. **The asset map will not draw its background until the place that
  hosts the screens is given that address.** It is written down rather than left
  to be found.
- **Screen ids no longer appear in the corner of any screen, in any
  environment** — the Product Owner asked for none. The ability to switch them
  back on for one environment is kept, and is one word in one file.

### Security
- **The sign-in cookie is now marked `Secure`** — it will not travel over an
  unencrypted connection. All three places the product issues one, from a single
  setting that is on by default. Nobody is signed out: neither cookie changed
  its name.
- **An action taken from a page that is not ours is now refused.** Both addresses
  end in `bynry.com`, and a browser treats those as the same place — so it would
  attach a signed-in clerk's cookie to a form sent from any page ending in
  `bynry.com`. Asking permission does not stop that form being sent; it only
  hides the reply, after the action has happened. The app now refuses it before
  doing anything. Scripts, payment providers and partner systems are unaffected.
- HTTPS-behind-the-load-balancer settings, and HSTS, are now configurable per
  environment. **HSTS ships switched off**, because it is the one setting a
  browser will not let you take back.

## [2.387.1] — 2026-09-28

### Fixed
- **A leftover number on a plan can no longer stop a customer's bill.** The base
  charge — the standing monthly amount for a service — is set on the charge code
  bound to the plan. A plan can also still *show* a base figure of its own, and
  where an old data migration left a different number there, the bill for that
  service **would not produce at all**: it stopped and said *"Two base charges
  for water. Clear 11.50 on the plan."* Every bill for that service, for every
  account on that plan, was held up over a number the product itself says does
  not set the price. **The bill is now produced from the charge code and the
  stale figure is ignored.** Nothing changes where the two already agree, which
  is every utility we have seeded: water still bills **$8.00** a month where the
  charge code says $8.00.
- **A utility that has not set up a base charge code is now told so.** It used
  to fall back to the plan's figure quietly. It now stops that one service's
  bill and says, in one line, *"No base charge for water. Declare one on Charge
  codes."* — naming the screen that fixes it rather than the plan, where typing
  a number would have changed nothing.
- **The customer portal can show a standing charge again on *Stop or restart
  service*.** The demo utility's own data said **$8.00** on the plan for every
  service while its charge codes said water **$12.00**, sewer **$8.00** and
  trash **$9.00**, so two of the three disagreed and the screen could show no
  figure at all. It shows one now.


## [2.387.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **The Units screen's *Missing services* block is gone, and the shortfall is a
  filter on the units list instead.** It used to be a second table above the
  list, with its own page controls, showing the same units a second time. You
  can now press **Missing services** on the toolbar and the ordinary list
  narrows to exactly those units — which means you can combine it with the
  search, with the four filters that were already there, page it with the list,

  **Missing**, which is shown, and **Offered here**, which you can switch on
  from the columns control. On the sample utility that reads *Missing services
  43 units*.

### Removed
- The separate service-gap report and the web address behind it. Nothing else
  was using it; everything it showed is on the units list now.

## [2.386.0] — 2026-09-28

### Changed
- **The report editor is now a page of its own instead of a narrow panel.**
  Pressing **Edit** on a report opens a full screen at its own web address, so
  the thing you are working on can be bookmarked, refreshed and sent to a
  colleague. The controls get about half again as much room as they had, which
  is most of the answer to *"I don't know what I'm doing and how fields are
  shown"*. **You still see your report while you build it:** the first five
  rows sit beside the controls and re-run every time you tick a column, and
  they stay in place as you scroll down to the grouping — which the old panel

- **The Filters box no longer lists every filter a report could possibly
  take.** On a report that declares thirteen of them it drew thirteen stacked
  rows and you had to scroll past all of them to reach the grouping. It now
  shows only the filters you are actually using, with **+ Add filter**
  underneath and a count of how many are on the bar. Clearing a filter's value

  (`DEF-REP-7080`)
- **The editor can no longer close itself while you are using it.** Changing a
  date, a class or the account a statement is about used to drop you back to
  the plain report mid-keystroke. The builder has its own address now, so there

- **A field's name no longer sits centred above its own box.** On the editor's
  first card the word *Dataset* was printed above the dropdown instead of
  beside it, which is not how any other row on the screen reads. It reads as a
  row now. (`DEF-REP-7201`)

### Still not fixed, said out loud
- **The builder offers a column called *teller*** on reports built from
  payments. That is the database's word, not ours, and it needs a proper name
  in all eleven languages. (`DEF-REP-7202`)
- **The Group & sort box offers three grouping levels and no *Subtotals* or
  *Sort* rows**, which the design drawing shows. The words for both are already
  translated into all eleven languages; what is missing is the report engine
  honouring them, and a control the engine ignores would do nothing.
  (`DEF-REP-7200`)

## [2.385.1] — 2026-09-28

*Written up on 2026-09-28, the day it was noticed missing. The build shipped in
`c8cc6e90c` and was superseded within the hour, which is how it came to have no
entry at all — see the note under 2.385.0.*

### Fixed
- **Opening a statement's editor cut the statement down to one column.** A
  statement is drawn with seven columns; pressing **Edit** left you looking at
  a single one, and nothing said why. Neither half was doing anything wrong on
  its own — the editor offered the columns the underlying data set has, and the
  report honoured exactly the list it was handed, and those two lists met in one
  word out of seven. There is now one place that answers *what may this report
  be asked for*, and the editor, the screen and the save check all read it.
  (`DEF-REP-7072`)
- **A statement could not be downloaded.** The download had been built and
  connected to nothing, so the button never appeared. It appears now, and the
  file that comes out carries the money at two decimal places exactly as the
  screen shows it. (`DEF-REP-7053`)
- **No statement said who or what it was about.** A statement opened with no
  heading naming its account or its unit, so a printed copy could not be told
  from any other. It now names them — *AC-2026-00032 · Hugo Faulkner* on an
  account, *163 Willow Bend Dr · Unit 1* on a unit — composed on the server, so
  a new kind of statement gets a heading without any screen changing.
  (`DEF-REP-7052`)

## [2.385.0] — 2026-09-27

*Written up on 2026-09-28. Both 2.385.0 and 2.385.1 shipped with no entry
because the check that asks for one only ever looked at the version that was
current at that moment, and on this branch a version is current for about
twenty minutes. The check now asks about every version it can see in the
project's history (`DEF-GOV-6930`, `DEF-GOV-6813`); these are the two gaps it
found.*

### Added
- **Two new reports.** **Bill run readiness** shows, for a billing cycle, what
  is standing between you and issuing the bills, built on the record the bill
  run already keeps rather than on a recalculation, so opening it costs
  nothing. **Plans & discounts** lists one row per enrolment across plans,
  tariffs and discounts together.

### Changed
- **The tolerance band on the revenue-variance report now has a test behind
  it.** The rule was agreed on 2026-09-27 and nothing checked it until now. On
  the worked example a bill of $84.00 made of $24 base and $60 usage carries a
  band of $9.00 — not the $12.60 you get by taking a flat percentage of the
  whole, and not the $12 drawn on the design sheet, which is an illustration.

### Still not fixed, said out loud
- **Bill run readiness has a Route column that is empty on every row, and no
  Route filter.** An account is not on one route — a house taking water and gas
  is on two — so there is no single route to print, and choosing one silently
  would be worse than leaving it blank. The column is drawn with its reason and
  the filter is deliberately absent, because a filter over a column that is
  empty everywhere is a control that cannot work. (`OQ-REP-12768`)
- **The revenue-variance report still does not open.** Its band is built and
  tested; what is missing is the part that gathers each account's expected
  figure, which means re-pricing a period through the rating engine.
  (`DEF-REP-7150`)
- **The *Winter average* basis is not built.** It was not covered by any
  existing rule, so it is served empty with its reason rather than guessed at,
  and it is left out of the band. (`OQ-REP-12769`)

## [2.384.2] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **AR Ageing gave the same answer whatever date you asked it for.** Asked for
  the receivable as at the end of last September, or the end of January two
  years ago, it handed back the figures for today with the older date's heading
  on them. On the sample utility seven different dates all read **$9,581.53
  owed by 30 accounts** — the same money, seven times. It now answers for the
  day you ask about: bills that had been issued by then, less money that had
  been posted by then. The same utility reads **$16,301.09 owed by 45 accounts
  at 31 August** and **$9,581.53 owed by 30 at 30 September**, and a date
  before its first bill reads **$0.00**. **Today's figures have not moved.**
  (`DEF-PAY-6940`)

### Still not fixed, said out loud
- **The Reports dashboard's Outstanding tile still reads *0.00% against the
  comparison*, and the AR Ageing screen still cannot be asked for an earlier
  date.** The report itself now answers correctly for any date. Two things in
  between do not: the dashboard asks the report for a date using a name the
  report does not read, and the *As of* box on the report screen moves only one
  end of the date range, so any earlier date comes back as *"the end date is
  before the start date"*. Both were already like that before this change and
  both are in the reports area. Shots and measurements are in
  `scratchpad/po-shots/ar-ageing-as-at/`. (`DEF-PAY-6940`)

### Known limitation
- A bill that has since been **cancelled or corrected** cannot be put back into
  a past date's position, because the product records the day a bill was issued
  and not the day it stopped being live. The report now says how many such
  bills there are rather than leaving them out silently. (`DEF-PAY-7020`)

## [2.384.1] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **The Billing Register fits twenty-two rows on a laptop where it fitted
  thirteen.** Counted from screenshots at 1440×1400, the width and height the
  Product Owner's own were taken at. Five things moved and none of them is a
  number being hidden.
- **The services are said once instead of forty-one times.** A utility that
  bills all six services on every account had the same six words in every row
  of the table, in about a quarter of its width. They are service chips now,
  and where every row carries the same set they collapse to one line above the
  table — *Every row · Electric · Fire · Gas · Sewer · Trash · Water*. Where
  the rows differ, which is what the column is read for, the column stays and
  each row gets its own chips.
- **The usage column shows what was used, and keeps a meter that read zero.**
  A cell read `0 cart · 0 connection · 0 kW · 15.2 kgal` — three zeros and one
  figure. A zero cart count means nobody has a cart, and that is not the same
  fact as a water meter that was read and read nothing. The first is no longer
  drawn; the second still is, and so is a cart count of one.
- **Two lines above the table instead of four.** The word *REPORT* is gone from
  over a report a clerk arrived at by clicking a report, and what one row is now
  sits on the same line as the window and the date basis.
- **The four filters are one row with their labels level.** The *Today*
  shortcut moved from under the date box to beside it, so *From* and *To* are
  no longer a line taller than *Bill type* and *Service*.
- **The tile band is shorter.** The tile with no figure still says *Not counted
  yet* — it is honest and it stays.

## [2.384.0] — 2026-09-27

### Added
- **A statement can now be run for a UNIT, not just an account.** Pick a unit
  and you get its running record — every charge and payment against that
  address, in date order, with the balance carried forward. Because a unit
  outlives the people who live in it, the statement also shows **who was living
  there** when each line was posted, so a statement spanning a move-out keeps
  each tenant's money under their own name. The heading shows the building's
  address and the unit's label; a unit never has an address of its own.
  (`BR-REP-043`, `CR-142-BRC07` `P2.15`)
- **Settings has a Delivery card** that opens Reports → Scheduled, where a
  utility says who each scheduled report goes to. It lists nothing of its own:
  recipients belong to a schedule, not to the utility. (`BR-REP-044`, `P5.5`)

### Known limitations
- **The Occupant column is blank on everything billed so far.** The system only
  began recording who held an account on 24 September, and past entries are
  never rewritten, so older lines have no name to show. The report says so
  rather than guessing — filling it in from whoever holds the account today
  would put the current tenant's name on the previous tenant's bills.
  (`DEF-REP-7051`)
- **No report yet prints a heading naming what it is about** — the account,
  customer, premises or unit. The information is served and nothing draws it.
  (`DEF-REP-7052`)


## [2.383.6] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **The new property statement was sending money with six decimal places
  instead of four.** Nothing on screen was wrong — the page rounds to two for
  display — but the figures crossing the wire carried two extra zeros, and a
  rule about how money is written is also a rule about how it is sent. Found by
  reading a real response rather than by any test. (`DEF-POR-7091`)

## [2.383.5] — 2026-09-27

*Written after the fact, from the commit (`3bf716c90`), by the gate triage lane
on 2026-09-30 — this version shipped with no entry and `G35` said so
(`DEF-GOV-8531`).*

### Added
- **Size is a column on the asset registry.** On *Meters* it sits between
  *Service* and *Mult.*, and on *Behind the meter* between *Meter* and *Export
  capacity*; it is in the column chooser too. It reads the utility's own name
  for the size — `Water 5/8"` — rather than the stored code, so it carries its
  unit. *Sub-meters* has no Size column, because a sub-meter cannot be given a
  size and the column could only ever show a dash.

## [2.383.4] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **A meter maker's name is printed as data, not translated.** The read-source
  column on reports read `AMI · Itron` and `AMI · Sensus`, and those two phrases
  were stored once per language — eleven identical copies of a company's name
  for a translator to look at. The words are translated now (*AMI feed*, *Flux
  AMI*, *AMI-Datenstrom*) and the maker is printed beside them exactly as it is
  stored. A utility that buys from a third manufacturer gets it on screen
  correctly with nothing edited anywhere.


### Fixed
- **The report editor now asks for the account before anything else, and every
  field on it is named in words.** Opening *Statement* to edit it used to show
  four empty tiles, the words *No rows match — widen the dates or filters*, and
  a list of boxes labelled `posted_on`, `account_code` and `narrative`. Widening
  the dates could never have helped: a statement is one account's record and no
  account had been chosen, and the one sentence that said so was four screens
  down. Now the account box is the first thing in the panel, with *A statement
  opens on one account* beside it; the reason an empty report is empty is at the
  top instead of the bottom; and every column, measure, filter and grouping
  reads as words — *Posted*, *Account code*, *Narrative*, *Source*, *Detail
  level*, *Ledger postings* — in all eleven languages. **The heading that read
  `ATTRIBUTES 7 of 5` now reads `1 of 5`**: it was counting the seven columns
  the report serves against the five it lists, which are two different things.
  On the billing register the same heading moves from `8 of 12` to `6 of 12`,
  because two of those eight are measures and are counted in the section below.
  While a report is being built and comes back with nothing, the screen now
  draws the SHAPE of the table it would produce — the columns, in order, with
  the ones that read right-aligned — as grey bars under the word *Example*.
  There is deliberately not one character in it, so nothing there can be
  mistaken for a figure from your own utility. (`DEF-REP-7070`)

⚠ **NO VERSION NUMBER IS CLAIMED FOR THIS ENTRY AND THAT IS NOT AN OVERSIGHT.**
`07-frontend/package.json`, `package-lock.json` and `06-backend/pyproject.toml`
were holding a sibling lane's UNCOMMITTED bump to `2.381.1` in the shared
working tree when this landed, over a changelog entry describing rating work
that is not on the branch. Writing `2.382.1` over that line would have reverted
their bump (law 11, mechanism two); committing the three files as they stood
would have published a release note for a fix nobody has pushed (`DEF-168`,
mechanism five). This lane's work therefore ships under whichever version the
next bump carries, and the choice is written down here rather than guessed. The
allocator answered `2.382.1` and it was still free at push time.

## [2.383.3] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **A finished tenant-isolation proof is no longer destroyed by an ordinary
  refresh of the working copy.** The only detailed record of a run — which cases
  failed, by name — was written inside the repository, so restoring files from
  the branch wrote an older copy over it. That happened to a 67-minute run
  earlier today: the counts survived in a lane's notes, the twenty case names
  did not. Every finished run is now also written outside the working copy,
  where a refresh cannot reach it, and the copy inside the repository is not
  replaced by a run that is older than the one already recorded or that reports
  no cases at all.


## [2.383.2] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **Five pieces of Reports colouring that were never arriving.** Three borders
  on the report builder's edit panel and the grey on five small labels across
  the viewer and its group rows were written against names the product does not
  define, so the browser threw the instruction away and drew each one in
  whatever colour it had inherited. They now use the product's own tokens and
  look like the rest of the screen. Nothing else about those screens changed.


## [2.383.1] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **A Settings rule page no longer shows an internal rule code to the person
  using it.** Under every field on every rule page — billing defaults, late
  fees, allocation order, remitting basis and the rest — sat a line reading
  *Set by BR-REP-018*. It answered a question nobody on that screen can act on
  (*who decided 200%?*) with a code that means nothing outside our own
  documents. **It is gone, and nothing replaces it.** What is left under a
  field is what a person types against: the unit the number is in, and whether
  it may be left empty.


## [2.383.0] — 2026-09-27

### Added
- **A landlord opening the portal now sees a statement for one of their
  properties — and only their own account on it.** At 1408 Elm Street the owner
  sees the $69.60 the building's shared supply cost them this month. They do not
  see Unit 3's $100.00, or any of the other flats. A tenant signing in sees
  their own flat and not the owner's shared-supply charge. Staff are unaffected:
  they still see the whole property, as they already did. (`CWP-078`, `P4.15`)
- **A scheduled report can now be delivered somewhere outside the product, by a
  web address that stops working after four hours.** A utility's administrator
  sets up the destination once; whoever writes the schedule picks from that list
  and cannot type an address of their own. Each address gets one file, for one
  utility, read-only, and every delivery is recorded. (`P4.14`)

### Not built, on purpose
- **Delivering a scheduled file into a utility's own SFTP folder is not offered
  yet.** Connecting to somebody's folder means deciding how we know we are
  really talking to their machine, and getting that wrong is silent: the file
  goes to the wrong place, the transfer succeeds, and our own record says it was
  delivered. That is a decision for a person to make, so the option is not shown
  at all rather than shown and failing later. It is written down as
  `OQ-REP-12767`.
## [2.382.2] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **Three builds that shipped with nothing written down now have their entry.**
  `2.377.1`, `2.377.2` and `2.380.3` were each live for a few minutes before the
  next lane bumped past them, and anyone told *"look in build 2.377.1"* found
  nothing between `2.376.1` and `2.377.3`. The entries are written from what
  those commits actually changed.

### Added
- **A check that every build we have ever published keeps its entry, not just
  today's.** The old one asked only whether the CURRENT version was written up,

  refused.

  was not moved with it, and the broken call was then reported as an ordinary
  refusal rather than as a fault. Every utility with a base charge code was

- The rate-change impact analysis's own suite gains one passing case back —

- **The Trend Pack was showing accounting entries, not a trend.** Opening it
  gave a clerk a list of ledger lines — posting date, account code, debit,

- A check the ledger had been carrying since August — *we cannot tell which bill

## [2.381.1] — 2026-09-27

### Fixed
- **The Plans & Rates list showed a monthly base charge of zero on every plan.**
  It was adding up a figure plans stopped carrying in August, when the charge
  code took over the base. It now adds up what the charge codes actually say —
  on the sample utility, twelve dollars for electric and eight for water, so
  twenty. Where we cannot work it out the cell is blank rather than showing
  zero, because a zero is a claim about a utility's own prices. **Sorting the
  list by that column has been withdrawn**, because the figure cannot be worked
  out in the database; every other column still sorts. (`BR-RAT-1040`,

- **Twenty-eight tests in the rating base-resolution area had been failing for
  four days and nobody had read them.** One of them disagreed by thirty dollars
  about what the sample utility's price list comes to. The data was right: the
  reconnection fee went from forty-five dollars to seventy-five on 21 September
  on the Product Owner's own instruction, and the test was still holding the old
  total. Three more test fixtures were still sending a field the product renamed
  on 23 September. Nothing a customer can see was wrong. (`DEF-RAT-6980`)

### Added
- **A check that notices when a set of tests has not been run.** A lane running
  one test file sees green beside a neighbouring file that is entirely red, and
  nothing in the repository was reading a test result. A run now leaves a
  receipt, and a merge check reads it: it fails on a new failure, on a failure
  parked without a defect number, and on a receipt taken before the code it

## [2.380.3] — 2026-09-27

*Written after the fact, from the commit, by lane FIX-SMALL (`DEF-GOV-6930`).*

### Fixed
- **Money on a report reads two decimal places, on all forty-six of them.** A
  trend pack footer read `15816.000000` directly under a tile reading
  `$15,816.00` for the same figure, so the number a finance officer quoted
  depended on where on the screen they looked. Walked at 1440 before the fix:
  **133 figures with more than two decimals in the body of six reports, and ten
  more in their footers. Afterwards: none.**
- **A column now says what KIND of thing it holds, so this cannot come back one
  report at a time.** The screen's only answer to *is this money* used to be a
  hand-typed list naming five reports out of forty-six; everything else was
  printed the way the database stores it. Money, percentages, quantities and
  counts are now each rendered from what the dataset itself declares —
  `100.000000` reads **100.00%**, `46754.000000` reads **46754**.
- **A report with no currency of its own stopped skipping the formatter
  entirely**, which is how `531.140000` reached a clerk in the tax remittance's
  cell, its footer and its tile. And a count under a grouped report no longer
  wears a currency symbol.
- **Nothing is rounded before it is displayed.** The queries still return the
  stored decimals and the wire still carries every digit, so a signed figure
  stays reconcilable against the report that quotes it.

- **On the new Reports Dashboard, the bottom panel's last two columns were
  touching** — the heading read *DifferenceResult* and a row read *$0.00Foots*.

- **The *Service mix* panel was a blank box in a month with no revenue**, which
