  owner record get created.** A user reported that importing premises with owner
  details did not generate the Master Account. The account was being generated —
  what was missing is that nobody owned it: no owner record, and the name kept
  only in a free-text box. The import will not guess what kind of owner somebody
  is from their name, and until now there was no way to tell it. Fill in *Owner
  category* — Landlord, Property manager, and the rest of the list on Settings —
  and the owner record is created and joined to the account. Leave it blank and
  the address still loads exactly as before; the rehearsal step now says what
  will and will not be created.
- **An import can record the owner's email.** An owner account is created active
  and it bills, and there was no way to supply an address to send anything to.
- **The receipt counts owner records, not just owner accounts.** Four new
  figures: owner records created, rows that did not say what kind of owner, rows
  whose owner could not be created, and rows whose Owner column names nobody.
  That last one was warned about during the rehearsal and then counted nowhere,
  so a run could show four zeroes and look clean.

### Fixed

- **The sample file no longer proposes values nobody could use.** *Lat* read
  *"Sample lat"* and *GIS parcel ID* read *"Sample gis parcel id"*. Both ship
  blank, like the other columns only a utility can fill in.
- **A saved column mapping that names a retired column no longer stops the
  run.** It used to refuse the whole import; the retired column is now left
  unmapped for the operator to decide about, and the rest of their mapping is
  kept.

## [2.308.8] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **A plan now shows what its rate schedules actually charge.** The price panel
  used to name the shape of each schedule — *seasonal*, *tiered* — and stop
  there, so a clerk checking a plan before publishing it, or looking one up
  afterwards, could not see a single price without opening the schedule itself.
  Each service's row now carries its prices: the blocks of a tiered ladder, each
  season's own ladder under its own name, and the price of every time-of-use
  window beside the window it prices. Capacity, demand and percent-of-another-
  service schedules show their figures too. It is the same panel on the last
  step of the new-plan wizard and on the plan's own page, so the two cannot
  disagree.
- **The usage column says *Time-of-use*, not `time_of_use`.** It was printing
  the value as it is stored, in English, whatever language the screen was set to.
- **The plan's base charge is just the figure now.** It read *"Plan base charge,
  from the server: $20.00"*; where a number is worked out is not something a
  clerk needs to read.

## [2.308.7] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **A plan can be built for more than one kind of customer.** The customer class
  on a plan used to be a single choice, so a utility charging Residential and
  Municipal the same prices had to write the plan twice and keep the two in step
  by hand. It is a list now, with the chosen classes shown as removable chips.
  **A plan that names no class is for every class**, which is what naming none
  already meant.
- **Penalties, deposits and adjustments can be added to a plan again.** Step 4
  offered only two of the five kinds of charge code, so late fees, returned
  payments, meter tampering, deposits and goodwill adjustments were simply not
  in the list — a utility could see the code in its own catalogue and had no way
  to put it on a plan.
- **A plan no longer restates a rule the charge code already owns.** The
  editable *Applied* box on each charge row is gone. Each row now states two
  facts the charge code itself declares: what kind of charge it is, and whether
  it lands on every bill or waits for something to happen. Where a code's own
  settings contradict each other, the row says so at the moment it is attached
  rather than at the next bill run.
- **Opening a published plan and saving it without changing anything no longer
  wipes its outside-city surcharge.** The screen was reading the plan and the
  save was sending a blank, so a plan that charged fifteen percent extra outside
  the city limits came back charging nothing extra. No bill already sent was
  changed.
- **The change-or-correction question is asked first, not last.** When you edit
  a published plan, *Change the plan* or *Fix an error* now sits at the top of
  step 1. It used to be the last thing on the review, after all the work had
  been done under a verb nobody had chosen yet.
- **You can type to find a charge code, a tax or a discount on a plan.** All
  three pickers were plain dropdowns for utilities with ten or fewer codes and
  search boxes for utilities with eleven — the same screen behaved differently
  depending on how many codes you happened to have. They are search boxes
  always, and wider.
- **Three empty lists stopped pointing the wrong way.** *No charges added yet.
  Add one below.* sat above the row it was pointing at. The lists state what is
  there now and leave the pointing to the control beside them.


## [2.308.5] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **The discount wizard asks a clerk to read a quarter of what it did.** Walking
  the five steps of a real discount, end to end, the screens carried **1,096
  words**; they now carry **411**. Three kinds of sentence went: the paragraphs
  explaining why a feature is not built yet (six of them, 199 words, none of
  which a clerk could act on), the block above the stepper that repeated *"Five
  steps · discounts reference the plan's normal rates…"* and *"There is no
  separate Save draft…"* on **all five steps**, and the opening description of
  what a discount is. What a clerk uses is untouched and in several places now
  says the same thing in fewer words.

- **The warnings a clerk needs are all still there, shorter.** A cap of zero
  still says it grants nothing, a bill floor of zero still says it can take a
  bill to nothing, automatic enrolment still says it cannot demand proof, and
  step 4 still says that saving enrols nobody. These are consequences of a
  decision someone is about to make, and the rule that shortened everything else
  protects them by name.

- **Money and percentages now read at two decimal places, as they are meant to.**
  On the edit door a 1.5% discount showed **`1.500000`** in its value box,
  **`0.000000`** as its bill floor and **`2383.000000`** as its budget cap, and
  the review step read back **`1.500000 as typed`** — six places is the precision
  the figures are STORED at, never the precision they are shown at. They now read
  `1.50`, `0.00`, `2383.00` and `1.50`. Nothing is rounded: a rate genuinely
  finer than two places, like `0.0625`, still shows every digit, and what the
  screen sends back to the server is the stored figure unchanged.

- **The phrase "as typed" is gone from the review step, because it was not true.**
  Nobody typed `1.500000`; the screen put it there when it loaded the discount.

## [2.308.3] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **Your bills, payments, documents, accounts and meter readings now arrive one
  page at a time.** Every one of those five lists used to send the customer's
  whole history to their browser before it drew anything — every reading a meter
  has ever taken, every bill since the account opened. On a property with an
  hourly-reading meter that is thousands of rows to show fifty. The page, the
  search box, the filter buttons and the column sorting all moved to the server
  together.
- **Searching a list searches the whole list, not the page in front of you.**
  Type a bill number, a cheque number, a meter serial or an address and the match
  is found wherever it sits. Typing a month name — *August* — still finds that
  month's bills, in every language the portal speaks.
- **The meter tabs on Readings show every meter, including one read only once a
  quarter.** They used to be built from whatever was on screen.
- **The *Pay* button, the *Download a year* button and the *"since you started"*
  line tell the truth on every page.** Each was counted from the rows on screen,
  so an unpaid bill on page two could hide the Pay button.
- **A phone can reach past the fiftieth row.** The card lists on Readings,
  Payments and My accounts had no page footer, because they used to hold
  everything.

## [2.308.1] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **A tamper fee was being charged every month to a customer nobody said had
  tampered with anything.** When a plan listed a charge, the product treated
  *listed* as *charge it every month* and never looked at what kind of charge
  it was. On the demo utility that meant a **$250.00** tamper fee twelve times
  a year, a **$30.00** returned-payment fee on all three plans and two
  **$45.00** one-off connection fees — **$955.00 a month, $11,460.00 a year,
  across ten units**. Listing a charge on a plan now makes it *available* to
  that plan, and the charge itself decides whether it belongs on a monthly
  bill. Those four fees now add **$0.00** to a monthly bill.
- **Nothing that was working stopped working, and it was measured rather than
  assumed.** The demo utility has no charge at all marked as a monthly
  automatic charge, so every fee the product could put on a bill was one of
  the wrong ones; the three sample plans carrying 78 of its 88 units list no
  charges whatsoever. A charge that is marked recurring and automatic still
  lands exactly as it did before.
- **No configuration was deleted and nothing was switched on for anyone.** The
  nine plan-to-charge links are untouched — they are harmless once the charge
  decides — and no charge had its *apply automatically* box ticked on a
  utility's behalf. That box is already on the charge-code screen, so a
  utility that wants a monthly fee can still set one up.

## [2.308.0] — 2026-09-19

### Added

- **A rate schedule can now say which charge code its base comes from.** On the
  first step of the rate schedule screen there is a searchable box listing the
  charge codes ticked as a base for that service; it shows the code and its
  name, not the amount, which is already on step 2 against every connection
  size. The review step names the bound code, and activating the schedule is
  refused if that code could not actually price the service — it is not marked
  as a base, it belongs to another service, or it only applies to customer
  types the schedule does not price.
- **Leaving the box empty is a real answer and it is what every existing rate
  schedule does.** The base is then worked out exactly as before, from the
  charge code that declares itself the service's base. **Nothing changes for
  any utility until somebody picks one**: the real billing calculation was run
  for all **78 accounts of the sample utility against both services — 156
  answers — on the old code and on the new, and all 156 came back identical.**
  Not one account's base moved by a cent.
- **What it is for:** a utility with a residential water base and a commercial
  one has two charge codes both ticked *this is the base*, and today the
  product refuses to bill such an account rather than let the order of a list
  decide what a customer pays. The rate schedule can now say which one it
  means.
- **The price itself has not moved.** The charge code still owns the base
  amount; the rate schedule names a code, it never holds a figure.

### Changed

- A minimum bill left blank now **means zero** rather than being unset. A
  minimum only ever tops a bill up, so no floor and a floor of $0.00 produce
  the identical bill. It is deliberately not pre-filled with `0.00`, because a
  stored zero prints as `0.00` in the rate matrix where the agreed design draws
  a dash for every size.

## [2.307.7] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **The notice record no longer ends at two thousand letters.** The list of
  everything a utility has told its customers — every disconnect letter, every
  reminder, and every account deliberately skipped, such as one on a medical
  hold — stopped at 2,000 rows. The two-thousand-and-first letter was on no
  page at all, and the total on screen read *2,000* however many had really
  been sent. A utility chasing forty thousand accounts writes past two thousand
  of these rows in a single night's run. The server now asks the database for
  the one page it is showing, so every letter is reachable however many there
  are and the total is the real total. On a test utility holding **50,050 notices**, asking for one page of fifty: the server used to fetch **2,000 rows for every page** and now fetches **50**. The total on screen used to read **2,000** and now reads **50,050**. And the one that matters most — **ask for page 1,000 and the old server handed you page 40**, the last page it believed existed; it now hands you page 1,000.
- The limit was **removed, not raised**: there is no ceiling anywhere on this
  path, and asking for the largest page the product offers returns all thousand
  rows of it.
- While the limit existed the server said so, in a note reading *"this read
  stops at 2,000 rows and the record may hold more"*. Nothing truncates now, so
  that note would be untrue and it was removed with the limit. The other stated
  absence on this list is unchanged and still true: a certified letter carries
  no tracking number, because no print provider is connected on any channel.
  (DEF-NOT-5750.)

## [2.307.6] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **The tax wizard's jurisdiction list asks for a page instead of the whole
  catalogue, and the box in front of it still offers every jurisdiction.** It
  was the last list in Plans & Rates that sent everything a utility has in one
  reply, with no count and no way for the screen to ask for less. A utility
  holds about **53** jurisdictions today, so nothing on screen changes — but
  nothing stopped one entering five thousand, and all five thousand would have
  been sent at once. Measured on a utility with 50,000 of them: **50,000 rows
  in one read before, 50 rows in two reads after**, and the same two reads
  whether you ask for page 1, page 40 or page 1,000.
- The jurisdiction box itself was deliberately left able to see the whole list,
  because it searches as you type and works out which jurisdiction is already
  chosen from the same list. Had it been given only the first page, you could no
  longer have found the fifty-first jurisdiction by typing its name, and
  **reopening a tax that used it would have shown the box empty** over an answer
  that was already correct. The screen now asks for the pages one after another
  until it holds them all — two requests for a utility with 1,001 jurisdictions,
  one for a real one.

## [2.307.5] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **The Disconnects tab stops reading the whole utility to draw one screen.**
  Opening it used to load every account a disconnection could touch — everyone
  on the collections ladder and everyone held back by a medical certificate, a
  payment plan or a weather moratorium — and then show forty of them. On a test
  tab of 120 accounts it pulled 320 account records out of the database to draw
  40, and pulled the same 320 whether you asked for 40 rows or 1,000. It now
  asks for the rows it is showing: 40 records for a page of 40, 120 for a page
  of 120. The numbers in the five tiles above the list, the rows themselves,
  their order and the total beside the pager are all unchanged. (DEF-CUS-5755.)
- **The "on hold" figure is worked out once per screen instead of twice.** The
  list and the `ON HOLD — PROTECTED` tile each asked payments whether every
  protected account's payment plan was still current; they now share one
  answer. On the same test tab that is 20 fewer questions to the database per
  screen, and it grows with the number of accounts a utility has put on hold.

## [2.307.4] — 2026-09-19

### Fixed

- **The Assets registry builds its page in a handful of database reads instead
  of five per row.** Opening the Assets list used to ask the database five
  separate questions about every row it was about to show — where the asset is
  standing, which property that is, which service it is on, what that service is
  called, and how many sub-meters hang off it — so a page of 40 cost about 201
  reads and the largest page a clerk can choose, 1,000, cost about 5,001. It now
  asks those questions once for the whole page: **6 reads for a page of 40 and 9
  for a page of 1,000**, and the number of rows the database has to hand back
  drops from 5,000 to 1,401 on the big page, because a thousand meters standing
  on two hundred properties are now looked up two hundred times and not a
  thousand. Every column shows exactly what it showed before.
- The same batched read now serves the Assignment history on an asset's own
  page, which was paying one lookup per row for the same reason.

## [2.307.3] — 2026-09-18

### Fixed

- **Route setup works on a real utility's list of properties.** Building or
  editing a route used to fetch every property the utility has before it drew
  anything, so the screen became unusable somewhere around five to ten thousand
  properties. It asks for the page it is showing now. On the same test data the
  server went from 82 database queries to 5, and stays at 5 as the utility
  grows. The Routes and Cycles tabs on the Meter Reads page do the same.
- **Searching a picker searches the whole list, not the page you can see.**
  Type a property number or a route code and the match is found wherever it
  sits — before, a search could only look at the rows already on screen.
- **Tick a property on page one and it still counts on page four.** The running
  "selected · units" figure, the "already on another route" warnings and the
  meter list on the next step all follow your selection across pages.
- **`Select all 9,412` selects 9,412.** It used to select only the rows on the
  page in front of you and say nothing about it.
- **Re-opening a route keeps its members.** The screen asks the route for its
  own properties rather than looking for them in the page on screen, so saving
  an edit can no longer drop the members you could not see.
- Two column headings on the property picker — Meters and Current route — no
  longer offer sorting. Neither is a value the list can be ordered by without
  reading every property in the utility, which is the thing being fixed here.
  (DEF-MET-5743.)

## [2.307.2] — 2026-09-18

### Fixed

- **The app builds again.** The frontend image would not build: a test added
  with yesterday's add-control change left out a value the shared table now
  requires, so the type check stopped and `docker compose build` died before
  the frontend image was made. Nothing a clerk sees changed. (DEF-SHL-5741.)

## [2.307.1] — 2026-09-18

### Changed

- **The add control sits above the list on a plan's charges, taxes and
  discounts.** A clerk arrives at those three steps to attach something, so the
  control they reach for first no longer sits underneath a list that grows. The
  divider moved with it, so the block still reads as belonging to the list.
  Nowhere else moved: the shared table keeps its old arrangement by default, and
  only these three steps ask for the new one. (PO ruling, 2026-09-18.)

## [2.307.0] — 2026-09-18

### Changed

- **Charges, taxes and discounts on a plan are one list each now, not two.**
  Each of those steps used to show the same thing twice — a catalogue on the
  left to pick from, and a panel on the right repeating what you had picked.
  There is one table: choose from the dropdown at the bottom, the row appears,
  and the × removes it. Whether a charge applies once or on every bill is a
  dropdown on the row itself.
- **A row shows the GL account you actually use** — `4000 Water revenue` — and
  shows nothing at all where a code has no account mapped to it.
- **The wizard says less.** Every step's wording was measured against the house
  rule that on-screen text is capped by what it is for; 28 sentences were
  shortened or split, and explanations of *why* the product works a certain way
  moved off the screen into the code, where the next builder reads them.
  Nothing a clerk needs in order to act was removed: the refusals that stop a
  plan being activated still name the codes, the services and the counts.


## [2.306.0] — 2026-09-18

### Added

- **A plan now shows you what changed underneath it.** A plan does not set
  prices — it binds the rate schedules and charge codes that do — so until today
  you could open *Sample — Residential*, see which water schedule it uses, and
  have no way of knowing that schedule's price went up last Tuesday. The Audit
  tab now lists every recorded change to something the plan binds: what changed,
  when, who did it and the reason they wrote down.
- **It is not a new version of the plan.** Something the plan binds changing is
  not a change to the plan, so the plan's version number does not move and
  nothing is filed against it.
- **It says what it cannot yet tell you.** Rate schedules and charge codes are
  tracked. Taxes and discounts are not recorded anywhere we can read them yet,
  and the screen says so rather than showing you an empty list that looks like
  reassurance. The sentence disappears by itself once that is fixed.

## [2.305.0] — 2026-09-18

### Added

- **A plan can now be CORRECTED, and a correction is not a new version.** Until
  today a typo in a published plan and a deliberate re-binding produced exactly
  the same record — *v4 supersedes v3, reason attached* — so the history said
  the plan changed when somebody had only mistyped. Editing a published plan now
  asks *"What are you doing?"*: **Change the plan** files a new version as it
  always did, and **Fix an error** restates the version already filed. The
  version number does not move, and the filing that was wrong is kept beside the
  one that replaced it rather than being overwritten.
- **Why the version number matters more than it looks.** Every unit assigned to
  a plan records which version it was assigned at, and those records outlive the
  plan. On the sample utility that is 75 units all pointing at version 1. A
  mis-click that was put right an hour later used to leave them pointing at a
  number that existed only because of the mis-click.
- **The Audit tab now says which of the two is which.** A corrected filing is
  marked *Corrected* and no longer wears the plan's own status; the correction
  is labelled as one and states what was fixed, in the words of whoever fixed
  it. Bills already sent keep their prices — the screen says so before you
  press, and it shows no count, because no number we can compute today would be
  the right one.

## [2.304.1] — 2026-09-18

### Fixed

- **Picking *Time-of-use* no longer shows you a *Seasonal* panel as well.**
  Seasons and their time windows are now one panel, and a window is added
  inside the season it belongs to. A time-of-use tariff really does have
  seasons — a window is priced per season and day type — but the screen never
  said so, so it looked as though you had chosen the wrong structure.
- **You can no longer type 31 April into a season.** The month is picked by
  name and the day only offers the days that month has. The season's dates are
  echoed back underneath — *1 Apr – 30 Sep* — and a gap or an overlap in the
  year is named while you type instead of when you activate.
- **Renaming a season no longer breaks its windows.** Windows used to find
  their season by its name, so changing *Summer* to *Peak* quietly detached
  them and activation refused. They now follow the season itself.
- **Connection sizes: pick, set the rate, then Add.** The size step listed
  every size your utility has with a control on each row, so pricing two sizes
  meant working down a table of ten. Nothing is listed until you add it, and
  the size list becomes searchable once it is long enough to need it.
- **Rows stopped repeating their own column heading.** The minimum-rate box on
  each size row announced *"Minimum rate for Solar panel 1 kW"* under a column
  already headed *Minimum rate*. Screen readers still hear it; it is no longer
  drawn.
- **Less text on every step of the rate schedule wizard.** Thirty-five
  sentences ran long; the explanations of *why* the product works a certain
  way have moved out of the screen and into the code, where they belong.


## [2.304.0] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **The plan wizard no longer offers your base charge for adding.** It sits in
  the *Monthly base* panel at the top of the same step, and it was listed again
  below as something to add — so one amount looked like two. It is excluded
  because the code is DECLARED a base, not because of how it is spelled, so a
  utility that calls theirs *SERVICE-CHG* gets the same behaviour.
- **Two dead sentences left the catalogue.** They promised a per-plan amount box
  that was removed months ago and that no screen has drawn since.

### Added

- **The product can now show a GL account the way a person reads it** — `4010`
  and its name, rather than the database id it has been showing. The chart is
  read from the ledger, and where an account is not mapped nothing is shown at
  all rather than a dash or an id. The screens that use this follow.
- **A table of things that have no order can now say so.** The shared editable
  table always drew a drag handle and up/down arrows; collections whose order
  means nothing — a plan's charges, its taxes, its discounts — can now turn them
  off. Nothing that reorders today is affected.

## [2.303.0] — 2026-09-17

### Changed

- **The plan wizard reads about half as long.** Across its eight steps it put
  **1,788 words** on screen and now puts **864** — counted in a browser, in the
  step panel itself. Nothing a step can DO has changed; what went was the *why*.
  Thirty-four sentences explaining how the product works internally — where a
  total is added up, why an amount cannot be edited here, why a field is absent
  — are gone from the screen and live in the code and the register instead.
  Every step is shorter: Basics 68 to 48, Services 211 to 61, Rate schedules 120
  to 74, Charges 325 to 221, Taxes 228 to 86, Discounts & billing 223 to 92,
  Eligibility 179 to 72, Review & activate 434 to 210.
- **The same three paragraphs left the plan's own page**, which shares its
  summary card with the wizard's last step.

## [2.302.0] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **The dates on a discount correction no longer accept typing that is thrown
  away.** A correction keeps the period the figure was recorded for — that is
  what makes it a correction rather than a backdated price change — and the
  server has always ignored any dates sent with one. The two date boxes are now
  refused on screen, with the reason under them, instead of looking editable.

## [2.301.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **A discount can be edited at all.** Until now there was no way to change a
  discount once it had been created — not its name, not its programme owner,
  and not even a draft version that nobody had submitted and that had priced
  nothing. Fixing `-15` where somebody meant `-1.5` took three separate acts
  and, above the approval threshold, a second person's signature, to correct a
  typo in something no customer had ever seen. A draft nobody has submitted now
  saves in place, and the name and owner can be corrected at any time.
- **A live discount can be corrected over the same dates.** When the value
  recorded for a period that has already run was wrong, `Fix this version` on
  the discount's page records the right figure over the SAME window, keeps the
  old one visible as the thing that happened, and asks for a sentence saying
  what was wrong. It is a different act from changing the price from a date,
  which is unchanged and still creates a new dated version.
- **The screen now says bills already sent keep their discount**, where
  somebody correcting a figure would otherwise assume the money was fixed too.

### Changed

- **Nothing about how a discount goes live.** Submit, approve and activate are
  untouched: the approval rules and the second-approval threshold behave exactly
  as before. A correction carries no signature it did not earn — it records that
  no approval check was performed, rather than copying one across.

## [2.300.0] — 2026-09-17

### Changed

- **A charge code's price can no longer be changed in silence.** Until now,
  anybody who could open the charge-code screen could move the paper-bill fee
  from $2.00 to $5.00 and press save: every plan carrying it billed $5.00 on the
  next run — $3.00 more per bill, every month — and the only record was an
  activity-log entry we delete after a time. Changing an amount on a code that
  is already in use now asks for a sentence saying why, and keeps that sentence
  beside the old and new figures for ever. A code nobody uses yet still changes
  freely, because nothing has ever been billed from it.
- **The price-by-size grid is guarded the same way.** A fire line is priced by
  diameter — one 6" line at $60.00, each 2" line at $12.00 — so a figure in that
  grid is the same money as the single Amount box and now asks for the same
  sentence.
- **Renaming a charge code asks for nothing.** The sentence is asked for when a
  figure actually moves, not whenever the form is saved.
- **The `Why this changed` box the blueprint drew is built**, on step 3 of the
  charge-code screen, and only on codes that are already in use. It says on
  screen that bills already sent keep their price.

### Fixed

- **The rate-schedule review step stopped promising something the product
  cannot do.** It read *"Edit the charge code and every schedule and plan
  carrying it follows on the same date."* There is no date: a charge code has no
  start date and no version history, so a new price applies at once, to the
  bills going out now. It now says so.

## [2.299.0] — 2026-09-17

### Changed

- **The plan wizard offers only the services you have switched on.** Step 2
  listed all eleven, nine of them greyed and reading *Not switched on* — nine
  rows nobody could pick above the two they could. They are gone. The one thing
  they were for survives as a link under the list: *Switch more services on in
  Settings*.
- **Step 2 lost six explanatory sentences.** It carried 211 words and now
  carries 71. What went was the *why* — why the other services were shown, why
  a plan with no multiplier charges the same everywhere, how step 3 narrows its
  own list. The controls say those things themselves.

## [2.298.0] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **The service filters now list only the services you have switched on.** On a
  utility running two services, the Plans, Rate schedules, Charge codes and Taxes
  & fees filters all offered eleven — every service the platform can bill, most
  of which could never match a row on your screen. All four read the same list
  now, and it is yours.
- **A retired rate schedule is no longer offered when you build a plan.** Step 3
  listed archived schedules alongside live ones, and picking one was refused at
  save with *"We don't recognise that rate schedule"* — about a schedule you had
  just chosen from our own list. Archived ones are gone from the list, and if one
  reaches the server another way it now says it is archived rather than unknown.

## [2.295.5] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **One bad property no longer stops the whole city-address sync.** The
  reconciliation now counts a property it could not update, says which ones and
  roughly why, and carries on with the rest — where before the first refusal
  ended the run and every property after it was lost. Proved against a real
  PostgreSQL database, which is the only place the old behaviour shows.
- **The city's address list is now in a sensible order.** When you type an
  address, the matches come back best first. Where the city ranks them itself we
  keep their order and say nothing; where it does not, we order them and the
  screen says so in five words: *Ordered by us, not the city.*
- **A paragraph left the address panel.** It explained why no match score is
  shown as a number. That belongs in our notes, not on a screen somebody is
  trying to work on.


## [2.295.4] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **Anyone you invited could not get in, and the temporary password was never
  the problem.** A person you added was given a temporary password and told to
  change it on first sign-in. Signing in worked — and then took them to a page
  that had never been built, so they saw an error about regional settings and a
  Retry button that could not help. Trying again landed in the same place, and
  resetting the password issued a new temporary one and sent them straight back.
  **There was no way through at all.** The page now exists: it asks for the new
  password twice, never for the old one, and takes the person into the product
  as soon as they set it. On our test utility a newly invited user went from
  invitation to dashboard in one go, and signing in again went straight there.
- **A person who sets their password is now a full user of your utility.** They
  showed as *Invited* on your Users screen until they did; that last step was
  already meant to happen and could not, because the page it depended on was
  missing.
- **Your own password rules are what the page enforces.** If the password is too
  short or too simple, the page says which rule it broke, in your utility's own
  terms — it holds no copy of your rules and cannot fall out of step with them.

### Changed

- **Roles & permissions now has its own tab and its own web address.** It used to
  be a button on the Users screen that unfolded a panel underneath, so you could
  not link to it, bookmark it or come back to it. It is now a tab beside *Users*
  under **Settings → Users & roles**. It is still read-only: the three roles are
  set by us, exactly as before.

### Known, not fixed here

- The **Change password** item in the account menu at the bottom-left is still
  greyed out. The page added here is the one you are *required* to use on first
  sign-in; choosing to change your password later is a different page and is not
  built yet.

## [2.294.2] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **A kind of customer you invent now works in four more places.** You told us a
  utility can set up its own kinds of customer. Four parts of the product still
  had our own short list written into them, so a kind you added did not exist
  there. They now read your list instead.
- **Taxes and charges.** A tax or a connection charge can be limited to certain
  kinds of customer. It refused any kind that was not one of ours, so a rule
  written for a kind you added was turned away and that customer was charged
  nothing by it. It now accepts your own kinds.
- **Bill layouts.** A bill can be given its own layout per kind of customer.
  Only four kinds could be chosen, and one of them — spelled *govt* — was never
  a real kind at all. No layout anywhere was using it. The four fixed names are
  gone and your own kinds are offered.
- **The deposit quoted before you sign up.** The page that says whether service
  is available at an address quotes the deposit a household would pay. It found
  that household kind by a name typed into our code, so a utility that calls it
  something else got no figure. It now reads your list. **If your utility has no
  household kind at all, the page shows no deposit rather than quoting a
  business deposit to somebody moving into a house.**

- **A connection fee priced for a particular kind of customer could be typed
  wrong and stored anyway.** A charge can set one price for homes and another
  for businesses. The kind of customer on that price row was never checked, so a
  misspelling was saved, matched nobody, and the customer quietly paid the
  every-customer price instead — $45.00 where the utility had typed $85.00, with
  nothing on screen to show it. It is now refused when you save it, and every
  price already stored is untouched.

### Known, not fixed here

- The same short list is still written into the **letters** side: a notification
  rule can be aimed at only two kinds of customer, and a letter template still
  offers four. Recorded so it is not lost.

## [2.294.1] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **A screen for the addresses we must not send to, with a way back.** Settings →
  Notifications → **Blocked addresses** lists every email address this utility
  has been told to stop using, why it was blocked and when. Until now the
  product kept that list and showed it to nobody, so a bounced address was
  permanent from a clerk's point of view.
- **Release.** A bounced address is most often a typo, so the repair is one
  click from the list: it names the address, says what will happen in two short
  sentences, and takes the date and a note in your own words. Sending to that
  address starts again and anything already waiting for it goes out.
- **Released addresses stay on the list**, stamped with the day and the note.
  That is deliberate: months later, *why did this customer stop getting email in
  March* still has an answer, and the same address going bad three times shows
  as three rows rather than as one.

### Fixed

- **A release dated today no longer shows as yesterday.** The date a clerk typed
  was being re-read in the utility's own timezone, so in Texas a release entered
  on the 4th appeared on the list as the 3rd.
- **Asking to release without a date** now says *Enter the date you released it*
  instead of a general sentence about delivery.

### Note

- **Nothing fills this list automatically yet.** No email service reports
  bounces back to us in this build, so on a live utility the list stays empty
  until that arrives. Everything on the screen works the day it does.
- **Paper is unaffected.** Blocking an email address never stops a printed bill.

## [2.294.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **The two email services can now actually send.** SendGrid and Postmark were
  listed on the connector page and could not be switched on. Both can now be
  connected with your own key, tested by sending one real message to an address
  you type, and used to send bills.
- **A new *Check the key* action** asks the service whether the key you pasted
  is allowed to send mail, without putting anything in anybody's inbox. A
  read-only key is now refused with a sentence instead of passing and failing
  later on a real bill.
- **The domain records your IT team must publish are now on screen** — the lines
  that make a consumer's mail say it comes from your utility rather than from
  us. The page opens instantly, before anything is checked, and already carries
  the one record we can always give you, so your IT ticket can start on day one.
  For SendGrid, pressing **Check** asks the service which of the others are
  published yet and shows each one as done or still waiting.

### Note

- **Accepted is not delivered.** When an email service takes a message it says
  *accepted*, which means it has the message and not that anybody received it.
  A bill therefore shows as **sent** and stops there, and the delivery figures
  keep saying *not reported* until a later change switches on the messages the
  services send back to us.
- **Postmark cannot yet tell us its domain records.** They are read with a
  different kind of password than the one a connection holds, so that page says
  so plainly and still gives you the one record that is ours to give.


## [2.292.1] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **A utility with no map service no longer sees map fields it can never
  fill.** Creating a property showed *Parcel — No parcel yet*, *Point — No point
  yet* and *Checked against GIS — Not checked yet*, with a *Change these*
  button, on every property — for utilities that have no city map connected at
  all. Those rows are now drawn only where a city is actually connected.
  Creating a property was never blocked and is unchanged.
- A city that is connected but **not answering** keeps the panel, on purpose:
  that is when somebody types a parcel in by hand.

## [2.292.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **The nightly parcel check can now be run by hand, and it offers two buttons
  rather than one.** On a connector's page, the *Nightly parcel check* row now
  carries **Preview** and **Apply**. Preview reads the city's register, works
  out every difference against your properties, and **changes nothing at all**.
  Apply is the one that writes, and it asks first.
- **Every run now records whether it was a preview or an apply, and who started
  it.** It shows in the connector's activity list beside the run.
- **The report says what it looked at, not only what it found.** *0 differences
  found* over a tidy estate and *0 differences found* over a button that did
  nothing read the same, so the report also states how many rows it read from
  the city and how many of yours it examined.

### Fixed

- **The parcel check could not have written a single property.** Several of the
  fields it writes were refused by name further down, and the first attempt
  would have stopped the whole run rather than skipping one property. Nothing
  had ever called it, so nothing had ever found out.

### Note

- **The first runs will change no addresses, and that is on purpose.** Until
  somebody turns an address field on, a run stores the city's parcel id and the
  date it was checked, and leaves every street, city and postcode exactly as
  they are. The report says so in words — *No address field is turned on.* — so
  a clean *0 applied* is not mistaken for a broken button. Turning a field on is
  not yet something the product can do.
- **Nothing here has been tried against a real city.** This build cannot reach
  Ann Arbor's map service at all; everything above was checked against a
  stand-in we wrote from their published field names.

### Added

- **The product can now tell a dead mailbox from a full one.** We are connecting
  two email companies, and each of them telephones us back to say what happened
  to every message we send. Until now we had one word for a bounce, and a bounce
  is two completely different things: an address that does not exist, which we
  must stop sending to, and a mailbox that was full on Tuesday, which we must
  keep trying. The product now has a separate word for each, and three more for
  the rest of what an email company reports — marked as spam, unsubscribed, and
  arrived. **Nothing changes on any screen yet**: no email company is connected,
  so nothing is reporting anything back, and this is the vocabulary those
  connections will need. When one is connected, a clerk will find that *send it
  again* is refused on an address the provider has told us is dead, with a
  sentence saying why, and that the customer's printed copy was never affected.

## [2.291.3] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **When the city's address service could not be reached, the whole address
  panel vanished as the clerk was typing into it — with their text in it — and
  said nothing at all.** It now stays where it is, keeps what was typed, and
  shows the amber note explaining that the property can still be created by
  typing the address; it just will not carry the city's parcel number until
  someone looks it up later. The product also now notices that the city is not
  answering, so it stops dialling a service that is not there instead of trying
  again on every keystroke.
- **The city's second reference number — the one for the address point, not the
  plot — was never stored on any property, and the screen said "No point yet"
  about properties the city had placed precisely.** Picking an address from the
  city now records both of the city's numbers and the city's own status word,
  and the map panel shows the point the city gave. Where a property is being
  recorded with several units at once the point is left for the overnight
  update, because one address point names one unit and guessing which would be
  worse than waiting.
- **The list of matches was cut off at eight and nothing said so, under a line
  reading "N matches from the City's records" — which reads as all of them.**
  When there are more, the list now says *Keep typing to narrow this.* beside
  the count. Nothing is said when nothing was cut.

## [2.291.2] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **Two connector screens disagreed about a connector's address, and one of
  them showed nothing.** Where an API's address comes from a door we publish
  rather than from a box a clerk filled in — Invoice Cloud's partner feed and
  the Aclarian ERP, eight APIs between them — the connector's own page showed
  the address and the set-up page showed a blank. They now show the same thing,
  because the address is worked out once, on the server, and both pages read
  that answer instead of each working it out their own way.

### Changed

- **Where an API's address is decided.** It was decided in seven places that
  did not agree with each other. It is decided in one now. Nothing a clerk sees
  moved: every connector and every API was listed before and after, all 286
  combinations, and every answer is identical. This was done before the
  customer-URL work adds another place, because the last time a new source was
  added the address went blank on every connector.

## [2.291.1] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **The green tick that said a property had been found on the city map, over
  three rows saying it had not.** Every new property drew a green box with a
  tick reading *Found on the city map* above *No parcel yet · No point yet ·
  Not checked yet* — before anybody had looked anything up. A clerk reading a
  tick believes the city's numbers are on that property. The tick now appears
  only when the city has actually answered and a row has been picked. The same
  panel is still drawn before that, headed *On the map*, so the boxes underneath
  can still be filled in by hand.
- **The parcel number, latitude and longitude a clerk typed in by hand were
  thrown away, and the save said it had worked.** Typing them into *Change
  these* and pressing Save gave a property with all three empty and no message
  of any kind. They are kept now, and the property is marked *not checked* until
  someone confirms it against the city — which is what was agreed for the case
  where the city cannot be reached. The city's own status word is still not
  something a person can type, and a property picked from the city still takes
  the city's numbers rather than anything typed over them.

## [2.291.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **Invoice Cloud can now be given a key, so they can read your customers,
  bills and payments — and download a bill.** This was built a fortnight ago
  and nobody could reach it: the key could not be issued at all. There are now
  **two Invoice Cloud rows in your connector list**, and that is deliberate.
  One takes card payments and is still coming later; the other lets Invoice
  Cloud read from you, and it is live today. The second one is named
  *InvoiceCloud (reads from us)* so you can tell them apart at a glance.
- **A bill can now be downloaded through the partner connection.** The address
  existed and no key in the product could call it.

### Note

- Two rows for one company is how we have unblocked this today. What we
  actually want is one connection that holds both halves — the key we give
  them and the secret they give us — and that is a separate change.

## [2.290.2] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **The State column on Connectors now always describes the connector, never
  one of its APIs.** On a connector with exactly one API it was showing that
  API's state instead. Custom SMTP read *Not working* — which was its API's
  word — next to *1 · 0 working* in the APIs column saying the same thing, on a
  connector nobody had ever tested. It now reads *Not tested yet*, which is what
  is true of the connector itself. State means this utility's own relationship
  with that partner; the per-API detail is in the APIs column and on the
  connector's own screen, both unchanged.


## [2.290.1] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **Clearing the allowed-addresses list on a connector now tells you what it
  means.** Emptying a list that had addresses in it opens that connector to
  every address on the internet, and nothing said so. A short red line now
  appears under the box — *This allows any address.* — only when you clear a
  list that was there when you opened the form. A box that was already empty
  says nothing, because you have not changed anything.

## [2.290.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **The city's address register can now be used as the source of your
  addresses.** Where a city publishes its qualified addresses, we read the whole
  list once, match it against the properties you already have, and remember the
  city's own reference for each one — the parcel for a building and the address
  point for a unit.
- **Two new references are kept on every property and unit**: what the city
  calls it, whether the city has confirmed it, and when. If a reference ever
  changes — a parcel split, merged or renumbered — we keep what it used to be
  and the date it changed, because a wrong reference quietly copies the wrong
  property's details for months.
- **Run it as a preview first.** A preview does everything a real run does and
  **writes nothing at all**, so you can see every difference before anything
  changes.
- **Nothing about your addresses changes until you say so.** Every field starts
  on *never touch*. The first runs store references and mark properties as
  confirmed, and change no addresses — the run report says so in those words, so
  it does not look broken.
- **Address search now groups results by building**, with its units underneath,
  and shows at most twenty buildings with *keep typing to narrow this*. The
  order is ours and the screen says so, because the city publishes none.
- **Nothing is ever selected for you**, even when there is exactly one result.

### Changed

- **The city's parcel reference has moved into a column of its own.** It used to
  share the column that holds the id from a utility's previous software. Any
  utility that had migrated its data would have hit a clash on the very first
  run and been told a parcel was already taken when it was not.

### Not in this release, deliberately

- No map and no map tiles.
- A city address you have no property for is ignored — it raises nothing.
- We never report anything back to the city.

## [2.289.1] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **You can now type a real service address into a connector.** The *Service
  address* box used to take a server name only, so the City of Ann Arbor's
  address service — whose web address carries a long path that is the part
  naming the map layer — could not be saved at all, while the bare server name,
  which answers nothing, was accepted. The box now takes the whole address.
  Nineteen connectors have the wider box; the mail server and the two folder
  hosts are unchanged, because those really are a server name and a port.
- **Nineteen connectors came pre-filled with an example address the same form
  would refuse.** Every one of them now ships an example that saves.
- **A rejected box now says what is wrong, under the box.** The set-up screen
  said *Check the highlighted fields* and highlighted nothing, on every
  connector, so a rejected save left you to guess which of up to nine boxes it
  meant.

## [2.289.0] — 2026-09-17

### Added

- **Invoice Cloud can now read your customers, bills and payments in their own
  words.** A partner's field names, date format and envelope come from the key
  they were given, so their own integration document works unchanged and they
  send us nothing extra to ask for it. Everything a shape may do is a rename or
  a re-spelling; **no figure a partner receives is ever recomputed on the way
  out.**
- **A customer record now carries the name in two halves, the account's status
  as a word, and both addresses** — the one where the meter is and the one the
  bill goes to. Where a customer has no separate billing address, the bill goes
  where they take service, and the record says so rather than leaving it blank.
- **`consumer-info`** — a partner can now ask for one account by its number, or
  several at once, instead of walking the whole list. It answers with the same
  customer record the list gives, plus the account's rate plan and what it owes.
- **`bill-download`** — one bill as the printed page, from the same renderer our
  own screens use, so a customer's copy and a partner's copy can never disagree.
- **`format=csv` on bills, payments and customers.** The same rows the JSON
  gives, as a table, one page at a time — never a download-everything. The
  counts move to `X-Total-Records`, `X-Page` and `X-Total-Pages`, and
  `rows=lines` gives one row per bill line with its GL code.
- **`limit` is accepted wherever `page_size` is**, and every partner address now
  works with or without a trailing slash, because a partner's document writes
  them both ways.

### Changed

- **A partner no longer has to tell us which utility they are.** The
  `company_id` they send is accepted, ignored, and recorded on the activity
  record so a manager can still see that a partner is pointed at the wrong
  utility. **Nothing about isolation changed**: which utility a partner can read
  has always come from their key and never from anything they send.

### Known limits

- Invoice Cloud runs in **both** directions — they read from us and we collect
  payments from them — and a connector in this product can only be set up to run
  in one. That has to be decided before the payment collection can be built, and
  the two new partner addresses cannot be switched on for a real customer until
  it is.
- We do not yet send `payment_received` on the customer record, because what it
  should mean has not been settled and it is a money figure.

## [2.288.1] — 2026-09-17

### Changed

- **A connector's own screen now puts everything you can do at the top.** Edit,
  the keys we issue, Disconnect and Regenerate key sit in the page head, where
  every other screen in the product keeps its buttons. They used to be at the
  very bottom, below the whole run history.
- **The connector heading now tells you what the connector IS.** It reads the
  category and the direction — *ERP · They read* — instead of the word
  *Connector*, and the line under the title carries the environment, where the
  connection reaches and who set it up.
- **Four figures across the top of a connector: how many APIs, how many are
  working, when it last ran, and how many keys are in use.** A figure we do not
  have reads as a dash rather than a zero, because a zero is a claim.
- **When a connector is not working, the reason now shows in red under those
  figures** — and it stops showing as soon as the connector is fixed.
- **"Cannot be tested until first use" is said once under the API table**
  instead of on every row.
- **Allowed addresses is now optional on the five ERP connectors.** Leave it
  blank and any address may call. ⚠ With no address listed the key alone is the
  whole door: anyone holding it can call from anywhere. Requested by the Product
  Owner, who was told this before confirming.

### Added

- **Regenerate key, on the connector's own screen.** It retires the old key and
  issues a new one, behind a red confirmation, and shows the new key once. You
  could only do this from the keys screen before.

### Fixed

- **You can change a connector's settings after it is set up.** Opening the
  set-up form on a connector that was already connected showed empty boxes and
  refused to save. It now loads what is really stored and saves the change.
  This is what blocked adding an address to the allowed list.
- **A connector whose settings included a field we have since removed could
  never be saved again.** The leftover value is now cleared instead of
  refusing every future change.

## [2.288.0] — 2026-09-17

### Changed

- **Connectors is a table now, not a wall of cards.** Settings → Connectors used
  to draw one card per connector — twenty-eight boxes you scrolled through. It
  is now one row per connector, all twenty-eight on a single screen, with the
  same search, filters and column chooser every other list in the product has.
  Asked for by the Product Owner: *"we are overriding the deciion and converting
  it form Grid -> Table - table only"*. There is no switch back to cards.
- **Each row carries ten things:** the connector's name, what kind it is, which
  way the information travels, whether it is working, how many APIs it has and
  how many of those are working, which environment it points at, where it points,
  when it last ran, and — only when something is broken — why. You can sort by
  **Last run**, which the cards could never do, and you can hide Environment,
  Where and Why if you do not want them.
- **Four buttons on every row — Connect, View, Edit and Keys — always in the
  same place.** Which ones you can press depends on the connector: *Connect* is
  available only on one you have not set up yet, and the other three become
  available the moment it is connected. A button you cannot press is greyed and
  tells you why when you hover it — *"Not connected yet"*, *"Already connected"*
  or *"Not built yet"*. The buttons never move or disappear, so a row always
  looks the same.
- **Two things a card used to offer have moved.** Turning a connector on or off
  is now done on the connector's own page rather than from the list. *Set up*
  and *Fix it* were two names for the same page and are both called **Edit**.
- **Disconnecting is still only on the connector's own page**, behind the
  confirmation box. It destroys every key on that connector and stops a partner
  working, so it is deliberately not a one-click button in a list.

### Known

- With all ten columns showing, the row of buttons sits off the right-hand edge
  on a 1440-wide laptop until you scroll the table sideways. Hiding Environment,
  Where and Why brings everything back on screen. We have written this down and
  will ask which you would prefer as the default.
- The **Mappings** link that used to sit on three connector cards is not one of
  the four buttons, so that page can currently only be reached by typing its
  address. Written down and raised.

## [2.287.6] — 2026-09-17

### Fixed

- **A utility's connector activity is now only ever that utility's.** Two
  utilities both using the same partner connector could see each other's
  records in four places. Nothing a customer holds was ever exposed, and no
  money moved anywhere it should not have.
- **"Who has been reading" now lists only your own reads.** The screen was
  gathering every read of that connector across every utility on the platform,
  so a manager could see another utility's partner traffic — and the key hint
  beside it. Reported by the Product Owner.
- **Authorising a partner now changes only your own connector.** The grant
  attached itself to the oldest connector with that name, which could belong to
  another utility. A System Admin could have authorised an outside system to
  read another utility's payments and bills.
- **Bills and letters now go out through your own mail server.** The dispatcher
  was picking the oldest mail connection set up on the platform, so one
  utility's post could have left under another utility's sending address.
- **Expiry warnings now cover only your own keys.** The nightly check was
  reading every utility's keys, so admins could have been warned about a key
  they do not hold.
- **With no utility open, all four now do nothing rather than everything.**

## [2.287.5] — 2026-09-16

### Changed

- **A connector card now says how many APIs it has instead of listing them
  all.** The Neptune card was printing one line for every one of its sixteen
  APIs, so it stood twice as tall as the cards beside it and pushed the rest of
  the grid down the screen. It now reads `16 APIs · 0 working` on a single
  line. Ten of our twenty-eight connectors have more than three APIs, so this
  shortens much of the grid, not just one card.
- **Nothing was lost.** Every API is still listed, with what it does and when it
  last ran, on the connector's own page — one press away on `View`. The card is
  the summary; the page is the detail.
- **A card with several APIs now shows its state word too.** Before, only a
  one-API card said `Working` or `Not working`; a card with three said nothing
  at all. Every card says where it stands now.
- **A connector nobody has tested yet says just `2 APIs`,** with no count of
  working ones — because `0 working` would read as a failure when the truth is
  that nobody has tried it yet.
- **The show-and-hide control on the toolbar now calls that line `API count`**
  rather than `Operation lines`, which is what it is.

## [2.287.4] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **The connector's own page now matches the drawing it was designed from.**
  *Keys we issue* and *Disconnect* used to sit ABOVE the run history, so you
  scrolled past *Disconnect* to reach the runs and then found nothing at the
  bottom of the page. They are now one row at the very bottom, under a
  dividing line, with *"Runs are kept exactly as they happened and are never
  edited."* on the right of the same line — exactly as the Integration
  Blueprint draws it. The heading over the run history used to read
  **RECENT ACTIVITY** in small grey capitals; it now reads **Recent
  activity** in the same dark, sentence-case heading as *Keys we issue* and
  *4 APIs on this connector* above it, and the search box, the filter chips,
  the column chooser, the table and the page footer are all inside that
  section's own box instead of floating loose under a heading. The password or
  key panel moved up to where the drawing puts it, above the run history.
  (`DEF-INT-5560`)
- **A connector with nothing run yet no longer offers a button that does
  nothing.** *Test it now* on the empty run history was not wired to anything:
  it was pressable and pressing it did nothing, with a line under it
  explaining why. Both are gone, along with *"Every attempt, newest first."* —
  three sentences on one section where our own rule allows one. What is left
  says *Nothing has run yet*, and where to look for it. (`DEF-INT-5560`)

## [2.287.3] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **The *Who has been reading* panel now tells you which of three things
  happened.** It used to say *"Nobody has collected anything yet."* in all three
  cases — while it was still fetching, when the fetch failed outright, and when
  the partner really had read nothing. On the one screen whose job is to show a
  partner reading things they should not, that is an all-clear over a question
  nobody asked. It now shows loading bars while it is fetching; **"The access
  log did not load — we cannot say whether anybody has read anything"** with a
  **Retry** button when it failed; and **"Nobody has read anything — this
  partner has a key and has not used it"** only when the read came back and
  came back empty. (`DEF-INT-5484`)

### Changed

- **Two small things on the same panel now look the way the Integration
  Blueprint draws them.** *"An access log, not a run history"* was an orange
  badge floated to the right of the heading and is now plain grey text under
  it; the **WATCH** note at the foot was a filled tan box and is now a quote
  with a grey line down its left side. (`CR-110-BRC04`, `ACC-01`)

## [2.287.2] — 2026-09-16

### Changed

- **The address we give an outside finance system no longer names the utility.**
  It was `…/api/brazosbend/partner/v1/bills`; it is now
  `…/api/partner/v1/bills`, and it is the same address for every partner and
  every utility. One base URL to publish, one to document, one to support.
- **Which utility a caller means now comes from their key.** When we hand a
  partner a key we record which utility it belongs to; a request arrives with
  the key, we look it up, and everything after that runs as that utility —
  exactly as if the utility had been in the address. A partner holding two keys
  calls one address twice and gets two utilities' records, and there is nothing
  left on the request for them to change.
- **Nothing about who may call, what they may read, how often or from where has
  changed.** Every check that decides those runs afterwards, inside the utility's
  own walls, exactly as before. A wrong entry in the new lookup would let a
  caller no further than a wrong key does.
- **A caller naming the wrong company is still told so, in five words, and told
  nothing else.** With the utility gone from the address, the company number is
  the last thing on a partner's request that names one — so it is checked, never
  used to choose.
- **No utility can be created named `partner` any more**, because that word is
  now the first segment of the partner surface and a utility of that name would
  be unreachable at its own address.

### Known

- `2.287.1` shipped without a changelog entry of its own. This release does not
  supply one: what that version contained is its author's to describe.

## [2.287.1] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **Setting up a partner who reads from you now works end to end.** The set-up
  form asked for a client id that nothing used, and it was required — so Save
  was refused and *Generate a key* could never be reached. The field is gone
  from all five finance connectors. A partner is identified by the key you give
  them, and by nothing else.
- **You choose which of a connector's APIs a key may call, on the APIs
  themselves.** There was one picker above the list and it took a single
  choice, so a partner who needed four could be granted one. Each API row now
  carries its own on/off switch, and the switches are what the key is issued
  with. The payment kiosk had no choice of any kind and now has the same
  switches as the rest.
- **The direction each API points is right in all four cases.** Every row where
  the other side places the call read *They send*, including the ones where they
  READ from you — so a row said *"Read payments · They send"*. It reads *They
  read* where they read and *They send* where they send.
- **The WHEN column answers when, not who.** It read *A partner*, borrowed from
  the run history's filter. It reads *They call us*.
- **A connector whose key you issue shows the keys you issued.** It showed a
  panel headed *Passwords on this connection* — over those very keys — and
  offered to replace a password that never existed. There is a *Keys we issue*
  panel now: the key, which APIs it may call, when it was issued, and whether it
  is still in use. Connectors you dial keep their password panel and gain no
  keys panel.
- **The ceiling a partner is held to is shown on the set-up form.** The column
  drew a dash on every row of every connector because it read a field no payload
  has ever carried.

## [2.287.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **A finance system now gets every line of a bill, with the accounting code
  each line posts to.** A bill used to leave as one flat record with room for a
  single code, which is right only when a whole bill posts to one account. On our
  own demo utility the first bill has seven lines across two services and five
  different codes, so four of the five had nowhere to go. Each line now carries
  what it is, which service it belongs to, its description, how much was used —
  **with the unit it was measured in** — the amount, and its accounting code.
- **A line with no accounting code is sent empty rather than guessed.** A default
  would post real money to an account nobody chose.
- **When a bill is corrected, both documents go and each says which replaces
  which.** We never change a bill: the first stands, marked *corrected*, and the
  correction is a new bill marked *rebill* that names the one it replaces. The
  receiving system has already posted the first one, and the correction is the
  thing that reverses it.
- **Three balances on a bill answer three different questions** — what the
  customer owed the day the bill went out, what is still owing on that bill
  today, and what the account owes right now across everything. The first is
  copied from the bill itself, so it is the same figure printed on the paper the
  customer holds. A figure we cannot work out is left empty, never sent as zero.
- **A payment now arrives with what kind of payment it was, what it was for, how
  it was paid and where it stands**, each as a code with a plain-English word
  beside it, plus the cash account it lands in and the reference it arrived with.
  The words are ours and are published rather than translated — the receiving
  system maps them at its end, from the list of codes we publish, which grew from
  seven lists to ten in the same release.
- **Both pulls say how many records exist**, so an overnight job can check it got
  everything rather than trusting it reached the end.

### Changed

- **The two older addresses for bills and payments have been retired.** They
  answer *this address has been replaced by …* and name the new one. The word
  `amount` meant the bill's own total on the old shape and means the account's
  balance on the new one, and no finance system could have seen that change.

## [2.286.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **A finance system can now pull the accounting entries behind the bills and
  payments — the general ledger, a month at a time.** Each row names the account
  money moved out of, the account it moved into, the amount, the date the entry
  is booked to, the customer it belongs to and the GL code it is filed under.
- **A bill that charges for four things arrives as four rows, one per account.**
  We hold a bill as one balanced entry — a single amount owed, split across
  electric, water and tax — and the receiving system's ledger takes one account
  pair at a time. Each row carries the amount that actually went to that account,
  so the four add back up to the bill and no account receives money it did not
  earn. A simple entry with one account on each side arrives as a single row.
- **Where an entry cannot be split without guessing, we do not guess.** If money
  moves between several accounts on both sides at once, each line is sent on its
  own with the opposite account left blank, so it is visible that we made no
  choice. No entry in the product does this today.
- **The dates are required and the totals are stated.** A caller has to say which
  period it wants, and is told how many rows exist in it, so its overnight job
  can check it pulled everything rather than trusting it reached the end.
- **Entries with no customer behind them — a bank charge, a period close — are
  sent too, with the customer left blank.** They are the difference between what
  the customer accounts say and what the books say, so leaving them out would
  make the two sides disagree by exactly that amount, silently.
- **A key can be ticked for the ledger alone.** It reads the ledger and is turned
  away from the customers, the bills and the payments with the same sentence a
  wrong key gets.

### Known

- **The rows carry no transaction number yet, and the response says so.** Our own
  rule is that a journal entry is numbered when it is posted, and the code that
  posts bills and payments has never done it — so every entry in the product is
  unnumbered. Rather than invent a number that would later clash with the real
  one, the response leaves the field empty and names the reason once, so a
  receiving system knows it is our gap and not its request.

## [2.285.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **A finance system can now pull the customer list, with the address the meter
  is at.** Each record carries the account number, the name, the email and phone
  we hold for it, the service address and the account's status in that utility's
  own words. The address is the one on the property — the same one the account
  screen shows — and never the address the bill is posted to, which for a
  landlord is a different building.
- **The list comes a thousand at a time and says how many there are in total**,
  so the receiving system can check it pulled everything rather than trusting it
  reached the end. Forty thousand accounts is forty calls.
- **A key can be ticked for the customer list alone.** It reads the customers and
  is turned away from the bills, the payments and the ledger with the same
  sentence a wrong key gets.

### Fixed

- **An account whose property record cannot be found is still sent**, with the
  address left blank rather than the customer left out. A missing customer would
  have made the receiving system's totals disagree with ours for a reason nobody
  could find.

## [2.284.1] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **Settings now calls them Connectors, everywhere a person reads the word.**
  The Settings tab and the heading under it said *Integrations* while the
  set-up screen beside them said *Connectors*; the back link at the top of a
  connector's connection screen said it too. Six sentences moved, in all eleven
  languages, and each language uses its own word for a connector rather than a
  translation of ours.
- **The grid's web address has not changed.** It is still
  `/settings/integrations`, so every link and bookmark anybody has saved keeps
  working. Only the word on screen moved.

## [2.284.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **A finance system can now read the ledger as well as the bills and the
  receipts.** Aclarian's connection screen grows a fourth line — *Read the
  ledger* — and the clerk's *What they may read* list grows a fourth tick. It
  cost one file and no change to any screen.
- **Every line on that screen now shows the address it answers at and the
  number of calls a minute it allows.** All three showed a dash before, because
  the column looked for the vendor's address and on this kind of connector the
  address is OURS.
- **We publish every code we can put on a partner's file, with a plain-English
  meaning for each.** A finance system reading our bills meets words like
  `storm_water`, `backbill` and `corrected` and has to know what each one means
  or it stops. One call now answers all of it: what a bill line is, the eleven
  utility services, the kinds of bill, the states a bill can be in, the ways
  this utility takes payment, its account statuses and its journal types.
  **Nothing in that list is typed out by anybody** — it is read from the
  product, so the day a twelfth service is added or a clerk adds a new way of
  paying, the partner's next pull already has it.
- **Four more addresses are published and answer honestly.** Customers, bills,
  payments and the ledger each say *not built yet* and name the release that
  will serve them — never an empty list, which a finance system would read as
  *this utility issued no bills* and post as such.

### Changed

- **We now check that the utility itself is switched on before serving anyone.**
  A utility whose sign-up stopped half-way used to be served; it is not any
  more. Being turned away still looks identical from outside whichever of the
  seven reasons it is — same words, same number, same time on the clock — and
  which one it was is recorded where a manager can read it.
- **A partner sends us their utility's id on every call and we only ever CHECK
  it.** We never use it to decide whose data to send, because then anyone who
  could send one utility's id could send another's.
- **A page of partner data is a thousand rows, not five hundred.** A month-end
  collection for our largest utility is forty calls instead of eighty.

### Fixed

- **The connection screen showed a speed limit of 100 calls a minute where the
  door actually enforces 60.** No clerk may change that number, so the screen
  was the only place a wrong one could ever be spotted.
- **A partner was shown another vendor's list of what it may call.** The
  published description of our partner API described whichever finance
  connector happened to come first alphabetically, which was harmless while all
  five were identical and stopped being so today.


## [2.283.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **When we turn an outside company away, we now write down why.** There are
  eight ways a partner can be refused at the machine door — called too fast,
  our own counter broken, a key we have never seen, a revoked key, an expired
  key, an address the utility never listed, a switched-off connector, and a key
  that may not call that particular API — and until today all eight said the
  same eleven words and nothing anywhere recorded which one it was. All eight
  are written down on our side now, so the *Who has been reading* screen can
  show **eight causes apart where it showed one**: *key expired · refused ·
  ••••7Q2F*.
- **Two of the eight are now told to the partner as well.** *You have had your
  hundred calls this minute* and *our own counter is broken, try later* come
  back as `RATE_LIMIT_REACHED` and `COUNTER_UNAVAILABLE` on the same `429`.
  Both can only happen to a company that already got in with a working key, so
  naming them tells them nothing they did not know — and the second is the one
  that mattered: a partner refused during an outage of ours used to read *rate
  limit reached* and go looking at the wrong thing.

### Changed

- **The other six stay one answer, deliberately.** Whatever is wrong with a
  key, an outside caller gets the same words, the same code, the same number
  and the same four hundredths of a second. A made-up key told *we have never
  seen that key* learns to keep guessing; a stolen one told *wrong address*
  learns the key is real. The distinction lives where a manager looks and an
  attacker cannot.


## [2.282.1] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **The connector cards now look like every other card in the product.** Each
  one had been drawn by hand rather than built from the shared panel, so it had
  no red line across its top, and its background was the exact same grey as the
  page behind it — a hairline box on grey rather than a card. All 28 now carry
  the 2px red rule the design draws and sit on their own lighter surface.
  Measured on the running product: a top border of 1px in grey became 2px in
  red, and the card's background stopped matching the page's.
- **The connector toolbar has all four of its parts.** It shipped with a search
  box and the category buttons and was missing the other two. **+ Filter** now
  narrows the grid by three things the category buttons cannot say — which way
  the data moves, whether a connector is working, and production or sandbox —
  and the **columns** button hides the per-operation lines, the failure reason
  and the environment line, which is what makes a grid of 28 readable when one
  card is sixteen lines tall and its neighbours are four. Both are the same
  controls every list in the product already uses, moved so a grid of cards can
  reach them rather than copied.
- **The line under the grid says how many are connected.** It read *"28
  services you can connect."* and now reads **"28 connectors · 11 connected."**
  The second number was already being sent by the server and nothing was
  printing it. When a search or a filter narrows the grid it says how many are
  on screen instead of claiming to show everything.
- **"integrations.category.erp" no longer appears on screen.** The five new ERP
  connectors introduced a category nobody had written a word for, so a machine
  word was printed on the filter button and on all five of those cards. It says
  **ERP** now, in all eleven languages, and a new check fails the next time a
  connector arrives with a category that has no word.

## [2.282.0] — 2026-09-16

### Added

- **A partner's speed limit is now the limit, whatever the server is doing.**
