  The ceiling on the APIs an outside company calls was counted separately by
  each of the three worker processes this product runs, so a limit written as
  **100 calls a minute was really 300** — and on a bigger box, more. It is
  counted in one shared place now, so **100 means 100**. Proved with four
  separate processes against one store: 20 admitted against a ceiling of 20,
  not 80. **If that shared place cannot be reached, the calls are refused
  rather than allowed** — a limit that switches itself off when its counter
  breaks is not a limit.
- **The limit is a number in the database, one per connector and per thing that
  connector does.** A bigger utility can be given a bigger allowance without a
  new release, and an outside company allowed six hundred meter readings a
  minute no longer gets six hundred refunds a minute for free. **No clerk can
  change it** — it is shown and never edited, because a ceiling somebody can
  raise for themselves protects nobody.
- **A key we hand an outside company now names exactly which of our APIs it may
  call.** Until today a key given to a finance system to collect payments could
  also read the bills and the whole customer list, because nothing recorded
  which ones it was for. **A key with nothing ticked cannot be issued at all**,
  and leaving the box blank grants nothing rather than everything. The record of
  issuing a key says what it was allowed to do, and replacing a key asks again
  rather than inheriting the old one's reach.

### Fixed

- **The door a payment machine posts through had no speed limit of any kind.**
  Only the two routes a finance system reads from were counted; the one a
  supermarket kiosk sends money events to was not. It is counted now, before the
  message is even read, and a machine that is going too fast is told to come
  back rather than told its key is wrong — which would have taken it out of
  service until a person intervened.

## [2.279.1] — 2026-09-16

### Fixed

- **New connect step 4 no longer grows a second scrollbar into an empty page,
  and its work order is a choice.** On a six-unit build the grid holds fourteen
  rows. The page carried 782px of blank grey under them that scrolled the whole
  application away — the panel ended mid-table with no border and the Back and
  Continue buttons were nowhere. The rows themselves were always reachable; what
  was wrong is that the window scrolled as well as the screen, because a
  visually hidden field label escaped the screen's scroller and made the page
  taller than it is. Every screen in the product that hides a label inside a
  table is fixed by the same change (`DEF-CUS-5480`, `DEF-SHL-5477`).
- **A clerk can now choose the job for one unit.** The WORK ORDER column printed
  the proposed job's name as plain text, so a clerk who wanted a different job on
  one unit had no way to say so. It is a dropdown, still opening on the job that
  fits that service, and it offers every job the build proposed. The INSTALL DATE
  column stopped repeating its own heading on every row, which is what put that
  one cell out of line with the rest (`DEF-CUS-5481`).

## [2.277.0] — 2026-09-15

### Added

- **Fix a bill is the four-step wizard end to end, and all five of its second
  steps are drawn.** Correcting **one bill** shows the answer first in a line a
  clerk can read down a telephone, then every charge line as it was, as it
  becomes and what changed, the tax per authority, whether the customer's
  discount survives, and what they have already paid. **Several months** shows
  one row per month; **a batch** shows which bills move which way, the rows that
  need a human eye, and every bill collapsed behind a search; **a goodwill
  credit** shows the concession, its excluded tax and what deliberately does not
  happen; **a fix to the page alone** shows that nothing moves, drawn as $0.00
  rather than implied.
- **The third step is the blueprint's four panels** — where their money goes,
  what your books do, what finance needs to know, and the loose ends — for one
  bill and for a batch. The tax panel shows one row per authority, before and
  after, from the bills' own tax lines.
- **The last step says what will be written before the button that writes it**:
  how many credit notes and replacement bills, that print is the only way a
  document leaves the building, that approval has bound these exact figures, and
  that nothing has been written yet.
- **A goodwill credit can be given at all.** The first step now asks for the
  figure beside the reason. Until today the screen sent no amount and the server
  refused every one of them, so the goodwill screen had never been reachable.
- **Past billing runs is a table instead of a grey panel.** Every run this year
  with its cycle, period, bill count, value, who ran it and what became of it,
  searchable and filterable, every row opening the run it names. On the demo
  utility: four runs, 80 bills, $27,224.65.
- **A bill run records what became of it** — issued, corrected or abandoned.
  Before this both writers wrote only at creation, so a run that had issued 39
  bills worth $15,453.63 still read *Draft*.
- **Print bills shows what the archive will contain before it is made**: how
  many bills will print, how many are held back and why, the page estimate, and
  a searchable list of the period's bills with each one's verdict on its row.

### Changed

- **A bulk correction now picks its accounts the same way a bulk bill run
  does** (Product Owner ruling). One closed customer no longer stops the whole
  batch: correcting a cycle on the demo utility went from refusing all **79**
  bills to offering **77**, with the closed account's two simply not there.
- **A month too old to charge more for is left out of the correction with its
  reason on screen**, instead of refusing the other six with it (Product Owner
  ruling). The cap itself has not moved: it applies to an increase only, a
  reduction is unaffected at any age, and theft is exempt.
- **A multi-month correction takes an unbroken run of that customer's billing
  periods** (Product Owner ruling, a new rule). A gap is measured against the
  billing period rather than the calendar, so quarterly and annual customers are
  not refused for nothing.

### Fixed

- **The demo utility can be seeded on an empty database**, and the correction
  that sets old runs' status now actually runs. It had reported success while
  seeing no rows at all, because it ran without a tenant and the database hides
  every row from that.
- **No rule id, question id or code name reaches a clerk** on the correction
  screens, the case list or the case status.

### Notes

- **Two things on these screens state an absence rather than guess.** Nothing
  records how long a bill run took, so that tile reads *Not timed*; and the
  posting period is not sent from the screen, because on a utility with a closed
  month the screen would have announced a closure that never happened.
- **Found and filed, not fixed:** on a correction where nothing changed, the
  line trail lists every charge twice; the person who approved a correction is
  stored only as an id, so no screen can name them; opening a case from the list
  leaves the clerk on the first step; and a bill whose connection size is not
  recorded refuses without naming the meter or pointing at the fix.

## [2.276.0] — 2026-09-15

### Added

- **Fix a bill is now the blueprint's four-step wizard, and step 1 is built as
  drawn** (`CR-101-BRC03` §06, screen 26 "What and why", pages 132–134 of the
  Billing blueprint, read as images). A clerk chooses what is being fixed six
  ways (one bill, a run, a cycle, a plan, a service, or a window of dates),
  narrows it, sees the bills that scope resolves to with what each asked, what
  was paid and a state of paid, part paid or unpaid, plus a totals row, then
  ticks one or more of thirteen reasons under three headings; the outcome
  sentence is derived from the strongest class and never chosen. Both doors
  work: Billing › Fix a bill, and Issue a credit from an account. Steps 2 to 4
  hold the previous bodies under a stated absence until the next release. On the
  demo utility's June run, 39 bills resolve with **$11,496.17** asked and
  **$10,802.57** paid.
- **The correction preview shows the discounts on both bills, with the
  programme version each names** (`CR-101-BRC03` §06). A $10.00 senior
  reduction present on the original and on the corrected bill reads as on both
  bills, −10.00 / −10.00 / 0.00, version 1; a goodwill credit says nothing is
  re-priced; a page-only fix says unchanged. The panel sits inside the money
  section, so the preview keeps its nine sections, and it is inside the figures
  approval binds.
- **A new read lists the bills a correction scope resolves to**
  (`GET /corrections/resolve`), fifty a page, with the totals summed in the
  database over the whole scope, and the paid money read through the payments
  seam.

### Fixed

- **Budget Bills reads as plain sentences again** (`DEF-BIL-5339`,
  `DEF-BIL-5340`, under `CR-103-BRC03`). Rule ids, question ids and code names
  no longer reach a clerk on that screen; the four things it does not do are
  stated in the clerk's language in all eleven catalogues, and an empty search
  says it searched only accounts on budget billing and links to Enrol an
  account. A shared test now reads rendered text for any such id, on that tab
  and across the fourteen routed screens the existing sweep covers. The same ids
  are still printed on two other screens, filed as `DEF-BIL-5344`.

### Notes

- **Found on the way and filed, not fixed:** nothing on the bill path stamps
  which discount version a bill used, so the version on the panel is
  reconstructed from the service date and labelled so (`DEF-BIL-5341`); the
  published API schema had fallen 175 endpoints behind the code and was
  regenerated in full (`DEF-GOV-5342`); "several months on one account" is drawn
  and its Continue refused in words because the server's window takes no
  account (`DEF-BIL-5348`); the case status reaches the clerk as a raw code on
  the carried step-2 body (`DEF-BIL-5349`); the gap-list heading's bracketed
  plural (`DEF-BIL-5346`).
- **Ruled by the Product Owner today:** the step-3 tax panel is the
  tax-by-authority figures shown again, from the bills' own tax lines, never a
  tenth section. It is built in the next release.

## [2.275.1] — 2026-09-15

### Fixed

- **The demo utility can be seeded on an empty database again**
  (`DEF-TEN-5343`). Since 7 September (2.219.7) the standing charge for a water
  or electric connection has been priced per connection size, and the single
  amount beside that price list is deliberately left empty. The demo seed read
  that empty amount as a blank to fill in, wrote the old single figure back
  beside the price list, and the product refused it, because a charge code
  states its price one way and not two. The seed then stopped before any tax,
  rate plan, premises, meter or reading existed. Measured on PostgreSQL 16 on
  15 September: the seed died after **2 min 52 s** with the tenant created and
  nothing past the charge step; after the fix a replay took **9 s** and created
  4 rate schedules, 3 rate plans, 6 premises, 10 units, 6 billing cycles,
  6 routes and 11 assets. No bill changes: the price list's smallest size
  already carries the very figure the seed was trying to write.

### Notes

- **Why nothing caught it for eight days.** The only test that runs the seed
  from start to finish is skipped on the everyday test database, which is not
  PostgreSQL, and every browser walkthrough since 4 September copies a database
  seeded before the change instead of seeding a fresh one. A test that runs on
  the everyday database now asserts the seed never sends a single amount beside
  a price list; it was shown failing on the old code before the fix went in.
  The copied walkthrough database still predates this fix and should be rebuilt
  from the tip before the next lane clones it.

## [2.275.0] — 2026-09-15

### Added

- **A clerk can see who is going to be trued up, when, and for how much**
  (§05 entry 25.2, the settle-up forecast). Budget customers pay a flat monthly
  amount and the difference against what they actually used is settled once a
  year, in a month copied onto each account when it was enrolled — so the
  settle-ups do not all land together. The new screen lists every enrolled
  account with the month it settles in, what it has paid on the level, what the
  year has actually cost, the difference, and whether that will be collected or
  credited. Four counts sit above it: how many settle this month, how much is to
  be collected and credited between them, and how many settle later.
- **The forecast has a read of its own** (`GET /budget-billing/settle-up-forecast`).
  It was the one budget screen with nothing behind it at all. The page and the
  ordering are cut in the database, and the two totals are withheld rather than
  added up when a utility's settling accounts carry more than one currency.

### Fixed

- **The Budget Bills tab's "actual to date" column counted one month twice**
  (`DEF-BIL-5327`). For any account that had already been through a settle-up,
  the column added that month's usage a second time and counted it as an extra
  month — on the worked example, **$921.77 over 4 months where $723.02 over 3 is
  true**. The month count moved with it, so the row looked consistent with itself.

### Known gaps

- **Export on the settle-up forecast is shown but cannot run yet**
  (`DEF-BIL-5328`). The button is on the screen, greyed, and says so.
- **Nothing on the forecast posts anything.** The settle-up is written by the
  ordinary bill run, on the customer's own bill, once per bill. The screen is a
  forecast and has no button, deliberately.


## [2.274.1] — 2026-09-15

### Fixed

- **A utility that bills sewer as a percentage of water can be back-billed
  again** (`DEF-BIL-5326`). Sewer priced off the water meter has no meter
  reading of its own, and the catch-up and theft bills were the only places in
  the product that had not been told. On the demo utility, one account and one
  month: the ordinary bill came to **$573.33** including **$28.35** of sewer,
  and the catch-up bill for the same account and month produced nothing at all,
  saying sewer had no reading. It now produces the same **$573.33** with the
  same **$28.35** on it. A real metered service with a real missing reading
  still stops the bill, exactly as before.
- **A theft bill can carry its tamper fee** (`DEF-BIL-5317`). A clerk who picked
  *Tamper* got a bill that restated the stolen water and charged nothing for the
  tampering, and the screen told them it could not be done. It could — the price
  list had been readable since 27 August and three other kinds of bill were
  already reading it. This utility's tamper fee is **$250.00**, so the bill now
  comes to **$823.33** instead of **$573.33**. The fee comes from the utility's
  own price list; a code with no price set on it is still refused rather than
  charged as nothing.

### Notes

- **Neither of these was a rule being wrong.** In both cases one file was
  keeping its own copy of something another file had already decided — which
  list of services are allowed to have no reading, and whether the price list
  could be read at all — and each copy was internally consistent, so every
  automated check passed over both for weeks. The copies are gone: there is now
  one list of those services, read by every kind of bill, and one place that
  turns a charge code into a price.
- **No signed figure moved and none was typed in.** Our own worked example and
  the design drawing both show **$500.00** for the tamper fee; neither was used,
  because a drawn figure is an illustration and every utility sets its own
  price. The **$250.00** is the platform default the Product Owner chose on
  10 August, and changing the price list changes the bill.

## [2.274.0] - 2026-09-15

### Added
- **§05 entry 25.3 `Asks` — a customer's request to pay the same amount every month now
  reaches a clerk's screen.** New `GET /budget-billing/asks` and a new page at
  `/:tenant/billing/budget/asks`, reached from the Budget Bills tab. The ask itself is an
  ORDINARY service request (`BR-CWP-066`) and lives in `customers.service_requests`;
  billing READS it through a seam and writes nothing there. Four figures at the top, one of
  them real — enrolments this month — and three withheld with their reason rather than shown
  as a nought. The rows are withheld too, and the screen routes the clerk to the requests
  queue where the asks actually are. `OQ-BIL-12359` asks where the ask's route, its account
  and the amount the customer was shown are kept; `DEF-CWP-5330`, `DEF-BIL-5331` and
  `DEF-BIL-5332` were filed alongside it.

## [2.273.2] — 2026-09-15

### Fixed

- **A brand-new customer's FIRST bill can be created again** (`DEF-BIL-5318`).
  Since 16 August, every attempt to create a first bill stopped with *"account
  … names no consumer category"*. The account always had a category; the
  billing code was asking the customers module for it by a name that module
  never answered to, so one missing entry in one list made the whole kind
  unusable — on every account, for three weeks. The customers module now hands
  the category over. Measured on the demo utility, account `E11-0006`: the
  first bill now creates — **25 lines, $618.33**, including the **$45.00**
  connection fee that only a first bill carries.

### Notes

- **We took the longer repair on purpose, and the reason is money.** The quick
  fix was to use the category's short name, which was already being handed
  over. The deposit table is filed by the category's identifier, so a lookup by
  short name finds nothing — and *nothing found* already means *this plan asks
  this customer for no deposit*. The bill would have been created successfully
  with the deposit **silently missing**: **$150.00** off a customer's first
  bill on our own worked example, on a document that can never be edited
  afterwards, with every automated check passing. No deposit figure changed and
  no frozen money rule moved.
- **The read that hid it now refuses instead of shrugging.** Billing asked for
  the category with a lookup that answers "nothing" when the field is absent,
  so a fault in our own hand-over read for three weeks as a statement about the
  customer's data. It now says which is which: a missing field names our read,
  a missing category names the account.

## [2.273.1] — 2026-09-15

### Fixed

- **Budget Bills: the override now asks about ONE account** (`DEF-BIL-5262`).
  The amount and the reason sat in two boxes under the table attached to no row,
  so a clerk typed a figure and only the pencil they pressed afterwards decided
  whose bill it changed — and an override fixes what somebody pays for a year.
  The pencil now opens a dialog headed with that account's number and customer,
  showing the computed level beside the box, because the ±30% bound is measured
  against the computed figure and hiding it is how an override gets typed blind.
  The pencil was also greyed on **every** row until those boxes were filled; it
  is live now.
- **Budget Bills: the account number is a link** (`DEF-BIL-5325`). The list drew
  the number as plain text, so there was no way to open the account from it. It
  opens the account, the same way the Bills tab beside it always has.
- **Budget Bills: a re-level month reads as a month** (`DEF-BIL-5324`). The
  `RE-LEVEL` column printed `2027-01`; it prints `Jan 2027`, in the language the
  app is rendering.

### Notes

- **The drawing's `Settle up the year →` button is still not on this screen**,
  because the screen it opens does not exist in the front end yet. A test now
  fails on the day that screen's route is declared and names the door that is
  then owed — a hold with no such test is a promise nobody is keeping.
- **The version literals in `package.json`, `package-lock.json` and
  `pyproject.toml` were NOT moved with this entry.** All three were held
  mid-edit by another lane at the time, showing `2.272.3` over a committed
  `2.273.0`. They are owed `2.273.1`.


## [2.273.0] — 2026-09-15

### Added

- **The one-time bill's step two, *What we bill on*, for all six kinds** (§04
  screens 22.1–22.6, blueprint p101 and p103–p114, read as images per B14 rule
  42). One screen with a fixed lettered spine — **who · where · what · readings ·
  how it prices** — then the kind's own group and, last and always, the block of
  what could still refuse. Interim is the fullest; the other five are that screen
  with groups removed, and a kind that does not need a group **keeps it and greys
  it with the reason on its face** rather than dropping it, because a group that
  vanishes looks like a bug.
- **A WHO group, first, ahead of WHERE** (PO ruling 2026-09-15). It carries the
  account number, the customer and how the account bills. An account with no
  customer linked reads *"Account with no name on file"*, which is the correct
  answer and not an error.
- **Each kind's own last block.** Interim names a missing fire-line size and a
  missing city-limits flag; a first bill names a deposit rule and whether a
  deposit was already paid; a final bill names the accrued interest and the
  transfer target; a back-bill and a penalty name a missing period boundary; a
  fee names an unknown code, a code with no live price and a code with no
  account. They are shown here because they refuse at pricing — better seen now
  than on the last step.

### Notes

- **Nothing on this step is written.** A reading typed here is destined for Meter
  Reads, where every other reading lives; billing may not store one. The route
  that creates a single read does not exist yet — the collection route is
  read-only — so the field collects and keeps the value and posts it nowhere, and
  a test goes red the day that route lands.
- **Money states are kept distinct.** *No deposit rule* produces no line rather
  than `$0.00`, which would read as a deposit that was assessed and waived; a
  deposit that cannot be read refuses rather than assuming none, because assuming
  zero takes the money a second time on a bill that foots perfectly. No amount is
  typed anywhere on this step, for any kind.
### Changed
- **A bill's own page is now seven plain groups, and the document is a download
  rather than a page inside a page** (owed a version — see below). Opening a
  bill used to put a full PDF viewer in the middle of the screen, with its own
  toolbar and page thumbnails, and the facts about the bill underneath it. The
  Product Owner asked for that viewer to go — *"we dont what full view of the
  document - you give a link to download but full view of document is not
  requires"* — so the page now answers the questions a clerk actually asks, in
  the order they ask them: how much, what it is made of, how much water or
  power, when it is due, the bill itself, where it came from, and the record.
  Nothing was lost. The due date, the past-due answer and the fee count moved
  here from the Charges tab, where they sat under a heading about charges; the
  two provenance groups are still there and simply start closed. New on the
  page: the customer's name and service address, both now links, where before
  they were only in the PDF; the date the bill went out; the cycle by its name
  — *Silver Creek — monthly* — instead of its code; what the customer owes
  TODAY beside what the bill said when it was issued, which are different
  numbers and were never both on screen; and how much each service was used
  this period against the account's twelve-month average. The bill itself is
  two buttons — download it, or open it in a new tab — with the number of pages
  in the saved copy stated beside them. And the two buttons at the top of the
  page swapped weight: seeing the bill the customer received is the loud one
  now, and correcting it is the quiet one, which is how the design always had
  it.
- **Budget Bills now shows the level three ways, and the list works like every
  other list in the product** (2.264.0). The tab used to show one *Monthly
  amount* column, every account the server held, and no way to search or page.
  It now shows what the twelve months worked out to, what a member of staff put
  in its place, and what the customer actually pays — three separate columns,
  because the ±30% limit on a hand-set amount is measured against the worked-out
  figure, and hiding it is how somebody types an amount blind. Beside them: what
  the meter has actually said so far, whether the customer is ahead or behind,
  and the month the amount is next due to be rechecked. Above the list are four
  counts — how many are on a level, how many are carrying a shortfall and what
  that comes to, how many are due a recheck, and how many customers have asked
  online. The list now has a search box, filter chips and a pager, so a utility
  with forty thousand accounts sees the same screen as one with three hundred.
  Nothing about enrolling changed: still one account at a time, still with the
  worked-out number shown first, and the three things this screen does not do
  are still written on it.
- **Raising a one-time bill is now three steps, not one long form** (2.263.1).
  *Who and when*, then *What we bill on*, then *Confirm and send* — the same
  numbered rail a clerk already knows from the bulk run, so one bill and a
  thousand bills are not two different products. Nothing was dropped: the
  customer search, the kind, the dates, the periods and the reason code are the
  same fields, the preview runs when you press Continue, and the bill is still
  created by one button at the end. Bills are still made only from the
  customer's plan and your charge codes — there is nowhere on any of the three
  steps to type an amount, and that has not changed.

### Added
- **A bill's header now says who it is for and what it says, before you open a
  tab.** The customer's name, their service address and the account number on
  one line; the amount, its due date, the date the bill was issued, the service
  period and the cycle on the next. The issue date was on no screen in the
  product and it is the date a clerk checks a posted payment against. The bill
  number has a copy button beside it, because it gets read aloud and pasted into
  Fix-a-bill all day.
- **A bill now has a Sent tab.** Which channels it went out on, when each was
  queued, whether any came back, and how this customer hears from us — their
  paperless choice, their email and their postal address. It was the last panel
  of the first tab, under four panels about where the bill came from, and *did
  they get it* is one of the first three questions anybody asks.
- **The Corrections tab now shows what actually happened, one row per event.**
  The bill being issued, the correction being opened and by whom, the approval
  and by whom, the credit note, the replacement bill — each with its date, its
  reason in plain words and what it did to the money. Underneath: **the net
  effect on the customer**, which is the one figure a caller actually asks for
  and which nothing computed before. On the tenant's real correction it reads
  −$0.55. And *Fix this bill* is now on the tab about corrections, where a clerk
  who finds none is exactly the person who wants to start one.

### Changed
- **The charges table is five columns instead of seven.** The accounting code
  and the rate version moved under the description, where the accounting code
  already half lived. Rate version was the widest column on the screen and the
  least-used thing on it, and it wrapped onto two lines on most rows. Nothing is
  lost — a line with no accounting code still says so. The total at the foot is
  bold now; it was not, while the same figure at the top of the screen was.
- **The delivery channels read as words.** *Print* and *Customer portal* instead
  of `pdf_print` and `portal`, and *Queued* instead of `queued` — in all eleven
  languages, where before there were no words at all and the machine code was
  the only thing there had ever been.
- **A credit note's reason reads as words** — *Wrong read* rather than
  `wrong_read` — on the tab that tells a customer why their bill was corrected.
- **The bill header has one status pill instead of two**, and four equal buttons
  instead become one primary, one quiet link and a ... menu. The bill still
  cannot be printed or cancelled from anywhere else; they are one click away
  with their reasons intact.

- **The bill run now tells a clerk whether billing is continuous, before the run
  starts.** Pick a cycle and a start date on step 1 and the screen says one of
  three things: *No gap, no overlap*; *3 days never billed: 1–3 August*; or
  *3 days billed twice: 29–31 July*. A gap is days nobody was charged for. An
  overlap is days charged twice, which a customer sees and which is then undone
  one bill at a time. Neither was visible anywhere in the product before, and
  both are money. It does not block the run — a mid-cycle change can make a gap
  legitimate — it says so, and says so early. On a cycle that has never been
  billed it says nothing at all, because "we have nothing to compare against"
  and "there is no gap" are different facts.
- **The billing cycle field now says which cycle you picked**, by its own routes
  and code, under the control. Billing against the wrong cycle is the most
  expensive mistake available on that screen.

### Changed
- **Step 1 of the bill run reads in a third of the words.** 138 words of help
  became 38, the longest sentence came down from 18 words to 6, and the heading
  from seven words to two. One explanation was removed rather than shortened —
  the sentence saying why an unticked service still counts as a recorded choice.
  It is true, and it is now in the code rather than on a clerk's screen.

### Fixed
- **The bill run offered fifteen kinds of case to filter by and the engine only
  ever produces nine.** Six of them — *Used a lot more than usual*, *No usage
  this month*, *Owes a lot*, *Way past due*, *Late fee due* and *Extra charges
  to add* — could never have a single account behind them, so a clerk could pick
  one, get an empty table, and have no way to tell "none this month" from "this
  can never happen". The six are gone. If the engine ever does raise one, the
  screen now names it rather than quietly leaving those accounts out of every
  list.

## [2.272.3] - 2026-09-15

### Fixed
- **The last step of the one-time bill now shows the money it was already being
  told.** Step 3 was drawing "the charge lines are not shown yet" and "the
  ledger entries are not shown yet" over a server that had started answering
  both an hour earlier. Each half was right when it was written and the pair was
  wrong, which is the hardest kind of mistake to see: nothing in the product
  checks whether a screen saying *not available* is still telling the truth.

  A clerk now reads, before they press anything: every charge line with the
  basis it was worked out on — the days a part-month was prorated over, the
  water with its unit, the tax with its rate — then what the bill charges, then
  the deposit and its interest coming off, then what is still to collect. Below
  that, the entries the bill will write into the books, each with its account
  number and name, and whether this bill posts, posts nothing, or is refused.

  **One number in that list means more than it looks like, and now says so.**
  *Still due · to collect* is not this bill minus the deposit — it is everything
  the customer owes, this bill and their arrears together, minus the deposit.
  That is how the product has always settled a move-out, and on a real move-out
  the difference has been as much as $120.84. The line beside the figure now
  says *"Everything outstanding, less the deposit"*, so nobody reads it as the
  bill alone. The same correction applies where the books refuse to apply a
  deposit: the figure shown is everything outstanding, and it is labelled that
  way rather than as what the bill charges.

  Two things on this screen are still genuinely not built, and still say so with
  no button over them: seeing a copy of the bill before it exists, and the list
  of which routes can carry it out of the building.

## [2.272.2] - 2026-09-15

### Fixed
- **The button that creates a one-time bill can now be dressed as what it is.**
  Creating the bill is the one step here that cannot be undone — it mints the
  bill's number and posts to your books, and the correction afterwards is a
  second bill rather than an undo. The shared footer these screens use offered
  only the ordinary button styling, so an irreversible act and a harmless one
  looked identical. It now carries the stronger treatment the rest of the
  product already uses for this kind of act, and the *Continue* button on the
  first step deliberately does not — nothing is written there, and a product
  that shouts on every screen has no way left to say which step matters.

## [2.272.1] - 2026-09-15

### Fixed
- **The last step of the one-time bill was finished and the wizard was still
  saying it had not opened.** Step 3, *Confirm and send*, landed earlier today
  and nothing pointed the wizard at it, so a clerk who filled in the first two
  steps met "Not open yet" over a working screen. It opens now. A check caught
  this by name within minutes of the screen landing — the door and the room are
  meant to arrive together, and this is the check that says when they have not.
- **The one-time bill's new screens now collapse the way the rest of the product
  does.** Their two-column groups and the step rail were written to widen on a
  big screen instead of to narrow on a small one. Both read identically to a
  person; only one of them matches how every other screen here is built, and
  writing the other kind is how layouts quietly drift apart.

### Changed
- **The sixth kind of one-time bill, *Fee*, can now be chosen.** It was listed
  and greyed out while the server did not yet accept it; the server does now, so
  the new screen offers it. The older *One-time bill* tab deliberately still
  does not — it has nowhere to enter the charge code a fee needs, so offering it
  there would be a dead end.
- **A fee bill asks for days to pay before it lets you go on.** Every other kind
  can be drafted without payment terms and simply cannot be sent until they are
  filled in — that is deliberate and unchanged. A fee bill cannot be drafted at
  all without them, so you are stopped on the screen that holds the field rather
  than three steps later.
- **Days to pay is saved.** What a clerk types for payment terms was being
  dropped on its way to the server; it is now stored on the bill.

## [2.272.0] - 2026-09-15

### Added
- **The last step of the one-time bill now shows the money, the ledger entries
  and how the bill will leave the building — before the button, not after it.**
  Step 3 is called *Confirm and send*, and it answers four questions in the
  order a clerk asks them. What it will bill: every charge line with the basis
  it was worked out on — *14 of 28 days*, *9.4 kgal, tiered*, the tax with its
  rate — then the charges, then the deposit and its interest applied first, then
  what is still to collect. What it does to your books: the journal entries with
  their account numbers and names, and whether this bill posts, posts nothing,
  or is refused because the customer is owed more than the bill charges. The
  specimen, which is the bill itself. And send, which lists every route out and
  says for each one whether it can carry this bill today and why.
  The clerk then chooses to print it now or leave it as a draft, and the button
  says which of the two it is about to do.

  Three things this screen deliberately does not do. **It never shows a zero it
  did not get.** Where something has not been worked out yet — the individual
  charge lines, the ledger entries, the routes out — it says so in a line you
  can open, and shows no number at all; on a screen where somebody is about to
  press a button that writes, *nothing is owed* and *we could not work out what
  is owed* are different answers and only one of them is safe. **It offers no
  amount box**, because a charge on a bill comes from the customer's plan or
  from one of your charge codes and never from typing. And **it does not put a
  button over something that is not built**: the specimen has no control while
  nothing can render one, rather than a button that does nothing when pressed.

  It also stops repeating something that stopped being true three weeks ago. The
  old tab tells a clerk a one-time bill *"can be drafted but not sent yet"*.
  That has been wrong since 23 August, when the question behind it was settled;
  the new screen does not say it, and a test now fails if anyone puts it back.

## [2.271.0] - 2026-09-15

### Added
- **A clerk can charge any one of the utility's own fees to one customer.**
  Until now the only fee the product could raise was the reconnection fee, and
  only automatically, at the moment somebody was cut off — a returned cheque, a
  tamper charge or a meter test had no way in at all. The one-time bill now
  offers *Fee* as a sixth kind: the clerk picks the charge from the utility's
  own list and the amount comes from that list, so a utility whose meter-test
  charge is $35.00 bills $35.00 and one whose charge is $95.00 bills $95.00.
  There is nowhere to type a figure, deliberately. Four things stop a fee and
  none of them quietly charges nothing — a charge that is not on the list, one
  that has been retired, one priced as a percentage (which needs a bill to be a
  percentage of), and one with no accounting code behind it. Each says which one
  it is, before anything is created.
- **The clerk sees the bill before they make it, and what it will do to the
  accounts.** Asking *what would this customer owe* used to answer with the
  account, the window and the services, and no lines and no money. It now
  returns every line with its amount, the tax, the deposit applied first on a
  move-out and what is still due — computed by exactly the same code that will
  produce the bill — plus the entries the bill would post to the ledger. Nothing
  is saved, no bill number is used up and nothing is posted: the clerk can look,
  fix a plan and look again.
- **A move-out whose deposit is worth more than the final bill now says so
  before the button.** A $153.50 deposit against $142.30 of charges would leave
  the books saying the utility is owed minus $11.20, and the only signed way to
  give money back pays out of an account where that customer holds $0.00. The
  posting has always refused this; what is new is that the clerk is told in
  advance rather than after the run has started.

### Fixed
- **Every one-time bill created through the screen drafted with no payment
  terms, so none of them could be sent.** The clerk's *days to pay* was
  collected, stored on the run by the code that makes it, read by the code that
  issues it — and never carried across the eight lines in between, so the due
  date could not be worked out and the bill stopped at issue. `DEF-BIL-5311`.
- **The one-time screen told every clerk that a tamper charge could not be added
  because the utility's charge list could not be read.** The list has been
  readable since 27 August and the new fee screen reads it. The sentence is
  corrected; the charge itself is still refused and is filed as `DEF-BIL-5317`,
  because changing what a theft bill charges is its own change.

## [2.270.0] - 2026-09-15

### Added
- **Raising a single bill is being redrawn as three steps, and the frame for it
  is now on the branch.** The screen you get today from the *One-time bill* tab
  is untouched and still works exactly as it did; this is a second screen beside
  it, reached one level deeper, which is what the Product Owner asked for when
  they said the redrawn screens should be written again rather than refitted.
  The three steps are **Who and when**, **What we bill on**, and **Confirm and
  send** — the same shape a clerk already knows from running the monthly bills,
  so nobody has to learn a second pattern for a single bill.
- **Each step has its own web address, and the answers travel in it.** That
  means a half-finished bill can be bookmarked, opened in a second tab, or
  reloaded without losing the account, the kind and the dates you had already
  chosen. A finished step stays clickable, so changing one date does not mean
  starting again.
- **A step you have not earned yet is not offered.** If you open the address of
  step 2 without having answered step 1, you are put back on the step you can
  actually work on, with your answers kept — never a blank screen, and never a
  button that looks alive and does nothing.

- **Step 1, *Who and when*, is built.** You choose the account and the kind of
  bill side by side, then the four dates and terms: billed from, billed to, the
  bill date, and **days to pay**. Underneath, a table names what each of the six
  kinds will ask you for on the next step — a fee needs no meter reading, a
  catch-up needs one for every period — so nobody reaches step 2 and discovers
  they needed the meter book.
- **The screen finally asks for days to pay.** A bill raised outside a cycle has
  no payment terms of its own, and until now there was nowhere to type them, so
  every one-time bill was created without them. The field is marked as expected;
  leaving it empty still lets you draft the bill, and the bill then cannot be
  sent — which is the rule saying so rather than the product inventing a due
  date and quietly starting a late-fee clock.
- **Under *Billed to*, the screen now tells you how much of a cycle you are
  billing** — for example, "9 days of a 30-day cycle" — worked out from the
  dates you chose rather than typed by anyone.

### Notes
- The second and third steps are mounted but empty for now, and each says so in
  one short line. Two other pieces of work are filling them in. A check goes red
  the moment either arrives, so the screen cannot sit there saying "not open
  yet" over work that is already finished.
- **A sixth kind of bill, *Fee*, is shown in the list and cannot be chosen
  yet** — the server does not accept it. It is shown rather than hidden so
  nobody has to wonder whether the product can do it, and it turns itself on the
  moment the server takes it.
- **Found while building this: what you type in days to pay would not have been
  saved.** The screen sends it and the part of the server that stores it is
  written, but nothing joins the two, so the value was being dropped. It is
  written up as a defect for the team working on that side; nothing about it is
  visible to a user today, because until now no screen asked the question.

## [2.269.0] - 2026-09-14

### Added
- **The bill run is four steps, and a clerk can open it.** The product has
  shipped a six-step bill run since it was first built; the Product Owner's
  blueprint draws **four** — *Scope*, *Check*, *Sign off*, *Send* — and argues
  for them in its own words: four words, each naming an act. The four-step run
  now exists as its own screen, reachable, with all four steps opening on real
  content. **The six-step run is untouched and still live**; nothing a clerk
  uses today has moved, and the switchover is a decision for later rather than
  a side effect of this work.
- **Step one now decides three things once, instead of asking about them one
  account at a time.** What to do when an account has no reading, when a reading
  goes backwards, and when an account has closed — answered for the whole run at
  the start. The clerk can still overrule any single account later, and no
  account is ever recorded as having been decided by nobody. The run also takes
  a **name** and the **bill template** it will print on, so the layout is chosen
  by a person before the run starts rather than resolved from whatever the last
  request happened to carry.
- **Step one says what a scope would cover before anything is created.** Pick a
  cycle and see how many units it covers, how many accounts would be billed, how
  many of those are master accounts, and which services those units take — all
  counts, no money, because pricing a scope on a forty-thousand-account utility
  takes about ninety minutes. Where a narrowing cannot yet be run safely it says
  so plainly instead of offering it.
- **Step two's findings read as seven plain groups.** The chips under each group
  are whatever the run actually raised, so a kind of problem the run did not
  produce does not appear as an empty filter. How long an account has waited is
  measured against **its own cycle** — a fortnightly cycle escalates at fourteen
  days and a quarterly one at ninety-two — rather than a fixed fourteen days for
  everybody, which marked a quarterly utility's whole queue as late before its
  first bill was due.
- **Steps three and four separate signing from sending.** Sign off is a check
  over bills that already exist and creates nothing; sending is the batch that
  issues them, renders the documents and dispatches them. Facts these two screens
  cannot yet answer say so in words — none of them is shown as a zero, because a
  fabricated nought directly above a signature is the most expensive kind of
  wrong on that page.
- **Eleven language catalogues carry the new wording**, so the four-step run is
  not English-only from the day it appears.


## [2.268.2] - 2026-09-14

### Fixed
- **The bill template a clerk picks when they scope a run is now the template
  the bills are actually printed on.** The choice was being stored and then
  ignored: when the bills went out, the system worked out the layout again from
  scratch, so what a clerk picked and what the customer received could be two
  different things and nothing anywhere said so.
- **And a run stops at sign-off if that template can no longer be printed.** A
  template can be retired or taken out of use in the days between scoping a run
  and sending it — that gap is exactly when people tidy their templates. Until
  now the problem was only discovered once the bills had started going out.
  A clerk is now told at sign-off, in a sentence they can act on, and the run
  waits.

## [2.268.1] - 2026-09-14

### Fixed
- **A billing period now opens where the last bill closed it, so no days fall
  between two bills.** A period used to start from whatever the meter's own
  history offered, and where that disagreed with the last bill, the difference
  was charged to nobody. Worked on the Product Owner's own case: May's bill
  closed the meter at 13,500 and the new read is 14,212, so the bill is now
  **712 units where it was 412** — the missing 300 were real consumption that
  no customer was ever charged for and no revenue was ever collected on. The
  bill also prints the same pair it charges; before, a bill could show one
  opening figure and bill from another, which is a document that does not add
  up in a customer's hands. **Two cases are read rather than assumed**: a meter
  that was physically swapped between the two bills, and a meter that rolled
  past its maximum and started again. In both the period opens on the meter's
  own history instead, because carrying the old meter's closing figure across
  either one invents consumption that never happened.
- **A bill run for one service no longer uses up the whole month.** A run was
  remembered by its cycle and its dates alone, so a water-only run for
  September consumed September: the sewer run for the same month was turned
  away as a repeat, nothing was recorded as left out, and those customers were
  never billed by anything. A run now remembers which services it covered, so
  the two runs are different runs. **A run with no narrowing is remembered
  exactly as it was**, so nothing already recorded changes meaning. This is the
  fix the scope screen was waiting for: it could show a narrowed scope and
  refused to run one.

## [2.268.0] - 2026-09-14

### Added
- **A bill run can now be asked what a scope would cover, before anything is
  created — and it says plainly that it cannot yet be narrowed** (`2.268.0`).
  The step-1 screen the Product Owner drew offers to bill a route, an area or a
  named set instead of a whole cycle, and the product has only ever been able to
  bill all of a cycle or none of it. There is now a read that answers, for any
  scope: how many units the cycle covers, how many are in the scope, how many
  accounts would be billed, how many of those are master accounts, and which
  services those units take. **Every figure is a count — no money and no
  forecast** — because working out what a scope is worth means pricing every
  account in it, which on a forty-thousand-account utility takes about an hour
  and a half. ⚠ **And it refuses to call a narrowed run committable, in words a
  clerk can act on.** A run is still remembered only by its cycle and its
  period, so a water-only run for September uses September up: the sewer run for
  the same month is turned away as a repeat, nothing is recorded as left out,
  and nobody is ever billed for it. That is a separate fix on the run-creation
  side; until it lands, the screen may show a scope and may not offer to run
  one.
- **The bill run's Check screen no longer needs the browser to add up the
  utility's own billing run** (`2.268.0`). Every one of the twenty-six counts on
  that screen was worked out in the browser, from the complete list of every
  account in the run — ten thousand accounts on the wire, every time anybody
  refreshed. The counts now come back as counts, and the list can be asked for
  one page at a time. **Nothing is remembered between refreshes**, on the
  Product Owner's own ruling: a clerk who fixes a plan and comes back must see
  the fix.
- **How long a held account has waited is now measured against its own cycle**
  (`2.268.0`). The waiting bands used to be a flat fourteen and sixty days for
  everybody. They are now one and two of the cycle's own periods, so a
  fortnightly cycle escalates at fourteen days and a quarterly one at
  ninety-two — a fixed fourteen would have marked a quarterly utility's entire
  queue as late before its first bill was even due.
- **The runs already made for a cycle now say who made them, what they were
  called, and which one is still open** (`2.268.0`). The name of the person who
  started a run has been recorded since the beginning and no screen has ever
  shown it.

## [2.267.0] - 2026-09-14

### Added
- **A bill run now makes three decisions once instead of hundreds of times, and
  picks its bill template before it checks anything.** The first screen of a run
  gains three standing answers a clerk sets for the whole run — what to do when
  there is no reading (estimate it from history), when a bill looks unusually
  large (hold it for review), and when the days are unusual (pro-rate by days).
  On a 1,284-account run those three answers stand in for up to 1,284 separate
  clicks. **Nothing about the record changes:** each account is still recorded
  one at a time, and the run names the person who set the three and when.
  **None of the three values is typed into the code** — each is a setting the
  utility keeps on its own Settings page, so a utility that would rather hold an
  unread account than estimate it says so once and every run afterwards follows
  it. A run already under way keeps what was in force when it began, so editing
  the setting never changes a run in flight.
- **The run also carries its own name** — *"September, after the water rate
  change"* — so two runs over one period can be told apart by a human, which
  until now they could not.
- **And the bill template is chosen on that first screen** (Product Owner,
  2026-09-14: *"in this step 1 scope - you will ahve to also decide on billing
  template"*). The bill still locks onto the exact version of that template at
  the moment it is issued, so a template edited between the first screen and the
  send cannot change a bill that was already approved. What is new is that a
  broken template is caught at the start: a template that is not this utility's,
  or that has only a draft and nothing published, now stops the run before
  anything is checked, where the same problem used to surface after the clerk
  had signed off.

### Fixed
- **Carried in this version, built earlier on this branch and previously
  unversioned** — recorded here so a tester has a build to look in rather than a
  commit they cannot run. Neither was authored in this version's work.
  - **A bill run now checks where each account's money starts.** Where May's
    issued bill closed a meter at 13,500 and June's read opens at 13,800, those
    300 units were real use on no bill at all. The period now opens at the last
    billed read.
  - **A decision now reaches the money**, through a re-price scoped to the
    accounts a decision actually touched, with the sign-off gate behind it.

## [2.266.0] - 2026-09-14

### Changed
- **A bill run that is interrupted now picks up where it stopped, instead of
  stopping for good** (2.266.0). If the machine working out a run of bills is
  killed part way through — a restart, a crash, a container replaced — the run
  used to sit there saying it was still working, for ever, with nobody working
  on it. It now comes back on its own and carries on from the last account it
  finished, rather than starting the cycle again. On a run of twenty-five
  thousand accounts that is the difference between an afternoon lost and a few
  minutes.
- **When nothing is available to work bills out in the background, a large run
  is now refused in a sentence you can read** (2.266.0). It used to start
  working the whole run out inside the page instead, and the page gave up long
  before the answer came back — so a clerk saw a dead screen and could not tell
  whether any bills had been made. Nothing is drafted and the screen says so.
  Small runs are unaffected: they are still worked out on the spot, exactly as
  before.

## [2.265.0] - 2026-09-14

### Changed
- **Fixing a bill is now four steps instead of one long page** (2.265.0). The
  Product Owner asked for this on 12 September — *"we will ahve to make it
  wizard - 4 steps"* — and it had reached the design document but not the
  product. The Fix a bill tab now walks a clerk through the same four stages the
  design draws: **What and why**, **The correction**, **What it changes**, and
  **Generate and send**. Nothing was taken away. The bill finder, the thirteen
  reasons, the sentence that tells you what the chosen reason will do, the
  approval and the final write are all still there — they have moved onto the
  step they belong to. Two buttons now say what they actually do: the one that
  used to read *Approve these figures* reads **Send for approval**, and the one
  that used to read *Make the correction* reads **Create the documents & post**,
  which is the last button and the only one that writes anything.
  ⚠ Nothing about the money changed. An issued bill is still never edited: the
  correction credits the original in full and issues a replacement, both as new
  records, and the original stays exactly as it was sent. That was watched
  happening in a browser on a real bill before and after this change.

## [2.263.0] - 2026-09-14

### Added
- **A bill's header now says who it is for and what it says, before you open a
  tab.** The customer's name, their service address and the account number on
  one line; the amount, its due date, the date the bill was issued, the service
  period and the cycle on the next. The issue date was on no screen in the
  product and it is the date a clerk checks a posted payment against. The bill
  number has a copy button beside it, because it gets read aloud and pasted into
  Fix-a-bill all day.
- **A bill now has a Sent tab.** Which channels it went out on, when each was
  queued, whether any came back, and how this customer hears from us — their
  paperless choice, their email and their postal address. It was the last panel
  of the first tab, under four panels about where the bill came from, and *did
  they get it* is one of the first three questions anybody asks.
- **The Corrections tab now shows what actually happened, one row per event.**
  The bill being issued, the correction being opened and by whom, the approval
  and by whom, the credit note, the replacement bill — each with its date, its
  reason in plain words and what it did to the money. Underneath: **the net
  effect on the customer**, which is the one figure a caller actually asks for
  and which nothing computed before. On the tenant's real correction it reads
  −$0.55. And *Fix this bill* is now on the tab about corrections, where a clerk
  who finds none is exactly the person who wants to start one.

### Changed
- **The charges table is five columns instead of seven.** The accounting code
  and the rate version moved under the description, where the accounting code
  already half lived. Rate version was the widest column on the screen and the
  least-used thing on it, and it wrapped onto two lines on most rows. Nothing is
  lost — a line with no accounting code still says so. The total at the foot is
  bold now; it was not, while the same figure at the top of the screen was.
- **The delivery channels read as words.** *Print* and *Customer portal* instead
  of `pdf_print` and `portal`, and *Queued* instead of `queued` — in all eleven
  languages, where before there were no words at all and the machine code was
  the only thing there had ever been.
- **A credit note's reason reads as words** — *Wrong read* rather than
  `wrong_read` — on the tab that tells a customer why their bill was corrected.
- **The bill header has one status pill instead of two**, and four equal buttons
  become one primary, one quiet link and a ... menu. The bill still cannot be
  printed or cancelled from anywhere else; they are one click away with their
  reasons intact.

## [2.262.0] - 2026-09-14

### Added
- **Billing has a seventh tab: Print bills.** The Product Owner ruled on
  12 September that print belongs on the Billing tab strip — *"We will need
  Print bills as tab at Billing level"*. The screen already existed and was
  reachable only from a button in the header; it is now the seventh tab, and the
  Print bills screen itself carries the Billing tab strip so a clerk can move
  between all seven from either side instead of using the browser's back button.
  The header button stays: the design keeps both.
- **The reason no bill is marked past due now opens on request instead of
  sitting on the screen.** It was 45 words of explanation above the table on
  every single visit. It is now one line under the table — *"Why no bill is
  marked past due"* — that opens to the same words, with a small ⓘ beside the
  Status column so the mark is where the fact is. Nothing was shortened and
  nothing was deleted.
- **The unresolved count on the Billing header is now a link** to the pending
  queue, so the clerk can go straight to the accounts the last run held back.

### Fixed
- **The three counters on the Billing header worked on one tab out of six.**
  On All bills they read the real figures; one click away on Fix a bill or Past
  billing runs the same header read "Not counted yet" three times — on a utility
  with 92 bills. The header sits above the tab strip and belongs to the whole
  screen, so it now asks for its figures whichever tab is open.
- **And the sentence behind them blamed the wrong thing.** Hovering a
  "Not counted yet" said *"Nothing serves that list yet"* — which told the clerk
  the utility's own system had not counted, when in fact the screen had not
  asked. Reworded in all eleven languages.
- **Column headings for money now sit over the money.** Every amount in the
  product is aligned to the right of its column and every heading above it was
  aligned to the left — on the Billing list the word TOTAL sat 35 pixels away
  from the figures it names. One rule in the shared table fixes 120 columns
  across the product.
- **Three notes in the code claimed the product could not do things it does.**
  One said the Billing tab strip is checked against the old prototype, which no
  check does; another said per-clerk column choices are not saved, which they
  have been for some time.

## [2.261.3] - 2026-09-13

### Added
- **The new account wizard shows a clerk the unit before they commit to it.**
  The Product Owner ruled that there should be no step for choosing a plan,
  because the plan is already on the unit — *"whenever the unit is selected,
  show all the details"*. The plan step is gone and the unit step now carries
  the unit's whole record: its number, label, type, floor, floor area, the
  building it belongs to, which point it is showing on a map, its plan, when
  that plan came into force, whether it is locked, the base charge, whether the
  owner is billed while it is empty, and the services available. Fourteen facts
  that were not on the screen at all. The wizard is five steps, not six.
- **Paperless billing and text reminders can be chosen when an account is
  opened.** Both were already real, writable columns; the screen refused them in
  writing and told the clerk they "were never built". Every account opened
  through this screen since 2026-08-31 elected neither. Print is still the
  floor — neither switches the paper off, and the step says so once.
- **Both creation wizards say which step you are on.** "Step 2 of 5 · Unit"
  under the title, the way the design draws it on every wizard screen, with the
  number read off the step list rather than written into a sentence. Each screen
  now carries its own title instead of one title repeated on all of them.
- **The review step groups what you entered by the step that captured it**, with
  a link back to each: Customer, Service address, Account preferences, and what
  will be on the account when it is created.

### Fixed
- The base charge on the new unit panel showed six decimal places. Money shows
  two.
- The unit type showed a database code (`residential_submetered`) instead of
  "Residential · sub-metered".
- The review step said the create "does not write a deposit". It has written one
  since the deposit step landed.

## [2.261.2] - 2026-09-13

### Added
- **The transfer screen now shows what is actually being sold.** Step 1 asked a
  clerk to hand over an account and told them six things about it: the number,
  the customer, the address, the balance, the deposit and the services. The
  design shows twenty-eight, in two named groups — everything on the account
  (who the seller is, the category, when it opened, whether autopay and
  paperless are on, the bill email, the phone, the preferred language and where
  post goes) and everything travelling with it (the unit and its type, the
  floor, the floor area, the building, the service address, the services, the
  meters and the plan). All twenty-eight are on the screen now, in the drawn
  order. Sixteen of them were already being sent to the browser and nobody had
  asked for them; three more — the floor, the floor area and the building's
  reference — were being fetched and thrown away one layer down.
- **Two panels that say what a sale does NOT do.** *The same customer
  elsewhere* answers the question a clerk on the phone actually asks: this
  seller holds three accounts and exactly one is changing hands. *What this sale
  will not touch* says that issued bills stay in the seller's name for ever,
  payments stay as taken, journal entries stay as posted, and the account
  number, the unit, the meters and the service agreements do not move.
- **The date step now shows what the date applies to.** It asked for a date over
  a blank page. It lists the unit, the building, the services, the meters and
  the plan, read-only, because none of it is chosen on a sale.
- **What the buyer takes on is now stated as a figure with a name.** The money
  step showed three numbers and no answer. It now carries the drawn
  *Taken on by the buyer* line and says which day the figures are as at. It is
  the balance, never a sum of the rows above it — the deposit does not move,
  because the account it sits on does not move.
- **Who gets told that figure.** The clerk sees it here, the record keeps it,
  and whether the buyer is told has never been decided — which the screen now
  says instead of leaving the row out.

### Changed
- **Every step of the transfer says which step you are on.** The line under the
  title read "Step 3 of 5 · one account changes hands, all at once" on all five
  screens — a number and a slogan. It reads "Step 3 of 5 · Date of sale" now,
  and the name comes off the same list that draws the numbered bar, so the two
  cannot disagree. It matters most on the journey nobody walks: a parked draft
  reopens at step 4, and step 4 of a slogan is not an answer.
- **The wizard no longer types out how many steps it has.** It said "Five
  steps"; it counts them. The move-in wizard told every clerk it had five steps
  over a six-step rail for weeks, in eleven languages, for exactly this reason.
- **Three rows on the transfer say plainly that we do not have the figure.** The
  base charge, the billing cycle and how long the account has been running are
  drawn on the design and nothing in the product can answer them for this
  screen. They are shown as rows saying so, rather than quietly left out, so
  nobody mistakes a missing row for a row somebody forgot to wire.

### Fixed
- **A database key could appear where the account number belongs.** If an
  account had no number, the transfer screen printed its internal id instead. It
  shows a dash.

- Two explanations a clerk had to read past on the new-request form: the

## [2.261.0] - 2026-09-13

### Added
- **A clerk can now record that a disconnection notice was served, which is what
  a cut has been waiting on.** Step 3 of the disconnect wizard told them "No
  final notice is recorded as served. Record it first." and gave them nothing
  that could record one. The door that does it has been open on the server since
  28 August and no screen had ever knocked on it, so **no cut could be scheduled
  from that screen on any account.** The step now opens on the letters that have
  gone out — what each one was, the day it went, how it was served and whether
  delivery is known — and under them a block for the channel, the reference, the
  day it was served and the day the receipt was signed for. Nothing here sends a
  notice; it records what a person did outside the product, which is what a
  regulator asks to see.
- **"Posted" can be recorded.** The screen offered four ways a notice could have
  been served where the database accepts five, so a letter that went by ordinary
  post could not be written down at all.

### Changed
- **The change plan and payment plan screens now read the way they were drawn.**
  Each step carries its own question as the page title — "Pick a plan", "When
  does it take effect?", "Confirm the change" — where all three used to say
  "Change plan"; the line under it names the step ("Step 1 of 3 · Plan"); and
  twelve labels are the drawn words rather than longer paraphrases of them, so
  "How often" is "Cadence" again and "Charge instalments to the method on file"
  is "Take by autopay". The change plan's first step shows the current base
  charge, which it was drawn with and did not have.
- **The payment plan's schedule says where the odd cents go**, and counts the
  instalments already paid — two lines the design has always had.

### Fixed
- **Nothing internal reaches a clerk on the change plan screen any more.** The
  cost preview printed five rule and open-question numbers and the name of a
  Python function to anybody changing a plan, and named the lines it left out of
  the total by their database codes. It says the same things in words now; the
  reasons live in the code, where they belong.
- **Two date columns showed 2026-10-01 to a utility that had asked for
  10/01/2026** — the payment plan's schedule and the change plan's confirmation.

## [2.260.0] - 2026-09-13

### Added
- **Close out account now shows whose account it is closing, and what was cut.**
  The screen showed three facts and two boxes; the accounts blueprint draws five
  panels of them and not one existed. It opens with the customer, their number,
  the category, the status, the service address, the unit, the services and the
  day the account opened — then the disconnection case, the reason for the cut,
  the services cut, the cut date and the balance. **Every row of the first panel
  was already served by the account read and nothing asked for it.** Four rows of

  every open service agreement ends, what happens to the disconnection case, and
  the one record of the act. Beside them, the five things it will NOT do — no
  final read, no deposit settled, no decision about the debt, no move-out record,
  and the balance survives it.
- **And the six ways it can refuse, listed whether or not one of them is live.**
  A clerk can see before they start that a customer still living there is a
  move-out and not a close-out.

  `Step 1 of 6 · Find account` under the title of all twelve wizard screens.
  Move-out drew the number without the name; move-in drew no line at all.

### Fixed
- **The move-in wizard told every clerk it had five steps while its rail drew
  six.** The rail grew a deposit step on 12 September by ruling and the sentence
  quoting the count did not move with it — in all eleven languages. It is
  derived from the declared step list now, so the two cannot disagree again.
- **The one date on the close-out that no correction can undo was printed in a
  format the tenant never chose.** `Account closed on` rendered the raw
  `2026-08-18` the server sends, on every tenant, where the rest of the product
  renders each tenant's own setting. It goes through the one date formatter now.
- **The balance at the cut is compared rather than asserted.** The screen says
  *unchanged since the cut* only when it holds both figures, and says nothing
  when it does not.
- **A refusal sentence on the close-out ran to seven words**, past the cap for
  on-screen text. It reads "No. It was read at the cut." Found by a new check
  that reads each sentence off the rendered screen and counts its words.
- **Ninety-four pieces of close-out and wizard copy were English-only.** They are
  written in all eleven languages now, so a clerk working in German, Hindi or
  Korean reads their own language on the screen that ends a customer's account.

## [2.257.2] - 2026-09-13

## [2.249.2] — 2026-09-13 · the front-end image would not build

**Fixed — two lines in a test file stopped the product's front end from being
built at all.** The image is built with the type checker switched on, on
purpose, so that a type error fails the build instead of shipping inside it. A
test added this morning reached for two of Node's own modules the direct way;
the type checker does not carry the definitions for those here, so the build
stopped with *"cannot find module"* and the container never finished. The tests
themselves passed the whole time — they run in a place where those modules
simply exist — so nothing in the ordinary run said a word.

The repository already had a settled way of doing this, used by two
neighbouring tests and documented in one of them. That way is now used here too,
and the real build command was run end to end to prove it: the type check is
clean and the bundle completes.

**The part worth recording is who saw it.** The type checker *did* report both
errors, and three separate pieces of work saw them, traced them to the commit
that introduced them, and correctly reported that they were not theirs. Each
followed the rule for a failure you did not cause. None of them fixed it,
because the work that introduced it had finished — so the first person to meet
it was the Product Owner, on a build that would not complete. A red that breaks
the build is not somebody else's to own later.

## [2.249.1] — 2026-09-13 · the version number stops naming two different builds

**Fixed — a release number could be used twice, and nothing in the product
noticed.** Three times in one afternoon, with eight pieces of work running at
once, two of them published the same version number for different changes — and
once, one change was published under two numbers. The oldest case had been on
the branch since **5 September**: one entry printed twice, eight days, nobody
looking. A version number exists so that somebody reporting a problem can say
which build they are on; when it names two different builds it answers nothing.

**Why it happened, and it was not bad arithmetic.** Every allocation was
correct. A version is *claimed* by editing three files, and in a shared working
space those edits sit there for as long as the work takes — but the tool that
answers *"is this number free?"* deliberately looks only at what has been
published, never at the work in progress beside it. With one person working that
is a rare coincidence. With eight it is the ordinary case, and the tool kept
answering "free" about a number already taken an arm's length away.

**Two changes, and they cover different halves.** The tool now says what the
work in progress already holds, beside its answer, while still refusing to
change the answer itself — it cannot know whether that number is yours or
somebody else's, and the person asking does. And a new merge check refuses a
changelog that publishes one number twice **or one change twice under two
numbers** — deliberately both, because the obvious check catches only the first
shape and the second is what happened next.

The eight-day-old duplicate is removed; the two entries were byte-for-byte
identical, so nothing was lost.

## [2.249.0] — 2026-09-13 · a statement of an account's activity, queued

**Added — the ✉ *Send statement* action can produce a real document.** Pick a
start and an end date on an account and the product builds a statement of what
happened on it over that period: the balance it opened with, every charge and
payment in date order with a running balance, and the balance it closed with.
It then puts that document on the outbound queue, on paper and by email.

**A statement is not a bill, and it says so on the document.** It restates what
is already recorded — nothing on it is a new figure, and nothing about it moves
a penny. The wording carries the line *"It is not a bill, and nothing is due
from this statement"* for the reason the rule gives: without it, customers pay
twice.

**"Send" means QUEUED, and the screen says queued.** Nothing in this product
sends anything to anybody — no email, no text, no post is connected, and none is
in this release. The statement is written onto the queue where the utility can
see it, and the form says so before the clerk presses, along with two other
things it will not do.

**Worked example.** Account `ACC-1042` for July 2026 opens at **45.00**, is
charged **247.87** on the 15th, pays **292.87** on the 25th, and closes at
**0.00**. Those are the ledger's own four figures; the statement copies them and
computes none of them.

**Almost none of this was newly built, and that is the story of the change.** The
wording had been set up and sitting unused. The part that gathers a period's
activity had worked since 11 August. The outbound queue has been there from the
beginning. Three finished pieces, and nothing joined them to each other — so
the action had been refusing for a month over a reason that had stopped being
true four days before it was written down.

**Known and stated rather than hidden.** The paper copy has no wording written
for it yet, so only the emailed copy has words in it today; the result says so
every time rather than letting a clerk assume otherwise. And the ✉ icon on the
account's own row of icons still refuses — the server can produce the statement,
but the one line that opens the form from that icon is in a file another piece
of work is currently in the middle of, and it was not worth disturbing that to
save a day.


## [2.247.0] — 2026-09-13 · a customer's own details can be corrected
### Added
- **A clerk can now fix a customer's name, telephone number and email address. Until today none of those could be changed anywhere in the product.** Open Customers, press the pencil on somebody's row, and correct their name, the number the old system knew them by, their date of birth, their telephone and their email. The account screen never reached these — a person's name is not one of the account's own details.
- **Correcting an email reaches every account that person holds.** A landlord with two accounts has two contact records; one save updates both, so no bill is left going to the old address. The form says so under the field.
- **Correcting a telephone number keeps the customer findable by it.** Type the corrected number into the search box and it finds them; the old number then finds nobody. That is worth saying because the number is stored scrambled with a separate search key beside it, and a version that updated only the number would have looked perfectly correct while quietly making the customer unsearchable.

### Changed
- **Correcting a name does not change a bill already sent.** A bill keeps the name it was issued with. The correction shows on the next one, and the form says so on screen.
- **Some details are refused, each saying which rule owns it.** The customer number is allocated by the utility's own series and is printed on letters already sent. A person cannot be switched to a company, because the proof of identity already on file would be left in a place the checks for the other kind never look at — the record would look corrected and quietly stop recognising them. A company is not asked for a date of birth, and a person is not asked for a Tax ID.
- **A Social Security number never appears in the record of who changed what.** Every correction is kept with who made it and what it was before; an identifier is written there as dots and its last four digits only.

### Known
- **Correcting an email does not change how that customer signs in to the online portal.** Those are two different addresses kept in two different places. Whether the sign-in should follow is with the Product Owner, because both answers can do harm: following it silently can lock somebody out, and never following it can leave a forgotten-password email going nowhere.
- **A mailing address still cannot be changed by a clerk anywhere in the product.** Only the customer can change it, from the portal. That is its own piece of work.
- **The customer edit is reached from the Customers list, not from an account.** There is still no customer detail screen and no link from an account to the person who holds it.

## [2.245.0] — 2026-09-13 · taking back a document you filed by mistake

**Added — a clerk can now take a document off an account.** Until today, a scan
filed against the wrong customer stayed there. There was no way to remove it: no
button, no menu item, nothing. The Documents tab has grown one more column, and
each row now carries a small bin.

**What "remove" means here, and the screen says it before you press.** The
confirmation reads *"This leaves the account permanently. The stored file is
kept."* Both halves are true and both matter. The document stops being part of
that customer's file — it disappears from the list, it stops being counted, and
