the link to open it stops working. **The file itself is not destroyed.** The
rule we work to keeps a filed document for seven years and nothing in this
product can shorten that, so the file stays in storage, locked, where it has
always been. A clerk who thought they had shredded a customer's passport scan
would have been told the opposite of what happened.

**Two kinds you cannot take back, and the bin tells you which and why.** A
contract and anything the product filed itself are locked. Their bins are greyed
out, and hovering one says *"Contract files cannot be removed."* or *"System
files cannot be removed."* — you learn the rule instead of looking for a control
somebody hid. The server refuses those two whatever the screen does.

**And it is not a quiet removal.** Every one writes a line saying who did it and
when, so somebody with the audit trail can always answer *"who took the lease off
this account, and on what day?"*

**What nobody can do, on purpose.** There is no way to put a withdrawn document
back. Nothing was decided about undoing one, so we built the narrower thing: it
is gone from the clerk's view, and getting it back is a job for somebody with the
audit trail rather than a second button. If that turns out to be wrong, it is one
ruling away — the row and the file are both still there.


## [2.246.0] — 2026-09-13 · Adjust works, and it always could
### Added
- **A clerk can take money off what a customer owes, from the account.** Open an account, press Adjust, type an amount, pick a reason from this utility's own list and say which bills it should meet. Worked, on an account owing **$247.30** on one bill: a **$25.00** adjustment for goodwill meets that bill, so the account then reads **$222.30** owing and **$0.00** credit, the books take the $25.00 out of revenue and off receivables, and the day's banking is untouched, because no money arrived.
- **The reason list is now on screen.** A utility's own reasons — billing error, meter error, leak, goodwill, dispute — are offered wherever a credit or an adjustment is recorded. The reason is also what decides which account in the books it lands in, which is why it is a list and not a note.

### Fixed
- **The Adjust button on the account said there was nowhere to post an adjustment. There was.** The way to record one has existed since 2 September; nobody had connected the button to it. It is the fourth control on that screen found refusing for a reason that had stopped being true, and it survived an earlier sweep because its wording blamed a missing address rather than an open question.
- **Record payments offered Credit and Adjustment and could not accept either.** The form let a clerk choose them and never sent the reason the server requires, so both choices came back as an error every time. Every test of that form had only ever used the third option, so nothing went red.

### Changed
- **The Adjustments tab now says where adjustments are and what is missing.** They appear on the Payments tab, marked Adjustment. The tab's own table still cannot be drawn, and it now says why: two of its six columns — the reason, and who approved it — are kept nowhere the product can read back.

### Known
- **An adjustment can only reduce a balance.** To charge a customer more, raise a one-time bill, so they receive a document for it. Whether a clerk should also be able to increase a balance directly is with the Product Owner.
- **The reason a clerk gives is kept only in the activity log, which is cleared on a schedule.** The money is permanent; which reason it was given under is not. That is with the Product Owner too, alongside the same question about who approved it.

## [2.244.0] — 2026-09-13 · putting an account back on the right unit
### Added
- **An account that was opened against the wrong unit can now be put right.** Until today the only way out of that mistake was to close the account and open another one, which threw away its number, its notes, its payments and its whole history to fix a typo. A System Admin or an Executive can now move the account to the correct unit, choosing from three set reasons, with the change taking effect today. The account's service, meters, route, cycle and plan all follow it to the new unit; the readings stay with the old one, where they were taken.
- **Every correction is kept.** Who moved the account, from which unit to which, why, on what day and who approved it — held in its own record so the answer survives, and shown alongside the account.

### Changed
- **A move is still a move.** A customer who has actually moved home still leaves through Move-out and arrives through Move-in. The three reasons this correction offers all describe a record that was typed wrong — opened on the wrong unit, imported onto the wrong unit, moved in to the wrong unit — and none of them says a customer moved.
- **Bills already sent are not touched.** A bill issued against the old unit stays exactly as it was sent; one that was wrong is credited and replaced the usual way.
- **A billing clerk cannot do this alone**, because the rule asks for a supervisor's approval and the product's permissions grid gives approval to System Admins and Executives.
- **Three refusals on the account edit form now say why.** Asking to change the unit, or the customer category, used to come back as "unknown field" — about columns that plainly exist. The unit now says an edit is the wrong door and points at the correction; the category says no rule yet covers changing it.

### Known
- A clerk cannot ASK for a correction and have a supervisor approve it afterwards — there is no such waiting list anywhere in the product. A supervisor has to make the change themselves. Whether a clerk should be able to raise one is with the Product Owner.
- An account's customer category still cannot be changed after the account is opened, and no rule yet says whether it should be.

## [2.243.0] — 2026-09-13 · every file anybody uploads is now checked for viruses first

**Added — a virus scanner now reads every file before this product keeps it.**
Whatever the file is and wherever it came in — an account document, a company
logo, a photograph from a technician, a bank file, a payment file, a meter
file — it is handed to a scanner and only stored if the scanner says it is
clean. If it is not clean, the upload is refused there and then and nothing is
kept: no copy, no holding area, nothing for anybody to release later.

**Why it matters.** We have promised this since 8 August and had not built it.
A utility's staff open what customers send them, and the list of file types we
allow was never protection — a PDF carries a virus perfectly well.

**What somebody sees when a file is refused.** One sentence, in their own
language: *"This file contains malware. Choose another file."* If the scanner
cannot be reached, they see *"The virus scanner is unreachable. Try again
shortly."* and the upload does not go through. That second one is deliberate:
when we cannot check a file, we do not keep it.

**How long it takes.** A 10 MB file was measured at about a third of a second.

### ⚠ WHAT A DEPLOYER MUST DO BEFORE THIS IS REAL — AND UNTIL THEY DO, UPLOADS ARE REFUSED

**1 · There is a new container, and the product does not work without it.**
`docker compose up -d --build` starts it; it is called `clamav`. A deployment
that does not use compose must add the service itself. Budget about 2 GB of
memory for it. Until it is running and reachable, **every upload in the product
is refused** with *"The virus scanner is unreachable"* — that is the rule
working as designed and not a fault.

**2 · The scanner downloads its virus definitions on first start** — roughly
250 MB from `database.clamav.net`, which takes a few minutes. A network that
blocks that address leaves the scanner with no definitions, and uploads stay
refused, because a scanner that has learned nothing recently says *"clean"* to
everything. The definitions are kept in a volume so this is a one-off.

**3 · ⚠ EDITING `06-backend/.env.example` REACHES NO HOST THAT ALREADY HAS A
`.env`.** The new settings are documented there, and a host already running
will not gain them by anyone pulling this release. **It does not need them to
be correct** — the built-in defaults are the compose service name and port, so
a stack brought up with compose works with nothing typed. It needs them only if
the scanner lives somewhere else.

**4 · There is no switch to turn this off**, deliberately. Turning the scan off
takes a change to the code, not a line in a `.env`.

**5 · Watch for one thing after the first week.** If the scanner's definitions
stop updating for three days, uploads start being refused with *"The virus
scanner needs updating."* That is the intended behaviour, and it is a signal
that the scanner container has lost its connection to its update service.

**Rollback.** There is no configuration rollback, because an unrecognised
scanner setting refuses uploads rather than accepting them. To go back, deploy
the previous release; the scanner container can then be stopped and removed,
and the only thing lost is the check itself.

## [2.242.0] — 2026-09-13 · the eight actions that used to take you off the account

**Changed — eight of the buttons on an account now open on top of it instead of
replacing it.** Move-out, Move-in, Close out, Print bill, Issue credit, Change
plan, Disconnect notice and Payment plan used to take you away from the account
you were reading. Each one now opens in a window over that account, with the
balance, the status and the tabs still there behind it. Eleven of the thirteen
buttons on an account now work this way; before today it was three.

**Why it matters.** Somebody who presses *Payment plan* is usually answering a
question about arrears they are reading on that very screen. Replacing the
screen took the arrears away at the moment they were needed.

**Nothing about the eight forms changed.** They are the same screens, with the
same steps, the same questions and the same buttons — they simply appear in a
window now. A half-finished move-out you saved yesterday is still there, still
on the step you left it on, and finishing it works exactly as it did.

**Every one of them still works from where it already worked.** The bill
document, the credit workflow and the disconnect wizard each keep the address
they have always had, so a link somebody saved or pasted into a ticket still
opens the same screen. The web address of each window is a real address too: you
can reload the page, share it, or come back to it later and land in the same
place.

**Close out is now translated.** The button had shown the English word on every
language.

## [2.241.0] — 2026-09-12 · writing to a customer from their account

**Added — a clerk can now write to a customer from the account screen.** There
is a new speech-bubble icon at the left of the row of icons on an account. It
opens a small window with two halves: one to write a message, one to see what has
already gone out to that customer.

**Writing a message.** You choose who it goes to — email, text, post or the
customer portal — type a subject and the message itself, say who it is signed by,
and choose whether it goes now or on a day you pick. A channel the utility holds
no address for is still shown, greyed out, so you can see what is missing instead
of wondering where the option went.

**It says *queue*, not *send*, and that is the truth.** Nothing in this product
posts a letter, sends an email or texts anybody: there is no postal vendor, no
mail provider and no text provider connected, and none is coming in this release.
So the button reads **Queue the message**, and every channel says in its own row
whether it will actually leave — today, on email, text and post, the honest
answer is that it waits. A screen that said "we emailed your customer" would be
wrong on every account.

**Seeing what has already gone out.** The second half lists every message that
was ever queued for that account — when, what, by which route, to what address,
and where it stands. Failed ones come first, because on a collections call that
is the row that matters. It pages like every other list.

**Four kinds of message are offered and refused, each naming who does it
instead.** A payment reminder and a disconnection notice are the collections
ladder's job — the wording there is fixed by the stage the customer is at, and a
letter typed here would not belong to any stage. A copy of a bill is a reprint
from Bills, and proof of a balance is a statement, which the product does not
produce yet. The window says so on the button rather than hiding the choice.

**What is not there, deliberately.** The design also draws a template picker, a
box to attach a statement, and *Save as a draft*. There is one template for a
clerk's own words, nothing produces a statement, and nothing stores a draft — so
all three would have been controls that do nothing, and they are left out rather
than shipped dead.

## [2.240.0] — 2026-09-12 · activating an account asks before it acts

**Changed — starting service on a new account is no longer one irreversible
click.** Open a draft account and press **Activate account**. Until this change
that button did the whole thing the moment you pressed it: no question, no date,
nothing to read back, and no way to undo it. It now opens a form over the
account, so the balance, the status and the tabs stay readable behind it while
you work.

**You can set the day service starts.** That was not possible before — the
account simply began on the day somebody happened to press the button. The form
also shows the plan the account will take from its unit, and says plainly that
the plan belongs to the unit and is not something you pick here.

**It reads back what will happen before it happens** — the status it is leaving,
the day service starts, the plan it will take, and one line saying the account
becomes active. Change the date and the read-back changes with it.

**And it says what it will NOT do**, in three short lines: no opening read is
taken, no deposit is charged, no copy of the plan is kept. Those three are real
gaps in the product today. Saying so before the click is the point; a clerk who
learns it afterwards has already told the customer something untrue.

**Why only this one action.** The account screen has thirteen quick actions and
the design asks for all thirteen to open this way. Eleven of them already open a
complete, working screen of their own — the move-in and move-out wizards, close
out, change plan, the payment plan, the disconnect notice, and the rest.
Rebuilding those as dialogs would mean writing the same forms a second time, so
they were left exactly as they are. Two more — **Adjust** and **Send statement** —
have nothing behind them to save to at all, and both keep saying so.

**Fixed — a form that cannot be saved now says so on its own button** rather than
letting you fill it in and fail at the end.

**Known, and recorded rather than quietly left:** the **Adjust** button on an
account currently does nothing at all when pressed. The Meters tab is not showing
a meter's last reading. Both are written down.

## [2.239.10] — 2026-09-12 · an account can hold a document, and the tab that said it could not

**Added — you can put a file on an account.** Open an account, go to
**Documents**, press **Upload document**, choose the file, say what kind of
thing it is, and it is filed against that account. It appears at the top of the
list straight away, with who filed it, when, and how big it is. You can search
the list by name, narrow it to just the contracts or just the identity papers,
sort it, and page through it.

Until this change that tab showed five column headings and one sentence saying
the product had nowhere to put a document. The rule that says an account should
hold documents was agreed on **8 August** — thirty-five days ago — and nothing
had been built for it.

**Five kinds of document**, and they are the five that were agreed: system,
contract, identity, payment and correspondence. A clerk may file four of them;
the fifth, *system*, is what the product attaches by itself, so it is not on the
list you choose from.

**What is accepted:** PDF, PNG, JPG and CSV, up to **10 MB**. Anything else is
refused with a sentence saying which limit it hit, rather than failing quietly.

**Nothing new was built to store the files.** The product has had a document
store since the end of August — the one that keeps bills and notices for seven
years, checks that the bytes have not changed, and refuses to let a record be
edited or deleted. Account documents go into that, not into a second place of
their own.

**Not in this change, and worth knowing:** a filed document cannot be removed.
There is no delete control, deliberately — contracts and system documents are
locked by agreement, and the files themselves are kept for seven years. And the
signed rule also asks for a virus check before a file is accepted; there is no
virus scanner in this product and nowhere yet to plug one in, which is the same
gap the company-logo upload has had since August. Only allowing four kinds of
file is not a substitute for one.

## [2.239.9] — 2026-09-12 · correcting an asset is a page you can link to, and three lists that only ever showed their first page now turn

**Added — the Edit form left its dialog and became a screen with an address.**
Correcting what was recorded about a meter — its serial, what kind of thing it
is, how its reads are collected, the size of the connection it stands on, its
unit of measure and its multiplier — now happens at
`/{utility}/assets/{asset}/edit`. That address can be sent to a colleague,
bookmarked and reopened, and a half-typed correction survives a refresh. None
of that was possible while it was a pop-up.

**And there are two ways in, where there was one.** The pencil in the asset
register still opens it; so does a new **Edit** button on the asset's own
header. Before this, a clerk reading a wrong multiplier ON the asset had to
leave it, find its row in a paged list, and press a pencil there. Premises and
Unit — the other two detail screens of the same menu — have had that button
since they shipped; the asset was the odd one out.

A retired asset still offers no Edit anywhere, which is the server's rule and
not the screen's: a retired asset is refused before anything is validated.

**Fixed — three panels inside an asset had page controls that did not exist.**
This morning's change taught the server to answer an asset's readings,
assignment history and repair log one page at a time. Only the readings panel
got a footer to turn the pages with, so **Export**, **Assignment history** and
**Work & maintenance** each showed their first fifty rows and no way to reach
the rest — and the maintenance panel never asked for a page at all. All three
now carry the same footer every other list in the product uses, and pressing
*Next* fetches the next page from the server rather than filtering in the
browser. Found by reading the linter's own output on the file, which had been
naming it since the change landed.

**Also fixed — a merge check that had been failing for five days with nobody
owning it.** The Runbooks work list shipped with a screen tag no register
defined, so the check that refuses an invented tag was red from the day it
landed and every lane since saw a failure it had not caused. The tag is real
and the registration was simply missed; it is registered now.

**Recorded, not fixed:** the drawing for the edit screen lists a field the
built form does not have (`Location note`) and omits one it does
(`Manufacturer / model`), while claiming its field list was read from the code.
Nothing was added or removed on the strength of it — the note that a crew
reads to find an asset is editable on the asset's Lifecycle panel, so putting
it on this form as well would be a second way to write one field.

## [2.239.8] — 2026-09-12 · a clerk can take a deposit, and it is the same deposit everywhere

**Added — a `Deposit` step on the move-in, and the new-account wizard's deposit
step now actually collects.** A clerk decides whether the account needs a
deposit, types the amount and says why, sets when it is due, and — if the
customer is paying there and then — records how the money arrived, the
reference, the posting day and the day it cleared. A footer shows what is being
handed over today.

**Worked, on the sample utility:** a move-in that takes **$150.00** by card
with the clearing date filled in writes, in one go, the new account, one
cleared payment marked as a deposit, the credit to the deposit-liability
account in the books, and **$150.00** against the account as money held. Leave
the clearing date empty and the payment is still recorded, the account reads
**$0.00** of deposit, and the screen says so before you commit — because the
money has not arrived yet, and the books say the same thing.

**Changed — the move-in has six steps instead of five.** The old
*Plan & deposit* step is now **Account preferences**, and the deposit has a step
of its own after it.

**Added — paperless billing and text reminders can be switched on at sign-up.**
Both were possible on the server since 31 August and neither screen offered
them. **A printed bill is still sent either way** — these add a channel, they
never replace the post, and the step says so in one line.

**Where the deposit amount comes from.** A clerk types it. A plan can carry a
standard deposit for a customer category, and when it does and the typed figure
is different, the answer says so — it does not overrule the clerk, because
sizing a deposit is a judgement.

**One deposit, not four.** The same step is used by both wizards and the same
single path records the money, so the deposit cannot behave one way at the
counter and another on a move-in.

**Still not done, and each is written down:** a deposit cannot yet be carried
over from a customer's earlier account; a deposit brought in by a data import
still reaches the account without reaching the books; and the new-account
wizard's deposit footer shows no currency symbol, because that screen has no
account to read the currency from yet.

**Rollback:** revert this release's commits. Nothing is migrated, no column is
added and no figure already recorded moves.

## [2.239.7] — 2026-09-12 · a clerk can log a complaint and raise a service, and each has its own page

**Added — two new tabs on the Accounts screen: `Complaints` and `Services`.**
They sit after `Disconnects` and before `Imports`, so the Accounts screen now
has ten tabs instead of eight. Each one lists the jobs of its own kind standing
on an account, with the reference, the account, the address, what it is about,
the priority, when it was logged, when we promised to respond and where it has
got to. Both have their own search and can be narrowed by status and priority.

**Added — a full page for logging each one, rather than a pop-up.** `+ Log a
complaint` opens a four-step page at its own address: who is complaining, what
happened, how fast we answer, then a review of everything entered before it is
saved. `+ Raise a service` is the same four steps in its own words. Because each
is a real address, a half-finished form survives a refresh and a colleague can
be sent the link. Nothing is written until the last step, so closing the tab
part-way leaves no half-made record.

**Why two tabs and not one list.** A container swap answered in three days is
good service; a missed collection answered in three days is not. The two carry
different response times — **8 hours** for a complaint against **72** for a
service — so they are counted and chased separately.

**Fixed — a complaint about a bill had no answer-by time at all.** Picking a
kind such as *Billing Issues* left the response time blank, because only some
kinds carry one of their own and the rest were meant to take their heading's and
did not. A complaint logged at 09:14 now reads **respond by 17:14 the same
day**. Twelve of the kinds a utility is given were affected.

**Fixed — filtering the work-order list by a heading found nothing.** Choosing
*Consumer Complaint* in the job-type filter returned an empty list even on a
utility full of complaints, because every complaint is actually filed under one
of the fifteen kinds beneath that heading. Picking a heading now includes its
kinds; picking one kind still shows only that kind.

**What these two forms do not yet ask for**, because there is nowhere to keep it:
the name and phone of whoever rang if it is not the account holder, the caller's
own words, an attachment, and a reason the complaint was upheld or not. A service
fee cannot be quoted or taken on the form either. Each is recorded as owed.

## [2.239.6] — 2026-09-12 · the owner's account for a building now lists every account at that address

**Added — an `Accounts` tab, right after `Overview`, on the account that owns a
building.** Open the owner's account for 1408 Elm Street and you see one table
of every account at that address: the owner's own and each tenant's, with the
unit, who is in it, the status, the date it opened and the balance — and you can
click straight through to any of them. The owner's own row is marked *This
account*, and its unit column reads **Common areas ×2**, because an owner's
account covers the shared parts rather than one flat.

**Before this there was no way to see a building.** To learn that one flat was in
collections and another on a vacation hold you had to leave the account, open
the accounts list, guess the address and read the rows. The tab has its own
search and a status filter, so *show me the ones needing attention at this
address* is now one click.

**The balances are deliberately not added up, and that is the point.** On the
building above the six rows come to **$810.95** — which is the owner's own
**$69.60** plus **$741.35** owed by three tenants who have nothing to do with
each other or with the owner. A total there would read as *what this owner owes*,
which is not true, so the column has no foot. The tab says the accounts are
related by their address rather than by any link, in a note you open only if you
want it.

**The tab only appears on an owner's account**, because no other account has a
building to show.

## [2.239.5] — 2026-09-12 · opening a meter's readings stopped working this morning, and now it opens one page of them

**Fixed — the Readings tab of a meter, the Assignment history of any asset, and
the Meters tab of an account all broke at 07:13 today and have been broken
since.** A change that made the server send these lists one page at a time went
in without the screens being taught to read the new reply, so instead of a list
they received the wrapper the list arrives in. The readings tab failed
outright; the export tab failed outright; the account's meters tab showed
nothing.

**And now they page properly, which is what the change was for.** A meter with
ten years of readings opens in the same time as one with three. The Readings
panel carries the standard footer you see on every other list in the product —
**1–50 of 1,460**, a rows-per-page choice, and first / previous / next / last.

**Why our own tests passed over a broken screen, because it is the part worth
knowing.** These tests hand the screen its data directly instead of asking the
server for it. That makes them fast and it means they cannot notice when the
server's answer changes shape — the test was handing over a list while the
product was handing over something else. Two of those fixtures now describe
what the product actually returns, and a new test asks through the real
connection with the real recorded reply, so this particular blindness is closed.

## [2.239.4] — 2026-09-12 · a step rail on the last two wizards without one, the import fix offered to the runs that need it, and two controls that stop lying

**Fixed — a clerk on the Decision tab was reading our internal code as the
reason a button was greyed out.** On a service request the *New connection*,
*Move-out* and *Transfer* buttons were disabled carrying
`customers.serviceRequest.verdict.moveOut.noAccountHere` and its two
siblings, as literal text, in the tooltip and beside the control. They read
*"A premise record already exists here."*, *"No live account at this
address."* and *"This applicant holds no live account."* now, in each of the
eleven languages, and *What the address lookup found* reads a sentence instead
of a key on both tabs that draw it. Eight keys the resolver mints were
declared in none of the eleven catalogues, and three screens printed a stored
key straight to the page.

**Fixed — the *Fix the rejected rows* action is on the runs that have rejected
rows.** It was chosen by a run's STATUS, so the two finished imports that had
lost rows — one of 1,251 rows with four rejected, one of 312 with two — were
offered only *Roll back this run*, while a three-row run with nothing rejected
was offered the fix. Roll back is now offered where something loaded and the
fix where something was rejected, and a run where both are true is offered
both. Reopening a finished run is still not switched on; it now says so on the
rows it is actually about.

**Fixed — Change plan and Payment plan show which step you are on.** Both drew
no step rail at all: the three step names existed in the code and nothing
rendered them. They use the same rail, Back/Continue row and confirm button as
the other nine wizards, so the numbers, the names and the *Step 2 of 3* line
come from one place. Clicking a finished step goes back to it.

**Fixed — the Requests list's filter said *All* while showing only the open
ones.** Six of eight requests under a control saying nothing was filtered. The
chip reads *Show: Open* now, which is what the list is showing, and pressing
*All* really does show everything.

## [2.239.3] — 2026-09-12 · the counter forms stop being cramped, a refusal names the field it means, and a drawn link opens where it says

**Fixed — a clerk taking a service request is told which field is missing.**
Pressing *Continue* on step 1 with the name typed said *"This step isn't
finished. Fill in what's marked above, then press Continue again."* over a
screen carrying **one** mark — and that mark on the field they had just filled.
The customer category the step actually refuses on carried no asterisk at all.
It carries one now, and screen readers are told the group is required.

**Fixed — a link to any step of that wizard opens on that step.** Six addresses
are drawn for it and all six landed the clerk on step 1: asking for step 2
painted *Step 1 of 6*, and so did steps 3, 4, 5 and 6. Out of range still
behaves — step 7 opens step 6, nonsense opens step 1 — rather than erroring.
It is now the same behaviour as the other four starting-service wizards.

**Fixed — the fields on these forms are no longer touching.** On the new
account wizard's step 1, the door every counter sign-up goes through, **eight
adjacent pairs of fields sat 0px apart**; the new connect wizard had them at
12px; and the request form's field grid set no gap between its rows at all, so
below 1024px, where it collapses to one column, every field touched the next.
All of them are **20px** now — the figure the Product Owner ratified after
saying *"the components are too much close"*. Measured in a browser at 1280 and
1440 before and after, not read off a stylesheet.

⚠ **That spacing fix reaches every form in the product whose fields sit
directly in a panel, not only these five screens** — which is what the rule
asks for in the Product Owner's own words, *"universally fit for the product"*.
707 tests across 38 files pass unchanged and the five wizards were re-measured
in a browser; no other screen was measured, which is said here rather than
implied.

**Corrected in the record, not built:** the Accounts blueprint's `NO
COMMITMENT` chip is applied exactly backwards on these screens — the new
account wizard carries it while three specifications name that wizard, and the
three screens no specification covers carry nothing — and the request form's
step-1 drawing claims to be a transcription of the built screen and is wrong
four ways, including omitting a control the Product Owner asked for. Both are
written into the screen index so a build lane does not follow them.

## [2.239.2] — 2026-09-12 · the warning band on a meter's page was invisible exactly when it was warning

**Fixed — the attention band at the top of a meter or device page drew nothing
when there was something to worry about.** It is the band that says a
certification is overdue or a test is due, and in that state it was meant to
show a red rule down its left edge, a pale red fill and red text. It showed
none of the three, so an overdue meter looked exactly like a healthy one. It
now draws all three.

**Fixed — the Back button on those pages' edit panels looked like plain text.**
It is a button and now looks like one.

**Fixed — on the printed-bill screen, the box where you paste a bill-run number
had its border in the text colour instead of the usual grey.** Cosmetic, and it
made the box look like an error state.

**Why none of these were caught.** All four were styling names that the product
simply does not have — a colour asked for by a name that isn't one of ours, a
button style deleted months ago, a rounded corner in a design that is square
throughout. A name that does not exist produces no style at all, and every
automatic check we have passes over it: the name is genuinely in the page, so
nothing can tell it apart from a name that works. The check that does catch
this had been failing since this morning and had not been read. It is read now,
and it has been extended to catch the one version of this fault it could not
see before — which is how the printed-bill border was found.

## [2.239.1] — 2026-09-12 · cutting off service could not be completed, and no scheduled charge could be raised

**Fixed — a clerk cutting off service could not finish the job.** The screen
asked, the account was right, and the last step failed with an error nobody
could act on — on every account, not an unlucky one. It had nothing to do with
the account: the part of the system that records *which person* ran a bill was
reading the wrong half of the clerk's sign-in, and trying to store the whole
login record where the books keep a single name. Cutting off service on the
demo utility now records the cut and its **$45.00** reconnection fee on the
first attempt.

**Fixed, and nobody had reported it — the same fault stopped every scheduled
charge.** The routines that add a late fee to an overdue account without a
person clicking anything were blocked by the identical problem on the identical
line, so no routine could ever have raised a fee. It went unreported because no
routine had yet been run against a real account: the test meant to cover it
only checked that the routine was *connected*, not that it worked.

**Why our own tests did not catch either.** Our test data described a clerk
more completely than a real sign-in does. Every test handed the billing code a
piece of information the real product never has, so the step passed in testing
and failed in use. That test data is now checked against what a real sign-in
actually produces, so the gap cannot re-open quietly.

## [2.239.0] — 2026-09-12 · a refusal that expired three weeks ago stops being repeated in ten places

**Fixed — ten places in the product said the owner of a new building cannot be
given an account, and the product has been able to give them one since
25 August.** Nothing a clerk sees changes here; what changes is what the next
person reading the code, the design documents or the published API is told. The
sentence they were told — *"`create_owner_account()` raises
`NotImplementedError`"* — sat in a field note **2,480 lines above the working
implementation, in the same file**, and had spread to a migration, a module
seam, a passing test, the OpenAPI document, three screens' comments and two
Work documents. Its stated reason was that an account must name a unit. It need
not: measured on the running database, `accounts.unit_id` is optional for a
master account, and Brazos Bend already holds one such account — active, naming
no unit — at the address of the very building the note said could not have one.

**The cost had already left the repository.** The Accounts blueprint read those
comments and drew a refusal on two of its pages — *"THE PRODUCT WILL NOT TAG
THIS ACCOUNT YET"* — over a screen that says the opposite; the product's own
step 7 reads *"The owner's account, created at step 9."* A stale comment did not
merely mislead a lane, it reached a design document a person will build from.

**The judgment those comments were supporting is unchanged.** A build is still
shown at its address rather than on an account, because a building may genuinely
have no owner account yet — nobody named an owner, or the build has no common
area and the rule refuses one by design. What changed is the proof: the column is
optional, not unwritten. Measured with the tenant in context: **8 Brazos Bend
connections, 0 with an owner account.**

**Found while proving it, and filed rather than fixed:** the new-connect wizard
collects the owner's name, kind, email and phone, and the account door it hands
them to reads none of those keys — so a build committed today is refused for
want of an identifier the wizard never asks for. Four payload shapes were driven
through the real function against PostgreSQL to establish that.

## [2.238.1] — 2026-09-12 · a property can be sold, a cut has a lawful date, and two screens stop lying about what they know

**Fixed — a property can now be sold.** The transfer wizard asked which unit the
customer was moving to and on what two dates; the product has asked *who is
buying it* since the Product Owner ruled on 1 September that a transfer is a
**sale** — the account, its number, its unit, its meters, its plan and its whole
ledger stay exactly where they are, and the customer changes. The screen was
never rewritten, so pressing *Complete transfer* was refused for a buyer nobody
had been asked for. **No property could be sold at all.** The five steps are now
*Find the account · The buyer · Date of sale · What they take on · Review &
confirm*, the refusal arrives on the step where the clerk is typing rather than
after they have set a date, and the commit says *Complete the sale ✓*.

**Fixed — the earliest lawful cut date is worked out.** A disconnection now shows
it: the final notice's served date plus the utility's own notice period, counted
in **business days** and skipped past that utility's own public holidays. A date
earlier than that gets a message and is still allowed — the clerk is informed,
not prevented.

**Fixed — the protections step on a disconnection was blind for fifteen days.**
The step that says whether there is a medical certificate on the household about
to be cut showed a dash against every check, under a sentence saying no endpoint
could answer them. The answers had been available since 28 August. It reads them
now, and an unanswerable check is never shown as a pass.

**Fixed — the close-out screen and the move-out money step reached no server.**
A missing character in two addresses sent both to a URL with the utility's name
welded onto the path, so both failed on every tenant and both dressed the
failure as something the product had chosen not to say. The close-out screen told
a clerk the balance *could not be read* while the server was answering with the
reason the account was not eligible, in plain English. Closing an account was
refused for a second reason behind the first, and both are fixed.

**Changed — the close-out screen speaks in its own words.** Repairing it revealed
that it was printing the server's internal notes to a clerk — rule numbers,
column names and four paragraphs of reasoning. It now states the same facts in
short sentences, and the outstanding balance carries its currency.

**Fixed — an amount with no currency.** The close-out balance read `8240.00`; it
reads `$8,240.00`.

## [2.238.0] — 2026-09-12 · every list on the Accounts screen opens on what was just created

**Changed — all eight lists on the Accounts screen now open with the newest
record at the top, and six of them gained a way to sort.** You asked for this on
the 10th: *"Whenever any account is created or any entry is created in the
system … It should always sort it by the creation order. The new newly created
entries should always show on the top."* And on the 12th, when we came back and
said that six of the eight had no sorting at all, you took the larger of the
three options: *"All eight open newest-first and the six gain a sort control."*

**What it looked like before, on the demo utility.** The newest account on the
books — Ridge Property LLC, created that morning — came back **58th out of 73**,
which is the second page. You had to know its name to find it. It is now the
first row on the first page.

**What a clerk can do now that they could not.** On Requests, New connects,
Move-ins, Move-outs, Transfers and Disconnects there was no way to change the
order of the list at all. Each of those six now has clickable column headings:
on Requests you can put the oldest request back at the top with one click, on
New connects the next one due, on Move-ins and Move-outs the next date, and on
Disconnects the account numbers in order.

**Four sentences under the tables have been rewritten, in all eleven
languages.** They used to promise an order that is no longer the one we use —
Requests said *"Sorted by age, oldest first"* — so leaving them would have been
the product telling a clerk something untrue. Each now says, in two short
sentences, what the list opens on and which heading to press to get the old
order back.

**Fixed — the Imports tab stopped showing the whole history after 200 runs.**
It asked the server for everything and the server quietly sent only the newest
200, with no count attached — so at the 201st import the list simply stopped and
looked complete. The limit is gone, the count is on the response, and the three
Imports tabs now show up to a thousand runs each instead of 200.

**Faster, on the screen that is opened most.** Drawing one page of accounts used
to build every account the utility has: asking for 1 row cost exactly as much as
asking for 50. It now builds only the fifty rows on screen. At the 73 accounts
on the demo utility nobody would notice; at the 40,000 a utility our size can
have, it is the difference between building 40,000 rows and building 50.

**Still owed, and written down rather than left.** If a clerk picks a column on
one of the six new lists and then reloads the page, the list goes back to newest
first. Only the main Accounts list remembers. Fixing that means changing how all
eight tabs share one web address, which is a decision on its own, so it is filed
(`DEF-CUS-5091`) rather than half-done here.

## [2.237.11] — 2026-09-12 · the account screen: money to the cent, a real sub-type, and four sentences that were no longer true

**Fixed — the Record payment box showed six decimals and filled itself in with
six.** On an account owing $2,410.00 the modal read `2410.000000 USD` and the
amount box opened holding `2410.000000`, one click away from the `$2,410.00` the
same figure shows in the list and in the header. A clerk who accepted that
default sent six decimals to the payment. It now reads **`$2,410.00`** and fills
the box with **`2410.00`**. Money is shown to the cent everywhere, which is the
standing rule.

**What was NOT wrong, said plainly because it is the tempting place to look:**
nothing is stored differently and nothing about the figure itself has changed.
The account's balance is held to six decimal places and always has been, and
that is allowed. Only what a person was shown was wrong.

**Fixed — the account's sub-type showed the word the database uses.** The panel
read `small_commercial` beside a Category that correctly read `Commercial`. It
now reads **`Small commercial`** — and it reads whatever the utility has chosen
to call it, because the sub-type list is the utility's own to edit. Where a
utility has added a sub-type of its own and given it no name yet, the screen
still shows the code rather than making a name up.

**Fixed — Close out was available on the one kind of account it is not for, and
switched off on the one it is.** Closing an account out is what happens after the
service has been cut. The button was live on a brand-new account awaiting
activation, where there is nothing to close, and refused everywhere else. It is
now offered only on an account whose service has been cut, and it explains itself
on every other kind.

**Fixed — four sentences told a clerk there was no customer portal.** There is
one: customers sign in to it. The note form said ticking *Visible to the
customer* did nothing "because there is no customer portal in this version", and
the audit trail said no entry could ever come from a customer — which is not true
either, since signing up for the portal writes one. Ticking the box still does
not show the note to anybody, and it now says only that, in all eleven languages.

**Also removed — three sentences that were written for screens that have since
been built**, and which no screen showed any more. One of them explained why the
usage chart was empty; the chart has been drawing real readings since last week.

## [2.237.10] — 2026-09-12 · booking in a meter: the dial reading, the share, and a way out

**Changed — the meter's opening reading is asked for on step 2, beside the
multiplier and the register digits, instead of on step 3.** It is the number on
the dial the day the meter goes in, and it belongs with the other facts about how
the meter counts — which is where the agreed drawing puts it, and where the
warning about a ×10 meter already lives. **It has MOVED, not been copied**: step
3 no longer asks for it.

**It is asked for on a METER and never on a device.** A backflow preventer has no
register and no multiplier, so there is nothing for the reading to mean and
nothing for the warning to describe.

**Added — a sub-meter is asked how its usage is shared, when it is created.**
Until today a sub-meter could be created that could never be allocated: the share
and the method existed in the database and on no screen in the product. The
method is chosen from the four agreed words — **Share of the building's total ·
By floor area · Split equally · Owner absorbs** — in all eleven languages.

**Added — both asset wizards now offer a way out that is not the back button.**
*Save & exit* leaves quietly and writes nothing of its own. The shared wizard
frame has supported this since it was built; neither asset wizard ever asked for
it, so a clerk part-way through adding or retiring an asset had no way to stop
without losing the lot.

**Fixed — a reading given without a date is refused where it is typed**, with the
sentence *"Your reading needs a date. Set one, or an install date."* rather than
at the end of the wizard.

⚠ **This release was assembled after the container restarted and stopped the lane
that built it.** Its work was complete and proved — the frontend typechecks, its
own suites pass and six backend cases pass — but it had not been saved. Three
things it was holding were repaired before saving, each of which would have
destroyed work that was already safe: the decision log would have removed another
lane's whole entry, all eleven catalogues would have removed the four agreed
allocation words, and two lanes had independently claimed the same two rule
numbers. All three are recorded in the decision log for 2026-09-12.

## [2.237.9] — 2026-09-12 · one asset: six panels, a pencil on each, and what it has cost us

**Changed — the asset Overview is re-cut into the six panels the agreed drawing
shows.** It used to open with one list of twenty-three rows that mixed what the
thing is, where it sits, how it measures, what it cost and when it was fitted.
It now answers one question per panel — **Assignment · What's due · Measurement ·
Device · Cost & value · Lifecycle** — in that reading order. **Not one row is
renamed and nothing is removed.** Two facts stop being printed twice: the asset
number is the title, and the status is the pill beside it.

**Added — a pencil on five of the six panels.** Press it and a small form opens
holding just that panel's fields, over the screen you were reading. Until today
the only way to correct anything about an asset was to leave it, find its row in
the register, and press the pencil there — on a form holding every fact about
the asset at once.

**Added — a warning line under the title when something needs doing, and
nothing at all when it does not.** A backflow preventer whose annual test has
lapsed now says so where you look first, with the *Raise work order* button
beside it. A warranty that has run out says so more quietly and offers no
button, because there is nothing to do about it. **A healthy asset shows no line
at all**, which is what makes it worth reading when it appears.

**Added — what this asset has cost us to keep running, as one figure with both
halves named underneath.** The product has been working that out twice, in two
places that did not know about each other: repairs a clerk types on the asset,
and labour and parts on work orders. The asset only ever showed the first, so
the better a utility used work orders the more wrong its own number got. One
figure now, **Repairs $84.01 · Work orders $138.42 → $222.43**, and the two
lines add up to the total exactly as shown.

**Added — how many jobs are open on this asset**, on the What's due panel.

**Added — the purchase date and the utility's own legacy reference can be
corrected.** Both were being stored and neither could be fixed from any screen:
the purchase date decides the age and the present value, both of which were on
display while the date itself was not, and the legacy reference could only ever
arrive through a file import.

**Added — a sub-meter's share of its building can be set for the first time**,
with the four choices written in words a clerk can read: *Share of the
building's total · By floor area · Split equally · Owner absorbs*. The three
rows were being stored and shown and there was no screen anywhere in the product
that could write them.

**Added — changing what a reading MEANS now asks before it saves.** The
multiplier, the unit and the connection size change what future bills are
computed from. Changing one now shows a second step naming exactly what changes
and what does not, before anything is written. Bills already sent are never
restated, which is the rule the product already followed and never said out loud.

**Added — the account on an asset is a link.** The chain read Premises → Unit →
dead end, and the dead end was the money.

## [2.237.8] — 2026-09-12 · an asset's history arrives a page at a time

**Changed — the Reads, Assignment history and Maintenance lists on an asset now
come back one page at a time instead of all at once.** Until now, opening a
meter asked the server for every read it had ever taken, every seat it had ever
occupied and every repair ever logged against it, in one reply. That was fine
while the biggest history anywhere was 26 rows. On a meter with two years of
readings the reply was **40,853 bytes and growing by one row at a time**; it is
now **14,199 bytes a page and stops growing**. The same three lists on the
registry's Inventory, Lifecycle and Map tabs are bounded too — the map used to
send every marker in the utility in a single reply and now sends fifty, together
with the total, so a screen can say how many more there are.

**Fixed — the Assignment history was asking the database one question per row.**
Nobody had ever seen it, because every asset in every sample utility has exactly
one seat in its history, so the loop had never run twice. Given a real history it
cost **64 questions to show 61 rows**; it now costs **4**, however long the
history is. The Inventory tab was doing the same thing once per spare meter.

**Fixed — the Inventory tab's three headline figures are now counted by the
database.** *Uninstalled*, *value at cost* and *aged over 12 months* were worked
out by walking every spare in the utility. The figures themselves are unchanged —
checked against the old ones item by item, including the money — and none of them
moves when you turn the page, which is what a headline figure is for.

**Note for anyone building against the API:** the three lists inside an asset now
reply in the same envelope every other list in the product uses. Details in
`04-docs/01-spec/11-api-contracts.md`, Addendum r7.

## [2.237.7] — 2026-09-12 · every page title is the size it was always supposed to be

**Changed — the big heading at the top of every screen is now 32px, not 40px.**
40px was reserved for a full-page wizard title; 32px was the size our own style
sheet called *"the app default, every screen head"*. The heading was drawing at
40 on **136 of the 137 screens**, so the size we called the default was the one
almost nothing used. Product Owner ruling: *"use 32 pixels — for every ordinary
screen"*. Nothing moves, nothing is removed, no text changes — the title is
simply less loud and the content below it gains a little room.

**Fixed — a screen no longer has to choose between the right title size and a
proper page title.** Until now the only way to get 32px was to demote the
heading, which leaves the page without the single top-level title that screen
readers and search rely on. That is why exactly one screen in 137 ever did it.
The size is now set on the heading itself, so the heading level is free to be
whatever the page's structure actually needs.

**Fixed — eighteen checks across twelve test files that were looking for the
wrong thing.** They matched the heading's raw markup rather than what they were
written to assert, so a cosmetic change made them stop finding an element that
was right there. One of them — a check that a particular page shows *no*
top-level title — had been left asking for text that can no longer appear, so it
would have reported success forever regardless of what that page did. All
eighteen now check the thing they exist to check.

## [2.237.6] — 2026-09-12 · one asset: the job you could not raise, the jobs you could not see, and readings you had to scroll past

**Fixed — a clerk standing on a meter could not raise a job on it.** The form
exists, its address is live, and four places in the product open it — a new
asset, a reassignment, a retirement and the lifecycle list. The asset's own
screen was not one of them, so anyone looking at a meter that needed work had
to leave it, find Work, and start again from the other end. *Raise work order*
now sits first in the header on every tab, and again under the new **Open
work** panel on the Maintenance tab.

**Fixed — a retired meter now says why it cannot have a job raised on it.**
The control is shown, greyed out, reading *This asset is retired.* rather than
quietly not being there. A control that disappears teaches a person the product
cannot do the thing; a greyed one with a reason teaches them why not.

**Fixed — the jobs raised against an asset were fetched and thrown away.** The
screen already asked the server for them on every Maintenance tab open and then
drew none of them. The new Open work panel lists what is outstanding — the work
order number, the type, the state, when it was raised, when it is expected and
who has it — and the number opens the job in Work.

**Fixed — the Reads tab printed `tou_on` and `tou_mid` at people.** The words
*On-peak*, *Mid-peak*, *Off-peak*, *Total register*, *Demand*, *Export* and
*Generation* already shipped in every language the product speaks; this screen
was not using them. A meter with more than one register also gains a **Channel**
column, so four readings on the same date stop looking like four identical rows.

**Fixed — the readings started a screen and a half down the page.** A meter with
four registers drew four full charts above the read log. It draws one, and the
rest are single lines that still show each register's name, its unit and its
average — nothing is hidden, and the readings are where a person opening the tab
is looking.

## [2.237.5] — 2026-09-12 · the Assets registry: real figures, a faster list, and a downloadable download

**Fixed — the four numbers at the top of the Meters tab were dashes.** *Meters
in service*, *Needs repair*, *In inventory* and *Past certification age* were
counted in the browser over the rows on the page, so they could only show a
figure when the whole list fitted on one screen. On a utility with 110 meters
that is never: the tab opened with four dashes under four headings, page two
showed four dashes, and a filter alone was enough to blank them even when the
filtered result was six rows. The counts are now worked out by the server over
the whole tab, so the cards read *Meters in service 104 · 7 masters · 9 subs ·
1% AMI* on first load, on page two, and with a filter applied. The same fix
covers the two counted cards on the Behind the meter tab.

**Fixed — pressing Download saved a file called `file.json` that would not
open.** The file was written by one background worker and looked for by a
different one, on two disks that were never connected, so every export failed
the same way every time. They now share one disk. Two other downloads nobody
had reported yet — the bill print set and the audit-log export — were broken
in exactly the same way and are fixed by the same change.

**Faster — filtering the asset list no longer asks the database one question
per asset.** Asking for the assigned meters on a 110-meter utility used to send
**111** separate questions to the database; asking for the water meters sent
**209**; both together sent **319** to bring back 53 rows. All of those are now
**2**, and the number no longer grows with the size of the utility. The map
behaved the same way — **241** questions to draw its pins — and is now **8**.

**Changed — the Lifecycle tab is three tabs instead of three stacked tables.**
*Certifications & tests due*, *Warranty & supplier* and *Age & replacement
forecast* are now separate, each with the search box, filters, sortable
headings, column chooser and page controls every other list in the product has
and none of these three had. The tests due open with the oldest lapse first.
Each tab has its own address, so a link opens the one you meant.

**Changed — the Asset value box has been removed from the Lifecycle tab**, as
asked. Its two figures (buy value and present value) are worked out nowhere
else in the product, so anyone who used them no longer has them.

**Fixed — two buttons on the Lifecycle tab looked usable to people who are not
allowed to use them.** *Raise work order* and *Set up an exchange rule* now show
as unavailable, with the reason, for a role that cannot make that change.

**Changed — four tab descriptions are shorter.** The Sub-meters, Inventory,
Lifecycle and Map tabs each explained themselves in two long sentences; each now
says it in one short one, in all eleven languages.
## [2.237.4] — 2026-09-12 · a clerk can name the technician, and a greyed-out button finally says why

**Fixed — logging a repair asked a billing clerk to type a technician's ID.** The
screen was written for that role, and it was the one role it could not serve: the
list of people it needs was for system administrators only, so everyone else got a
plain box and a note saying to type an identifier nobody can look up anywhere in
the product. Choosing a person from a list now works for every office role. The
list shows a name and an email and nothing else, and the administrators-only list
it used to ask for has not been opened up.

**Fixed — when that list cannot load, the field stays a list.** It is shown
greyed out with a short line saying the crew list did not load and that the repair
can be saved without it. It used to turn into a text box and blame your role,
which was untrue for an administrator whose connection had simply dropped.

**Fixed — *Raise work order* on an asset with no matching template was a grey
button with nothing to explain it.** The sentence above it now says what to do
next, and the button itself carries the reason so it reads aloud too. The template
list is greyed out rather than offering an empty choice.

**Fixed — three date fields now refuse the dates the server was going to refuse
anyway**, and each says so: a repair cannot be dated in the future, a retirement
cannot be dated before the asset was installed, and a move cannot be dated before
the assignment it closes. The calendar greys those days out instead of letting you
pick one and be told off after saving.

**Fixed — three screens proposed no date at all.** Reassign, Log repair and Retire
were supposed to offer today's date already filled in, and were offering an empty
box. They now propose today in the utility's own timezone.

## [2.237.3] — 2026-09-12 · adding an asset: the utility service is a list you pick from, and the form says what happens to your answer

**Fixed — *Adding an asset* asked which utility service the meter measures as a
box you type into, and never showed you the list.** It is a dropdown now, holding
the services your utility actually sells — two of them on Brazos Bend, Electric
and Water — read from your Settings rather than from anyone's memory. Typing a
code that does not exist is no longer possible.

**Fixed — the form did not say the service was required and the server did.** An
empty one used to be accepted on step 1, accepted on steps 2 and 3, and refused
at the very end with a message about a box three screens back. It is marked
required and refuses on the step it is on. A behind-the-meter device still needs
none, which is unchanged and correct.

**Fixed — reloading the page half-way through threw away everything you had typed
and left you on the same step.** You came back to a form that looked part-finished
and held nothing. You now land on the first step with one line: *"Your answers
weren't kept — start again."* Keeping the answers across a reload is *Save as
draft*, which is coming.

**Fixed — the *Opening read* box you cannot fill in looked exactly like the boxes
you can.** It is greyed now, so a reading typed into it is not lost in silence.
The sentence under it already said why.

**Fixed — a backflow preventer was told a field was for "inverters and batteries
only" while being offered that field.** Both sentences on that step now describe
whatever device you are adding.

**Fixed — the summary you read before pressing *Add asset* printed our internal
codes.** It said `meter · water`; it says **Meter · Water**.

⚠ **Known, and now stated on the screen rather than left silent: a meter you book
straight onto the shelf does not keep the service you were asked for.** Choose
*Assign to a unit* and it keeps it; leave it in inventory and it does not, because
the product has nowhere to put that answer until the meter is fitted. Step 3 now
says so before you commit, naming the service. Where it ought to be stored is an
open decision.

## [2.237.2] — 2026-09-12 · an asset's type now actually saves, and its purchase date is on the page

**Fixed — changing an asset's type did nothing.** On the Edit form for a meter,
sub-meter or device, *Asset type* is a required box a clerk can open and change.
Pressing **Save asset** reported success and the type stayed exactly as it was —
every time, since the form was written. It now saves. Nothing else on that form
changed, and the same Save still sends the serial number, meter type, read
method, connection size, unit, multiplier and manufacturer it always did.

**Fixed — an asset's purchase date was recorded and then never shown.** It is
typed once when the asset is added, and after that it appeared on no screen at
all — while the age, the depreciation to date and the present value are all
worked out from it and are all on the page. It now sits on the asset's
*Warranty & supplier* panel, between the purchase cost and the present value, and
reads as a dash when nothing was recorded.

⚠ **The purchase date still cannot be CORRECTED from any screen.** Seeing a wrong
date is the half this release fixes; changing it belongs to the *Cost & value*
edit form, which is drawn and not yet built.

## [2.237.1] — 2026-09-12 · every form in the staff app: the help line moves under the box it is about

**Fixed — the help sentence sat between the field name and the box you type in.**
It now sits under the box, which is where the Product Owner asked for it and
where a reader expects it. This is every form in the staff app, not one screen:
the change is in the six shared field controls the whole product is built from.

**Fixed — fields were crowded together and the crowding was uneven.** Two fields
now sit a consistent 20 pixels apart everywhere. They were 14 apart inside pop-up
dialogs and 16 apart on full-page forms, and no form in the product used the
agreed figure.

**Fixed — two boxes side by side no longer sit at different heights.** When one
of a pair had a long help sentence and the other had none, the left box dropped
below the right one. Measured on the asset screens, four rows out of six were out
of line; all six line up now, at both laptop and desktop widths, whatever the
length of the sentences.

**Added — a date field can now be given an earliest and a latest date.** Until
now no screen could limit a date even where the rule limiting it was already
written down, and a help line saying *"cannot be in the future"* sat over a box
that happily took next year. The limits are not switched on for any screen yet —
that comes with the screens themselves.

## [2.237.0] — 2026-09-11 · the customer portal, redrawn: nine screens that hid their own name, and a pay flow a customer can follow

**Added — paying a bill when you are signed in is now three screens instead of
one.** *Pay now* → *Check before you pay* → *Payment made*. The middle screen
shows what will leave your account and which card or account it leaves from
before anything moves; the last one shows the receipt number and your new
balance. ⚠ **The two new addresses were built in 2.236.0 and could not be
reached — a customer pressing Pay went to an address that did not exist.** They
are switched on in this release. A receipt opened cold — from a bookmark, days
later — says *"We cannot show that receipt here"* with two working doors, not a
blank *Payment made*.

**Fixed — a payment that is declined no longer empties the screen.** It keeps the
amount and the card on screen and offers two things to do: use another card, or
go back and change something.

**Fixed — the portal's on/off switch reached one route out of ten.** At a utility
that had not opened its portal, the front page held and *sign in*, *enrol*,
*forgot password*, *track*, *report*, *help*, *find a service centre* and two
detail pages all served their full screens anyway. A switched-off portal now
asks the server for nothing at all.

**Fixed — a member of the public with no counter near them got a staff error
panel**: a red *Failed* chip, *"the address may be wrong"* said to somebody who
had typed nothing, and a **Download error report** button, all outside the page
frame so there was no utility name and no way back. It now says what is absent
and puts the utility's phone number next to it, as a number you can tap.

**Fixed — nine screens could not say their own name.** The worst was Usage,
which had no title at all: the only heading in the document was a panel heading
inside the first card, and on a failed read even that disappeared. A screen
reader announced the assistance panel as the page. Every one of the nine now
carries its title on every branch, loading and failed included.

**Fixed — a failed read used to be a dead end.** Across roughly twenty screens a
failure left one grey sentence and nothing to press. Each now carries **Try
again** — and it genuinely re-reads, which is asserted by making the first read
fail and requiring the second to draw the figure. The screen a customer opens
when their bills swing, *Budget billing*, was the worst: it said *"We could not
find an account to work this out for."* and offered no button, no phone number
and no link back.

**Fixed — bills and documents fit on a phone.** Four columns as drawn, with the
amount still owing on a second line wherever it differs from the bill total, so
a part-paid bill reads as neither paid nor unpaid. The payments list keeps its
search box and its year filter at phone width, where they used to vanish.

**Fixed — the address the utility prints on the bill now signs you in.** Opening
`/{utility}/portal` while signed in landed on the public page with a *Sign in*
bar on it, rather than on your own home page.

**Fixed — thirty things a customer reads were English in every language.**
Twenty-five new entries are now written in all eleven, including the label on
the biggest number on the home page; seven more were pointed at words the
product already ships rather than inventing a second set.

**Fixed — a fire service line now states its size**, `Fire service line · 2"`
beside its `$12.00`. The size decides the price and the count multiplies it, so
this was the one charge on the screen whose figure could not be checked against
anything visible. The same cell also read *"Fire Fire service line"*.

**Fixed — a help answer a clerk had pinned to the Usage screen had been
publishing into nothing for six days.** The setting offered three screens; two
of them showed it.

**Fixed — smaller things a customer would notice:** an instalment due in
eighteen days now offers *Pay $82.43*; the overdue screen says which day it is
counting from; a customer asking for a thirteen-month plan is told *"Choose
between 2 and 12 months"* instead of being asked to check dates they filled in
correctly; autopay shows `08/22/2026` rather than `2026-08-22`; *Postcode*
reads *ZIP code* on the guest screens; *"1 payments bounced"* is gone; and the
first step of a service application now names the address you are applying for.

**Internal — the checks, which is where most of this wave's lessons are.** The
branch stopped compiling twice in two days and no gate in this repository runs a
typecheck or a test suite, so both times it was found by a person looking. Lint
is back to zero errors across the front end. A ratchet that allowed nineteen
screens to hide their own id from three source scanners now allows seven, and
names all seven when it fails. Roughly a dozen checks were found that could not
have failed — or could not have passed — and each was fixed with the reason
written beside it.

**Known, and deliberately not fixed here:** seven screens still declare their id
in a way two gates cannot read; thirty-two browser walkthroughs still use a
readiness check that stopped meaning what it used to the day failed reads
started carrying the screen mark; the server still answers six guest endpoints
at a switched-off utility, so only the browser half of that switch is closed.

## [2.236.0] — 2026-09-11 · the customer portal: a heading that survives a failed read, and a way out of every dead end

**Fixed — a screen that failed to load threw away its own title and the only way
off it.** On nine screens the page head was built inside the success path, so when
a read failed a customer was left with one grey sentence on a blank page: no
title, no back link, nothing to press. The head is now drawn on every branch, so
a failed bill still says *Your bills* and still offers *← Bills*. Two of the nine
were worse and showed **nothing at all** while loading.

**Fixed — the customer portal told people bad news and gave them nowhere to go.**
The budget-billing screen said *"We could not find an account to work this out
for"* and offered no button, no phone number and no link back; the browser's back
button was the only way out. Every such message now carries what to do about it,
in the same card, directly under the sentence. This is a rule the Product Owner
ratified today in these words: *"when a screen tells a customer something bad, the
thing they can do about it must be on that same screen, next to the message."*

**Fixed — "still loading", "nothing here" and "we could not load this" all drew
the same card.** A customer could not tell an empty screen from a broken one.
Each now says which it is, in its own words, in all eleven languages.

**Fixed — the guest header took three rows on a phone.** It measured 147 pixels
tall at phone width against the signed-in bar's 57. It is now 57 at both widths,
with the errands and the language control in a band beneath it.

**Fixed — spacing the Product Owner described as "too much close".** Form fields
across the portal now sit to one scale: the label 5 pixels above its input, the
helper 6 pixels below it, and 20 between fields. The helper used to sit **17**
pixels from its own input and about the same from the *next* field's label, so it
read as belonging to the wrong one. The cause was a stylesheet giving every
paragraph the browser's default margin, which changed with the font size and so
could never be pinned by any scale.

**Fixed — six headings were the wrong size.** Four screens drew their title at 25
pixels where the other thirty draw 40.

**Changed — the bills list shows the four columns the design asks for**, down
from nine, and the documents list four, down from six.

**Changed — paying online is three screens, not one.** Choose, check, then a
receipt — so a customer can stop, go back, and keep the last page. ⚠ **The two new
addresses are not switched on in this release**; the screens are built and the
routing lands next.

**Known and not fixed:** five screens still set their own gap between form fields
and measure 12 or 16 rather than 20. The staff-side forms still put the helper
text *between* the label and the input, which is the same rule broken on the
other side of the product.

## [2.235.0] — 2026-09-10 · Plans & Rates, redrawn — all five tabs against the blueprint

**Added — a discount can now name the services it applies to.** Creating a
discount asks whether it covers **all services** or **specific services**, and
the specific list is a searchable multi-select. The choice shows on the
discount's page and can be changed when you edit it. Until now a discount could
not say which services it touched at all.

**Added — the two empty tabs on taxes and charge codes are built.** A tax and a
charge code each now have a **Plans** tab listing what uses them and an **Audit**
tab showing what changed and when. The charge code's Plans tab also counts the
plans that reach it through a rate schedule, which the old count on the overview
missed entirely — it read `0` over a code pricing every connection.

**Fixed — `Edit` on a tax that is already in force did nothing useful.** The
button opened a form and the server refused the save, because a live tax is
corrected with a new dated row rather than edited. The correction path is wired
now, the dates it must keep are shown as fixed rather than as boxes you can type
in, and the step asks for a reason. Found by opening the screen against a real
server: every one of the five seeded Texas rates offered a save that could not
succeed.

**Fixed — the plan wizard asked for a figure it should read.** A plan's minimum
charge was typed on the plan and again on the rate schedule, so two screens could
disagree about one number. The rate schedule now carries the base rate, the rates
and the minimum, and the plan shows what it is attaching. The plan sets nothing
it does not own.

**Fixed — a charge code could not be limited to a customer type from the
screen.** The wizard said it had no such setting; the setting had existed for
three weeks and only the API could reach it. The refusal is gone and the control
is there.

**Fixed — the discount screens told clerks things that stopped being true.**
Picking one discount type described a different one. A percentage read back the
stored fraction instead of what you typed. Three sentences still said an uncapped
discount always needs a second approval, after that rule was changed to apply
only where a utility sets a threshold — and the threshold now starts unset, so
nothing asks for a second approval unless a utility turns it on.

**Changed — a status is shown once.** The tax page drew its status twice, as the
badge under the title and again as a tile. The badge stays.

**Changed — the eleven-service picker is a proper control.** Choosing which
services a plan covers was a grid of eleven checkboxes; it is the same searchable
multi-select used everywhere else.

**Known and not fixed:** a charge code's Audit tab is sized but not built — it
needs history to be recorded before it can be shown. Rebuilding the discount
overview's tiles to the blueprint is recorded and not done. Roughly 255 pieces of
text across the eleven languages are still English, unchanged by this release.

## [2.234.19] — 2026-09-10 · the two search boxes on Add units say what to type, and one of them keeps its promise

**Fixed — the building box would never find a property by its parcel, however
you typed it.** The line under the box said you could search *"by address,
property number or parcel"*, and the search only ever looked at the address and
the number. Typing a parcel returned "no matching options" — the same answer you
get for a property that does not exist. Parcels are searchable now, and are still
not printed in the list, because the box is meant to read as a street address.

**Fixed — neither box said you could type in it.** The building box read
*"Any premise"*, which is the wording from the filter on the units list, where it
correctly means "no filter applied". On a box you have to type into it says
nothing. It now reads **"Search by address, number or parcel"**. The plan box read
*"Set the plan when somebody moves in"* — a sentence about leaving it blank, on a
box you type into, and repeated word for word by the control just below it. It
now reads **"Search plans"**.

**Known and not fixed:** the building box loads the first 200 properties and
searches them in your browser, so a utility with more than that cannot find the
rest by any term. Recorded; it needs the search to move to the server, which is a
change rather than a wording fix.

## [2.234.18] — 2026-09-10 · saving an edited property no longer answers "something went wrong"

**Fixed — typing a Parcel ID that another property already had crashed the save.**
The clerk saw *"Something went wrong on our side. Nothing was saved."* and no
indication of which box caused it. A parcel identifies one property, so a
duplicate has to be refused — but it was being refused by the database rather
than by the form, which is what produced the crash instead of a sentence. It now
says **"That Parcel ID is already used."** and puts the cursor back on the
Parcel ID box.

**Why it survived the fix for the same thing on the create form.** The check that
turns a duplicate parcel into a sentence was written a day earlier and switched
on only for *creating* a property. The reasoning was that on an edit a property
would otherwise be refused for clashing with its own parcel — which is true, and
the way round it is to ask "does another property have this" rather than "does
any property have this". Until then, editing kept the crash.

## [2.234.17] — 2026-09-10 · CR-089 · the twelve unit screens meet their drawing

**Changed — every screen a clerk uses to look at or edit a unit now matches the
design that was agreed for it.** Twelve screens were read against the blueprint
