and came back with about 145 differences; this closes them. The unit's Overview,
Assets, Plan, Account, Occupancy and Audit tabs, the units list, both steps of
Add units, and the three dialogs for editing, moving and taking a unit out of
service.

**Fixed — two ways of doing one job, where one of them kept no record.** Taking
a unit out of service could be done from a row on the list or from the proper
dialog. Both refused when an account was still open, so nothing unsafe was ever
possible — but the one on the list asked for neither a date nor a reason, and
those two facts live only in the history log. A clerk who used it left nothing
behind saying when or why. There is one door now, and it asks.

**Fixed — editing a unit opened two different forms depending on where you
started.** The pencil on the list and the button on the unit's own page each
opened a form the other did not have: one could set a common area and not a
plan, the other the reverse. They are the same form now.

**Fixed — pressing `+ New unit` on a building forgot the building.** The clerk
was handed an empty box and had to find the address again. The building now
comes with them.

**Fixed — columns the product already had the data for.** Nine facts were absent
from unit screens although the server was already sending them on the very
request the screen made: a meter's service, size and last reading; what a
departing tenant left owing; the last bill; the previous occupant and the gap
before the current one.

**Fixed — three sentences on screen that had stopped being true.** One told
clerks the meter readings could not be joined onto a meter, while the query that
joins them ran on the same page. One advised deleting a unit and recreating it
elsewhere to move it, three weeks after the Move button shipped. One explained
why two columns were missing that the design had since removed on purpose.

**Fixed — an empty audit tab offered the same link twice, and one of them did
nothing.** The cause was in the shared kit, so it could have happened on any
empty list: the control was mandatory, and a screen with nothing to offer had no
way to say so except a button wired to nothing.

**Fixed — hiding a column on one building's history hid it on every flat in it.**
The property and the unit shared one saved layout.

**Fixed — a plan list you could not type into.** Adding units offered every plan
in a plain menu while the edit form offered the same plans with a search box.
Both search now.

**Fixed — twenty-two lines of English that could never be translated**, on the
unit pricing panel, including the whole date-range picker. They were not missing
translations; the words existed in no catalogue at all, so every language saw
English permanently.

**Fixed — a Japanese bill line read "bicycle charge".** The billing *cycle* had
been translated as the vehicle, in Japanese and French, on an invoice line a
customer sees.

**Fixed — three empty pickers that all said the same thing.** A route box read
"No route yet" whether you had not chosen one, the utility had none, or the list
had failed to load. Only the first is a prompt; the second is a job on another
screen and the third is a reason to reload. They say which now.

## [2.234.16] — 2026-09-10 · CR-089 · the property's tabs get their table back

**Changed — three tabs on a property gain a search box, filters, a column
chooser and a footer that counts.** The Assets, Work orders and Audit tabs were
drawing the small in-panel table meant for a few rows of figures, so none of
them had any way to search, filter, choose columns or page — on screens that can
hold a property's whole history. They now use the same table the rest of the
product uses, which is what the agreed design named for each of them. One
change, three screens.

**Added — the columns those tabs were drawn with.** Assets shows **Service** and
**Size**, both of which the server was already sending and neither of which was
on screen. Work orders shows **Where** — the unit a job is on — which until now
could only be seen by opening the job. Common areas shows **Billed to**, which
is the question that tab exists to answer: who pays for the corridor light.

**Fixed — column headings that were English on every tenant.** Ten headings and
helper sentences were written with an English fallback and no catalogue entry at
all, so a utility working in Spanish, Japanese or Hindi read them in English and
nothing reported it. All ten are now written in each of the eleven languages.

## [2.234.15] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave G · Assets on a unit

**Added — the depot can be searched in the words a clerk is holding.** The
picker behind *+ Assign from inventory* asked for an asset NUMBER and nothing
else, so a person standing in the depot with a 5/8-inch water meter in their
hand had to go and find its number somewhere else first. Typing **5/8 water
meter inventory** now comes back with three chips — **Water 5/8"**, **Inventory**
and **Meter** — and the two spares that match. The words are read against the
utility's OWN catalogues (its asset types, its meter classes, its lifecycle
stages, its ratified connection sizes), so a utility that renames a stage
renames the word that finds it. A word the catalogues do not hold is said back
rather than dropped: *Not one of your words: depot*.

**Added — choosing one attaches it, on the unit.** It used to open the asset's
own reassign page with the unit preselected, so a one-step job finished on a
different screen and the clerk lost the place they were standing. **Assign ✓**
on a row puts the meter in the table above. Walked on `brazosbend`:
`W-5100` assigned to **SCW-U-001 · Unit 1, 101 Silver Creek Rd**, and
`GET /units/{id}` lists it a second later. A row the server would refuse keeps
the button and says *Not free to assign* — the state is read from the row, never
re-derived on the screen.

**Added — an attached meter's status changes from its own row.** There was no
way to do this from the unit at all; the tab drew a status column and offered no
control anywhere on the page. The row's **✏ Status** takes the new stage, the
day and the reason, and writes the append-only entry the asset register already
keeps. `W-5000` at the same unit moved from **Installed** to **Needs repair** on
8 Sep 2026 with *Register glass cracked at the meter pit*, and stayed on the
unit — a status change is not a removal. **Retiring is not offered here**: it is
terminal, it is the System Admin's own wizard with a reason, a date and a
book-value treatment, and it must not be one click away on a screen about a
flat.

**Fixed — `f.assigned=false` answered the whole register** (`DEF-AST-4734`). The
registry accepted the parameter, ignored it and returned 200: on `brazosbend`,
**142 rows where 10 are unattached**. A caller could not tell that answer from a
correct one.

**Fixed — a spare on the shelf now says what size it is** (`DEF-AST-4735`). No
seeded inventory spare has ever recorded a connection size, so *5/8* matched
nothing anywhere and the search above could not be demonstrated on the product's
own demo. Newly seeded tenants give a spare its service's smallest ratified band;
an existing demo is corrected through `PATCH /assets/{id}`, which is the clerk's
own door.

## [2.234.14] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave F · The unit's page answers what a person is standing there to ask

**Added — the Overview shows the ACCOUNT, not an occupant's name.** It read
*Occupant / account · Miller, Sarah · A-10432* on one line, with the number
demoted to a qualifier. It now leads with the number as a link and carries the
holder, the status and the date it opened, what is owed, the deposit held and
whether autopay will take it, closing on one button out. Walked on the demo
utility at **1408 Elm Street**: *A-10432 · Miller, Sarah* · *Active · since
02/05/2024* · *$247.30* · *$150.00 · taken 02/05/2024* · *On — the account is
not cash only, so it will be taken*.

**And when it is due is still a stated absence, deliberately.** The due date is
the oldest STILL-OPEN bill's, and nothing in the product answers which bill is
open — only the total. The Overview reuses the account screen's own sentence for
that gap rather than wording a second one, so the two surfaces cannot come to
disagree about it.

**Added — the unit's own number is on its Overview,** first, ahead of the
premise. It was in the page title, the tiles, the Plan tab, the Account tab and
every audit row, and missing from the one panel headed *Overview*.

**Changed — the four tiles are the page's, and they are the four that were
ruled.** `Account · Plan · Meters · Since` becomes **Assets · Owed · Plan · Open
work** on all six tabs. The Assets tile splits what is read and bills from what
the utility owns and does not read, from the server's own category. **The cost
was measured rather than estimated**: all three new figures arrive with the page
the screen already asks for, so moving between tabs costs **no extra request at
all**, and the units list pays nothing for them.

**Added — a vacancy is a row.** The occupancy tab listed tenancies and nothing
between them, so *how long did my flat stand empty* could not be answered from
the tab that exists to answer it. On `SCW-U-042 · 301 Mill Pond Ln`, whose
tenant's account closed on 31 July: **Vacant · 08/01/2026 · Current · 40 days ·
Base charges bill to the owner.** The gaps are derived from the tenancies either
side and nothing new is stored. What the row does NOT say is what the owner is
charged — base-only or full is `OQ-316` and still open.

**Added — a unit can be edited from the unit.** The pencil was on the units
LIST, so a wrong label had to be fixed from a table rather than from the flat
you were looking at. `✏ Edit` sits on the unit's header beside Move, changes the
label, floor and floor area, and carries the **plan** on the same form.

**Fixed — `PATCH /units/{id}` accepted a plan and threw it away.** The field has
been in the endpoint's ignored set since the unit wizard was built, so a request
carrying a plan answered `200`, changed everything else and left the plan
untouched, silently. It is applied now, through the same code the create and the
plan modal use, in one transaction — so a refused plan takes the label change
back with it instead of leaving half an edit behind.

**Fixed — the edit form drew a blank plan picker on a unit that has a plan**
(`DEF-MET-4728`). The value was right and the control a clerk can see said
nothing, which on that field reads as *no plan*. Found by reopening the form in
a browser and by nothing else.

**Verified, not built — the unit's audit tab.** It draws its own rows with the
old value beside the new and no expand controls; that arrived with wave C's
shared component. Every one of the demo utility's 131 units carries audit rows,
so the empty state the task was written from is not reachable there.

## [2.234.11] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave H · One date, one floor sentence, and a zero that explains itself

**Fixed — the unit's Plan tab used to write one date four different ways.** The plan's
start date read `06/01/2026` in the fact list and `2026-06-01` two inches below it, and
the two period boxes underneath printed **day first** — `01/09/2026` — under a sentence
that read `2026-09-01 to 2026-09-30`. A clerk reading `06/01/2026` cannot tell 1 June
from 6 January, and the screen supplied evidence for both readings. Every date on the
tab now reads **1 Jun 2026**. A named month cannot be read two ways.

The two period boxes are the browser's own control and render in the browser's language,
which nothing in the product can change — so each now carries the same named-month line
directly beneath it, which is the only place the two can be compared.

**Fixed — one sentence printed seven times.** *"No floor is set on this plan."* appeared
once for the plan and once for each of six services, taking more of the screen than any
figure on it. It is printed **once** now, as *"No floor is set — a bill can be any
amount, including nothing"*, and each service row reads **none**.

**Changed — the eligibility row is written for the person reading it.** It said
*"Nothing checks a plan's eligibility rules yet. The rules are stored as they were
written and no code reads them…"* — true, and about our software rather than about the
clerk's job. It reads **"Not checked — no plan here asks for proof before it applies"**.

**Added — a `$0.00` now says what the service is priced on, on the same row.** Three of
the services on a plan can show a base charge of nothing — Trash, Solar and **Fire** —
and every one of those zeros is correct. Fire is priced by the size of the line
multiplied by how many there are, so a warehouse with a 6" line and two 2" lines pays
`$60.00 + 2 × $12.00`, and its standing charge really is nothing. A new **Priced on**
column says so: *By the size of each one, times how many* for fire and trash, *By
capacity — the kW installed* for solar. The wording comes from the service's own
ratified size classes, so a twelfth service needs no change here.

**Still wrong, and written down.** The **ON PLAN SINCE** box at the top of the page
prints the tenant's numeric format, so that one date still has two shapes on the screen.
That box belongs to a piece of work being changed at the same moment; it is
`DEF-MET-4725`, and a check goes red the day it is fixed.

## [2.234.10] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave J · Moving a unit tells you what moving it does

**Added — the move screen lists what will happen, before you press.** It asked the four
right questions and then described the consequence in two sentences, one of which was
about the ledger. It now itemises **seven** things, each built from a figure the server
read rather than one the screen worked out.

**Two of them were readable nowhere in the product.** An address is kept on the property
and nowhere else, so **every meter, sub-meter and cart on the unit changes address the
moment the move commits** — the screen says how many first. Walked on the demo utility:
unit `SCW-U-002` moved from `103 Willow Bend Dr` to `412 Cypress Row`, the screen said
*"All 5 assets tagged to this unit travel with it and take the new address"*, and
afterwards `CART-0001`, `CART-0002`, `CART-0003`, `E-5001` and `W-5001` all read
`412 Cypress Row`. And a unit takes its **route and cycle from its building**, so a move
also changes who reads the meter and when it bills: `U-00101-A` was told
*"Electric leaves Route RT-002 · Cycle CY-002 and is on no route at the new property"*,
and after the move it is on no route.

**Changed — the button is the red one now.** A move decides where the unit's next bill
lands, and moving it back is a second move with its own date and its own reason — the
record then says it moved twice and neither date is wrong. So it commits like a
disconnection rather than like a save.

**Fixed — the warning stopped speaking like a machine.** *"This unit has carried 2
account(s)"* now reads *"This unit has carried one account"* or *"…2 accounts"*, in all
eleven languages.

**Fixed — a refusal stopped asking for a wire format.** A date that could not be read said
*"Enter the date as YYYY-MM-DD"* — which is what a screen says when it has no calendar,
and this one has always had a calendar. It says **"Pick the date from the calendar."**

**Fixed — pressing *Move unit* on an empty form did nothing at all.** No message, nothing
highlighted, no cursor moved: the three errors were being filed under names none of the
three fields could look up. All three now say what is missing, under the field it is
missing from, and the cursor lands on the first one.

**Fixed — a refusal was printed twice, one line under itself.**

**Still missing, and said out loud rather than filled in:** the screen cannot say how many
bills the unit has produced, because nothing in the product counts bills for a single
unit. It says so in words. It does not show a zero, because a zero would mean the unit has
never billed — which is exactly the thing that makes a move harmless.

## [2.234.9] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave E · Adding units, and finding them

**New — the units list shows what each unit owes.** Across 1,109 units it showed
no money at all, so finding the arrears in a building meant opening each unit in
turn. The column reads `$158.10`, `$225.46`, `$1,202.40` on the demo utility. It
is the same figure the customer's account screen shows — not a second sum worked
out a different way — and where nobody is renting the unit it reads a dash, not
`$0.00`, because a zero there would look like a settled account on a unit that
simply has nobody in it.

**Changed — the list is scanned by the two things a person actually looks for.**
It opened *Select · Unit ID · Premise · Unit*, so the first thing on every row
was a series number and the street was buried as the second half of a cell whose
first half was a property code. The **address** is now the second column with
the property number beneath it, and the unit's own name leads the next column
with its number beneath that. Nothing was taken away: both old columns are still
there and still sortable, one of them now in the column chooser.

**New — adding units starts by naming the building, and shows you what it
lends.** Pressing **+ New unit** on a building used to forget the building: it
landed on a four-way *"How many?"* chooser whose first required box was an empty
*Premise* picker, so a clerk standing on `P-00043` was asked to find `P-00043`
again out of seventy-nine addresses. Now you name the building first and it
stays on screen — its number and street, its type, its status, how many units
are there today **and what they are called**, the services the address offers,
the reading route and billing cycle the new units will join, and the owner.

**Changed — the plain case is plain.** Adding three flats meant typing a pattern
language — `{floor}`, `{seq}`, `{seq:00}` — and the box came pre-filled with
`Apt {floor}{seq:00}`, so three flats came out `Apt 101, Apt 102, Apt 103` when
what was wanted was `1, 2, 3`. Type how many, press Continue. The pattern
language is still there, one line down, folded away, for the block that really
is numbered `Apt 101` to `Apt 310`.

**New — a plan can be attached while the units are being created.** The rate
plan could only be set afterwards, one unit at a time, from a list. Pick it here
and it is on every unit the run creates. Leave it blank and the screen says what
blank means: *Set the plan when somebody moves in*.

**New — a last look before anything is written.** Adding a property got a review
step; adding units — which creates the rows that actually bill — got none, so a
mistyped *how many* or a wrong pattern was found afterwards, on a list, one row
at a time. Step 2 now lists the building, what it lends, every label, the
numbers the units will get, and states the things it is *not* setting (there is
no floor). The button says **Create 3 units ✓**.

**One thing worth knowing, and it matters at a busy counter:** the numbers on
that review are **not reserved for you**. If a colleague is adding units at the
same moment they are shown the same three, and whoever presses Create first gets
them. We chose that because holding a number every time somebody opens the
screen and walks away would burn numbers nobody ever sees.

**Fixed on the way — the review's numbers were wrong the first time we built
it.** It said `U-00421`, `U-00422`, `U-00423`; the three units it created were
`U-00001`, `U-00002`, `U-00003`. Every test we had was green. It was found by
adding three real units in a browser and comparing, which is now how it is
checked every time.

## [2.234.5] — 2026-09-09 · CR-089 wave K · Finding things by an address

**New — type a street into the accounts list and you get everyone at that building,
the owner included.** The list could already find an address, but only through the
unit somebody lives in — so the one account at a building that has no unit, the
owner's, was invisible. Searching **500 Main St** returned five of the six accounts
standing there and left out the account that owns the building. It returns all six.

**New — the payments list and the bills list can be searched by address at all.**
They could not before. Searching **301 Mill Pond Ln** on the payments list returned
nothing while nine payments had been taken from the six households there; on the
bills list it returned nothing while eighteen bills stood against them. Both now
return what is really there. It is the commonest question at a counter — *someone
is on the phone about this house* — and it took three screens' worth of looking up
account numbers first.

**Changed — the search boxes on those two lists now say they search an address**,
in every language the product speaks. A box that does not offer something is a box
nobody types it into.

**One thing worth knowing:** typing a street also matches the town, the property
number and the owner's name, because that is exactly what the Properties screen
already searches. The two screens are asked the same question so they cannot give
different answers about the same building.

## [2.234.4] — 2026-09-08 · CR-085 wave 4 · What happened to the thing you asked us for

**Fixed — a customer's own list of requests was showing them our filing note.** When Ana
queried a bill, her list of requests read *"Queried through the customer portal bill
BL-2608-000044 (2026-07-01 to 2026-07-31, 843.36 USD): The bill is higher than usual.
Their reason: We were away for three weeks in July and the house was empty.. They read
the meter themselves today: 41988."* — 271 characters written for a clerk, about her, in
the third person. It now reads **"A bill you queried — BL-2608-000044"**, and what she
actually typed is kept and shown as her own message on the request. The note the clerk
reads has not changed.

**Fixed — a request disappeared the moment it finished.** She withdrew the query and her
list went empty; there was no page anywhere that could show it to her again, so the
reference we had given her opened nothing she could find. The panel now offers **Still
open** or **All of them**, and the choice appears only once she has something finished.

**Fixed — the page for one request never said which request it was.** Every one of them
was headed *"Track your request"*. It is headed by the request itself now, with the
reference above it and **"Raised 09/08/2026"** under it, and each step of the progress
list says what happened — *through this website*, *You called it off*, *We are waiting
for: …* — instead of only a date.

**Fixed — the screen where you say a bill is wrong never showed the money.** Checked on a
phone and on a desktop: not one figure anywhere on it. It now says **"You are querying
bill BL-2608-000044, $843.36."**, shows the bill, the amount and the period on the
confirm step, puts *what this means* directly above the send button instead of off to the
side, and offers a **Back** button that keeps what you typed.

**Unchanged, and worth saying:** nothing about the bill moves, no bill is re-issued, and
we still do not stop the clock on a queried bill — the product keeps no record of a
disputed amount, and the screen says only what we actually do.

## [2.234.3] — 2026-09-08 · CR-085 wave 3 verified · A refusal on the payments list that was not true

**Fixed — the payments list refused to open a bill and blamed a missing receipt.** When
one payment settles two bills there is no single bill to open, so *See what this paid*
is greyed out — correctly. The sentence beside it said *"No receipt for this row."*,
which is about a different document, and on those very rows the receipt sitting next to
it is a working download. It now reads *"No single bill to open."*, in all eleven
languages. Nothing else about the row changed.

**Verified — a customer can take a copy of their payment plan agreement.** The button was
released a day earlier and nobody had ever pressed it: the demo customer has no payment
plan, so the automated walkthrough skipped that step on every run and still reported
success. The walkthrough now sets a plan up, presses the button and checks a real
document comes back — and it refuses to pass at all if it cannot.

## [2.234.1] — 2026-09-08 · CR-089 wave A · A property can say where it is, and a unit can differ

**Added — the property page shows where the property is, which it never has.** Every
property has been able to carry a position on a map since August, and **73 of the 79 on
the demo utility have carried one all along** — on no screen. Open one now and the
Overview reads its parcel number, its position, and whether anybody has ever checked that
position against the city's map. All three are asked for when a property is created, and
the position can be corrected afterwards on the edit form: until today the server refused
to change one, so a property recorded on the wrong side of the street stayed there.

**Added — the property list can find the ones with no position at all.** Six of the
seventy-nine. Before this you found them by opening properties one at a time.

**Added — a single unit can have its own position, and the screen says which one it is
showing.** A flat reads its building's and says *from the building*; a cabin in a park can
be given its own and says so. That matters on the equipment map, where twelve cabins used
to draw one pin on the site office with eleven hidden underneath it.

**Fixed — the address lookup was refusing in silence.** On a utility with no city mapping
service connected, typing an address got no candidates, no marker and no sentence. It now
says *Address lookup unavailable — type the town, state and ZIP* and gets out of the way.

**Changed — the field called *External / GIS ref* is now called **Parcel ID***, on the
create form, the edit form and the property's page, in all eleven languages. Same field,
no data moved: it was empty on every property in the product.

**And one thing worth knowing about the tick-box.** There has always been a yes/no flag
for *checked against GIS*, and it read *no problem* on every property — because that is
what the box defaults to, not because anyone had looked. The screen now says **Checked**
only where somebody actually pressed the button, and records who and when; everything else
reads **Not checked yet**.

## [2.233.0] — 2026-09-08 · CR-087 · One charge code can price two kinds of customer, and reading a plan takes one click instead of ten

**Added — a charge code can now charge a house one amount and a shop another.** Until
today a code stated one price per connection size and nothing else, so a utility that
charges **$45.00** to connect a home and **$85.00** to connect a business had to keep two
charge codes wearing the same name and remember which was which. One code says both now,
on a grid: connection sizes down the side, customer types across the top. The first
column is the price for everybody, and you only get a column for a customer type you
actually price differently — a utility with eight account types does not get eight
columns for a charge that varies by none of them. A blank cell means **this size is not
served**, and a bill for it is refused rather than charged $0.00.

**Fixed — and this one was quietly charging the wrong price.** The reading that works out
a customer's base charge already knew which customer type it was billing, and used it to
pick which charge codes applied — then built its per-size list with no ordering at all.
The moment two prices could exist for one size it kept whichever the database happened to
return last. A residential 5/8" water connection was quoted **$34.00**, the commercial
price, with no error and no refusal anywhere.

**Changed — the tax wizard asks three things instead of four.** A tax has 37 pieces of
information; nineteen lock the moment the first bill goes out, and the whole step that
was removed held none of them. Nothing was lost: every field still saves and is now typed
on the tax's own page, where it is also read. The date the rate starts — the one locked
field on that step — moved next to the rate it dates.

**Fixed — the count on that first tax screen stopped lying.** It counted the boundary and
ignored the other two restrictions, so a fee meant for commercial water customers
reported the whole utility. On the sample utility's 85 properties it now reads: no
restrictions **85**, Commercial **5**, Residential **58**, Water **71**, Gas **0** — they
sell no gas. Ticking Commercial moves the number before you leave the step.

**Changed — a discount can no longer be set to something that means nothing.** Enrolment
was a mode and a *proof is required* tick-box, which between them could say *enrol
everybody automatically, and also demand a document*. It is one dropdown of the three
answers that do mean something, and the server refuses the impossible pair by name if
anything sends it anyway. The type is a dropdown too, each option carrying its own
sentence instead of five radio cards sharing one.

**Changed — the plan wizard asks for a percentage, not a multiplier.** The outside-city
surcharge asked a clerk to type `1.15` to charge 15% more. Typing **15** — the number
printed in the label — would have charged fifteen times the bill. You type 15 now, the
screen reads back *"15% more. A $100.00 bill outside the city becomes $115.00"*, and the
conversion happens on the server.

**Changed — reading a plan takes one click.** Seven tabs all answered the same question,
so checking one plan meant opening seven screens. A plan's page is now **Overview ·
Units · Audit**, and the Overview is one card in the order a bill is made: rate schedule,
charge codes, discounts, taxes, terms. The last screen of the wizard draws that same card,
so the thing you approve is the thing you see afterwards.

**Added — the Units tab, which did not exist.** A plan showed a count of 74 and never said
74 of what. It lists them now, paged from the server, and a vacant unit says *base charges
still bill to the owner* instead of showing a dash a clerk reads as "nothing is billed".

**Changed — every one of the five definition screens offers the same three actions**, in
the same order, with Retire on the danger tier: **Duplicate · Edit · Retire**. There is no
longer a fourth spelling of Edit.

**Fixed — a plan's deposit showed its money under a name that read "not set".** Every
other row in that block names itself by its charge code; a deposit has none, so the name
fell through to the wording that means *there is nothing here* — in grey italic, next to
**$150.00**. Four deposits are seeded and all four read that way. It says **Deposit** now.

## [2.231.0] — 2026-09-08 · Where else a notice goes out, a seeded town that is finally in one state, and a starter file for every shape of meter reading

**Changed — the template screen now tells you, at the top, where else the notice goes.**
Open any notice under Settings → Configure → Templates and the panel listing its other
forms — the SMS, the printed letter — is the first thing beside the document instead of
the fourth. It used to sit below the merge fields, *Where it's used* and the version
history, so somebody editing the e-bill email only discovered an SMS version existed
after scrolling past three panels. It also says what it is rather than naming itself:
**"This notice also goes out as: SMS · Printed letter"**, with one line underneath —
*"Each is edited and published separately, so a change here changes only the document
you are looking at."* **Nothing on that screen has ever said that**, so a person who had
just reworded the email had no way to know the SMS still says the old thing.

**Fixed — the sample utility's addresses are all in one place now.** One seeded account
showed three different answers to the same question: the header said *Silver Creek,
Texas 68901*, the mailing box on the same screen said *Silver Creek, NE, 68901*, and the
postcode belonged to Nebraska. **124 seeded addresses moved to `Silver Creek, TX
78611`** — 73 properties and 51 mailing addresses. `78611` is Burnet, Texas, the post
office that serves Silver Creek Village in Burnet County, so the town, the state and the
postcode finally name one real place. The state is written the way an envelope writes it
— `TX` — everywhere, and the demo utility's own settings still show the word *Texas*
they picked from the list.

**Added — a starter file for each of the four shapes a meter reading file takes.** The
reads upload screen offered one example file: an energy row and a peak row. A utility on
time-of-use meters had to work out for itself that three rows share one date, and a
utility with solar that an export reading is a row and not a column. There are four
buttons now — **Flat or tiered · Time of use · Demand · Net metering** — and each hands
you the same columns with that shape's rows filled in. Every one of them uploads with
nothing to map by hand.

**No seasonal starter, on purpose.** A season is part of the price list and is worked out
from the date on the reading, so a seasonal reading file is a flat one. A fifth button
would have sent people looking for a column that does not exist.

## [2.230.0] — 2026-09-08 · Sewer is charged on the water you actually use, not on what your water cost

**Changed — every bill with a sewer line on it.** Until today sewer was billed
as **40% of what the water on the same bill came to in money**. From today it is
billed the way real utilities bill it: **90% of the water you actually used**,
priced at **$5.00 per thousand gallons** of its own.

On the reference household — 8,000 gallons of water in July — the sewer line
was **$15.80** and is now **7,200 gallons at $5.00 = $36.00**, and that bill's
total goes from **$292.87 to $314.97**. Five other worked bills move the same
way; the largest is the small-commercial one, from **$853.46 to $885.24**.

**Why 90%.** It is not the old 40% put up. The 40% said *what sewer costs
compared with water*. The 90% says *how much of the metered water actually
reaches the sewer* — real utilities use 79% to 95%, and most use 90%.

**A note for whoever reads this next:** a garden hose is water that never
reaches the sewer, so it is tempting to lower the 90% to allow for it. That is
the wrong lever, and doing it would under-charge every flat and every shop that
waters nothing. The trade's answer is to bill sewer on the customer's *winter*
water instead, which this product does not do yet.

**Also — the sewer line now shows its working.** It reads *"sewer usage — 90.00%
of water volume · 7.2 kgal @ $5.0000 · $36.00"*, where before it showed only an
amount. A utility that meters water in hundreds of cubic feet bills sewer in the
same unit.

**What has not changed, and is with the Product Owner.** Six sewer figures were
re-signed. A seventh, on the move-in example, and six later examples in the
payments and finance workbooks that start from the old total, were not put to
them and are untouched (`OQ-RAT-12347`).

## [2.229.3] — 2026-09-08 · Revenue & AR is back, and two screens stopped showing their own code names

**Fixed — Finance → Revenue & AR.** This tab has been showing an empty grey
panel headed *General ledger* instead of its own figures. Everything on it was
missing: what you billed this month, what came in, what is still owed, revenue
by service, who owes you, the write-off and refund queues and the tie-out. It
now opens on its own numbers again, and the Finance tab strip highlights
**Revenue & AR** rather than General ledger while you are on it.

**Fixed — Billing → Budget Bills.** The two buttons above the list read
`billing.budget.filter.enrolled` and `billing.budget.filter.off_budget`, and
every row's Status said `enrolled` in lower case. They now read **On budget
billing** and **Taken off**, in all eleven languages.

## [2.229.2] — 2026-09-07 · Opening a work order by its number now works, and a work order that cannot be opened says so

**Fixed — the work order you open from its number.** Every work order has a number you
can read, like `WO-0016`, and it is the only reference the product ever shows you. If
you put that number in the address bar, the screen came up completely blank: a dash in
every field, no error, nothing to tell you anything had gone wrong. It looked like a
work order with nothing in it. Opening the same job by clicking it in the Orders list
always worked, which is why this went unnoticed. **Both ways now open the same job.**

**Fixed — a work order that cannot be found.** Ask for a number that does not exist and
the screen used to show you the same page of dashes. It now says **"This work order
could not be opened"** and names the number you asked for, with a reference you can
quote to support.

**Fixed — a screen that is still loading no longer looks finished.** While a work order
is being fetched the page now shows that it is loading, instead of drawing every field
as a dash. A page that is empty because it is still working and a page that is empty
because something failed used to look identical.

**Fixed — the Checklist tab no longer guesses why it is empty.** It used to say the job
was *"raised without a template"* even when the job was raised from one that simply
plans no steps, which contradicted the Overview tab on the same screen. It now says
which of the two it is.

**One related problem was found and written down rather than changed here.** The work
order **template** screen has the same fault as the one fixed above and is worse about
it: when it cannot load a template it shows the word *Loading* for ever, with Edit,
Duplicate, Deactivate and Delete sitting live over nothing.

## [2.229.0] — 2026-09-07 · Your parts list has a door on the Parts screen

**Added — Work → Parts → ↑ Import parts.** The parts upload that arrived a few
releases ago now has a button to reach it. It opens the same five-stage screen
premises, units, meters, sub-meters, assets and accounts already use — download
the sample file, fill it in, and every column maps itself.

**Fixed — undoing a parts upload.** Rolling one back now actually removes the
parts it added. A part that has already been issued to a job is kept and
switched off instead, because deleting it would take that job's record of what
it used with it.

## [2.228.0] — 2026-09-07 · A plan says where its late fee comes from

**Changed — Plans & Rates → the plan editor, step 6.** A plan now names the charge
code its **late fee** is taken from, and the fee is the one that code says. Until
today the figure came from Settings → Billing defaults for every plan on the utility,
and a plan could only nudge it.

**What a utility sees.** Step 6 has a new **Late fee charge code** picker, loaded with
that utility's own codes. Every existing plan already points at **LATE**, the late-fee
code every utility is seeded with, so **no bill changes**: `LATE` says 1.5% with a
$5.00 minimum, which is exactly what the Billing defaults screen said. A $5,247.31 bill
six days past its due date is charged **$78.71** before and after.

**What is new is the choice.** Point a plan at a different code and that plan charges
that code's figure. **Leave the picker empty and the plan charges no late fee at all** —
the option says so in those words, *No late fee on this plan*, rather than sitting
blank. It does not fall back to the utility's default any more; empty means nothing.

**Nothing goes quiet.** A plan charging nothing is listed by
`manage.py cr078_late_fee_codes` and a merge check refuses one that nobody meant. Every
plan on every utility was pointed before the change took effect — 27 of 27, across 9
utilities.

## [2.227.0] — 2026-09-07 · Thermal/heat is billed on the size of the connection, not on a meter

**Changed — how a chilled-water utility charges.** Thermal/heat used to be a metered
service: a meter on every unit, a reading every month, and a bill based on how much
cooling the customer drew. The Product Owner has ruled that it is **capacity based**,
charged on **connected tonnage** — *"i will ahve 100 tonne or 200 tonne etc"*. So a
thermal customer now has **no meter and no readings**. What is recorded instead is how
many tons of cooling their building is connected at, and they pay for that size every
month.

**The sizes you can connect a building at.** Eight of them — **5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200,
400 and 800 tons** — replacing the three old groupings (*up to 25 tons*, *25 to 100*,
*100 and over*). The old three could not survive the change: you cannot multiply a
price by "25 to 100". 25 and 100 are kept as sizes of their own so nothing you already
had disappears from your list. **A ton here is the cooling ton** — the standard measure
of air-conditioning capacity — not a metric tonne.

**Sizes add up.** A building with a 100-ton connection and a second 25-ton one is
treated as **125 tons**, the same way solar panels on one roof add up to a total. It is
not counted as "two connections".

**The starting price is $12.50 per connected ton per month**, so a **100-ton** building
is **$1,250.00 a month** and a **200-ton** one is **$2,500.00**. It replaces the old
price of 4.5 cents per ton-hour, which no longer has anything to multiply now that
there are no readings. **Gas is unaffected** — its own new $1.15 per ccf, added earlier
today, is untouched. Like every seeded price, it is a starting value you change on
your own Settings screen.

**On a demo bill this reads:** *Thermal / Heat — 5 ton at $12.5000 = $62.50*, plus the
separate $20.00 monthly base added earlier today, so **$82.50** for a five-ton house.
A house outside the city limits pays 1.5 times the rate, $18.75 a ton.

**Nobody's bill changes.** Thermal was switched off on every utility, with no
connections, no equipment and no bill line ever raised on it — so this moves settings
only. **Your own sizes and prices are yours to edit** under Settings → Service sizes.

**Steam is unchanged and still unavailable.** Thermal has two halves — chilled water and
steam — and only chilled water has sizes. Steam is still waiting on the sizes only you
can give us.
## [2.226.0] — 2026-09-07 · The customer portal becomes a way of reaching people, and the template list stops calling itself empty

**Added — Settings → Notifications → Bill ready.** *Customer portal* used to sit in the
Channels table greyed out, under a sentence saying this product had no customer portal.
It has had one for days. The switch is real now: turn it on and every bill is published
to the customer's own portal, where they read it under *Your bills* and *Documents and
letters* after signing in. It is an **extra** route and never a replacement — a bill
still goes out on paper whatever this switch says.

**Fixed — in-app notifications had quietly stopped being deliverable.** Since 3 September
the one channel this product can actually deliver on was being asked whether an outside
provider was connected, and answering *not connected* — so staff notifications sat in the
queue instead of arriving. They arrive again.

**Fixed — Settings → Configure → Templates.** Twenty-three of the thirty-eight templates
told you they had no wording written for them, or that nothing was sending them. Both
were untrue: the wording was there and, for most of them, something sends it. Each row
now says what actually fires it — *"Sent when a payment comes back."* — and a check
refuses any future sentence that contradicts the wording beside it. The template page's
*author not recorded* line now appears only when nobody is on record.

## [2.223.0] — 2026-09-07 · The bill has a design

**Fixed — every bill, and Settings → Configure → Templates → the bill page layout.**
The five layout previews were showing plain typewriter text with the columns held
apart by spaces. They were not broken: each one renders a real bill of yours through
the same code that prints the bills you send, so what they were showing is what your
customers were actually receiving. **The bill was the thing with no design.**

It has one now, and it follows the drawing we agreed. The utility's name in bold with
its address and phone beneath; **UTILITY BILL** and the bill number on the right; a red
line under that block; the customer, the address, the account and the period; then the
charges with the description on the left and the amount on the right, a hairline
between each; a heavier line and **Total due** in bold; a dashed tear-off line and the
remittance stub along the bottom of the page; the ways to pay at the foot. Amounts line
up on the decimal point down one column, the way a bill should read.

**The five layouts now look different from each other**, which is the whole point of
choosing between them — Compact drops the usage and rate columns, Amount due first puts
the total above the charges, No remittance stub leaves off the tear-off, and Pre-printed
letterhead leaves the top of the page empty for your own stationery.

**Both the printed page and the e-bill email changed together**, from the same design,
so what you post and what you email cannot look like two different companies. On the
demo utility's own bill the page went from two sheets to one.

**Bills you have already sent are untouched.** Every bill keeps the exact page it was
printed on and always reprints that way; this changes bills issued from now on.

**Removed — the note above the layouts.** *"Changing this affects bills issued from now
on…"* is gone at the Product Owner's request. Only the sentence went: the rule it
described is still enforced.

**Changed — the note under *Send test to me*.** *"Queues, does not send"* is true and
stays. It is now worked out from the same check the sending machinery uses, rather than
being a fixed sentence, so it will start telling the truth by itself on the day a mail
provider is connected instead of having to be remembered.

## [2.222.0] — 2026-09-07 · Eight services stop being free to have

**Added — every bill.** Until today a customer paid nothing each month for simply
having a sewer, storm-water, broadband, battery or district-heating connection.
Only water, electricity and gas carried a charge for the connection itself. All
five of them now do, at figures taken from what North American municipal
utilities actually charge: **sewer $9.00**, **storm water $2.00**, **broadband
$30.00**, **battery $5.00** and **district heat $20.00** a month. Storm water is
the clearest example of how the figure was picked: this product already charges
$4.50 for each ERU of a property, so a $2.00 connection charge puts a
single-family home at **$6.50 a month** — the national average across the 2,202
US storm-water utilities counted in the 2026 Western Kentucky University survey.

**Left at $0.00 on purpose, which is a finding and not a gap.** Solar and private
fire lines charge nothing for the connection. Most municipal utilities levy
nothing monthly for a customer's own rooftop panels, and where they do it is per
kilowatt, which this product already charges. A private fire line is charged by
the width of its pipe everywhere we looked, and this product already bills that —
$12.00 for a 2-inch line up to $230.00 for a 12-inch one — so a second monthly
charge would bill the same connection twice. Trash stays at $0.00 too: it is
billed per cart.

**⚠ None of these figures has been approved yet.** They were researched, not
ruled. Every one carries the utility and the year it came from, and any single
one can be changed in a word.

**Who sees a difference.** Only utilities set up from today onwards. A utility
already running on SMARTBillHub keeps exactly the charges it has.

## [2.221.0] — 2026-09-07 · A new utility's Integrations screens have something on them

**Added — Settings → Integrations, on every utility created from today.** A new
utility used to open this screen and find nothing at all: no connections, no runs,
nothing to click. It now arrives with **three connections already set up** — the
mail server the bills go out on, the meter-reading cloud and the bank's lockbox
file — and **five sends recorded against the mailbox**, so the Runs screen shows
what a real month looks like: one where every message got through, one where seven
addresses were refused and are listed by name, one the provider never confirmed,
and **one that failed**, with the mail server's own sentence about the password
underneath ours. The failure is deliberate; a demo where everything worked teaches
nobody what to do when something does not.

There is also **one payment notification from a kiosk** and **one month handed over
to the accounting system**, so the finance and payments screens that count those
are no longer empty either.

**None of the three connections claims to be working.** They all read *Untested*,
because no provider can actually be dialled in this release and a green tick would
be a promise the product cannot keep.

**Added — importing your parts list.** Parts joins premises, units, meters,
sub-meters, assets and accounts on the same upload screen: download the sample
file, fill it in, and every column maps itself. A row with no part number, a
duplicate number, or a category you do not have is caught before anything is
written.

## [2.220.2] — 2026-09-07 · A gas customer is charged for the gas they use

**Fixed — every bill on a gas utility.** Until today a gas demo charged **nothing at
all** for gas. The bill line said *40 ccf* and then *$0.00*, so the whole bill was the
$6.00 monthly charge for having gas, plus twelve cents of tax — while the same estate's
heating meters were correctly billing $1,350.00.

**What a bill says now.** The price list we work from has always priced gas at **$1.15
for each ccf**. The reference customer uses 40 ccf a month, so their usage line now
reads **40 ccf × $1.15 = $46.00**, and the bill before tax goes from **$6.00 to
$52.00**.

**No price was changed and none was invented.** The $1.15 was already written down; it
was simply never used. The reason it could not be used is worth stating, because it was
a good one: the gas meter used to be recorded in *therms* while the price is quoted per
*ccf*, and those two measure different things — a therm is heat and a ccf is volume — so
there was no honest way to multiply them without inventing a conversion nobody had
agreed. The meters were moved onto ccf on 2 September so the price could be applied as
written, and the price itself simply never followed. It has now.

**Nothing else moved.** Water, electric, heating and every other service bill exactly
what they billed yesterday. If your utility does not sell gas, no bill of yours changes.

## [2.220.1] — 2026-09-07 · A gas utility stops being offered water's jobs

**Fixed — Settings → Reference data → Work order types.** Earlier today this screen
started giving every utility the same eighteen jobs, whatever it sells. That was the
list as the Product Owner wrote it, and it left a gas-only utility looking at **No
Water Supply** and **Water Truck Services**. They have now said a gas utility should
carry gas's jobs, so **each job type follows the service it belongs to**, the way the
gas ones already did.

**What each utility gets now.** The nine headings — Consumer Complaint, Meter
Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Connection, Corrective Maintenance,
Infrastructure Development, Water Quality Monitoring, Consumer Services and Reading —
go to everybody, always. Underneath them: a **water-only** utility gets eighteen jobs;
**water and gas** gets twenty-two; **electric and water** gets twenty-one; a
**gas-only** utility gets gas's four; a utility selling all eleven services gets
forty-two. Switch a service on later and its jobs arrive then.

**If your utility already had the water jobs and does not sell water, they are
switched off, not deleted.** Any job already recorded against one still reads
correctly, and switching one back on is a single click. **A job you had renamed is
left exactly as it was and stays on** — a renamed row is one you made your own.

**Two things are still with the Product Owner and nothing is guessed meanwhile.**
Eleven of water's eighteen name no service at all — *Billing Issues*, *Meter Change*,
*Re-read*, the four *Connection* rows and four more — so a gas utility no longer has
job types it does every day; whether those should go to everybody is with them now.
And job types are to carry a default priority again, which they have agreed to; which
priority each one gets sets the response time your customers are promised, so the
proposed list is going to them in plain words with the hours beside it before anything
is switched on. Until then the priority is blank and a clerk sets it on this screen.

## [2.220.0] — 2026-09-07 · A new utility's customer portal opens with something in it

**Added — every newly provisioned utility now gets a working customer portal, and one
customer who can sign into it.** Until today the portal's own self-service data was
seeded on two hand-built demo utilities and on nobody else: a utility that signed up
through the real path got a portal with **no branding, no answers, no tips, no service
counter and no login at all** — zero rows in all seven of its tables. Product Owner
ruling, 2026-09-07: *"before step 29 this - you ahve to set all the self service data
in settings -> configure -> Customer portal - {overview, branding, Help & Answer, Tips
+ service centers }"*, where step 29 is the customer login, so the configuration is
seeded first. `CR-082`.

**What a fresh utility's portal holds now**, measured on one provisioned through the
sign-up endpoint: the portal switched **on** and branded with the utility's own
services as its front-page chips, its own office hours and an emergency number;
**8 questions and answers** in eleven languages (88 translations); **6 tips** across
six screens; **3 service counters** with **21 rows of opening hours**; and **1 customer
login** on a sample account. Before: nothing, on any of them.

**Not one line of seeding content was written for this.** Both seeders already existed
and worked — they were reached only by the demo command that builds the two showcase
utilities, and were never named in the sample-data registry. The fix was a
registration.

**Fixed — the tip slot on a customer's Usage screen has never been able to show
anything.** It asked for a tip aimed at a screen name no tip can carry, so the lookup
answered *nothing today* on every utility, forever — and *nothing today* is also the
correct answer on a quiet day, which is why no test could tell the two apart. Found by
opening the screen on the first utility that ever had a Usage tip to show.
`DEF-CWP-4510`.

**Fixed — two seeding steps were missing from the sign-up screen's progress list**
since 2026-09-06, so an operator watching their utility being built saw 19 steps of 21.
The check that catches this had been failing the whole time and nothing ran it; the same
assertion now also runs in the backend suite. `DEF-TEN-4509`.

## [2.219.7] — 2026-09-07 · The base charge learns the meter size

**Fixed — a 6-inch water main and a household 5/8-inch meter no longer pay the same
standing charge.** `charge_code_amounts`, the table that prices a base charge per
connection size, held **zero rows on every tenant this product had ever created** —
counted on PostgreSQL 16 across four seeded utilities and a freshly provisioned
eleven-service one. The rule it exists for has been CONFIRMED since 2026-08-20 and
its writer was built on 2026-08-28; neither reached the seed, so a utility opening
the per-size table met a blank screen. `DEF-4497`.

**What a base now costs, per size.** The seeded sample steps water from **$8.00** at
5/8" to **$204.00** at 6", electric from **$12.00** for an ordinary house to
**$114.00** for a CT-metered service, and gas from **$6.00** to **$15.00** — 40 rows
on an eleven-service tenant. Commercial and industrial customers take the same ladder
at their own price level, which is how one service carries two prices.

The ladder is `half a customer component every connection pays + half scaling with
reserved capacity`, and it was not invented for the occasion: it reproduces
`BR-RAT-108`'s published `5/8" $8.00 · 1" $14.00` exactly and fire's six PO-ratified
prices to within a rung.

**No existing bill moves by a cent.** Each ladder is anchored on the figure its charge
code already states, so the smallest size is unchanged — which it had to be, because a
charge code that disagrees with the plan REFUSES the account rather than mis-billing it.

**Also found, not fixed.** A `government` account has no base charge for water or
electric and its bill would refuse by name — fifteen combinations, present identically
before and after this change, so it is on the customer-class axis and not the size one
(`DEF-4503`). And eight of the eleven services still charge **$0.00** for having the
connection; trash is deliberate (it bills per cart by PO ruling) and the other seven
have never had a figure signed, so none was invented.

## [2.219.5] — 2026-09-07 · Nine of the eleven services billed nothing, and the reason was not the seeder

**Fixed — the demo estate now connects every service a utility sells.** A tenant selling
all eleven services was producing bills that carried only electric and water. The cause
was not a broken seeder: **nine of the eleven services were switched off on the tenant**,
and the estate is built from the enabled set, so creating nothing for them was correct.
On a tenant that actually sells all eleven, every service now reaches a bill.

**Added — a Fire service line is a kind of equipment (`OQ-1361`).** Fire is the eleventh
utility service and is priced by counting what stands on the property, and there was no
equipment type it could ever be recorded against — so a utility selling fire protection
got connections with nothing on them and a zero on every bill. A property with a 6-inch
line and two 2-inch lines now bills **$60.00 + 2 x $12.00 = $84.00 on two separate
lines**, each naming its own size so a customer can tell them apart. It is its own type
rather than a backflow preventer, because backflow preventers sit on water connections
and sharing the type would have let a water device be counted as a fire line.

**Fixed — every meter was the smallest size the product sells.** Fifty electric meters
were all single-phase 100A against a six-size list, and fifty-one water meters were all
5/8-inch against a nine-size list, because the seeder took the first size on the list for
every meter of every service. A price list that charges more for a bigger connection
would have been tested at one point on the curve. Connections are now sized to match the
customer, reaching all six electric sizes, six of the nine water sizes and all four gas.
Nothing a finance sign-off depends on moved: the demonstration properties those figures
are calculated from keep the size they already had.

**Fixed — twenty meters and sub-meters had no size recorded**, which meant those
connections could not work out what to charge. A sub-metered apartment building was the
first case that would have failed. Each sub-meter now takes the same size as its own
building's meter.

**Fixed — the Next-test date was blank on every piece of equipment of every demo
tenant.** The backflow preventer has carried a twelve-month test interval since the day
it existed, but the date is worked out from the last test and no seeded equipment ever
had one. The preventer on the laundromat's connection now carries a real annual test
date, so the rule that finds overdue tests has something to find.

## [2.219.4] — 2026-09-07 · Work order types are your own list, in two levels

**Changed — Settings → Reference data → Work order types.** The eight job types this
product came with were not the right list, and the Product Owner replaced them. There
are now **nine types with sub-types underneath them**: Consumer Complaint, Meter
Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Connection, Corrective Maintenance, Infrastructure
Development, Water Quality Monitoring, Consumer Services and Reading. Under those sit
eighteen jobs a utility actually raises — *Low Pressure*, *No Water Supply*, *Billing
Issues*, *Meter Change*, *Meter Dispose*, *Routine Inspection*, *Meter Replacement*,
*Survey for New Connection*, *Residential*, *Commercial* and *Industrial Connection*,
*Leak Repairs*, *Electrical Line*, *Main Extension*, *Water Pressure*,
*Disconnection/Reconnection*, *Water Truck Services* and *Re-read*.

**And you get the jobs for the services you sell, and no others.** A water-only utility
gets exactly those eighteen. A utility that sells water and gas gets those eighteen plus
four gas ones — *Gas leak call-out*, *Odour complaint*, *Pressure test* and *Line
purge*. There are twenty-four of these altogether, across gas, electric, trash, storm
water, solar, battery, broadband, thermal, fire and sewer, and they all sit under the
same nine headings rather than adding headings of their own. **Switch a service on later
and its job types arrive then**, without anybody having to ask for them.

**The eight types you had are switched off, not deleted.** *Reconnect after payment*,
*Main repair*, *Disconnect — non-payment*, *Leak investigation*, *Meter exchange*,
*Backflow inspection*, *Read verification* and *Move-in activation* are still there,
marked inactive, so every job already recorded against one still reads correctly and
nothing is lost. They no longer appear when you raise new work. If your utility was
using one of them, switch it back on in one click. **If you had renamed one, it is left
exactly as it was and stays on** — a renamed type is one you made your own.

**None of the new types carries a default priority.** The Product Owner gave the names;
the promises are yours to set, on this same screen, where they show up as the SLA hours
each priority carries.

**On screen.** The card now has a **Parent type** column, and a type shows how many
sub-types sit under it — *Reading · 1 sub-type*. Adding an entry asks first whether you
are making a **Type** or a **Sub-type**, and the heading follows what you pick; choosing
Sub-type shows a **Parent type** dropdown offering only the nine headings. A type that
already has sub-types under it cannot be deleted until they are moved or removed, and
the message says how many are in the way. Types go two levels deep and no further.

## [2.219.3] — 2026-09-07 · The monthly filing job now says what it actually filed

**Fixed — the scheduled job that files away records older than two years.** Every
month the product moves old audit history and old meter readings out of the live
tables and keeps them on the side, and it writes a short receipt saying how many
records it moved and a checksum of them. **The receipt said `0 records` and carried
the checksum of an empty file** — over a month that really did hold records — and it
wrote nothing into any utility's own history to say the filing had happened. The
records themselves were moved correctly and nothing was lost; only the description
of them was wrong.

**Why it happened.** Those tables are locked so a query can only ever see one
utility's rows, and the job was counting them without saying which utility it was
asking about. So the database answered honestly: nobody's rows. The obvious repair —
letting this one job read across every utility — was refused a fortnight ago and
stays refused.

**What it does now.** The job asks each utility in turn, counts and checksums that
utility's share inside that utility's own account, and adds them up. On the two
records this was measured against, the receipt now reads **2 records with a checksum
of those two records**, and each utility gets a line in its own history saying **one
record of mine was filed**, with nothing about anybody else's.

**It takes longer, deliberately.** A month holding forty thousand records across
forty utilities takes about **four tenths of a second** to account for, where it used
to take a couple of milliseconds — and the old speed was the speed of reading
nothing. The job runs at two in the morning.

**And it now refuses rather than guesses.** If the job cannot read one utility's
share, it leaves that month exactly where it is and the run says so on screen,
instead of filing it away under a receipt that under-counts it.

## [2.219.2] — 2026-09-07 · The reading-checks screen stops going blank, and you choose how a missing reading is estimated

**Fixed — a settings page that ended in empty space.** Settings → Reference data →
Read validation & estimation shows one section per utility service you sell, with the
high and low thresholds a reading is judged against. On some loads it drew its heading
and its list of always-on checks and then **nothing at all** — every service section
missing, with no message. Nothing about the page looked broken, which is the problem:
it read as a finished page, and it was only noticed by someone who had seen the
complete version minutes earlier.

**Why it happened.** The page draws a section for each service that is switched on,
and if none is switched on it drew none — and said nothing about it. Switching your
services off and on under Services & UoM is enough to see it. The page now says so in
plain words: *"No services are switched on, so there is nothing to check yet — switch
one on under Services & UoM and it appears here."*

**Fixed — the boxes on that page line up now.** The two columns of settings sat at
different heights wherever the left one had a line of explanation under its label and
the right one did not, so a pair that belongs together stopped reading as a pair.

**Changed — there is much less to read.** The page carried a sentence of explanation
under nearly every box, on top of a two-sentence introduction and a paragraph over the
checks. It now carries one sentence per section, and the unit a threshold is measured
in has moved into the label beside it — *High-use floor (kWh)* — where it is shorter
and harder to miss. The services you have no meters for are now one line naming them
all rather than a paragraph each.

**Changed — a panel with unsaved edits says so when you close it.** Each service is
saved on its own, so *Save Water thresholds* saves water and nothing else. If you
typed into one service and collapsed it, your typing was still there and the Save
button had gone with the panel. The heading now reads **Unsaved changes** while
anything is waiting.

**Added — the estimation method is now a choice.** When a meter cannot be read, the
product estimates the reading. Until now that was a fixed value on screen with no way
to change it. There are now seven methods to choose from, each with a line saying when
you would pick it: the daily average of the last 3, 6 or 12 periods; the same period
last year, for irrigation and other seasonal use; repeating the last real reading; the
average of similar accounts on the same route; and the average from the plan.

**Your setting has not changed.** Every utility is still on the daily average of the
last 3 periods, exactly as before — how a missing reading is estimated decides what a
customer is billed, so it changes only when somebody chooses to change it. The last
two methods in that list are shown greyed out, each saying why: we have not yet been
told which accounts count as "similar" on a route, and a rate plan does not hold an
average for us to read. Both questions are with the product owner.

**Fixed — two checks were listed by their internal name.** In the list of checks that
run on a reading, two appeared as `row_key` and `unit_mismatch` among thirteen plain
English names. They now read *Reading row matches its meter* and *Unit matches the
tariff*.

## [2.219.1] — 2026-09-07 · The customer portal offers two languages

**Changed — the language dropdown in the portal's top menu, and the one on
*My details*.** Both offered eleven languages. The Product Owner asked for two:
*"currently in drop down show only 2 elnglish and spanish"*. Both now list
**English** and **Español**, each written in its own language, and the same two
on both — they read one list from the server instead of each deciding for
itself.

**Nobody's saved choice was changed.** A customer whose account is set to
German still reads German everywhere, exactly as before. Their own dropdown
shows **three** — English, Español and Deutsch — so the setting they have is
visible and not silently blank. The moment they pick English or Spanish, German
stops being offered to them too.

**A utility set to a language outside the two behaves the same way**: its
guests read the utility's language and see it listed alongside English and
Español.

**Nothing was removed from the product.** All eleven translations are still in
the build and every one still draws; what changed is only what a customer may
pick.

**The top menu is still two lines in English, and this did not fix that.** It
was worth checking: the language control shrank from 186 pixels to 105 when the
list narrowed. The menu was already too wide before the control was added, so
it still wraps. That one is a separate piece of work about the wording of the
menu.

## [2.218.9] — 2026-09-07 · The Add-entry screen now says which one you are making

**Fixed — Settings → Reference data → Areas & sub-areas.** Pressing **+ Add entry** used
to open a dialog headed *"Add to Areas & sub-areas"* with a Code box, a Name box and a
**Parent area** dropdown. It made either an area or a sub-area, and the only thing that
told you which was one line of small print above the dropdown: *"Leave blank for an
area."* The Product Owner opened it and said there was no difference on screen between
adding an area and adding a sub-area. There was not.

**Now you choose first, in a control.** The dialog opens with two buttons at the top —
**Area** and **Sub-area** — with **Area** already chosen, and the heading follows what
you pick: *"Add an area"* or *"Add a sub-area"*. Choose **Sub-area** and the **Parent
area** dropdown appears, marked required, offering only the districts that can actually
hold one. Choose **Area** and there is no dropdown at all, so there is nothing to leave
blank and nothing to get wrong. The small print explaining what blank meant is gone —
one fewer sentence to read, not one more.

**Editing opens on what the row already is.** Open a sub-area and the dialog says
*"Edit a sub-area"* with its parent already named; open a district and it says *"Edit an
area"* with no dropdown.

**And a value nobody typed can no longer change what gets made.** The Product Owner's
screenshot showed the dropdown reading *Downtown* on a dialog that had just been opened
— a browser filling the form in. A dropdown filled that way never told the screen it had
changed, so what appeared on screen and what would have been saved could disagree. The
two buttons now decide, so a stray value in the dropdown can no longer alter the result,
and the Code and Name boxes tell the browser not to fill them in the first place.

## [2.218.5] — 2026-09-07 · Two prices no other utility can see

**Fixed — the database would have shown one utility another utility's price.** Two of
our tables hold what each utility agreed to pay us: the setup order, with its price,
currency, length and how many instalments it is paid in, and any add-on, with its
agreed monthly figure. Both tables say which utility each row belongs to, and neither
was locked down in the database itself. One line of our own code was doing the whole
job. It is now the database's job as well: with nobody signed in to a particular
utility, both tables answer **zero rows**, and from inside one utility's account the
other's price cannot be reached at all — not even by someone who knows the exact
record to ask for.

**Nothing on screen changes.** Settings → Billing plan shows the same plan, the same
setup order and the same add-ons it did yesterday, to the same people.

**Our own order numbers still run as one series across every customer.** They used to
be worked out by reading every utility's orders, which is exactly what we have just
stopped anyone doing — so the count now lives on a record of ours instead. The first
two customers still read **IMPL-26-0001** and **IMPL-26-0002**, and no two utilities
can be handed the same number.

**Why it was missed for five days:** the check that would have caught it could not run.
It needs a real PostgreSQL database and a login that the rules genuinely apply to, and
until 2026-09-07 it had been quietly reporting "skipped" — which reads exactly like
"nothing wrong".

## [2.218.3] — 2026-09-07 · A sign-in code is not a letter

**Fixed — a text-message sign-in code was listed among a customer's documents.** On
*Documents and letters* in the customer portal, the one-time code we text somebody when
they set up their portal login appeared as a row reading *A letter from us · Letter ·
How: Text message*, with no name, nothing to open and no reason given. A six-digit code
is not a document — there is no envelope for it and it stops working after ten minutes
— so it is no longer listed. The code is still sent and still recorded exactly as
before; it simply is not filed alongside bills and receipts.

**Sending it by text is correct and has not changed.** When we hold a mobile number for
a customer, that is where the code goes.

**Not a defect, and left alone deliberately:** a receipt that reads *Text message ·
Email · Post — We could not send this by Text message* is the product being honest.
Three copies of the receipt are prepared, and the texted one says plainly that we hold
no mobile number for that customer rather than quietly going missing.

## [2.218.2] — 2026-09-07 · The bill on screen again

**Fixed — the printable bill was an empty grey box saying the content was blocked.** On
a bill's Document tab, and on the customer portal's copy of the same bill, the page
showed a browser message instead of the bill. We were blocking ourselves: a new security
header added the day before told the browser that no page here may display an embedded
document, and both of those screens display exactly that — the real printed bill, in the
browser's own PDF viewer, with its print and save buttons.

**The header now permits this product to show its own documents and nothing else.** No
other site may embed our pages and no outside content may be embedded in them; the only
thing that changed is that our own bills are allowed on our own screens.

**Checked by opening both screens in a browser**, because this is the kind of fault no
test in the project can see: the bill now renders inside the frame on the staff screen
and inside the viewer on the customer's, with nothing refused.

## [2.218.1] — 2026-09-07 · A customer receipt with the numbers on it

**Fixed — every value on a payment receipt was a dash.** A receipt waiting to go out
read *"Hi ——, Amount —— Date —— Method —— Confirmation ——"*, with both balance lines
blank as well. The letter was written correctly and the part that fills its blanks in
worked correctly; what was missing is that the payment screen never handed it any of
the numbers, and it will not guess one — a value it cannot fill it marks as blank
rather than inventing it.

**What a receipt says now**, from a real payment on the demo utility: Dev Duval owed
**$855.27**, paid **$255.27** by cheque number **8842**, and the receipt reads *Amount
255.27 USD · Date 09/07/2026 · Method Check · Confirmation 8842 · Applied to
BL-2607-000004 · Balance before this payment 855.27 USD · Balance after this payment
600.00 USD*. The text-message version and the printed copy carry the same figures, so
the three cannot say different things about one payment.

**The two balances come from the accounts and from nowhere else** — the same place the
Finance page asks — so a customer's receipt and the utility's own screen can never
disagree. If the books cannot answer, the two balance lines are blank and the rest of
the receipt still goes out.

**Fixed — the list of details beside a waiting message showed money to six decimal
places.** It read `Balance 0.000000` two inches under a letter saying *0.00 USD*. Money
is shown to two decimal places there now, and a date wears the utility's own date
format.

**New — the product now says which fields on a queued letter will be blank.** It does
not stop the letter: a run of five hundred bills must never die because one line of one
letter is empty. Expect it to name gaps on other letters, each of which is its own job.

## [2.218.0] — 2026-09-07 · Which meters are due for change-out, and which budget levels the year no longer supports

**Two more of the catalogue's runbooks, and they are the first two that were only ever
named.** Every runbook before these arrived with a card describing its scope, its steps and
its screens. These two arrived with one sentence each, so the rest is written down as a
judgment rather than presented as a specification — each card marks it, and the decision
log carries the reasoning.

**Meters past change-out age or never tested** is the Assets category's first runbook, so
that category stops being empty and starts drawing its filter chip. A clerk presses Run and
sees every meter older than its own expected life or with no test on file, biggest revenue
first, each with **Order a test →** or **Schedule change-out →** beside it. On the demo
utility that is 8 meters, and the tile that matters most is the one that is not a finding:
**8 of 8 cannot be judged on age**, because no meter there records an expected life. A
runbook that reported *0 past change-out age* and left that out would be telling a utility
its meters are young when the truth is that nobody has written down how long they last.

**Budget billing re-level** shows each budget-billing account's current level, the level the
last twelve months support, and what would change. **It changes nothing, and it says so on
the screen**: nothing in this product moves a budget level yet, so the *Apply the new levels*
button is drawn disabled with its reason and every row reads *"has to be changed by hand"*.
Nobody is written to either — telling a customer their monthly payment is changing when
nothing can change it would not be true. The level itself is billing's own arithmetic and is
not recomputed here.

**Fixed.** The empty state of a result table rendered as a blank strip on the screen — the
sentence explaining that there was nothing to do was being passed in a shape the page could
not read. It now says *"Every level is where it should be."* It was found by looking at the
page in a browser, which is the only place it was visible.

## [2.217.0] — 2026-09-07 · Price the whole estate before you go live, and find every open item on one screen

**An implementer can now put a utility's own accounts through the real bill engine, as a
grid, before the utility commits to anything.**

Pick *Coverage grid*, press Run, and the product chooses one account for every combination
of plan, service mix and billing cycle the utility has — automatically, and the same way
twice, so two runs can be compared. Each of those accounts is then priced by the **test
bill**, exactly as a real bill run would price it, and the answers are laid out as coloured
cells: green where the bill came out clean, amber where a reading behind it was an estimate,
red where the utility's own configuration stopped it.

**A red cell opens that account's test bill.** Not a summary of it — the bill itself, with
every line explained and the refusal in the engine's own words. Fix the rate that caused it,
run the grid again, and the cell turns green.

**And the grid says what it left out.** *All 3 plan and cycle combinations were priced. Left
out: 32 sample.* A screen that silently priced the first twenty-five of forty combinations
would look identical to one that covered the estate; this one cannot.

**Sample and demonstration accounts are never picked.** A utility trying the product on
