demo data and a utility going live on its own are two different questions, and the grid only
ever answers the second.

---

**Everything waiting on a person is now on one screen.**

Open **Work list** and you get findings from the checks, exceptions from the actions and
human tasks from a cutover plan, together, heaviest and oldest first. Each row says what
needs doing, which runbook found it, who owns it, how long it has been sitting there, and
carries a button to the screen that fixes it.

**The important part is the age.** If the morning sweep finds the same missing reading every
day for thirty days, that is **one item, thirty days old** — not thirty items, and not one
item that says *today* every morning. The thirty days is the number that tells a clerk
something has been ignored.

**And an item closes itself.** Fix the tax region, run the check again, and the row goes
away because the finding stopped coming back. Nobody has to remember to tick it off. A clerk
can still resolve or reopen one by hand; what they cannot get is a resolved item quietly
re-appearing as a brand-new row with its history lost.

### Fixed

* Every cell of the coverage grid would have opened onto a blank screen: the grid handed the
  browser a half-written address. Found by pressing a cell rather than by reading the code.
* One account the grid could not even start would have taken the entire grid down with it,
  reporting nothing at all instead of the other twenty-four cells and one refusal.
* The grid drew nothing at all on the demonstration utility, because every account there is
  demonstration data and the grid is right to skip it. The demo now carries some accounts of
  the utility's own, which is what a real one looks like.
* A runbook added by a script rather than from the library could become permanently
  unrunnable, refusing with *Review the template update* over an update that did not exist.
* A run's result screen answered an error for a few minutes this morning, over a name
  collision inside the server. Caught in the browser before anyone else saw it.

## [2.216.0] — 2026-09-07 · It runs at six in the morning without anybody there

**The product does something while the utility is asleep, and it does it on the utility's
own clock.**

Until today every job in Runbooks was something a person pressed. A runbook could carry a
schedule — *Daily at 06:00* — and the screen would show it, and nothing would ever happen.
Now it happens.

**Six o'clock means six o'clock where the utility is.** A utility in Texas and a utility in
New York can set the same runbook to the same time and they run an hour apart, because the
time on the screen is the time on their own wall clock and not a time in London. In winter a
06:00 Texas job runs at 12:00 UTC; in summer, 11:00. Nobody has to know that, which is the
point.

**And on the two Sundays a year when the clocks move, it does the right thing twice over.**
When the clock goes back and half past one happens twice, the job runs **once** — being late
is a delay, running twice is a duplicate that cannot be taken back. When the clock jumps
forward and half past two never happens at all, the job runs **an hour late rather than not
at all**, because a job that quietly did not happen is the one thing this whole change
exists to prevent.

**If a run is missed, you find out.** The old worry with anything scheduled is that it stops
and nobody notices for a fortnight. A firing that does not happen now appears in the history
as **Failed**, in plain words: *"This runbook should have run on 5 Jan 2026 at 06:00 CST and
did not."* Ten missed mornings are **one line saying ten**, not ten lines — and the same
missed stretch is never reported twice.

**A new screen: Run history.** Every run this utility has ever started, newest first —
when it started, which runbook, whether a person or the schedule started it, what happened,
how many records it touched and how long it took. Filter it to Checks, Actions, Failed or
Stopped, search it by name, and open any row to read that run's own result exactly as it
was written on the day.

**And the runbook's own page finally says when it runs next.** That line used to read *Not
set* on every runbook in the product, because nothing scheduled anything. It now says a real
date and time, in the utility's own zone.

Runs get their own worker, so a sweep over forty thousand accounts cannot sit in front of
somebody waiting for a download.

## [2.215.0] — 2026-09-06 · The county's list beside ours, and the letters that came back

**Two more jobs a clerk can press, and neither of them changes anything yet.**

**The county's property list, put beside ours.** Somebody uploads the county's file and the
job says what the two disagree about — which differences it is set to correct on its own,
which need a person, and which it will never touch whatever the file says. On the demo
utility, over nine county records against six of ours, it reads **"2 to apply. 5 need
you."**: two postcodes it would fix, five things to decide, one it refuses to change, and
two properties the county serves that we do not. **Every row you have to decide shows our
value and theirs side by side**, with *Accept theirs* and *Keep ours* beside them, so
nobody reads two systems and tries to remember which said what.

**Three things it will never change from an outside file** — inside city limits, city and
state. Those three decide what an address is charged, and a utility cannot add to that list
from a settings screen. A disagreement on one of them is shown and nothing is touched.

**The letters that came back.** When a letter is marked returned, the job stops using that
way of reaching the customer and **says where it falls back to instead**. On the demo
utility, over five returned letters, it reads **"5 to suppress. 0 have nothing left."** and
the table says *Post 5 → Email 5*. An account nobody can reach at all would be listed with
what it owes beside it, because that is the collections job's next problem.

**Neither job writes anything, and both say so on the screen** — the tiles read *To apply*
and *To suppress* rather than the past tense. Turning them on is a later, deliberate act.

**A job that finds nothing connected says so and stops.** No red errors, no crash: one step
marked, the rest reading *Never reached*, and a box saying what to do — upload the file, or
connect the service. That is the screen a new utility sees on its first morning, and it is
meant to be readable rather than alarming.

**Still missing, and named rather than implied.** Nothing in the product yet hears an email
bounce or a failed text from a provider, so today the only feedback anyone can act on is a
letter somebody marks returned — and the screen says that instead of showing a confident
zero. And nothing yet fetches the county's list automatically; a person uploads it.

## [2.214.1] — 2026-09-06 · The collections ladder could not run at all, and now a month of it has

**A month of the collections ladder was run against a real utility with sending switched
off, and it found six things.** Nobody was written to and nothing left the building: the
job plans what it would do, records it, and stops. Over five Mondays on a utility with
**1,035 accounts past due**, it planned **835 notices in the first week** — 323 reminders,
250 ten-day notices, 170 five-day notices and 92 certified final letters — and **878 across
the whole month, never sending the same letter to the same customer twice**. Sixty-two
accounts were never even looked at, because they are on a medical hold, in dispute, or are
demo records: those are excluded before anything else happens and cannot be reasoned back
in.

**Fixed: the job could not finish a single run.** On a real database it stopped on the very
first of a thousand accounts, every time, because of how it wrote down which piece of
software had made the decision. Nothing in the product could have told you — every
automated check passed. One line.

**What the month showed, and why the live half is NOT starting yet.** Four things have to
be right before a real letter is posted and none of them is today: switching the job to
live does not actually switch it on; with it switched on, every letter is refused because
nothing says what to put in the envelope; the screen that shows a clerk what would be sent
crashes rather than showing it; and the ladder does not climb — a customer would get the
first reminder and never the notices that follow it. All four are written down with the
figures behind them, and the decision to hold is recorded rather than assumed.

## [2.214.0] — 2026-09-06 · The runbook buttons do what they say, and the change log says who changed what

**Add, Clone and Change limits are buttons now.** The last release opened those three
doors in the product and left the screens pointing at them with *"Not connected yet."* —
so a utility could read about a feature it could not press. Pressing **+ Add** on a
template card puts the runbook on the utility's own list and opens it. Pressing **Clone**
on a row asks for a name, makes an independent copy — its own schedule, its own limit, its
own history — and opens that. Pressing **Change limits** sets how many records one run may
act on and who has to approve it, and the change takes effect from the next run.

**The runbook page was blank, and nobody could have seen it.** The page that shows a
runbook's settings had been drawing nothing at all since the morning of 6 September: the
screen and the server had each been built correctly against a different shape of the same
answer, and every test on both sides passed because neither test ever put the two together.
It now draws the real answer — the schedule, the steps, what the runbook may never touch,
the limits and the runs — and there is a check that fails if the two sides ever disagree
again.

**The Activity tab reads like a person wrote it.** Every change to a runbook is recorded,
and the tab now says what moved in words rather than in field names: *v2 · Cap set to 400 ·
Dana Whitfield · 09/06/2026*, newest first, with the version each change made. A copy's
first line names what it was copied from. Nothing on that tab is an internal code.

**Three things the screens deliberately do not say**, because the product does not know
them yet: the one-line description of what a runbook does, the sentence under each step
explaining the rule that decides it, and a schedule written out in words. Each is left
blank rather than filled with a guess or with the raw setting behind it.

**What still cannot be pressed, and why.** **Run** — starting a run is the next piece of
work. **Change scope** — a utility can already see which accounts, services and cycles a
runbook covers, and there is nowhere yet to save a change to them. Both say so in three
words, and both now carry a test that fails on the day the missing half arrives, so neither
can sit refusing over something that works.

**This closes the first phase of the runbooks work**: a utility can see what runbooks
exist, add one, copy it, change it, read a past result, and see who changed what and when.
Running one is phase two.

## [2.213.0] — 2026-09-06 · What would this customer's bill be? Ask, without billing them

**A clerk can now price one account exactly as the bill run would, see every line explained in
words, and nothing is written.** Pick an account, press Run, and the screen shows the total,
each charge with the quantity and the rate that produced it, a sentence saying why that amount,
and the same lines set beside the customer's last issued bill with the difference on each row.
No bill number is used, no draft is created, no books move. Press Run again as often as you
like — that is what it is for.

**When the account cannot be priced, it says so in one sentence and says where to go.**
*"Electric: no July price."* over *"Nothing was priced. Add a rate schedule to the plan, then
run this again."* That is not an error screen; it is the answer, and for a utility that has not
finished setting up it is the answer they will meet most. Nothing else is drawn beside it — no
row of empty tiles, no half a bill.

**The number this screen shows is the number the bill will show, and that is now true because
there is only one of it.** The five pricing stages a bill run walks were pulled out into one
function that both the run and this screen call, so the two cannot compute different lines: the
only difference is that the run then writes a draft and this does not. On the sample utility,
six of six accounts re-priced to the penny against bills the real pipeline issued weeks ago —
account `AC-2026-00001` came back `$160.52` over seven lines, matching its bill line for line.
The test that guards it compares at four decimal places rather than the two a person reads, and
it was proved by planting a quarter-of-a-cent difference and watching it be caught: at two
decimals both figures read `$49.44`.

**And the screen says which date it priced on, because that date changes the answer.** A bill is
priced on its bill day, not on the last day of the period, and rates change between the two. The
same account and the same July come to `$160.52` priced on 2 August and `$158.10` priced on
31 July, because water went from `$4.00` to `$4.24` a kgal on the first. Both figures are right;
what was missing was anything on screen saying which question had been asked. There is a tile
for it now, and without it a clerk comparing this screen with a bill would report a fault in a
bill that is correct.

**Known, and named rather than left to be found:** every money tile on a runbook result carries
the words *posting date* beside it, and a test bill posts nothing at all — the strip contradicts
its own sentence card two inches below. Filed; the fix belongs to the screen that draws the tile.

## [2.212.0] — 2026-09-06 · Add a runbook, copy one, change it — and be asked before we change yours

**A utility can now take a runbook out of the library, make a copy of it with different
settings, and change either one.** *Add* puts the shipped runbook on their own list. *Clone*
makes a second copy under a name they choose — the same dunning process for commercial
accounts, say — with its own schedule, its own limit and its own history. Editing either one
changes what it does from the next run onwards and writes down what moved, who moved it and
when.

**The part that matters most is what we stopped doing.** When we improve a runbook we ship,
every utility that has a copy of it used to get our change automatically, at their next run,
having been asked nothing. Now they are told: their runbook page says *Template updated · 1
new step · Review →*, and until somebody presses Review their copy keeps the steps it had.
A copy with an unreviewed update does not quietly run the new steps under the old version
number — it stops and says *Review the update first.*, which is one press away from being
fixed.

**A past run cannot be rewritten, and now the database is what says so.** Edit a runbook
twenty times and every earlier version is still there, exactly as it was, and a run that
happened last month still names the version that produced it and still shows the report it
produced. That was written down as a promise before and enforced by nothing.

**Two smaller things.** A runbook that has been edited runs as a rehearsal only until somebody
has looked at a clean rehearsal — a check that changes nothing is never held that way, because
it changes nothing. And the runbook list now shows people what belongs to their job: a finance
user sees the finance, payments and collections runbooks and not the platform ones, an
administrator sees everything, and an administrator can widen or narrow any single runbook by
hand. It decides what is SHOWN and never what is allowed.

**What a person still cannot do from these screens.** Press Run — starting a run is the next
piece of work. The three doors this release opens are Add, Clone and Change.

## [2.211.1] — 2026-09-06 · A billing clerk can run the by-premises report again

**Two screens a billing clerk is meant to use were quietly refusing them.** Reports →
By premises said *"Set the fiscal year start to see the current period."* at a utility whose
fiscal year start is set, and never ran the report at all — the sentence pointed at a Settings
screen only a system administrator can open. Payments → Refunds, the screen a clerk raises a
refund on, carried the same sentence in its heading.

**Why.** Both asked the Settings service which month the books are in, and Settings is
administrator-only. That is the same fault that made the whole product unusable for a clerk
between 21 August and this morning; fixing it moved the two things the app frame needs and
left everything else where it was.

**What changed.** The read every signed-in person may make now also carries the current
accounting period — which period it is, the dates it covers, and whether it is open. It still
carries none of the utility's close policy: the accounting method, the close cadence, the
close day, the closed-period lock and the hand-off deadline stay with Settings, so a clerk is
told which month they are working in and not when the books are due. Settings itself did not
move: a clerk opening it is refused exactly as before.

**And the product is now walked as a clerk, twice.** Every browser walkthrough in this project
signed in as an administrator until this morning, which is why a total lockout went unnoticed
for sixteen days. There are now two that sign in as a billing clerk: one that clicks through
their ordinary day, and one that runs the report and opens the refunds queue.

## [2.211.0] — 2026-09-06 · The screen that shows what a check found

**Runbooks can now show you an answer.** When a check has run, its result opens as a screen:
what stopped billing, in a sentence at the top; how many blockers and warnings; the ten steps
it walked, with the failed ones red and each one naming what it found; and a table of
findings where every row carries a button that takes you to the screen that fixes it.

**A green step now says what it looked at.** *"No findings"* over a utility with nothing set
up and *"no findings"* over a correctly configured one used to read the same. A step that
found nothing now says what it examined — *2,907 service points* — so you can tell a clean
result from an empty one.

**Behind it, a fault worth naming.** The part that runs a check and the part that draws its
answer had drifted apart: every one of the six things a result contains was being produced in
one shape and expected in another, including two lists of status names with nothing in common.
Both halves were correct on their own terms and every test passed, because the only thing
being checked was that the two sides used the same *names* for those six things — never that
they agreed on what was inside them. The result screen would have drawn nothing at all.

That is fixed, and it cannot happen again quietly: a real check run is now kept as a reference
sample, the engine is tested against it, and the screen is tested by drawing it. Neither side
can change without the other noticing.

**Not yet.** You cannot press a button to start a check — that arrives with the half of
Runbooks that acts on what it finds. What this release adds is the screen that shows a
finished one.

## [2.210.0] — 2026-09-06 · When a computer does something to a bill, the history says which computer job it was

**Until today, if one of our automatic jobs charged a customer, the account history left the
"who did this" column blank.** A blank looks exactly like a bill run, like an import, and like a
bug — so a clerk taking a call about a charge she did not make could not tell the customer
anything at all. The only alternative was worse: an automatic job could be set up under a staff
member's login, and then the history said *that person* had done it.

**Why it matters, with real numbers.** An overnight job adds a **$25** returned-payment fee to
**43** accounts — **$1,075** charged while nobody is in the office. Six weeks later a customer
rings about theirs. The clerk opens that account's history and it now reads
**"Returned payments, version 4"**. She can look up what version 4 of that job does and answer
the question properly, instead of saying she does not know.

**A job can no longer sign a colleague's name to its work — and not merely by convention.** Our
code refuses it, and the database itself refuses it as well, so somebody writing new code next
year cannot bring the problem back without the database stopping them.

**Nothing already in your history changed.** Every entry reads exactly as it did yesterday: a
person's entry still shows the person, and a job with no name of its own still reads
*System job*. The audit trail does not allow anything to be edited, ever, and that includes us —
so this adds a new kind of entry rather than rewriting any old one.

**And you can now filter for it.** The Actor filter on the audit log has an *Automations* entry
beside *System job*, so "show me everything a computer did" is one click.

## [2.209.2] — 2026-09-06 · Both maps draw again

**Two map screens were broken, and neither fault was in a map.** They were reported from
the running product: the asset map used to work and had stopped, and the work map had never
placed a single job.

**The asset map had lost its background.** It showed the right filter line — *Showing 115 of
115 assets* — over a flat grey rectangle with the zoom buttons working and a few black blobs
on it. The blobs were the 115 asset pins, drawn correctly on top of no map at all. Yesterday's
release added a security rule to every page that says which outside addresses the page is
allowed to fetch from, which is a good thing to have and was built to say *none* until a
utility connects one. But nothing has ever created that connection for any utility, and the
map still went on asking the map service for pictures. The browser refused every one of them,
silently: **18 tiles asked for, 0 arrived.** The map and the security rule now read the same
single fact, so the address the page is allowed to call and the address it actually calls can
never disagree again. If a utility switches its map service off, the map draws no background
and says *"Background map is switched off."* rather than showing the same grey square.

**The work map had never placed a job.** It said *"No job on this list has a place on the
map yet."* over *"NOT ON THE MAP · 17 JOBS"*, and it was telling the truth: none of those jobs
had a location to be drawn at. A job takes its place from the property it is at, and the demo
data only ever gave coordinates to the first batch of properties we invented — the ones the
accounts and bills use. Every job in the demo stands on a *later* batch, added for new
connections and move-ins, and those were skipped without a word. **All 17 jobs are now on the
map and the *not on the map* list is empty.** The step that fills coordinates also now names
any address it could not place, so the next batch of demo properties cannot be skipped in
silence.

⚠ **The work map needs one command run against an existing utility.** Coordinates are data,
not code, so a redeploy alone does not add them: run `load_sample_data --tenant <utility>`
once. It is safe to re-run — it fills only blanks and never moves a pin somebody has set by
hand. The asset map needs nothing but the redeploy.

## [2.209.1] — 2026-09-06 · A Billing Clerk can use the product again

**For sixteen days a Billing Clerk could not use SMARTBillHub at all.** They could sign in,
they reached the dashboard, and then every single screen showed *"We couldn't load your
regional settings."* with a Try again button that could never work. Not one screen in the
product was usable. This started on 21 August and was found on 6 September, by signing in as
a clerk and looking.

**What was wrong.** Before it can draw anything, the app has to know two things about your
utility: how you write dates and numbers, and what your name and logo are. It was asking for
both through the Settings screens — and Settings is deliberately closed to a Billing Clerk,
because your date format sits on the same page as your accounting method and your
close-period lock. So the app was refused the one thing it needed to draw a date, and
correctly so.

**What changed.** Those two facts now come from their own place. Formatting and branding are
not settings *administration* — they are what any screen needs before it can print a date or
draw your logo in the corner — so anyone signed in to your utility can read them, and nobody
can change them from there. Settings itself has not moved an inch: your accounting method,
close cadence, close day and closed-period lock are still yours and your executive's alone,
and a clerk is still turned away from every Settings tab exactly as before.

**And a check that did not exist.** Every one of this product's 92 click-through walkthroughs
signed in as a system administrator, which is why nothing caught this. One of them now signs
in as a Billing Clerk and works through the product the way a clerk does.

## [2.209.0] — 2026-09-06 · Runbooks is on the menu, and what "configurable" actually means

**Runbooks now has a place on the left-hand menu, above Reports.** Clicking it opens an
honest page that says what Runbooks will do and what it is waiting for, because the part
behind it is built and the screens are next. Showing the door before the room is finished is
deliberate: hiding it would tell a utility the product is smaller than it is. There is also a
new check that turns red the day those screens land and the menu item is still pointing at the
holding page — so the door cannot stay shut over a room that is ready.

**And a much bigger change, which makes the work smaller rather than larger.** A runbook is
one fixed process. Nobody rearranges its steps — not a utility, not us at setup time. What a
utility changes is its **inputs**: which services, which cycles, which kinds of account, how
much is "past due". Each input offers only what that utility actually has, so a two-service
utility sees two services and not eleven.

**"All" now means all, permanently.** If a utility says *all services* today while it sells
water and sewer, and adds trash next month, the next run covers **three**. That sounds
obvious and it is the thing this kind of software usually gets wrong: the alternative is to
write down the two services on the day someone ticks the box, after which adding a service
quietly drops it out of every one of these jobs, with nothing on any screen to show it.

**Who does the assembling, and why it is us.** The building blocks these jobs are made of are
ours, not a utility's: 173 pieces of work across 26 jobs, which turn out to be 137 genuinely
different ones. A utility never has to assemble anything out of them. That is a deliberate
choice and the reason is that this is a new idea for everyone — nobody running a two-person
utility should have to build a process out of a hundred parts before they can use one.

**One check turned out not to be checking.** The test that makes sure every item on the
left-hand menu opens a real screen had been looking at a loading placeholder rather than at
the screens themselves, so it would have passed over a product where nothing opened at all. It
was found by adding the Runbooks item and watching three things fail at once. It is fixed, and
it now proves it can tell a working screen from a missing one before it checks anything else.

## [2.208.1] — 2026-09-06 · A billing clerk could not use the new address lookup at all

**The one person the new screen was built for was locked out of it, and everything we run
said the release was fine.** Looking up an address against the city's records, and creating a
property from what came back, were both restricted to system administrators — by accident,
because they were added next to the settings screens and picked up the settings rules. A
billing clerk asking the city for an address got a flat refusal, and the panel read that
refusal as *this utility has no city connection* and quietly took itself off the screen. So
she saw no error and no explanation: the feature simply was not there.

Both are now open to the same people who may already add a property by hand, and creating one
is still refused for everybody else — twice over, at the door and again at the write.

**A second fix in the same area.** The address panel used to draw itself for every utility,
including the great majority that have no city records connection at all: a heading and three
boxes that did nothing, sitting directly above the property form's own address field, until
somebody typed three characters into them and they disappeared. It now asks once, quietly,
when the screen opens, and appears only where there is a city to ask.

**And a refusal that said nothing.** If someone typed something that was not a number into a
map coordinate, the field refused with no words at all — the message existed in the code and
in none of the eleven languages. It reads *"Enter a number, like 30.2672."* now, in all
eleven.

**And picking the same address twice used to break the page.** A city parcel number can only
belong to one property, which is right — but choosing an address that already has one gave a
blank failure with a database message behind it, instead of saying what was wrong. It now says
*"Another property already has that parcel."* This is an ordinary thing to do: two people
adding properties, or the same person coming back to a page they left open.

**What found all of this:** a test on a neighbouring screen went red for what looked like a
cosmetic reason — two boxes on one screen both called *Address*. Following that one failure
is what turned up the lockout.

## [2.208.0] — 2026-09-06 · A checklist now physically cannot write to your accounts

**Still nothing on screen, and still the right order.** Yesterday Runbooks got seven tables of
its own and a wall around them. Today it got the thing that decides what a runbook IS — and the
first thing that shape does is make one promise impossible to break.

**The promise: a checklist has nothing to write with.** Runbooks come in two kinds. A **Check**
looks at your data and tells you what it found. An **Action** does something — sends a notice,
applies a payment, adds a fee. Until today, *"a Check does not write"* was a sentence somebody
had written down. From today it is a fact about how the software is built: if an engineer wrote
a Check and gave it the ability to send a letter, **the product would refuse to start**, and the
message would name the checklist and the exact ability it should not have had. Not a warning in
a log. Not a mistake found on a Monday. The thing does not run.

**Why that matters more than it sounds.** The dangerous version of automation is not the one
that does nothing — somebody notices that. It is a badly set-up job quietly sending three
thousand wrong shut-off letters in four minutes, and **a letter cannot be unsent**. So the part
built first is the part that makes the safe answer the only possible one.

**And a checklist that meets one bad record no longer loses the whole run.** If a run looks at
a thousand accounts and one of them cannot be written for some reason, the other nine hundred
and ninety-nine still count. That sounds obvious; it is the single most common way this kind of
job goes wrong, it does not show up in ordinary testing, and it was proved here against a real
database rather than assumed. With the protection removed, one bad record out of four cost
**three** of them.

**What this buys a utility later, in one line:** adding the twenty-third checklist to this
product is one file written by one engineer, with no new screen — which is why there can
eventually be thirty-four of them rather than three.

## [2.207.2] — 2026-09-06 · The new security header would have turned off the product's own typeface

**Caught before anybody saw it, and only by opening a browser.** Yesterday's release gave
every page a list of the outside addresses it may fetch from — the first this product has
ever had. The list left out the one this product uses itself: the web address the SMARTBillHub
typeface is served from. The browser would have quietly declined it and drawn every screen in
whatever plain font the computer had to hand. Nothing on our side would have noticed: a
refusal like that is a line in the browser's own console and nothing else — no error, no
failed request, no test that can see it.

The typeface's address is on the list now, in both of the two places the list is written
down, and there is a check that fails if those two ever disagree again.

**And the walkthrough that found it now looks for this on purpose.** It opens the map — the
screen the list exists for — watches for anything the browser refuses, and stops if it
refuses anything at all.

## [2.207.1] — 2026-09-06 · Two fixes the browser found: the map's own address, and the two search boxes the design drew

**The security header named the wrong address, and would have blocked the right one.** Every
page now tells the browser the exact list of outside addresses it may fetch from. For a
utility whose city runs both an address service and a map server — two different machines on
one relationship — the list named the **address service** and left out the **map server**. So
the city's own map would have drawn nothing, and an address service the browser has no reason
to talk to was on the permitted list. It names the map server now, and a utility that has not
set one gets a list with nothing outside on it at all.

**And the address search drew one box where the design draws three.** *Unit* and *Zip* are
back, and they do something: what a clerk types into them narrows what the City is asked for,
so knowing the unit or the postcode gets fewer and better matches rather than the same long
list.

Both were found by opening the screen in a browser and reading what came back — the only
thing that can see either of them.

## [2.207.0] — 2026-09-06 · Runbooks exists, and the first thing it can do is refuse

**Nothing on screen changed today, and that is the honest headline.** This is the
first line of code of Runbooks — the part of the product that will let a utility
press one button and be told exactly what is stopping billing, and later do some
of the work itself. What landed is the shape of it: seven tables of its own, and
a boundary that stops it reaching into anything else.

**What a utility gets from this, even though they cannot see it.** The dangerous
thing about a feature that acts on your accounts is not that it does nothing —
somebody notices that. It is a badly set-up job quietly queueing three thousand
wrong shut-off letters in four minutes, and **a letter cannot be unsent**. So the
first thing built is not the acting; it is the wall. There are **thirteen doors**
out of this new part of the product to the rest of it — queue a notice, apply a
payment, add a fee, write a reading, flag an account, and eight more — and today
**not one of them is connected to anything**. A checklist that only looks at your
data holds none of those doors at all: it is not that it is told not to write, it
is that it has nothing to write with.

**Nothing here can touch another utility's data**, proved on the real database
under a login that gets no special treatment: with nobody signed in, all seven
new tables answer **zero rows**, and under one utility's session not one row of
another utility's is reachable in either direction. That is checked on
PostgreSQL, where the protection actually exists, and the check is **skipped
rather than pretended** on the small local database that has none.

**And the same run twice cannot do the same thing twice** — the database itself
carries the lock that makes a repeat impossible. ⚠ **One honest caveat, written
down rather than smoothed over:** *what* gets locked — the fingerprint we work
out for each letter — is written two different ways in our own documents, and one
of those ways would let a second run send everything again. Nothing sends
anything yet, so nothing is at risk; the fingerprint is settled when the
collections chase-up is actually built, with the real thing in front of us
(`DEF-RBS-4246`, `OQ-RBS-1737`).

**For the team.** `06-backend/apps/runbooks/` is the twelfth code module: seven
tables under RLS FORCE, nine read seams, thirteen unbound ports.
`07-frontend/src/features/runbooks/` is on the Route B ledger **before** its first
component, because a Tailwind class in a file the ledger does not cover renders
as nothing while every test passes. `G115` is the boundary gate and was shown red
on two planted violations through `run_gates.py` — a foreign import in
`selectors.py` and a write inside a seam — then green. `13-selector-inventory.md`
lists the fourteen reads no module exposes yet, with the owning module named for
each, so wave Q does not discover them on the day.

## [2.206.0] — 2026-09-06 · A payment machine can now tell us about a payment, and telling us twice does not charge anybody twice

**A customer puts $42.10 in cash into a kiosk in a supermarket at two minutes
past two, and the kiosk tells us.** Until today there was nowhere for it to
say so: the door a machine posts to did not exist, and the only way that money
reached an account was a clerk typing it in from a report the next morning.

**The door exists now, and the thing it is built around is the second call.**
Payment machines re-send. They re-send on a timeout, on a slow reply, and
sometimes days later, and they are right to — from where they stand, silence
and failure look the same. So the interesting question was never *what happens
when a payment arrives*, it was *what happens when the same payment arrives
twice*. **It is recognised as the same one, answered before anything is
written, and there is exactly one record of it, not two.** A second record
would be $42.10 the customer never paid, sitting on their account, and the
product would quietly spend it on their next bill.

**A refund carrying the same reference is not a duplicate, and getting that
wrong would have been invisible.** When the cash comes back two days later the
kiosk tells us about the return — and its own system reuses the reference of
the payment it is reversing. A door that simply remembered references would
have refused **every refund the product ever saw**, with an answer the kiosk
reads as *we already have that*. The reference is stored with a word saying
which of the two it is, so the payment and its return are two records and
neither hides the other.

**Nobody who is not the kiosk gets in, and they cannot tell why not.** The
kiosk presents a key we issued it and calls from an address it published in
advance. A call with the wrong key, a call from an address that is not on the
list, and a call naming a connection this utility does not have all get the
same six words and the same number — so somebody holding a stolen key learns
nothing about how close they got. **Both checks happen before we read what was
sent at all**: a stranger cannot make this product open their message.

**What this release deliberately does NOT do, and it matters for anyone
planning around it.** The money does not reach the customer's balance yet. The
Product Owner ruled this morning that landing what a partner sends and
*deciding what it means* are two separate jobs, and only the first one is built
here. So a kiosk payment today is a record on file — authenticated, recognised,
and exactly what the kiosk sent, kept unaltered — waiting for the half that
puts it on the account. That half is scheduled and it is not late; it simply is
not this release, and the product says so rather than looking finished.

**A number that was wrong in the settings, and would only have shown up in
front of a customer.** When the kiosk asks *what does this account owe* and the
account does not exist, our configuration said to answer *this address does not
exist*. The kiosk network reads that as *the utility's system has gone away*
and stops asking — for every account, not just the missing one. It now answers
normally and says *no such account* in the reply, which is what their
specification asks for.

## [2.205.0] — 2026-09-06 · Type an address, see the City's own records, and know which properties were never checked

**What a clerk can do now that they could not.** On *Add premises*, type the start of an
address and the City's matching records appear in **about a third of a second** — up to
eight of them, each with the City's parcel number and one word: **strong match** or
**close match**. Press **Use this** and the address, the city, the state, the postcode and
the City's own map pin fill in. Press **Create** and the City is asked one more time, at
that exact moment, whether it still holds that parcel — because a city can split a parcel
between the moment you looked and the moment you pressed.

**Nothing is written while you are looking.** The list is an offer. Until somebody picks a
row and presses Create, not one row exists.

**When the City cannot be reached, the screen says so — and you can still get on with your
day.** No spinner, no spinning wheel that suggests waiting will help. An amber box says *we
cannot reach the City's address records right now*, you type the address yourself, and the
property is created carrying **no parcel number** and the words **Address not checked with
the City** — everywhere that property is shown, until a later run checks it. That mark is
the point: without it, a property attached to a parcel the City may have split looks
identical, on every screen, to one the City confirmed a second ago.

**Two calls this product has been making since August now have a card, a switch, and a
home.** The asset map draws its background from Esri — hundreds of small images per pan,
each telling them roughly where the utility's equipment is — and the address service the
product uses to put pins on the map is the US Census one. Both were accepted by ruling in
August, both were written into the code's notes, and **neither had anywhere a utility could
see it or turn it off.** Both now appear in Settings with a health state and a switch, and
the map's background server is a field a utility can point at its own city's map service.

**And the browser is now told what it may fetch.** This product had **no page-security
policy at all** — which meant the browser's answer to *what may this page load* was
*anything*. Every page now carries one, and it is **generated** rather than typed: it lists
exactly the outside addresses the utility has connected, and no others. Switch the map card
off and the list becomes none. Point it at a city's own map server and the policy follows,
with no change to any code.

**What is not here.** The nightly check of the City's whole parcel file against the
utility's properties — that is a separate, larger piece of work. And the same address job
as a scheduled overnight batch, or as a *run it once* button, both of which the Product
Owner asked for in the same breath as this one: those run on the engine that has not been
built yet, and neither is started.

## [2.204.0] — 2026-09-06 · Collect two years of meter readings, and nothing gets billed from a guess

**A utility can now connect its water meter cloud and collect from it.** The card
was already on the Integrations screen; pressing **Connect** answered *"Cannot be
connected yet."* This release is the part that makes it work.

**Two years of readings, collected in one go.** The supplier hands them over a
week at a time, so a two-year backfill is **105 weekly chunks** and takes about
two hours. If it stops half way — the supplier restarts, the network drops — it
picks up at the chunk it reached. **Chunks 1 to 60 are not fetched again.**

**The pass the supplier issues lasts ten minutes, and the collection takes two
hours.** So we swap the utility's stored key for a fresh pass about a dozen times
while it runs. Those passes are never written down, and **the key history a clerk
reads still shows one entry before and one after** — not the 144 entries a day it
would otherwise fill up with, on one connection.

**Four things every reading request now says out loud, and two of them are about
money.** This supplier's system has defaults that are not safe for us: if the
request does not say *actual consumption*, it sends back its own **estimates**,
in the same shape as real readings, and a utility would bill them. The other two
are the unit — their default is gallons at one site and cubic feet at the next —
and the time zone, because a midnight reading landing on the wrong day is a
reading in the wrong billing period. **A request that leaves any of the four
unsaid does not run, and the screen says which one was missing:** *"not started —
actual_consumption was not set"*. Nothing is sent.

**When the supplier builds a file while you wait, the screen says so and you can
leave.** *They are building the file. We will collect it when it is ready · asked
them 4 times · checking again in 30 seconds.* Close the tab, come back, and the
file is there with a link. If they never finish, the run reads **Unconfirmed**
with *they never finished the file* — never "done" over a file we do not have,
and never "failed" over a supplier who is simply still working.

**An export that closes billing routes on the supplier's side happens once.**
That request changes their system, not ours, and closing twice is a mistake we
cannot undo from here. A second attempt for the same month reads **"already
closed on 1 Sep"**, naming the day the first one happened, and nothing is sent.

**Fixed:** the print vendor's hand-over said *"they build it while we wait"* and
never said how often to ask or what the answer would look like — a print job
handed over would have waited for ever. It now asks every minute for an hour.

## [2.203.0] — 2026-09-06 · The month's journal has somewhere to go, and it remembers

**What a utility can do now that it could not yesterday.** Alex, who does the
books at Brazos Bend, can save where the month's journal goes — *Month-end
journal · QuickBooks · downloaded here* — and the product remembers it. Before
this, the export screen offered four file formats every month and recorded
nothing about the destination at all; a clerk who chose IIF in July had to
remember to choose IIF again in August, and nothing anywhere would have told
them if they had not.

**Press *Test it now* and it answers *Wrote an empty QuickBooks file.*** It
means what it says: a real QuickBooks Desktop file, with QuickBooks' own header
lines in it and no entries. That is deliberate — it proves the product can
build and place a file **without asking anybody what belongs in one**, which is
the only thing a test is allowed to prove on a live production destination at
four in the afternoon.

**Ask for the same month twice and the second one is refused, in words.** *July
was already exported on 5 Aug* — naming the day the first one went, so a clerk
can go and look at it. An accounting system that is handed July twice books
July's revenue twice, and the failure nobody asks about is the third one: a
second July file that quietly DIFFERS from the first, leaving an accountant
holding two files that both claim to be the same month and cannot be told
apart. Asking for August still works, and asking for July in a different format
still works, because those are two accountants rather than one
double-handover — both are checked, because a door that refused everything
would look exactly the same as one that refuses correctly.

**Ask for a format nobody registered and it says which ones exist.** *xlsx is
not a registered format — QuickBooks, Xero, CSV, IIF*. A clerk told only *no*
is left guessing.

**What is deliberately still missing, said plainly.** The file the product
builds today has no figures in it. Deciding which of a month's numbers becomes
a journal line, and whether three accounts are still missing their accounting
code, is work that belongs to a different part of the system that has not been
built yet — and the boundary was drawn by the Product Owner rather than assumed
by us. Two doors are open on this side waiting for it, both answering nothing,
and a test fails the day either one starts answering something without the
boundary being moved on purpose.

**Two problems were found by building this and both are written down rather
than quietly worked around.** The accounting export column in the books mixes
up *where the file goes* with *what shape it is in* — QuickBooks is a place and
CSV is a shape, and they were four values in one list, so a utility that wanted
a plain CSV dropped in a folder for its Xero bookkeeper could not say so. That
is fixed on the connection and left alone in the books, where changing it would
move a signed rule. And a utility can save only ONE accounting destination
today, so the QuickBooks handover and a CSV copy for the auditor cannot both be
remembered — the handover itself works either way.

**Bank statements in the newer ISO format can now be read**, though the product
does not yet claim to support them: that claim needs a real statement from a
real bank recorded in the repository, and nobody can decide one into existence.


## [2.202.0] — 2026-09-06 · Runbooks is written down — and a utility can do nothing today that it could not yesterday

**Start with the honest part: nothing in the product has changed.** No screen is
new, no button does anything it did not do before, and no utility can do one
thing today it could not do yesterday. This release is a **specification** —
the written-down shape of a feature nobody has built a line of yet — and it is
in the changelog because the shape itself was agreed this week and because four
things that were missing from it are now in place.

**What Runbooks will be, in one paragraph.** One engine that walks a set of
things — every account past due, every meter that has not been read, every
setting a bill needs — applies the utility's own written process to each one,
and either **tells you what needs fixing** or **does the work**. Those are two
different kinds and the difference is built into the machinery rather than
promised in a document: the telling kind is constructed **without the ability to
write anything at all**, so it cannot change a customer's record even by
mistake. The doing kind writes only after a dry run you can read, a batch
approval that carries the count you agreed to, a limit that **refuses** the run
rather than quietly doing the first four hundred, and a stop button that works
mid-flight. **Thirty-four of these are described, one screen set draws all of
them**, and the first one a clerk would press answers *"can we bill?"* in ten
steps with a button beside each thing that is wrong.

**Four things that were missing from that specification, and now are not.**
Three end-to-end journeys — get to billable, prove it on their data, and a
guarded send — were **named thirty-eight times across ten documents and did not
exist as files**; they exist now, each one written so that a wrong build fails
it. The screen inventory did not know the runbook screens existed. The database
brief carried **none** of the seven tables the feature needs — two teams closed
that within the same hour, one writing the tables and one writing the complete
list of every way the feature is allowed to reach outside itself, and the second
found the first only at the last moment, which is worth saying because the near
miss was a whole section of somebody else's work. And this entry is the
changelog line the feature did not have.

**Three mistakes were found inside the source documents and corrected while this
was written, and they are worth naming because each would have cost real work.**

* **The list of everything the automation can ever do to a customer is thirteen
  things, not four.** The source said *four* in seven places and *thirteen* in
  one, and it was wrong in two ways at once: the count, and one of the four it
  named. *Raising a note for a person to look at* is not one of the thirteen —
  it is something the engine does on its own — and that distinction is the only
  reason the *telling* kind of runbook can put items on your work list while
  still having no ability to write anything. **Building the four-item version
  would have given every one of them the ability to write.**
* **One rule number was being used for two different rules** — a tie-out
  tolerance for tax of $0.00, and an unrelated rule about how a new category
  gets added. Anyone following that number for the second rule would have landed
  on a money figure. The tax rule keeps the number; the other was dropped,
  because two rules already say what it said.
* **Six error codes read `RBS-001` to `RBS-006`, and `RBS-001` is now the name of
  a screen.** They were also the wrong shape for this product, which names its
  refusals in words rather than numbers. They are now named — *the plan changed*,
  *too many for one run*, and so on — in all eleven languages.

**And two contradictions found in the source were NOT resolved, deliberately,
because they are somebody's decision and not ours.** Whether a re-run of a
collections batch may send a letter a second time — the documents disagree with
themselves, and the wrong answer means **496 letters where 248 were meant** —
and whether the money column on a run's records needs a currency beside it.
Both are written up where the work will start, so the first person to build this
meets them before writing code rather than after.

## [2.201.1] — 2026-09-06 · The integrations screens stop wasting your time, and say what they mean

**The Product Owner opened Settings → Integrations, tried to use it, and could
not finish anything.** Sign-in did nothing on Microsoft 365 and did nothing on
Google Workspace. No connection could be added. No test would run. This release
does not build the missing plumbing — two other teams are doing that right now —
it stops the screens pretending the plumbing is there.

**Half the cards were offering a connection this product cannot yet make.**
Seven of the fourteen live services — the print vendor, the bulk mailer, the
city's address lookup, the map tiles, the accounting file, the meter head-end
and the census geocoder — drew a **Connect** button, opened a full form, and
waited while a clerk chose an environment and typed a server name, a port, a
user name, a password and an address. Only then, on the last press, did they
answer *"Cannot be connected yet."* Now the card says so up front: the button is
there, greyed, with the words **"Not ready to connect yet."** underneath it, and
pressing it opens nothing. **You find out before you type, not after.**

**Nobody has to remember to switch those seven back on.** The card asks the
server, on every single draw, whether this product has anything that can talk to
that service. The day one of them is built, its card goes live by itself. There
is no list to update and no second job to forget — which is exactly how four
buttons on the customer portal stayed greyed out for days over screens that had
already shipped.

**Signing in to Microsoft or Google is now one press, at the bottom, where every
other button is.** It used to be a quiet grey button halfway up the form, inside
a box, inside another box — and the only button at the *bottom* of that window
was **Cancel**. So the one thing that finishes the job looked like a detail and
the way out looked like the main event. It is now the main button in the footer,
and it reads *Sign in with Microsoft*.

**And the box asking where to send bills from is gone from that window.** It was
marked as needed, it could not be skipped, and nothing was ever done with what
you typed — the address is settled by whoever you sign in as, which is the whole
point of signing in. It was collecting keystrokes and throwing them away.

⚠ **Sign-in will still refuse, and that is not fixed here.** It refuses because
the registration that identifies us to Microsoft and to Google has never been
filled in on any server we run — it is a setting that lives with the
installation, not in the product. That is written down and handed on. What has
changed is that you now spend one click finding out instead of a filled-in form.

**The window stopped looking like a sketch of itself.** It carried a bordered
box headed **WHAT THIS CONNECTION NEEDS** in shouty capitals, wrapped around a
second grey box, with four more shouty captions and several lines set in
typewriter type. All of that came from the design drawing, where it was a note
to a developer explaining how the *drawing* worked — not a part of the screen.
The fields are simply the form now. Typewriter type is kept only for the masked
last four characters of a password, where you actually compare characters.

**Required boxes are marked.** *Send bills from* was an empty box with no
asterisk, no example and no hint, on a form where the other boxes were optional.

**"There is no Save here — the round trip is the save."** is gone. A round trip
is our word for our own machinery. It now reads *"Signing in is all there is —
nothing else to fill in."*

**"Nothing to test"** on the Third-party GL card was read as *this is broken*.
It is not — there is genuinely nothing to test until the partner calls us for
the first time. It now says so the right way round: *"Ready. It starts working
when they first call us."*

**You can search the services now**, which matters at eighteen cards, and a
search that finds nothing says so and offers the way back. Before this, filtering
to a category with nothing in it drew a silent blank page.

Eleven defects were written up on the way, including three this release does not
fix and does not pretend to: the sign-in registration above, two comments in the
back end still claiming features are unbuilt after they shipped, and a mappings
screen that manages to say *"Every word is mapped."* and *"Nothing recorded
yet."* at the same time.

## [2.201.0] — 2026-09-06 · Eleven days' warning before the mailbox stops

**A utility is now told, in words and with a date, that its mailbox is about to
stop sending bills — eleven days before it happens.** Silver Creek connects
Microsoft 365 by signing in rather than by typing a password, and Microsoft asks
for that permission again every ninety days. Until today nobody found out it had
run out until a Friday when Tuesday's bills had never left. Now the connection's
own screen and the dashboard both read **"Needs re-authorising by 09/17/2026.
After that, bills stop going out."** — the date written the way that utility
writes dates, so a tenant on the European format reads *17.09.2026*.

**Re-authorising takes about a minute and loses nothing.** Press *Re-authorise
now*, sign in with Microsoft, come back: the warning is gone, the connection is
on its second permission, the first one is still recorded, and every one of the
twenty nightly sends from before is still listed on the screen. That last part
is the promise the whole feature turns on — a renewal is not a fresh start.

**Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace can both be connected now.** A utility
sends bills from its own mailbox, signs in at the provider's own screen, and we
never see or store the password. What we keep is the permission they hand back,
shown as `••••A17C` and never readable by anyone, us included.

**One thing this release does NOT do, said plainly:** the warning reaches the
dashboard and the connection's own screen, and it does **not** send an email to
the system administrators. That half needs a piece of the notifications module
that does not exist yet, and rather than send a message that would have read
*"Sign-in about to lapse: 1 of 1 failed"*, it sends none and says so.

## [2.200.0] — 2026-09-06 · A key you hand a partner, shown once, and revoked in a heartbeat

**A utility can now give its finance system a key of its own, and take it back
without warning anybody.** Alex opens *Third-party GL* under Settings →
Integrations, presses **Issue key**, and the key appears once — in a box of its
own, with a Copy button and the sentence *"Copy it now. This is the only time it
is shown."* Close the panel, reload the page, come back tomorrow: the screen
shows `••••b8e3` and nothing more, for ever. There is no button anywhere that
brings it back, and no support call can produce it either, because **we do not
keep it**. What is stored is a one-way fingerprint that can recognise the key
and cannot reproduce it. If the finance company loses their copy, the answer is
to issue a new one, which takes one click and retires the old one on the spot.

**Revoking is immediate, and immediate means the next request.** Not the next
nightly collection, not when a cache expires — press *Revoke*, and the very next
call that partner makes is refused. We proved it as three requests in a row with
nothing in between: their call succeeds, the key is revoked, the same call one
statement later is refused.

**And a refusal gives nothing away.** A key that was mistyped, a key that was
revoked an hour ago, and a key that never existed all come back with the same
answer — the same words, the same bytes, and the same time on the clock. That
last part matters more than it sounds: if a revoked key were refused a fraction
of a second more slowly than a made-up one, somebody holding a stolen key could
learn from the delay that it used to be real. They come back within a whisker of
each other.

**A key belongs to one utility and cannot be pointed at another.** Brazos Bend's
partner presenting Brazos Bend's key at Lone Star Ridge's address is told
exactly what a complete stranger is told. That one is proved against a real
PostgreSQL server rather than the everyday test database, because the protection
is the database's own row-level security and the quick test database does not
have it — a pass there would have meant nothing.

**Every issue and every revoke is written to the audit log**, with the four
visible characters and never the key.

### Fixed on the way

* **A partner connection could not be created at all.** Saving the *Third-party
  GL* card answered *"Cannot be connected yet."* — because the code asked
  whether we had software to dial that provider, and a partner who reads *from*
  us is the one relationship we never dial. Both connectors of that kind were
  affected. (`DEF-INT-4215`)
* **A test that two files described in detail was not in the repository.** The
  partner door's own notes explain that the three refusals are compared
  byte-for-byte and by the clock, and name the file that does it; there is no
  such file. The comparison is now written and runs. (`DEF-INT-4216`)

### Still to come

Nothing on this screen is waiting for a decision. The partner's own reading
surface — the addresses they call, the allowed-address list and the log of what
they took — shipped the same day beside this.
## [2.199.0] — 2026-09-06 · A finance system can now collect a utility's payments, and the manager can see it happen

**A utility can hand an outside finance system a key and let it collect their
payments and bills on its own schedule — and every page it takes shows up on a
screen the manager reads.** Until today that whole direction did not exist:
every connector in the product was the utility reaching out to somebody else,
and this is the first one where somebody else reaches in.

**The screen is called *Who has been reading*, and it is the point of the
work.** It lists every collection with the date and time, what was taken
(*Payments, 1–30 Sep*), how many rows, and which key was used — shown as
`••••7Q2F`, never the key itself. A collection that is much larger than the
others is drawn heavier so it catches the eye. The example that made this
worth building: a partner with a perfectly valid key collecting **48,000**
payment records — two years of history — at twenty to three in the morning.
Every single request properly authorised, and there was previously nowhere in
the product that would have shown it.

**Three ways of being turned away, and they are deliberately identical.** If
the call comes from an address the utility has not listed, or the key is wrong,
or the key was revoked this morning, the answer is the same five words —
*We cannot serve this request* — with the same status and nothing else in it.
It is also held to the same minimum time, four hundredths of a second, because
a faster answer for one of them would tell somebody holding a stolen key that
the key is real and only the address is wrong.

**One partner cannot slow another utility's partner.** A key may make a hundred
requests a minute; the hundred-and-first is told to wait. The count is kept per
key *and* per utility, so a busy partner at one utility leaves the others
untouched — proved with two utilities side by side rather than reasoned about
with one. Honest limit, stated rather than implied: the count is kept inside
one web process, so if the product runs four of them a determined caller gets
four hundred a minute rather than a hundred. Closing that needs a shared
counter this product does not have yet.

**Which utility's data a partner sees comes from the web address, not from the
key.** A partner is given a link with the utility's own name in it. Present one
utility's key at another's address and it finds nothing and is refused in
exactly the same five words. That is the database refusing, not a check
somebody wrote, so it cannot be deleted by accident.

**And the register that answers "who else has our customers' data" now has a
row pointing the other way.** It reads as a sentence — *Aclarian — reads
payments, bills and customers — authorised by Dana Whitfield on 2026-09-03* —
and it is worked out from the live connection every time it is read, so nobody
has to remember to add a partner to a list. Where nobody recorded who gave
permission, it says *authorisation not recorded* rather than going quiet,
because that is exactly the thing an auditor is looking for.

**What is deliberately NOT in the payload.** A partner gets our own receipt
number, the date, the amount and the currency, and nothing else. Translating
our *Bank transfer* into their word for it, and naming the account in their
chart, is work that belongs to Runbooks rather than here — the rule the
Product Owner set on 5 September and sharpened on the 6th. A test asserts those
three fields are absent, so the day Runbooks fills them in, it will say so out
loud rather than happening quietly.

## [2.198.0] — 2026-09-06 · The same bank file, sent twice, is now refused the second time

**A utility can name the bank it gets its lockbox files from, and send us one.**
Until today the *Bank & lockbox file* card sat on the integrations screen looking
connectable and refused every attempt with *Cannot be connected yet.* — the card
was there, the settings behind it were there, and the one line that joins the two
was not. It is joined now. You give the connection a name (*Chase lockbox*), say
which format the bank sends and whether the file arrives by hand or sits in a
folder, and it is a connection like any other.

**And the point of the whole thing: if the same file arrives twice, the second one
is refused.** Someone uploads Tuesday's lockbox file on Tuesday. On Wednesday they
are not sure it went through and upload it again. The second upload comes back
**refused duplicate — the same file as Tuesday 06:10**, naming the first arrival so
they can go and look at it, and nothing is applied twice.

**We check the file BEFORE we read it, and that turns out to matter in two
directions.** We take a fingerprint of the file exactly as it arrived, before
anything opens it up. So a file that is identical is recognised as the same file
*even if we have since changed how we read bank files* — the answer to *have we had
this before* cannot be altered by us editing our own code. And a file that differs
by a single character is treated as NEW *even though it would read out to the same
payments*, which is the surprising direction and the safe one: we only ever refuse
something we can prove we already took.

**What we deliberately did NOT build, and why you will not see it yet.** Deciding
which payment in that file matches which customer account, and writing those
payments, is not this piece of work — the Product Owner drew that line on 5
September: *integrations connects to the bank, pulls the file, records that a batch
arrived — and stops.* So today the file arrives, is fingerprinted, is recorded, and
is refused if we have had it; what happens to the rows inside it is the next piece
of work and is not pretended at anywhere.

**Two things on screen were wrong before this and are fixed.** A run that we
deliberately declined to make — because it was a duplicate, or because a provider
was in trouble — was showing as **0 of 0**, which reads as a job that tried nothing
and succeeded. It now reads *Not attempted*, in all eleven languages; the word was
missing from every one of them, so what actually reached the screen was our own
internal word `skipped`.

**Proved by driving it, not only by testing it.** Against a real PostgreSQL and in a
real browser: connect the bank, send Tuesday's file (accepted), send it again
(refused, naming Tuesday), **and then send a genuinely different file and watch it
be accepted** — that last step is not decoration, because *nothing was written* is
also a perfect description of a door that is simply broken.

## [2.197.14] — 2026-09-06 · The panel comparing this August with last August was empty for everybody

**The screen that tells a customer why their bill went up has a panel down the
right-hand side comparing this month with the same month a year ago — and it
was blank on every bill, for every customer, on every account.** Not broken,
not showing an error: simply absent, because a panel with nothing to say is
supposed to disappear rather than sit there empty. So it looked like a design
choice.

The cause is one number. To compare August with last August you have to be able
to reach back **thirteen** months, and the screen was asking for twelve. The
code that fetches the history knows this and says so in its own notes; the
screen that calls it asked for the shorter window anyway, and nothing ever
compared the two. Measured on a real account with the readings present: one row
of history at the correct window, none at the one we shipped. It is fixed, and
a customer now reads *Water 4171 gal → 4820 gal* beside two bars. (Those
figures are missing their thousands comma, which is a separate fault we already
had written down against every screen that shows a quantity.)

**We drove that screen against four different bills to check it is actually
working things out, rather than repeating itself.** Every bill in our demo data
had gone UP, so a test that only ever looked at one of them would have been
satisfied by a screen with the words *cost more* painted on. Given a bill that
rose it says *this bill cost $3.74 more than last month* and lists four
reasons that add up to exactly $3.74; given one that fell it says *cost $3.74
less* with all four reasons reversed; given a bill that came to precisely the
same total as the month before it says *cost the same* — **and still names two
things that moved**, water up five dollars and tax down five, cancelling each
other out. That last one is the case that proves the reasons are worked out
from the bill rather than reverse-engineered from the total. On a customer's
very first bill it offers no comparison at all, rather than telling somebody
who has just moved in that they are paying $100 more than last month.

**Six things the drawing asks for that the product does not do are now written
down** rather than left to be noticed again later. The two most useful: the
chart labels both of its bars *Aug*, so you cannot tell this August from last
August; and the screen explains the bill and then offers no way to act on it,
where the design puts *Send a reading* and *Query this bill* underneath — both
of which are screens we finished days ago.

**And the second half of this piece of work is deliberately not built.** There
is a designed screen called *Your usage looks high* that would warn a customer
mid-month that they are using twice their normal water. Nothing in the product
can raise that alarm, and nothing pretends to: raising it needs a daily or
weekly meter reading and these utilities read once a month, so the earliest we
could ever tell somebody is on the bill itself — which is not a warning. The
design was drawn to force that decision, and it is recorded as decided rather
than as outstanding.

## [2.197.13] — 2026-09-06 · A payment receipt was dated tomorrow, and we could not make one settlement count twice

**Somebody who pays a bill without an account is shown a receipt, and the date
on it was wrong.** It read `2026-09-06T03:59:13.769308+00:00` — a computer's own
way of writing a moment — and worse, it was written in London's clock rather
than the utility's. A customer in Texas paying at eleven at night was handed a
receipt dated the NEXT day, on the one piece of paper they are most likely to
keep and the one they would quote back to us in an argument. It now reads
`09/05/2026 23:09`, in the utility's own format and its own time zone. The due
date on the page before it, and the *added* date on the saved-cards page, had
the same fault and are fixed the same way.

**We tried hard to make one payment count twice, and could not.** Card companies
routinely send us the same message about the same payment more than once, and if
we recorded it twice the customer would appear to have paid money they never
sent — money the system would then quietly spend on their next bill. So the same
settlement was sent again, byte for byte, and it was recognised and ignored. Then
the SAME money was sent under a new reference, and that one WAS recorded — which
is the part that matters, because it proves the first was ignored deliberately
rather than because the door was shut. Two copies sent at the same instant left
one payment. A message with a forged signature was refused.

**Three of the customer portal's payment screens had never been opened by
anybody.** Every one of them had passing tests. Opening them found four problems
tests cannot see, and each is now written down: the two dates above, a card
company's *we are taking that money back* message being recorded as money
arriving, and the fact that the whole message-receiving feature cannot be
switched on by any installation of this product at all — there is no setting to
put the shared secret in.

**One thing this build deliberately does not change.** The receipt page offers a
download and an *email it to me*, and both are drawn greyed out with the reason
written on them. Neither works yet. Showing the buttons and saying why is the
choice we keep making over hiding them.

## [2.197.12] — 2026-09-06 · Every date on the request screens was written the way a computer writes it

**A customer who asks us for something — to stop their supply, to query a bill,
to ask a question — now reads the dates on those screens the way their utility
writes dates.** All five of the screens where a customer makes a request were
printing `2026-09-06` where Pine Hill's own setting asks for `09/06/2026`: the
date a request was raised, every step of the progress ladder, the day a supply
would be turned off, and every bill in the *Which bill* list. The helper that
formats a date properly has existed for days and two other groups of screens
already use it; these five had never been moved onto it. One of them was worse
than it looked — the progress ladder was cutting a timestamp down to its first
ten characters, which shows the wrong day to any utility west of Greenwich.

**Would it be cheaper to stop your supply for the winter, or to close the
account?** That screen answers with two figures and names the cheaper option,
and this is the first time anyone has watched it do so in a browser. Stopping
for five months costs about `$92.50` in standing charges against `$335.00` to
close and reconnect, so stopping wins; stop for nineteen months and it is
`$351.50` against the same `$335.00`, and the screen changes its answer. **The
answer really does change** — a screen that always said *stopping is cheaper*
would have passed every test we had.

**Three things a browser found that no test could.** A bill query writes a
summary for the office to read, and that summary is shown back to the customer
on their own requests list — including an amount printed as `142.1800` where
money is meant to read `142.18`. **The amount is fixed here**; that a note
written for the office is shown to the customer at all is recorded, because
what that column should say to a customer is a decision rather than a
formatting error. The demo utility every
walkthrough uses **cannot work out that stop-or-close comparison for a single
one of its 73 accounts**, because its sample price list states the same monthly
charge in two places and they disagree; the product refuses rather than guess,
which is right, and the sample data is what is wrong. And the plan for this work
still said one unbuilt screen was waiting on a question the Product Owner
answered two days ago.

**What the drawings ask for and the product does not have yet** is recorded
rather than described: the screen that tracks a request never says what the
request is about or what we are waiting for; the screen where a customer
disputes a bill never shows the bill's amount; and there is no way from the
requests page to see a request that has already been closed.

## [2.197.11] — 2026-09-06 · The last bill a customer ever sees had no title on it, and a customer still cannot send us a reading

**A customer moving out opens one final screen: what they owe or what is coming
back, and the meter reading it was worked out from. That screen had no heading
at all.** No *Your final bill*, no *Moving out* above it — the page simply began
with two panels of figures. The title was there on every version of the screen
where there was nothing to show: while it was loading, when the reading failed,
and for the customers who are not leaving. It disappeared the moment there was a
real bill on it. A test now checks the heading on the version that has a bill,
which is the one nobody had checked.

**Four dates on the same screen were written the way a computer writes them** —
`2026-09-17` where a person expects the 17th of September. The same helper the
rest of the product already uses now formats all four, so they read in whatever
style the utility has chosen.

**What that screen now prints, watched in a real browser rather than asserted:**
service of `$63.40`, a deposit of `$150.00` held since March 2021, `$16.50` of
interest earned on it, and **we owe you $103.10** — with the three figures
adding up to the total underneath them, checked by reading them off the screen
the way a customer would. The closing meter reading is `154,310`, taken on the
day they left, `1270 gal` used since the last one, and read by a meter reader.

**Three things on that screen are wrong or missing and are written down rather
than quietly fixed.** When a leaving customer already owed money from before,
the column does not add up: it lists `$289.10` less a `$150.00` deposit and
`$16.50` of interest, then states `$296.82`, and nothing on the screen names the
`$174.22` they already owed. There is no way to download a copy of this bill,
which is the last one they will ever get from us. And the *query this reading*
button — the customer's last cheap chance to say a closing reading looks wrong —
