can only ever appear for people who owe us money, never for the people we owe.
Each of those needs a decision or a piece of wording that is not a
developer's to invent, so each is recorded with the figure that shows it.

**A customer still cannot send us their own meter reading.** For a utility with
one or two staff that is the most valuable thing this portal could do — a
reading that arrives on time is a walk nobody had to make — and it is the largest
single thing the customer portal does not do. The design for it exists in full:
which meter, the day they read it, the dial figure in a wide meter-shaped box, a
warning in plain words when a figure looks about nineteen times their usual, and
a panel saying what happens to it next. The product has none of it, and the one
button that points at it says so honestly. The question that was holding it up
was answered on 4 September; six sentences across our own documents were still
saying it was blocked, and they now say what was actually decided.

## [2.197.10] — 2026-09-06 · The last warning before we cut somebody off could never appear on their screen

**A customer behind on their bill is shown a ladder of what happens next. It had
four rungs where the design has six, and the missing one was the final notice —
the last warning before the supply is disconnected.**

It could never have been drawn. The screen was never sent the date, so both the
code that would draw that rung and the sentence it would print were unreachable.
Somebody in arrears was told the day their water goes off and never told the day
of the last warning before it. It is there now.

**Fifteen dates across those four screens were being shown to customers in the
format a computer uses** — `2026-11-30` where a person expects the 30th of
November. One of them was the day a doctor's certificate stops protecting
somebody's supply. The helper that formats dates properly already existed; these
four screens had simply never used it.

**What those screens now print, checked in a real browser rather than asserted:**
`$412.60 is overdue by 19 days`, a reconnection fee of `$95.00` read from the
utility's own charge row rather than written into the code, a closing total of
`$507.60` that the check adds up from the parts on screen, and a refund of
`$89.80` in four dated steps.

**Four things the design asks for and the product still does not have** are now
recorded rather than described: there is no way to pay from the overdue screen
although the payment screen is one click away; no protection card offers the
action its drawing gives it, so the certificate names its expiry and offers no
way to renew; a payment plan that is not yet holding says *Not started yet*
beside a start date in the past; and credits and refunds are one column where
the design has two. Each is a decision for the Product Owner rather than a
preference, and each now goes red the day the product grows it.

## [2.197.9] — 2026-09-06 · The plan-acceptance screen promised something we do not do

**On the screen where a customer commits to a payment plan, the box headed *what
accepting this does* ended: "Miss two payments and the plan ends, and the whole
balance falls due."** We do not do that. The Product Owner ruled the opposite on
11 August — *we chase for payments until write-off* — and the code agrees: a plan
is still active on the tenth missed payment. The sibling screen one click away
had printed the true sentence all along.

So one release said two opposite things about one rule, and the false one was on
the screen where the customer signs. It now prints what the code does, in each
language's own words rather than one English sentence translated eleven times.

**Why no test caught it:** the guard exists on the other two plan screens, and
this screen's own test *fed it the forbidden sentence in its fixture* and then
asserted nothing about it.

**Three more, all found by opening the screens:** every screen in this release
printed raw dates like `2026-09-14` to a utility that has asked for
`MM/DD/YYYY`; four held controls pointed at a question id **that was never
issued**, so a customer's *ring us about this* waited on a question nobody could
answer; and the screen told a customer their last instalment carried a rounding
even when all six were exactly `$20.00`.

**What the screens now print:** a plan of `$22.03 · $22.03 · $22.03 · $22.03 ·
$22.03 · $22.05` totalling `$132.20`, and a live preview on an account owing
`$585.94` giving five of `$97.66` and a final `$97.64` — with the run adding the
six up and checking they equal the total the same screen printed.

## [2.197.7] — 2026-09-06 · The demo utility now has a year of water behind it, and three customer screens finally have something to show

**Three screens in the customer portal — Usage, Every reading, and Meters and
equipment — were finished and shipped, and anyone who opened them on the demo
utility saw nothing at all.** Not broken: empty, and honestly so. The screens
were built correctly and the demo customer simply had no meter, no readings and
no equipment recorded against her address, so there was nothing to draw. Every
test passed, because the tests bring their own data with them.

**She has all three now.** The demo now records two years of water readings on
her meter at 1408 Elm St, the water meter itself, her rubbish cart, and the
backflow device in her front boundary box. Opening the Usage screen shows a
year of bars with gallons named on the axis, the highest month and the lowest
month marked, and a switch to two years. The sewer and rubbish panels say what
they are billed on — the water she uses, and the 96 gallon cart at the kerb —
and draw no chart at all, because neither is measured and a chart of nothing
invites the question "where is my graph".

**One reading was estimated and later put right, and the screen now says so in
plain words:** *"We estimated 144,600 and corrected it to 144,130 when the meter
was read on 2026-07-03. You were not charged twice."* That sentence is the whole
reason the Every reading screen exists, and until now no demo could produce it.

**Three faults were found and fixed while doing it:**

* Every month of usage the sample data creates was invisible to the "remove the
  sample data" button — 774 rows of 775 on a freshly built utility. A month
  decides once whether it is sample data and never reconsiders, and it decides
  before the readings behind it have been marked. The months this release plants
  are marked properly; the older ones are recorded as still outstanding.
* The demo utility priced water per thousand gallons while its meter measured
  single gallons, so the most recent reading was flagged as a unit mismatch —
  which would have stopped a bill run on that account. The two now agree, and the
  price per thousand gallons is unchanged.
* A reading upload could report "posted" while posting nothing, if the reading's
  date fell outside the range the database is prepared to store. The sample data
  builder now refuses out loud and names the date instead of quietly planting a
  shorter history.

**And eight things the drawings ask for are still missing, named rather than
glossed over.** The Usage screen writes `4820 gal` in one place and `43,300 gal`
in another — the same kind of number, two formats, on one screen. The drawing's
third summary tile, *next reading due*, is not built. The drawing asks for a
daily average and the screen shows a monthly one. The correction sentence writes
its date as `2026-07-03` rather than as a person would. And the signed-in help
screens and the tip slot the wave was named for do not exist yet, so a customer
looking for help reaches the public help page — a working page, and not the one
that was drawn.

Each of those is filed, and the browser check that walks these three screens
counts them out loud on every run and goes red the day any of them is quietly
fixed without the record being updated.

## [2.197.8] — 2026-09-06 · Somebody opened the payment screens in a browser for the first time

The four screens where a customer's money actually moves — paying a bill,
setting up automatic payment, seeing a refund on its way, and paying the fees to
start service — had been built, tested and released, and **nobody had ever
opened them in a browser.** Somebody has now, and here is what they found.

**A customer looking at a cancelled refund was shown a line of computer
gibberish.** Where the screen should have said the money was stopped on 27
August, it printed `2026-08-28T02:08:26.806734+00:00`. The dates on the refund's
four progress steps had the same problem, in a milder form. All of them now read
the way this utility has asked for dates to be written, in this utility's own
time — which also means they show the right day, not the day before or after.

**And that same cancelled refund was headed "A refund on its way".** It was not
on its way; it had been stopped, and the panel said so on the very next line.
Every refund carried the same title regardless of what had happened to it. A
refund we have cancelled now says so at the top, where somebody reading quickly
will see it.

**On the automatic-payment screen, a small link had swollen into a button
stretching the width of the card.** Nothing was broken behind it, but a control
that size reads as the main thing to press, and it was not. It is now the size
it was meant to be.

**What was checked and is right.** Paying the whole balance took the money once
and once only, put it on the oldest bill first as this utility has configured,
and the payment appeared as cleared on the customer's list the same minute.
Paying part of a balance showed which bill it would land on and what that bill
would still owe **before** anything was committed. When the card processor did
not answer, nothing at all was recorded and trying again used the same reference,
so nobody can be charged twice. And the fees to start service added up correctly:
$185.00 plus $150.00 is $335.00 to pay now, with a waived $25.00 still listed,
crossed out, and in neither total.

**Two things this build still cannot do, said plainly rather than left to be
discovered.** Automatic payment can be looked at but not switched on — nothing
in the product can yet take a payment without somebody pressing a button, and
the screen says so. And the deposit line on the fees screen does not appear for
customers whose price plan does not set one; that is the plan, not the screen.

## [2.197.1] — 2026-09-06 · Meter reads showed the wrong day, and now they show the right one

**Every meter reading in the product was displayed one day early.** A reading
taken on 14 August was drawn as 13 August — on the meter's own history, on the
account's read log, on the main Reads list, on the reading's own detail page,
and on the customer's bill in the portal. It was not a few screens or a few
readings: it was the whole reads history, everywhere, and it had been that way
since the meter history screen was first built.

**Who it affected: any utility whose clock is behind UTC.** That is every
American one. A utility on Central time — Brazos Bend, in the demo — saw every
reading a day early. A utility in Europe saw the right day all along, which is
part of why this went unnoticed for so long.

**What was wrong.** A meter reading's date is a *calendar date* — the day
somebody stood at the meter. We stored it correctly, and we sent it to the
screen as though it were a precise moment in time instead of a day. The screen
then quite properly translated that moment into the utility's own timezone, and
midnight in London is the evening before in Chicago. So the day moved back one.

**What changed: only what we send to the screen. Nothing about what we store
has moved.** That distinction matters more than it sounds. The stored value is
also what stops the same meter being read twice on the same day, so "correcting"
it at the storage end would have quietly switched off that protection while
making the screens look right. We did not go near it.

**One thing you will notice beyond the date.** The main Reads list used to print
a time next to each reading — `08/13/2026 19:00`. That time was never real; it
was an artefact of the same fault. The list now shows the date alone.

**The reading's own page also stops contradicting itself.** It had been showing
a previous reading of 31 July and a current reading of 13 August while telling
you the gap was 14 days. It now says 14 August, and the arithmetic agrees.

**A separate, smaller thing is still open and is not fixed here.** A register
reading is drawn as a bare number with no unit beside it — `2147` rather than
`2147 kWh`. Whether an odometer-style reading should carry a unit at all, and
where it should appear, is a genuine product question rather than a bug, so it
has been put to the Product Owner rather than decided by us.

## [2.197.0] — 2026-09-05 · The search box at the top now finds the work, the people and the price list

**Type into the one box at the top of any screen and you can now reach six more
kinds of thing.** Before today it found premises, units, meters, accounts,
customers, bills, payments and service requests. It now also finds:

* a **job** by its number — `WO-0011` opens it;
* a **job template** by name — *Meter set* brings back one per service;
* a **part** by its number or by what it is — `MTR-W58`, or just *Water meter*;
* a **person or a crew** by name — *Patel*, *Crew B*, *Apex Utility Svc*;
* a **plan** by its code or name — `RES-W`, *Residential Water*;
* a **charge code** — `LATE-FEE`, which is what someone reads off their bill
  when they telephone to ask what it is.

**Meter reads and finance are deliberately not in the list.** They were
considered and left out, and so were work-order rules, rate schedules, taxes,
discounts and rate changes — every one of them for a reason written down in
`CR-073`, so nobody has to guess later whether they were forgotten.

**People, crews and contractors come back as ONE heading**, because the crews
screen already shows them as one list. Their rows open that list with the name
already typed in, rather than a person's own page — a crew does not have one,
and a link that works for some rows and not others is worse than one more click.

**Nothing about money changed, and no result shows a price.** A part's cost has
no meaning without a quantity, and a charge code's amount is a starting figure
the bill run can override — showing either in a search result would state a
price that is sometimes wrong.

**Also fixed:** the Jobs, Templates, Parts and Crews lists ignored a search term
arriving in the address, so every *View all* link from the search box would have
opened the full list while promising a filtered one (`DEF-WRK-4094`). And the
tool that hands out defect numbers was calling a lane's own number "already
taken" and telling it to pick another — every time (`DEF-GOV-4095`).

## [2.196.0] — 2026-09-05 · Jobs that raise themselves overnight, and one form for a meter in front of you

**A utility can now tell the product what to watch, and stop typing the jobs.**
A supervisor writes a rule once — *when a meter passes its certification date,
raise a meter exchange* — and at two in the morning the jobs appear. By seven
the dispatcher's screen has them, and each one says **Raised by: Asset age
rule**, so nobody has to guess where a job came from.

**Five things can be watched, one per part of the product:** a final notice that
has run out with the bill still unpaid, a billing problem nobody has resolved, a
meter past its certification life, a flow that never stops, and somebody moving
in.

**Running the night's work twice raises nothing the second time.** A rule that
is switched off raises nothing at all — and switching it back on months later
does not then raise everything it missed while it was off. It remembers what it
has already done.

**A clerk standing on a meter can raise a job for it, from one form.** Only the
templates that apply to that kind of meter are offered. The job is for that
meter and is not tied to a new connection, and the maintenance history's Work
order column stops being a dash.

**Seven controls that said *Work R5* now do something.** The *raise a work
order* tick on adding, moving, servicing and retiring a meter; *Parts in Work*,
which had been refusing over a parts register that shipped days earlier; the
wrench beside a certification that is falling due; and the replacement-programme
panel, which now sets up the rule that raises those exchanges by itself.

**Rules is a new tab in Work**, between Templates and Performance.

## [2.195.0] — 2026-09-05 · A technician works a day with no signal, and the reading they typed reaches the meter

**PHASE 2 IS LIVE: a dispatcher assigns work to a crew, and the technician works
it on a phone.** Walked end to end on a running product — a phone with its
network switched off and a supervisor's desktop — rather than declared on an
intention. Three jobs worked with no signal, one sync, and a second sync that
changed nothing: the approval queue stayed at 19 and the meter's history at 4.


**A technician can now work a whole day with no signal and lose nothing.** Every
tick, every reading, every photograph and the close itself are recorded on the
handset the moment they happen. When the signal comes back the phone sends the
day once. Send it twice and nothing is added a second time. The button says which
of those is about to happen — *Close job*, or *Close job · send when back online*
— so nobody finds out at six o'clock that the office never heard.

**Closing a job still does not switch anybody's supply on.** A technician says
the work is done; a person in the office reads it and accepts it. Those are two
acts and they stay two acts.

**The reading the technician typed becomes a real meter reading — dated to the
day they read it.** D. Ortiz reads 1,204 kWh at four in the afternoon on the
15th; the office accepts it at nine the next morning; **the meter's history shows
1,204 kWh on the 15th, not the 16th.** That is the day the electricity was used,
so that is the day it has to be billed in — and it gets there through the same
door and the same checks as a reading typed by a clerk at a desk. A number with
no unit beside it never reaches the meter at all.

**Two things the product refuses to guess, and says so.** A meter *exchange* has
two meters, and nothing in the product yet records which reading belongs to
which; rather than pick one, it declines to approve that job and asks. And the
*your service is live* letter still cannot be sent, because the message system
has no kind of message for it — it is queued, refused, and the screen says why,
rather than being filed under a heading that would quietly spoil every monthly
count of notices.

**Four buttons on the work-order screen did nothing, and now they work.** *Mark
complete*, *Reassign…*, *Put on hold…* and *Cancel order* were drawn, looked
live, and went nowhere — over a screen that was otherwise finished and tested.
Every one of the four things they needed already existed. Cancel now asks first,
because it cannot be undone.

## [2.194.1] — 2026-09-05 · The bugs found today, counted honestly: twenty of the thirty-six were already fixed

**Thirty-six problems reported today were still marked unfixed. Twenty of them
had already been put right** — somebody fixed the thing, and nobody went back to
tick the box. That is the single most repeated bookkeeping failure in this
project, and it makes the list of outstanding work look almost twice as bad as it
is. Every one of the twenty was checked against the actual code before it was
ticked off, and the note on each one now says what was checked rather than just
that it was.

**Eight were real, and are fixed.**

* **The check that stops the field-work code reaching into the metering code was
  crying wolf.** Three of its four complaints were about tables the field-work
  module owns itself; the fourth was real and is fixed. A guard that is wrong
  three times out of four is a guard somebody switches off.
* **The tool that hands out reference numbers could only see one list.** If a
  number had already been used in the code or in a commit, it handed it out
  again. Two people were given the same number an hour apart. It now looks
  everywhere — and the moment it did, it found eight numbers already taken that
  nobody could see, two of them already claimed twice.
* **Ten rule numbers that a refusal at the counter points you to led nowhere.**
  A clerk told a cheque cannot be voided, with a rule number to look up, could
  look it up and find nothing. The rules were decided on 1 September; they
  reached the code and never reached the rulebook. They are written down now,
  word for word as they were decided, with nothing added.
* **The setting called "Bill accent" was translated into Portuguese as a way of
  speaking and into Italian as a man named Bill.** Both now read as what they
  are — the highlight colour on a bill — in each language's own words.
* Three tests still counted seventeen connectable services after an eighteenth
  arrived, so they had been failing for everyone. Corrected after checking the
  product, not the test, was right.
* A merge check reported *what kind* of problem it found and never *which file*.
  It names the file now.

**One was a duplicate** — two people found the same broken colour on the
dispatcher's map and fixed it the same way.

**One was already decided and stays as it is**: the usage screen shows a monthly
average where a drawing asked for a daily one, and a daily figure would be an
arithmetic the rest of the product cannot reproduce. The note now says what would
have to change instead.

**Eight remain open**, each for a stated reason rather than by omission — the
largest being six failing test files that each need their own module to judge
whether the product or the test is right, which is not a thing one person should
sweep through.

**This release also records a mistake made while doing the work.** Publishing a
fix, this session accidentally removed 160 translated phrases and another
person's explanatory note, because it told the safety check to compare the branch
with itself. Nothing was lost — it was caught by reading the numbers, restored
within minutes, and the safety check now refuses to be told that.

## [2.194.0] — 2026-09-05 · What the phone sends back: a reading with its unit, a photograph, and a signature or a refusal

**Until today a technician could open a job on their phone, tick the safety list
and work through the steps — and had nowhere to put what they found.** The
readings the template asked for, the photograph of the dial, the customer's
signature: none of them had a screen, and none of them had anywhere to go.

**There is now.** Three panes on the job:

* **Readings** — every reading with its unit beside it, a box for the number and
  a camera on the row.
* **Photographs** — the ones that belong to the job rather than to one reading:
  the state of a cupboard, a damaged seal.
* **Signature** — the customer signs with their name printed beside the mark, or
  they refuse, and the crew records why and photographs the door hanger.

### The two things on this screen that look alike and are opposites

**A reading outside its expected range is recorded, shown in red, and the job
still closes.** If the meter says 1,204 on a dial the template expects to read
between 0 and 999, then 1,204 is what the meter says. Refusing it would leave
the true reading unrecorded because of a limit somebody typed in last year.

**A missing photograph that the template REQUIRED does stop the job closing**,
and it is shown in amber with a different sentence. The screen says which is
which in one line: *Required means the job will not close without it; out of
range never blocks.*

They are deliberately not the same colour and not the same words. A screen that
showed both as one shade of "check this" would teach a technician that neither
matters — and one of them is the one that stops a job closing at five to five on
a Friday.

### Photographs are made small on the phone, before they are sent

Every photograph is compressed on the handset to **at most 100 KB** — usually
50 to 60 — before it leaves. The original never goes anywhere. This follows the
Product Owner's instruction of 4 September, from a problem they had lived
through: photographs arriving at one and two gigabytes until the storage ran out.

For one utility the difference is about **59 GB over seven years becoming about
3.4 GB**, and it stops growing rather than climbing. If a photograph cannot be
made small enough, the phone says so **while the technician is still standing at
the meter**, rather than failing silently at the end of the day.

### How long these are kept

**Twelve months**, and then the utility is offered a download before anything is
removed from our storage — the Product Owner's ruling of 4 September.

⚠ **Nothing is deleted today, and nothing can be.** The download does not exist
yet, and an export that does not exist is not a retention policy, so the job that
would delete old files refuses to run until it is built. A photograph attached to
an open dispute is not deleted while that dispute is open.

### Also in this release

* A job's photographs and its signature can never be edited or deleted
  afterwards, and the database enforces it rather than the screen. To correct a
  photograph you take another one; both are kept, so a supervisor can see that a
  correction happened.
* A photograph sent twice — the phone retrying after losing signal — writes one
  row, not two.
* A link to a photograph works for four hours and then stops working.
* A reading is always sent with its unit. A number with no unit beside it is
  refused, because a wrong unit here becomes a wrong bill later.

## [2.193.0] — 2026-09-05 · What a finished job cost, and the total that is not in the books

**Until today a finished job had no price.** A technician could spend an hour
replacing a meter, use a meter and a seal, close the job — and nothing anywhere
said what it had cost.

**Now it does, and the report says so in three lines a person can add up.**
Fifty-two minutes on site by a field technician at `$48.50` an hour is
**`$42.20`**; one electric meter is **`$96.00`**; one seal is **`$0.22`**; the
job cost **`$138.42`**.

**The lines add up to the total on purpose.** The hours are rounded to two
decimals before they are multiplied — `0.87 h`, not `0.8667` — because `0.87` is
the number printed on the report, and printed hours times printed rate must give
the printed amount. Anyone checking the document with a pen reaches the same
figure. (Kept to four decimals the labour line would read `$42.03`, seventeen
cents adrift, on every job.)

**There is no tax on a work order.** The original drawing of this report showed
`$8.65` and `$2.77` of tax and a total of `$149.84`. None of it is built, and a
permanent check now fails the build if anyone adds it.

**And the total goes nowhere near the books.** The drawing said this figure
feeds the O&M line in Finance; it does not, and there is no link, button or note
on the page that offers to send it there. **Payroll already pays that hour —
putting it in the books again would count the same hour twice.** The figure is
*recorded*, and that is the word the screen uses.

**An approved report cannot be changed.** Once a supervisor accepts a job the
report is frozen — the database itself refuses an edit or a deletion, and so do
the three cost lines underneath it, because freezing the total while leaving the
lines loose would let a document stop adding up to itself. A correction is a new
version beside the old one, and pressing Accept twice produces nothing the
second time.

**A rate is dated, and a job keeps the rate it closed at.** Set the field
technician to `$48.50` in January and `$50.00` in April, and a job closed on 15
March still prices at `$48.50` — as do the 184 meter exchanges that closed
before it. Changing a rate writes a new row; the old one is never edited.
Contractors carry one rate and a dash, because an agency invoices its own
overtime.

**Two new screens.** *Performance* on the Work strip — how the field did against
its promises and what it cost, by job type. *Labour rates* under Settings, which
is the one screen in the product that shows money to four decimal places,
because it is the screen where those decimals are set.

**Parts are recorded, and nothing is counted.** Who took what, when, and what
for — and no on-hand number moves anywhere, because this product keeps a parts
register and an issue log and no stock at all. A return is a new row, never a
deletion of the issue that took the parts out.

## [2.192.0] — 2026-09-05 · The job reaches the technician's phone, and safety is a lock the server keeps

**Until today there was no field app at all** — no phone screen, nothing that
worked without a signal, and no way for a job to reach the person doing it
except somebody ringing them.

**A technician now opens the app on the phone they already carry**, signs in
with the login they already have, and sees the day.

**The day is in appointment order, and it stays that way.** A job marked Urgent
shows an *Urgent* label — and it does **not** jump the queue. A technician
drives a route, and a job across town does not move ahead of the one they are
standing outside.

**The top of the screen always says when the phone last reached us** —
*◍ offline · synced 08:12*. If it has never reached us it says so, in those
words, rather than showing a time that would not be true.

**Tap a job and everything is already there** — the customer and their number,
the safety checks, the steps with their minutes, the readings to take, the parts
and the help pack. None of it is fetched when you tap: it came down with the
job. That is what makes it work in a meter pit with no signal, and the
supervisor's number and the procedure document open there too.

**Safety is a lock, and it is not just a grey button.** The steps stay locked
until every required safety check is ticked. Two of three ticked is locked — not
nearly unlocked. And the same rule is kept by our server, not only by the
screen: if a job is sent back as finished with a safety check still outstanding,
it is refused, and the refusal **names the check that is missing**. A greyed-out
list is a courtesy; the server refusing is the guarantee.

**Assigning a job pushes it to the phone.** The job's history then reads
*Dispatched · pushed to phone · 14:02*.

**And where there is no phone registered, the history says that instead** —
*Dispatched · waiting for the phone*. It will never say a job was pushed to a
phone we did not reach. The technician still gets the job the next time the app
checks in; nothing is lost either way.

⚠ **What is not here yet, so nobody is surprised:** taking photographs, entering
readings, capturing a signature and closing the job are the next two releases.
The app shows them as coming rather than hiding them, so a technician can see
the job is not finishable there yet.

## [2.191.0] — 2026-09-05 · A dispatcher can change a job after it exists, and everyone who needs to know is told

**Until today a work order could be raised and assigned, and then nothing about
it could be changed.** There was no screen for the ordinary thing a dispatcher
does all day — move the visit to the afternoon, hand it to somebody else, put a
note on it about the dog in the yard.

**There is now.** Open a job from the orders list and you get one form: status,
priority, the promised date and time window, the area, who is going, and what
to tell the crew. One Save.

**Before you press Save, a box tells you what pressing it does** — because this
is the one screen in the product that changes something a person may already be
acting on. It says three things, and each is something you cannot take back:

* **the customer is told the visit moved** — Sarah Miller gets a message saying
  her appointment is now 12:00–17:00;
* **the technician's phone changes immediately** — D. Ortiz's copy of the job
  updates while he is in the van, and nobody asks him first;
* **every field change is logged with who changed it and when.**

**Nothing that has already been done gets undone.** Moving a job from one
technician to another records that the first one lost it and the second one
gained it, and keeps both. A safety step a crew ticked at 09:40 stays ticked at
09:40. The job gets a new promise; it does not get a new past.

**Cancelling a job asks first, in red, and deletes nothing** — the order keeps
its number and its whole history.

**A message about a moved appointment is now filed as an appointment.** It used
to have nowhere to go, and the nearest place to put it was beside disconnection
notices — which would have quietly inflated the monthly notice count with
appointment changes, every month, with nothing on the report to show it.

**And there is a map.** The same open jobs, placed where the work is, with an
outline instead of a filled pin wherever nobody is going yet. **Any job whose
address has no position is listed underneath rather than dropped**, because you
cannot count pins: a map that quietly left jobs out would be lying about the day
and nothing on the screen would say so.

**When a crew reports that a job FAILED, something now happens.** A follow-up
visit is raised automatically, linked to the one that failed, and the build it
belongs to goes on hold with the crew's own words in *Waiting on* — *pressure
test failed at 2.1 bar*, not a generic sentence. A failed one-off job with no
build gets the follow-up and says plainly that there was nothing to put on hold.


## [2.190.0] — 2026-09-05 · A job keeps its own copy of the instructions it was given

**Change the template tomorrow and the job somebody did yesterday does not
move.** A template says what a job of that kind involves; an order is what one
job actually was. Until this build an order had no checklist at all, and the
cheap way to give it one — point at the template and read the steps off it —
would have meant that publishing a new version this afternoon silently rewrote
what every finished job says its technician did. Not a row would change and
nothing would appear in any history.

**So a job now takes its own copies at the moment it is raised:** the safety
list, the steps, the readings, the parts and the help numbers, plus the version
they came from. `WO-4822`, raised from version 2 of *Meter exchange —
residential*, has **seven** steps. Publish version 3 with an eighth, *Apply
tamper seal*, and `WO-4822` still has seven. So does every other job already
out. Only jobs raised from now on get eight.

**A dispatcher can raise a one-off job in three steps** — where and what, when
and who, then confirm — and nothing is written until Confirm, so closing the tab
on step two leaves no half-made order and burns no order number.

**The order opens as six tabs** — Overview, Checklist, Parts, Location, Customer
and Audit — and every figure on them is the job's own.

**Safety is a lock, not a suggestion, and the server holds it.** The task list
stays shut until every safety line is ticked: two of three ticked is locked, not
two-thirds unlocked. The greyed control on screen is a courtesy; the refusal is
on the server, so it holds for a phone that was offline and hopeful.

**One thing is deliberately blank.** The Location tab has a *gate code* and
*access notes* box and both are empty on every job — this product does not hold
that information anywhere yet, and a guessed entry code against a real address
is worse than a dash.

⚠ **2.187.0 HAS NO ENTRY OF ITS OWN, AND THAT IS THIS LANE'S DOING.** Wave H's
first commit set **2.187.0** in all three version literals and wrote **no
CHANGELOG entry in the same commit** — exactly the half of change-process
step 7 that gets skipped. A sibling lane numbering its own work then read
`package.json`, found 2.187.0 sitting there with nothing explaining it, and
had to renumber its entry to 2.188.0 mid-flight, noting *"another change had
already taken 2.187.0 in `package.json` between this one being numbered and
being pushed."* **They caught it; this lane did not.** The whole of wave H —
the copy tables of 2.187.0 and everything since — is recorded here at 2.190.0,
so 2.187.0 remains a number with a bump and no story. `DEF-GOV-4039` files it.
**The lesson is the timing, not the number:** bump the version and write its
entry in the SAME commit, or the cost lands on whoever numbers next.

## [2.189.0] — 2026-09-05 · One place to see every open job, and drive it

**The dispatcher (`CR-070` wave G).** Work → Orders was a list of what exists;
it is now the screen somebody runs the day's work from.

* **Five figures across the top** — how many jobs nobody is going to, how many
  are due today and how many of those are urgent, how many crews are out right
  now, how many finished jobs are waiting for somebody to accept them, and what
  is late. Each counts the whole utility, so none of them moves when you type in
  the search box.
* **A job now has an owner, a promise and a place.** Every job carries who is
  going, when it is due, which area it is in, and why it exists — a job raised by
  a move-out says so, and so does one a dispatcher raised by hand. The due date
  is worked out from the priority's own promise: an Urgent job with a four-hour
  target reported at 09:00 is due at 13:00, and nobody types a date.
* **Filter on six things and drive many jobs at once.** Search, type, status,
  priority, technician and area. Tick the rows and assign them, move them to
  another day, or change their priority — and each job gets its own record of
  what happened, not one record for the batch, so *who was sent to 77 Cedar Ct
  and when* is answerable for that job alone.
* **Raising a job's priority moves its due date with it**, re-dated from when
  the job was reported. A leak reported at 09:00 and made Urgent at 15:00 reads
  as already late, because it is.
* **The record of who was sent where cannot be edited or deleted.** If somebody
  was assigned by mistake, the fix is two new entries — taken off, given to — so
  the history reads as what happened. The database refuses the alternative.

## [2.188.0] — 2026-09-05 · Why your bill is different now says why

⚠ *Released as 2.188.0 and not 2.187.0: another change had already taken
2.187.0 in `package.json` between this one being numbered and being pushed.
The earlier claim keeps the number.*

**"Why is this bill different" showed two totals and said it could not explain
them.** It read *"We are still working out how to show you the reasons line by
line"* — which was true when it was written, and stopped being true the day the
decomposition was signed off. The screen was telling the truth about itself,
which is why nobody noticed.

**It now lists every reason with its share, which is what was decided.** A bill
that went up by $27.36 reads: electricity used +$16.00, electricity standing
charge unchanged, water used +$10.82, water standing charge unchanged, tax
+$0.54. The shares add up to the difference exactly — checked against all 49
comparable bills on the live system, and a breakdown that does not add up is
not shown at all rather than shown with a penny missing.

**A charge that ENDED is one of the reasons.** A summer discount on last
month's bill and not on this one is the whole of why this month costs more, and
it is listed as such rather than quietly left out.

**A charge that did NOT move is listed too, as "unchanged".** Someone looking
for what changed is also asking what did not, and a service missing from the
list reads as a service that has stopped being charged.

**This is the screen the blueprint calls the single biggest deflector of phone
calls** — a customer whose bill went up either understands it here or telephones
the office.

*One difference from the drawing, stated rather than hidden:* the drawing writes
each reason as a sentence — *You used more water +$8.83*. This writes the thing
that moved — *Water used* — and lets the signed figure beside it say which way.
The information is the same and the row is shorter.

## [2.186.1] — 2026-09-05 · One copy of a function two of us wrote

**Nothing a customer can see changed here.** Two of us needed the same small
piece of plumbing within an hour of each other — the bit that fetches an answer
a clerk pinned to a screen — and both wrote it. The code ran the second copy and
quietly ignored the first. There is one now, and it carries both explanations.

## [2.186.0] — 2026-09-05 · A lost reply no longer tells you your payment vanished

**If the reply to a card payment got lost on its way back, the customer was
told there was nothing to pay.** Their money had gone through — one payment,
correctly, never two — but the page they were looking at said the bill was
already settled, with no receipt and no reference. From where they were
sitting, that reads as *your payment did not arrive*, and the obvious thing to
do about it is to pay again.

**A retry now hands back the receipt they already earned** — same reference,
same amount, and the time the money was actually taken rather than the time
they pressed the button again. Nothing new is charged and nothing new is
recorded; the page simply shows them what already happened.

**It still costs them the bill number and the postcode**, exactly as the first
attempt did, so this cannot be used by anyone else to find out whether a bill
has been paid.

**Separately, the guest payment form has stopped asking for an email address
for the receipt.** It was collecting one, checking it, and then doing nothing
with it — the product cannot send receipts by email yet, and the note under the
box said *"We use it only for this receipt."* The form now says plainly that
email receipts are not available yet. Sending a receipt to an address a
stranger typed, against somebody else's account, is a decision about who may be
told what, and that is yours to make rather than ours to assume.

## [2.184.2] — 2026-09-05 · An answer a clerk pins to a screen is now actually shown there

**A utility could tick "also show this answer on the overdue screen", get a
confirmation, and the customer would never see it.** The whole feature was
built — the setting, the picker, the summary line a clerk reads back, the place
in the database that holds the choice, and the card that draws it — and none of
the pieces were joined to each other. It has been that way since the feature
shipped.

**It works now on the overdue screen**, which is the one where a pinned answer
matters most: a customer who has just been told what happens if they do not pay
is exactly the customer with a question. The answer is written once, on the
help page, and shown in both places — never typed twice and never able to
disagree with itself.

**Nothing is drawn when nothing is pinned.** An empty card headed with a
question is worse than no card, so the slot closes up completely.

**Read in the customer's own language**, and where an answer has not been
translated yet they get it in English with a line saying so, rather than a
blank space.

**The other two places a clerk can pin an answer — the bill and the usage
screen — are not wired yet.** The plumbing they need now exists and is tested;
what is left is one line on each of those two screens, and both are being
worked on by other people today.

## [2.184.1] — 2026-09-05 · The level-pay screens show you the gap, not a count of it

**If you are on level pay, you can now see what you paid against what it
actually came to, month by month.** That screen has always known both numbers —
it was showing you how many months it had counted, which is the one thing about
them that does not matter. The whole point of level pay is the gap between the
two, so now you see the gap.

**The chart on the joining screen is the same chart.** It was drawn separately
before, in its own screen, which is how two pictures of the same thing slowly
stop matching. There is one now, and both screens use it. Nothing about what it
shows you has changed.

## [2.184.0] — 2026-09-05 · The record repairs, and the isolation proved on a real database

Three corrections and one proof, all of them about this build rather than new
behaviour.

**A defect row this lane filed was deleted by somebody else's push an hour
later.** It had been written, committed and pushed correctly; a later commit
rebuilt the register from a copy that predated it, and the row simply was not in
the version that landed. Nothing looked wrong at either end — the commit that
dropped it shows only its own work, because a row removed by rebuilding a file
never appears in a difference at all. It is restored, under a new number,
because the old one had been handed to another team in the meantime.

**The migration in the last build was missing its ownership marker**, so the
check that watches sensitive files was refusing the merge. Anything that changes
the shape of the database is reviewed by a person before it is signed off, and
that file now says so and has its review note written in plain English.

**And the isolation this wave is about is now proved on a real database rather
than the test one.** The test database cannot express row-level separation at
all, so a passing test there says nothing about whether one utility can see
another's data. Run against real PostgreSQL, under a restricted login rather
than an administrative one: one utility's record of *this provider has stopped
answering* is invisible to the other, a missed window is a genuine row with the
reason on it, and turning that row into a success is refused by the database
itself — which matters, because that single change would erase the evidence that
a utility's bills did not go out.

## [2.183.0] — 2026-09-05 · The portal stops sending customers our engineering notes

**The portal was sending customers our own engineering notes.** Not on screen —
the screens never showed them — but in the data behind every page, where
anything can read them. On the customer home page the note read:

> `apps.billing.selectors.issued_invoices_for_account is not published, so no
> bill states its usage+base / taxes / tenant-defined / fees balances…`

That names our internal modules, our rule numbers and our open questions to
somebody who does not work here. A worse one, on the payments side, quoted the
caller's own account reference back at them, which is the thing we specifically
promise not to do.

**These notes are useful and they are staying — for staff.** They are how a
clerk is told why a screen is showing less than it would like to. What has
changed is that they are now removed on the way out to a customer, on every
customer page, including the ones a person can reach without signing in.

**It is done once, at the edge, rather than page by page.** The same fault was
fixed on one page in an earlier release and could not travel; eight pages still
had it. Half of these notes are not even written by the portal — they arrive
from the billing and payments code and are passed straight through — so a fix
that listed the known ones would have missed the next one written.

## [2.182.1] — 2026-09-05 · A revert of our own, undone

**Nothing a customer can see changed here.** A commit of ours earlier today
carried an out-of-date copy of two bill screens and their tests, which quietly
undid another day's work on the same files — the bill's own line detail, its
currency and unit labels, and the date formatting behind them. All of it is
back, alongside the work that overwrote it.

Recorded rather than tidied away, because the check that was supposed to catch
this reported success while doing it.

## [2.179.2] — 2026-09-05 · …and the tool now works out the next number from every file, not one

The fix shipped an hour ago taught the version tool that the number lives in
three places. **It then worked out its own next number by reading one of them**,
which is the same mistake one layer down.

At that moment the branch carried `package.json` at 2.179.0 and the backend file
at 2.180.0 — out of step in the *other* direction, from somebody else's one-sided
bump. Reading only the frontend, the tool answered 2.179.1, and the fix for
version numbers going backwards moved one backwards. Nothing real was lost: no
release ever carried 2.180.0, it had no changelog entry and no other file had
ever held it. The arithmetic was still wrong, and next time it would have moved
a number somebody had shipped.

The next number is now the highest across every authoritative file, in this
checkout and on every branch. One detail worth recording: the first attempt
scanned the lockfile too and answered **7946.0.17**, because a lockfile pins a
version for every dependency it holds — so that file is read when asking *do
these agree* and never when asking *what comes next*.

## [2.179.1] — 2026-09-05 · The version number lives in three places and the tool that hands it out knew about one

**The product version is written in three literals across two files.** The
frontend's `package.json`, the two copies inside its lockfile, and the backend's
`pyproject.toml`. A merge check compares them and refuses to let anything
through while they disagree.

Today they disagreed: the frontend said **2.178.1** and the backend still said
**2.177.0**. Two lanes in a row moved one and not the other — and one of them was
this lane, which moved the frontend number four times in four commits and never
once touched the backend.

**That has now happened four times**, and each previous fix corrected the numbers
rather than the reason. The reason is this: the tool a lane uses to ask for the
next version reads the frontend file, prints a number, and writes nothing. It
never mentions the other two files, so a lane is handed one number and left to
edit two files it was never told about. Its `--verify` check compounded it — it
answers *has somebody else taken this number*, said "still free" three times
today, and was read as *the version is fine*.

**Both halves are fixed.** All three literals now read 2.179.1. And the tool
reads all three: it prints what each file currently says next to the number it
gives you, and `--verify` now fails outright when they disagree — so a lane finds
out while it is asking, not seventeen minutes later in a merge suite with
twenty-nine other failures in it.

## [2.179.0] — 2026-09-05 · You can look at your bill, and the answer is where the question is

**The bill we posted you is now on the screen, not just behind a download
link.** Open *the bill we sent* and the actual letter appears, page-shaped and
centred, the way you would see it on paper. It is the same file that went in
the envelope — not a copy redrawn from the figures — so nothing on it can drift
from what you were sent. The download is still there.

**An answer your utility attaches to bills now shows up on the bill.** Staff
could already tick *also show this on the bill* against any of their published
answers, and until today nothing put it in front of you: the answer sat in the
help section and the bill never mentioned it. Now it sits under the charges,
with a link to the full answer, in your own language. If nothing is attached
the space simply is not there.

**Three smaller things you may notice.** The six-digit code we text you when
you set up a login has its own wide, spaced-out box, so you can check it digit
by digit against your phone instead of squinting at a box shaped like a
surname field. The *is anyone in danger?* panel on the report-a-problem page
now carries your utility's colour down its edge, so it no longer looks
identical to the quiet note underneath it. And nothing was renamed, moved or
recalculated.

## [2.178.2] — 2026-09-05 · The buttons a customer came to press are back at the top of the page

**Every signed-in screen has a heading now, and this puts the controls back
beside it.** The design puts each screen's main buttons in the row next to its
title — *Download CSV*, *Download the agreement*, *Call this office*. On four
screens the heading had arrived and the buttons had not followed: they had
drifted to the bottom of the page, under a table or below a card, which is
where you look last.

**Four screens fixed.** Your payments (Download CSV), your payment plan
(Download the agreement), the plan we have offered you (the same), and a service
centre's page, where *Call* sat in a strip of its own directly underneath the
heading it should have been part of.

**Nothing was re-drawn and no button changed what it does.** Each one is the
same control with the same wording, moved to where the design puts it — so a
button that is not available yet still says so, in the same few words.

**And the suite now checks this against the design itself**, rather than against
a list somebody typed out. It reads the drawing, finds every screen whose
heading is supposed to carry buttons, and fails if one of them has none. Five
screens are still outstanding and each says in one line why — two belong to
other work in progress, and three would need a new control rather than a move,
which is not a layout fix.

## [2.178.1] — 2026-09-05 · The screen that answers "can I get service here?" is finally tested, and dead wording is now a list

**CWP-008 is the screen a stranger uses to find out what it costs to be
connected. Until today nothing tested the answer it gives.** Five cases existed
and every one of them checked the screen *before* anything was typed — the
address box, the panels, no priced table yet. What a person sees *after* their
address matches — the four services, the connect fee, the deposit, the row for a
service we do not carry — was untested, and it had already been broken twice
this week without anything going red.

Six cases now type `31 Palm Ct`, press Check, and check the answer: four rows,
**$185.00** to connect, **$150.00** on the first bill, sewer *included* rather
than zero, trash a real **$0.00**, and the electric row greyed and quoting **no
money at all** — because telling somebody a service we do not sell costs $0.00
reads as *free*.

We proved the cases can fail before trusting them: with the screen changed to
print the stored figure instead of the formatted one, two go red; with the
unavailable row un-greyed, one; with that row quoting $0.00, two. The screen was
put back exactly as it was each time.

**Also: wording written for screens that do not say it is now a list you can
act on.** Fifty-one phrases are translated into eleven languages and called from
nowhere, thirty-six of them the customer portal's. The check that finds them
could only report a count and three examples; it now names every one, grouped by
the part of the product it belongs to. That matters because a dead phrase means
one of two opposite things — either the wording should go, or **a control
somebody wrote the words for was never built** — and you cannot tell which from
a number. The phrases themselves are still there; this makes them findable.

## [2.178.0] — 2026-09-05 · Your documents are now named after what they are

**Every row in *Documents and letters* was named after its KIND, so five of the
six on screen read *A letter from us*.** A list whose whole purpose is finding a
document could not be used to find one — the only thing telling one row from
another was a reference number, so a customer had to know their own bill numbers
to find their August bill.

**Each row is now named after the document itself.** A bill is named by the
month it covers, a receipt by what it was for — *Receipt for $38.44* — and a
letter keeps the plain description it always had. The kind stays in the *Kind*
column, where it belongs; it used to be printed twice on every row.

**And the bills were not filed as bills.** Every bill in the list was sitting
under *letters*, and the *Bills* filter found none of them — because the row
the system writes when it queues a bill for printing does not say which
template it used, and the screen was taking its word for it. A document made
from a bill is now filed as a bill whatever was or was not written on that row.
This corrects all 100 bills already on the live deployment, not just new ones.

**Where a bill has no period recorded, or a receipt no amount, the row still
says what it can** rather than showing a name with a gap in it.

## [2.177.0] — 2026-09-05 · One utility's dead mail server stops being everybody's

If a utility's mail server stops answering — not breaking, just going quiet for
a minute and a half at a time — that used to be everybody's problem. Every one
of the eight background workers that dialled it went to sleep waiting, and every
other utility's bills queued up behind the silence.

The guard that prevents this was written yesterday. **Nothing was calling it.**
All four places in the product that actually dial an outside system went
straight past it, so the protection existed, its tests passed, and the outage it
was written for was exactly as possible as before. It is wired up now, and three
further things turned up in the wiring:

* **A run nobody sent was being recorded as sent.** When the product decides not
  to dial a mail server that has gone quiet, it writes down that it skipped the
  window. The arithmetic that picks the word had no word for *we did not ask*,
  so it chose *succeeded* — and the connection's history would have shown
  *93 of 93* over ninety-three bills that never left the building. It now says
  **Skipped**, with the reason in words.
* **The cap was holding the workers it was meant to free.** Two calls at a time
  are allowed to one connection. The other six were made to wait thirty seconds
  each for a turn, so the connection still occupied all eight workers and the
  other utility still waited. They now give the worker back after two seconds.
* **A restart could have held a healthy connection shut.** The note of *when to
  try this server again* was written on a clock that means nothing once the
  process that wrote it is gone.

**What a utility sees:** a connection that has stopped answering reads *Not
working* with its own reason — *The mail server is not answering* — the windows
it missed are listed rather than passing in silence, and everyone else's bills
go out on time. Nothing is lost: the queued messages stay queued and go when the
server comes back.

Also in this build: the integrations plan now records waves A to E as built,
against the files and line counts they were checked against, and the two version
numbers agree again after three builds of drift.

## [2.176.5] — 2026-09-05 · The ten screens we have drawn and not built now say what happens when they arrive

**Ten screens in the design have no address in the product.** That is not new
and nothing is broken today: where a control points at one of them it says so
honestly, and where nothing points at one, a customer never learns it was
meant to exist.

**The risk is the day one of them is built.** Landing a screen and releasing
the button that was pointing at it are two separate jobs, and only the first
one feels like work. That has already cost us a week once: the portal's front
page spent days with two working doors out of eight, every refusal message
written correctly and every one of them untrue by the time a customer read it.

**So each of the ten is now written down with what would have to be released
when it lands**, and the test suite fails on that day and names the control.
Three of the ten are pointed at by something live today — the Messages word in
the header, the *Moving out* card on the requests page, and *Send a reading* on
the readings page — and each was already protected, but by three separate
mechanisms in three different places, so nobody could answer "are all three
covered" without reading three codebases. That is one question in one place now.

**Seven of the ten have nothing pointing at them at all**, which means no check
anywhere can notice the day they arrive. That number is written down too, and
it can only go down on purpose.

## [2.176.4] — 2026-09-05 · One way of writing a responsive layout, not two

**This changes no pixel and it is worth doing anyway.** Our styling has a rule
written in capitals at the top of the theme file: layouts are described
starting from the desktop and narrowed for smaller screens, never the other way
round. Eight places in the customer portal were written the other way round.

**Nothing looked wrong, and that is exactly why it lasted.** In the simple
two-column case the two ways of writing it produce the same result, so no
screen was broken, no test failed and nobody noticed. The cost is to the next
person: someone opening one of those components to see how it is done here
found the opposite of the rule, and copied it. That is how eight became eight —
one component written correctly the same week sat beside them with a note
explaining why.

**There is now a check that refuses the wrong direction**, so this cannot come
back quietly. The customer portal is at zero and stays there. The staff side of
the product has thirty of the same and they are written down: that number can
go down and cannot go up.

**We also found and fixed a real trap while converting.** Collapsing a
twelve-column layout onto a phone needs each panel told to take the full width
as well; without that the panels quietly spill into columns that do not exist.
That would have been invisible to every automated check we have and visible to
anyone holding a phone.

### Fixed
- The version number recorded in `package-lock.json` had fallen behind the one
  in `package.json` — 2.174.3 against 2.176. It is back in step. Nothing was
  installing the wrong thing; the file simply disagreed with itself about which
  build this is, which is the exact confusion version numbering exists to end.

## [2.176.3] — 2026-09-05 · A test that failed once over a screen that was fine

**One autopay test went red yesterday on correct code and passed the next four
times it was run.** It cost the person who hit it fifteen minutes proving a green
change was green, and it would have cost the next person the same.

The reason is small and worth writing down. The test waited for the autopay card
to appear and then, in the same instant, looked inside it for the held switch —
assuming the switch is drawn at the same moment as the card around it. That is
true on an idle machine and not guaranteed on a busy one; a build and a browser
running alongside it were enough.

It now waits for the switch itself rather than for the box it sits in. Three
assertions in that file made the same assumption and all three were changed.

**A test that goes red at random is worse than a test that is missing**, because
it teaches people to run it again instead of reading it — and that is exactly how
a real failure gets waved through.

Also here: the version in `package-lock.json` had drifted two releases behind
`package.json`; both now read the same number.

## [2.176.1] — 2026-09-05 · The meter reading on screen now reads the way it does on the meter

**A customer comparing our screen with the box on their wall was reading
`153040`.** The wireframe has always drawn it `153,040`, and this is the one
number on the whole portal a customer checks digit by digit, so the commas are
not decoration — they are what makes the comparison possible without counting
places with a finger.

**Half of this had already been done and the other half was still wrong**, on
the same screen, two lines apart. The Reading column was grouped; the sentence
underneath a corrected reading — *"We estimated 144600 and corrected it to
144130"* — was not. One screen printed the same kind of number two different
ways. Both are grouped now.

**Nothing was checking any of it.** The grouping had no test at all, and the
one assertion that touched the corrected sentence was written against the
ungrouped text, so it actively held the old form in place. That assertion is
why the first pass stopped at the column. There are now nine checks on how a
dial figure prints, including one that fails if someone "corrects" it by
running it through the helper that adds units — which would replace the number
with a dash on a customer's screen.

**The reading keeps no unit, and that is deliberate.** The figure on a meter's
face is a running total for the life of the meter, not an amount used; the
*Used since* column beside it is the amount used and still carries `gal`.

## [2.176.0] — 2026-09-05 · Your bills now say which month, how much you used, and how long you have

**A customer opening *Your bills* could not tell which month a bill covered
without opening it.** The list showed the bill number, the day it was issued,
the day it is due and the money — and not the service period, even though the
server had been sending the period on every row all along. Someone looking for
their August bill had to open bills one at a time to find it. The period is now
a column, in the date format the utility chose in Settings.

**Nor could they see what they had been charged for.** *Usage* is now a column
too, and it carries its unit — `4,820 gal`, `31 therm` — with each unit
separate, never added together. A bill that only charged a fixed monthly
amount shows a dash rather than a zero, because a zero would say the meter
read nothing.

**And the status now counts.** It said *Due*, which is equally true of a bill
payable tomorrow and one payable in five weeks. It now reads **Due in 12
days**, **Due today**, or **Overdue by 3 days** — so a customer scanning the
list can see which bill to deal with first. The count is worked out by the
server, on the same clock that decides whether a bill is due or overdue, so
the words and the number can never contradict each other on a phone whose
clock is a day out.

## [2.174.0] — 2026-09-05 · Dates in the portal follow the setting you chose

**You set a date format and a time zone in Settings, and until today the
customer portal ignored both.** Every date a customer saw was a raw computer
string — `2026-08-14` on their readings, their bills, their documents and their
payments — while the staff side of the same product had been following the
setting since yesterday. That is the half of the problem that was still open.

**It follows now, and changing the setting changes what a customer sees.** Set
the format to `25-Aug-26` and that is what their readings say; set it to
`25/08/2026` and it changes on the next page load. No re-sync, no re-import.

**The time zone travels with it**, which matters more than it sounds: a payment
taken at half past seven in the evening in Texas was showing as the next day,
because the portal was reading every timestamp as UTC.

**If a utility has not chosen a format yet, the portal says the date the plain
way rather than guessing one.** Guessing is what caused the original fault: the
product quietly assumed an American format and a UTC clock everywhere, which is
right for some utilities and silently wrong for the rest, with nothing on screen
to show it had assumed anything.
## [2.174.3] — 2026-09-05 · And it now checks that a list has its search box and its footer

The check added in 2.174.2 asked whether a screen composes the shared list at
all. It did not ask whether that list was given its **toolbar** — and those are
different questions: a screen can draw the table and pass it no search box, which
is most of what the audit found wrong with the six lists in the first place.

It asks now, from the same drawing: where the drawing says *"toolbar search"* the
screen must pass one, and where it says *"no footer"* the footer must be off —
and where it does not, on. Seven lists are covered and all seven are correct
today, so nothing changes on screen; the next one built without a search box goes
red instead of shipping.

This was the third of the three things the layout audit asked for. The first — has
every screen got a page heading — is a census that landed yesterday; the second —
has it got a rail where the drawing gives it one — landed in 2.174.2 with the
rest. The audit finding that said nobody was comparing portal screens with their
drawing is closed.

## [2.174.2] — 2026-09-05 · The check on portal layouts now reads the whole drawing, and asks for components that exist

**A gate landed yesterday to compare every customer-portal screen with the
drawing that says what is on it. Measured, it was checking about one part in
ten of that drawing, and part of what it did check could never come true.**

The drawing calls the portal's list a `DataTable`. The portal does not build one
— it has its own list table, deliberately, because the staff version paints a
grey background that is wrong on a white page. The gate compared names, so it
recorded **seven lists as missing a shape six of them already had**: bills, all
my accounts, documents, readings, meters and payments had all been given a
search box, sortable headings, row icons and a footer days earlier. Its worklist
said of them *"not one of them draws a table"*, and that was untrue the day it
was written.

**It also read one line per screen.** Each entry in the drawing names the
template on its heading line and then the actual pieces underneath, and only the
heading was being read — 49 questions where the drawing makes 378 statements,
and **thirteen screens asked nothing at all**.

Both are fixed. The check now reads the whole entry, resolves the drawing's
names to the names the product builds them under, and takes its vocabulary from
the component kit itself so a new piece is covered the day it is drawn. **It
asks 229 questions of 50 screens instead of 49 of 46.** Twenty-five real gaps
remain and each is written down with the reason it is owed — the six false ones
are gone.

Nothing a customer sees changes today. What changes is that the next screen
built in the wrong shape is caught by a machine instead of by the Product Owner
opening it.

## [2.174.1] — 2026-09-05 · Two screens that should have been split down the middle

**Your final bill and your details each drew two panels, and one of them was
squeezed.** Both screens are meant to show two panels of equal width side by
side; both were drawing one wide panel and one narrow one, so the closing meter
reading on your final bill — and your sign-in details on the details screen —
sat in a column about half the width of the one beside it. They are equal now.

**On the details screen the narrow column also held two cards with no gap
between them**, so they read as one box with a line through it. They are spaced.

Nothing moved, nothing changed what it says, and no figure is different. This is
the layout catching up with the design.

## [2.173.5] — 2026-09-05 · The utility's own colour, checked rather than hoped for

**Your colours were already reaching the portal — this makes sure they keep
doing it.** We put a real browser on the customer portal with three different
utilities: one whose colour is teal, one purple, and one that has set no colour
at all. The teal utility's *Pay a bill* button came out teal, the purple one's
came out purple, and the utility with no colour of its own got our house red.
That last one matters as much as the other two: it is the promise that our
style guide is the starting point and a utility only ever paints over it.

**The Branding screen was telling clerks something untrue, and we have stopped
it.** It listed four things — your logo, your trading name, your brand colour
and your bill accent — under the heading *How the portal looks to your
customers*, and said all four were "used by the bill, the letterhead and the
portal". Three of them are. The bill accent is not: we measured it in a browser
and it reaches nothing on the portal, by an earlier decision that we will not
invent a rule about where a second colour appears until someone tells us what
it is for. So a clerk could pick an accent colour, save it, look at their portal
and see no change anywhere. The screen now says which of the four goes where,
in all eleven languages, each written properly in its own rather than run
through a translator.

**Two new checks, for the one mistake this product keeps making: a value that
is stored, fetched, and read by nobody.**

The first catches text that is styled with a size name we do not have. Our type
sizes are a fixed, deliberate list, and asking for one that is not on it does
not fail — it silently does nothing, so the words come out at ordinary body
size and every automated check stays green, because the instruction really is
there in the page. That is how the portal's front door came to show the
utility's own name at the size of a sentence. A check for it existed but never
ran when work was merged; now one does, and on its very first run it found a
live one nobody had reported — a red *this did not work* message on the field
work panel that was drawing in ordinary black. A colleague fixed that same line
within the hour, from the other direction.

The second catches the same component being written twice under one name. The
portal had grown its own copies of three pieces the product already had; those
were folded back last week, and this makes sure a fourth cannot appear
unnoticed — the trouble with two components of one name is that nothing can see
it, since each screen quietly uses whichever one is nearer. Writing this check
turned up one more, in the staff Settings screens, where a panel used on 187
screens is a second copy of the one used on 98. That one is written down rather
than fixed: choosing which of the two is the right one is a job of its own, and
guessing at speed is how the last such merge went wrong.

## [2.173.4] — 2026-09-05 · Ten written promises checked against the product, and the one that mattered

**Some of our own documents described a product we had not built.** Ten of them
were checked against the code this release. Three turned out to be already right
and only needed confirming. Six were wrong and have been corrected. **One is a
genuine gap in the product, and it is written down plainly rather than tidied
away.**

**The gap: a clerk still cannot say anything to a customer about their own
request.** A customer can add a note to a request and see it on their own
timeline. A clerk reading that same request can only write notes marked
*internal · never shown to the customer* — there is no control anywhere that
marks one visible. So a clerk who needs two more documents from somebody cannot
say so on the page that person is watching; they have to telephone. The rule we
signed says a customer's history shows the notes flagged customer-visible, and
half of that rule has nothing behind it. **Nothing was quietly reworded to match
what we built.** What made this costly was a note in the code saying a
customer-visible path "must not" exist because there was no portal — true when it
was written, wrong from the day the portal went live, and it would have talked
the next person out of building it. That note is corrected.

**The other one worth knowing about:** the *how we contact you* screen draws a
grid of forty-eight switches — every kind of letter against every way of sending
it. The product holds three answers, not forty-eight: one for email, one for
text, and printing, which is always on. The screen already says so honestly above
the grid and no customer's settings were ever saved to the wrong place. **But the
document behind it pointed that grid at the utility's own settings row — where
one customer's choice would have changed what every other customer receives — and
declared it had no open questions.** It has one, and now says so. Whether to
build per-letter choices at all is the Product Owner's to decide and nobody
invented an answer meanwhile.

**Also fixed, all of them signposts that led nowhere:** a question two live files
told you to go and read, which had been renumbered out from under them; a note
pointing at a bug report that has never existed; five files naming the wrong
story for the sign-in and enrolment screens, one of them citing a test file that
is not in the repository; and a mapping table telling the next builder to use a
database column nobody ever created.

**And the demo utilities stop looking broken.** Every piece of equipment on every
demo tenant showed a dash where its location should be — not because the screen
was faulty, but because no sample utility ever recorded one. Two separate reviews
on the same day hit that dash and neither could tell a missing feature from an
empty field. Meters now read *Front boundary box*, sub-meters *Rear alley*.

## [2.173.3] — 2026-09-05 · The drawing of each portal screen is now something a check can read

**We have a drawing for every screen in the customer portal and nothing in the
product had ever compared a built screen with it.** Somebody opened all fifty
portal addresses in a browser yesterday and found that twenty-five of the
thirty-nine they could judge were short of their own drawing — a missing
right-hand column, a list with no search box, a row of headline figures that was
never built. Forty-two test files and 391 test cases passed over every one of
them, because each test checks the facts its screen shows and none of them checks
the shape. **A screen that shows the right facts in the wrong shape passed
everything we had.**

A new check reads the drawing itself and asks a handful of questions of each
screen: does a list use the shared table with its search box and footer, does a
page that is drawn with a right-hand column have one, do two panels drawn as
equal halves sit as equal halves. **Sixteen screens are short today**, and each
one is written down with the reason it is owed — seven lists that do not use the
shared table, seven pairs of panels drawn equal and built lopsided, the usage
page's three service panels, and one row of headline figures. That list can get
shorter and cannot get longer.

The part that lasts is where the expectation comes from. Every other check we
have that knows anything about a portal screen carries its own copy of the
screen list, so it quietly stops being true the day the design moves. This one
reads the design each time it runs: change a screen's drawing and the check
changes its mind in the same breath.

## [2.173.2] — 2026-09-05 · A held control now says what would release it

**A greyed button that says *"arrives later this year"* over something that
shipped last week is the most repeated fault in this product.** It has happened
four times in a week: the portal front page had two working doors out of eight;
*Something else* was grey for 32 hours over a screen that had been live since
the small hours; the bills list held *Pay* after *Pay now* shipped; and, in
Settings, *New answer* was disabled over a save that has worked since 2.138.0.

The reason it keeps happening is not carelessness. **Holding a control until
its screen is built is correct on the day you write it, and wrong on the day
the screen arrives** — and building the screen and releasing the control are
two separate jobs, only one of which feels like work. Nothing was watching.

**Now every one of the 35 held controls in the customer portal writes down what
would release it**, and a check refuses to merge any change where a control is
still refusing over something that now exists. Of the 35: **one** waits on a
screen and is watched; **22** cannot go stale at all (they are answers about
this account, or about a form nobody has filled in yet); and **12** wait on
something no automatic check can see — and the check reports that number out
loud rather than implying it is guarding all of them.

**A clerk can write a help answer again.** *New answer* was disabled with
*"Writing answers arrives later"* over a save that has worked for two days. It
is a live button now. A second fault came with it: the only *New answer* button
