in the product sat on the "no answers yet" panel, so a utility that wrote one
answer could never write a second. There is a *New answer* button at the top of
the list, where the sibling tips screen already had one.

## [2.173.1] — 2026-09-05 · Three gates that were telling the truth about the wrong thing

**A gate said a live screen was dead code.** *Connections · one connection* is a
screen a clerk opens; the check that looks for components nothing draws had been
reporting it as unused, because the router imports it under a second name and the
check only ever searched for the first. Acting on that reading would have deleted
the screen. It now understands a renamed import, and it proves it can still spot a
genuinely dead one before it trusts itself.

**The same gate was reading half the question from yesterday.** It listed files
from the last commit and then read them from disk, so a lane that had just written
a new screen and the piece it draws — neither committed yet — was told the piece
was dead. That is exactly the moment the build process asks a lane to run it. It
reads the files as they are on disk now.

**And two new migrations were missing the one line that says a human must review
them.** The review entry had been written; the marker in the file had not, which is
the half that does not feel like work. The check that guards our sensitive files
is green again for the first time since yesterday morning.

Versions: the front end said `2.173.0` and the back end said `2.168.1`. They agree
again.

## [2.173.0] — 2026-09-05 · The rest of the signed-in pages get their heading

**Twenty of the twenty-eight pages that had no heading now have one**, and the
last of them arrived in this release: your payment plan, level pay and where it
stands, a plan we have offered you, your final bill, the printed bill, why a
bill is different, one bill line by line, add another account, track a request,
stop or restart service, and ask us something.

**A bill now opens with its own number as the title**, which is what is printed
on the paper a customer is holding, and *Why is this bill different?* moved
from a stray link into the row of actions beside it.

**Three pages had a back control that looked like a button** — a bordered
control sitting exactly where a page's main action goes, which teaches people
to ignore the main action. All three are plain `←` text links above the title
now.

**And *Look something up* was drawing its own heading by hand** — a small label
and a sub-heading arranged to look like the real thing, inside the card. It
composes the same page head as everything else, so it finally has a proper
page title rather than an imitation of one.

**A new check keeps it that way.** Nothing in this repo has ever compared a
built portal page against the design that describes it; there is now one
question it does ask, for every page at once — *does this page compose the
product's page head* — and a page born without one fails the build. Pages a
colleague is still working on are listed by name, and the check fails the day
they gain a heading, so the list cannot quietly go out of date.

**And the number on your meter is now printed the way a number should be** —
`153,040`, not `153040`. It is the figure you check against the box on the
wall, and grouping the digits is the difference between reading it once and
counting the zeros.
## [2.172.3] — 2026-09-05 · The portal's screens get the shape their drawings give them

**The customer portal has been showing the right facts in the wrong shape.**
Somebody opened all fifty of its addresses in a browser and compared each one
with the drawing that says what should be on it. Every screen worked. Most were
laid out differently from the picture, and in several cases that cost a
customer something they could not see.

**Your usage screen was a stack of boxes and is now the page it was drawn as.**
Three big figures across the top — what you have used this period, your monthly
average, and when your next reading is due — then one chart panel per metered
service with every bar dated and a legend under it, then your services three
across in a row instead of six panels running down a very long page. A service
that is not metered sits in that row with no chart and says what it *is* billed
on, which is the design rather than a gap.

**Two screens got the right-hand column they were drawn with.** *Your account*
now shows your tax exemption, when it runs out, whether your certificate is on
file and when the account was opened — none of which had anywhere to appear
before. *Add another account* now lists the accounts already on your login,
with a count, so you can see at a glance whether the number you are about to
type is already there instead of finding out after we text a code to somebody
else's phone.

**A tip a clerk switches on now actually says something.** It was publishing an
empty box: the screens were reading a field the server has never sent. Nobody
would have reported it, because the person writing the tip saw it correctly in
the editor and the customer saw a bordered box with no words in it.

**The word *Messages* at the top of every signed-in page has gone** until the
screen behind it exists. It looked like a link, sat next to one that works, and
went nowhere. It will come back on its own the day that screen lands.

**Right-hand panels were grey where every other panel on the page was white.**
One colour setting, and the two halves of a page look like one page again.

**And *why did this bill cost more* now shows you the picture.** Two bars, this
month against the same month last year, instead of four numbers in a sentence.

Behind all of it: two components that existed twice under one name are one, a
number formatter that dropped six decimal places onto a customer's screen is
the ruled one, and the shared layout piece now carries a mark so a test can ask
*does this screen have its second column* without counting elements.

## [2.172.2] — 2026-09-05 · Every list in the portal can now be searched, sorted and paged

**Eight lists could not be searched, sorted or paged, and no row carried an
icon.** Your bills, your accounts, your documents, your payments, your readings,
your meters and your open requests all printed every row they had and left you
to scroll. There was no way to find one bill by its number and no way to put a
list in date order.

**Every one of them now opens with a search box and sortable headings.** Type a
bill number, part of an address, a meter serial or a document's name and the
list narrows as you type; click a column heading to sort by it, click again to
reverse, click a third time to put it back the way it was. If what you typed
matches nothing, the screen says so in a sentence rather than showing you an
empty table.

**The lists that can get long now say how long they are and let you page
through them** — *Showing 1–50 of 120 · Page 1 of 3 · Rows per page* — and the
count is the count of what you are actually looking at, so it follows your
search rather than reporting the whole pile.

**Rows end in the small controls the design draws.** A bill row opens the bill
or the copy we sent you; a document row opens the printed page; a payment row
opens the bill that money settled; a reading row opens the bill it landed on.
Where an action cannot be offered — a payment that was returned by the bank, a
reading not yet on a bill, a letter we kept no copy of — the control stays
visible and says why, instead of quietly disappearing from that row.

**Two lists deliberately have no footer**, because the design gives them none:
your meters and your saved payment methods are three or four rows about your own
property, and a page counter over three rows is furniture standing on nothing.

**Staff lists gain something too:** the shared pagination footer now says *Page
x of y*. It has always shown the range and the arrows and never the page number,
so you could move through a long list without being able to tell how far through
it you were.

## [2.172.1] — 2026-09-05 · What you have paid, and a bounced cheque you can read

**The reference against every payment was our own internal string.** The column
read `SAMPLE-BL-2608-000077` — a bill number wearing a fixture prefix, in the
place the design puts the thing a customer would recognise. Two of those rows
were worse: a payment against an instalment plan printed the plan's internal
database identifier as the customer's reference.

It now reads what a person would say on the telephone: **#10188** for a cheque,
**Chase ••••4021** for a bank transfer, **Visa ••••8812** for a card, and for a
cash payment the receipt number, because a cash payment has no reference at all.
**A utility that was set up before today keeps the old value until its demo data
is loaded again** — changing how data is written changes nothing already written.

**A returned cheque is drawn in red, all the way across.** It has always been two
rows, which is right — nothing in this product edits a payment, so the money
coming back is a new line rather than a change to the old one — but only the
small `Bounced` badge was red. The date, the cheque number, *Returned by the
bank* and the negative amount all read exactly like a payment that went through.
The whole line is red now, and the payment it undoes sits directly beneath it in
grey. That is the one row on this screen a customer must not skim past.

**The page says what it is.** It read `YOUR PAYMENTS` in small grey capitals — a
section label, not a heading. It is now *What you have paid* under a `PAYMENTS`
kicker, the same shape as every other page.

**And the seven buttons at the foot are seven cards.** *Your payment plan*, *A
plan we have offered you* and *Credits on the account* were three near-identical
phrases in three identical boxes, and a customer had four words each to tell
them apart. Each now carries one line saying what it is for.

## [2.172.0] — 2026-09-05 · Four flows can now send somebody, and none of them waits

**When a clerk is closing Sarah Miller's move-out at 221 Oak Ave, the screen
offers to send somebody for the final read.** It offers the utility's OWN
published jobs — not a list we invented — and the account closes and settles at
the same moment whether or not that job could be created. If it could not, the
screen says so in one sentence. A field module that could stop somebody moving
out is the thing this is built to prevent.

**The same offer now appears at three more moments a clerk is already standing
in:** taking the opening reads on a move-in, doing the changeover reads on a
property sale, and routing an approved application. On the application it is the
*Route* button that opens it — the page gains no seventh tab, because the offer
belongs to the act and not to a place somebody has to go and look at.

**Every job now records WHY it exists and which record asked for it.** One of
fourteen reasons — dunning, asset age, high usage, payment received, billing
exception, move-in, compliance calendar, the dispatcher, move-out, assets, new
connect, service request, transfer, reconnect — and the flow's own number, so
from the move-out you can find the visit and from the visit you can find the
move-out. **Nothing is filled in for jobs that already exist:** they keep a
blank reason and the screen shows a dash, because guessing one would put a false
fact on a real record.

**An application now closes itself when EVERY job it raised has been accepted,
not the first.** A new water connection is three jobs days apart — inspection,
tap and service line, meter set — and closing on the inspector's report would
mark it finished before anybody dug the trench.

**The reconnect can book its visit at last.** The code has carried a written
note since it was first typed saying nothing books it; that note is now dated
rather than deleted, because it still describes a reconnect where nobody was
sent. ⚠ **What is NOT there yet: the reconnect has no button on any screen.**
The ladder on screen still stops at *schedule the cut*, so this is reachable
only through the interface behind the screens. Said plainly rather than left to
be discovered.

## [2.171.0] — 2026-09-05 · Five more pages get a heading, and status words stop whispering

**Struggling to pay? · What is protecting your supply · Money coming back to
you · What do you need? · Where things stand** all open with a real heading
now, the same one the rest of the product uses. That is ten signed-in pages
carrying a title in two releases, out of twenty-eight that had none.

**On the overdue page, *Ask for a payment plan* moved to the top.** It was one
of three links in a side panel; the design puts it beside the title, because it
is the thing to do about the situation the page describes.

**Status words are now printed the way the design draws them** — `CLEARED`,
`IN SERVICE`, `DUE`, `BOUNCED`, in small letter-spaced capitals rather than
ordinary sentence case. It is one decision in one place and it reaches every
badge in the portal. The words themselves are untouched, so nothing is shouted
at a screen reader and the languages that have no capital letters are
unaffected.
## [2.170.1] — 2026-09-05 · Cards and bank accounts, drawn the way it was signed off

**The page is called what the design calls it** — kicker `PAYMENTS`, heading
*Cards and bank accounts* — and **`+ Add a method` now sits beside that heading
instead of inside the notice about card security.** An information bar explains
something; it is the one place a button to press should never be, because it
reads as part of the explanation.

**Each saved method says what kind of thing it is.** The row used to read
`Chase ••••4021` and leave a customer to work out from the brand whether that
was a card or a bank account — which is the difference between money leaving
today and money leaving in three days. It now reads **Chase ••••4021** over
*Bank account*, and **Visa ••••8812** over *Card · expires 11/27*.

**The row ends in the two small controls the design draws** rather than a red
`Remove` button on every line. The pencil is deliberately greyed and says
*Changing one is not ready.* — nothing in the product changes a saved method in
place, and a control that is missing tells a customer the product cannot do it
at all.

**And *Set up autopay* is no longer a switch spanning the whole card.** It read
as something live and large; it is an ordinary button now. The card also says
plainly what autopay's standing is — **Autopay cannot be switched on yet** —
instead of leaving a customer to press through and find out.

## [2.170.0] — 2026-09-05 · Every signed-in page now says what it is

**Twenty-eight screens inside the portal had no heading at all.** You signed in,
opened your bills, and the page began with a small grey label inside a box —
no title, and nothing for a screen reader to land on. Of the forty-nine
addresses walked, thirty-three had no heading anywhere in the page.

**The title was the small half of it.** The design puts each page's main
buttons in that same top row, so they were missing too — and where one had
survived it had slid to the bottom of the page. *Pay* sat under the table of
bills with no amount on it. *Download a year* sat under the documents, switched
off. Both are back at the top, where a person looks for them.

**Your bills · All my accounts · My details · How we contact you · Documents
and letters** open with a real heading in this release, and *Add an account*
now sits beside the accounts title instead of being reachable only from
somewhere else.

**On *How we contact you*, the back link stopped being a button.** It was a
bordered control sitting where a page's main action goes, which is how you
learn to ignore the main action. It is a plain `← My details` above the title
now, the same as everywhere else in the product.

Nothing new was drawn to do any of this: the page head the rest of the product
has used since B14 rule 2 was simply put on the screens that had never composed
it.
## [2.169.3] — 2026-09-05 · A customer with no card could not pay at all

**Pay now is the screen that takes money, and three faults on it stopped a
person finishing.** All three were found by holding the drawing beside the
running product; not one of them could fail a test we had.

**A customer who had never saved a card reached a dead end, and the screen told
them to do the one thing it would not let them do.** The list showed saved cards
and bank accounts only, so with none it said *"Cards and bank accounts you save
will show here."* over a Pay button greyed out with *"Add a card or bank
account."* — and there was no way to add one anywhere on the page. Both halves
were right on their own, which is why nobody looked further. The drawing has a
third choice we had left out — **A different card or bank account** — and it is
there now, already chosen for anyone with nothing saved, with a link straight to
*Cards and bank accounts* behind it. The instruction is now something a person
can follow.

**We had invented a step and put the payment behind it.** *Show me where it
goes* was ours; the Pay button refused until it was pressed. The panel it
revealed — which bill the money lands on — is drawn as a standing panel, visible
the moment the screen opens, and it exists precisely so somebody paying part of
a balance can see where it goes **before** they commit. We had taken the thing
that informs the decision and made it a toll gate. The step is gone and the
panel is simply there.

**And the sentence that told a customer what was about to happen to their money
read "Takes $155.45 from ."** — naming no method and ending on a bare full stop,
because it was written whether or not one had been chosen. It is not written at
all now unless there is something to name.

Also on that screen: the *What this will do* summary has moved inside the card,
under the payment method, where the drawing puts it; **Pay** and **Back** are a
row at the foot of that card instead of a lone button floating above it with no
way back; and the refusal *"That is not an amount we can read."* is now the five
words the copy rule allows.

## [2.169.2] — 2026-09-05 · Four buttons that never said what they switched

**On *How we contact you*, four buttons reading `On` and `Off` floated above the
table with nothing to say which pair was email and which was text.** The
Product Owner reported it looking at the running product. The control had a
label all along — it was written where only a screen reader could reach it, and
drawn nowhere.

That matters beyond the one screen, because it is the shape of fault that
survives being checked. An invisible label still counts as a label to every
accessibility rule there is, so a test asserting *this control is labelled*
passed, correctly, over a control nobody could read. The test written for the
fix asserts the words are **on the screen**, and it was shown failing on the old
control first.

The same one line labels *12 months / 24 months* on Usage and *All / Owing* on
your accounts.

**And the chosen one of the pair is no longer a solid red block.** Red is this
product's colour for *this cannot be undone* — disconnect, reverse, write off —
so a red `Off` read as something having gone wrong rather than as the setting
you picked. The pair is now the same joined switch the rest of the product uses.
## [2.169.1] — 2026-09-05 · Which meter is that, and what is it called

**A customer with two meters could not tell their own readings apart.** Every
reading on the account went into one list, so the electric reading and the water
reading sat on the same date with nothing on either row saying which box on the
wall it came from — only the unit was different. The screen now opens with a
meter column: *Water · 2007*, the name the utility gave the service and the
serial printed on the meter. Nothing is hidden and nothing has to be chosen; the
screen is still every reading.

**On Meters and equipment, two rows both said `Meter`.** Each row is named for
what it is now — *Water Meter*, *Trash Container / Cart* — and a device that
stands on no service, like a backflow preventer, keeps its own name.

**The state column was showing a stored code with a slash in it.**
`Installed/Active` is how the system files a status; it is not a thing a person
says, and in ten of the eleven languages this portal speaks it could not be
translated at all. It now reads *In service*, in the reader's own language, and
*Test due NOV* when a check is coming.

**The date a meter was fitted reads *Mar 2021*** rather than a computer date.
The other two date columns on these screens still do not, and the reason is
recorded rather than hidden: the tenant's date format and time zone reach the
staff side of the product and reach none of the customer portal's fifty screens.

*Send a reading* now appears where the design puts it, switched off, saying
*Sending readings is not ready yet* — with a test that turns red the day that
screen is built, so nobody has to remember to switch it on.

## [2.169.0] — 2026-09-05 · Who works for you, and what they are allowed to do

**Until today the product could not say that D. Ortiz exists.** There was no
list of the people who do the work, nothing recording what each of them is
trained on, and no way to know that J. Kaur's confined-space certificate runs
out on 20 August. A dispatcher had names in their head and a spreadsheet.

**Work → Crews is that list.** Four people, a crew of three and a contractor sit
as six rows in one table, with what each one can do, what they are certified
for, their hours and whether they are on shift today. A crew and an outside
contractor are rows beside a person on purpose: whoever the job is offered to,
the test of *can they do this* is the same one.

**A certification about to run out is now something you see here, not on a
failed dispatch.** The watch names the person, the certificate and the date —
*J. Kaur, confined space expires Aug 20*.

**And whether an expired certificate STOPS a job or only warns is your choice,
per utility.** A new utility starts on *warn*, so a two-person operation can
still send J. Kaur out on 21 August with the expiry shown beside her name; an
operation with a safety officer switches blocking on and she is refused. The
sentence saying she is blocked appears only where blocking is switched on — a
screen should not promise something the setting has turned off.

**Open a technician** to see every skill your utility has, marked held or not
held, and what each one lets them be sent to. The *not held* rows are the point:
they say exactly which jobs a training course would unlock. *Assign skills*
walks through three steps and updates the row.

**A technician is a profile beside a login, never a second login.** People are
still invited in Settings → Team; Crews is where you say what they can do.

**Two access rules you asked for are now real.** A field technician's login
opens the phone and is refused on the web with *Sign in on the field app.* —
they are staff like anybody else, in the same user list, invited and
deactivated the same way, and the only difference is which app the login opens.
And *accept field work* is now a named permission that a billing clerk holds,
because accepting a finished job is day-to-day work and must not wait for a
supervisor. A technician cannot accept their own work — not because of a second
rule, but because the button lives on the web app their login does not open.

**Nothing changed for anyone already signed in.** Every existing login opens
both apps exactly as before.
## [2.168.1] — 2026-09-05 · Dates and times now follow the tenant's own settings

**The date format and time zone a utility chooses on Settings → Regional now
reach every screen.** Until this release they reached none of them. The Product
Owner reported it from the running product: *"date and time format is set in the
settings, plus we save location - but date shown everywhere in the product does
not change with that format change. If I change the language it changes across
entire app, date does not change."*

The two settings sit side by side on one page. Language was applied to the whole
app at the shell, so it worked. The date format and the time zone were handed
down screen by screen as optional values that the root never set, so all
**83 screens that draw a date** fell through to a built-in `MM/DD/YYYY` and
**UTC** — a plausible date in the wrong format, and a clock five or six hours
out for a Texas utility. A payment taken at 7pm local read as the next day.

What changed: the shell publishes the tenant's zone and date format once, for
the whole application, from the settings response it was already fetching. No
screen renders a date until they are known, and there is no built-in default
left behind them — a screen with nothing to render a date against now says so
instead of guessing.

Measured on Pine Hill Water & Power (`America/Chicago`, in a real browser,
against the running product): a staff member last active at `11:43` UTC read
**`09/05/2026 11:43`** before and **`09/05/2026 06:43`** after. Switching the
tenant to `DD/MM/YYYY` and `Pacific/Honolulu` moved **135 of 135 dates** across
Users, Bills and Accounts; before this release it moved none of them.

### Fixed
- `DEF-SHL-3964` — the tenant's `date_format` and `timezone` never reached a
  screen. Fifteen files carried their own hand-written `MM/DD/YYYY` / `UTC`
  fallback below the first one; all are gone.

## [2.168.0] — 2026-09-05 · A utility can write down its own jobs, and the wizard proposes them

**This is the first release in which a small utility can author a work order
template.** Until this morning the Work section listed the twenty-four starter
templates every tenant is seeded with, and there was no way to open one, change
one, or write a new one. The screen the Product Owner designed — eight steps,
starting from a ready-made pack — had never been built.

**What a person can do now that they could not this morning:**

* **Write a job down, in eight steps.** Work → Templates → *New template*.
  Step 1 offers four tiles: *Meter exchange*, *New connection*, *Inspection*
  and *Start empty*. Picking one fills in the safety checks, the steps, the
  parts, the readings and the help pack, and every one of them stays editable.
* **Put the steps in the order the technician does them**, and change that
  order by moving a row up or down. The order is what the phone shows, so it is
  data and not decoration.
* **Say what has to be measured**, with a unit, a range, whether a photo is
  needed, and whether the value posts to the meter's read history when a
  supervisor accepts the job.
* **Say how the job closes** — whether the customer signs, whether a refusal is
  recorded with a reason, whether a card is left when nobody is in. Those three
  answers had nowhere to be stored before today.
* **Save a draft and come back to it.** Nothing reaches a work order until
  *Publish*, which is the one button that gives the template its `ST-` number
  and its version. Editing a published template never changes work already out
  in the field, and the screen says so before the button.
* **Edit a template that already exists** — the pencil on a row, or *Edit
  template* on its detail. Both of those controls were absent yesterday.
* **See the jobs a new build needs.** Step 6 of the New Connect wizard — the
  step called *Plans & work orders* — has said since the day it shipped that
  *"those templates are not built yet, so no orders are proposed here."* It now
  lists them: one row per template, the job that completes the service flagged,
  a *Remove* beside each, and a count underneath. Nothing is written until the
  last step, exactly as before.

**The twenty-four seeded starters are real templates now.** They were rows in a
table nothing read: no bundle, no number, and marked as drafts, which meant the
New Connect wizard would never have offered one. They are published, version 1,
each with its own `ST-` number, and a new check refuses a build where a seeded
row has no screen to appear on.

**One figure moved and it is worth naming:** the *Inspection* pack's tile said
*3 tasks* where the design says **4**. The counts are counted from the pack's
own contents now, so the tile and what the tile fills in cannot disagree again.

**Rollback:** hide the Work → Templates section and keep the data. Nothing
billed, nothing posted, and every template row survives untouched.


## [2.167.3] — 2026-09-05 · A way into every screen the portal has

**Twenty-six of the customer portal's fifty screens had no door into them.**
Every one was built, working and answering correctly at its own address — a
customer simply could not get to it. Following every link and pressing every
button, a signed-in customer's whole clickable product was **twelve
destinations**.

**The worst of it was the bills list.** The only control on it was a greyed-out
*Pay*, and the bill numbers were bold text rather than links. So a customer
could see every bill we had ever sent them, could not open one of them, and
could not pay one either.

**What a customer can do now that they could not this morning:**

* **Open a bill.** The bill number is a link. Behind that one bill are four more
  screens they also could not reach — the bill as we printed it, why this month
  cost more than last, querying the bill, and asking us about it.
* **Pay.** *Pay* on the bills list opens *Pay now*, which reads what they owe,
  lets them choose an amount and shows which bills the money settles. Card
  payments still cannot be taken — no provider is connected — and *Pay now*
  says so per account, in words, which is where that belongs.
* **Reach the money screens.** From *Payments*: their cards and bank accounts,
  automatic payment, their payment plan, a plan we have offered them, credits
  and refunds, and fees to pay. Two of those — payment methods and automatic
  payment — linked to each other and to nothing else, so they were a closed
  loop with no way in.
* **Find their other accounts.** From *My details*: all my accounts, this
  account, and from there their final bill; and from the account list, adding
  another account.
* **Get help when they cannot pay.** From *Bills*: where things stand, and what
  help there is. From there: asking for a payment plan, and what is protecting
  their supply.
* **Open a request they have raised.** The reference in the open-requests list
  is a link.
* **Ask for a quick service without an account** — it is in the top bar now,
  beside *Track*.

**Four links on the two arrears screens went nowhere at all.** They were missing
a leading slash, so they resolved to an address no page serves. Nobody had met
them, because neither of those screens had a door either.

**Measured, in a real browser, by following links rather than typing addresses:
22 of 50 screens reachable before, 46 after.** Of the four the crawl still does
not reach, three are opened by a button rather than a link — the quick-pay steps
and the start-service draft — and the fourth needs an open request on the
account, which the demo does not plant.

**Two controls that were greyed out over screens that had already shipped are
open**: *Pay* on the bills list, and *Query this reading* on the final bill,
which now opens the dispute screen for that bill. Each carries the test that
fires if the door ever closes again.

**A new check refuses a merge that leaves a portal screen unreachable** — and it
walks from the front page rather than counting references, because two screens
linking only to each other are exactly as unreachable as neither being linked at
all.

## [2.167.2] — 2026-09-05 · Work looks like the rest of SMARTBillHub

**Field work's tabs did not look like anything else in the product.** Payments,
Premises, Accounts, Bills, Assets, Plans & Rates and Finance all draw the same
row of tabs — plain words with a coloured underline under the one you are on,
sitting under the page title. Work drew boxes instead, above the title. Nothing
was broken; it simply looked like a different product for the two seconds it
takes a person to notice.

**Work's tabs are now the same tabs.** Same words, same places, same links — a
tab still opens in a new window if you hold the key down — drawn by the one
piece of the product that draws every other module's tabs. Held up side by side
with Payments in a browser, every measurement matches: the colour, the weight,
the size, the underline, the spacing.

**And the one line of explanation under each Work title now stops at 80% of the
column**, like every other screen. It was running the full width of a wide
monitor.

**One more thing a person would have seen:** the search box on Work → Templates
was printing `work.templates.search` at people instead of *Search templates, job
types…*. It reads the words now.

Underneath: the template history table was drawing itself instead of using the
product's table, so its type was the wrong size and its dates came out
`2026-09-02` rather than in the tenant's own format. Both fixed.

## [2.167.1] — 2026-09-05 · The sign-up code you can actually read

**A customer signing up on the portal reached step 2 — *we sent you a code* —
and waited for a message that could not arrive.** The six digits were made and
put in the outbound queue, and nothing on the utility's side sends a text or an
email until a provider is connected. The back-office queue listed the message
by type, status and recipient and never showed what it said. So on a utility
that has not connected anything yet, nobody could finish signing up at all.

**The message now opens from its own row on Settings → Notifications →
Messages needing attention.** Click *Show the message* on the row and the code
is there to copy, beside how long it lasts.

**It shows only while nothing is connected to send it, and it stops on its
own.** Connect a text or email provider and the button disappears from every
row on that channel the moment the screen is next opened — there is no setting
to remember to turn off. The two channels are separate, so a utility that
connects email first can still finish a sign-up over text.

The code is never skipped instead. An account number, a postcode and a surname
are all printed on the paper bill; the code is the only thing that is not.

**Every time somebody opens a message this way it is written to the audit
trail** — who looked, at which message, and when. The code itself is not
written there.

Also fixed: five kinds of message showed an internal name in the Type column
instead of a word — including the portal's own.

## [2.167.0] — 2026-09-05 · The front page shows everything it can do

**A utility looking at its own portal saw four cards where the design has six,
and nothing anywhere told it why.** Two cards were being filtered out on the
server before the page was ever built, and an absence cannot explain itself.

The Product Owner compared the two and ruled: *"Yoi ahev these cards - may be
disable them, but for completess have them on screen"*.

### All six cards, and the two that cannot be used say so

The front page now draws every card, in the same order as before. A card a
visitor cannot use is plainly disabled and carries one short sentence:

* **Pay a bill · Report a problem · Start service** — *Not offered online at
  the moment*, when the utility has that switch off. It can turn it back on
  itself, in Settings → Customer portal.
* **Check my area** — *No status page here yet*. This one waits on us, not on
  the utility: a public status page needs somebody keeping it current out of
  hours, and until that is settled it stays parked.
* **Help & answers** — *Nothing published here yet*. Publishing one help answer
  turns it on, for that utility, the same day.

**The point of the change is that those three now look different.** Before, all
three looked like a card that was not there, so a five-minute job and a
permanent decision were indistinguishable from the utility's chair.

### What deliberately did not change

**A card you can see is not a door that is open.** The endpoint behind a
disabled card refuses exactly as it did when the card was hidden, so switching
quick pay off still stops payments — the card being visible changes nothing
about what the server will accept.

**The words in the top bar still come and go.** *Help* and *Visit us* appear
only when there is something behind them. A row of cards is a list of what this
product does; a word in a navigation bar is a promise that pressing it takes
you somewhere, and a greyed one that goes nowhere is worse than none.

**A portal that is switched off is still a holding page** — the utility's name
and colours, and no cards at all.

## [2.166.0] — 2026-09-05 · A utility can write down how its own jobs are done

**Until today a job template was one line — a name and a service — and there was
no screen to author one.** The Work section's Templates tab said, in as many
words, *not built yet*. It does not any more.

### A template is now a bundle, and the list shows what is in each one

A template carries the safety lines a crew must tick before it starts, the steps
in the order a technician does them with how many minutes each takes and whether
a photograph is required, the parts it fits, what has to be measured and **in
what unit**, and the documents and phone numbers a technician needs on site.

The Templates list shows one line per template with what it contains — *7 tasks
· 3 parts · 3 readings* — and counts them at the foot: how many are published,
how many are drafts, how many are switched off. A template with nothing behind
it reads *0 tasks · 0 parts · 0 readings* rather than going blank.

### Two Water templates can exist at once, which yesterday was impossible

A utility that wanted *New connection* **and** *Leak investigation* for Water
could not have both. It can now. The name is unique per service, so a second
*Leak investigation* for Water is still refused, and *Meter set* can exist for
electricity, water, gas and heat — which is what every utility we seed already
has.

### Publishing is the one act that reaches a job

Editing a template changes nothing. **Publish** is what makes a version, and
every work order raised from then on carries the version it came from. Publish
version 2 and the jobs already raised from version 1 still read version 1 —
nothing in the field is rewritten. The template's own screen shows both versions
side by side with how many jobs each produced.

Pressing Publish twice in the same second makes **one** version, not two.

### A template that has produced work cannot be deleted, and the screen says so

**Delete** is greyed out with the number on it — *35 work orders came from this
template* — and the server refuses independently, so it is not merely a greyed
button. **Deactivate** is the answer instead: it stops new jobs being raised
from the template and leaves every job already raised readable. **Duplicate**
makes a draft copy carrying every step, part and reading.

### What is not here yet

The eight-step builder that authors a template on screen arrives with the next
release; today a template is authored through the API. **The buttons that would
open it are not drawn**, rather than drawn and dead. The 24 starter templates
every utility is seeded with now read as drafts until that same release
republishes them — they have never carried steps or parts, and nothing has ever
raised a job from one.


## [2.165.0] — 2026-09-05 · Customers can pay us

**Until today the customer portal could show somebody what they owed and give
them no way to settle it.** Every Pay button on every screen was visible and
greyed out. This release turns them on.

### Paying a bill you are holding, with no login at all

Somebody with a paper bill and no account can now pay it in three steps. They
type the bill number and the service postcode, see what is owing, pay it, and
get a reference to keep and a receipt they can download on the spot — or have
emailed anywhere, which matters because it is often a neighbour or a relative
paying.

**No account is created and none is asked for.** A login is offered afterwards
and declining it costs nothing: come back with the reference and the receipt is
still there.

**They are shown almost nothing about the customer** — a masked name and the
amount, and not one other fact about who lives there. A wrong postcode and a
bill number that does not exist are refused in exactly the same words, so
neither answer tells a stranger which of the two they got wrong. Six wrong
tries from one address and that form locks for fifteen minutes.

A bill that is already paid opens showing nothing owing and simply has no Pay
button — not a refusal. A bill that was corrected says so and sends the payment
to the one that replaced it.

### Paying when signed in, and seeing where the money lands *before* pressing

Signed-in customers can pay the whole balance or an amount of their choosing.
**The screen names the bill the money will land on before they commit** — and
where it will split across two open bills, it shows that too, in the order the
utility's own rule will apply. Nobody finds out where their $40 went after the
fact.

If the payment service does not answer, the screen says so and **no payment is
recorded**. Pressing again does not risk paying twice: the request carries the
same reference it was given before it first left.

### A saved card, and a code before anything changes

Customers can save a card or a bank account and see it as *Visa ••••8812 ·
expires 11/27*. **We never store a card number** — the payment service holds it
and gives us a token, a brand and the last four digits, and there is no column
in this product that could hold more.

**Adding or removing a payment method needs a fresh one-time code**, sent to the
contact we already hold. The code from signing in ten minutes earlier will not
do; changing where money comes from is its own decision.

### Money coming back

The refund screen now says where money came in, where it is going, and why. A
refund of a card payment reads *"the money came in on the card ending 8812; we
have sent cheque 10241 instead"* — **because we cannot yet return money to a
card**, and saying so beats a bare *sent*. A refund where the credit came from
several payments says that too, rather than picking one and looking certain.

### What starting service will cost

Somebody applying for service sees the whole cost broken out: what is due before
we start, what waits until the first bill, and what has been waived — the waived
line struck through and still listed, because a fee somebody was excused is a
thing they should be able to see.

### Three things that are visible and still switched off, each saying why

We would rather show a control that says what it is waiting for than hide it.

* **Turning autopay on.** The screen is live and tells a customer exactly where
  they stand — the amount, the date it would be taken, what happens if it
  bounces. Switching it on is held, because **nothing in the product yet drafts
  a payment on its own**: today somebody presses a button and we ask; autopay
  means asking without anyone pressing, and that machinery is not built.
* **Paying the fees to start service.** The figures are right and the total is
  right. Taking the money is held: those fees are a quote that has not yet
  become anything payable, and only the counter can collect one.
* **A card surcharge.** No fee line is drawn anywhere, because whether the
  customer or the utility carries it is a per-utility setting and beta ships
  with the utility absorbing it.

### And the plumbing behind all of it

When the payment service tells us a payment settled, **it can tell us twice and
only one payment is recorded** — proved with the same message sent twice and
sent simultaneously. A reversal carrying the same reference is correctly a
second row and not mistaken for a duplicate.

⚠ **No real money moves yet.** Beta runs against a test payment service, which
behaves like the real thing and settles nothing. The five processors a utility
will be able to choose between are named and listed; each becomes connectable
when its adapter is written.

## [2.164.4] — 2026-09-05 · The prices a stranger is quoted, put back

Yesterday's fix for the demo utility's missing bills carried a fault of its own.
The check it added asked the database the wrong kind of question — it compared a
service to the word *water* where the database holds a reference to the service,
not its name — and that check sits directly under the step that sets up the
priced address a stranger sees when they ask *can I get service here?*

So the bills came back and **`31 Palm Ct`'s prices and the occupied flat at
`1408 Elm St` did not**. One word, and it is corrected: the demo seeds both
halves again.

Found within the hour, by reading the whole of a test run rather than its last
few lines.

## [2.164.3] — 2026-09-05 · The demo utility could not produce a bill

**Pine Hill Water & Power — the utility whose portal is switched on, and the
one anyone opens to look at this product — had 73 accounts, 129 meters and 402
meter readings, and not one bill.** Oak Ridge, which nobody opens, had a
hundred.

So on the customer portal, Bills said *"Your first bill will appear here"*,
Payments was empty, and Documents, Your plan, Level pay, Your final bill, What
happens if this is not paid, and Credits and refunds were all showing their
empty state. Every one of those screens was built and working. There was simply
nothing to show.

**The cause was two base charges for the same service.** The demo builds Pine
Hill in two passes, two seconds apart. The first sets up the prices a stranger
is quoted before they have an account, and creates a base charge for water,
sewer and trash. The second sets up the estate — meters, accounts, readings —
and creates its own base charge for the same three. Neither says which sort of
customer it applies to, so both apply to everybody, and the billing run then
refused **49 of 50 properties** rather than guess which one to charge:

> service sewer: 2 charge codes declare themselves the base and all of them
> apply to this account. The bill refuses rather than charging.

**Refusing was right.** A bill that quietly picks one of two base charges is a
bill that might be wrong by a few dollars a month on every account, forever, and
nobody would know. What was wrong is that the demo handed it two answers.

Nine further pieces of the demo failed behind that one — the payments, a refund,
a cheque covering three properties, a corrected overcharge, the second month's
billing, its collections, and a payment plan with its instalments — each
correctly reporting that it had no issued bill to work from.

**Fixed by having the first pass reuse the base charge that already exists for a
service instead of adding a second, and by building the estate before the
prices.** On a clean database: before, no bills and no payments; after, **100
bills and 83 payments** — the same estate Oak Ridge had all along. No price changed and no billing rule was touched.

Found by asking why every bill screen in the walkthrough was empty. The
walkthrough itself could not tell — thirty-eight screens came back correct, with
no errors, because an empty screen that is empty for a good reason looks exactly
like a healthy one.

## [2.164.2] — 2026-09-05 · The engine's diagnostics were printed on the customer's home page

**Under their balance, a signed-in customer was shown this:**

> apps.billing.selectors.issued_invoices_for_account is not published, so no
> bill states its usage+base / taxes / tenant-defined / fees balances. The
> payment meets the right BILLS in the right order (BR-PAY-001 oldest-first)
> and its WITHIN-bill breakdown is not computed — B5 GT-7's own shape, and a
> legal input to the allocator. Two facts have to land before it can be: a
> published kind→class map (OQ-128, `minimum_adjustment` belongs to no named
> class) and the tenant's own definition of the fourth class in the ledger
> (BR-PAY-038, PO 2026-08-11).

Two module paths, three rule references, a date and an internal test name, on
the first screen a customer sees after signing in. The same paragraph appeared
on **All my accounts**.

**What it was meant to be** is a short honest line saying what a figure does
*not* include — the product tells you when a total is incomplete rather than
quietly showing the wrong number. That intention is right and stays. What was
wrong is that nobody had written the sentence a customer reads, so the screen
printed the note the engine writes for whoever is fixing it.

**Six sentences now exist, in all eleven languages**, and they say what the gap
means to the person reading: *"A credit on your account is not in this total."*
*"One bill has no due date, so it is not in this total."* *"Your accounts use
different currencies, so there is no single total."*

**And a gap nobody has written a sentence for now shows nothing at all.** Not a
placeholder, not the engine's note. The figure above it is still honest and the
customer is no worse off; writing the sentence is what makes a line appear.

Found by opening the product and reading the page. Every test was green over
it, because every test fixture had an empty list of gaps — the branch that
fires on a real database had never been drawn in a test.

## [2.164.1] — 2026-09-05 · Six shut doors on the portal's front page, over screens that were already open

**A customer arriving at the Pine Hill portal had two working doors out of
eight, and was told in writing that the other six did not exist yet.**

Five of the six cards on the front page showed a greyed *Start →* with
*Opens with the next release* under it. The bar at the bottom said
*Sign-in opens with the next release*. Along the top of every public page,
*Help*, *Visit us* and *Pay a bill* were words that did nothing when
pressed, and *Sign in* was a button that could not be clicked.

**Every one of those screens was built, live and tested.** Paying a bill
without an account, checking whether service is available at an address,
help and answers, where you can walk in, and the sign-in page itself all
shipped over the past two days. Nothing was broken — the front page had
simply never been told they had arrived, because each of them was built
and tested at its own address and nobody went back to the door.

*Report a problem* and *Track* worked throughout, which is why the page
looked healthy: it had links on it, they just were not the ones a customer
needs. **All six now open the screen they name.**

**One card is still greyed, and correctly**: *What things cost* has no
screen anywhere in the plan and no prices are published, so the card says
so rather than opening an empty page.

This was found by opening the product in a browser and pressing things —
not by a test. Forty-two portal test files and 391 cases were green over
it the whole time. Three new checks now hold every door by the address it
opens, and each was shown to fail against yesterday's build before the
fix was written.

## [2.164.0] — 2026-09-05 · Four customer screens, and a deposit that could not come back

**Four screens ship, and building the last of them found a fault that had
stopped every closing account in the product from settling.**

**What do you need** (`CWP-046`) gives a signed-in customer six cards in their
own words — *move out* · *move to a new address* · *add a service* · *stop
service for a while* · *report a problem* · *something else* — and lists what
they already have open with us. The six are the utility's own list rather than
words written into the product, so a utility that renames *Move out* to
*Leaving the property* sees the new words the same minute. **Four of the six are
greyed out today, with the reason under them** — *Not online yet — ring us* —
because the forms behind them are not built; a card that looked live and led
nowhere is a failure this product has paid for before. The two that work are
*Stop service for a while* and *Report a problem*. The `Requests` tab in the
menu had pointed at nothing since it was drawn; it goes somewhere now.

**Stop or restart service** (`CWP-052`) does the arithmetic a customer would
otherwise do on the back of an envelope, and tells them the answer **even when
the answer is to leave us**. Stopping the supply from 1 November to 1 April is
five months of standing charge — about **$92.50** — against a **$185.00**
connection fee and a **$150.00** deposit to start again, so **stopping is
cheaper** and the screen says so. Ask for nineteen months instead and it is
**$351.50** against **$335.00**, and the screen says **closing the account is
cheaper**. The verdict is worked out every time from the utility's own prices;
there is no sentence in the product that always says one or the other. And the
line the whole screen exists for: **the account stays open and the standing
charges keep running.** That sentence is on the form, on the confirmation, and
in the note the clerk reads — because assuming a stopped supply stops the bill
is the most expensive misunderstanding a customer can make here.

**Your final bill** (`CWP-032`) settles up on the way out: service to the day
you left, the deposit we hold, the interest it earned, and **we owe you** — or,
where the service came to more than the deposit, what is still to pay. Money
coming back is a **refund and never a credit**, because there is no next bill to
put a credit on, and the screen says so. It also carries the closing meter
reading with one last route to query it — and once the account has settled that
route is replaced by a sentence explaining that a correction takes longer now,
rather than quietly disappearing.

⚠ **AND THAT SCREEN FOUND SOMETHING.** No final bill on an account holding a
deposit could settle at all. The part that works out interest was fitted a day
earlier and works correctly; the part that closes an account **never told it
which day to work the interest up to**, and it refuses to guess — deliberately,
because a figure worked out to a day nobody named is a figure nobody can check.
So closing an account that took a deposit produced no settlement, with a message
blaming the interest calculation. At a utility that takes deposits that is every
household. It now uses **the day the customer moved out**, taken from the bill
itself rather than from today's date, so re-opening a settlement next month
gives the same figure. Our own note claiming this had been fixed the day before
has been corrected in place.

**Where your level pay stands** (`CWP-066`) is the screen an enrolled customer
did not have: what they pay each month, whether they are **ahead or behind and
by how much in words**, the month it settles up, and every time the amount
changed with what happened that year. It shows an amount set by hand where there
is one and never the office's private note about why.

Copy for all four screens is written in all eleven languages, in each language
rather than translated out of English.
## [2.163.0] — 2026-09-05 · Ask us about a bill, question one, and see where your request got to

**Three screens, and every one of them ends on a reference you can look up.**

**You can now question a bill without ringing up.** Open a bill, press *Query
this bill*, say what looks wrong and why, and add your own meter reading today if
you took one. It reaches a person at the utility with your bill number, the
period, the amount and your own words already on it, so nobody has to ring back
to ask which bill you meant.

**Nothing about the bill changes, and the screen says so before you send.** The
bill you are questioning is exactly the same afterwards — same amount, same due
date. If the utility agrees with you they issue a new, corrected bill and the old
one stays in your list so your bank statement still adds up. Anything you are
*not* questioning is still due on time.

**What it does NOT do, said plainly because the design asked for it and the
product cannot do it yet.** The design showed the screen promising to hold
collection on the disputed amount and charge no late fee while it is looked at.
Nothing in this product records *how much* of a bill is being questioned, so
there is no way to hold exactly that much — and printing the promise would be a
promise a customer could act on and nobody could keep. The screen says what
actually happens instead: the bill stands, its due date keeps running, tell us if
that worries you. The question of whether to build the hold is with the Product
Owner.

**Asking a question is its own door, and the bill goes with it.** *Ask us about
it* on a bill carries that bill's number into the question; if your question is
not about one bill you can leave that blank and it is still accepted. Before you
send, up to three published answers are offered — and when the utility has
published none, that panel is simply not there rather than sitting empty. The
office and emergency numbers are shown as two separate lines, because they are
two different numbers. **Attaching a photo is still not possible** and the box
says so rather than pretending; that was deferred on 2026-08-08 and has not been
re-opened.

**And you can now see where a request got to.** Every reference — from a query,
a question, or anything else raised through the portal — opens a progress screen:
six steps from *you sent it* through *we decide* to *finished*, marked where
yours has reached, with the dates. You can add a note answering whatever the
office asked you for, and withdraw the request while it is still open. Withdrawing
stops the request and **does not touch your account** — the screen says that
beside the button, and a test compares the account row before and after.

**What a member of staff writes to themselves stays with them.** A clerk's
internal routing note — *"route to Tuesday crew, low priority"* — never reaches
this screen, and does not even leave the server. What you see is the steps, the
dates, whatever the office wrote *for you*, and the reason if a request was
turned down. A refusal always carries a reason, and if one somehow has none the
screen says the office will explain rather than showing an empty box.

**A request is matched to you by the telephone number on your account.** A
service request is not attached to an account anywhere in this product, so there
is no account to check it against; the phone number on your own accounts is what
is used, and that is narrower than the reference-plus-postcode check the public
tracking page already ships with. Two customers of one utility who share one
telephone number would see each other's requests, which is why the durable
answer is a question for the Product Owner rather than a decision made here.

Written in all eleven languages. Phone layouts are still deferred at the Product
Owner's instruction of 2026-09-03 and nothing here changes that.

## [2.162.0] — 2026-09-05 · The overdue screen, the three ways we can help, and what is protecting your supply

**Four customer screens ship, and they are the ones a person is most likely to be
looking at late at night.**

**What happens if this is not paid** (`CWP-057`) shows the real timeline from
that account's own record — payment due 14 August, reminder sent 21 August, the
ten-day notice on 1 September, and what comes next. Beside it, what letting it
run would cost: **$412.60 owed now, $95.00 to get reconnected — $507.60 so far.**
The blueprint had a third line, a $150.00 deposit, adding up to $657.60. **We
looked, and nothing in this product sets that $150.00.** The record says a new
deposit *will be required* and no rule anywhere says how much. So the screen
shows the two figures it has, says in words that a deposit will be needed on top,
and asks the customer to ring us for the amount — rather than printing a number
nobody agreed on the screen most likely to frighten somebody. The question is
with the Product Owner.

**A stage we cannot name shows as a gap, not as somebody else's date.** One rung
of the collections ladder has no name in our screens. Showing a customer at that
rung as though they were at the ten-day one would move the date they think they
have, so the screen says plainly that we cannot name their stage and to ring us.

**Help paying** (`CWP-056`) puts the three things we can do in front of the
customer: spread it over up to twelve months, send a doctor's certificate, or
level out next year. The certificate card says **in words that the hold has an
end date and is not permanent** — a customer who believes it is permanent stops
paying and is cut off the week it lapses. Sending one raises a request a person
looks at; **nothing on that screen puts a hold on anything by itself**, and the
confirmation says so and asks for the certificate to be brought to the office.
Below the three, one line states that nobody in this state is disconnected
between 1 December and 1 March, whatever they owe — **with no button, because
nobody applies for it.**

**And past the final notice, all three are still offered.** The drawing said
"ask before the final notice and all three stay open", which reads as though
something closes afterwards. Nothing in this product closes any of them — a clerk
can still grant a plan, a certificate is still accepted, level pay is unrelated.
Turning somebody away from help they could still get is the worst thing this
screen could do, so it says instead that time is short. That one is also with the
Product Owner.

**What is protecting your supply** (`CWP-064`) shows each hold with its own
lifetime, because the three are genuinely different. A doctor's certificate names
the day it ends and says the account carries on from there. **A payment-plan hold
carries no date at all** — it holds while the plan is kept and lifts the day an
instalment is missed — and the screen says that in a sentence rather than leaving
a blank where a date would be. The winter window states both its dates, read from
the record, with no button. One line runs across all three: **a hold stops a
disconnection; it does not stop the debt.**

**Credits and refunds** (`CWP-045`) separates two things customers say
interchangeably. A refund of **$89.80** shows its four steps with their dates —
raised 18 September, approved the 19th, sent by cheque #10241 on the 21st, and
*not yet* cleared, which usually takes up to ten working days. Two credits of
**$25.88** show the bill they came off. And one line does the work: *a credit
comes off your next bill; a refund is money sent back.* A cancelled refund stays
on the list marked cancelled, because somebody told money was coming and then
shown nothing has no way to ask what happened to it.

**Nothing on any of these four screens works out a figure of its own.** The
balance, the reconnection fee, the credits and the refunds each come from the
part of the product that already owned them, and which rung an account is on is
answered by the same read the staff screen uses — so a customer and a clerk on
the phone cannot be looking at two different answers.

24 backend tests and 33 screen tests, all in eleven languages.

## [2.161.0] — 2026-09-05 · Quick pay finds your bill, and a customer can say how we reach them

**Find your bill without a login.** Somebody holding a paper bill can type its
number and the postcode of the service address and be told what is owing —
`BL-2608-0141` and `78702` answer **$142.18**, with the name masked to
`M. A••••••` so a bill left in a hallway does not disclose who lives there.
Five wrong pairs from one address close the form for fifteen minutes. A bill
that is already paid answers **$0.00** rather than refusing, because somebody
who has paid should not be told their bill cannot be found; a cancelled one
says so; a corrected one names the bill that replaced it. **Paying is not
open yet** — the Pay control is on the screen, disabled, saying why.

**How we contact you.** A customer can now see the six kinds of document we
send and how each reaches them, switch email and text on or off, choose a
language from eleven, and read the day they agreed to paperless billing —
with a *Go back to paper* that records the change instead of erasing the
agreement. **Post is marked ALWAYS on every row and has no switch**, because
we print everything; the screen says that in a line rather than offering a
control that would quietly do nothing. One choice covers every document and
every account the login holds, and the screen says that too.

**Three screens that shipped without any test of their own now have one.** The
enrolment flow — the one-time code, the masked contact, the password and the
panel naming what the login cannot do — carried a comment claiming a test file
that had never existed. It exists now, 13 cases. So does the application's
final step, 7 cases, including that the paperless tick actually reaches the
server both ways.
## [2.160.0] — 2026-09-05 · A clerk can now write a tip, and a utility can add its first service centre

**Three buttons that looked deliberate were wired to nothing.** *New tip* on the
Customer portal settings, and *New centre* in Reference data, were both shown
greyed out with a sentence beside them — *"Writing tips arrives later"*, *"Adding
centres arrives later"* — while the server had accepted both since the day before.
Nothing in the build could tell the difference: every test passed, the screens
looked finished, and the sentences read like a plan rather than a mistake.

**Tips.** There is now an editor behind the pencil on every row, and behind *New
tip*. You write the line, choose which of the **six** customer screens it belongs
on, choose whether it runs all year or only between two months, and turn it on.
A tip longer than the **fifteen-word** guidance is still accepted — it is flagged
while you type, and now on the list as well, because the rule belongs on the
screen and not in a policy document. Beside the text sits **the tip exactly as the
customer will see it**, updating as you type; write nothing and the preview shows
nothing, which is what the customer's screen does too. A new tip starts **off**,
so nothing reaches a customer until somebody says so.

**Service centres.** *New centre* opens the same editor the pencil opens, with
seven closed days ready to fill in. A new centre arrives **hidden**: the address
is not on the portal until somebody shows it, because a published address is one
customers will drive to. Removing a centre is still the red button behind a
confirmation, and hiding is still what the screen recommends.

**And eighteen refusals that said nothing now say something.** If the server
turned a tip, an answer or a centre away — a month out of range, opening hours it
could not read — the screen showed **nothing at all**: you pressed Save and the
page sat there. All eighteen now have a short sentence, in all eleven languages.
## [2.159.0] — 2026-09-04 · The account switcher now actually changes the account

**Three faults in the frame every signed-in customer screen sits inside.**

**Switching account used to change nothing, and then quietly undo itself.** A
landlord holding four accounts could pick *22 Palm Ct* in the header, press the
Bills tab, and be put back on *1408 Elm St · A* without being told — every page
remembered the choice only for itself. And on the Bills and Payments tabs the
choice never reached the server at all: the header said *22 Palm Ct* over a list
of all four accounts' bills. Now the choice is held once for the whole portal, it
survives every tab change, and Bills and Payments ask the server for that one
account. Asking for an account the sign-in does not hold is refused by the server
with the same answer it gives for an account that does not exist — before this
change that request was quietly answered with all three bills.

**Two of the six tabs led to a blank page.** *My details* pointed at an address
the product does not serve — the screen is there, one word off — and *Requests*
pointed at a screen that has not been built yet. Both drew an empty page under a
working header, on all 31 signed-in screens. *My details* now works. *Requests*
is not shown at all until its screen exists, because a tab that goes nowhere is
worse than a tab that is not there; it comes back on its own the day the screen
ships.

**The messages bell counted nothing and never could.** It was built to show how
many unread messages a customer has, and nothing in the product ever gave it a
number, so the count never appeared on any screen. The bell stays; the empty
counter is gone until the piece of the product that knows what a customer has
read is built.

**Home and *All my accounts* are deliberately unchanged** — those two show every
account on purpose, so a landlord still sees $142.18 + $0.00 + $318.04 + $412.60
= $872.82 as four rows and a total.

Phone layouts are still deferred at the Product Owner's instruction of
2026-09-03 and nothing here changes that.
## [2.157.0] — 2026-09-04 · A bounce is two rows, and the last instalment carries the rounding

**Three customer screens ship: the money list, asking for a payment plan, and the
plan itself.**

**Your payments** (`CWP-041`) shows everything that moved money — payments,
credits and write-offs — newest first. **A bounced cheque appears as TWO rows and
that is correct rather than confusing.** Nothing in this product edits a payment,
so a reversal is a new negative row against the original: the customer sees
`2 Jul · Cheque #10174 · Returned by the bank · −$129.02 · BOUNCED` sitting
directly above `2 Jul · Cheque #10174 · BL-2606-0147 · $129.02 · REVERSED`. The
word *Reversed* on the second row is worked out from the first; the payment row
in the database still says *cleared*, and it always will. A goodwill credit of
`−$25.88` shows with its date and its plain reason. **A write-off of `$84.20`
shows its amount and its date and never its reason** — *bankruptcy* is the
utility's judgment about a person, and the amount is the person's own money.

**Ask for a payment plan** (`CWP-042`) lets somebody `$172.20` behind spread it.
`$40.00` up front over six months is **five instalments of `$22.03` and a final
`$22.05`, totalling `$132.20` exactly** — and the uneven last one is deliberate
and is shown, because a customer comparing the plan against their bank statement
will notice a cent. **Not one of those figures is worked out by the portal:** it
calls the same instalment engine a clerk's screen calls, so the two can never
hand out different numbers. Thirteen months is refused, naming the two-to-twelve
range. The consequence box says **five** payments then one, counted by the server
rather than by the screen. Pressing *Ask for this plan* raises a request a person
works — **a plan is set up by the office, never by the customer** — and the
confirmation says so with its reference.

**Your payment plan** (`CWP-043`) shows the whole record instead of a monthly
summary of it: six instalments with *paid on time*, *paid late*, *due in 9 days*
and *to come*; the `$40.00` paid up front; the cadence read from the record
rather than assumed; and — for the first time — **which payment cleared which
instalment**, so a plan can finally be reconciled against a bank statement. A
finished plan disappears from the portal today and now stays, marked closed with
its date. The right-hand panel says the thing customers get wrong: **a plan holds
the arrears, it does not pause the current month's bill. New bills still arrive
and still have to be paid.** Where the office left late-fee suspension off, it
says fees still apply rather than promising they stop.

**One sentence is deliberately absent, and it is worth saying why.** The design
ends the consequence box with *"miss two and the plan ends"*. This product does
not do that — nobody is dropped off a plan; we chase until write-off — so the
screen says what actually happens (*if you miss a payment we get in touch; the
plan stays open*) and the contradiction is a question waiting on the Product
Owner. Printing the design's sentence would have promised a customer something
nothing behind the screen keeps.

Every Pay, Receipt, Download and Agreement control renders in its place,
**disabled with its reason**, because a control that is not there makes a
customer ring up to ask where it went.

All eleven languages. 36 backend tests and 29 screen tests, and none of the money
arithmetic is new.


## [2.156.0] — 2026-09-04 · One bill line by line, the bill we actually posted, and why it moved

**One bill, line by line** ships. A customer opens `BL-2608-0141` and sees what
they were charged for, grouped by service — water, sewer, trash, then taxes and
fees — with a quantity, a rate and an amount on every line. The point of the
screen is that **the column adds up**: `18.50 + 17.80 + 34.12 + 35.67 + 22.00`
is `128.09` before tax, and `128.09 + 5.42 + 8.67` is `142.18`, from the figures
on the page and not from anything recomputed behind them. A penny of
disagreement there is a telephone call, so the server rounds each figure once
and the screen adds up nothing at all.

**Every quantity carries its unit and there is now no way for it not to.**
`2,000 gal`, `1 cart`, `4,820 gal`. A line whose unit we do not know is served
without its number rather than with a bare one — `4,820` in a column headed
*Quantity* is read as whatever unit the reader assumes.

**The readings behind the bill are the readings that priced it**, named by the
bill's own frozen record rather than by asking the meter what it says today, and
each says how it was taken: *Both taken by a reader. Neither was estimated.*

**The bill as it was printed** ships, and it is the file we actually posted.
The utility keeps a copy of every bill at the moment it is issued, and that copy
is what downloads — checked on the way out to make sure the bytes have not
moved. Redesigning the bill template or changing the logo cannot touch a bill
already sent. **Where no copy was kept — every bill issued before we started
keeping them — the screen says so in one sentence and offers a route to ask,
rather than quietly building a fresh one.** A rebuilt page can differ from the
one in somebody's drawer, and handing it over under the words *exactly as it was
printed* is the single thing this screen exists to prevent.

**Why this bill is different** ships in part, and the part that is missing is
named. A customer whose August bill went up sees *This bill cost $3.74 more than
last month* — `142.18` less `138.44`, which needs no ruling — with last August
beside it, `4,090 gal` against `4,820 gal`, and the sentence about what a jump
like that usually is. A first bill offers **no comparison at all**, not one
against zero.

**The four-line breakdown underneath it is not built, deliberately.** Which
reasons we list, and which one gets the credit when a customer uses more water
AND the rate moves in the same month, is a finance decision and not an
engineering one: both attributions give four lines that add to `$3.74` and there
is no arithmetic that chooses between them. It is on the register as an open
question with that worked figure, and the panel says in plain words that we are
still working it out. What IS built is the rule that survives whichever answer
comes back: **whatever lines are listed must add to the difference exactly**,
with no tolerance — proved by moving each of the four proposed figures a single
cent in both directions and watching the check refuse all eight.

**A defect found while checking our own work.** On the portal's front door the
utility's name is asking for a text size no stylesheet declares, so it renders
at ordinary body size. The check that catches this exists and is correct; what
is missing is that nothing runs it on a merge.

Twenty-nine backend tests and thirty-nine screen tests, all passing.


## [2.150.0] — 2026-09-04 · A year of usage, every reading, and the meter that is yours

**Usage ships.** A customer sees what they have used, month by month, for twelve
months or twenty-four. Maria Alvarez's water reads **4,820 gallons** this
period, her lowest month is **3,050** and her highest **4,820**, the axis is
labelled in gallons, and a `Download CSV` gives one row per month **with the
unit as a column** rather than only in the heading.

**The services that are not measured say so, and draw nothing.** Sewer reads
*Billed on: the water you use · Not separately metered*. Trash reads *Billed on:
your 96 gal cart · Not measured*. **Neither draws a graph and neither draws a
zero** — a chart with no bars says *you used nothing*, which is a different
claim from *nobody measures this*. An account with only trash gets no chart
anywhere on the page and the page still makes sense.

**A month nobody read is marked as unread, not drawn as zero.** On 2 September
Maria has eleven read months and one that has not been read yet; the eleven have
bars, the twelfth has a gap. A month that includes an estimate keeps its full
height and gains a dashed outline, so a customer looking at a figure knows part
of it was estimated.

**Every reading ships, with how it was taken.** *Read by a meter reader*, *You
sent it in*, *Estimated, then corrected* — as prominent as the number itself,
because *"you estimated and overcharged me"* is the most common dispute in
metered billing. Opening the corrected row says it in full: **we estimated
144,600 and corrected it to 144,130 when the meter was read on 3 July, and you
were not charged twice.**

**A reading we have not billed yet leaves the bill column blank** rather than
naming the nearest bill — which would tell somebody they were charged for a
reading nobody has billed. A meter that has passed its maximum shows what it
used *through* the rollover: `999,900` to `000,400` is **500 gal**, never
minus 999,500.

**Meters and equipment ships.** The water meter `88-40219` in the front boundary
box, the refuse cart `C-11840` in the rear alley, the backflow device `BF-2210`
reading **TEST DUE NOV** — each by the number stamped on it, never by a database
id. **The cart's *last read* cell is blank**, because a cart is never read; a
`0` there would say it measured nothing. A sub-meter belonging to the flat next
door does not appear. And the note says what to do: *damaged, buried or leaking?
Tell us rather than touching it — the meter belongs to the utility.*

**One number on the live home page was wrong and is fixed.** The usage tile
printed **`4820.000000 gal`** where the ratified display is **`4820 gal`**
(`DEF-CWP-3770`). It reached a customer because the test that guarded it handed
the screen a hand-typed `4820` that no server has ever sent.

**And the figures behind all of it moved to where they are measured.** The home
tile used to add up BILL LINES; it reads `metering`'s stored months now, the
same read the staff Account details Usage tab has drawn since August. The
practical difference is the one above: a bill line has no row for a month nobody
read, so *no use* and *no reading* were the same thing on that tile and are not
any more. Product Owner ruling, in their own words: *"We are mainiting last 12
month usage details on account - you canuse it."*
## [2.158.0] — 2026-09-04 · What we sent you, a plan waiting for your signature, and paying the same every month

**Documents and letters** ships. Everything the utility has sent this customer,
newest first, with the route each one went by — *Post · Email*, *Email*, *Post*
— filtered to bills, receipts or letters. *"I never got it"* is the second most
common call a small utility takes, and until now the only person who could
answer it was whoever could open the database.

**And it says what we SENT, never that it ARRIVED.** That distinction is the
whole screen. A row is written the moment a document is made, so it says one of
