four things — *sent*, *waiting to go*, *on hold*, *could not send* — and the
page carries one sentence above the table: *we cannot confirm that anything
arrived; post and email remain the record of delivery*. There is no green tick
anywhere on it, deliberately: green reads as *arrived*, and no provider on any
channel reports a delivery to this product. A customer ringing up about a
letter that never came must not be shown a tick.

**A bill posted and emailed is ONE row, not two**, and a route that failed is
named beside the ones that went — *we could not send this by Email* — rather
than quietly dropped. An account with no email address is normal, and the
screen says so instead of leaving a blank the reader fills in themselves.

**A plan the utility has offered you** ships. A clerk builds a plan covering
`$172.20` — `$40.00` already received and six payments of `$22.03`, `$22.03`,
`$22.03`, `$22.03`, `$22.03` and `$22.05` — and until today the person it was
for could not see it, could not accept it, and heard about it only if somebody
rang them. Now they see every figure, the day each payment falls due, and what
accepting would do: late fees stop on that balance, no disconnection for that
debt, **new bills still arrive and still have to be paid**, and missing two
ends it. Those four are read from that plan's own settings, so a plan that does
not suspend late fees says fees still apply rather than promising they stop.

**Accept, Ask for different terms and Decline are on the screen and are all
held**, each with the reason under it. A signature starts a payment schedule,
and the portal is allowed to write six kinds of row — a payment, a service
request, a meter reading, a preference, a contact detail, an account link — and
a signature is none of them. Widening that list is the Product Owner's ruling
to make, and it has been asked. Meanwhile the customer can read every figure
and ring the office, which is one telephone call fewer than before, not one
more.

**Two things the screen cannot say, it says it cannot say.** Nothing in the
records holds when an offer stops standing, and the only trace of which clerk
set it up is an audit row that gets deleted on a retention schedule. So the
page states both absences in words rather than printing a deadline this product
could not enforce or a database id in place of a person's name. Both are asked.

**Level pay** ships. Twelve months totalling `$1,501.09`, a monthly average of
`$125.09`, and the rounded level of `$125.00` a customer would actually pay —
both figures shown, because *"$125.09 rounded to $125.00"* is the sentence that
explains the number. The month it settles up in is read from the utility's own
settings and named on the page; a utility that settles in September is told
September. Where no month has been chosen the box says so rather than printing
June. An account with four months of history is not offered it, with the reason
in words, and an account already on level pay is shown where it stands instead
of being offered it twice.

**All three screens read the reads that already existed** wherever there was
one — level pay works out the same figure the counter staff see, from the same
code, so a customer and a clerk cannot end up arguing about two different
numbers on the telephone. Documents genuinely had no read anywhere, so one was
written in the part of the product that owns the records, which means the staff
screen can be built on it rather than on a second copy.

## [2.149.0] — 2026-09-04 · A customer can fix their own details, and add an account

**My details** ships. A customer changes their own email, mobile and postal
address, and it updates the utility's master records — the first thing this
portal has ever been allowed to CHANGE rather than create. Maria Alvarez holds
four accounts, and **one save reaches all four**, because her contact sits on
each account separately and fixing one would leave three bills going to an old
address with no way to find out which. The screen says so above the button.

**What it will not change, it shows anyway.** The name on the account and the
account holder are on the page, read-only, next to *Ask us to change this* —
those are what a deposit carry-forward and a duplicate check are decided on, so
they go through a person. Posting one straight at the endpoint is refused by
name, before anything is written, so the read-only box is not the security.

**Post that came back shows above the address field**, not below it, and
correcting the address clears it. A banner under the thing it is about is a
banner nobody reads.

**Add another account** ships. Account number and postcode, then a code — and
**the code goes to the contact on the account being added, never to the person
adding it**. Both facts are printed on a bill anyone could pick up, so matching
proves nothing; reading a message sent to that account's own phone does. A
wrong postcode and an unknown number answer the same sentence, so the form
cannot be used to find out which account numbers exist. Nothing is combined —
the panel says so before the button, because *add this account to my login*
reads as though the bills become one.

**There is no second password prompt on either screen.** Product Owner ruling,
2026-09-04: the checks belong at the door — the one-time code, three tries, the
lockout, the session's lifetime — and a customer who is in is not asked to
prove themselves again to fix their own record. Every query is still filtered
on the accounts that login holds.

The rule these two sit under moved from four kinds of write to six. The fifth
is that ruling; the sixth was a miscount of our own, filed as a defect rather
than as a change, because the original design had specified it all along.

## [2.148.0] — 2026-09-04 · Bills, with what is still owed beside what was charged

**Your bills** ships. Every bill in one list, and the two columns the screen
exists for: what the bill **charged** and what is **still owed**. A bill of
`$142.18` with `$40.00` against it shows both, and reads **Part paid** — its
own state, because a list that had to call it paid would ask nobody for the
`$102.18` and one that called it due would ask for the `$142.18` twice.

**A corrected bill stays in the list.** `BL-2606-0137` at `$154.90` is greyed
and reads *Replaced by BL-2606-0147*, and the replacement at `$129.02` sits
beside it naming what it replaced. Dropping the original would leave somebody
holding a bank statement they cannot reconcile against anything.

The **Pay** control is on the screen, visibly held, carrying its own reason —
*Online payment arrives later this year*. A control that simply isn't there
makes a customer ring up to ask where it went.

A customer with no bills yet gets a sentence saying what will fill the page,
never a table of dashes.

## [2.147.0] — 2026-09-04 · The home page is a whole page

The first screen a customer sees now carries what it was drawn to carry: what
they owe and by when, a panel of things they can act on, their last bill, their
last payment, what they used this period **with its unit**, and their three
most recent bills.

**Every panel can be absent, and absent renders as nothing.** No amount owing
means no attention panel — not an empty box saying *no items*. No tip in season
means no slot, closed up so completely nobody can tell it was there. A
trash-only account with no meter gets no usage tile **and no empty chart**,
because a chart with no bars reads as *you used nothing*. A customer in their
first week sees no bill tile rather than `$0.00`, which would say *you were
billed nothing*.

### Two decisions worth knowing
- **The usage figures are read from issued bills, not from meters.** Metering
  publishes no per-account consumption read, and building one inside the portal
  would put billing arithmetic in the wrong place. A bill line already holds
  the answer with its unit attached. The cost, stated plainly: usage since the
  last bill does not appear, because it has not been billed yet.
- **The twelve-month chart is not drawn, and its data is already being sent.**
  What is missing is a chart in the shared component kit; hand-rolling one on
  this screen is how four screens end up with four different charts. Adding it
  to the kit is its own piece of work.

## [2.146.0] — 2026-09-04 · Your account: the deposit we are holding, and the exemption that runs out

**Your account** ships. A customer sees the four facts about their account that
never appear on a bill: the deposit we hold, the services they are on and since
when, the plan they are billed under and what came before it, and their tax
exemption with the date it expires.

The deposit panel says three things in order — **we are holding $150.00, taken
on 4 March 2021**, that it comes back at closing with the interest, and, the
sentence that saves a phone call, **that it is not money off a bill in the
meantime**. A customer who reads a held deposit as credit stops paying, and
then owes money *and* still has the deposit.

An account with no deposit gets **no panel at all** — not a `$0.00`, which
reads as *we took nothing from you* rather than *there is nothing here*.

### Two things the build refused to invent
- **The interest is read from the signed accrual engine, never recomputed
  here.** When that engine cannot work a figure out it says so, and both places
  that pay this money out stop rather than paying the principal alone. The
  screen does the same in words. A `$0.00` here would be a number disagreeing
  with the customer's own final bill.
- **The move that opened the account is not shown** (`DEF-CWP-3767`). The story
  asks for it from a table that has never existed, and a move-in record carries
  no link back to the account. The panel says the date the account opened,
  which is a real column, and stops there.

### Fixed
- The story's own worked interest figure of `$3.20` cannot be produced by the
  signed arithmetic at any whole number of months. The test asks the engine
  instead — which is what the story's *a figure here that disagrees with the
  final bill is the defect this test exists to catch* actually asks for.

## [2.145.0] — 2026-09-04 · A landlord sees all four accounts on one screen

**All my accounts** ships. A landlord signs in and sees every account they hold
on one screen — the address, what each is billed for, when it is next due, what
it owes and whether it is clear, due or overdue — with **$872.82** totalled
above them. The four balances stay four: nothing on that screen can be paid as
one amount, and there is deliberately no control anywhere near the total.

The common-areas account reads **Billed to you as owner** and the others read
**Tenant billed**. That is a billing fact, not a permission: the master confers
nothing, and a tenant's own account appears neither in the table nor in the
total — which is what you ruled this morning.

*Owing* drops the paid-up account from the view. A householder with one account
gets one row and no total line, because a total of one number is noise.

### Added
- `CWP-023` at `/{tenant}/portal/accounts`, in all eleven languages — each
  written in that catalogue's own words for *records as Other*, not translated
  from English.
- `GET /portal/my-accounts`, never cached, built from the session's own account
  set so there is nothing for a screen filter to widen.
- `Home.dom.test.tsx` — the balance tile had no test at all, and its file
  header had cited one since the day it shipped.

### Fixed
- `DEF-CWP-3765` — the portal decided *is this a master account* from the shape
  of the row rather than from the column that records it, and was right only by
  coincidence: the rule that made the shape true was superseded on 1 September,
  so a master created before that migration would have been labelled as the
  tenant's.
- `DEF-CWP-3766` — 150 file headers across the repo claim a test that does not
  exist. `G95` now refuses new ones and the list can only shrink.

## [2.144.0] — 2026-09-04 · Twenty rulings land, and five are held back on purpose

The Product Owner answered sixteen integration questions and nine Work questions
in two messages. Twenty are recorded as ruled and implemented where they touch
code; five are not, and the five are the part worth reading.

**What changed on screen.** The mapping screen's `R02` row used to say *Waiting
for a decision*. The decision was made — a bank's *account closed* code always
records as **Other**, with the raw code kept — so the row now says **Always
records as Other**, in all eleven languages, and the writer refuses to map it
with a sentence a clerk can act on instead of a server error.

**What changed in the rules.** The bulk-email connector becomes mandatory above
**2,000 bills a cycle**, not the 6,000–10,000 the rule carried since it was
written: a mailbox is capped at about 2,000 external recipients a day, so the
larger figure was a promise it could never keep. A partner reading a utility's
payments is authorised by the **System Admin**, as an audited grant. Green Button
consent is **out of scope** — not later, not conditionally. Hourly interval data
is **not in this product**, which is about 26 million rows a year per utility not
taken on. Field work keeps **no parts stock** and posts **no cost to the books**.
A job's photographs are kept **twelve months**, exported before deletion, and
compressed **at capture to 100 KB** — which turns the blueprint's 59 GB over
seven years into about 3.4 GB standing.

**What did NOT change, and why that is the point.** Two of the sixteen
integration answers name a question whose text does not match them: each is,
word for word, the recommendation written for the NEXT question in the register,
and three questions are missing from the message entirely. One of them decides
which system is master of the link between a meter and an account — getting that
wrong bills the wrong customer. Both stay open with the mismatch written down.
A third question came back as *"I did not understand"*; it had been put with an
endpoint path, a rule id and a meter serial, to ask who may press a button. Its
plain-English form is now in the register, and that is what goes back.

### Fixed
- `DEF-GOV-3763` — the gate that validates the question register knew three of
  the register's four lifecycle states. The first question ever routed outside
  this team failed for spelling the register's own header correctly.

## [2.143.0] — 2026-09-04 · Your customers can sign in

> ⚠ **This entry read `2.141.0` until it was noticed that another lane had shipped
> the same number the same afternoon** (`DEF-GOV-3756`). Two builds sharing a version
> defeats the one thing a version is for: a customer saying *"this happened on
> 2.141.0"* would have named two different products. `2.142.0` was already taken by
> the time it was found, so this moved rather than the other.

### A login of their own, set up from the bill in their hand

Until today a customer could pay a bill with its number, report a burst main and
ask for service — all without ever telling us who they were. There was no way for
somebody you already bill to **sign in and see their own account**.

Now there is. On your portal's sign-in page, *first time here* asks for three
things, and all three are printed on the paper bill you already send: the account
number, the postcode of the address you serve, and the surname or company name.
If those match, we send a six-digit code — **to the phone number you already hold
for that account, and nowhere else**. They type it, choose a password, and they
are in.

### What they see, and what they cannot do

They land on a page that answers the question they came with: **what do I owe, and
by when**. A landlord with four accounts sees four separate figures and a total
beneath them — never one merged bill, because they are four bills.

The login is deliberately narrow. It cannot close the account, cannot change whose
name the account is in, and cannot end the service. The screen says so, before the
button, alongside the balance they are about to get access to.

### The four things we refuse, and why they are worth saying out loud

* **A wrong surname and an account number that does not exist get exactly the same
  answer.** Nobody can use this form to find out which accounts are real.
* **The code goes only to a phone or email already on the account.** If we hold
  neither, enrolment stops and says *ring the office* — it never falls back to
  something easier.
* **Forgotten password answers the same words whether or not that address has a
  login** — and quietly sends nothing when it does not.
* **Your staff sign-in does not work here.** A member of staff typing their office
  email and password into the customer box gets the same message as a typo. The two
  are separate systems with separate passwords, on purpose.

### What is not here yet

**Paying online.** Every *Pay* button appears where it belongs, greyed, with the
reason beside it. **Text messages and emails are queued but not sent** — the
sending switch comes on in a later wave, so today a code exists in your outbound
queue rather than on a phone.

## [2.142.0] — 2026-09-04 · Your own mail server, connected from a form instead of a deployment

### You can now type your mail password into the product

Settings → Integrations → **Custom SMTP** asks for five things — mail server,
port, username, password, and the address bills should come from — and
**Save and test** sends **one real message** to an address you type. If it
arrives, the card turns **Working** and shows the address your customers will
see. Nothing else has to happen; nobody has to put anything on a server.

Until today that password was not stored here at all. This product held only
the *name* of a secret kept somewhere else, and connecting email meant asking
whoever runs your hosting to place a file. Anyone who already had that set up
is moved across automatically, once, the first time this version starts — same
mail server, same address, nothing to re-type. If we cannot find the secret
where it was named, the card appears reading **Mail password needs entering**
rather than looking ready and failing on your first bill run.

### When the password is wrong, the mail server tells you so in its own words

Type it wrong and the screen reads **"The mail server rejected the password."**
Underneath, in smaller type, is what your mail server actually said —
`535 5.7.8 AUTHENTICATION FAILED` — because the first sentence is the one you
act on and the second is the one your support person needs.

### Pasted the wrong one at five on a Friday? One button puts it back

**Replace password** keeps the old one standing by. If the new one does not
work, **Go back to this** makes the previous one live again immediately. You do
not have to ask your mail provider for anything, and the history of everything
this connection has ever done stays exactly where it was.

You will never see either password again — only the last four characters,
like `••••kbox`. **Nobody can read them back, including us.** That is
deliberate, and the price of it is that a forgotten password is re-typed rather
than looked up.

### And you can take it back out

**Disconnect** destroys every copy of the password immediately. Before it does,
it tells you plainly what stops — *bills and notices stop going out* — and what
stays: every past run is still on the page, and any messages already waiting
simply keep waiting. **Nothing is sent from anybody else's address in the
meantime**, and nothing already recorded is deleted. You type the connection's
name to confirm, because it is not a button to press by accident.

### Fixed: a refused setting said nothing useful

Saving a bad sender or dispatch setting on Settings → Notifications used to
show a general sentence instead of the actual reason — so a port of 70000 read
as *"That dispatch setting was refused"* rather than *"port 70000 is outside
1–65535"*. The reason now reaches the screen, in all eleven languages.


## [2.141.0] — 2026-09-04 · One place to look at a build

### The work on a building is where the building is

Until today, a build — a developer's twenty-six flats going in at *1408 Elm St*
— had a screen of its own. You reached it from the New connects list, and it
showed the progress, the units, the jobs, the meters and the charges. The
premises screen for the very same address showed none of that, and the account
showed none of it either.

**So there were two places to look at one address, and the Product Owner said
so:** *"you are duplicating this — there is nothing called connections;
Connection = Account only — you cannot have two different screens — this is an
integration problem."*

**Now there is one place.** Open **Premises → 1408 Elm St** and the build is
there: a **Build** tab with how it is going — *In progress · Our crew · target
14 Apr · $14,435.00* over twenty-six units, and five of eight jobs done — and a
**Work orders** tab listing every job at that address, finished ones included,
newest first. The eight things you could do to a build are on that tab: hold it
with a reason, release it, cancel it, say what it is waiting on, add a service,
write down what is still outstanding, close one of those, and raise a job.

**And from the account too.** An account now has a twelfth tab, **Work**, next
to Meters. It lists the jobs on that account and the jobs at the address it
shares, and each row says which — so the final read on a move-out sits beside
the meter exchange outside, and you can tell them apart.

### Your old links still work

Anything you bookmarked, and every *Open this connection* link the New Connect
wizard has handed out, still opens. It now takes you to the premises — the same
screen as above — rather than to a page that no longer exists.

### What did not change

Nothing was migrated and no data moved. The build's own record, its number, its
services and its jobs are exactly where they were. The New Connect wizard is
untouched. The **Awaiting approval** queue is untouched except for where its
`CON-…` column takes you, which is now the same one place as everything else.
## [2.140.0] — 2026-09-04 · One reference, and it is the number of the job you asked for

### The report you send is now the request we work

Yesterday, telling us about a burst main created **two records** — the job on
your clerk's worklist, and a separate outage record — and the person who
reported it was handed the number of the second one. Two places to look, and the
number in the customer's hand was not the number of their own request.

**Now there is one record and one number.** Somebody standing over the water
picks what is wrong, says roughly where, leaves a name and a phone, and gets
back **SR-26-0049** — the very request your clerk opens. They can check it any
time with that number, without signing in, and see the same three plain words
they always did: *Looking into it*, *Crew on site*, *Resolved*.

### Deciding it is an outage is now a person's job, and it takes one click

A form filled in by a stranger cannot tell you whether a street is out. So a
report no longer opens an outage record by itself. On the request, your clerk
sees **"Nobody has opened an interruption for this yet"** and one button:
**Open an interruption**. Press it and the operational record exists — with its
own number, the status your crew moves, and the stretch of street it affects.

**And when three people ring about the same burst, they can all be put on the
one record.** The second and third reports offer **Add to RP-26-0412** beside
the button, so you are not left with three "outages" on one street. Everybody
who reported it then sees the same crew arriving, off the one record you are
actually keeping.

### Smaller things you may notice

* *"Someone has already reported this street"* still appears on the
  confirmation, and now counts the reports themselves as well as any outage you
  have opened.
* A brand-new utility can take a report before anybody has set up outage
  numbering — that used to fail outright.
* Nothing about a payment or a meter reading you send us has changed.


## [2.139.1] — 2026-09-04 · Your public page is in YOUR colours now, not ours

### The colour

Open your public page and the buttons are the colour you chose on
**Settings → Company**. Until today they were **our** red — `#EC3013` — on every
utility, whatever colour you had set, because the page read a product constant
instead of your setting. Your colour was being fetched and carried all the way
to the page, and then nothing used it.

**If you have not chosen a colour, you get our red on purpose.** That is the
style guide's own accent and it is the default; choosing a colour replaces it,
and clearing it puts the default back. Nothing goes grey either way.

**Hover and press match too.** The two darker shades a button uses when you
point at it and press it are worked out from your colour, so a teal button no
longer flashes red under the pointer.

### Why nobody spotted it sooner, in one line

The sample utility we test against happens to use the same red as the product,
so on every test the wrong colour and the right colour were the same pixels.

### Underneath

The public page had quietly grown a second set of its own building blocks —
its own panels, its own status chips, its own buttons — beside the shared ones
every other screen uses. Those hand-drawn pieces were the ones the colour could
never reach. They are gone, and the page is built from the shared set, so the
next time a colour, a size or a spacing is corrected it is corrected everywhere
at once.


## [2.139.0] — 2026-09-04 · Somebody standing over a burst main can tell you, without an account

### Report a problem, and keep a reference

Your public page now has a form anybody can use — a neighbour, a passer-by, a
delivery driver — with **no account and no sign-in**. They pick what is wrong
from six choices, say roughly where it is in their own words, leave a name and a
phone, and press send. They get a reference on screen, **RP-26-0412**, and the
job reaches your worklist as a request whose channel reads **Customer portal**.
That column is new on the requests list, and until today nothing in this product
had ever written a value into it.

**The address is free text on purpose.** Somebody watching water come up through
the pavement does not know your premises number, and a form that insisted would
turn them away. One of your clerks decides which property it is, later.

**A smell of gas is routed, not queued.** Choosing it gives them your emergency
number and creates nothing at all — no request, no record. A form that quietly
accepts *smell of gas* and puts it behind a missed collection is worse than no
form.

**A second report of the same burst is welcome**, and the screen says so. People
suppress a second call assuming it is a nuisance; for a burst main it is the
opposite.

### Track anything, with a reference and one more fact

One box for any reference you have handed out. The reference plus the postcode
or the phone number they gave you shows **the status and the dates, and nothing
else** — no name, no balance, no other reference. A reference is not a login.
Five wrong tries from one place locks that form for fifteen minutes, on your
utility only.

### And the piece your office has never had: a record of what is off

A burst is now a record with a life — *looking into it*, *crew on site*, *closed
off* — and, on the request it came in on, **the stretch of street it affects**.
Type *Elm St, 1400 to 1500* and the screen tells you which addresses that is and
how many homes are on them. A stretch with nothing on it yet is fine: an
interruption can exist before you know who it touches.

**Photographs are not accepted yet.** Every place that would want one shows the
box and says so, and the server refuses a file rather than pretending to keep it.

### ⚠ If your utility was set up before today, do one thing

Report numbers are a new numbering series, and a utility created before today
has no counter for it — reporting will refuse until it does. Running the
reference-data refresh for that utility creates it. New utilities get it at
sign-up.


## [2.138.0] — 2026-09-04 · Answers your customers can read, tips where they help, and where to walk in

### Write an answer once, and it is on the portal the same minute

**Settings → Configure → Customer portal → Help & answers** is where you write
the questions people ring you about. An answer has three states and only one of
them reaches a customer: a **draft** is yours until you are happy with it, **not
shown** is finished and deliberately withheld, and **published** is live. There
is no approval step — publishing shows it to customers at once — and the screen
says so before you press it.

**The order you put them in is the order on the portal**, and the column that
makes this worth opening is *read this month*. A question read 1,204 times in a
month is usually a bill-design problem rather than a help problem, and now you
can see which one it is.

**One field puts the same answer under a bill as well as in the list**, so you
write it once. And each answer has a row per language with its own state, so you
can see at a glance which of your Spanish-speaking customers are not being shown
what everybody else reads. **A language you have not written yet shows the
English answer and tells the reader so** — a missing translation is better than
a missing answer.

### One short line of advice, on the screen where it helps

**Tips** are one sentence a customer did not ask for, on the screen where it is
useful. A tip shows only when it is on **and** today is inside its month range,
so a freeze warning appears in December and disappears in March without anybody
touching it. **One tip per screen**, and when nothing matches, the screen simply
does not have a tip on it — no empty frame, no older tip, nothing.

### Where a customer can walk in, and what each place can actually do

**Reference data → Service centres** publishes your counters: the address, the
phone, how to find the door, what a customer can do there, what you take payment
in, and the hours for each day. **What you leave out is an answer too** — the
customer's screen shows plainly that an account cannot be opened at the north
counter, which saves somebody a wasted journey.

**Hiding a place is not deleting it.** A depot stays on your list and off the
public page, one control from coming back. Removing one warns you that a printed
bill may still carry the address.

**And public holidays close every counter without anybody typing them in.** The
closure comes from the holiday calendar you already keep, so 26 November is
already Thanksgiving Day for a utility that has done nothing at all.

**Nothing empty ever appears.** Publish nothing and there is no help page and no
link to one; hide every counter and the *Visit us* page and its link are gone.

### Two things every screen in the product now shares

An **on/off control** and a **chip picker** — the kind of field where you choose
several things and see what you chose — are now single shared components rather
than something each screen drew for itself. Three screens changed to use them,
including the portal's own Branding page, which had been drawing a column of
tick boxes where the rest of the product uses chips.

## [2.137.2] — 2026-09-04 · An application could be filled in correctly and still not send

Three faults, all found by clicking the screens rather than by any test, and all
in the last few seconds of the application — the part where somebody has already
done the work.

**Send is no longer refused after the form was filled in.** Pressing *Send my
application* answered *"Something went wrong on our side. Nothing was saved."*
The cause was ours and it was in the database: the rule that a consent may never
be dated in the future was written against the clock at the START of the piece of
work rather than the clock on the wall. Since the application is numbered and the
draft stamped before the consent is written, the consent was always a few
thousandths of a second "in the future" by that reading, and every honest
application was turned away. The rule itself has not changed — a consent dated
nineteen days out is still refused by the database — it now means what it always
said.

**The last thing typed is no longer the thing that is lost.** The public pages
deliberately take only two requests at a time, so a fast typist could have six
saves in the air at once and one would be turned away. That was harmless for
every field except the last one, because each save carries the whole form and the
next one repairs it — and there is no next one after the last. The applicant was
then told to *"finish an earlier step first"* about a step they had finished. The
form now sends one save at a time, keeps the newest values, and *Send* waits for
anything still on its way.

**A card that was not there is no longer read as a card.** The check that proves
the quick-service cards are really drawn was looking at the page after it had
moved on, and would have reported the same thing whether the styling worked or
not.

## [2.137.1] — 2026-09-04 · Eight screens now look like the rest of the product

The Product Owner walked eight screens shipped today and found every one of them
off the house style. They are corrected — not patched one at a time, but built
from the shared set of parts the rest of the product already uses, so the next
screen gets them for free.

### The connect form stopped looking like a sketch of itself

Four panels inside *Settings → Integrations → Connect* were drawn as blue dashed
boxes with typewriter capitals over them — a drawing of a form rather than a
form. They are ordinary panels now. The boxes you type into are the same boxes
as everywhere else in the product, and when the server refuses something it says
so in the same red strip you see on every other screen.

### Buttons are the right size, the right colour, and there is one of each

Every card on the Integrations page had a *Connect* button stretched right
across it. They are ordinary buttons now, the size the design has always drawn
them. On *Settings → Customer portal → Branding*, **Reset to defaults** — the
one that wipes your strapline, your opening hours, your emergency number and
your whole service list in a single press — now wears the warning colour, and
**Save** wears the ordinary one. It was the other way round. And an empty parts
register offered *+ Add part* twice in the same red; there is one.

### The portal preview shows what a customer will actually see

The preview panel on the Branding screen was squeezing your front page into a
column so narrow it printed one word per line for eleven lines, with the *Sign
in* button sitting on top of the information icon. It now draws the page at the
width a visitor's browser really gives it and shrinks the picture to fit, so
every line break in the preview is a line break your customer will see.

### The QR code for your bills appears

*Settings → Customer portal → Overview* offers a QR code of your portal address
to print on your bills. It has been showing a broken-image icon since the day it
shipped. It draws now.

### Smaller things

The category filter on the Integrations page is the same chip the rest of the
product uses. *Register | Issue log* on the parts screen now shows clearly which
one you are looking at — the chosen one was painted almost the same colour as
the page. And the work-order templates page has lost three paragraphs explaining
itself and a back arrow that pointed somewhere it does not go.

## [2.137.0] — 2026-09-04 · Find out what you can get here, and ask for it, without an account

### Type an address and see what it costs

Somebody moving in can now go to your website, type an address and read what you
can supply there and what it costs to connect — before they fill anything in. At
`31 Palm Ct` they see **Water · yes · $185.00 to connect · $150.00 deposit**,
**Sewer · yes · included**, **Trash · yes · $0.00** and **Electric · not here**,
greyed out, with a box that says **$185.00 before we start · $150.00 deposit on
your first bill · about three working days**.

The three quiet cells mean three different things and are drawn differently on
purpose. *Included* means there is no separate charge for connecting it.
*$0.00* means you priced it at zero and meant it. A dash means there is nothing
to quote, because the service is not there at all — a service you do not supply
never reads as free.

**An address you do not hold is not a refusal.** It says a person will look at
it, and the *Apply* button stays where it is. Somebody you turn away at the
first box never becomes a customer.

### A form that survives a closed tab, and carries no promise until it is sent

Everything an applicant types is saved as they type it, so closing the tab loses
nothing — the link brings all of it back. Until they press send there is **no
reference at all**, because nothing has been promised. The number arrives with
the send, and it is the first thing this journey shows anybody.

The form works out whether the address already has somebody living at it. If it
does, this is a **move-in** rather than a new connection — quicker, cheaper —
and the screen says so **without naming who lives there**.

### The paperless tick is a record of the words they read

When somebody agrees to have bills and letters by email, we do not store a yes.
We store **when** they agreed, **which version of the words** they were reading
and **which screen** they were on. Reword the sentence later and the old record
still describes the old sentence. **We print them as well**, and the screen says
so beside the box — paperless never stops the paper.

The application takes **no money and demands no documents**. The two you will
need are listed and marked *after you apply*, which is when you will ask for
them.

### Six small things anybody can ask for

*A meter reading looks wrong · my collection was missed · I need a copy of a
bill · my water pressure has dropped · a question about my bill · something
else* — each ends on a reference, each reaches the clerk's list, and each is
read from **your own list of cards**, so renaming one renames it on the website.
Anything that changes whose account it is, or moves money, still needs a sign-in
or a telephone call, and the page says that in one line.

### Under the covers

An applicant's unsent form and their consent are two new tables of the portal's
own, both walled off per utility by the database rather than by a screen. The
database refuses a consent dated in the future outright. Every money figure a
visitor reads is two decimals of a four-decimal stored value, formatted once, on
the server.

## [2.136.0] — 2026-09-04 · A clerk can raise, hold, cancel and close a job

**This closes phase 0 of the Work module.** Its promise was one sentence — *a clerk can
raise, hold, cancel and close a job this week* — and it is now true on a running build,
clicked rather than asserted.

### One list of everything the field has finished and nobody has approved

**Work → Awaiting approval** is a new screen. It shows every job your crews have closed
that nobody has accepted yet — the order and what it was, the connection (or a dash, when
the job stands on an address instead), the premise, the service, how it went, when it was
finished, and how long it has been waiting. Oldest first, so you work down the list.

The footer says how many and how long the oldest has waited — *4 orders · oldest waiting
6 days* — and that second figure is about the whole queue, not about the page you happen
to be looking at.

Accepting a job is still one act in one place: open it and accept it, and only then does
the service go live and the customer hear about it. There is deliberately no *accept them
all* button, and deliberately no search box: this list is short by design and the server
hands it to you oldest-first.

### Thirteen things that only a developer could do, a clerk can now do

The acts that used to need somebody at a Python prompt are buttons: **Hold…**,
**Release…**, **Cancel…**, **Waiting on…**, **Add service**, **Mark outstanding work**,
**Close** and **Raise order**. Hold asks for a reason in a few words, and the job then
reads *On hold* with that reason beside it; Release puts it back. Only Cancel is drawn in
the warning colour, because only Cancel destroys something.

**Every button that cannot be pressed says why, in a few words** — *"This build is not on
hold."*, *"Nothing is outstanding here."*, *"This build is cancelled."* — rather than
disappearing. A control that vanishes teaches you the product cannot do a thing; a greyed
one with a sentence teaches you when it can.

### A job can now be raised on an address, with no connection at all

A leak reported at **77 Cedar Ct** could not be recorded before this release — not by a
clerk, not by anyone, because a job had to belong to a connection. It can now stand on an
address, an account or a meter instead, and it appears in the approval queue like any
other. A job standing on nothing at all is still refused, by the database itself.

### Fixed: releasing a build that was not on hold quietly erased a note

Pressing Release on a build that was never held used to be accepted, and it **wiped
whatever the build was waiting on** while recording that the build had been released. The
screen had always greyed that button out; the server had not. Both now refuse it, and the
note survives. Nothing needs doing to a live system — notes already erased cannot be
recovered, but no further note can be lost this way.


## [2.135.0] — 2026-09-04 · A run says what it did, and says so when it cannot

### Read eight characters down the phone, and find the run

Every connection now has a page of its own — **Settings → Integrations → Recent
activity** on any card you have set up. It lists what that connection has done,
newest first, with the result written the way you would say it out loud: *93 of
93* · *86 of 93 · 7 bad addresses*.

**Every run carries a support reference** — eight characters, printed on the row
and on the run itself. Read it over the telephone and one search finds the run,
the connection it belongs to, and the mail server's own sentence about what went
wrong. The search looks across all your connections, because the person ringing
does not know which one those eight characters came from — that is what they are
ringing to find out.

**Open a run and you get the ones it could not do, by name.** A send of 93 bills
that lost seven shows the seven addresses, each with the mail server's own reason
— *No such mailbox*, *Domain not found* — so somebody can go and fix them
instead of guessing.

### And a new word, for when we do not know

Some providers accept a batch and will not say how many of it they took. Until
today the honest answer to that had nowhere to go.

**A run like that now reads *Unconfirmed · 93 sent, provider did not say*, in
amber**, and the connection's card shows it as needing attention rather than as
working. Open it and the counts read **93 handed over · — · — · —**: dashes, not
zeroes, because a zero would be a claim that nothing was sent and nobody knows
that. A run is only ever called done when the numbers add up **and** the far end
said so.

### What a run keeps, and what it never repeats

A run is written once and never edited. A correction is a new run, and the
database itself refuses anything else.

When a provider's message quotes somebody else's customer back at us — it
happens; a mail server will tell you which account and which street address it
refused — the account number, the street and the town are **taken out before the
message is stored**, and what is left is shown on that one screen to the utility
that owns the run, and nowhere else. The provider's own error code is kept,
because that is the part support actually needs.

## [2.134.0] — 2026-09-04 · Settings tells the truth about Work

### Six lists that said "arrives with Work" now hold your own rows

For three weeks the Work group in **Settings → Configure → Reference data** showed four
cards with a grey sentence saying the feature had not arrived. That sentence is gone, and
the group now holds **six cards you can actually open and edit**: job types, priorities,
skills, safety kits, parts categories and parts.

You start with sensible defaults and change any of them. **Eight job types** — reconnect
after payment, main repair, disconnect for non-payment, leak investigation, meter exchange,
backflow inspection, read verification and move-in activation. **Four priorities, each with
the response time it promises**: Urgent 4 hours, High 8, Normal 72, Low 168. **Eight skills**
your crews can hold, **four safety kits** with their contents, and **four parts categories**.
Add a skill called *Backflow* and it is there the moment you save, and in every picker that
reads skills.

### A parts register, with what each part costs you

**Work → Parts** is new. It lists the parts your crews fit — part number, description,
category, how you count it, and what one costs — and you can add a part without leaving the
page. A cost is kept to four decimals and shown as two, so a meter entered at `92.4000`
reads `$92.40` on screen and stays exact underneath.

**It does not count your stock, and that is deliberate.** There is no *on hand* column, no
*reorder at*, no location, and no reorder banner. The drawing for this screen shows all of
them; every written rule for it says the opposite. Rather than guess, the register ships as
a price list and the question of whether this product should track stock at all is with the
Product Owner. Nothing here has to be unpicked whichever way it is answered.

### Each utility's lists are its own

All six lists are walled off per utility in the database itself, not merely in the
application. With no utility signed in they return nothing at all, one utility cannot see
another's job types or part prices, and an attempt to write a row into somebody else's
utility is refused by the database. That was measured on PostgreSQL 16 under a role with no
special privileges, because the ordinary developer login is exempt from such walls and would
have proved nothing.

## [2.133.0] — 2026-09-04 · The customer portal exists, and a utility can switch it on

### Your customers now have an address, and you decide when it opens

Every utility has always had a web address of its own — the name you chose when you
signed up, the first part of every page you open — and until today the back office
never showed it to you again. **Settings → Configure → Customer portal** now shows it,
lets you copy it, and gives you a QR code you can print on your bills.

**The portal is off until you turn it on.** A brand-new utility's address shows a
holding page that says so, in your name; your bills and letters go out exactly as before.
Turn it on and your customers see a front page in your own colours with the errands
they came for — pay a bill, report a problem, start service, what things cost — and a
bar for those who already have a login. Each of those doors opens with the release that
builds what is behind it; today every one of them says so beneath the button rather
than pretending to open.

**Five switches decide what customers may do**: quick pay, sending their own meter
reading, payment plans, service requests and outage reporting. All are on for a new
utility except sending a reading, which is off until you choose otherwise. Turn quick
pay off and the *Pay a bill* card is simply not there — not greyed, not disabled, gone.

**Branding reads what you already keep.** Your logo, trading name and two brand colours
are edited once, in Company → Profile, and the portal shows them read-only with a link
to that one place, so you can never end up with two logos. The four things that are
portal-only — the sentence under your name, which services appear as chips, the office
hours and the emergency number — are edited here, with a live preview of the front page
that changes as you type.

### It is built for many utilities at once, from the first day

A busy afternoon at one utility no longer counts against another's customers, and a
rush on the portal cannot take every worker the back office needs: each utility's
visitors have their own allowance, one worker is always kept free for a clerk, and a
visitor over the limit is told to try again in a second rather than made to wait. The
front page costs three small reads and nothing that grows with a utility's history.
What the portal is *held to* in seconds is a question still put to the Product Owner;
nothing here claims a target was met — the walkthrough prints what it measured.

### Fixed along the way

The sentence shown when the product refuses too many requests at once had no words in
any language since the day it was written — a person saw a code where a sentence
belonged. It now reads plainly in all eleven.

### Not in this release

Nothing behind the front page's doors — paying, reporting, starting service, help
answers — arrives yet; each says so. The customer sign-in and the portal's own queue
arrive with the sign-in release.

## [2.132.0] — 2026-09-04 · Every integration card opens a form, and the server refuses what the button cannot

### What you can do now

**Every card on Settings → Integrations has a button.** *Connect* on a card
that is not set up, *Test it now* on one that was saved but never tried,
*Manage* on one that works, *Fix it* on one that does not, *Turn on* on one
that was switched off. Pressing *Connect* opens one form for every provider:
how it signs in, whether this is the real thing or a sandbox, the fields that
provider needs, how often it should run, and *Save and test*. The fields are
the provider's own — your mail server asks for a server, port, username,
password and the address bills go out from; Microsoft 365 asks for one address
and a *Sign in with Microsoft* button and **has no password box at all**; the
payment kiosk network shows the key we will hand them and the addresses it may
call from, and says nothing about tokens. Nine providers do not become nine
forms.

**A card marked *Coming soon* takes no press, and the server agrees.** Its
Connect is drawn dashed, and if anything asks the server directly — a script,
a stale tab, a mistake — it is refused in six words, *This connection is not
available yet.*, and **nothing is saved, not even a partial record.** The same
is true of a form filled in wrong: a port that is not a number is named under
the field, and no row is written until every field is right.

**In this release every live provider's *Save and test* is refused too**, with
*Cannot be connected yet.* and nothing saved. That is deliberate: the part
that talks to a real mail server arrives with the next release, after the
encryption behind a stored password has been reviewed and signed, and no real
password is stored before then. The form is real, the refusal is real, and the
card does not pretend.

### Underneath, for the people who run it

Integration work — a test message, a manual run, later the nightly sweeps and
the kiosk's incoming payments — now runs on **its own worker queue** with its
own worker, so a mail server that hangs for ninety seconds holds one of those
slots and never a clerk's screen or a bill run. A gate refuses the build if
the queue exists without the worker or the worker without the queue, or if
the default worker is told to drain it too.

A test request is answered *accepted* with a link to poll, and **the job's row
is written before the message is sent and before the reply goes back** — a
lost message loses nothing durable. Connecting, testing, changing, replacing a
password and disconnecting each write one audit row with the actor and the
masked reference, and never the secret. A password is stored in versions;
replacing one deactivates the old; disconnecting destroys every version and
keeps every run ever recorded.

The rules a provider adapter must obey are now a written contract with a
thirty-seven-case check that every adapter runs unchanged; an adapter that
answers *true* instead of counting what it sent is recorded as *unconfirmed*,
never as a success.

### Three things found on the way

Wave A's card colours never rendered — the theme deliberately has no
`slate` or `emerald`, so the state words drew in the body colour while every
test stayed green (`DEF-INT-3580`). Both integrations screens now use the
product's own colours, and the browser walkthrough reads a state word's
colour in a real engine.

The Settings screen's own test suite had carried one red case since the
Integrations grid replaced the last tab that said *arrives with* — the case
looked for a sentence that no longer existed (`DEF-INT-3632`, and wave D's
`DEF-INT-3622`). It now proves the honest-state mechanism on a tab of its
own and checks that Integrations renders the grid and never the absence box.
The colour finding above was also filed by two other lanes as `DEF-INT-3621`
and `DEF-INT-3630`; all three close here.

Two more things, filed for their owners and not fixed here: two of the job
kernel's test files cannot share one process — one reloads the kernel and
empties the queue list billing filled at start-up, so the billing-queue
suite fails three cases when it runs second (`DEF-BIL-3581`); and the tool
that hands out defect numbers cannot see a number already used under a
module tag, so it offered 3580 twice (`DEF-3582`).

The eleven catalogues gain about seventy-six lines each for the form and the
refusals, written in each language rather than translated word for word.
The ten non-English sets are marked as owed a native reader's review.

## [2.131.0] — 2026-09-03 · Their words, mapped on one screen — and the same payment as JSON to one partner, XML to another

### A partner's words for your things are rows you map, not columns we add

The payment kiosk network sends fourteen words for how a customer paid —
`CASH`, `CHECK`, `ACHCHECK`, `ACHSAVINGS`, `VENMO` and the rest. Until today
there was nowhere to say what each of them means to *your* utility. Now the
kiosk card on Settings → Integrations carries a **Mappings** link, and the
screen behind it lists all fourteen, every one red until you point it at one
of your own payment methods. Two of theirs may mean one of yours — `ACHCHECK`
and `ACHSAVINGS` both become *Bank transfer* — and the screen says how many
are still unmapped and that an unmapped word records as *Other* rather than
being refused. A word the kiosk sends that nobody has mapped appears on the
same screen, red, with when it was last seen. Nothing here needed a database
change, and the next partner will not either: the bank file's return codes
use the same screen, and an accounting partner's account codes will too.

One word is deliberately left for the Product Owner: the bank's *account
closed* return code maps to none of the four signed reversal reasons, so its
row is shown and its control is disabled with *Waiting for a decision*.

### One definition of a payment, two file shapes

The same payment now leaves as JSON to one finance system and as XML to
another from one definition, and both carry the same eight fields. Asking for
a file format is asking for a name; a name nobody has registered is refused
with the list of what exists, never quietly replaced. The print vendor's
format list, which shipped on 1 September, now runs on the same registry.

### Two things put right on the way

The seventeen integration cards had shipped with borders and state colours
that did not draw — the product's own palette does not carry the stock
colour names they used — and they draw now. And connecting with a misspelt
environment or cadence answered a server fault instead of a refusal; it
refuses properly now.

### Still to come

The format picker on the Connect screen appears with the Connect screen
itself, which the next wave brings. The eleven translations of the new
screen were written in each language rather than translated from English
and are owed a native speaker's read.

## [2.130.0] — 2026-09-03 · Work becomes its own part of the product, and a job no longer needs a new connection to exist

### The Work menu opens a screen

Pressing **Work** on the left-hand menu used to land on a page that said field work
was still being decided. It now opens the Work area: a strip with two tabs —
**Orders** and **Templates** — and the Orders tab lists every open job across every
new connection and every account, with the order number, what the job is, the
address, the service, where it stands, how it ended if it has, and which
connection it belongs to. A job that belongs to no connection shows a dash there
rather than a blank.

The strip has two tabs on purpose. Awaiting approval, the map, crews, parts, rules
and performance each arrive with the screen behind them; a tab that opened
nothing would be worse than no tab.

### A job on an existing meter can be recorded at all

Until now every job in SMARTBillHub had to belong to a new connection — the
database would not accept one without it — so a leak investigation on a meter
that has been in the ground for years could not be written down anywhere. From
this version a job stands on at least one of four things: the connection, the
address, the account, or the meter. Nothing already recorded changes; every
existing job keeps its connection.

The database itself refuses a job attached to nothing, and that refusal was
proved on a real PostgreSQL rather than on the test suite's stand-in.

### For the operator

The Templates page no longer says the module is undecided; it says the module is
being built and that page becomes its templates list. The sample utility's
addresses gain **77 Cedar Ct**, a house with no new-connection build, so the
demonstration has somewhere to raise its first job.

### Underneath

A new `work` module holds the code, reads the other modules only through one
read-only file per module, and a check fails any file in it that writes another
module's table. The screen is in all eleven languages, written in each language
rather than translated word for word from English; a native reader is still owed
a look at each.

## [2.129.0] — 2026-09-03 · Settings stops apologising about integrations, and the bell can finally tell you something

> **THIS VERSION CARRIES TWO THINGS.** The notification work below had been
> finished and waiting without a number, because two lanes were mid-flight on the
> version literal and a third bump would have collided with theirs. The
> integrations grid moved the version, so it attaches the waiting entry, exactly
> as it was left to do.

### Settings → Integrations shows you what you can connect

The Integrations tab held one grey box telling you that accounting, payment,
meter and email connections *"arrive with the Integrations feature"* and that no
connection could be made there yet. That sentence had been true and had stopped
being true.

It now shows **seventeen cards** — your mail server, your bank file, your
accounting export, your meter supplier, the payment kiosk network, and the rest.
Each one says in a few words what it does and which way it runs: some things we
send out, some we go and fetch, some they send us, and some they only read.
Every card reads **Not set up**, because on a new utility nothing is connected
yet, and a card that claimed otherwise would be inventing it.

Where one connection does several jobs — the kiosk network looks up accounts,
takes payments and handles returns — each job gets its own line and its own
word. There is deliberately no single word above them: *"three of three
running"* would be a summary of something that is not one thing.

**There is no Connect button yet.** The next wave builds the form behind it, and
a button that does nothing when pressed is worse than no button.

Underneath, the tables that will hold your connections are in place, and a
utility's data is walled off from every other utility's at the database itself
rather than by our code remembering to ask. A password or key is never stored on
the record the screens read, is kept in versions so a mistyped one can be rolled
back in a single step, and the database itself refuses to let two be active at
once.

The screen is in all eleven languages, written in each language rather than
translated word for word from English.

### The bell can finally tell you something

### What was wrong

You told us: *"this says - staff notification - but we dont get any notification"*,
with the bell reading **"You're all caught up."** That was true, and it was going to
stay true forever. Three separate things had to be true for a notification to reach
you, and none of them was.

**Nothing raised an alert when your setup came up short.** When we set up a new
utility and one of the seventeen parts fails to load, we are supposed to do three
things: name it on the setup screen, write it down, and tell somebody. The first two
worked. The third had never been built — the place it was meant to call did not
exist, and every run wrote down "not delivered" and moved on.

**The bell had two places to keep things and only ever used one.** An unfinished
second store had been sitting behind it since early August: nothing ever put
anything in it, and nothing ever read it.

**Nothing was actually being sent out.** Messages were being written correctly and
queued up. The part that takes them off the queue every five minutes needed to be
told which utilities to send for, and nobody had ever told it — so it woke up, found
no utilities, and went back to sleep. Every five minutes. On every server.

### What is different now

**A setup that comes up short now reaches the people who look after the utility.**
The person who started it, and every System Admin, get one message — one, however
many parts failed — reading, for example, *"Sample data setup finished. 18 processed
· 12 failed"*. It names the count, never the internal part names; the setup screen
already lists those in words you can read.

**Sending happens on its own again.** With nothing configured, we now send for every
utility that is set up, rather than for none of them. If you have deliberately named
a list of utilities on your server, that list still wins and nothing changes for you.

**The unused second store is gone**, so there is one place a notification lives and
one answer to "what is in my bell".

### What has not changed

The five kinds of thing the bell is meant to show are exactly the five you agreed:
billing run finished, payment failures, approvals waiting, import results,
integration broken. **One of those five has something in the product that actually
fires it today** — a finished billing run. The other four still have nothing to fire
them, and that is tracked; this change did not add or remove any of them.

## [2.128.2] — 2026-09-02 · The audit log now tells you what a record IS, instead of showing you its database key

### What was wrong

Three things on the audit log screen, all reported from a live deployment.

**The Entity column showed a database key.** Every row read something like
`tenant · 01a062a7-9f7d-73e6-96e4-700cba033c73`. That long code is how the database
finds the record; it is not something a person can read, look up or repeat down a
phone, and it took up the whole column.

**Some rows explained themselves in our language, not yours.** One summary read *"the
named sample_data_runs rows this run stored (BR-TEN-060)"*. That is one of our internal
rule numbers and the name of a database table, in a sentence written for you.

**The filter row did not line up.** Six boxes — Actor, Action code, Entity type, Entity
ID, From, To — and the Action code box sat three lines lower than the other five,
because a long paragraph of help text underneath its label pushed it down. The export
and column buttons then sat under a ragged block and looked adrift.

### What is different now

**The Entity column says what kind of record it is.** *Utility*, *Bill*, *Payment plan*,
*Meter read*, *Park*. Nothing on the screen is a database key any more, including the
Actor column, where a deleted colleague used to show as `User 01a0…` and now reads
*User no longer listed*.

**Support has not lost the key.** Hover the Entity cell and the full reference is there,
it is still what the Entity ID filter searches, and the row's own *Entry details* panel
shows it in full under *Stored record* — the fold that already says "exactly as it was
saved, technical".

**Eighteen of those internal sentences were rewritten**, across bills, corrections,
payments, payment plans, message templates and setup. The one above now reads *"the
setup screen names every part that did not load, and why"*. Nothing was deleted from the
trail: every entry still records exactly what it recorded, in words.

**The six filter boxes sit on one line.** The help paragraph is gone; the one thing it
usefully said — what an action code looks like — is now a hint inside the box itself.

### What has not changed

**Nothing about what is recorded.** The audit log is still append-only, still shows
every entry exactly as it was stored, and still cannot be edited or removed from this
screen or any other.

**No money, no rule and no calculation moves.** Not one figure changes anywhere.

**Every filter still works the same way**, including searching by an entity's ID, which
is unchanged.

## [2.128.1] — 2026-09-02 · A customer whose type none of your charges covers now shows up on the review step instead of quietly going wrong

### What was wrong

Every base charge you set up carries a list of the customer types it applies to. If a
customer's type is not on any of those lists — an agricultural account, a housing
association, anything you added yourself — then no charge covers them.

**The bill run said nothing about it.** The account sat in the run alongside everybody
else, did not appear in the blocked list, did not appear anywhere, and either lost its
standing charge or was quietly billed from an old price list we retired. You found out
when the bill did not arrive.

We fixed the seeded data for this last week, which fixed the customer types we ship. It
did nothing for the ones you add yourself, and that was always the bigger half.

### What is different now

**The account appears on step 2, in the blocked list, with the other accounts that need
you.** Under Plans, because that is where the fix is. It reads:

> this account's customer type agricultural is not covered by any charge for water — the
> base charges for water apply to commercial, industrial, residential only. Add
> agricultural to one of those charges, or add a charge that covers it; the run continues
> for every other account.

The rest of the run bills as normal. There is no *retry now* button on it, deliberately:
the edit is on the charge code, not on this screen, so a retry here would only fail again.

**An account with no customer type at all says so too**, in the same place, naming the
other repair.

### What has not changed

**A utility that has never scoped a charge by customer type is untouched.** If your
charges name no customer types, they cover everyone — exactly as before — and every bill
comes out the same.

**A service with no base charge at all is untouched.** That is a different situation with
a different answer, and it still bills from the plan the way it always has.

**No price moves.** Not one. This changes what the run tells you, never what anything
costs.

## [2.128.0] — 2026-09-02 · Setting fire rates no longer shows you electric and gas sizes, and you can label a size you add yourself

### What was wrong

You opened the **Fire** rate schedule to set its prices and the size list offered you *Electric 3φ
400A*, *Electric CT-metered*, *Gas 250 CFH* and *Gas 1,000+ CFH* alongside the seven fire lines.

It was doing that on every service, not just fire. There are **sixty** size classes in the product —
water pipe diameters, electric amperages, gas meter ratings, trash carts, solar panels, fire lines —
and every rate screen offered all sixty to everybody. A water schedule was offered solar panels.

The reason is small and slightly annoying: **the product already knew** which service each size
belongs to. It has known since the sizes were written down. That knowledge lived in one place the
seeding step read for the size's code and its name and then dropped everything else, so what reached
your database was sixty names with no service attached to any of them. The screens were not ignoring
a label. There was no label.

### What is different now

**Every size class says which service it belongs to.** The fire schedule shows seven fire lines. Each
service now offers its own: electric 6, water 9, gas 4, trash 7, storm water 5, solar 10, broadband 3,
thermal 3, battery 6, fire 7 — and sewer none, because sewer is charged as a share of the water bill
and has nothing to size.

**You can set the label yourself**, on Settings → Utility service size classes. That matters for a
size you add: if you enter a 14-inch fire line next week, you are the only one who can say it is a
fire size, and now you can.

**Leaving it blank is a real answer and it is the safe one.** A size with no label shows on every
service, exactly the way all sixty behaved before today. Nothing you have added disappears, and
nothing gets labelled on your behalf.

### What has not changed

**No price moves.** Not one. This changes which sizes a screen offers you, never what any of them
costs, and nothing already billed is touched.

Every utility that already exists gets its sixty sizes labelled automatically when this ships — the
ones the product shipped you, and only those. Anything you typed in yourself keeps its blank label
until you fill it in.

### Still to do

The **meter** screen's connection-size picker has not been narrowed yet, so adding a fire meter still
offers you every size. It is recorded and it is next; the reason it is not in this release is that a
meter you are editing may already hold a size from another service, and we are not going to change
what your form saves without deciding that properly first.

## [2.127.0] — 2026-09-02 · Every charge on a new utility now has an account to post to, so a bill with a fee on it goes out

### What was wrong

When you created a utility, it came with 28 ready-made charges: a late fee, an after-hours
call-out, a paper-bill fee, a hydrant rental, and so on. **Not one of them said which income
account it should be recorded against**, and a bill that carried any of them was refused when you
tried to issue it — the whole bill, not just that one line.

The Accounting screen said so plainly. It read *"28 charges have no account to post to."* What it
could not tell you was that there was nowhere to point most of them: the accounts a field-service
call or an equipment recovery would need did not exist in your chart, so there was nothing to
choose.

It stayed hidden because ordinary bills were fine. Water, sewer and trash lines take their account
from the SERVICE, not from the charge, so a demo utility produced 95 perfectly good bills beside a
screen correctly reporting 28 charges that could post nowhere. The moment a utility switched on
its paper-bill fee — which lands on every bill, every month — the run stopped.

### What is different now

**A new utility arrives with all 28 charges already pointing at the right account, and nine new
accounts to point them at**, approved on screen before anything was built:

* **4600** Connection & new-service fees · **4610** Disconnection & reconnection fees
* **4630** Field-service & meter fees · **4640** Equipment recovery & penalties
* **4650** Billing & payment fees
* **4700** Billing adjustment · **4710** Leak adjustment · **4720** Rate / meter correction ·
  **4730** Customer credit

Your monthly service charges follow your own service revenue accounts, so a utility that sells
electricity, gas or heat gets those charges filed against electricity, gas and heat — not against
a list somebody typed once for water.

Your five adjustment reasons — billing error, leak, meter error, goodwill, dispute — each now
carry an account too. **That changes nothing about how a credit is recorded today**; a credit still
reverses whatever account the original bill credited. It is there so your books can tell one kind
of credit from another when the product starts using it.

And **Settings → Accounting has a new Discounts section**, so you can see and change where a
discount is filed. It has no warning banner and does not need one: a discount already goes to
*Customer discounts (contra-revenue)* whether or not you choose something.

### What did not change

**No price moved.** This says where money is recorded, never how much it is. Every rate, every fee
amount and every figure on every bill is exactly what it was.

**Nothing you set yourself is touched.** If you had already pointed a charge at an account of your
own, it stays where you put it — now and on every future update.

**Bills already issued keep the accounts they were stamped with.** This applies to bills issued
from here on.

### One thing still being decided

An **impact fee** is filed as income for now. Some utilities treat it as a contribution toward
construction rather than as revenue, and that is a question for your accountant; you can re-point
it on the Accounting screen at any time.


## [2.126.0] — 2026-09-02 · When we set up your utility you can now watch all seventeen steps, and see exactly which one stopped and why

### What was wrong

When you created a utility, the screen told you we were loading your sample data and showed a
count that went up. If something did not load, it said *"Part of it did not load"* — and that was
all it said. There was no way to tell **which** part, or **why**, without leaving the screen and
going to Settings afterwards.

That is not enough to work with. If a utility comes out empty, the first question is *where did it
stop*, and the product could not answer it while it was happening.

### What is different now

The screen lists **all seventeen steps** we run, by name and numbered, **from the moment you press
the button** — before your utility even exists. You can read the whole list before anything has
started:

    1. Sample staff logins
    2. Plans and rates
    3. Properties, units and connections
    …
    6. Meter readings, first month
    …
    17. A move-in left half finished

Each one ticks over as it finishes — **Waiting**, then **Working**, then **Done**. A step we could
not run says **Skipped**, and a step that broke says **Not loaded**, and either way **the reason is
printed on that step's own line, in the words the system itself produced**. So instead of *"part of
it did not load"*, you now read, on line 6:

    6. Meter readings, first month                                   NOT LOADED
       relation "meter_reads" does not exist

A step we have not reached yet says **Not started** — never *Done*. That sounds small and it is the
thing we were most careful about: a list that claims a step finished because we have no record of it
would be worse than the single line it replaces, because it would be confidently wrong.

**"Skipped" and "Not loaded" are now different words**, and they used to be the same one. A skipped
step means nothing broke — a part of the product is not switched on yet — and a broken step means
something failed. Reading them as the same thing is how a real fault used to hide in plain sight.

If we lose contact with the server altogether, the list says so and prints a short reference you can
read aloud to support, rather than sitting silently.

### What has not changed

Everything the screen used to say, it still says: your utility and owner login, the reference lists
with their counts, and the accounting setup all still tick off above the seventeen. The button that
takes you into your utility still waits until the work is finished, exactly as before.
Nothing about how your utility is built has changed — only what you can see of it.

## [2.125.8] — 2026-09-02 · A solar or battery customer could not be billed at all, and the ten panel types finally reach the utilities that already exist

### What was wrong

**A solar customer's bill had no solar line on it. Not a wrong figure — nothing.** The same was true
of battery, storm water and broadband.

Yesterday we changed what a *size* means for those four services. It used to be a label that picked
a price, the way a water pipe's diameter does. It is now a real quantity: a **4 kW panel**, a **10 kW
battery**, and we add them up. A customer with three panels of **2 kW, 4 kW and 8 kW** has a **14 kW**
system, and at **$14.00 per kW** their solar line is **$196.00**.

Underneath the billing code was an old assumption: *if a service has a list of sizes, its price must
depend on which size you have.* That was true for every service that had a list — until yesterday,
when four of them got a list of **equipment** instead of a list of **prices**. So the product looked
at a solar customer, saw ten panel types, decided the price must depend on which panel they own,
found the utility had not priced any panel individually — and produced no line at all.

It was in **three** places, and the third was the check we built to watch the new pricing rules before
they touch real money. That check was quietly reporting every solar and battery customer as *"cannot
be evaluated"*.

### What changed

The product now asks the question it actually meant: **does this service's price depend on the size?**
For a solar panel or a battery the answer is no — the price is per kilowatt and the kilowatts add up.
For a water pipe or a rubbish bin the answer is yes.

That question is asked in one place and used by all three, and **no service is named anywhere in it** —
so it is already right for Fire, the eleventh service that arrived the same day.

### The ten panel types now reach utilities that already exist

The list of installable sizes grew from **40 to 60**: ten solar panel types (1–10 kW), six battery
capacities (5–30 kW), five storm-water property sizes, and the **seven fire sizes** that arrived with
the eleventh service hours later and had never reached the delivery list either. Four old solar inverter bands and four old
storm-water bands are **withdrawn** — they were superseded on 27 August and had never been removed.

Growing the list is not the same as delivering it. Reference data reaches an existing utility only
when its version moves, so without that step the new panel types would have reached **newly created
utilities only**, and every utility already set up would have kept the four withdrawn bands for ever.
The version moved with the content, in the same change.

**Nobody loses a size they already have.** Seed data never deletes: a utility already holding one of
the eight withdrawn codes keeps it and can switch it off on its own Settings screen.

### What deliberately did not change

**Rubbish is still never added up.** Its bins are measured in gallons and its skips in cubic yards,
and there is no unit in which a 96-gallon bin plus a 4 cubic-yard skip is a quantity — so the product
refuses to total them rather than inventing a number. Rubbish is billed the way it always was: the bin
size picks the price and the count multiplies it.

**A utility that has not priced a size still gets a refusal that names that size**, rather than being
quietly charged at some other size's rate. That is the choice made on 28 August with its cost stated.

**No signed billing figure moved.** The two capacity figures on record, **$40.00** solar and **$24.00**
battery, are exactly where they were.
