## [2.125.7] — 2026-09-02 · Sewer can be saved, and the demo now tells you which of your services it could not set up

### Two things that were wrong, and both were the product failing to say what it knew

**A clerk who opened Sewer in Settings and pressed Save was told to pick a unit of
measure — and there was none to pick.** Sewer is billed as a percentage of the water
charge. It reads no meter and counts nothing, so it has no unit; that was ruled this
morning. The screen and the server both went on demanding one anyway, so the save was
refused and there was nothing the clerk could do about it.

**And a utility that ticked three services could get sample data for only two, with a
green tick on every step.** The demo estate put one meter on a unit, water took it, and
electric got no meter, no reading and no line on any of the 95 bills — not even its
`$12.00` monthly charge, which is **`$576.00` a month across 48 units**. The product knew
why and wrote the reason to a server log file, where no clerk will ever see it. That cost
a whole conversation about whether the billing engine was broken. It was not: it billed
95 bills correctly, from the data it was given.

### What changed

**A unit of measure is asked for only where there is something to measure.** A metered
service is read from a dial and the reading is in something. A capacity service is billed
by a count and the count is in something — three carts at `$15.00` is `$45.00`. A service
billed as a percentage of another has neither, so its unit boxes are simply not shown, and
sewer still bills 40% of the water usage charge: on `$28.75` of water usage, `$11.50`.

⚠ **The check for the other two did not weaken, and there are tests whose only job is to
prove it.** A metered service with no unit is still refused, on the screen and on the
server.

**The Sample data panel now shows the reason a step could not set a service up, even when
the step SUCCEEDED.** Until today it showed a reason only when a step FAILED — so a step
that built most of the estate and left one service out looked perfectly healthy. The
sentence is the same one that used to go to the log.

A worked example of the sentence a utility will actually see: a utility that sells sewer
and not water gets no sewer connection in its sample data, because sewer is a percentage
of a water charge that does not exist. **That is correct rather than broken**, and it is
now said on the screen instead of assumed.

### What did NOT change

No billing figure moved. Nothing already issued moved.

## [2.125.6] — 2026-09-02 · A Trash unit was told its bill could not be produced, while that utility was producing 96 bills

### The things that were wrong

**The pricing panel on a Trash unit carried a red warning saying a bill could not be produced from
that price list, and it was not true.** The sentence read:

> *"This schedule prices in cart and the service is billed in , with no conversion recorded. A bill
> cannot be produced from it until that is settled."*

Trash bills perfectly well. A household with three bins is billed **3 × $15.00 = $45.00**, and the
same utility, set up from scratch on a real database, produced **96 bills** with that warning on its
screen. There are two separate faults in that one sentence and both are fixed.

**First, the warning should never have appeared at all.** Yesterday the product learned to compare
the unit a price is written in against the unit the meter reads. That check earns its keep: a gas
price of **$1.15 per ccf** sitting over a meter that records **therms** overcharges by roughly
**4% — about $1.72 a month on one meter** — on a bill that adds up correctly and that nothing used
to flag. **But Trash has no meter.** It is priced by counting bins, so there is no reading and
nothing to compare a price against; the product was holding *"per cart"* against *"per month"* and
calling the difference a fault. **The check now applies only to the services a utility has declared
it measures with a meter** — the three-way choice made this week: metered, a share of another
service, or capacity. The product no longer keeps its own list of which is which; it reads what each
utility has declared on its own Settings screen.

**Second, the blank.** Where that sentence should have named a unit it named nothing, on **three
screens**: the unit's pricing panel, the rate-schedule page and the New Rate wizard. All three were
reading a settings box that has never been filled in on any utility we have ever set up. The unit
they should read — and now do — is the one the meter actually records.

**Gas still fails the check, and that is how we know this is finished rather than undone.** A test
drives the gas case and requires it to be refused; if it ever passes, the fix that caught the 4%
has been removed.

### What did not change

**Bills.** Thirteen utilities were provisioned on a real PostgreSQL database before and after this
change — one per service, plus three realistic combinations — and both runs produced the same
result: **nine of the ten services a person can tick at sign-up produce bills.** The tenth is Sewer,
which cannot be sold on its own because it is priced as a share of the water bill. **The frozen
billing figures are unchanged**, checked before and after.

### Repaired on the way through

Four checks in the price-unit test file had stopped running earlier the same day, when this week's
change to the seeded units moved Gas from *therms with ccf as its alternate* to the reverse. They
failed on a settings refusal before reaching the thing they were written to check, so the product
looked tested where it was not. All four run again.


## [2.125.5] — 2026-09-02 · A reading in the wrong unit is now caught while somebody is still standing at the screen

### The thing that was wrong

**A gas meter that measures in therms, on a price list quoted per ccf, uploaded without a
word of complaint.** The reading was accepted, the batch posted, and the mistake only turned
up when the bill run refused it — which is the middle of the night, with nobody there to
answer. The clerk who could have fixed it in three seconds had gone home hours earlier.

**What it costs when it slips through the other way.** One therm of gas is about 0.964 ccf, so
a 42-unit reading priced at the signed $1.15 per ccf bills **$48.30** where the honest figure
is about **$46.58** — roughly **4% over, $1.72 a month on one meter**, on a bill that adds up
perfectly and that nothing objected to.

**Why nothing caught it.** The product compared the two units at the price list, and at the
bill run, and nowhere in between. The upload screen — the one place a person is holding the
batch and can correct the row that caused it — had never been asked to look.

### What changed

**The import screen now refuses a reading the price list cannot price, and names both ways
out.** It says which unit the reading is in and which unit the schedule charges by, and it
offers the two remedies plainly: change the meter's unit of measure, or change the rate
schedule's. It does not guess which of the two is the typo, because guessing would send
somebody to the wrong screen.

**One bad meter no longer holds up the file.** The row is held for a decision; every other
reading in the batch posts as normal.

**A meter that measures peak demand is deliberately left alone.** Demand is recorded in kW
beside energy in kWh, and those are meant to differ — checking one against the other would
refuse every demand bill there is. The check says so on the row rather than going quiet.

**Where the units differ only in size — kilogallons against hundred cubic feet — it warns
rather than refuses**, unchanged, because that is what was signed off. Where they are
different kinds of measurement altogether, like energy against volume, it refuses, because no
conversion number can ever reconcile those two.

**Nothing was invented and no signed figure moved.** The frozen billing figures check out
unchanged, and the billing engine's own refusal is untouched and still stands behind this one
— a reading can be older than the price list it meets.

### Still open

**The refusal shows its internal name on screen until the wording is translated.** The message
a clerk needs — *"Unit does not match the rate schedule"* — has been handed to the team that
owns the eleven language files and is not in them yet.

**Whether a utility may switch this check off is with the Product Owner.** Today it can, the
same as every other judgment check; it fails safe if they do, because the bill run still
refuses.

## [2.125.4] — 2026-09-02 · Solar, Broadband and Battery utilities now get bills — nine of the ten services a person can buy

### The thing that was wrong

**A utility that signed up to sell only Solar, only Broadband or only Battery got the whole demo
estate and not one bill.** 70 addresses, 118 units, 48 connections — and then every one of its 48
customers was refused, because there was no price list for the service it sells. Thirteen of the
seventeen pieces of the sample load fell over behind that. It looked like a different problem from
the one fixed the day before, and it was: that fix gave these three services an estate, this one
gives them a price.

**Why nothing caught it.** A service the price list has no entry for is simply absent from the
price list — which looks exactly the same as a service the utility does not sell. Nothing in the
product compared *the services a utility sells* against *the services its plan prices*.

### What changed

**Each of the three now produces 96 bills**, the same number a Trash utility produces, measured one
utility per service on a real database through the same sign-up the product uses. **Nine of the ten
services a person can tick at sign-up now produce bills.** The tenth is Sewer, which cannot be sold
on its own because it is priced as a share of the water bill — that refusal is correct and is not a
gap.

**They are billed the way Trash already is** — on the equipment recorded at each unit, not on a
meter reading — so they get the same three things Trash has: a price-list entry, a line on the plan
and a base charge.

**Every figure on those bills is $0.00, and that is the decided answer rather than a hole.** Nobody
has yet said what a solar, broadband or battery customer is charged, or how their service is sized.
The rule for exactly that case was already set — bill it as zero, and say so on the bill — so a
customer's June bill carries a line reading **$0.00** instead of carrying nothing. The day the price
and the sizing are decided, those lines carry real money with no further change to the product.

**Nothing was invented and no signed figure moved.** The frozen billing figures check out
unchanged, and the two capacity examples that price from real records still read **solar 4 × $10.00
= $40.00** and **battery 2 × $12.00 = $24.00**. A water utility's bills are identical to the byte.

**A small piece of wording was repaired on the way through.** A plan belonging to a utility with no
metered service used to describe itself as *"Sample plan.  at a $0.00 monthly base"* — with a gap
where the service name should be. It now reads *"Sample plan. Trash — billed on the equipment
recorded at each unit, with no monthly base."*

### Still open

What a solar, broadband or battery customer is charged, and what their service is measured in, are
one decision and have not been made. Until they are, those lines read $0.00 on the bill rather than
being left off it.


## [2.125.3] — 2026-09-02 · Four services that produced an empty product now get a demo estate, and a battery can be billed

### The things that were wrong

**A utility that signed up to sell Solar, Broadband, Battery or Thermal/Heat received an empty
product.** Not a thin one — an empty one. No addresses, no units, no connections, no customers, no
bills. Fourteen of the seventeen pieces of the sample load fell over behind the first one. A water
utility on the same day got 70 addresses, 118 units and 95 bills it could open and read.

The two reasons were different and both were honest. For Solar, Broadband and Battery the sample
data simply had no idea what an estate for them looks like, and said so. For Thermal/Heat the
product had never been told what unit that service measures in, and would not invent one — a meter
with no unit on it is the one thing this product refuses outright.

**And a battery customer could not be billed at all.** The bill run stopped on the very first
account, asking a question about battery sizes that the Product Owner had already answered five
days earlier — by deciding there are no battery size bands, because capacity services are not sized
that way. The answer reached our records and never reached the code.

### What changed

**All ten services can now be given a demo estate.** Solar, Broadband and Battery ride on the unit
with no meter — exactly the way Trash already does, and for the same reason: they are billed on
what is installed rather than on what is measured. Thermal/Heat is metered, so it now carries the
unit our own catalogue already reserved for it (**ton-hours** for cooling, **thousand pounds** for
steam). Each of the four goes from **nothing at all** to **70 addresses and 118 units**.

**Nothing was invented to do it.** No price, no size and no capacity figure is made up for any of
the four; where a number has not been decided, the line bills **$0.00** and says so, which is the
rule the Product Owner already set for exactly this case.

**A battery customer can be billed.** Two kW blocks at $12.00 each now bill **$24.00**, alongside
solar's $40.00, produced from real records rather than from a test.

**A heating/cooling utility now has a working demo.** Once Thermal/Heat had a unit it was an
ordinary metered service, and a separate piece of work landing the same day priced it with no
further change: **70 addresses, 118 units, 70 customers and 95 bills** — the same number a water
utility gets.

### What is still not done, said plainly

**Solar, Broadband and Battery still produce no bills.** They now have the whole estate — 70
addresses and 118 units each — and stop at one thing: **nothing has priced them yet.** The demo's
price list knows how to price the metered service a utility is built around and the two that hang
off water, and it has nothing for a service billed on what is installed. Until it does, no plan
exists for a unit to carry and no customer can be opened on it. That is filed on its own so it
cannot be mistaken for the part that is finished.

## [2.125.2] — 2026-09-01 · A clerk can record a bounced cheque, and a refund can be paid out

### The thing that was wrong, and it was on the screen

The Payments list carried a panel, in eleven languages, telling a clerk that reversing a payment and
issuing a refund **were not built** and that two decisions the Product Owner had not made yet were
holding them up. All three of those statements were false when a clerk read them. Both jobs were
built the day before. The two decisions were made on 11 and 12 August — a bounced cheque may take an
account's credit below zero and the utility chases it, and the chasing sequence restarts from the
beginning. Left alone, that panel would have sat on the same page as the new Reverse button and
contradicted it. The panel is gone, in all eleven languages, and the developer-facing note that said
the same thing about five web addresses that now exist has been corrected rather than deleted.

### What you can now do that you could not do yesterday

**Record a returned cheque.** Every payment row on the Payments list — and on an account's own
Payments tab — now carries a Reverse action. It asks for the bank's return date, your own bank's
charge if there was one, and whether to restart chasing, and it shows you which bills come back
before you commit. A worked example: a **292.87** cheque comes back, the list gains a **−292.87**
row of its own, and **292.87** goes back on the two bills it had settled, at their original due
dates. The customer's own returned-cheque fee is billing's charge and is not added here — the screen
says so every time.

**Only an administrator can do it**, which is the rule as it was decided. A billing clerk sees the
button and is told why it is greyed out rather than being left to hunt for it.

**Pay a refund out, end to end.** Finance has a new Refunds page. A clerk raises a refund against an
account, an administrator approves it and sends the money, and whoever reconciles the bank marks the
cheque cleared. A worked example: **57.13** is raised against an account, approved and sent as cheque
**#10241**, and the account's credit goes to **0.00**. Marking it cleared five days later posts
nothing to the books — the money left when the cheque was sent, and posting again would take it out
twice. Until now none of this was reachable: the approval queue existed and could never hold a row,
because nothing in the product could raise a refund in the first place.

**A refund is refused while the same customer owes money on another account**, which is also the rule
as it was decided, and the screen shows the refusal rather than a spinner.

### What these screens still cannot tell you

The refunds list cannot say which account a refund belongs to, and the form cannot show how much is
refundable before you type an amount. Neither figure is served by anything today, and neither is
guessed — the page says so instead. Filed as a defect with the two reads that would close it.


## [2.125.1] — 2026-09-01 · An electricity, gas or storm-water utility now gets a demo that bills

### The thing that was wrong

**A utility that sells electricity got a complete demo and not one bill in it.** Signing up as an
electric company produced 70 addresses, 118 units, 75 connections, 70 meters and three months of
meter readings — everything you would expect — and then stopped dead. Not one customer account
could be opened, so there were no bills, no payments and no collections either. Nine of the
seventeen things the demo sets up failed. A gas utility and a storm-water utility got exactly the
same. Only a water company got a working demo.

**The cause was a single mismatch.** The part of the product that builds the demo *estate* — the
addresses, the meters, the readings — had been taught to follow whatever service the utility
actually sells. The part that builds the *prices* had not: it still only knew how to price water,
sewer and refuse. So an electric utility got electric meters and a water price list, no price list
matched anything, and every customer account was refused because the unit it sat on had no plan.

### What changed

The price list is now built for the same service as the estate. An electricity company gets an
electricity price list and two plans; a gas company gets gas; a storm-water company gets storm
water. Both of the demo's plans — Residential and Commercial — carry it, and each one states the
monthly base charge for that service.

**The monthly charges come straight out of the billing workbook we have been working from all
along and none of them is invented:** electricity **$12.00** a month for a household and **$48.00**
for a business, gas **$6.00**.

### What is deliberately still missing, and it is a question for you

**There is no price per unit used, so the usage line on these bills reads $0.00 and says so.** We
would rather show a zero and tell you about it than put a made-up rate on a demo bill. The reason
is different for each service: the workbook prices electricity only by time of day (22 cents in the
afternoon, 9 cents overnight) and the demo meters record one number a month rather than three; it
prices gas per **ccf** while the demo gas meters read in **therms**, a different unit that would be
about 4% out if we pretended otherwise; and it never prices storm water at all.

**To show the size of it: a demo house uses 800 units of electricity in June. Its bill today is
$12.00. With the workbook's time-of-day prices it would be about $100.** If you would like a single
price per unit for each of these three, tell us what it should be and the demo will use it.

### Nothing about a water utility moved

A water company's demo is unchanged to the letter — the same three price lists, the same wording on
both plans, and the same figures on the reference bill.


## [2.125.0] — 2026-09-01 · A discount is no longer filed with the money you earned

### The thing that was wrong

A customer discount was being recorded in the same part of the books as revenue.

When a utility gives somebody $10.00 off a $100.58 bill, the $10.00 has to be
recorded somewhere. Since 28 August it went into an account called *Customer
discounts*, numbered 4300 — its own account, correctly, so the subsidy is
visible — but that account was **classified as revenue**. On a chart of accounts
it sat in the revenue block and it was labelled *Revenue* on the trial balance.

The Product Owner read that and ruled: **"no, you cannot file discount under
revenue"**. A discount is not something you earned; it is something you gave
away. It belongs in a category of its own.

### What changed

**There is a sixth kind of account: contra-revenue.** For the whole life of the
product there were five — asset, liability, equity, revenue, expense. Contra-
revenue is a revenue account that runs the other way: it lives in the revenue
ladder, carries a debit balance, and states a reduction the utility *granted*
rather than netting it into what the utility *earned*.

**The discount account moved from 4300 to 4760.** The reference chart of accounts
the Product Owner supplied uses 4300 for *Electric Energy Revenue*, and files
adjustments like this one in the 4700s alongside billing adjustments, leak
adjustments and rate corrections — every one of them a debit. 4760 is the first
free slot in that block, so adopting the rest of it later moves nothing.

**The revenue report still subtracts the discount.** This is the part that could
have gone wrong quietly. Exactly one report in the product picks its lines by
account type, and while the discount account was *revenue* it was included by
accident of that label. Re-classifying it and changing nothing else would have
made the revenue table, the Revenue-by-service report and the Dashboard's service
mix all read **$100.58** where the books hold **$90.58** — ten dollars of revenue
that was never earned, on a journal entry that did not move by a cent.

### What did not change

**Nothing about the bill or the books.** The $100.58 bill with a $10.00 discount
still asks the customer for **$90.58**, and still records: accounts receivable
$90.58 and customer discounts $10.00 on one side, electric usage $82.08 and
electric base $18.50 on the other — both sides $100.58. Every frozen billing
figure was re-checked before and after and none moved.

**Finance has still not signed off the account.** The ruling settles which kind
of account a discount belongs in and gives permission to renumber it; it is not a
finance signature on the chart. Every screen that offers 4760 still says finance
has not signed it off.

### What this does not do

The Product Owner also said the chart of accounts needs **more codes and more
categories** — they tried to use the existing ones and ran out. That is the larger
half and it is not built here: it is a 111-row chart of accounts that renumbers
accounts across the whole product, and it needs sizing and agreeing before any of
it starts.

## [2.124.3] — 2026-09-01 · The Dashboard says what its figures are, and the search box admits it cannot search

### The things that were wrong

Four screens were showing a person something only a programmer could read.

**Every figure on the Dashboard was labelled with its internal code.** The first screen after every
sign-in read `AR-OUTSTANDING`, `UNBILLED-READS`, `FAILED-PAYMENTS`, `MTD-REVENUE` and
`ACTIVE-CONNECTIONS` above its five numbers. The Recent-activity rows and the To-do rows did the
same thing whenever they carried something we had no wording for — and the six set-up steps a brand
new utility sees had no wording at all, so a new customer's very first To-do list was six machine
codes.

**The search box at the top of every screen took what you typed and did nothing with it.** There is
no search yet — that is honest and known — but the box looked and behaved like a working one right
up to the point where nothing happened.

**The unit screen flashed a plan's database identifier** — 36 characters of letters and digits —
in the moment before the plan's name arrived, and left it there permanently if the plan could not
be read at all.

**The Finance › Revenue & AR screen printed the same explanation twice** and showed internal rule
numbers to the utility. (That one was repaired earlier the same day; this release closes its
record.)

### What changed

The five Dashboard figures now read **AR outstanding · Unbilled reads · Failed payments · Revenue
this period · Active connections**, in all eleven languages. An activity row reads *Bill run*,
*Payment*, *Meter reads*; a set-up step reads *Fill in your company profile*, *Invite your team*.

The search box is now **greyed out and says "Search is not available yet"**. Nothing is hidden and
nothing is pretended: the day search exists the box comes back to life on its own, with no other
change.

The unit screen says **"Loading the plan…"** while it is fetching, and **"This plan cannot be
read."** if it cannot. The identifier is still there for support — it is on the tooltip — it is
just no longer the thing a clerk reads.

### Why it lasted this long

The five Dashboard labels *were* written, and translated eleven times — under a slightly different
spelling than the one the server sends. So the two automated checks that guard our wording each
looked at it and each reported everything fine: one only follows labels written out in full, and
the other treats `dashboard.kpi.` as covering everything beneath it. A figure with no label was
built to fall back to naming itself rather than going blank, which is a sensible thing to do and is
exactly why nothing looked broken.

There are now two checks that ask the question the other way round: for every code the server can
send, is there wording for it? One runs against the server's own lists; the other runs against all
eleven languages. Both were shown failing on this defect before they were trusted.

The unit-screen identifier lasted because it was on screen for a fraction of a second — every test
we had waited for the data to arrive and then looked. It has its own test now, which looks *before*
the data arrives.

## [2.124.2] — 2026-09-01 · A utility that collects refuse gets bills again

### The thing that was wrong

**If you ticked Trash when you signed up, your new utility produced no bills at all.** Not fewer —
none. Every account was held back, and eight of the seventeen steps that build your sample data
failed behind it: no bills meant no payments, no refund, no correction, no payment plan and nothing
in collections. The set-up screen still said it had finished.

The reason was one thing nobody had written down. Trash is not measured by a meter — it is priced by
counting the bins standing at the property, three bins at $15.00 being $45.00. The product has always
been able to be told that a service works this way, and the Services settings page has had the switch
for it. Nothing ever set it. So every new utility said all ten of its services were metered, and
billing then asked a refuse connection for its meter size and its meter multiplier, got no answer,
and correctly refused rather than guessing — because a guessed size picks a price.

### What changed

**A new utility that sells refuse now says so properly, and its bills come out.** The sample data
declares refuse as priced by what stands at the property rather than by a meter, which is what it
always was. Measured on the real sign-up path: 0 bills before, 96 after — the same number a utility
without refuse has always produced — and all seventeen set-up steps run.

**Three bins bill $45.00, one bills $15.00, and none bills $0.00 on a real bill.** The last one
matters: a property the crew looked at and found no bins is a real answer and it must still get a
bill. Nothing else on any bill moved.

**You can now record what size the bin is, on the bin.** Every seeded container carries its size, and
the add-equipment wizard, the equipment edit form and the equipment page all show and record it — the
same three places that have handled a meter's connection size since August. Before this, a size could
be recorded for a meter and for nothing else, so a refuse connection had nowhere to put one.

### If you are already running

Nothing you have is changed and no issued bill moves. A utility already set up with refuse should
open **Settings › Services**, find Trash, and set it to *Unmetered* — that one switch is the whole
fix, and it takes effect on the next bill run.

## [2.124.1] — 2026-09-01 · A budget-billing customer who pays what we asked for now owes nothing

### The thing that was wrong

A customer on budget billing pays the same amount every month — a **level** — instead of whatever
that month's usage happens to come to. On the worked example the utility already uses, July's
actual charges are **$292.87** and the level is **$242.00**, and the Product Owner ruled in August
that **the level is what is due**: pay the $242.00 and the month is settled.

Billing knew that. Payments did not. Everywhere payments asked *"what does this customer still
owe?"* it read the bill's **total**, so a customer who paid the $242.00 they were asked for was
recorded as still owing the **$50.87** difference. Every month. With three consequences, all of
them things the customer or the clerk sees:

* the debtors list counted them as owing $50.87 when they owed nothing;
* the collection ladder ran on that figure, so reminder and disconnect notices went to a customer
  who had paid in full and on time;
* the *"which bill is this payment for?"* list offered a clerk a bill nobody owed.

### What changed

Payments now asks billing what each bill **asks for** instead of what it totals. For an ordinary
bill those are the same number and nothing at all changes. For a budget bill it is the level, so
$242.00 settles July and the customer disappears from the debtors list, the ladder and the picker,
which is where they should have been all along.

Paying **less** than the level still leaves a real balance and is still chased — $200.00 against a
$242.00 level leaves **$42.00** owing. Paying **more** carries the extra as credit on the account,
exactly as an overpayment on any other bill already does.

### One thing that had to move with it

The next bill's *"previous balance / payments & credits / open balance"* box is built from the same
figures. Left alone, it would have printed **"Previous balance $292.87 · Payments & credits $50.87
· Open balance $242.00"** for a customer who had paid nothing — three lines that add up, and one of
them a claim about a payment that never happened. That box now reads $242.00 · $0.00 · $242.00.

**No signed figure moved.** $292.87 is still what the July bill charges, $242.00 is still what it
asks for, and the frozen worked examples the bill layout was built on are unchanged to the cent.

### Also in this release

* The three comments that told a reader the R1–R7 pricing chain has no live caller are corrected.
  It has had one since this morning — the base charge of every bill goes through it — and one of
  those comments claimed a refusal path could never fire, which is exactly the path a utility with
  no base charge code declared hits on its next bill run.
* Three defect records that had been fixed and never closed are closed, with the commit that fixed
  each one written into the row.

## [2.124.0] — 2026-09-01 · You can finally record payroll, insurance and rent — and you cannot record a truck

### The thing that was wrong

The Costs tab let you record a cost against a service you sell, plus exactly two others — general
maintenance and infrastructure. **That was the whole list.** There was nowhere to put payroll,
insurance, a legal bill, postage, printing, office rent or fuel, so the promise that this is the one
place your costs live was not true. A utility keeping half its costs here and half in a spreadsheet
is keeping them in the spreadsheet.

### What changed

**Sixteen categories now, grouped the way an operating statement reads them.** General maintenance
splits into labour, materials and contract work. Customer costs — billing and collection, postage
and printing, meter reading — arrive. So do payroll and benefits, insurance, professional fees,
office and rent, and vehicles and fuel. So do your own property, franchise and payroll taxes, which
are a different thing from the taxes you collect from customers and remit.

**And one thing the tab now refuses.** If you try to record a truck, a building, plant or equipment,
it stops you and points at the asset instead: *record it on the asset*. This matters more than it
sounds. A $40,000 truck recorded as a cost overstates this year by $40,000, understates the next
five years by the depreciation that never happens, and leaves the truck off your balance sheet
altogether — the most common bookkeeping mistake at this size of utility. It has a home already:
Assets holds the purchase price, the depreciation method and the expected life, and works out the
book value. Depreciation is refused for its own reason and says so: it is worked out from the
asset, so there is no invoice to record.

**Payroll says what it is.** A single figure is a record of what left the bank. It is not payroll
accounting — the amounts you hold back from an employee and pay to the government are a liability
this product does not carry — and the form says so where you choose the category.

**The bought-versus-billed figure is protected.** Payroll and insurance have no delivered quantity,
so they can never enter it. Water still reads 9.00% and electric 5.50% whatever else you record,
including a payroll entry with an hours figure typed on it.

### What has not changed

**Recording a cost still posts nothing to your books** and the export's cost section still says it
comes from the register. Nothing here moves a trial balance.

### If you are already using the product

The fourteen new categories bring fourteen new accounts, and they arrive in your chart the first
time you use one — nothing to run, nothing to re-import. If you retired one of those account
numbers, it stays retired and the form asks you to pick an account instead.

## [2.123.0] — 2026-09-01 · An uploaded spreadsheet stops leaving Social Security numbers lying about

### The thing that was wrong

When somebody uploaded a spreadsheet of customers or properties, the file sat in our database with
**every Social Security number readable**, and the checking screen showed them back in full. It sat
there until someone pressed commit — which can be days — and for a utility migrating three thousand
customers that is three thousand readable government identifiers in one place, waiting.

### What changed

The number is scrambled the moment it is uploaded, and the checking screen shows the last four.
A clerk who used to see `123-45-6789` now sees `••••6789`, exactly as they already do everywhere
else in the product. The same is true of a driving licence and a Tax ID. Both uploads — properties
and accounts — changed together.

**Nothing changed about the spreadsheet you send us.** It still carries the whole number, which is
what the Product Owner ruled this morning, and it has to: recognising a customer we already hold is
done on the whole number, and four digits cannot do it. A landlord already on file still comes back
as the same customer with the same number rather than being written in a second time.

**Nothing changed about the file we hand back when rows fail**, either. It still carries your own
values, so you can fix two cells and upload it again.

**And nothing already uploaded is disturbed.** A file parked before today keeps its readable
numbers, and it can still be checked and committed exactly as it is.

### Two smaller things worth knowing

* A phone number is still shown in full, on this screen and on every other one — it is a contact
  number rather than a government identifier.
* On the *"fix the rejects here"* editor, a masked cell now opens **empty**, with the masked value
  shown behind it. Type the whole number to change it, or leave it alone. It can no longer be
  cleared from that box; clear it in your own spreadsheet instead.
* **Fixed on the way in (`DEF-2991`):** an earlier commit of this same change dropped the header
  line from the *"rows that did not land"* download, so the file came back with its columns
  unlabelled. It never reached a build anybody ran, and there is now a test that reads the first
  line of that file rather than only its contents.

## [2.122.1] — 2026-09-01 · Every account in the demo now has a customer, through the rule rather than around it

### What changed

When the rule that an account needs an ID landed this morning, the demo data seeder was let off it —
its 48 sample people did not say whether they were a person or a business, so the rule would have
refused all of them and a rebuilt demo would have had no accounts, no bills and no payments at all.

That exemption is gone. Those 48 people are now identified from what the demo already held: the
`555-` phone numbers already printed on their contact details, and for the two businesses the
made-up tax number the demo already uses. **Nothing was invented for anybody**, which is the same
answer another part of the product reached earlier the same day.

### Why it is worth doing

The seeder plants 48 accounts every time somebody rebuilds the demo, so it is the busiest path in
the product — and it was the one path the new rule never ran on. It now runs on all 48. And a demo
where every account has a customer is the demo people actually look at when they judge the product.

### It immediately found a gap in the rule itself

The rule let an account through whenever it quoted a reference to an existing customer. It never
checked that the reference found anybody — so any value at all opened the door. It does now.

### Nothing about the demo's numbers moved

Same 70 accounts, same 48 customers, same bills, same books. The identity was added alongside; it
replaced nothing.

## [2.122.0] — 2026-09-01 · One landlord, three buildings, **one customer number**

### The thing that was wrong

A landlord who gave their name and a Social Security number at three different buildings was
written into the system **three times**, under three different customer numbers, all holding the
same Social Security number. The system had recognised them each time — it said so, in as many
words — and created a duplicate anyway.

### What changed

Every door that opens an account now asks the same question in the same order: **is this somebody
we already have?** If the name and a government ID both match somebody on file, that customer is
used. If nothing matches, a new customer is created. Three buildings, one number.

A phone number is deliberately not enough to match somebody this way. It is enough to create a
customer, and it always was — but two people in a house share a phone, and reusing somebody's
record on that basis would hand a stranger their file. A driving licence, a Social Security number
or a business Tax ID is what counts.

### Nothing about deposits or money changed

Recognising somebody well enough to reuse their number is **not** the same as recognising them well
enough to move their deposit. That still needs the full check the finance team signed, date of birth
included. Reusing a number changes how many records exist and nothing about what they are allowed
to do.

### And an account now needs an ID

Following the ruling that we cannot create a customer, a regular account or an owner's account
without an identifier, both counter screens now ask for one before the account can be opened, and
say which one is missing while the clerk is still typing. **A phone number is enough**, so somebody
who gives a phone still gets served in one visit. The door that closes is the one where a name is
typed and nothing else.

### Both counter screens now say what happened

Opening an account and moving somebody in both tell the clerk which of three things the system did:
added the account to a customer already on file, created a new customer, or created none and why.
On a match it says *"this looks like a customer you already have"* rather than linking quietly.

### Two places deliberately left alone, and one of them needs a decision

The **bulk import** and the **demo data seeder** both create accounts from files that carry a name
and no ID at all. Under the new rule neither could create anything — which for the import means a
utility could not migrate its customers onto the product. That consequence is with the Product Owner
rather than shipped; both keep working exactly as they did today.

## [2.121.0] — 2026-09-01 · The accounts spreadsheet asks who the customer is

### A name and one identifier, or the row loads nothing

The Product Owner ruled this morning that we cannot create a customer, a master account
or an ordinary account for somebody nobody can identify. The premises spreadsheet learned
that hours ago. **The accounts spreadsheet learns it now, and it is the file that carries
the volume** — a utility migrating in loads its whole customer base through it.

Four new columns, all optional: whether the customer is a person or a company, a Social
Security number, a driving licence and a Tax ID. **The phone is the column the file has
always had** rather than a second one beside it — asking a utility for the same telephone
number twice is how the bill contact and the identity end up disagreeing.

A row with a name and one identifier loads its account, and its customer is either matched
to somebody already on file or created. A row with a name and nothing else **loads
nothing** — no account, no customer — says so in plain words next to the row, and is
counted on the receipt. That count is the point: without it a migration that identified
half its customers looks exactly like one that identified all of them, and the utility
finds out at its first bill run.

A file saved yesterday still uploads and still maps. What changed is what a row is allowed
to create, not what a file is allowed to contain. And a corrected re-upload of accounts
already on file is untouched, because it creates nothing.

### The Customer # column is finally read

The template has offered a **Customer #** column since March, the help text promised it was
used, and nothing read it — so a utility migrating with its own customer numbers lost every
one and could not reconcile against their old system. A number already on file now links
the account to that customer; a number we have not issued is kept exactly as sent; an empty
cell still takes one from your own series. Your own numbering then moves clear of whatever
the file brought in, so the next customer added by hand cannot collide with it.

### There is one accounts upload, not two

An older three-step accounts import lost its screen months ago and its web addresses stayed
switched on. It still handed out rules that have since been reversed: it invented an account
number when the cell was empty, and it did not ask for a customer name at all. It now
refuses, and says where to go instead. Nothing was deleted — a batch someone staged last
week can still be read.

## [2.120.1] — 2026-09-01 · The bill-day check now tells you what it did not look at

### The test estate catches up with the new pricing rules

Turning on the two new pricing rules on 1 September stopped about 77 of our own
tests. None of it reached a customer — the rules are right and the test data was
out of date — but the test data was out of date in **four** different ways, and
each one was hidden behind the one in front of it. A rate plan needs a base
charge code, a meter needs its connection size recorded, a published plan needs
a start date, and a rate schedule needs to say which connection sizes it prices.
All four are things a real utility fills in on screen; our test data had been
written before any of them existed. Every figure we filled in was taken from
figures the business had already signed — water $8.00 a month, electric $12.00,
the connection sizes the Product Owner ratified — and none was invented to make
a test go green.

### The check that said "all clear" about a service it had never looked at

Before a utility can have the new rules switched on, we run a check that asks
*would any bill stop?* On three utilities it answered **all clear**, and it was
answering about the accounts that happened to be in a billing cycle at the time.
One of those utilities sells electricity. Not one electricity account was in that
population, and every electricity meter on it has no connection size recorded —
so every electricity bill would have stopped, with **all clear** on the screen.

Worse, and this is the part that would have caught us out again: water *was*
looked at and *was* reported fine, while two of the three utilities each hold
**21 water accounts** whose meter has no size recorded either. Those accounts are
not in a cycle, so the check could not see them however carefully it looked.

The check now asks the whole utility rather than the accounts in front of it: for
every service, how many connections have no size recorded and **how many billable
accounts that touches** — because the account count is the number somebody has to
act on. Across the three utilities that is **84 accounts**. All three now read
**not met**, which is the true answer. It also names the services it examined
beside the ones the utility sells, so "nothing wrong" can never again be confused
with "nothing looked at".

None of this is a fault in the pricing engine. It is configuration a utility has
not finished — you cannot charge for a connection size you have not recorded —
and the only question the check settles is whether they find out beforehand or on
billing day.

### Not moved

No money figure moved. The billing tests that run the real pricing engine give
exactly the same answer with the new rules on and with them off.

## [2.120.0] — 2026-09-01 · Meter readings are taken a month at a time, the way a meter reader takes them

### Reads, bill, reads, bill, reads

The demo utility used to be built by handing in three months of meter readings on the same
morning, before a single bill had been issued. The Product Owner put it plainly — *"you can not
add reading data once for 3 months"* — and they are right: no meter reader works that way, and a
seeded utility built that way cannot be read as a sequence of billing cycles.

Each month's walk now happens where it belongs: the first month is read, then billed and paid;
the second month is read after that money has landed, then billed; the third month is read last
and is the one left ready to run. **Not one reading, date or figure changed** — only which step
plants which month. The same 197 readings, the same 48 and 47 bills, the same third cycle of 44
bills for $3,762.22, and the books balance at the same $35,466.09.

Each walk also counts itself now. A meter that should have been read and was not does not fail a
bill run — it quietly drops that customer onto the exception list, where it looks like a billing
problem rather than a walk that did not finish. Each step checks its own month and refuses if it
comes up short, naming the meters by serial.

### Loading the sample data twice no longer records money twice

Pressing **Load sample data** a second time used to record **82 duplicate payments** across three
months and issue a second refund behind them — and because payments can never be deleted, that
utility was permanently wrong. The collections step was only ever correct by accident of when it
ran: it paid every issued bill it could see, and on a first run the first month happened to be the
only one issued. It is scoped to its own month now, and a second load records one row instead of
eighty-four.

The seeded disputed reading had a quieter version of the same fault: it flagged *the most recent
reading not yet disputed*, so each re-run disputed one more month and dropped that customer out of
one more bill run. It asks for the month it is actually about.

## [2.119.0] — 2026-09-01 · A bill run that gets stuck is stopped and says so, and a printer's file has a name

### A stuck bill run used to stay stuck for ever

Until today nothing bounded a bill run in TIME. There was a limit on its SIZE — a run of more
than 25,000 customers is refused before it starts — but a run that wedged held one of the two
background workers indefinitely, and the only way to get that worker back was to restart the
server.

A run now stops after **2 hours and 17 minutes**, and it tells the clerk what happened, on the
screen they are already looking at: *"This stopped after about 137 minutes, which is the longest
one background job is allowed to run on this system. Everything it had already finished is kept —
start it again and it carries on from where it stopped rather than beginning over."*

**Pressing the button again really does carry on.** The run keeps its place, so a run stopped at
9,000 customers out of 10,000 does not pay for those 9,000 a second time.

### Where two hours and seventeen minutes comes from

Not from a round number that felt safe. The biggest run this system accepts is **25,000
customers**, and the slowest a bill run has ever been measured going — on a real database with
every security check switched on — is **0.219 seconds a customer**. That makes the longest honest
run about **an hour and a half**. We allowed half again on top of it, and then **five more
minutes** for the run to write down what happened before the worker is killed outright.

The five minutes is the one number we assumed rather than measured, and it says so in the settings
file beside the value. Every other background job finishes well inside the same limit: printing a
whole cycle's bills is about five minutes at the largest size, the findings screen about fifty, and
the biggest file upload we have ever benchmarked about four.

Both limits can be changed per installation without a code change.

### Two settings said they could be changed and could not

The two size ceilings — the largest bill run and the largest print set — both told whoever read
the code that an operator could raise or lower them from the server's own configuration. Neither
was actually connected: setting them changed nothing at all, and nothing said so. They are
connected now.

### A printer's file now has a name, and asking for one we do not have is refused

The list that goes to a print vendor with the bills is now written in a **named file shape**.
There is exactly one shape today and it is the one already being sent — the same fourteen columns
per bill agreed on 30 August, in the same order, in the same file.

What is new is that asking for a shape nobody has set up **refuses and says which shapes exist**,
rather than quietly sending the default. A printer given a file in the wrong shape can read the
wrong column into the wrong field, and that is bills posted to the wrong people.

**We still do not know what any particular printer wants.** Which shape, which fields in which
order, and how a batch is delimited are all things the printer has to tell us, and nothing here
guesses at any of them. When they do tell us, adding their shape is a small, contained change
rather than a project.

## [2.118.0] — 2026-09-01 · A spreadsheet can now say who owns an address, and selling a property transfers the account instead of replacing it

### What changed, in one sentence

Two things a utility does every week: **loading a list of addresses**, which can now say who the
owner is and give them an account, and **recording a property sale**, which now hands the existing
account to the buyer instead of closing it and opening a new one.

### Loading addresses — the spreadsheet gained six columns

The premises upload template used to have one Owner column and nowhere to say who that owner
actually is. It now has six more:

* **Owner is a person or a company**
* **Owner Social Security number**, **Owner driving licence**, **Owner phone** — for a person
* **Owner Tax ID** — for a company
* **Owner account type** — what their account is charged as

**Every one of them is optional**, so a file saved before today loads exactly as it did.

**What you get back.** A row with an owner's name **and at least one identifier** now gets the
address an owner account and a customer number. A row with a name and nothing else loads the
address and creates nothing — which is what it did before — and the receipt now says how many of
each, so a half-finished migration no longer looks identical to a finished one:

    Owner accounts created                        3
    Waiting for the owner to be identified        1
    No account type given — needs a choice        1

A landlord who is a company and owns three buildings ends with **three accounts and one customer
number**, not three of each.

### Selling a property — the account moves, it is not replaced

Recording a transfer used to close the account and open a new one at a new address. That is what a
customer **moving** looks like, not what a **sale** looks like. Now the same account moves to the
buyer: same account number, same meter, same unbroken history. **The buyer takes on what is
outstanding**, and the clerk is shown that figure before completing the sale.

Bills already sent to the seller are untouched, in the seller's name, permanently.

**A customer who is moving to a new address is now sent to a new service request instead**, and the
transfers screen says so in one sentence with a link, where a clerk would otherwise reach for the
wrong door.

### Fixed

* An address's owner account was something the product could create and nothing ever asked it to.
  The premises upload is now the first door that walks through it.

## [2.115.0] — 2026-09-01 · R3 and R4 are switched **on** — the ruled pricing rules now bill for real

### What changed, in one sentence

The two pricing rules the Product Owner asked us to wire in — the one that decides **whether a
connection's size is priced at all** (R3) and the one that decides **what the base charge is**
(R4) — now run on real bills instead of running quietly beside them.

### What a utility must have set up before this is safe for them

**Every service you bill needs a base charge code, marked as the base.** That is where the base
charge now comes from, and there is deliberately no fallback to the old figure. If a service has
none, the product tells you **when you activate a rate schedule** — on a settings screen, naming
the service and what to add — rather than letting the bill run fail on the day the money is due.

**A banded service needs its connection sizes priced.** A meter whose size nothing prices stops
that account's bill by name. That is not new behaviour we chose today: it is the cost the size
ruling accepted in August, and it only becomes visible now that the rule is live.

### What we measured before turning it on

Three utilities, **163 accounts**. Every account was put through the switched rules inside a
transaction that was rolled back, and the base charge each would be billed was compared with
the one it is billed today: **163 the same, 0 changed, 0 refused.** Every service on all three
carries its base charge code, and every connection size in use is priced.

### If a bill comes out wrong

Set `SBH_BILLING_RESOLUTION_STEPS=` (empty) and restart. That is the whole rollback — one line,
no release, and the old pricing path takes over on the next bill. It is covered by a test that
prices a real bill through the rolled-back path, so it is checked rather than promised.

### Also in this release

- The base-charge-code check now follows the switch, so it protects **every** utility once the
  rules are on, not only utilities that had already adopted base charge codes (`DEF-2923`).
- Both switch preflights now report **which services have no base charge code**, and both now
  print what is actually live rather than a sentence written when nothing was.

## [2.117.0] — 2026-09-01 · a bill with nothing on it is no longer printed

### What changed, in one sentence

When a customer's account has nothing to charge for this month, the billing run now produces **no
bill at all** instead of an empty one — and the run screen says *"Nothing to bill this period"*
beside that account rather than showing a blank table.

### Why

The Product Owner ruled on 31 August that **every address gets its owner an account**, whether or
not anything is shared. An owner who lives in his own house therefore has two accounts: the ordinary
one he is billed on, and an owner's account that covers nothing. That second account must not
produce a `$0.00` bill every month — *"a customer who receives one telephones to ask what it means,
and several hundred a month is real postage and a real support load for a document that says
nothing"* — and it must not appear on the screen that lists accounts a clerk has to go and fix,
because a list that fills with normal outcomes is one a clerk stops reading.

### What a clerk sees

* **A new figure on the billing-run screen: *Accounts with nothing to bill*,** beside *ready to
  bill* and *cannot be billed*. Which accounts they were opens with one click and stays closed
  until asked.
* **The words, not a blank table.** Each of those accounts reads *"Nothing to bill this period"*.
* **Fewer false alarms.** An empty flat whose standing charge the owner IS paying was being listed
  as *"has no billable account"* every month; it no longer is. An empty flat that reaches **nobody**
  is still listed, because that one is a real problem.
* **New Connect can create the address it is building on**, instead of demanding one be typed into
  the Premises screen first — and it can open the owner's account at that address in the same step,
  when asked to.

### What did NOT change

**A bill that shows a charge of `$0.00` is still printed and still sent.** That was a separate
ruling (27 August) and it stands: the rule here is *no lines, no document*, not *no money, no
document*. `1408 Elm Street` still bills `$41.20` of hallway lighting plus `$28.40` of shared
irrigation = **`$69.60`** on one owner document.

### One thing found and NOT fixed here

**The `1408 Elm Street` regression itself is currently failing on this branch, and not because of
this change.** Switching the two new pricing rules on last week made the billing engine refuse any
account whose utility has not declared a base charge code, and the test's own fixture has not
declared one. The figure is measured here with those rules switched off, which is how it was signed;
the failure belongs to the lane that owns the switch and is written down for them.

## [2.116.0] — 2026-09-01 · The day a tenant moves out owing money now has an answer, end to end

### When a tenant leaves, the empty flat's standing charge goes to the landlord — and the screen says so before you commit

That has been true of the money since August: the moment nobody occupies a unit, its standing charge
moves onto the owner's bill, which is the same thing that happens when an account is cut off. On the
building the rules use as their example, a landlord's bill of **$69.60** for the hallway lighting and
the shared irrigation becomes **$81.60** the month one flat stands empty — the extra **$12.00** being
that flat's electricity standing charge, and nothing else, because nobody is living there to use
anything.

**What was missing was being told.** The move-out screen's "What happens next" step now says, in one
sentence and before anything is committed, which account the empty unit's standing charge will be
billed to, and that it comes off that account again the day the next tenant takes the unit. It also
shows how many units are still occupied afterwards, who the owner is, and what standing charge each
service on that unit's plan carries. All of that used to read "not served".

**And where the address has no owner on file as an account, the screen now says THAT** — plainly,
where it used to say nothing at all. It is a fault a person can act on, not a blank.

### A departing tenant's unpaid balance can now be put on the landlord's account

If a tenant leaves owing more than their deposit covers, a clerk has always been offered four
choices, and one of them is to put the remainder on the landlord's account. **On a house, that choice
could never actually be taken.** The product worked out who the landlord was by looking at who paid
for the building's hallway — so a house with no hallway had no landlord it could find, and the option
refused. That is now read from who the address's owner actually is.

**What still does not happen, and it is written down rather than glossed over:** the money does not
yet move in the accounts. The decision is recorded with who made it, which account it names and how
much, but nothing in the general ledger changes, because nobody has yet said which two ledger
accounts a balance moving between two customers should touch. It is a question, not a guess.

### An owner who lives in his own house can now let it out without anything breaking

He has two accounts and gets one bill, because the second one has nothing on it. The day he lets the
house out, his own account closes and the house's standing charge moves to the account he already
had — no new account, no duplicated customer, and nothing for a clerk to remember.

### Also fixed

* A warning saying "the owner is a name, not an account — nothing can be billed to them" appeared on
  **every** move-out, including the ones where the owner does have an account. It now appears only
  when it is true.

## [2.114.0] — 2026-09-01 · The demo seed runs on a database created today, and it now prepares the cycle you run yourself

### A brand-new database could not be seeded at all, and that is fixed

`manage.py seed_demo` followed by `manage.py load_sample_data` — the documented way to fill a
new utility with demo data — stopped on the very first metering step and took **ten of the
fourteen steps down with it**. The tenant ended with no accounts, no customers, no bills and no
payments, so every customers screen on a freshly installed box was empty.

The cause was a counter standing behind its own data. `seed_demo` writes six billing cycles and
six routes under names it chooses itself, which never moves the numbering counter — so when the
next step asked the counter for a code, it was handed `CY-001`, which already existed, and the
product correctly refused it. The product already had the repair for exactly this (it was built
in August for premises and unit numbers) and it had simply never been wired to cycles and
routes. It is wired now: the counter catches up past everything on file and hands out the next
free code.

**Every one of the seeding steps now loads on a database that started empty** — fourteen when this
was fixed, sixteen once the two steps below were added — verified end to end on PostgreSQL 16.

### A new step: the readings for the cycle you run, and the money against the one before it

The Product Owner asked for one more step after the second bill: *"after second bill is
generated, I want to add another step which will add - meter reads and payment data - so that We
can run the next bill cycle on our own"*. There are now two, one per module, and they sit
directly after the second bill run:

* **Meter reads for the cycle YOU run** — the third month's walk, posted after the second bill
  rather than before the first, which is when a meter reader would actually walk it. The step
  counts its own coverage and refuses if a meter that should have been read was not, because a
  missing reading does not fail a bill run — it quietly holds that account out of it.
* **Collections against the second cycle** — the second month's bills paid in a mix: about half
  settled in full, a quarter paid in part, a quarter not paid at all, and one account overpaid
  so a credit balance exists. A demo where everybody pays leaves the arrears, dunning and
  collection screens with nothing to show.

The seeded utility now arrives with two months billed, a month read and waiting, and a real
spread of who has paid — so the next bill run can be started and watched from the screen.

## [2.113.0] — 2026-09-01 · A customer number now needs a name **and one ID**

### What changed, in one sentence

Until today, typing a name was enough to create a customer number. It is not any more. To
create one we need a name **and at least one ID**: for a person a Social Security number, a
driving licence **or** a phone number; for a business its Tax ID.

### The account still opens either way

This is a rule about the customer number and not about service. Somebody at the counter who
will not give an ID still gets their water — the account opens, it bills, it takes payments.
What it does not get is a customer number, and the screen says so while the clerk is still
typing rather than after the account is saved. Everything that hangs off a customer number —
carrying a deposit forward, recognising somebody who comes back — follows from not having one.

### Four doors, four answers

* **The New-account wizard** now asks whether the customer is a person or a business and
  collects the right ID for each. It also sends that information for the first time: the
  server has accepted it since yesterday and no screen had ever posted it, so every account
  opened at the counter had a blank customer column.
* **The owner's account at an address** carries the address's owner name, which is free text
  and may name a person or a limited company. It opens the account and creates no customer
  number, and says which fact is missing.
* **The bulk import** carries a name and an old system's reference and no ID at all, so it
  creates nobody. **The accounts still load.** Each such row is flagged so somebody can
  identify the customer later, and the import receipt counts them.
* **The service-request screen** links a customer a clerk has already found. It never created
  one and still does not.

### What it does not touch

Customers already on file with a name and no ID stay exactly as they are. Nothing is migrated,
nothing is deleted, and no screen refuses to show one.

### One thing that is deliberately not tidied

What is enough to **create** a customer number is not what is enough to **match** one. A phone
number alone creates a customer; a phone number alone is still a weak match and still carries
no deposit. Both are true at the same time and they are different questions.

## [2.112.0] — 2026-09-01 · The charge code says which connection sizes you price, and R3's release condition is now something you can read off a screen

### The size of a connection is priced where its money already lives

Until today the product asked two halves of one question in two different places: **what does a
5/8" water connection cost** was read off the charge code, and **is a 5/8" water connection priced
at all** was read off the rate schedule. A utility could price a 2" connection on the charge-code
screen and still have that meter refused by a rate schedule that knew nothing about it.

The Product Owner ruled on it in one sentence — *"rate schedule will not provdie the size, charge
code will provide"* — and both halves now come from the same place. Where a service declares a base
charge code with a per-size table, that table says which sizes are priced. A size missing from it
refuses the bill by name rather than being charged at another size's rate.

**Nothing on any bill changes.** A base charge code that prices one flat figure for every size — which
is every utility on this database — makes no statement about sizes at all, so the rate schedule
still answers exactly as it did yesterday. The day a utility prices per size, its answer moves with
no further work.

### A refusal now names the screen you have to open

*"This size has no row on rate schedule version 8f2c…"* was the only sentence the product could
produce, and after this change it would sometimes have sent a clerk to the wrong screen. The refusal
now says *the base charge code pricing water* when that is where the answer came from.

### And the check that decides whether this rule is safe to switch on

The comparison we had been relying on for the connection-size step was asking the same place the
same question twice and reporting the echo as agreement, so *47 of 47 agree* was never evidence. What
replaces it reads the configuration itself: for every utility, does every connection size its
accounts actually carry have something pricing it? On this database — three utilities, 163 accounts —
**every one does**. The report says so per utility, names the object that priced each size, and can
be made to say the opposite on demand, which is how we know it is reading anything at all.

## [2.111.1] — 2026-09-01 · What you approved is downloadable, and the line between the parts of the system is held by a check

### The release approval can be read back

When a run is signed off, the product keeps a record of what was on the screen at
that moment: how many accounts, how many bills, how much money, the four
confirmations, who confirmed and when. Since the sign-off screen started
recalculating live, that record has been the only thing that can answer *"what
did I approve on 1 July?"* — and there was no way to read it.

It downloads now, one row per approval, newest first. Every figure is the one
that was stored at sign-off and none is recalculated, which is the whole point:
a bill voided next week leaves the screen's total and does not leave this file.
A run approved twice — a catch-up, a resumed batch — appears twice, because both
happened and both were authorised by somebody. There is no screen for it and
there is not going to be one; that was decided on 11 August.

### A check now holds the line between the parts of the system

The billing code is supposed to reach the rest of the product through a small
number of named doors. Nothing anywhere read whether it actually did, so the
arrangement held only for as long as everybody remembered it — and it slips one
import at a time, with every individual one looking reasonable and nothing going
red. There were seven such shortcuts on 31 August and more a day later.

They are written down now, and a new one fails the build. The list is allowed to
shrink and never to grow.

### The pricing cutover table says which steps can actually be switched

The new pricing engine is being brought in one rule at a time. The table used to
decide which rule moves next answered *do the old and new agree here* and never
*can this one be switched on at all* — so a rule with nothing behind it looked
exactly like a rule ready to go, and a whole wave of four turned out to be a wave
of none. The table now says both, and it works it out from the switch itself
rather than from a list somebody typed.

## [2.111.0] — 2026-09-01 · A business is recognised by its Tax ID, and nobody is filed as a person by accident

### A company could not be recognised at all, and the rule that should have done it is why

You ruled today that a customer is a person or a company: a person is identified
by a Social Security number, a driving licence or a phone, and *"if it is Company
then we ask for Tax ID"*.

We already had the person half, built yesterday. The company half did not exist —
there was no Tax ID anywhere on a customer. Worse, the rule that decides whether
somebody is a returning customer needs **a name, a date of birth and one
government identifier**, all three, and **a company has no date of birth.** Read
exactly as written, that rule made every business permanently unrecognisable: a
landlord's company could give a perfect Tax ID and still be treated as a
stranger, so the deposit it was owed could never follow it to a new account.

Both halves are fixed. A business now has a Tax ID on its record, stored
scrambled the same way a Social Security number is, and only the last four digits
ever reach a screen. A business is recognised when **its name and its Tax ID both
agree** — nothing else. A person's test is untouched.

**Neither is asked for the other's details.** A business is never asked for a
driving licence, and a person is never asked for a Tax ID. If one is sent anyway
the form says so rather than quietly dropping it, because a box that is asked for
and left blank eventually gets filled with something.

**A wrong Tax ID still opens the account.** As you ruled, a duplicate or mistyped
identifier refuses to *link* two customers together; it never refuses to *save*.
The account opens under its own customer number, nothing is merged, and the
screen shows **no amount at all** — because a figure on a refused offer is an
invitation to type it in by hand.

You can now also find a business by typing its Tax ID into the customers search
box, which is often the only number on the letter in somebody's hand.

### Nothing is filed as a person by accident any more

Until today, opening a customer needed only a name. Person-or-company was
silently set to *person*, and nobody was told. That is now the difference between
being asked for a Social Security number and being asked for a Tax ID, so it
cannot be a guess.

- If any identifier is being entered, **the type has to be stated** — otherwise
  the form asks *"Is this a person or company?"* before it accepts the number.
- If no identifier is being entered — a spreadsheet import that matches on an old
  system's reference, or an address whose owner is only a name — the account
  still opens, still as a person, but **the record now says nobody chose it.**
  Refusing to open an account over a missing dropdown would be the same one-way
  door you turned down this morning.

### Two things we did not decide

Neither of these is guessed anywhere in the product; both are waiting on you.

- **Does a business get a founding date**, the way a person has a date of birth?
- **Is a sole trader a person or a company?** They trade as a business and are a
  human being, and the two answers ask for different documents.

### One error message a clerk could not read

Opening a second master account on one address is correctly refused — one address
holds one owner account — but the refusal had no sentence written for it in any
language, so it arrived on screen empty. It now says which account is already
there.

## [2.110.4] — 2026-09-01 · The pricing comparison stops reporting an agreement it never made

Nothing on a bill moves in this release. The new pricing rules still price no
customer's charge — the switch that would turn one on is still off — and every
figure the finance-signed tests pin is unchanged.

### The connection-size check was comparing a number with itself

We are moving the pricing rules across one at a time, and a rule only moves once
we have watched the old way and the new way agree on real accounts. The
connection-size rule had been reporting **47 accounts agreeing out of 47**, and
that reading was worthless: both sides were asking the same place what size the
connection is, and the new way simply hands the answer back. The size makes four
hops and ends where it started.

We proved it rather than argued it. The one place both sides read was made to
answer *2 inch* for connections that are *5/8 inch* — the wrong price ladder for
every account, in both implementations at once — and the table went on reading
**47 agree, 0 disagree**, unmoved.

So the check is now stated as what it actually is. If the two sides ever differ
it stops and says the two paths are looking at different connections, which is
the only thing a difference could mean. And the report no longer counts it as
agreement: the connection-size row reads **cannot be evaluated**, with the reason
written beside it. A count of zero disagreements is only worth something where
the agreements were earned.

**What the rule can still be judged on is its refusal.** Where a rate schedule
does not price a connection's size at all, the new way refuses to bill rather
than quietly using the every-size price the old way falls back to. That is a real
difference between the two, it is money, and it can be checked exhaustively
against every size class the utility can have — which we now do, for all forty of
them, without needing more accounts.

### A service with no meter no longer stops a whole account

Sewer has no meter of its own — it is priced as a share of the water usage — so
nothing records a meter factor for it. The comparison was refusing to look at any
account with a sewer connection at all, because it asked for a factor that cannot
exist and treated the missing answer as a fault.

**Measured across three utilities: 116 of 163 accounts could not be examined for
this reason** — every account of two whole utilities, at every step, while the
bills those utilities send out were being produced perfectly well.

The order of two questions is swapped: where there is no meter reading to scale,
there is nothing to multiply and the factor is not asked for. Where there *is* a
reading and the factor is missing, it refuses exactly as before — that case is
the one the check was written for, and a ×10 meter with no recorded factor would
bill a tenth of a customer's usage on a document that looks entirely normal.

All 163 accounts are now examined, up from 47.

### Known gap, stated

The one demand meter and the one master account in the sample data sit on
addresses that belong to no billing cycle and have no account, so neither can
appear in a bill run. Two of the things we most want to compare are therefore
still not being compared. Written down rather than worked around.

## [2.110.3] — 2026-09-01 · The basic service charge question is decided, and four checks that could not fail now can

### A box nobody filled in is no longer read as "this connection is free"

A utility's rate table has a box for the basic service charge. This product
stopped using that box on 20 August, when the charge code became the one place
that figure lives, and the rate-schedule screen has had no control for it since.
On a utility set up before that day the box very often holds **0.00** — because
nobody ever typed in it.

Today's bill run reads that as *nobody filled this in* and charges the plan's
**$8.00**. The new pricing engine, which is being brought in one rule at a time
and is switched on nowhere, read it as *the charge is nothing* and charged
**$0.00** — worth **$8.00 a month per connection**. Both readings are
defensible; only one can be right.

Both now read it the same way: **a stored 0.00 means nobody filled it in.** The
other reading would give the standing charge away because somebody left a box
alone rather than because they decided anything, and a genuinely free connection
is something a utility should have to state.

**No bill moved.** The new engine prices nothing on any installation, so this
changes what it would say and nothing a customer receives. A non-zero figure is
still a figure: a rate table really carrying $4.25 still yields $4.25.

### The new engine can no longer mix two rate tables on one bill

The engine's rules can be switched on one at a time. There was already a guard
stopping it from changing WHICH rate table prices a customer while leaving the
basic charge behind. The same bill can be built the other way round — the basic
