charge from the new engine, every other price from the old one — and there was
no guard at all. That account is now stopped by name, with both tables named.
Nobody has ever been billed this way.

### Four checks that were measuring nothing

- A bill whose printed page cannot be made must not be issued. The check for
  that had been faking the failure at a door the product stopped using on
  16 August, so it proved nothing and had been failing for days.
- A check asserting that two decisions could not be recorded was left behind
  when one of them gained real choices, and had been failing since.
- A correction to the message printed on a bill was accepted, recorded, and
  changed nothing on the page: it was written under one name and the bill is
  drawn from another. The names now match, and a new check runs the renderer to
  prove every correctable field actually reaches a page.
- Nothing anywhere read which other part of the system the billing code reaches
  into directly. There were seven such places on 31 August and ten a day later.
  The ten are now written down and an eleventh fails the build.

### The twelve-month usage block reads in every language

The four sentences on the bill's usage history had been left in English in all
ten other catalogues since they were added, which held a merge-blocking check
red. They are written now, each in that language's own existing words for
*usage* and *an estimated read*.

## [2.110.2] — 2026-09-01 · Step 2 of the bill run: one number per fact, and every figure says what it counts

Three things the Product Owner found on one screen while working the deployment.

### Two numbers called "Accounts", disagreeing with each other

The band at the top of step 2 read **Accounts 0** while the row of figures just
below it read **Accounts 48**. Both were right and they were answering different
questions: the band counted accounts that already have a bill from this run, and
the row counted accounts the run had gathered. Before the bills are worked out
the first is always nought.

The band no longer shows an account count at all. It already shows Draft bills
beside it, which is the same set counted in bills, so a second tile would have
been one number twice under two names. On the list of past runs the column is
now called **Accounts billed**, because there the figure is worth having and it
needed saying which one it is.

### A row of six figures counting three different things

It read 48, 47, 1, 95, 0, 31 under Accounts, Ready to bill, Cannot be billed,
Waiting on you, Decided, Days in the cycle — and the fourth one counts
questions, not accounts, so it looked like 95 customers and was larger than the
total. One account can raise several questions.

Every heading now begins with what it counts: **Accounts in this run · Accounts
ready to bill · Accounts that cannot be billed · Decisions waiting on you ·
Decisions you have taken · Days in the cycle**. Reading across, that is
accounts, accounts, accounts, decisions, decisions, days — so the row falls into
three groups without needing a line between them. Translated into all eleven
languages.

### "Cannot be billed: 1", and no way to find out who

The run had already worked out which account it was and why. Those rows were on
the screen, but spread across the six tabs by the kind of problem, so finding
the one account meant opening up to six of them.

Underneath the figures there is now a line reading **Which accounts cannot be
billed**. It is closed until you click it, and it opens to every blocked
account, what we found, and which tab to go and fix it on. When nothing is
blocked it is not there at all.

## [2.110.1] — 2026-09-01 · The bill document reads like a bill, and a run too big says so

Five more of the same kind: places where the product showed a person our own
notes instead of theirs.

### The bill you open now looks like the bill that was posted

The platform offers five page layouts and a utility picks one. The screen that
shows a bill "as it was sent" printed the name of the layout it had used and
then drew the same page every time — so a utility on the compact layout was
shown a page that announced compact and looked standard, with the usage and
rate columns the compact page does not have. It now draws what the layout
actually says: the compact page loses its services band and its usage and rate
columns, the letterhead page leaves the top blank for pre-printed paper, and the
no-stub page has no tear-off. The amounts are untouched in every one of them.
That page also used to name the layout as `platform-layout-compact-letter-v1`.
It now says "the compact letter layout".

### The bill document stopped explaining itself to an engineer

Where a bill had nothing to show for a field, the screen printed the note our
own code carries — A19 section numbers, rule references, database column names
in backticks, and in one case a file path. Under "Utility" a clerk read a
seventy-word paragraph about what the snapshot does not stamp. Every one of
those now reads "This bill did not record it.", and the two panels underneath —
the things worth looking at, and what the printed page could not show — read as
sentences too. The original notes are still attached to the page for support.

### A run that is too big now says how big, and what to do

The largest run this system accepts is 25,000 accounts, and a bigger one is
refused before anything is drafted. Until now the clerk was told only "This
billing run can't go ahead as asked." It now says how many accounts the run
covers, what the limit is, and to split it — in all eleven languages.

### One more repeated sentence, and one more Portuguese word

The accounts billed on standing charges only still carried the long instruction
on every row: "account AC-2026-000NN is on a base-charges-only status… whether
this run bills it at all is your call." That row already has a dropdown offering
exactly that choice. It now reads "Standing charges only, no usage".

And the Portuguese fix of the last release covered four lines. Twenty-nine more
lines of the bill run used the same word for a bill as for an account; they now
use the word for an invoice, as the rest of the product does. One Italian line
did the same thing and is fixed with them.

## [2.110.0] — 2026-09-01 · Two reading screens stop over-explaining themselves

The Product Owner said four times in twenty minutes that there is too much
writing on our screens for a clerk to read. That became a rule, and this is the
rule applied to the two windows a clerk opens when a reading is wrong.

### Disputing a reading

The window used to carry a hundred and twenty-seven words. It now carries
ninety-five, and nothing a clerk acts on was taken out: the reading is not
changed, the account leaves the next bill run until a System Admin clears it,
and — where the reading has already been billed — the bill stays issued and due,
the disputed amount earns no late fees while the dispute is open, the rest of
the bill ages as usual, and the way to fix it is a billed correction. What went
was the sentences explaining what does NOT happen.

### Correcting a reading

Sixty-four words down to forty. The three lines of guidance under the two boxes
went from fifty-two words to twenty-eight. The window still says the one thing
that matters before someone types over a register: the new value becomes the
current reading and this one stays in the history. It still asks for the value
in its own unit, because a reading without a unit is not a reading.

### The version numbers agreed again

The previous release moved the number the browser shows and left the server at
the older one, so the automatic check that keeps them together had been failing
for every piece of work on the branch. Both now read 2.110.0.

## [2.109.1] — 2026-08-31 · The bill run says what it means, in words a clerk can read

Seven things the Product Owner found while running bills on the live system.

### It bills accounts, and it now says "accounts"

One column of the run said ACCOUNT and listed AC-2026-00001, while the heading
above it said "47 customers ready", the tile beside it said CUSTOMERS and a
section further down said "Customer by customer". One customer can hold several
accounts, so "47 customers" could have been forty people. A bill run bills
accounts, so every place in the run that counts, lists, holds or bills something
now calls it an account. "Customer" is kept for the person — the name beside the
account number, and the person an email or text is sent to.

Changed in all eleven languages. In Portuguese this turned up a second problem
worth naming: four lines used the same word for a bill as for an account, so
"calculate the bills" and "the accounts" read identically. Those four now use the
Portuguese word for an invoice, which the rest of the product already used.

### No more internal codes on the screen

The run screen was showing our own shorthand to whoever was using it:
`BR-MET-121`, `trailing_3_avg`, `cycle_span`, `no_read`, `no_meter`,
`account_held_by_disputed_read`, and a Decision column that printed the word
`estimate` where it had offered "Estimate the reading" a moment earlier. All of
them now read as sentences. The codes are still attached to the page for support
to read, and nine reasons an account can be held back had never been given words
at all — they have them now.

### The same sentence stopped being printed 93 times

Every row of the missing-readings list carried the same 24 words: "account
AC-2026-000NN: no usable read for water in this period. Estimate it, hold the
account, or bill without this service — nothing is assumed." The row already
showed the account number in its first column, and the three choices were the
row's own dropdown. Each row now reads "No water reading this period", and the
one thing worth saying — that nothing is decided for you — is said once, at the
top of the step.

### Six empty columns are gone

The decisions table drew METER, METHOD, CONSECUTIVE, DAYS SINCE PRIOR, CYCLE
EXPECTS and JUDGED AGAINST on every row, and most rows had nothing to put in any
of them. A column now appears only when something in the table actually fills it.
Where one kind of row fills a column and another does not, the column stays and
the empty cell still shows a dash — that dash means something.

### The decision dropdown shows its whole option

It was narrower than its longest choice, so it offered "Estimate the re…". It is
now wide enough to read, and the table still does not scroll sideways, because
the two changes above gave the width back.

### Two sentences that read wrong

The note on the past-runs list ended mid-thought — "The customers billed and the
number held back are." It is one short line now. And the line under the utility's
name in the sidebar, "Connections and plan not shown yet", read as part of the
utility's name on every screen; it is gone from there. Your subscription plan is
on Settings → Billing plan, which now exists, and that page says the one figure
still not counted.

## [2.109.0] — 2026-08-31 · Bills you can hand to a printer

You can now produce, in one go, everything a printing company needs to post a
cycle's bills: one print-ready page set for every bill, and a list with one line
per bill giving the account number, the bill number, the customer's name, the
address in separate columns, how many pages the bill has, the bill date, the due
date, the amount due and the name of its page file.

**Billing → Print bills.** Choose a bill run or every issued bill, look at what it
would produce — *"93 bills · about 1.8 seconds"* — and press **Build the print
set**. What lands is a single archive holding the pages, the list, a report of
anything held back, and a short note for the printing company.

### A bill whose address is incomplete is held back and named, never sent short

A printing company cannot standardise, barcode or rate an address that has no
town, state or postcode, so a bill missing any of the three is **kept out of the
file and reported by name**, with a sentence saying which part is missing and
what to do about it. We do not fill the gap in ourselves: a guessed address is
post delivered to the wrong house.

For the same reason the address travels in **separate columns**, exactly as it is
recorded, and is never cut up or joined together on the way out.

### We say plainly what we have not done

The note in the archive states that the addresses have **not** been
CASS-certified, have **not** been NCOA-processed, and carry **no** Intelligent
Mail barcode. Your printer does all three; this product does none of them, and a
silence there would read as a claim that we had.

It also says that we change a customer's address only when the account holder
tells us to — so if the printer's checks find that somebody has moved, that is
something to tell us, not an instruction we act on.

### Two gaps this found, both recorded

The list has a column for a second address line and a column for a country
because that is the agreed shape, and **both are always empty**: there is nowhere
in the system to record either. They are left empty rather than guessed at.

And the sample utility's addresses had a town and a postcode and **no state** —
all forty-nine of them — so the first run held every single bill back. That is
the rule above doing its job. The sample data now carries a state so the feature
can be shown.

### Under the bonnet

A print set runs on billing's own background worker and does not hold the browser.
Measured on real data: **0.012 seconds and 6 database reads a bill**, so ten
thousand bills is about **two minutes** and a **13 MB** file. A run larger than
25,000 bills is refused before a single page is drawn, and the refusal says how
long it would have taken and how to make it smaller.

Every page comes from the layout that bill was issued on, not from today's — a
reprint next year is the same document.

## [2.108.0] — 2026-08-31 · The reads upload asks which services the file covers, and four finished pieces of work finally appear in the record

### The upload screen now asks which services this file is for

Step 1 of the reads upload has always asked for the reading month, the cycle, the
route and how the meters were read. It now also asks **which of your services this
file covers**, and it starts with all of them chosen. Remove the ones that do not
apply, exactly as you would anywhere else in the product — the services show as
small removable tags with a picker beside them.

Choosing a single service is the useful case: every row in the file that does not
name a service of its own is then treated as that service, which is what lets the
product tell you a water meter has turned up in a batch you said was electric. If
you leave more than one chosen, the screen says so plainly — *"Each row states its
own service."* — and each row in your file decides for itself.

The screen used to carry a 36-word note explaining why this field was missing. The
note was wrong: the list of your services has always been readable by a billing
clerk. Both the note and the gap are gone.

### Four things that were built three days ago and were not written down

None of this is new behaviour and nothing on screen changes because of it. The
pre-filled reading sheet — the file you download with every meter and register the
cycle expects, the previous reading already in it, and only the readings left to
type — was finished on 30 August and the change record never said so. It has now
been re-checked end to end and written down:

* the sheet for the sample utility's August cycle is **18 rows across 5 meters**,
  because four of those meters are on a time-of-use tariff and need one row per
  window and one for the total. A clerk is never asked to know that.
* a demand meter's two rows carry **kWh on one and kW on the other**, so a peak is
  never typed into a column measured in the wrong unit.
* changing a meter number on the sheet and uploading it produces
  **"row 15 was M-7450, now M-7210 — was the meter replaced?"** — a question, not a
  rejection, because replacing a meter is normal and the clerk is the one who
  knows.

### Nothing internal is printed on the sheet, and there is now a check that says so

The sheet carries a `key` column so the product can spot a swapped meter. It was
reviewed against the rule that says no internal identifier is ever shown to a
utility user, and it passes: the key is built from your cycle's code and the
meter's own number, and the register is named in the words the screens use —
*On-peak*, not `tou_on`. Three tests now hold that, each shown to fail first when
an identifier was deliberately put into the key.

## [2.107.0] — 2026-08-31 · An account you have already dealt with leaves the exceptions list, the *Charges to add* tab can store a reply, and three sentences that said a worker cannot exist stop saying it

Nothing a customer is billed has changed. The golden figures are the same before
and after — **33 of 33** — and the 130 signed money figures in the two frozen
finance documents are byte-for-byte identical.

### An account you had already dealt with stayed on the exceptions list for ever

The billing rules give a failed account exactly two ways out: fix it and retry it
now, or hold it for the catch-up run. **Only the first one took the account off
the clerk's exceptions list.** Hold an account and its exception row stayed open —
so the list showed work that was already done, and the rule that says a run cannot
be signed off with an open exception would have stopped a run that was ready.

Both doors now close the row, and they say which door it was: *drafted* means the
account was billed on this run after all, *held* means it is waiting for the
catch-up run. A supervisor looking back at what a run struggled with gets the
right answer for each account instead of one answer for both.

### The *Charges to add* tab offered Apply on every row and the server refused every one

The screen shipped yesterday with Apply and Waive on each row, and the server had
no way to store either reply — a clerk's answer went nowhere. It can store them
now.

**What is honest to say about it, plainly:** applying a charge does not yet put
money on the bill. The amount of a service charge comes from the utility's own
charge code, and nothing in the product yet produces one of these rows to decide
on at all, so the tab is empty on every database there is. Rather than bill the
account WITHOUT the charge somebody asked to add, or invent a figure no rule
produced, an applied charge holds that account for the catch-up run and says so.
Waiving changes nothing and the account bills normally.

### Three places still told callers there was no background worker

There has been one since 19 August, and bill runs have had a worker of their own
since yesterday. One of the three was not a note in the code — it was **a sentence
sent back on every single bill release**, telling whatever read it that the
product could not do something it had been doing for twelve days. All three are
corrected, and a check now looks at every such sentence the billing module sends
rather than at the two somebody remembered.

## [2.106.4] — 2026-08-31 · The basic service charge now comes from the charge code, which is where you ruled it lives

Nothing a customer is billed has changed, and that was checked before anything was
switched rather than afterwards. The basic service charge on the sample utility is
exactly what it was — **$8.00** on the reference account and **$390.00** across the
47 accounts of the July run — printed account by account before and after, with the
two lists identical.

### You ruled this on 20 August and neither pricing path had read it

On 20 August the ruling was that the **charge code** owns the basic service charge
and a plan only displays it. That reached every document in the repository and
neither of the two places that actually work out a bill.

The bill run went on reading the figure typed on the **plan**. The new pricing
engine — the one being brought in a step at a time, and switched on nowhere — read
a box on the **rate schedule** that the same ruling retired, and which the
rate-schedule screen has had no control for since. So a utility that did exactly
what the ruling told it to do could not be priced by the new engine at all: on our
own sample utility it **refused all 47 accounts**, every one of which the bill run
was charging correctly.

Both now read the charge code, including the per-size price list a clerk can
already type in and which nothing had ever read.

### The new engine asks two questions where it used to ask one

*Does this rate schedule serve this pipe size* is one question; *what does that size
cost* is another. One piece of code answered both, which is why it ended up asking
for a figure the product had removed the box for. They are separate now — which is
the ruling's own wording — and a pipe size the utility has never priced still stops
the bill, exactly as before. Nothing about **whether** a bill refuses changed; only
**where the price comes from**.

A consequence worth knowing: all eight steps of the new engine can now be checked
against the old one individually. Two of the eight could not be, because they shared
a figure — so on a run where they agreed on all 47 accounts, both reported "nothing
could be checked". Both now report their own result, and each was proved able to fail
before it was trusted.

### One thing in the sample data disagreed with itself, and no customer was affected

The sample utility's Industrial plan says the electric basic charge is **$180.00**
while the charge code said **$12.00** — a **$168.00** gap that nothing could see,
because the two halves were read by different code and never met. **No account is on
that plan**, so no bill ever carried either figure. The $180.00 was moved onto its
own charge code rather than a figure being picked, and the seeding script now stops
with an error if a plan ever states a basic charge no charge code states.

### From now on, two disagreeing figures stop one bill instead of picking one

If a plan and a charge code state different basic service charges, that one account
stops with both figures named and the rest of the run bills normally. Silently
preferring one of two numbers a person typed is exactly how every bill this product
produced once printed $0.00.

## [2.106.3] — 2026-08-31 · The new pricing rules now charge the state tax to the commercial customers who owe it

Nothing a customer is billed has changed today: the new pricing rules are still
switched off everywhere, so every bill is still produced by the old ones.

### What was wrong

Two of the sample utility's customers are businesses, and Texas charges them a
6.25% state utility tax that households do not pay. **The old rules charge it. The
new rules did not** — they were never told what kind of customer they were pricing
for, and a tax that only applies to some kinds of customer is dropped when nobody
says. The same thing happened to a tax that only applies in certain places, to a
tax that only applies to certain services, and to a customer holding an exemption
certificate — that last one the wrong way round, so the new rules would have
charged a tax to somebody who had proved they were exempt.

Nothing could see it. When a tax does not apply, the correct outcome is no line on
the bill and no error — so a tax that was dropped by mistake looks exactly like a
tax that was correctly left off.

### What it was worth, per authority

On the two business accounts, before and after, with every other figure held still:

| account | authority | old rules | new rules, before | new rules, after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AC-2026-00047 | Local | $6.64 | $6.64 | $6.64 |
| AC-2026-00047 | Texas State | $20.76 | *not charged* | $20.76 |
| AC-2026-00048 | Local | $4.77 | $4.77 | $4.77 |
| AC-2026-00048 | Texas State | $14.91 | *not charged* | $14.91 |

Across all 47 accounts of the July run: **$35.67** of state tax, charged by the old
rules and by nothing else, now charged by both. The county tax was **$87.03** on
both sides throughout and did not move.

### The eight-step comparison now reads clean

The run that found this compares the old and new rules step by step over a whole
bill run. The tax step read **45 agree, 2 disagree** and now reads **47 agree, 0
disagree**; the whole run has no disagreements left. The comparison was checked by
deliberately removing a tax from one account and confirming the count moved.
## [2.106.2] — 2026-08-31 · The new pricing rules can now be checked against the old ones, and the sample utility can be priced by them at all

Nothing a customer is billed has changed. Both figures on the sample utility are
exactly what they were: the water base charge is **$8.00** on the reference
account and **$390.00** across the 47 accounts of the July run, before and after,
checked account by account rather than as a total.

### The sample utility could not be priced by the new rules at all

The product is being moved onto a new set of pricing rules one rule at a time, and
before a rule is switched on we run it beside the old one and count where the two
disagree. On the sample utility that count could not be taken: the new rules
refused **all 47 accounts** at the third step, because nobody had ever typed a
price for the meter size those customers have — a 5/8-inch domestic water
connection — and the sample data has never contained one.

Both seeders now write that price list. A newly seeded utility carries a row for
every meter size its own service can have, so the new rules resolve rather than
refuse, and a repair script brings an already-seeded utility to the same state.

### Four of the eight new rules were not being checked against the old ones

Of the eight steps a bill goes through, only four were ever compared. The other
four reported "no disagreements" on every run — and that was true only in the
sense that nobody had looked. It was proved by putting a thousandfold error into a
customer's meter reading and re-running: **nothing moved anywhere**.

All eight are compared now — the quantity billed, the out-of-city surcharge, the
discounts granted and the taxes charged — and each one was proved able to fail
before it was trusted.

**It found something on the first run.** On the two commercial accounts the old
rules charge the state utility tax and the new rules do not, because the new rules
never get told which kind of customer they are pricing for. Nobody has been
mischarged — no rule is switched on — and it is now written down as a defect with
the fix named.

## [2.106.1] — 2026-08-31 · Our question numbers can go past 999, and the tools can finally read them

The Product Owner asked for question numbers five digits wide. They already needed to be:
we passed 999 some time ago, and our own tools could only read three digits.

- **A four-digit number was not being ignored — it was being read as a different, real
  question.** `OQ-1190` was read as `OQ-119`. Nothing failed and nothing warned; a note
  saying *"this is waiting on question 1190"* was quietly filed against question 119
  instead. That had already happened for real: a question about how vacant flats are
  charged was, for two days, recorded against an unrelated accounting question.
- **Twelve of our 434 open questions were invisible to every automatic check**, including
  two that were answered and closed today. The checks reported them as unanswered.
- **Nothing has been renumbered.** `OQ-291` is still `OQ-291`. What changed is how much
  room the numbering has and what the tools can read — not how anything is written.
- **The business-rule numbers were the urgent part and nobody had hit them yet.** Rating
  rules stand at 962 of a possible 999, and three more were written this afternoon. Once
  they passed 999, a rule about pricing would have pointed at the wrong rule — on the part
  of the system that works out what a customer owes.
- Two further faults were found while fixing this and are written up rather than left:
  one question with a tick in front of its status that made the status unreadable to the
  checks, and one place that hid internal reference numbers from customers but had never
  recognised one of the four kinds it claimed to cover.

## [2.106.0] — 2026-08-31 · Two decisions about discounts, turned into working rules

### A free allowance now knows what it is free of

A programme can give a customer "2 free" of something. Until today the product
stored the **2** and nothing anywhere stored what the 2 was **2 of** — so two free
kilogallons of water and two free kilowatt-hours of electricity were the same
saved row. A programme attached to the wrong service would quietly have given away
two of whatever that service happened to measure.

**The allowance now takes its unit from the service it is attached to**, which is
how it was decided. The same saved row is worth very different money depending on
which service that is, and those are the two numbers worth seeing:

- attached to **water**, a customer who used 18.72 kgal goes from **$90.78** to
  **$76.38** — the allowance is worth **$14.40**
- attached to **electricity**, a customer who used 620 kWh goes from **$71.80** to
  **$71.52** — the same row is worth **28 cents**

**The unit is now printed next to the figure** — the screen says `2.00 kgal`, not a
bare `2.00`. That is deliberate. The product is now working the unit out rather
than being told it, and showing the answer is how a member of staff spots a
programme attached to the wrong service. If a utility has never said what unit a
service is measured in, nothing is guessed: the product says so and stops.

### And it has to apply to one service, which it now says while you are typing

An allowance that applies to the **whole bill** has no single service to take its
unit from, so "2 free" would mean nothing. Choosing that combination is now refused
**on the form, as it is being filled in**, in plain words: *"A usage allowance is
counted in the unit of one service, so it has to apply to a single service."*

The timing is the whole point. The same refusal arriving during a bill run would be
an outage; met while somebody is setting the programme up, it is a correction that
costs a few seconds.

### A subsidy no longer pretends to be a different price list

A discounted programme like "Residential Electric — subsidised" was going to be
built as a **swap to a second, cheaper price list**. It is not, and will not be.
**A subsidised customer is charged the normal price and given a discount**, and
both numbers appear on the bill.

Worked on a real customer using 620 kWh:

- the normal price list charges **$71.80**
- the low-income credit takes off **$25.00**
- the customer pays **$46.80**

Built the other way, the bill would have shown **one line of $35.90** and nothing
on it would have told the customer they had been given anything. A discount line is
visible; a swapped price list is not. That is the reason, and it also restores a
rule the product already had — a discount is an overlay, never a rate.

### Nothing about anybody's bill changed

Both of these settle how the product will work. **No invoice, no total and no
figure moved**, and both kinds of discount are still switched off until the wider
billing changeover reaches them. The 33 finance-signed billing figures were checked
before and after and all 33 still pass.

### Two things found and fixed on the way

**A warning on the discount form was telling people the opposite of the truth.**
Setting up a *charge waiver* said it could not go live — it can. Setting up a
*usage allowance* said nothing — that one cannot. Both are now correct.

**The same discount could show a different value on two screens**, because two
pieces of the product were building that row separately and had drifted apart.
They now agree.

## [2.105.0] — 2026-08-31 · A tax return is filed per authority, and now something adds it up

### What was happening

A bill can charge two tax authorities and the only figure this product published
was the two added together. On the seeded bill `BL-2608-000094` that is **$4.77**
of Bexar County tax and **$14.91** of Texas State tax, and the product printed
**$19.68**. A remittance return is filed **per authority**, monthly, so the one
number a clerk actually has to write down was the one number nothing computed.

### What changed

The Product Owner ruled on 2026-08-31: *"(a) Add a per-authority subtotal to the
bill and the finance screens"*. Both surfaces now carry it.

* **On a bill** — the Charges tab gives each authority its own subtotal under its
  lines, and says whether they add up to the tax the bill already showed. On
  `BL-2608-000094`: Bexar County Tax Office **$4.77**, Texas Comptroller of Public
  Accounts **$14.91**, footing exactly to **$19.68**.
* **On the finance screen** (Finance → Taxes & Remittance) — a *Billed on bills*
  column beside what the books hold for the same authority, the authority named
  the way a return names it, and per row whether the two agree. A disagreement is
  shown with both figures and neither is moved.
* **A figure that cannot be answered says so rather than showing 0.00.** On a
  screen a return is filed from, a zero reads as *"this authority is owed
  nothing"*.

**Nothing about how a bill is priced changed**, and no signed figure moved: the
subtotal adds the ROUNDED printed lines, which is the rule finance already signed.

### And an address still only changes when its owner says so

The same day the Product Owner ruled that a mail vendor's mover lookup — which
finds people who have moved and hands back a new address — **is not something we
write onto an account**: *"(a) Ignore it — mailing only, our record unchanged - we
cannot make chnges until account confirm it"*. Nothing in the product did that
already, which was checked rather than assumed, and a merge check now keeps it
that way.

## [2.104.1] — 2026-08-31 · The tests were not testing that each utility's data stays separate

### What was happening

Every utility on SMARTBillHub shares one database, and what keeps one utility from seeing
another's customers is not our own code being careful — it is the database itself refusing.
The app tells the database, on every single connection, which utility it is working for, and
the database will not hand back a row belonging to anyone else. That refusal is the strongest
guarantee this product makes.

**Our automated tests were not telling it.**

A piece of shared test setup, written when the tests only ever ran against a small local
database that has no such feature, swapped the real database connection for a stand-in. The
stand-in wrote the utility's name into a list in memory and threw it away. Nothing ever reached
the database.

That was the right thing to do for the small local database — it genuinely cannot do this — and
the mistake was that it was never limited to it. The helper switched itself on automatically,
without any test asking for it, and it spread through shared imports to **447 test files
covering 6,575 individual tests**.

So when those tests passed against the real database, they were not showing that the separation
works. They were not exercising it at all. And nothing looked wrong, for a reason worth stating
plainly: the login the tests used to reach the database was an administrator account, and an
administrator is exempt from the separation entirely. With no utility named and no rule applied,
every query simply returned its rows and every test went green.

### What changed

The stand-in is now used only on the small local database that needs it. Against the real
database the tests use the same code the live product uses, so the utility is named on the
connection exactly as it is in production.

Four other, near-identical helpers in the same test suite were already written this way, each
with a note explaining why. This one was the only holdout.

### What it does not change

**The product itself was never affected, and that is measured rather than assumed.** Signing up
a new utility was run against a real database with the separation fully enforced, under a login
that genuinely cannot bypass it. It worked end to end. This was a fault in how we test, not in
what we ship.

### The part that is still open

Turning the stand-in off means those 447 files run for real for the first time, and a large
number of them fail — not because the product is wrong, but because the test setup itself never
said which utility it was working for, and the database is now correctly refusing it. Nearly all
of them fail for one single shared reason rather than for hundreds of separate ones. The repair
to that shared setup is in this release; what remains is recorded with a count so it can only
get smaller.

A new automatic check now reads all 569 test files and refuses any shared setup that switches
itself on automatically and replaces the real connection without first asking which database it
is on. It was proved to fail before it was trusted to pass.

## [2.104.0] — 2026-08-31 · Billing gets its own lane, so it can be given a share of the machine without slowing anything else down

### What was happening

Everything this product does in the background went through **one lane**: working
out a utility's bills, exporting a list to a spreadsheet, taking in an uploaded
file of meter readings, and sending customers their notices. All of it, through
the same two slots.

That was fine until we measured what a clerk feels while a bill run is going. In
a utility that was not billing at all, with two other utilities' bill runs under
way, the list of accounts went from just over half a second to nearly three, and
opening one bill went from a fiftieth of a second to a tenth. It is not the
database — the runs never once waited for each other there. It is that the part
doing the billing and the part answering the screens share the same processors,
and **nothing limited how much the billing could take**.

The obvious fix is to give billing a share of the machine and no more. **It could
not be done.** With one lane, limiting billing meant limiting the customers'
notices too, and adding capacity for billing meant adding it for everything.

### What changed

**Billing now has a lane of its own, and a worker of its own to drain it.** The
three billing jobs — work out the bills, check what we found, and issue them — go
there. Everything else stays exactly where it was, in the lane it always used,
with nothing changed about it.

**That worker is allowed one processor.** A normal installation has four, so the
other three stay with the screens a clerk is clicking. What it costs is stated
rather than hidden: a bill run for a ten-thousand-customer utility takes about
**forty-eight minutes** instead of about **twenty-four** when a second utility is
billing at the same time. A bill run finishing at three in the morning instead of
half past two costs nobody anything; a clerk waiting three seconds a click costs
them the morning.

**Two numbers can be changed by whoever runs the installation** — how much
processor billing may use, and how many billing workers there are — in one
settings file, without any change to the product, and **without affecting any
other kind of background work**. Nothing decides either number by itself; this is
an ability, not an automation.

**And one thing is now refused outright: a second scheduler.** Two schedulers do
not clash and do not complain — they both fire, so anything on a timetable simply
happens twice. The person who scales the billing workers is exactly the person
who would scale that too, so an automatic check now refuses any change that does.

### What a customer sees

Nothing different, and nothing about any bill has moved. No price, no total and
no rounding is touched by this — the billing arithmetic checks read **33 of 33
passing before and after**, run both times.

### Measured, before and after, on the same database

Four screens a clerk uses, timed in a utility that was **not** billing, while two
other utilities' bill runs were under way the whole time. p95 — the one click in
twenty that a person actually notices — against the same screens with nothing
running:

| screen | with two bill runs, no limit | **with the limit** |
|---|---|---|
| the list of accounts | 3.2× slower | **1.3×** |
| one customer's page | 4.7× slower | **1.4×** |
| one bill | 5.3× slower | **1.3×** |
| the bill run's own results page | 2.7× slower | **1.3×** |

The list of accounts, which is the screen most people open first, went from
**4.1 seconds to 1.3** at that mark.

## [2.103.1] — 2026-08-31 · A utility that signs up now gets customers, not just buildings

### What was happening

A utility that signed up got its buildings, its flats and its meters — and **not
one customer and not one account**. The sign-up said it had worked. The list of
customers, which is the first thing anyone opens, was empty, and so was
everything that follows from it: no bills, no payments, no payment plan.

Seventy buildings and a hundred and eighteen flats, and nothing to bill.

### Why

The forty-eight sample accounts were being created correctly. A later, unrelated
piece of the same setup step then asked the database a question it could not
answer, noticed, wrote a quiet note in the log and carried on — and on this
database that is not something you can carry on from. Once one question fails,
every later question in the same piece of work fails too, and the whole piece is
undone at the end. So the forty-eight accounts that had already been made were
thrown away, along with everything downstream of them.

What got recorded was a message about the database rather than about what
actually went wrong, so it pointed at the wrong thing. And nothing ever compared
the number of accounts created against the forty-eight that were meant to be
there — the number was worked out and then read by nobody.

### What changed

**One refusal now costs one row, not the whole set.** Twenty-five places in the
setup code that say "if this one fails, skip it and keep going" now genuinely
can. Measured: with one flat deliberately made to fail, the other **forty-seven
accounts still land**, where before all forty-eight were lost.

**And the count is now checked.** If nothing at all could be created, the setup
says so in a sentence naming what refused, instead of a database message naming
nothing. If some were created and some refused, the ones that worked are **kept**
— forty-seven accounts is a utility you can look at and none is not — and the
shortfall is written down with both numbers, so it can be found later and acted
on rather than discovered by a customer.

### Measured, before and after, on the same database

|  | premises | units | meters | accounts | customers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 70 | 118 | 69 | **0** | **0** |
| after | 70 | 118 | 69 | **73** | **65** |

Eight of the fourteen setup steps failed before; none does now.

### Fixes

- `DEF-2722` — a newly signed-up utility got sample premises, units and meters
  but no customers and no accounts.

## [2.103.0] — 2026-08-31 · A premises upload can no longer throw away a row because of how the owner's name is spelt

### What was happening

When you upload a list of addresses, one of the columns is the owner. If the name
in that column was close to two owners you already have on file — *Ridge Property
LLC* and *Ridge Property, L.L.C.* — the upload **threw the address away**. It came
back in the failed-rows file, and nothing about it was wrong except the spelling.

On a migration of a few thousand addresses that is a real stall: the addresses you
cannot load are the same ones your meters and your accounts then cannot name.

### What changed

**The address loads, with no owner, flagged for someone to fill in later** — exactly
what already happens when the owner column is simply empty. The upload now accepts a
row whatever the owner column says: blank loads, a name you already have is reused,
a name that looks like two of yours loads with nobody attached, and a name nobody
has yet loads and keeps the name.

**We still never pick between two owners for you.** That was offered and turned down
on purpose: the owner is who gets the bill, so choosing the wrong one eventually
sends somebody else's bill to the wrong person. The upload names both and leaves the
choice to a person.

**Adding one address by hand is unchanged.** That screen still asks for an owner,
because somebody filling in a form knows the answer or can find it.

### What to watch on the receipt

An address with no owner has **nobody to charge**. It is a real address — it holds
units, it holds meters, it can be read — and no bill can be produced for it until
somebody says who owns it. The receipt at the end of the upload has always counted
those rows, and now it splits them into the two kinds, because they need different
work from you:

* **No owner named — needs research.** Somebody has to find out who owns it.
* **Matched two parties — needs a decision.** We name the owners it looked like, so
  you are choosing between two names rather than searching again.

Both are settled on **Premises → Owner matching**.

## [2.102.0] — 2026-08-31 · A bill run now has a size limit, and we can finally say what ten utilities billing at once costs

### What was happening

Nothing bounded a bill run. If a billing cycle was set up wrongly and picked up a
hundred thousand customers instead of a thousand, the run started anyway and
worked through all of them — for hours — holding half the background capacity
while it did. Nobody was told and there was no way to stop it short of
restarting the worker.

Two other things had never been established. How much work IS one bill, in reads
and writes rather than in seconds? And what happens when several utilities on the
same installation press "work out the bills" at the same time? Every figure the
project had was one utility alone on an idle database.

### What changed

**A bill run above twenty-five thousand customers is refused before it drafts
anything.** The refusal names the count and the ceiling and gives the two ways to
make a run smaller — put fewer services on it, or run one billing cycle at a
time — both of which the product already does. It does not truncate the run and
it does not start and hope. Checking the size costs two queries, so the check is
never a reason to skip it, and a deployment that genuinely needs more can raise
the ceiling with one setting (zero switches it off).

Twenty-five thousand is **eight times the largest utility this product is for**.
SMARTBillHub is built for utilities under three thousand connections, so a run
that size is a misconfigured cycle rather than a big customer — and at the
measured rate it would already take seventy minutes.

**One bill costs about a hundred reads and five writes**, and that does not move
between a hundred customers and ten thousand. Ninety-eight per cent of the work is
reading. Nothing about the run gets worse as a utility grows.

**Several utilities billing at the same time do not get in each other's way in
the database.** Ten were set up and fired at once, and no run ever waited for a
lock held by another — not once, in six different combinations. What they share is
the machine's processors, and the queue the product already uses is what stops
that hurting between runs: put through it, each utility's run went at its normal
speed and everybody finished sooner than when all ten were fired at once.

⚠ **But a bill run DOES slow the screens down, and that is now measured rather
than guessed.** With two bill runs going — which is the most this installation
runs at once — a clerk in a different utility saw the accounts list go from just
over half a second to nearly three, and a single bill from a fiftieth of a second
to a tenth. The cause is not the database; it is that the part of the system doing
the billing and the part answering the screens share the same processors, and
nothing currently limits how much of them the billing may take. **The fix is a
setting on the deployment, not a change to the product**, and it is written up
with the numbers so whoever runs the servers can make the trade deliberately: give
the billing worker a share of the machine, and a run that took twenty-four minutes
takes forty-eight while the clerk keeps their morning.

**The review step of a bill run got about a fifth faster** — the same work,
asking the same questions fewer times. It still re-checks everything from scratch
each time it is opened, deliberately, so a plan somebody has just corrected shows
up straight away.

### What a person sees

A run inside the ceiling behaves exactly as it did. A run above it stops at the
door with a message instead of running for hours.

⚠ The refusal's reason — the count and the ceiling — reaches the log and the audit
record but not the screen, which shows the shorter "This billing run can't go
ahead as asked." That gap is recorded as a defect rather than half-fixed here.

## [2.101.2] — 2026-08-31 · The list of rejected rows arrives with the rejected rows in it

### What was happening

When a clerk uploads a thousand readings and two of them are bad, we promise them a file
at the end listing those two. **That file was arriving empty** — the column headings and
nothing under them. A clerk reading it would conclude that nothing had been rejected,
which is the opposite of true, and the screen one click earlier was correctly saying
*"2 rows will not post"*.

The same was true of the file the account import hands back at the end of a migration.
Two different features, written a day apart, with the identical fault.

### Why nobody saw it

The file is sent as a stream — the rows are read out of the database as the download is
being written, rather than all at once, so a fifty-thousand-row file does not have to sit
in memory. That work happens **after** the request has finished, and the marker that tells
the database which utility is asking is cleared the moment a request finishes. So the
database was being asked *"which rows failed?"* by nobody in particular, and it answered,
correctly, with nothing.

It did not error, and it did not look wrong anywhere: the download succeeded, the file had
its headings, and every automated test passed. Two of those tests download this very file
and check the headings — which are written before any row is fetched, so they were true
over an empty file. It became visible only when a database account stopped being an
administrator, because an administrator is exempt from the rule the whole thing turns on.

### What changes

Both downloads now re-open the utility's own context for exactly as long as they are
reading rows, and close it again the moment the file is finished. **Nothing about who can
see whose data changed** — the download simply asks under the same utility the clerk was
already signed in to, and it asks under the one the request was granted rather than one
read back off a record.

A new merge check refuses any future streamed download built the other way, so the next
person to add one cannot repeat this, and a new test holds the behaviour against a real
database under an account the isolation rules genuinely apply to.

### Proof

Downloaded through the screen in a real browser: the button said **2 rows will not post**,
and the saved file held **0** rows before this change and **2** after — each with the
reason it failed and how to fix it.

## [2.101.1] — 2026-08-31 · Three screens that told you a number that was not true

### What was happening

All three were found the same way: somebody opened the screen, read the number, and then watched
what the product actually did next.

**A cycle that was only half read drew a full bar and said it was 100% done.** The Cycles page was
dividing the number of readings collected by the number of meters on the cycle — and those are not
the same kind of number. A meter on a time-of-use tariff owes four readings a month; a plain meter
owes one. So on the demo utility the sum came out at 300%, 500% and 400% on three different cycles.
The bar could not draw past full, so all three showed a complete bar reading **100%**, and a clerk
looking for meters still to chase was told there were none.

**The step before you press Post said "Rows that will become readings: 0" and then filed five.** It
was counting rows a person had explicitly ticked. Since a ruling on 26 August, a reading with a
warning on it is filed anyway — we do not throw a real reading away — so on a file nobody had ticked,
the count said nothing would be filed and everything was. The receipt on the next screen then called
those same five readings *"left without a decision"*, under a heading saying **1** row had not become
a reading. Six statements about the same five rows, and they disagreed with each other.

**One sentence contradicted itself.** *"This cycle expects 5 readings. This batch and the readings
already on file cover 5. 1 have not been read."* Fully covered, and one meter unread, in the same
breath. A meter that had been read before and appears in the file again was being counted twice.
And the same sentence called a count of **meters** a count of **readings** — the cycle it said
expected 5 actually expects 18.

### What changed

**The Cycles page now measures completeness the way the rule defines it** — required readings
collected against required readings expected — and the demo utility's deliberately-short cycle now
reads **10 of 18, 55.6%**, with a button to chase the three meters still owing. It used to read a
full bar.

**A figure over 100% is now shown, in red, saying the real number.** This is the part worth calling
out: capping the bar at full is what hid the fault for five days, because a full bar reads as good
news. A percentage above 100% means the sum behind it is wrong, and that has to be visible.

**The step before Post now states what will be filed and what will be held back**, worked out once,
from the same rule the server uses. We proved it across the button: it said *Commit 2 rows*, and the
post created 2. The receipt stopped describing filed readings as failures.

**The coverage sentence is now shorter, truthful and in the right unit:** *"2 of 2 meters covered.
0 meters still unread."* It used to be three sentences and twenty-four words.

**And the checks that watch these screens were tightened**, because two of them could not fail: one
passed when the short cycle it was meant to inspect was absent, and one passed when the sentence it
was meant to read was missing entirely. Both now insist the thing exists, and both compare what the
screen says against what the product then does, rather than against itself.
## [2.101.0] — 2026-08-31 · The last twelve months of usage now print on the bill

### What was happening

A bill showed this month's charges and nothing about the months before it. The
twelve months of usage had been copied onto every bill since 30 August, frozen
at the moment the bill was issued — and nothing served them, so no screen and no
printed page could show them. They were on the bill and invisible.

### What changed

Every bill now shows the last twelve months of usage, one row per service, as a
chart on screen and as a table on the printed page.

**The figures come from the bill itself, not from today's meter data.** They were
copied onto it the day it was issued and they stay there. If a reading for one of
those months is corrected next year, this bill still shows what the customer was
sent; only bills issued after the correction show the new figure. Reading the
account's current usage instead would mean a bill from 2026, reopened in 2033,
displaying 2033's twelve months above 2026's charges.

**A month nobody read is left blank, not drawn as zero.** A zero would tell a
customer we read their meter and it had not moved. Months that include an
estimated reading are marked.

Worked, on the sample utility's account A-10432: electricity 412, 842 and 628
kWh and water 8, 9 and 4 kgal across the three months that have readings, and
nine blank months before them.

### Note

The printed page carries a **table** of the twelve months rather than a plotted
graph. A graph would need extra software installed on the servers, which the
16 August layout decision deliberately keeps out; a table needs none, and the
request was for *a last-12-month consumption table or graph*.

## [2.100.2] — 2026-08-31 · No database keys left on the bill screens

### What was happening

Three places on a bill showed a long internal code instead of something a person can read.

Open a bill, click **Charges**, and when the accounting code or the rate version behind a line
could not be looked up, the column printed the raw key —
`dead0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001` — under a heading that says ACCOUNTING CODE. And on the
first tab, the row headed **Billing run** always showed the run's internal key, never its name.

Each of those was a deliberate choice at the time, and each had a good reason. The accounting
code showed the key so the column could never go blank, because a blank there reads as *"this
line did not post"*. The billing run showed its key because the run screens did not exist yet,
so there was nowhere to send anyone.

### What changes

**Nothing internal is on these screens any more, and nothing reads as missing either.**

- **Accounting code.** Where the code cannot be looked up, the column now says
  **"Accounting code not readable"**. That is not a blank, so the reason the key was there in
  the first place still holds — nobody will read it as an unposted line.
- **Rate version.** The same, in the same words: **"Rate version not readable"**.
- **Billing run.** The row now shows the run's own number — **RUN-0001** — and clicking it
  opens that run. If a run is old enough to predate run numbers, the row says **"Open the run"**
  and still takes you there.

The internal codes are not thrown away. They are on the cell, where support can read one off a
screen share, and out of the sentence a clerk reads.

### Why you can trust it this time

The bill screens are now opened in a real browser and read the way a person reads them: every
cell of the charges table and every visible line of the first tab. **Seven cells and one row
carried a key before this change; none does now.** The run link is clicked, not just checked, so
a link that goes nowhere cannot pass.

### Nothing else changed

No money figure, no rounding, no rule about how a bill is calculated. The change is what three
cells display.

## [2.100.1] — 2026-08-31 · The app now refuses to start if the database is not keeping tenants apart

### What was happening

Every customer's data in SMARTBillHub is kept separate by the database itself, not just by our
code. The database is told "only ever show this utility its own rows", and it does — for almost
every kind of login.

There is one exception, and nobody had ever written it down where it mattered. If the username
the app connects to the database with happens to be an **administrator** account, PostgreSQL
skips that separation entirely. Not partially — completely. And there is no sign of it anywhere:
the settings still say the protection is switched on, the rules are all still there, and every
screen still shows sensible-looking data. The only difference is that a check nobody can see is
no longer being made.

We found this the hard way. A test utility that had been set up with **no customer accounts at
all** reported **73 accounts** when we looked at it. Those 73 accounts belonged to a *different*
utility. Nothing had gone wrong, nothing was logged, and every test was green.

### What changes

**The app now asks the database, every time it starts up, whether the separation is actually
being applied to it — and says so out loud.**

- **In a real deployment it refuses to start** if the answer is no. That is a deliberate choice.
  There is no legitimate reason to run the product this way, and a version that starts anyway
  would keep serving pages and quietly mix two utilities' data together. Not starting is the
  safer of the two failures, and it prints the exact command an administrator needs to fix it.
- **On a developer's own machine it prints a warning instead**, because working with an
  administrator account there is normal and convenient. Getting that leniency requires
  deliberately switching to development settings; it cannot happen by accident on a real server.
- **When everything is correct it still says so**, naming the database user. That one line is
  what lets anyone reading a performance measurement or a support log afterwards tell which of
  the two situations the numbers came from.

### Also in this release

- **Performance figures published earlier today are marked as measured with the separation
  switched off.** The bill-run timings of 136, 137 and 141 milliseconds per account were taken
  on a connection that was skipping the per-utility check. With it applied the same work
  measures about **172 milliseconds** per account. The original numbers have been kept and
  labelled rather than deleted, so the record stays readable.
- **Checked, and it is good news: signing up a new utility still works when the separation is
  switched on.** A sibling team saw every one of its database tests fail the moment an
  administrator account was taken away, which looked like signup being broken on any correctly
  configured server — the one thing this product cannot afford. We ran the real signup service
  against a properly restricted account with every protection applied: it created the utility
  end to end. The failures are in the **test scaffolding**, which stands in for a piece of the
  database machinery so the tests can also run on a simpler database, and therefore never set the
  "which utility am I" marker. On an administrator account that was invisible, because the marker
  was not being checked anyway. Tracked separately; no customer-facing behaviour is affected.

- We have also written down that **we do not currently have a record of which database username
  any deployed environment actually uses** — so we cannot yet say, from the repository alone,
  whether a live environment was ever affected. Establishing and recording that per environment
  is now a tracked item.

## [2.100.0] — 2026-08-31 · The bill run's review step stops being one long list

### What was happening

Before a single bill goes out, the run shows the clerk what it found. That screen had six labels
across the top and, behind five of them, the same thing: a grouped list of reasons. Three of the six
drew nothing else at all. The step after it was worse — **fifteen separate lists down the left-hand
side**, one per kind of question, and the only way to answer any of them was to tick a box at the top
and confirm a dialog. A clerk with one late fee and one high reading clicked through two lists, two
tick boxes and two dialogs to say two words.

Nothing on either screen moved when a decision was recorded. The server stored it correctly and
answered; the screen kept showing *Not decided* until somebody reloaded the page by hand.

### What changes

**Six real sub-screens.** Consumers, Plans & Rates, Meter reads, Open balances, Credits and Charges to
add each draw their own thing now, and the two the run genuinely cannot fill say so — with the columns
they will have — rather than sitting empty.

**Meter reads is one table with a filter for every situation.** All · Collected · Missing · Not metered
· Estimated · Looks high · Looks low · Days threshold · Meter factor · Meter changed · True-up · No
usage. Each filter carries its own count, and the decision a flagged reading needs is taken **on its
row**.

**Estimating a missing reading now asks for the figure.** Choosing *Estimate the reading* opens a small
window that asks for the usage and its unit and will not commit without both, because that figure goes
on the customer's bill as their consumption. Before today the option was there, and pressing it did
nothing a clerk could see.

**Step 3 is three groups, not fifteen lists** — *Readings and usage*, *What the customer owes*, and
*What goes on the bill* — grouped by where a clerk goes to answer the question. The kinds inside the
open group are a row of filters, and the answer is chosen on the row. **Bulk is untouched**: a run with
a thousand late fees still takes one click, which is the whole reason bulk exists.

**Six figures above the step, and four of them move as you decide.** How many will bill, how many
cannot, how many are waiting on you, and how many you have answered — each with a word beside the
colour, so the strip reads the same to someone who cannot tell the colours apart.

**Step 4 opens with what happens if you continue now** — how many bills are ready to go out, and how
many accounts are held back, split into what could not be worked out and what a person chose to hold.

### What is honestly not there, and says so

**No late fee or extra charge is gathered yet.** The *Charges to add* screen is built and reads the
right place, but the run produces neither kind of row on any database today, so the screen names that
rather than showing an empty table that would read as *nothing to add this month*.

**Open balances and Credits are still not gathered by the run.** Both now show the table they will be,
with no rows and the reason.

### Also in this release

The *Over charges* tab is now called **Charges to add**, which is what the glossary has always said it
holds and what the design has always drawn in it. The other meaning of that phrase — a bill far above a
customer's own average — keeps its own place on step 4 under *Unusually large bills*.

No customer's bill changes. Nothing on these screens works out a price, a total or a usage; every
figure shown is one the server had already decided, and where there is no figure the screen says so
instead of showing a zero.

## [2.99.1] — 2026-08-31 · The disconnection bill stops charging a whole month for part of one

### What was happening

When a utility turns a customer's supply off, the product raises that customer's last bill
there and then. It was charging the **whole monthly standing charge** for however few days
the customer had actually used.

On the worked example we have been using all along: a customer cut on **18 August**, on a
**$40.00 a month** standing charge, had used the service since the 1st — 18 days out of 31,
worth **$23.23**. They were billed **$40.00**. That is **$16.77 too much on a final bill**,
in the customer's disfavour.

The rule for splitting a standing charge was never wrong, and it has not changed: days used
divided by days in the billing month, times the charge. What was missing was the second
number. Nothing in the product would say how long that customer's billing month was, so the
sum divided by the length of the *billed stretch* instead — 18 days over 18 days — and the
answer came out as the full month, every time.

### What changed

Metering now works a customer's billing month out from the cycle they are on. A utility
already tells us when a cycle starts, how often it comes round and when its first run is, and
that is enough: this customer's month is **1–31 August**, so the bill is **$23.23**.

Nothing about the splitting rule moved, and no new setting was added — every part of the
derivation is something already decided (the first run sets the day; a cycle set to the 31st
falls back to the 28th or 29th in February). It is also the same length the product already
works out when a bill run asks whether a meter reading covers 15, 30 or 90 days; the
disconnection path simply was not asking.

Two more things came with it:

- A cut recorded **late** now uses the month the cut happened in. A customer cut on 18
  February whose paperwork lands in March is split over February's 28 days, not March's 31 —
  **$25.71**, not $23.23.
- A **mid-cycle plan change** preview splits the month the change falls in, rather than the
  month today falls in.

### What still happens when the month cannot be worked out

Some cycles were set up before the product asked for those facts and carry none of them, and
a property could be on two billing cycles at once. In those cases nothing is guessed: the
full standing charge is billed exactly as before, and the bill record says that the customer's
billing month could not be read and by how much that leaves them over-charged.

### Was anyone actually over-charged?

No. There is no button anywhere in the product that performs a disconnection — the only
disconnection a screen can do is *schedule* one, which charges nobody. The cut can currently
only be triggered by talking to the system directly rather than through a screen, so this is
fixed before the button exists.

## [2.99.0] — 2026-08-31 · The screen catches up with the file that already posts what it can

### What was happening

Yesterday the upload learned to file the good rows and hold back the bad ones. **The screen
did not.** It still refused to move past the review step while any row carried an error
nobody had decided, and it still said so on screen:

> *"1 error row(s) still need a decision before this batch can post."*

So a clerk with two bad meter numbers in a thousand-row file could not reach the button at
all. The behaviour was built, released and unreachable through the only door to it.

### What changes

**The review step stops refusing and starts telling you what will happen.** Where the red
box was, the screen now says:

> *"1,178 rows will post. 2 will not, and you can download them."*

**The button says what it is about to do.** It read *Commit load*; it now reads
**Commit 1,178 rows** — and it is the same number the sentence above states, worked out
once so the two can never disagree.

**The spreadsheet of what will not post is offered before you press it, not only after.**
That was the Product Owner's own instruction — *"create csv file at loading stage itself"* —
and it is now on the review step as well as on the receipt.

**Three things the screen was saying that were no longer true are gone.** The load step said
*"Posting is all-or-nothing"* and counted *"Rows that will become readings: 0"* over a batch
that then filed five; the receipt described those same five filed readings as *"left without
a decision"*; and the cycle-coverage line managed to say a cycle was fully covered and had an
unread meter in one sentence.

### Cycles: a collected count that finally has the right denominator

The Cycles page showed **Expected 5 · Collected 25 · Progress 100%** for a cycle that was
**83.3% complete**. The two figures were never comparable — one counted meters, the other
counted readings, and a time-of-use meter owes four readings where a flat one owes one. The
column now reads **15 of 18 · 83.3% · 0 days left**, and **Chase 2 meters** opens the list of
which meters are short and which registers each one still owes, by name.

### A tiered customer whose read date was changed

A tariff with bands cuts those bands to the length of the billing period, so a mistyped read
date on a tiered customer silently re-prices every band and the bill still looks right. When
a reading on a tiered tariff is dated outside the reading month you chose, the screen now
says so — and says why, in one sentence.

### What is deliberately unchanged

The batch still closes when it posts, and posting it twice is still refused. A reading with a
warning on it is still filed. Nothing here decides whether a clerk *should* post a meter whose
bill will refuse — that stays a warning and stays the clerk's call.
## [2.98.0] — 2026-08-31 · A bill taken apart: what each service cost, whose tax it is, and what the utility never wrote

### What was happening

Open a bill and click **Charges** and you got one long list of lines. It was accurate and it
answered almost none of the questions a clerk is actually asked.

*"How much of this is water?"* — nowhere. *"Who is this tax paid to?"* — the line said
**Tax Local** and nothing else. *"Is this a discount or a fee?"* — a discount, a deposit and a
minimum-bill top-up all sat under a heading called *Taxes & fees* looking exactly like a usage
line. *"What happens if they pay late?"* — the due date was in the page header and there was no
answer at all to the rest.

And on the bill document, the utility's own message and its ways to pay were squeezed into a
narrow label-and-value box, with the line breaks the utility typed collapsed into one run-on
line.

### What changes

**The Charges tab now answers five questions in the order they are usually asked.**

- **What each service cost.** A subtotal per service, plus one clearly-labelled row for
  everything charged to the bill rather than to a service — tax, fees, a minimum-bill top-up —
  with those kinds spelled out in words so nobody has to guess why money is sitting outside every
  service heading.
- **Every line, in full.** All seven fields stay on screen, the accounting code and the rate
  version included. Under each line that is not usage or a base charge, a short note says what it
  is: **Tax · Bexar County Tax Office**, **Discount**, **Minimum bill adjustment**.
- **Whose tax it is.** A panel groups the bill's tax by the authority it is paid to. On a real
  seeded bill that is `$6.56` to Bexar County and `$13.12` to the Texas Comptroller.
- **When it is due**, whether the bill is past due, and how many fee lines are on it.
- **What the customer already owed**, which the amount-due panel above already showed.

**Every figure on that screen is the server's own.** Nothing is added up in the browser. Where
the server states that its lines and the bill's total disagree, the screen says so in both
figures and changes neither.

**The bill document draws the utility's message and ways to pay as what they are** — paragraphs,
at a readable width, with the line breaks the utility typed. And when a utility has written
neither, the bill says what that costs: *"What this utility has not written is not on the bill.
That includes any late-payment terms, which are theirs to write. Add them on the Templates
screen."*

### What is deliberately unchanged, and said out loud

- **Nothing here writes a utility's late-payment terms for them.** Those are the utility's own
  words, in their own jurisdiction; the product charges the fee whether or not the wording is
  printed, and it will not invent a legal disclosure on a utility's behalf.
- **Tax is not split across services.** A tax is charged on the bill and nothing in the records
  says which service it belongs to, so the screen does not pretend otherwise.
- **A total per authority is not shown**, because nothing computes one yet. The screen says so
  rather than adding the lines up itself — a remittance return is filed per authority and that
  figure needs to come from one place ({OQ-1190}).
- **A minimum-bill top-up shows where it actually is.** It is charged per service and recorded
  against none, so it appears in the bill-level row with a note saying the total is right and
  only the heading is wrong. It is not quietly moved on screen.
- **The twelve-month usage block is not drawn.** It is frozen onto every bill and no endpoint
  hands it to a screen yet, so it is reported rather than faked from today's readings — a reprint
  in 2033 must show 2026's twelve months ({DEF-2714}).

## [2.97.0] — 2026-08-31 · Turning the supply off now sends the bill for the days they used

**CR-052 wave W0, task 1 — the disconnect is the whole event** (PO ruling 2026-08-30,
closing `OQ-1170`).

Until today, marking a cut customer's account **Disconnected** quietly took them out of
next month's billing run — so the days they had used before the cut were billed to
nobody. On a **$40.00** a month standing charge, a customer cut on the 18th had used 18
days of 31: **$23.23**, plus every gallon and every kWh, gone.

Now the bill goes out on the day the supply goes off, priced by the same engine that
prices every other bill. The **$75.00** reconnection fee is charged as before, whatever
is still owed stays owed on an account that is **still open** — nothing is written off
and nothing is closed — and when the customer settles up and the crew turns the service
back on, the account returns to exactly the status it had before the cut, so it is
billed normally again.

* Raising the bill is billing's job, not the disconnection screen's, so it asks through
  a new published door (`apps.billing.services.raise_and_issue_cut_bill`).
* Cutting twice cannot bill twice: the second bill is refused by the database, not by a
  check that a race could lose.
* If our own pricing cannot produce that customer's bill, we still cut the supply but we
  do **not** mark the account Disconnected — they stay in the billing run so the days
  are not lost.

**Known and stated, not hidden (`DEF-2708`):** to split a monthly standing charge fairly
we need to know how long that customer's billing month is, and nothing in the product
answers that yet. Until it does, the disconnection bill charges the whole **$40.00**
rather than the **$23.23** that 18 of 31 days is worth — **$16.77** too much on that one
bill — and it says so on the record every time.

Also fixes a test fixture that had left four billing checks failing since 27 August
(`DEF-2709`), and reports one more that belongs to another change (`DEF-2710`).

## [2.96.0] — 2026-08-31 · The bill run is timed for the first time, and a run that is interrupted picks up where it stopped

### How long a bill run actually takes

Until today nothing in this product had ever been timed. It has now been
measured on a real database at three sizes, and the answer is **about a seventh
of a second per customer**, whatever the size:

| customers | time | of which looking things up | bills written |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 13 seconds | 12 seconds | 413 lines |
| 1,000 | 2 minutes 15 seconds | 2 minutes | 4,123 lines |
| 10,000 | 23 minutes | 19 minutes | 41,245 lines |

Nothing gets worse as a utility grows — ten thousand customers take a hundred
times as long as a hundred, not more. The figures are published in the decision
log and reproducible with one command.

### It now asks the same question once instead of ten thousand times

**84% of that time was spent looking things up before a single bill was
written**, and most of those lookups were the same question over and over:
*what does this plan charge for water?* has the same answer for every customer
on the plan, and a small utility has three or four plans, not ten thousand.

A run now asks each of those questions once. **1,000 customers: 2 minutes 15
seconds becomes 1 minute 48.** Nothing about anybody's bill changes — it is the
same question, asked fewer times, and the amounts are identical to the penny.

### A run that is interrupted carries on rather than starting again

If the machine doing the work stops half way through a run, it used to begin
again from the first customer. On ten thousand customers that is twenty-three
minutes of repeated work. It now continues from where it stopped, and it cannot
bill anyone twice: a customer is skipped only when the run had already got past
them **and** their bill is already there.

## [2.95.0] — 2026-08-31 · A bill picks its own layout, a customer can ask to be emailed, and the conservation surcharge finally charges

### Four things a utility could set up and this product could not honour

**1 · The bill template is now chosen per customer, not once per run.**
The rule has always been *this account's own template first, then whatever this
kind of customer gets, then the utility's standard one*. What the billing run
