actually did was pick the standard one and stamp it on every bill in the batch.
A utility that had made a different layout for its commercial customers got the
residential one on every bill, and the system reported this on every response
rather than doing it. It now works down that list for each bill as it is issued,
and the run says how many bills answered for themselves.

**2 · A customer can ask to be emailed or texted — and still gets their paper
bill.** The two preferences existed on the sign-up screen and had nowhere to be
stored, so the billing run had been asking a question nothing could answer since
March. Now: a customer who has asked for nothing gets **one** delivery record —
paper. Paperless on gets **two** — paper AND email. Both on gets **three**.
Nothing ever gets none, and the paper record is identical in all three: going
paperless is a request to be *told* about the bill, never permission to stop
sending it.

**3 · A per-unit tax charges what the rule says it charges.**
A water conservation surcharge of **25¢ per thousand gallons above 15,000**
billed **nothing at all** — the code that prices taxes could do percentages and
flat fees and had no way to price this third kind. On a customer who used
**18,720 gallons** it now charges the **3,720 gallons above the threshold**, so
**$0.93**. Charging it on the whole reading would be **$4.68** — the customer
paying a conservation surcharge on the first fifteen thousand gallons the rule
deliberately exempts.

The tax has to say what unit it is charged per, and the system refuses rather
than guessing: a surcharge written per kilowatt-hour cannot be applied to a
water meter, and it says so in those words instead of quietly multiplying.

**4 · The two discount kinds that could not be switched on are built as far as
the data allows.** A *rate override* puts a customer on a cheaper price list;
a *usage allowance* gives them so many units free. Both refuse at set-up today
because neither is a simple subtraction — a rate override changes every price on
the schedule, and an allowance has to come off the READING before the bands are
worked out. Worked: a 2,000-gallon allowance on a customer using 18,720 gallons
is worth **$14.40**, because those two thousand come off the most expensive band.
Handed to the discount step as money at the average price it would be **$9.70**,
and the customer would be $4.70 worse off for a discount the utility believes it
gave them.

**Both still refuse at set-up, deliberately.** Two things are missing and only a
person can supply them: nothing records WHICH price list a rate override points
at, and nothing records WHAT UNIT an allowance is measured in — 2 free of what?
Both questions are with the Product Owner.

### Nothing that was already correct moved

Every existing tax rule and every existing account behaves to the digit as it
did: the finance-signed worked examples read **33 of 33 correct** before and
after, and the two new columns default to *not asked for*, which is true of
every customer in the product.

## [2.94.0] — 2026-08-30 · Two bad rows stop holding back a whole meter reading file

### What was happening

A clerk uploads a month of meter readings — often more than a thousand rows. If **two** of the
meter numbers in that file were wrong, the system filed **none of them**. Not the two: all of
them. Every customer on that file waited on two typos, and the screen said so in as many words:
*"The batch cannot be posted until every one of them has one."*

The clerk's only way forward was to open the file, find the bad rows among a thousand, make a
decision about each one by hand, and try again — for a fault that had nothing to do with the
other 1,178 customers.

### What changes

**The upload now files what is correct and holds back what is not.** The same 1,180-row file
with two unknown meters in it now files **1,178 readings** and holds **2**.

**The two come back as a spreadsheet the clerk can fix and upload again.** It is their own file —
same columns, same order, the values they typed — with two columns added on the end:

| why it failed | how to fix it |
|---|---|
| There is no meter called M-9999 on this utility. | Check the meter number against the one on the meter itself. If the meter is genuinely new, add it first — a reading cannot be filed against a meter that does not exist. |

No rule numbers, no error codes, no database words. They correct the cell, upload the file, and
those two readings go in as well.

**The file is offered before the commit as well as after it.** The moment a clerk most needs the
list of what is wrong is *before* they press the button, not on a receipt afterwards.

**A reading with a warning on it is still filed, and is not in that spreadsheet.** That has been
true since 26 August and has not changed: a reading somebody actually took is stored, flagged,
and worked afterwards.

### What is deliberately unchanged

**A batch cannot be posted twice.** Once a file has been posted — even if two of its rows were
held — that file is closed. Pressing Post again says so; uploading the identical file again says
so, and names who posted it and when. That is what stops a customer being billed twice for the
same reading, and it is the reason the held rows come back as a *new* corrected file rather than
by re-opening the old one.

**A reading a person decided to keep out stays out.** Rejecting a row, sending someone out to
re-read a meter, or skipping a row all still do exactly what they did before, and the spreadsheet
says which of those happened rather than blaming the data.

### Also in this release

Two things the reads screens describe as missing turned out to have been built. The upload's
first step carried a 36-word note saying no endpoint a Billing Clerk may call lists this
utility's services; one has, since the day the product shipped. And the check that catches a
water meter in a file tagged Electric was described in its own source as unable to reach a
verdict; it has warned with both values named since 26 August. Both are now covered by tests, so
the next reader believes the assertions rather than the prose.

## [2.93.0] — 2026-08-30 · The reads upload hands you the file

### What was happening

To get a month of readings into the product, a clerk downloaded a blank template with
eight columns and two example rows. To turn that into a file they had to work out six
things themselves, and the product told them none of them: which meters are in the cycle,
which of them need more than one row, that a time-of-use tariff needs four, how to spell a
register name that appears on no screen, that a peak is measured in kilowatts and not
kilowatt-hours, and which service each meter is on. The system already knew every one of
those answers.

Once the file was uploaded, the screen still did not say what was in it. A file covering
half the meters looked exactly like a file covering all of them until the bill run, weeks
later, refused to bill the ones that were short.

And the screen said several things that were not true. It offered to save the column
mapping as a template for next time — this import deliberately keeps no mapping and said
so six lines further down. It headed the last screen before the commit *"Dry run first"*
over an import that has never had a dry run. It explained, in thirty-six words, why a field
a clerk had not asked about was missing. On the screen where readings are reviewed before
they become money, the date read `2026-08-03T00:00:00+00:00`.

### What changes

**You can download a reading sheet for the cycle, already filled in.** One row per meter
per register it needs, with the premise, the unit of measure, the previous reading and the
date it was taken. The only column left blank is the reading itself. The button names what
you are about to get — *"Reading sheet for CY-002 · 18 rows"* — and the blank template is
still there beside it for anyone whose meters are read by a hand-held device.

**The moment a file is staged, the screen says what is in it**: how many rows, how many
meters, which services, which dates, and how many readings arrived for each register. A
time-of-use cycle uploaded with one row per meter now shows that on the second screen
rather than at the bill run.

**A new table says which meters are short of what their plan needs**, grouped by the kind
of tariff — how many registers the plan expects, how many arrived, how many are missing and
which ones. Two buttons act on a whole group at once: estimate them all, or send someone
out.

**The upload now looks and behaves like the other six imports in the product** — the same
cards, the same file panel, the same rules table. It states the file's fingerprint the
moment it is accepted, and shows a sample of your own data beside each column it matched,
so you can see what your headings became before anything is checked.

**The screens say less, and what they say is true.** Roughly half the words are gone: every
sentence explaining something that is not built has been deleted, every sentence explaining
a rule has been shortened, and every sentence that tells you what will happen before you
commit has been kept. The two false promises are fixed. The read date reads `08/03/2026`.

### Fixed

* The read date on flagged rows printed the raw timestamp instead of a date (`DEF-2443`).
* The cycle-coverage sentence on the last screen before posting printed three blanks where
  its three numbers should be — it had been asking the server for fields the server does
  not send (`DEF-2440`).
* Table captions in every import screen rendered below the header row instead of above it
  (`DEF-2439`).
* Columns of counts in every import screen were left-aligned instead of right-aligned
  (`DEF-2438`).

### For the record

Four of those were found by opening the screens in a browser and reading what came back,
after 3,485 automated tests had passed over them. Two of the four are only visible by
measuring the finished page — no test that reads source code could ever have seen them.

## [2.92.0] — 2026-08-30 · Every bill keeps a year of usage, and your own words

### What was happening

Two things were designed into the bill years ago on paper and had never been on a bill.

**A year of usage.** The bill was meant to show the customer their last twelve months, the way
most utility bills do. It showed one month — the one being billed — because that is all the bill
kept. The rest of the year existed, and the account screen already drew it, but the bill could
not reach it without going and looking things up at printing time, which is exactly what a bill
is not allowed to do: a bill has to say the same thing in 2033 as it says today.

**Your message and your ways to pay.** The bill has a place for both and nothing ever filled it.
The visible cost of that: the late-fee terms this product charges — the ones a customer is
entitled to be told about — have never appeared on a single bill it has printed.

### What changes

**Every bill now freezes twelve months of the customer's usage into itself when it is issued.**
It comes from the same stored figures the account screen already shows, so the two can never
disagree, and it is frozen rather than looked up later, so a reprint years from now shows the
year as it stood on the day the bill was sent. The window ends at the **bill's own period**, not
at today: a June bill issued in September shows July 2025 to June 2026, and so does the same
bill reprinted in 2033.

**Every bill now carries your message and your ways to pay**, taken from the bill template that
bill is pinned to and frozen with it. Rewrite your message next year and the bill you sent this
year still says what you sent. Type your late-fee terms once on the Templates screen and every
bill from then on carries them.

If you have written neither, the bill says so plainly rather than printing a blank line, and the
bill run tells you once, with the one edit that fixes it.

### What is still owed

**No bill layout draws the chart yet.** The year of usage is on the bill — kept, reprintable,
and correct — and the printed page does not plot it. That needs a drawing engine we deliberately
keep out of the product, and it is the next piece of this change.

**We do not write your late-fee sentence for you.** It is your disclosure, in your language, and
a product that composed it would be writing one English sentence for every utility. The bill
carries whatever you type.

### What has NOT changed

No money moves. Nothing here prices anything: the 33 signed money checks pass unchanged, and a
bill whose usage history or message cannot be read still goes out — the run records why, by
name, and the bill is unaffected.

## [2.91.0] — 2026-08-30 · The minimum bill is actually charged

### What was happening

A utility can tell this product *"water is never billed at less than $15.00 a month"*. It is on
the plan screen, a clerk can type it, and finance signed the rule for it weeks ago.

**It did nothing.** Not "did it wrong" — the figure never reached the part of the product that
prices a bill at all, so every customer who used very little water was billed for exactly what
they used and the minimum the utility had set was never applied to anybody.

The code was honest about it. The stage that owns the rule said so in its own words: the two
amounts *"cannot travel on the seam, so there is no input to apply"*. That sentence had been
sitting there for three weeks.

### What changes

Both amounts now reach the pricing engine, and both kinds of minimum are charged:

**The per-service minimum.** A household that used 0.4 thousand gallons of water is charged
**$1.60** for the water and **$8.00** for the standing charge — **$9.60**. Because the utility
set a $15.00 minimum, the bill now carries a line reading **Minimum bill adjustment $5.40**. Tax
is charged on the full **$15.00**, which comes to **$1.42**, and the bill totals **$16.42**.
That is the worked example finance signed, and the product now produces it.

**The whole-bill floor.** A utility can also say *"no bill on this plan is ever under $40.00"*.
When both are set, each service is brought up to its own minimum first, and only then is the
whole bill brought up to the floor: electric $18.10 and water $9.60 becomes electric $18.10 and
water $15.00 — $33.10 — and the floor then adds a further **$6.90**.

**A late fee does not help a customer reach their minimum.** A $20.00 late fee on that $9.60
water bill still owes the full $5.40 adjustment. A penalty is not spending.

### What has NOT changed

**No bill that has already been issued moves, and no bill on any tenant configured today moves
either.** Every plan in the database has these two boxes empty, and empty means "no minimum" —
not "a minimum of zero". The bill you would get this morning is the bill you would have got
yesterday, to the penny. The 33 signed money checks pass unchanged, before and after.

### Still open

* If a utility typed a minimum on the **rate schedule** screen instead of on the plan, it is
  still ignored. The signed rule names the two figures on the plan and says nothing about a
  third one, so we report it rather than guess which wins.
* A customer away on holiday, and every empty flat in a landlord's building, are charged their
  standing charge and nothing else on purpose — and today they are topped up to the minimum like
  everybody else, because the rule has no exception for them. On the building we use as our
  standing example that is **$42.00 a month** across six empty flats. It is a question for the
  Product Owner, not something we decided.

## [2.90.0] — 2026-08-30 · The demo utility gets meters you can actually check

### What was happening

The sample utility we hand you to click around in had **199 meter readings, and every single one
of them was the meter's plain total.** No reading anywhere in it said which register it came
from.

That matters more than it sounds, because three of the checks the product runs on an uploaded
reading are checks about registers, and none of them had anything to look at:

**"This meter is missing half its readings."** A customer on a time-of-use tariff has a meter
with four dials on it — peak, mid-peak, off-peak, and the total — and the product knows that,
because the tariff says so. If a crew hands in one number where four were needed, the product is
supposed to say so before the bill runs. On the demo it never could: not one meter there was on
a tariff at all. All ten of the demo's addresses had **no price plan attached**, which also means
nobody could have been connected at any of them.

**"These three windows do not add up to the total."** Same idea, the other way round: peak plus
mid-peak plus off-peak should come to roughly the total, and the product checks it. With no
meter reading four dials, the check simply reported that it had nothing to compare.

**A peak demand reading did not exist on the demo at all.** A large commercial customer is
billed partly on the highest power they drew in the month — a number in kilowatts, not kilowatt
hours. Earlier this month we fixed a fault where the product treated that peak like an ordinary
counter and subtracted last month's from this month's: it billed **$154.00 where the correct
charge was $4,532.00**. The fix is in, and until now there was no way to see it working on the
demo, because the demo had no peak reading.

**And solar.** A household with panels sends power back to the grid, which is a second reading
on the same meter. The demo had none of those either.

### What changed

The demo utility now carries **24 readings across five kinds of register**, on four meters, for
July and August.

* **A time-of-use meter reading all four of its dials**, whose peak, mid-peak and off-peak add
  up to its total exactly. The check runs and passes.
* **A meter deliberately left short** — one number where four were needed — so the warning has
  something to fire on. It reads, in the product's own words: *"expects
  total/tou_on/tou_mid/tou_off, file has total only."*
* **The industrial meter's peak demand**, **412 kW**, recorded in kilowatts and marked as having
  been reset at the start of the cycle. That reset box exists on the upload template and nothing
  in this product had ever filled it in.
* **A solar household's export reading**, **122 kWh** sent back to the grid in August.
* **Every demo address is now on a price plan** — seven residential, two commercial, one
  industrial — which is what makes all of the above possible and what would have stopped anyone
  being connected there.

None of these readings is priced: the demo still has no customers and no bills, so no money moves
on any of them. Every number either comes from a figure already written down and agreed, or is an
opening dial position that prices nothing. The readings are loaded the same way a clerk loads a
file — upload, check, accept, post — and not written straight into the database, so anything the
checker would refuse from a clerk is refused here too.

### Still true, and worth knowing

Every one of the 24 readings is marked **"vacant"**, and that is the product being right: the
demo has no customers yet, so no address has anybody living at it. Seeding customers is a
separate piece of work.

## [2.89.1] — 2026-08-30 · Housekeeping: we now run the build that actually ships

### What was happening

Nothing on any screen changes in this release. It closes three holes in our own checking, and the
first one stopped you deploying earlier today.

**We were not running the command that builds the product.** You ran the build yourself and it
stopped on a broken line of code. The person who wrote that line had run a check and it passed —
and they were telling the truth. The problem is that the check they ran and the build that ships
are two different commands, and only the second one looks at every file. So a branch could be
green on every check we own and still refuse to build, and nobody had any way to tell the two
apart. That is the difference that cost you a deploy.

**Our defect list could say a problem was still open after it had been fixed.** We keep a list of
every fault, and we plan the next day's work from it. Rows in that list are marked done by hand,
and a row whose fix has already shipped but whose mark was never changed sends somebody off to fix
work that is finished. Today there were at least nine such rows, three of them serious — and the
fault about the broken build was itself one of them.

**Two people running the tests at once could stop each other.** The tests need a scratch copy of
the database, and every person on the team was using the same one by default. One run creates and
deletes it; another run expects it to be there. Neither crashes — they simply grind. Today that
cost fifty minutes and produced no result at all, on a set of tests that takes three minutes when
it has the machine to itself.

### What changed

**The build that ships is now one of the checks that must pass before anything merges.** It reads
the build instructions themselves rather than a copy of them, so if the way we build changes, the
check changes with it. It takes about 45 seconds. We proved it works by putting the broken line
back and watching it stop, with the same message you saw.

**A change that claims to fix a fault is now checked against the list.** If a change says it fixed
something and the list still says that thing is open, nothing merges until the two agree. Separately,
the report we plan from now prints how many open faults have been touched by work already done —
119 of them today — and says plainly that this is a list to look at, not a list of things that are
fixed, because only a person can tell those apart.

**Everyone now gets their own scratch database automatically**, named after the folder they work in.
Nobody has to remember to set anything, which is the only kind of safety that survives a busy day.
We measured it: two people running the same tests at the same time used to leave one of them with
thirteen errors in two seconds, and now both finish normally in a minute and fifty seconds each.

## [2.89.0] — 2026-08-30 · When somebody changes the wording of a letter, we write down what changed

### What was happening

You told us this on 30 August, and this release is the middle part of it:

> *"any legal document when send - it is freezed - we should keep all underline data, but actual leter
> and PDF should be freeze - **any changes to tempalte or any items hsould be noted as changed**; that
> way it will keep the santity of the legal documents; otherwie everytime we reproduce it using data in
> table, we might change something about it and that is not correct"*

The letters and the bills are already kept as they were sent — that landed earlier the same day.
**Noting a change as a change had never been built at all.**

The product did already keep every version of every letter, and it would not let anybody rewrite one.
Open a letter's history and you got a list: v1, v2, v3, each with a date and a line like *"pinned by
3,412 sent"*. Two things were missing from that, and the second is the one that matters when somebody
complains.

* **It never said what an edit had actually changed.** Not on the screen and not in the audit trail —
  the trail recorded that somebody saved a new version and not one word of what they wrote. Answering
  *"did last March's edit touch the paragraph about disputing a bill?"* meant opening two versions and
  reading them side by side.
* **That count of 3,412 was a dead end.** It told you how many letters used the old wording and gave
  you no way to see a single one of them — and *which* is the question a regulator or an angry
  customer actually asks.

### What is different now

Open a letter's version history and every version says **what moved**: *Letter*, or *Subject ·
Letter*. Hover it and you are told which versions it sits between; click it and you get the rest —
how many lines were added and removed, and **the letters still standing on the wording you moved
away from**. The newest twenty are listed with the total beside them, each one linking to the exact
copy that customer received.

The audit trail records it too. The entry an edit already wrote now names which parts of the letter
moved and which version it followed.

### What we deliberately did NOT do

**Nobody is asked why they changed it.** There is still no box for *"softened the wording"*, and the
history still says *"no change note recorded"* — because that is something a person writes and we
would only be guessing. It is a small piece of work if you want it; say so and we will add it.

**This is letters and notices, not the bill's page design.** A bill is printed from one of five page
designs rather than from words somebody typed, so "the wording changed" does not mean anything there
yet. That is written down as an open question rather than guessed at — and it changes nothing you can
see today, because a bill's own sent copy has been kept since this morning's release.

## [2.88.0] — 2026-08-30 · A bill is kept as the bill, and you can see the one that was sent

### What was happening

You told us this on 30 August:

> *"any legal document when send - it is freezed - we should keep all underline data, but actual leter
> and PDF should be freeze - any changes to tempalte or any items hsould be noted as changed; that way
> it will keep the santity of the legal documents; otherwie everytime we reproduce it using data in
> table, we might change something about it and that is not correct"*

The letters were done earlier in the day. **The bill was not**, and the bill is the most important
document this product makes.

The screen called *"The bill as it was sent"* was rebuilding the bill from scratch every time somebody
opened it. All the figures were right — a bill's own data is locked the moment it is issued and cannot
be edited — but the DOCUMENT could still come out different, and here is the way it actually could:

* a bill prints on one of the page designs we publish. **Change what we publish — a new build, or a
  rollback to an older one — and a bill already sent re-opens on a different page.** We proved it: a
  bill issued on the standard design, opened after that design was no longer in the published set,
  came back with a whole section missing. "Services this period" was simply gone from a document a
  customer was holding.
* the same is true of any change we ship to how a bill is drawn. One improvement to a heading, and
  every historical bill in the product quietly re-opens looking different, with nothing anywhere
  recording that it happened.

**Two things were already safe and stayed safe**, and it is worth saying so rather than leaving you to
wonder: a bill's own figures cannot be edited after it is issued, and neither can the page design a
bill is pinned to — the database itself refuses that. **What nothing could protect was our own code**,
and that is what this change fixes.

Nothing was edited, nothing was lost, and no record was wrong. The bill on screen was just no longer
provably the bill in the customer's hand.

### What changed

**Every bill is now kept, as a document, the moment it is issued** — both the page you read on screen
and the printable page — in the same locked store the letters went into. Nothing can change them: they
cannot be edited, they cannot be deleted, and every time one is opened we re-check it against a
fingerprint taken when it was stored.

**Keeping it is a condition of issuing it.** If a bill cannot be kept, it does not issue: it stays a
draft you can still correct, rather than becoming a permanent record of a document nobody has a copy
of. That is only possible because nothing has gone to a customer yet, so we have taken it now — after
the first real bill run it could not be done.

**And the screen tells you which of two things you are looking at**, with no third answer:

* **the bill as it was issued** — the kept copy, with the date it was sealed and its fingerprint, so an
  auditor holding their own copy can check it matches without asking us; or
* **rebuilt from the data, not the original** — said plainly, in a warning, for any bill issued before
  today. The figures under it are still right; the page is not guaranteed to be the one that was sent.

If a kept copy ever fails its fingerprint check, the screen says THAT, rather than quietly falling back
to a rebuild. Those are different problems and only one of them is recoverable.

### What this does not do

The kept page still is not handed to a printing company — that part of the job is unbuilt and is now
the only half of the print rule still owed. And the page itself is still the plain one: no logo, no
usage graph, no barcode, because the product has no page-design engine yet. What gets kept is exactly
what the product produces today, and the day a designed page lands, that is what will be kept instead.

## [2.87.4] — 2026-08-30 · Housekeeping: three broken checks fixed, nothing on screen changes

### What was happening

Nothing a utility would have noticed — this release changes no screen, no figure and no rule. It
clears up three checks of our own that were failing, and a failing check nobody has claimed is
dangerous: the next person to break something real cannot tell their breakage apart from the noise.

Three things were wrong.

**The close-out screen had no name.** When we added the separate "close out an account" page on
27 August, we forgot to add it to the list the product keeps of every screen and its number. The
page worked fine; it just was not on the list. So the little screen tag in the bottom-right corner
showed nothing on it, and the check that is supposed to tell us "a screen has shipped without a
name" could not see the page at all — it was reporting on 103 screens when there were 104.

**Four tests were still asking for a button you removed.** On 27 August you told us every import
should offer two choices and not three: *"in all imports - we need 2 option on step 1 insert,
insert & update; replace option is not required"*. We took the third choice out of the product
correctly. We did not go back and update four tests that were still looking for it, so they had
been failing ever since — and two later people each spent time working out that the failures were
not their fault.

**One of our internal checks was counting the wrong things.** It looks for places where our own
internal codes could leak onto a screen you read. It was also counting demo data, command-line
tools and database upgrade steps — none of which has a screen at all.

### What changed

The close-out page is on the screen list now. It carries no number, because it is newer than both
of the numbering schemes we inherited, and we would rather record that honestly than invent one.

The four tests now check the world as you ruled it: two choices, and the third one is now actively
checked for its ABSENCE, so if anyone ever puts it back by accident a test says so immediately.

The internal-codes check no longer counts places that have no screen. It is still failing, and we
have left it failing on purpose and written down why: the remaining count is our engineers' own
notes to each other inside error messages, which have not reached a customer screen since your
ruling of 19 August, and deleting them would cost us a lot and gain you nothing. Making it pass by
quietly raising its limit is exactly the thing that check exists to prevent.

We also fixed the version number itself, which had drifted between two files.

## [2.87.3] — 2026-08-30 · The letter about a returned payment is now a letter, not an email printed out

### What was happening

When a customer's payment comes back — a cheque that bounces, a bank that returns a direct debit —
the product puts a letter for them on the outbound queue. On 29 August you told us print should never
be switchable off: *"don't switch of print for any document it is awayls on"*. That rule is doing its
job, and a paper copy of that letter is queued on every bounce whatever else a utility has turned off.

The problem was which document was being queued. There was only ever one version of the
returned-payment notice written, and it was the **email**. So the paper copy was the email, pinned for
printing — the wrong shape, the wrong greeting, and the wrong thing to put in an envelope.

There was a second, smaller wrong. If a utility had switched the emailed version off, the screen still
reported *"the returned-payment notice was queued by email"* right next to *"email is switched off"*,
with no email anywhere. Two contradictory sentences about the same action.

### What changed

The printed letter now has its own entry in your template list — **Payment failed / NSF · letter** —
separate from the emailed one, and the paper copy is queued against that.

**It is deliberately blank, and it will stay blank until somebody writes it.** Nobody has written the
wording for a printed returned-payment letter, and we will not invent it: this is a letter telling
someone that money they believed had reached you did not, and that is not wording for us to guess at.
So the letter is queued and then held, rather than going out with something made up. Open it, write
what you want your customers to read, and publish it — the same as any other template.

Your template list therefore goes from 37 documents to 38, and for the first time one of them has no
wording at all. That is the honest state and the screen says so.

The receipt panel also stops contradicting itself: it now reports the printed letter and the emailed
one separately, and it only says a channel was used when something was actually queued on it.

**Nothing reached a customer either way** — no printer, email or text provider is connected yet — so
no wrong letter was ever posted. This was fixed now because from today every document that does go
out is kept, unchangeable, for seven years under the name of the template it was made from. Left
alone, the first bounce letter printed after a provider is switched on would have been filed forever
as an email.

## [2.87.2] — 2026-08-30 · A tax can now be written for farms, schools, city departments and developers

### What was happening

Back on 24 August you were shown the four customer categories the product had — Residential,
Commercial, Industrial and Government — and you said *"Expand the signed list to seven"*. Since that
day a utility has been able to file a customer as **Agricultural, Institutional, Municipal or Builder
or developer**, and to price a plan for them.

They could not be taxed. The Taxes & fees screen offered the old four in its *"applies to these
customer classes"* box, and behind it the server refused the four new spellings outright. If you had
tried to write a 6.25% levy that applies only to farms, the save would have been rejected — and the
nearest thing that did work, leaving the box empty, means *every* class, so the levy would have
landed on every customer you have.

It failed in the safe direction, which is why nothing ever looked broken: the tax was simply never
created, so nobody was over-charged. It looked exactly like a tax somebody had forgotten to set up.

### What is different now

The box offers all eight categories — your seven, plus Government, which is kept because accounts
created before the change still carry it and a tax already restricted to it has to keep working.
A 6.25% levy restricted to Agricultural now charges a farm **$6.25** on a $100.00 taxable bill and
charges a house **$0.00**, which is what a restriction is for.

**No existing tax changed.** Widening the list of categories a tax may *name* re-points nothing:
every tax you have keeps the exact classes it was saved with, an empty box still means every class,
and a misspelled category is still refused rather than quietly dropped. No figure on any bill moves —
the 33 signed billing examples produce the same numbers to the cent.

The same box on a base charge code widened with it, for the same reason and through the same check.

### Under the hood

The product used to keep a second, typed-out copy of the category list inside the rating module, and
that copy is what went stale. It is gone: rating now reads the list from the one place the categories
are defined. There is nothing left to re-type, and a test now compares the screen's list against the
server's in both directions, so the next time the categories move, a mismatch fails the build instead
of shipping.

## [2.87.1] — 2026-08-30 · The customer rights wording and the email sender each get their own page

### What was happening

You walked the Notifications settings and said two things:

> "Create a seperate tab for this - under notification only"

> "Email sender (SMTP) - create seperate tab under notification"

You were pointing at the same problem you had been naming all day, one size larger. Everywhere else it
was a sentence too long for a table cell. Here it was two whole **sections** too long for a settings
page: the wording that prints on a disconnection letter, and the form for your outgoing mail server,
both stacked underneath six cards of ordinary configuration on a screen somebody opens to change one
setting. Neither block is too long. Each one is a different page.

### What changed

Notifications now has four tabs instead of two: **Settings · Messages needing attention · Email sender
(SMTP) · Customer rights wording**. Each of the two new ones holds exactly what it is named after and
nothing else, and each has its own web address, so you can send somebody a link straight to it and the
Back button works.

The settings tab is now **2,584 pixels tall where it was 4,367** — a little over 40% shorter, measured
in a real browser at the same window size, because two whole sections became two pages.

### The one thing we were careful not to break

The red warning above the rights wording travelled with it. That warning is there because those five
paragraphs are **not ours to write**: disconnection rules differ from state to state and from utility
to utility, so what we ship is a starting point for you to check against your own commission, not your
regulator's words. Leaving that warning behind on the old page would have quietly turned our
placeholder text into something that looks like legal advice, on the most serious letter this product
sends. It moved with the clauses, in full, unchanged — and there is now a check that opens the page in
a browser and fails the build if it ever goes missing.

The sender card kept its two important facts the same way: that **filling it in does not switch email
on** (that is a separate setting, on the dispatch card), and that the secret box holds the **name** of a
password kept in your own systems, never the password itself. Both are now three or four words on the
page, with the full sentence when you rest your pointer on them — the same shape you approved that
morning.

### And one sentence on that card was simply wrong

It read: *"…so under C-12's rule email would fall back to the platform ESP … Configure SMTP on Settings
→ Notifications, or wait for the platform sender."*

Two faults in one sentence. **C-12** is our own internal shorthand and means nothing to anybody running
a water utility. And it told you to go and configure SMTP on the very page you were already standing
on. It now says what is actually true, in plain words — that no sender is set up yet, that a mail
server and a from-address are the minimum, and that the shared sender that would otherwise cover it is
not built either — and it stops there, because the boxes underneath it *are* the configuration. Our own
reference numbers are still recorded, where our support people can read them and you never have to.

We found the same fault on the other half of that card — the version you would see once you *had* filled
it in — and fixed that too, so it is closed for every utility rather than only the ones that cannot
send yet.

## [2.87.0] — 2026-08-30 · You can now open the letter we sent, and it is the letter we sent

### What was happening

Earlier today this product started KEEPING every letter and message at the moment it goes out, exactly
as it went out. That was your instruction, and your reason for it was the right one:

> *"otherwie everytime we reproduce it using data in table, we might change something about it and that
> is not correct"*

But keeping a copy and being able to look at it are two different things, and only the first one was
built. **There was no way, anywhere in the product, to open one of those kept letters.** The copies were
piling up in a drawer nobody had a key to — which means that if a regulator had asked to see the exact
disconnection notice a customer was sent last July, the honest answer would still have been "we have it,
but we cannot show it to you".

### What changed

On **Settings → Notifications → Messages**, every message in the list now has a **Show what we sent**
button. Press it and you get one of two things, and they are meant to look different:

* **The letter as it went out** — the actual words the customer read, the date we sealed it, and a
  fingerprint that proves it has not been altered since. You can download it; the download link works
  for four hours, as you asked for.
* **Or a plain sentence saying no copy was kept — and nothing else.** No letter, not even a greyed-out
  one. This is deliberate. Showing you a rebuilt version with a warning above it is exactly how somebody
  ends up reading the wrong document and believing it is the real one.

**The letter is never rebuilt.** Not once, not as a fallback, not if something goes wrong. If a stored
letter ever stops matching its fingerprint we refuse to show it and tell you to report it, rather than
quietly falling back to a rebuilt copy.

There is also a **register**: every document sealed between two dates, which is the list a regulator
would ask for. That one is System Admin only, and we record who opened it and when.

### What this does not do yet

**Bills still rebuild themselves when you open them.** The "view the bill as sent" page has not been
moved onto the kept copy, because bills are not being kept yet — that is the next piece of this work.
Notices, receipts and the other letters are covered; bills are not.

## [2.86.1] — 2026-08-30 · The template screen stops explaining itself and starts showing you the letter

### What was happening

You walked the product screen by screen and found the same fault ten times in one sitting, and said so
plainly: *"again too much text content breking the UI"*, and *"just use 3 or 4 wrods and fix the UI"*.

You were right, and it was one fault wearing ten costumes. Wherever this screen had something to
explain, it printed the whole explanation on the page — under buttons, inside table cells, in stacked
helper paragraphs. Text is what decides how tall a thing is, so those sentences were not just wordy,
they were pushing the actual work off the screen.

The worst of them was in the version history. One cell was printing a note meant for the people who
build this product — a sentence about which database column does not exist — and it was drawing a box
**645 pixels tall**, in a panel only 344 pixels wide, on every row of every template. Two other places
were printing a file name from our own source code and an internal question number on your utility's
screen.

### What changed

Everywhere that happened, the fact stayed and the paragraph went. On screen you now get three or four
words; rest your pointer on them and you get the whole sentence. That is the same shape you approved
that morning for a different note: *"keep the fact, kill the paragraph — a small greyed marker on the
row, and the full sentence only when you open that event. Same protection, no wreckage."*

Nothing was deleted. That mattered more than the tidying, because several of those sentences are the
only answer to *"why is this button dead"*, and a button that refuses without saying why is a worse
problem than a long sentence.

The measured result, on the two templates you had open:

- The note under a disabled button: **114 characters down to 24.**
- The preview said "nothing is sent" three times within a few hundred pixels; it now says it **once**.
- The merge-field table carried a small "engineering spelling" badge under **every single row**, so it
  told you nothing. We counted: of the 41 letter types that have a field list, **31 have it on every
  field**, one has it on none, and only nine are a genuine mix — and both templates you had open were
  in the first group, 13 fields out of 13 and 5 out of 5. It is gone from the screen. The tallest row
  in that table went from **143 pixels to 80**.
- The version history came off the edit tab, as you asked: *"this may not be required on edit tab - you
  give a link on top and allow user to open it as seperate page"*. There is now a link at the top
  reading "Version history (1)". On its own page the table gets **1328 pixels** of width instead of
  being squeezed into 312, and that 645-pixel cell is **50 pixels**.
- The whole page is shorter: **3862 pixels down to 2524** on the corrected-bill email, and **3055 down
  to 1796** on the bill-ready text message.

Separately, opening the account-closed email showed two blocks explaining how our rendering works
instead of telling you what to do about it. A missing support phone number now reads *"Support phone
will print blank — add it under Settings → Company"*, which names the field and where you fix it. And
the list of fields the preview does not invent used to repeat one identical sentence once per field,
three and four times in a row; it now says it once for the group.

### Worth knowing

We found a third place with the same fault, on the account close-out screen in a different part of the
product. It is written down and not fixed here, because that screen belongs to another piece of work
and this change could not prove it looked right afterwards.

There is now an automatic check that measures the real height of these blocks in a real browser and
fails the build if any of them grows back. It was shown failing on the old screens first, so we know it
works rather than assuming it.

## [2.86.0] — 2026-08-30 · Nineteen more kinds of letter can be sent — and every one of them is kept

### What was happening

When this product tried to send a customer their statement, a refund or credit confirmation, a deposit
or account-closed letter, an autopay confirmation, a write-off notice, a "your bill is ready" email or
text message, or one of four field-service messages, **it stopped and refused to send it at all.**

That sounds like a bug and it was the right call. On 30 August you ruled that a legal document is frozen
as the document when it is sent — a copy kept exactly as the customer read it, never rebuilt afterwards
from the data. But the product only had filing categories for the 21 kinds of letter your own scope list
had named. For the other nineteen it had nowhere lawful to file the copy, and it would not invent a
filing category for a document that has to survive seven years. So it held them.

Nothing was lost while it did. No email, text or print provider is connected yet, so nothing was going
out on those channels anyway.

### What changed

You were shown the count — the product has 41 kinds of letter and message, your scope list named 21, and
the other 20 had never been ruled on — together with the recommendation to keep all of them, because
storage is a few kilobytes a message and the risk only runs one way: keeping a document you did not need
costs almost nothing, and failing to keep one you did need loses it permanently. You answered:

> "My recommendation is to keep all of them. - OKY KEEP THEM"

So **nineteen of those twenty are now kept at send, and they can be sent.** The twentieth is the in-app
summary a clerk sees inside the product after a bulk action, which you ruled out separately on 26 August
because those are for information rather than letters to a customer.

### What did not change

**The refusal that made this safe is still there.** A message still cannot be marked as sent unless the
letter was kept first — there are no exceptions to that, and there is no era before the rule, because
nothing has ever been sent from this product. A kind of letter nobody has ruled on is still held rather
than guessed at.

**And the four field-service messages got a filing category and nothing else.** The appointment,
work-completed, outage and door-hanger messages have approved wording but nothing in the product sends
them yet — that is the field-work part of the product, which is not built. Your ruling says only that
when they are sent they are kept, and that is all that was done.

## [2.85.0] — 2026-08-30 · The Templates and Notifications screens stop explaining themselves at you

### What you were seeing

You walked both screens and said the same thing about ten different places on them. Every template row
carried a sentence where a status should be — *"Not in use yet — closing an account does not send this."*
The autopay row carried several sentences of our own internal reasoning about banking rules. One template
printed its own name twice, one under the other. "Past-due reminder" took three rows because it goes out
three ways. Twelve rows of the notification list each carried three lines of red text saying nothing
fires that event yet. And the Notifications screen held three whole sections nobody needed: four switches
of which three admitted in their own text that nothing read them, a table about the collections ladder
that is set on a different screen and already shown on a third, and a copy of the Templates screen.

### What was actually happening

**One mistake, made ten times: a sentence was being printed inside a table cell.** A sentence in a cell
sets the height of the whole row and wraps at whatever width the column happens to be, so an honest,
correct explanation on twelve rows turns a list you can scan into a wall you have to read. Measured on
the running screen at your window size: the longest "Used by" value was 123 characters and wrapped to six
lines; four template rows carried a paragraph box up to 160 pixels tall in a table whose ordinary rows are
40; the tallest row on the list was 235 pixels.

Nothing in our build could see any of it. Every check we have reads the source code, and a paragraph
compiles exactly like a number.

### What changes

* **"Used by" is now a short status** — In use, Not in use yet, Wording not written, Placeholder wording,
  or Mixed where one document's channels disagree. The full sentence is on the chip when you hover, and on
  the template's own page. Longest value on the screen: 19 characters, down from 123.
* **The autopay explanation is off the row.** That row now says "Placeholder wording", and the reason —
  the wording has to come from your bank, not from us — is on the hover and on the page the row opens.
  Nothing was deleted; a list row is not where a paragraph belongs.
* **A template's name is printed once.** It was printed twice whenever a template had only one version.
* **"Kind" is icons.** An envelope for email, a bubble for a text message, a printer, a page, a signature,
  a bell. Each one still reads out the word it replaced, so nothing is lost to a screen reader, and the
  three compound values that used to wrap to three lines now fit on one.
* **One row per template, with a button for each way it goes out.** "Past-due reminder" was three rows —
  print, email, text — and is now one row with three buttons in the Kind column, each one click to that
  version. Same for "Payment receipt", "Disconnect notice", "Payment plan" and "Bill ready". The list is
  27 rows where it was 38.
* **The caption under the Templates title is one line.** "What messages say. Not when they go out."
* **"Messages needing attention" has its own tab** under Notifications, with its counts beside it.
  Everything else on that screen configures something; that block is today's work.
* **Three sections are gone from Notifications** — the four send-time switches, the tone/letter reference
  table, and the letter library. **The one switch that is actually live moved rather than went**: whether
  recording a payment sends the customer a receipt is now on the "Payment received" rule page, where the
  rule it belongs to lives. Its stored setting is untouched, and so are the three dormant ones, which stay
  in the database ready for the features they were built ahead of.
* **The red "nothing fires this event yet" paragraph is a small grey marker.** It still appears on every
  event nothing fires, and the switch for such an event is still disabled — that protection is the whole
  reason this work was raised. The full sentence appears when you hover the marker and on the event's own
  page. Measured: three lines and 78 pixels became one line and 18.

### How we will know if it comes back

The browser check that measures these screens now fails the build on each of them: it counts the line
boxes in a cell, the characters in a status, the height of the tallest row, and whether an icon still
carries its word. Every one of those checks was shown failing on the screens as they were before it was
trusted passing on the screens as they are now.

## [2.84.0] — 2026-08-30 · A letter you have sent is kept as the letter, and nothing can change it afterwards

### What changes

Until now this product kept everything a letter was made FROM — the account, the balance, the wording it
was built from — and kept no copy of the letter itself. So every time you asked to see a notice again, it
was rebuilt from that data, using today's settings. Rebuilt letters usually look right, which is what made
this worth fixing rather than living with.

**The sharpest example, and it is the one this was proved on.** A disconnection notice carries five
paragraphs about a customer's legal rights — how to dispute the bill, the medical hold, the weather rule,
the number to call the commission. Those five are yours to edit in Settings. Before today, correcting one
of them changed what a notice you served last year *appeared* to have said, and nothing anywhere showed
that it had. On a 48-hour certified notice, that paragraph is the part with legal weight.

**From this build:** when a message is sent, the exact letter is kept at that moment. Editing a clause
afterwards changes the next letter and never a letter already served.

### What you will notice

* **A message cannot be marked as sent unless the letter was kept first.** No exceptions. Nothing has ever
  been sent to a customer from this product — no print, email or SMS provider is connected yet — so there
  is no older batch of messages that misses out.
* **If a copy is ever missing, you are told.** Anything shown in its place says *re-rendered from data, not
  the original* rather than being presented as the letter. That should never happen, and it is there so
  that if it ever does, nobody is misled.
* **Two things deliberately do not get a sealed copy**, and both say so plainly: the in-app alerts your own
  staff see, which already keep their own copy, and a *Send test to me* rehearsal, which is not a document
  sent to anybody.
* **Some letters cannot be sent yet, and that is deliberate.** Of the 41 letter and message templates in
  the product, 21 are on the list of documents that must be kept when sent. The other 20 — the *your bill
  is ready* email, the statement, refund and credit confirmations, deposit and account-closed letters, the
  field-service messages — are not on that list, and rather than guessing whether they are legal documents,
  the product holds them and asks. None of them could be sent today anyway.

## [2.83.0] — 2026-08-30 · Uploading a thousand accounts no longer fails after a clean rehearsal

### What you were seeing

You uploaded 1,048 accounts for Ottumwa Water Works. The rehearsal was clean — *will create 1048, nothing
updated, nothing rejected* — and then Commit load sat there for a long time with no sign of progress and
finished with *"Something went wrong. Nothing was saved — try again."*

### What was actually happening

**The upload was still running when the server gave up on it.** A web request in this product is given
sixty seconds; creating one account takes about an eighth of a second, because each one also picks up its
unit's services, its plan, its meters, its opening balance and its entry in the books. A thousand of them
is over two minutes, so the request was cut off at sixty seconds with the work half done. Nothing was
saved — that part of the message was true — and nothing was left behind either.

The size at which an upload moves off the request and into a background job was one number for every kind
of file: five thousand rows. That number was measured on address files, where a row is one small write. It
was never measured on accounts, where a row is about sixty times the work.

### What changes

* **An accounts file of more than 100 rows now runs as a background job**, which is the size you asked
  for. Measured on a real database: 100 accounts take 12.7 seconds — comfortably inside the sixty the
  request has — while 500 take 60.5 and 1,048 take just over two minutes. The screen shows the progress of
  the background job instead of waiting in silence. Other kinds of file are unchanged.
* **The list of rows that will not load can now be downloaded before you commit**, not only from the
  final screen. That was the one moment you could not get it, because an upload that fails never reaches
  the final screen.
* **If nothing is running to process a background job, the upload is refused rather than accepted.** It
  now says *"Nothing is running to process a file this size. Start the background worker and try again, or
  upload a smaller file."* An upload that says it worked and quietly does nothing would be worse than the
  error you saw.
* **A background job that nothing has picked up now says so on screen** after half a minute, along with
  the thing you most need to know: nothing has been written.

### Still true, and worth saying

Creating an account is still about an eighth of a second's work. That is now slowness in a background job
rather than a failure in front of you, and the reason for it is written down and being worked on
separately.

## [2.82.1] — 2026-08-30 · The Notifications, Templates and Numbering screens were being squashed by the page they sit on

### What you were seeing, and what was actually causing it

You have reported these three screens as wrong for about three weeks, and each round of fixes made them a
little better without ever making them right. We now know why, and it is one thing, not seven.

All three screens sit inside an older page wrapper that lays a Settings tab out as **a row of equal
cards**. That wrapper is the correct thing for a tab that really is a handful of same-sized cards —
Company, Users and roles, Security and Regional all still use it, and all three are untouched by this
release. It is the wrong thing for a screen that has a layout of its own, because it hands that layout one
narrow slot and the screen then arranges itself correctly **inside a third of the page**.

Measured in a real browser on a 1728-pixel-wide screen, before this release:

* the **template designer** was drawn in a 448-pixel slot of a 1424-pixel page. Its own left-hand controls
  and right-hand document were split correctly — three to one — but of 448 pixels, which left the controls
  **108 pixels wide**. That is why "Save as new version" came out on four lines and the message box was a
  few characters across;
* the **Notifications screen** was ten cards all exactly 330 pixels wide. The agreed design is a list with
  a rail down the side; ten identical columns is what "there is no rail" looks like when you measure it;
* five tables on that screen were between 14 and **692 pixels wider than the card holding them**, which is
  the table you saw running underneath the card next to it.

**Every fix until now was made inside the screens, and the thing squashing them was one level up, in a file
none of those changes touched.** Nothing in our own checks could see it either: they all read the code, and
the code was right. The screens are only wrong once a browser draws them.

### What the three screens look like now

* the **template designer** takes the whole page: the controls are 344 pixels and readable, and the letter
  itself has 1032 pixels;
* **Notifications** is what was agreed — the three channel switches in a strip across the top, the list of
  thirty events across the full width, and the two read-only panels (what has gone out, and pacing) in a
  rail down the right;
* the **rule page** stacks its four cards down the page instead of tiling them three across, so the
  channels-and-templates table has room and no longer runs behind the card beside it;
* **no table on any of these screens now runs past the card that holds it**, and no page scrolls sideways.

### The four smaller things in the same report

* **"Next Counter" no longer wraps onto two lines.** That column label needs 146 pixels and the column was
  130, so it broke in half and took the whole header row with it. The column is 152 pixels now, and every
  column label on that table is told never to wrap, so the next long one cannot do the same thing.
* **"How they appear together" no longer disappears when you scroll.** On a large monitor it was already
  staying put; on a normal laptop the panel is taller than the window, and because it is pinned at the top,
  the bottom of it could never be reached. It now scrolls inside itself when it outgrows the window, and it
  is fully readable at 1280 by 720.
* **The red "not finished yet" boxes can no longer set the height of the card or the row they sit in.** The
  worst was 318 pixels tall inside a 330-pixel card; four more on the Templates list made four rows of a
  38-row table the height of a paragraph each. **Not one word has been removed** — the whole sentence is
  still there and still readable, because a refusal that does not say why is worse than no refusal. What is
  capped is how much of the card it may take.
* **The two lists that had no page footer now have one.** The letter library was putting all 38 kinds of
  document on the page and the queue all 50 messages, with no "showing 1 to N", no page arrows and no
  rows-per-page control.

### One thing we have not changed, and we would like your decision

You asked for these lists to show **10 rows a page**. The rows-per-page choices across the whole product are
**50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000, starting at 50** — and that is a decision you made yourself on 9 August, so we
have not quietly overridden it on two screens. Changing it would change every list in the product, which is
the right way to do it if you want it changed. Tell us and we will.

### One thing we looked for and could not find

You reported a field label sitting beside its box instead of above it. We measured every label on both
screens — 29 on Numbering, 31 on Notifications, at five different window widths, 300 measurements in all —
and every single one was already stacked, with the box below its label. Our best guess is that it was read
from a screenshot of the crushed 108-pixel and 330-pixel columns, where a short label and a narrow box can
look side by side. Those columns are now 344 and 1056 pixels. If you see it again, the two things that would
settle it are which tab, and how wide the window was.

### So that this cannot happen again

The reason this took three weeks is that **nothing we own looks at a drawn screen.** Every check reads the
source code, and the source code was correct the whole time. There is now a check that opens these four
screens in a real browser, measures fifty things about them, and fails when any of them moves out of range —
including one that confirms Company, Security and Regional are still laid out the way they were, so the
shared wrapper cannot be widened underneath them by a later fix. It was proved to fail first: with these
fixes backed out it reports ten problems and reproduces the original numbers exactly.

## [2.82.0] — 2026-08-30 · There is now somewhere to keep a document — and once one is kept, nobody can change it.

### The gap this closes, said plainly

Until today this product could produce a bill, a disconnection notice or a receipt and **keep no copy of
it.** It kept the figures the document was built from, and every time somebody asked to see the document
again it built a fresh one from those figures. That is the thing you told us was not correct — *"everytime
we reproduce it using data in table, we might change something about it"* — and it is also something our
own written rules had required for three weeks with nothing built behind them.

**This release builds the place to put them.** Nothing is being kept in it yet: filling it is the next
piece of work, and it is deliberately separate so that this half can be checked on its own.

### Once a document is in there, it cannot be changed or deleted

Not by us, not by a mistake, not by anybody. The database itself refuses. We tested that by taking the
guard out and trying it: without the guard, one command quietly rewrote a stored notice's fingerprint and
another deleted the record outright. With it, both are refused and say why. A corrected document is always
a **new** document, exactly the way a corrected bill is a new bill.

### One utility can never see another's documents, and the reason is worth knowing

The documents are filed in folders named after each utility — but **that is only a naming convention, and
it is not what keeps them apart.** What keeps them apart is that the only way to learn where a document is
kept is to look it up in a table that already knows which utility is asking. A utility asking for another
utility's bill gets exactly the same answer as one asking for a bill that never existed: **nothing** — it
cannot even learn that the document exists.

### A link to a document lasts four hours

You asked for hours rather than minutes and that is what it is. Worth saying plainly: the link does not
check who is clicking it, so if it is forwarded, the person who receives it can open **that one document**
for the rest of the four hours. It cannot be used to find any other document. The four hours can be
shortened at any time without a new release.

### What it will cost, and the one setting that has to be right from the start

Documents go to storage in the cloud rather than into our database. For a hundred utilities keeping seven
years of bills, receipts and notices — around a terabyte — that is **about $27 a month**, or **about $8**
once a rule is set to move anything older than a year to cheaper storage.

**Two things have to be set up in the cloud account that no amount of code can set**, and one of them
cannot be fixed afterwards: the storage container has to be created with its lock switched on, because
Amazon does not allow that to be switched on later. The other is the cheaper-storage rule, which is only
money.

### And if it is not set up at all, the product refuses rather than pretending

A deployment that has not been given a place to put documents will **refuse to store one**, loudly, the
first time it tries. It will not quietly write them onto the machine it happens to be running on, where
the next restart would destroy them. That refusal is the correct behaviour and not a fault.

## [2.81.1] — 2026-08-30 · You can send yourself a test of a template, and the screen stopped saying you could not.

### "Send test to me" works on the Templates screen

Open a template that goes out by email, text message or in-app, and **"Send test to me" is now a button
you can press.** One real message goes onto the outgoing queue, addressed to you and to nobody else,
rendered from exactly the wording a real message would use. It is a rehearsal of the real thing rather
than a mock-up of it — that is the point of it.

**It does not send, and the screen says so plainly rather than leaving you to wonder.** Nothing is
connected to a mail, text-message or print provider yet, so what you get is a sentence telling you the
message is on the queue, who it is addressed to, and that it will sit there. Pressing the button twice
gives you two test messages, not one — a second press means you wanted a second rehearsal.

### The screen had been telling you something untrue for nearly two weeks

The button was greyed out beside the words *"No test send in this release, on any channel."* That was
true when it was written on 17 August. It stopped being true a few hours later, when the same feature
shipped on the Settings → Notifications screen — and nothing brought anybody back to correct the
sentence, because a greyed-out button with an explanation beside it is not something any of our checks
re-examine. **We have made the screen work this out for itself instead of remembering it**, so the
explanation can no longer outlive the fact it describes.

### What is still greyed out, and why it is not the same thing

**"Download sample PDF" is still unavailable**, with its own separate explanation. The two controls sit
side by side and have always needed two different fixes: only one of them has been done. The part of the
platform that writes PDF pages writes bills, so a notice shows you its text rather than a printable page.
Turning that control on beside its neighbour would be exactly the thing we try never to do — offering a
button that would refuse you after you pressed it.

**Where a test genuinely cannot be queued, the button stays visible and greyed out with the true reason.**
On a printed template it says there is no way to post a test letter to yourself, which is honest: we hold
an email address and a mobile number for you, and no postal address.

## [2.81.0] — 2026-08-30 · Your notification settings now decide what actually gets sent — and your logo finally appears.

### The settings screen stopped being decoration

Switching *Bill ready — email* off on Settings → Notifications used to change nothing at all. The
switches were stored, editable and audited, and **nothing on the sending path ever read them.** A utility
could turn a message off, watch the screen agree, and keep sending it.

They decide now. When a document is queued, the utility's own switches are read and applied, and a
channel that was switched off is not used. When a message is suppressed, the run report **says so in a
sentence** — *"this utility has switched email off for this notification on Settings → Notifications"* —
rather than leaving a clerk to work out why a customer with an email address got no email.

### Paper always goes, whatever the switches say

**A utility can now silence every channel it was offered and the paper copy still goes out.** This is the
answer to a question that was live and wrong: the print floor covered bills only, which left a utility
able to switch off the `notice` kind — **the one that carries the disconnection letter**, a document the
law makes a precondition of cutting somebody's water off. A setting about reminders could suppress a
legal instrument and no screen would have said so.

Print is now the floor on all four things a customer receives — the bill, the receipt, the notice and the
payment-plan letter — and no setting on any screen can remove it.

*The visible cost, stated rather than discovered: every receipt, notice and plan letter now queues a print
row it did not queue before. No provider is connected and nothing leaves the building, so what you will
see is a larger print queue — which is the honest picture of what you would actually be posting.*

### Three messages that could never be sent, can be

Move-in welcome, move-out final bill, and the missed payment-plan instalment all had their wording
written and seeded on every utility, and no way to send them. Each now has a switch on the settings
screen and something that fires it.

The missed-instalment letter had two faults underneath it, both invisible and both fixed. It pointed at a
wording that does not exist, so it would have rendered from nothing. And **every payment-plan letter
shared one identity**, so the second one a customer should have received silently became a duplicate of
the first — a customer chased once and never again, with no error anywhere.

### Your logo, at last

A utility could upload a logo and nothing in the product ever drew it — not the settings preview, not the
header, nothing. **No route could even read the bytes back.** The preview that claimed to show a
letterhead was a 26×26 coloured square, identical whether a logo was on file or not.

The logo now appears in Settings → Company and in the sidebar. Where there is no logo yet, the product
draws **two letters from the utility's own name** on the utility's own colour — *Silver Creek Water* → SC.

**We never change your colour.** The letters are drawn in black or white, whichever stays readable on it,
and the rule cannot produce an unreadable mark for any colour you could pick.

### The notification screens, rebuilt

One flat sortable table instead of cards. Channel status as a strip across the top, so the go-live
switches stop reading as a second copy of the per-event toggle. A right-hand panel giving the rule in
plain English, thirty days of real delivery counts, and who last changed it. The template pickers are
wide enough to read — they showed `Bill re ⌄` — and the sentence that escaped its card fits inside it.

The escalation ladder — the reminder day, the two notice tiers, the final-notice hours, the balance floor
and the partial-payment pause — is now **shown here and changed in Settings → Collections**, so the
collections run and the notice can never disagree about the same numbers.

### The template designer works output-first

Three quarters of the screen is the page you are actually writing, with the controls in a rail beside it.
Each kind gets its own editor: a page, a subject and preheader, a phone bubble with a live segment
counter, a bell panel. The merge fields offered are the ones that class actually allows, and the locked
mandatory blocks are **visible as locked** rather than enforced only when you hit save.

### Still ahead in this change

Thirteen more customer messages have wording seeded and no switch yet — statement, credit, refund,
write-off, deposit, autopay, plan change and the rest. And the two template systems have not yet been
merged into one; that needs a decision about which tables survive and what happens to versions already
pinned by documents that were sent.

## [2.80.0] — 2026-08-29 · One bad row costs one row, not your whole migration — and your notification settings finally decide something.

### An upload no longer loses everything to one bad row

Uploading accounts used to be all-or-nothing. If a single row was refused as it was being written,
**every account that had already loaded was undone** — 1,213 rows in, row 63 refused, nothing on file,
one error message and no receipt.

Now each record stands on its own. A row that cannot be written is skipped, named on screen with the
reason and a fix, and the rest of the file loads. This applies to **all six uploads** — premises, units,
meters, sub-meters, devices and accounts.

⚠ This was not a new feature. `BR-CUS-051` has said *"skip-errors ON · N created · N failed"* since the
import was first specified. We signed that rule and did not build it. It is filed as a defect
(`DEF-2519`), not as a change, because filing our own gap as a "change" would quietly turn our mistake
into the customer's new requirement.

### Two files at the end of every run

**successes.csv** — every record that landed. **failures.csv** — *your original row, unchanged, in your
own column order*, plus two columns: what went wrong and how to fix it. Correct the two cells in the
spreadsheet you already know, upload that file on its own, and the second run is small.

### An imported account now inherits its unit, always

An account created by an upload takes its unit's services, plan, route, cycle and meters **whatever its
status** — everything held by reference, so changing the unit's plan tomorrow changes the account's
billing the same day. Previously this only happened for accounts with a billing status, so the simplest
file a utility could produce loaded accounts wired to nothing and counted them as successes.

### Your notification settings now decide what happens

Switching *"Bill ready — email"* off used to change nothing at all — the rules were stored, editable, and
never read when a message was queued. They are read now. Bills and payments obey them, staff alerts land
in the bell on a schedule, and the settings screen reports how many notifications are built against how
many the requirement named.

**Print can never be switched off on a customer document** — bills, receipts, notices and payment-plan
letters. The disconnection letter is a legal instrument, and a setting about reminders must not be able
to suppress it.

### Fixed

- A **9,000-account upload failed with an authentication error.** Above 5,000 rows the work moves to a
  background worker that carries no permission role by design — and one function on the write path still
  demanded one. It bit hardest on the *second* attempt at a migration, after you had already fixed your
  file. (`DEF-2515`)
- **A failed payment sent no notice.** Every bounce since 11 August recorded "nothing is queued and
  nothing is sent". A letter is now queued.
- Three refusal messages showed a placeholder's name instead of the value — *"your changeover date
  ({given}) is in the future"*. (`DEF-2517`)
- The **failures file came back with your columns re-ordered**, which made it unusable for the one thing
  it is for. (`DEF-2513`)

### Known and honest

No email, text or print provider is connected — by instruction. Messages are composed and queued and you
can read every one of them; **in-app is the only channel that delivers today.** The queue count on the
notifications screen is the true picture of what a utility would be posting.

## [2.79.25] — 2026-08-28 · A price plan must say when it starts, and the two pricing engines stopped disagreeing about every single customer.

### The gap

A rate plan has a status — draft, published, archived — and, separately, an
optional date saying when it starts charging. Nobody had ever decided what it
means to publish a plan and leave that date empty.

**The two halves of this product had quietly decided opposite things.** The code
that produces bills today looks only at the status: a published plan charges
customers, date or no date, forever. The newer pricing rules — the ones being
brought in to replace it — require the date, so the very same plan is treated as
never having started, and every customer on it is refused outright.

Both readings are defensible. Neither had been chosen.

**Measured on the sample utility, through the real bill run, three times over:
47 of 47 customers were refused by the new rules** while the old path billed
every one of them. Because that is the *first* of seven pricing rules, and each
one gates the next, **nothing further down could be compared at all** — the
report that exists to show where the two engines differ could not get past its
first question on a single customer.

### What changed

**You can no longer publish a plan without saying when it starts**, and you can
no longer clear that date on a plan already published. Both halves are needed:
without the second, the situation the ruling removes comes straight back one
save later, on a plan already charging customers. Leaving a **draft** undated is
