still fine — a draft charges nobody, and coming back to finish it later is what a
draft is for.

**Plans already published without a date were given one.** Not today's date, and
not an arbitrary old one: **the day the prices they actually use came into
force** — a date somebody at the utility typed, about that plan's own rates.
On the sample utility the two plans that have really billed customers were dated
**1 June 2026**, which is exactly the first day of the earliest period they ever
billed. The three plans that have never billed anyone took the date their rates
begin.

Dating them today would have been the tempting shortcut and would have put **90
already-issued invoices outside their own plan's window** — the new rules would
then refuse to explain bills the utility has already sent and been paid for.

### What has NOT changed

**No bill moved, and no bill can move.** This decides which plan is considered
in force; it does not change a price, and issued invoices are immutable. The
finance-signed figures are untouched: 33 of 33, before and after.

**The new pricing engine still prices nothing.** It has no caller in the bill
run. What changed is that the comparison between the two can now see past its
first question — it reaches the third rule instead of stopping dead at the first,
which is what makes the remaining differences findable at all.

## [2.79.24] — 2026-08-28 · The message you get for a bad conversion factor was pointing at nothing, and would have shown you its own key.

### The gap

Yesterday's release let a utility state the unit a service is billed in, and the
number that converts the meter's unit into it. Typing something that is not a
number was refused correctly — and the sentence explaining why did not exist.
The screen would have printed the internal name of the missing sentence where
the explanation belongs, which is the same fault the Product Owner photographed
on the Notifications screen last week.

### What changed

One sentence, in all eleven languages: *"Enter the conversion factor as a
number, like 0.748052."* It now covers both ways of getting it wrong — a word
where a number belongs, and a number sent in a form the money path will not
accept — because to the person typing it those are the same event, and a second
sentence about number formats is not something anyone can act on.

## [2.79.23] — 2026-08-28 · A utility can now enter its own bank accounts, so the bank half of reconciliation is reachable at last.

### The gap

To reconcile a bank statement you first have to say which bank account it came
from. The product knew that — the import screen's first step asks for it, and
the picker was built to render *"Chase Operating ••4021"*.

**No utility could ever put an account in that picker.** There was a place to
store bank accounts, a rule that two cannot share a name, and two screens
reading them — and nothing anywhere in the product that could create one. The
only thing that had ever created a bank account was a test. So the picker was
empty on every real utility, on the first day and on the hundredth, and bank
reconciliation could not be started at all.

It stayed invisible for eleven days because every automated test made its own
bank account first, which is exactly the step a real person cannot do.

### What changed

**Settings → Configure → Reference data now has a Bank accounts card.** Add
*"Chase Operating"*, type the last digits *4021*, and it appears in the bank
statement import as **Chase Operating ••4021**. It sits with the other
tenant-maintained lists and behaves like them: search it, edit it, switch one
off when you close it.

**The last digits are the last digits — not the account number.** Four digits at
most; a fifth is refused. We deliberately do not store a full account number
anywhere, because a number we do not hold is a number that cannot leak. Two
accounts at the same bank are told apart by their **name**.

**Switch an account off rather than deleting it.** It disappears from the import
picker straight away, but every statement you have already imported still shows
the account it came from. An account with statements against it cannot be
deleted at all.

**Only this card creates a bank account.** The import screen chooses from the
list and can never add to it — two places to create one is how two screens end
up disagreeing about which accounts a utility has.

### What this does not do

**It does not add a ledger account to a bank account.** Reconciliation already
knows which account cash lands in, and which ledger account a bank account maps
to is a question nobody has answered yet — so nothing was guessed.

**It does not seed anything.** A brand-new utility sees the card at zero, and
that is correct: nobody but you knows what your bank accounts are called, and a
made-up example sitting in a picker that imports real money would be worse than
an empty one.

### Rollback

Revert this commit. The card disappears from Reference data and the import
picker goes back to being empty. Any bank accounts already entered stay in the
database untouched — nothing is deleted — and reappear if the commit is
restored.

## [2.79.22] — 2026-08-28 · Before a bill run commits, you can now see where the new pricing rules would have answered differently — and on how many customers.

### The gap

The product has been working every bill out twice for a day: once the way it
bills today, and once with the new pricing rules, keeping both answers. **That
comparison existed only inside the code.** No screen showed it and no address
served it, so the one thing it was built to produce — a list of the places the
two ways of pricing disagree — could not be read by anybody.

It was held back deliberately, and the reason was a good one: until yesterday
the comparison could not be run on a single real customer, so the panel would
have reported *"nothing disagreed"* on every screen it was ever shown on. **That
reading is exactly the one nobody should trust**, because it is also what a
comparison that never ran looks like. The last missing piece landed yesterday
and the comparison now runs on real customers, so the panel can be honest.

### What changed

**"Check what we found" — the step that shows every input before anything
commits — now carries a section called Compare the new pricing.** It opens with
one sentence:

    We worked out 1 of 1 customers both ways. 1 came out differently.
    0 could not be worked out at all.

**Those numbers are deliberately in one sentence.** *"1 came out differently"* on
its own can be read as good news or bad; *"0 came out differently"* on its own
can mean everything matched **or** that nothing was checked, and those are
opposite things. So the count of customers actually worked out both ways is
always beside the count that differed, and when nothing was worked out the screen
says so in words rather than showing a zero.

**Then a table of what came out differently, and how many customers each thing
touches.** One customer and four hundred customers can be the same finding and a
completely different decision, so the count is on the row and the biggest is
first. Each row shows **both answers side by side** — what billing says today,
what the new rules say — and the product does not choose between them or work
out the difference. Which one is right is a decision for a person.

**On the seeded utility there is exactly one thing to decide today.** Customer
ACC-1042 is billed now on **Residential Standard, version 1 — an 18.50 monthly
base on electric**. The new rules **refuse to price that customer at all**,
saying *"account ACC-1042 has no plan version in force on 2026-07-01"*. The two
are not arguing about an amount; they mean opposite things by the words *a plan
in force*, and the one that produces a bill today is the old one.

**Customers nobody could check get their own table**, with the reason and the
count — *"No connection size on the meter"*, *"This customer has no rate plan"*.
A customer nobody could ask about has not agreed with anything, and this is the
one place that distinction could quietly have been lost.

### What did NOT change

**No bill changes. Not one.** Reading this panel writes nothing — no bill, no
line, no decision, no exclusion — and it sits on no path a bill travels, so if
it broke entirely the run would carry on unaffected. Every finance-signed figure
is untouched.

## [2.79.21] — 2026-08-28 · A utility can finally tell us it does not put a meter on trash — and a property with three carts bills $45.00 without anyone touching the database.

### The gap

Eight days ago the Product Owner ruled that a utility says whether a service is
metered or unmetered. Everything downstream of that ruling was built: a refuse
utility's bill is priced from the carts standing on the property — three carts
at $15.00 is $45.00, take one away and the next bill is $30.00, and nobody types
the number.

**There was nowhere to say it.** No screen, no API and no part of the product
wrote that setting. The only way to make a service unmetered was to edit a row
in the database by hand, so every figure above was unreachable for a real
customer. The same was true of the unit a service is billed in: three parts of
the product read it and nothing anywhere could set it, so every utility's answer
was blank.

### What changed

**Settings → Services now states, for every service, whether it is metered.**
The row shows it whether the service is switched on or off, and the row's edit
form is where it changes — together with the unit the service is billed in and,
where that unit differs from the one the meter reads, the conversion factor
between them.

**Changing it never touches history.** Bills already issued keep exactly what
they charged, and readings already recorded still bill. The change applies to
the next bill that has not been priced yet, in full, and the form says so before
you commit. The save tells you how many accounts take the service, so the size
of what you have just changed is on screen rather than discovered later.

**A service billed in a different unit from the one its meter reads must state
the factor between them**, and it is refused in the field rather than three
weeks later inside a bill run. A service with no meter at all is asked for no
factor — there is no reading to reconcile.

**The demo utility now declares trash unmetered and billed per cart**, through
the same audited settings call the screen makes.

### What did not change

No money rule, no rounding and no signed figure moved — the finance-signed
golden checks stay at 33 of 33. A utility that has declared nothing bills exactly
what it billed yesterday.


## [2.79.20] — 2026-08-28 · Switch a service on after you are already running, reload the sample data, and you can actually sell it.

### The gap

A utility signs up for water and sewer, runs the demo, and then decides to sell
refuse. They switch **trash** on at Settings → Services & UoM and press *Load
sample data* again — which is the only thing the product offers them — and
almost nothing happens. Measured on a booted tenant, before and after that
second press: the plans still priced water and sewer, no address offered trash,
no unit held a trash service point, no bin was recorded anywhere, and no bill
ever mentioned it. The one thing that did arrive was a trash rate sheet that no
plan pointed at.

That is why the Product Owner's own demo customer, Ana Alvarez, was showing
water, sewer **and** trash on her account while her bill charged for two of
them. The bill half of that was fixed last week — the missing service now
appears on the document as a `$0.00` line instead of vanishing in silence. This
is the reason the data was in that shape at all.

### What changed

Reloading the sample data now fills in what is genuinely missing rather than
skipping anything it has seen before:

* the demo **plans gain the new service** and the price sheet that goes with it;
* the demo **addresses offer it** and the **units take it**, which is what
  lets the bins be recorded at all;
* so the household with three bins on the walkthrough property bills
  **3 × $15.00 = $45.00**, where before it was billed nothing for refuse.

Reloading a second time still changes nothing at all, which is the rule this had
to keep. Nothing overwrites a price you typed yourself, and a plan a real
customer is already on is never touched.

**And a price that had been ruled and never reached the product.** On the 27th
the Product Owner ruled that a refuse customer pays **$15.00 a bin** and that the
old **$18.00 a month for having the service is gone**. The demo was still
charging the $18.00, so a three-bin household was billed **$63.00** where it
should have been **$45.00** — across the demo's 48 refuse customers, **$864.00 a
month** that had been withdrawn. It is now the ruled figure.

### What is still missing, and is written down

* **Switching a service on does not itself set it up.** The toggle creates the
  accounting codes and stops there; filling the rest in still means reloading
  the sample data. Whether switching a service on should add it to plans you
  have already published is a decision nobody has made yet — it is recorded and
  waiting (`DEF-2492`).
* **The account's service tags lag the bill by one step.** A customer is now
  charged for the new service before their account page lists it (`DEF-2491`).
* The run now says plainly which of the services you sell no published plan
  prices — a read, on the seeding report. There is no screen for it yet.

### Rules and records

`BR-RAT-830` · `BR-RAT-831` · `BR-RAT-832` · `BR-MET-830` · closes `DEF-1250`
and `DEF-2490` · files `DEF-2491` and `DEF-2492` · implements `OQ-317`
(closed 2026-08-27, option A). Golden harness 33 PASS / 0 FAIL — no frozen
finance figure moves.


## [2.79.19] — 2026-08-28 · A single pricing rule can now be handed over to the newer engine, one at a time, and none has been.

### The gap

The Product Owner asked a direct question: *when a bill generates, will it use
R1 to R7?* The answer was no. The seven-step engine whose rules were signed has
never priced a real bill, and the reason was mechanical rather than a decision:
**there was no way to let it price one part of a bill without letting it price
all of it at once.** The approved plan says to switch one step at a time and
*never swap and hope*, and the product had no seam a single step could cross.

### What changed

**A switch, and it is off.** Three of the engine's eight steps can now be handed
over individually — the two that decide a customer's fixed monthly standing
charge, and the one that decides the extra charged to a customer outside the
city limits. The other five say plainly that they cannot be switched yet rather
than accepting the instruction and doing nothing.

It is a setting on the server, not a screen and not a per-utility option: this
is our changeover, not something a utility chooses, and it is reversible at the
next restart rather than at the next release. Every bill also now records which
rules priced it, so nobody has to guess later.

**If a handed-over rule cannot price a customer, that customer's bill is held
and named on the exceptions list, and every other bill in the run still goes
out.** It never falls back to the old code quietly — a bill nobody can attribute
to either engine is worse than a held bill.

### What did NOT change

**No bill moved, and none can yet.** Nothing is switched on: a full run before
and after this change produces identical figures, and the standing charge on the
sample water plan reads $8.00 both times. The signed billing figures are
untouched — 33 of 33 still reproduce exactly.

Worth stating because it is the reason nothing is switched on: on that same
sample plan the two engines disagree by **$4.50 a month per water connection**
($8.00 against $12.50), because the newer rules read the standing charge from a
charge code and no utility has been migrated onto one yet. That disagreement is
the finding; it gets ruled before anything is switched.

## [2.79.18] — 2026-08-28 · A bill with a discount on it can be issued. Until today none could — not for any customer, on any utility.

### The gap

A utility could set up a discount programme, enrol a customer in it, and watch
the reduction appear on the draft bill and in the preview. **Then the bill would
not issue.** Every bill, for every discounted customer, refused with a message
about an unknown kind of line — and the reason was not a bug in the code but a
decision nobody had made: where in the books a discount lands.

Two ways to book it were on the table, and they are genuinely different. The
reduction could come off the electricity revenue the utility recorded, or it
could sit in an account of its own. The Product Owner ruled: *"you will need
differnt GL code for these - dont keep them in same, create differnt category as
required and keep them in it."*

### What changed

**A discount now has its own account in the chart, and the revenue it does not
touch stays whole.** On the reference bill — 82.08 of electricity used, an 18.50
monthly base, and a 10.00 discount — the books now record:

    accounts receivable                    owes  90.58
    customer discounts (contra-revenue)          10.00
    electric usage                               82.08
    electric base                                18.50

The customer is asked for **90.58**; the entry adds up to **100.58** on both
sides. That difference is the discount, stated as its own readable figure.
Booked the other way, electric usage would have read **72.08** — the utility
reporting revenue it never earned at that price, with the 10.00 it gave away
gone from every report.

**Every new utility gets the account automatically** — the seeded chart goes
from 33 accounts to 34, numbered 4300 and named *Customer discounts
(contra-revenue)*. Like every other account, it can be renamed or renumbered
under Settings → Configure; nothing in the product looks it up by its number.

**Correcting a discounted customer no longer charges them full price.** A
correction and a back-bill both re-priced the period without the discount, so a
corrected bill handed back less than the customer was owed. Both now carry it,
resolved as of the period being corrected rather than today — so a September
correction of a July bill reproduces July's programme. A back-bill applies it
once for the whole catch-up rather than once per stretch of it.

**The safety rule that was already in place is untouched.** A bill whose books
do not add up still refuses to issue; the only case that now passes is the
discount itself, and it passes because it is recorded on the other side rather
than as a negative.

### What this does NOT do

Nothing already issued changes — no bill carrying a discount could ever issue,
so there is no old entry of this shape in anyone's books.

Two things are still missing and are written down rather than quietly left: the
running total of subsidy actually given is not recorded, so a programme's budget
and its per-customer caps do not go down as bills are issued; and a programme
whose funding runs out is not marked as suspended. Both need the discount line
on a bill to say which programme it came from, and today it carries only the
customer-facing name.

### Under the hood

`DEF-536` and `DEF-537` closed. `discount_contra_revenue` is the thirteenth GL
designation (ledger migration `0009`), seeded as 4300 with `signed=False`
pending a finance re-sign of the code and the name. `PostingBucket` carries a
`side`, so the sign travels as a side and never as a negative amount. New rules
BR-BIL-790/791/792 and BR-LED-790. New defect rows `DEF-2430` and `DEF-2431`.

## [2.79.17] — 2026-08-28 · The last screen of sign-up no longer invites you to leave before your utility is built, and its footer stopped saying two things that were not true.

### The gap

Two faults on the same screen — the hand-over at the end of sign-up, the first
screen a brand-new utility ever sees. The Product Owner found both on a fresh
database.

**You could leave while the work was still running.** *Go to your utility* was
live and inviting from the first frame, while the list underneath it read
*"Sample data so you can see it working — WORKING — Block 2 of 14"*. The screen
already knew better: the automatic redirect three lines above the button waited
properly for the work to finish. The button simply never asked.

**The footer was false in both halves, in all eleven languages.** It read
*"Account and meter data migration happens separately in Settings — this only
captures configuration."* There is no import screen in Settings — they are on
Accounts, Assets and Premises — so it sent every new utility to the wrong place.
And sign-up does far more than capture configuration: the block running
underneath that very sentence creates **48 accounts**, each with its contact,
its billing address and its service agreements, plus their units and meters.

### What changed

**The hand-over button now waits for the work.** It stays on screen the whole
time — visibly not ready rather than vanishing and reappearing — and becomes
usable the moment the sample data is finished. A screen reader reads out why it
is not ready yet.

**One exception, deliberately.** If part of the sample data fails to load, the
button stays usable. That screen never moves you on by itself, on purpose: you
need to see which block did not land before you go, and the button is the only
way off it.

**The footer now says what is really happening**, in all eleven languages, each
naming its own sidebar sections:

> Any accounts and meters we load now are sample data, so you can see how
> everything works. Import your own from Accounts, Assets and Premises when you
> are ready.

### Rollback

Revert this commit. The button returns to being clickable from the first frame
and the footer returns to the old sentence; nothing is stored either way, so
there is no data to undo.

## [2.79.16] — 2026-08-28 · A utility that collects three carts now bills three carts.

### The gap

Some services a utility sells are not measured by a meter at all. Refuse
collection is the obvious one: nobody reads a dial on a wheelie bin. What a
utility charges for is the **number of carts** standing at the property — one
cart, three carts — and the price is per cart.

This product could not express that. A property with three carts did not get a
cheap bill or a wrong bill. **It got no bill at all.** The bill run looked at
the trash connection, saw equipment standing on it, concluded that a meter
reading was missing, and stopped the whole account — the water and sewer
charges with it. The better a utility had recorded its carts, the more
certainly its bills stopped.

### What changed

**Three carts on a property now bill 3 × $15.00 = $45.00.** Take one cart away
and the next bill is **$30.00**. Nobody types a quantity: the product counts
the carts standing on the property on the last day of the billing period, so
adding a cart in the field changes the next bill by itself, and a cart
collected back stops being charged from the next period — while the period it
was there for keeps the charge it earned.

**A property that has been looked at and genuinely has no carts bills $0.00 for
carts, and its bill still goes out.** That is a real answer.

**A property whose carts have never been counted stops, and says so.** This is
the distinction the whole change turns on, and it is deliberately not a
convenience: *"nobody has counted this property"* and *"this property has no
carts"* are different facts, and only the second one is a bill for nothing.
Treating the first as zero would send a three-cart household a document that
adds up perfectly and charges them nothing, and nobody would ever notice. The
bill refuses instead, and the message says the work is to go and count the
carts — not to estimate a meter reading that does not exist.

### What is unchanged

Nothing already issued moves. No price, rounding rule or signed figure changed
— the billing golden tests still pass 33 of 33. A meter that exists and simply
was not read still stops the bill exactly as it did before; that has always
been the point of the distinction and it is asserted both ways. And a utility
that has not declared a service unmetered is not affected at all.

### Still to come

Declaring a service unmetered still cannot be done from any screen — the
setting exists and nothing writes it (`DEF-2310`), so this billing is reachable
today only by setting that flag directly. The sample utility also still carries
an $18.00 monthly trash base that a ruling retired (`DEF-2312`).

## [2.79.15] — 2026-08-28 · A big water connection and a small one can finally be priced differently.

### The gap

A utility charges more to have a 2-inch water main at your building than a
5/8-inch one, because the bigger connection costs more to stand ready to serve.
The product agreed with that in August: the standing charge belongs to the
charge code, and the worked example everyone signed off on was a 5/8-inch water
base at **$8.00** and a 2-inch at **$34.00** on one code.

The table that holds those two figures was built. Nothing could put a number in
it. The save refused the field, so a utility could type ONE amount and every
connection was billed it, however big. On that example a 2-inch connection was
billed $8.00 where the utility meant $34.00 — **$26.00 a month, per 2-inch
connection**, that the product had no way to ask for.

Nobody could see it, either: with the table empty, "look up the price for this
size" and "use the one price" give the same answer for every customer, so no
test could tell them apart.

### What changed

The charge-code screen's second step now has a table with one row per connection
size you have configured, and a box for what each one costs. The sizes are the
same list the meter screen offers, so a price you set here is a size a meter can
actually be given — there is no box to type a size into, which would have stored
a price nothing ever looks up.

Three answers stay different, because two of them look identical and mean
opposite things:

* **blank** — you do not serve this size. A bill for it is refused by name, not
  charged $0.00.
* **0.00** — you serve it free. The bill carries a zero line.
* **no row at all** — nobody has priced it yet.

A charge code states one amount **or** a table of them, never both. If you fill
in the table, the single Amount box goes read-only and says why.

The rate schedule screens already show these figures, attributed — `$8.00 · from
BASE-W` against the 5/8-inch row and `$34.00 · from BASE-W` against the 2-inch —
so nothing needed changing there.

### What did NOT change

**No bill moves.** The pricing path that reads these figures still has no
production caller, and the sample utility's seeded $8.00 water base is
deliberately left as one flat amount. This release makes the price settable.

### Also

* The per-size amount column's own documentation said it stored six decimal
  places, two lines above a field that stores four. It has stored four since
  21 August; the note is corrected. No stored number was ever wrong.
* Eight things the charge-code specification asks for had nowhere to be stored.
  Per-size amounts was one of them; seven remain, and the screen still says so
  against each one rather than quietly leaving it out.

## [2.79.14] — 2026-08-28 · The new pricing engine stops refusing every bill, and stops trying to charge the whole price list.

### The gap

A utility's price list holds every charge it can ever make: a monthly paper-bill
fee, a one-off connection fee, a fee for a bounced payment, a fee for tampering
with a meter. On the sample utility that is **23 charges**. Only a couple of them
belong on an ordinary monthly bill.

The new pricing engine — the one being brought in to replace the old one, and
which does not yet touch a single real bill — could not deal with that list in
two separate ways, and each one on its own was enough to stop it being turned on.

**It could not express a late fee.** The engine could hold one price, or a table
of prices by pipe size, and nothing else. A late fee is *one and a half percent
of what is overdue, with a five dollar minimum*. Four more charges are quoted per
job. So when the engine met any of those **five charges, it refused to produce
the entire bill** — and the reason it printed was *"this charge states no amount
for connection size None"*, which would send somebody out to look at a meter for
a problem that lives on a price list.

**And it could not tell a monthly charge from a one-off one.** It knew a water
charge from an electric one, and a residential price from a commercial one, and
it could not tell a `$45.00` connection fee from a `$2.00` monthly paper-bill
fee. Turned on as it was, it would have put **every charge on the list onto every
monthly bill: 18 charges adding up to `$799.95`**, including a `$250.00` tamper
fee, on top of a bill whose basic service charge is **`$8.00`**. About a hundred
times the bill.

The second problem was hidden by the first: the engine always refused on the late
fee before it ever got as far as the other eighteen.

### What changed

The engine now reads the two boxes a utility already fills in when it creates a
charge — **what kind of charge is this**, and **apply it automatically** — and
only charges with both set ride a monthly bill. That is a rule the Product Owner
gave on 22 August; it had reached one part of the product and not this one.

On the sample utility, **none of the 23 charges has both boxes set**, so **`$0.00`
is added** where `$799.95` would have been. Nothing is guessed on a utility's
behalf: an unticked box is taken as the utility saying no, and no existing charge
is quietly switched on behind them.

And **none of the 23 stops a bill any more**. Not because the late fee got a
price — it did not, and it must not, because the engine is never told what a
customer owes — but because a late fee is not a monthly charge, so the engine
never has to ask what it costs. Where it genuinely cannot price something it now
says which rule is in the way instead of blaming a meter.

The basic service charge is deliberately exempt from the two boxes, because it is
already governed by its own rule. Without that exemption the sample utility's
`$8.00` water, `$15.00` commercial water and `$18.00` trash charges would all
have gone to `$0.00`.

### What has NOT changed

**No bill is different today.** The new engine still has no caller; it is being
proved against the old one first, one step at a time. This is what it *will* do
when its turn comes.

Two things are written down for later: a charge the Product Owner ruled is
*priced per job* and a charge nobody has priced are still stored identically, so
one message has to mention both possibilities; and the report that compares the
two engines keeps its own list of refusal types and cannot see a new one, so one
of its counts runs short.

### Also in this build — a guard-list check, and why it is recorded here

This build also carries a check nobody planned for it, and the honest reason it
appears under someone else's heading is that **the lane that wrote it did not cut
a version, and this is the release its commit landed inside.**

The check itself: fifty files say in their own text that a human must review
changes to them, and none of them was on the list of files anyone watches —
about **42,000 lines**, including the fourteen-line file holding the
money-rounding rule that twenty-seven other files depend on, and the key that
stops a repeated payment being recorded twice. The existing check reads the list
and inspects what it names, so a file that was never added is invisible to it and
its absence reads as compliance. Four money paths had escaped that way, each
found by a person reading code for something else.

The new check asks the other way round, and it **adds nothing to the list** —
that stays a decision for the Product Owner. It pins the number at exactly those
fifty by name and fails the moment a fifty-first appears.

## [2.79.13] — 2026-08-28 · The deposits a utility holds are on its balance sheet, and they match its own records.

### The gap

A deposit is money a customer hands over that the utility has to give back. It
has to show up in two places: on the customer's own record, and on the balance
sheet as something the utility owes. This product kept both and never connected
them.

**When a customer paid a deposit, only the balance sheet heard about it.** When
a utility brought its existing deposits across at go-live, **only the customer
records heard about it.** On the sample utility that meant customer records
showing **$750.00** of customers' money held — five customers, **$150.00**
each — and a balance sheet showing **$0.00**.

Both directions balanced perfectly, which is why nobody met it: the accounting
entry was not *wrong*, it was never made at all, and every check that looks for
an out-of-balance book passes over that.

### What changed

**A deposit that clears now reaches both.** The customer's record goes up by the
amount that actually cleared, at the same moment the balance sheet does. If the
payment later bounces or is reversed, both come back down together.

**A deposit brought across at go-live now reaches both too.** It is recorded on
the balance sheet as an opening entry dated at the changeover — *the last day
your old system was in charge of the money* — which is the date every other
figure brought across already uses. **The original date the customer paid it is
kept**, because that is what any future interest on their deposit is worked out
from; the two dates answer different questions and are both stored.

**In money, on the sample utility.** Deposits held: **$750.00**. Deposits on the
balance sheet: **was $0.00, now $750.00**. Receivables are unmoved at
**$5,171.18** on both sides.

### The check that stops it coming back

The Finance screen's tie-out panel already asks *"does what we hold match what
the books say we owe?"* — it now gets a straight yes, and it goes red the moment
the two differ by a cent. Two more checks were added behind it: one that fails
if a re-run of a migration books a deposit twice, and one that fails if any
money column a customer can type into a migration spreadsheet ever again lands
in a record without reaching the books.

### Nothing already issued changes

No bill, no payment and no accounting entry was edited. Every correction is a
new entry, which is the rule. The signed billing figures are unmoved.

### Fixed along the way

The panel that compares the two figures was comparing them over different
periods — it read the balance sheet up to the end of a chosen month and the
customer records as they stand today. That reported a difference on a correct
book, and it is what showed the fix as still broken. Both sides are now read the
same way.

## [2.79.12] — 2026-08-28 · Tax is charged on the full service value, as ruled.

### The gap

A customer with a senior discount was taxed on the **discounted** amount. The
person who runs the utility had already said it should be the other way: *"Tax
the full amount before discount — the utility remits tax on the full service
value; the discount is the utility's cost, not the tax authority's."*

The product could already do exactly that, per tax authority, and had been able
to for a week. **Every tax rate on every utility said the opposite**, nothing
anywhere ever set it, and no test in the repo combined a discount with a tax —
so both readings looked right and the wrong one shipped.

### What changed

Each tax authority still carries its own answer, and both answers are still
offered on screen. What changed is the answer a tax starts with, and the answer
tax rates already set up now carry: **the full service value**.

**In money, on the bill that was reported.** A **$62.14** bill with a 25% senior
discount of **$15.54** was taxed at 6.85% on **$46.60** and charged **$3.19**.
It is now taxed on the full **$62.14** and charged **$4.26** — **$1.07 more per
discounted bill, every cycle**, and the customer's total moves from **$49.79**
to **$50.86**.

**Bills already sent do not change.** An issued bill is a permanent record here;
this takes effect on the next bill run. Re-pricing past bills would be a
separate correction run, and nobody has asked for one.

**A utility can still say the opposite for one authority.** Some authorities do
levy on the discounted amount. That is one choice on the tax screen, it stays
chosen, and the two can sit side by side on the same bill.

### The check that was missing

The spreadsheet of signed billing figures had no case combining a discount with
a tax — the word *discount* appeared in it zero times — which is the only reason
this survived. It has one now, kept in its own section marked as coming from
the ruling rather than from the finance sign-off, because the sign-off never saw
this number. The 33 finance-signed figures are untouched and all still pass.

## [2.79.11] — 2026-08-28 · A utility could not tell us its own prices. Now it can.

### The gap

Four things a utility charges for were fully built in the engine, fully tested,
and **impossible to type in anywhere in the product.**

**The out-of-town surcharge.** Lots of small utilities charge more to serve a
property outside the city limits. The maths for it has been in this product
since the day the pricing engine was written — every standing charge and every
usage line gets multiplied by it. **There was no box anywhere to put the number
in**, so the multiplier was always one, and every bill this product has ever
produced charged the in-town price. Because multiplying by one changes nothing,
nothing ever failed, no test went red, and no figure looked wrong.

**Deposits.** The plan screen said deposits were coming later. They were not
coming later — the storage, the checks and the endpoint had all been finished
weeks earlier, and only the box was missing. The person who reported it put it
in three words: *"Deposite unable to add."*

**Standing charges on the sample utility.** When a rule moved the standing
charge from the plan onto the charge code, the sample data was not moved with
it, so step 4 of the plan builder read *"No base charge code for this service"*
for water, sewer and trash on the very tenant we ship as an example.

**Tax rates.** A new utility is set up with the names of its tax authorities and
none of their rates. If they chose not to load the sample data, **every bill
they issued carried no tax at all and nothing anywhere said so.**

### What changed

The plan builder gained the missing boxes: the out-of-town multiplier and a tick
per service that is flat everywhere, on the step where services are chosen; and
a deposit amount per kind of customer.

**In money, on one real address on the sample utility.** 161 Silver Creek Road
used 18 thousand gallons of water in June. Inside the city that is a standing
charge of **$8.00** plus **$109.00** of water — **$117.00**. Outside the city on
a plan set to one and a half, it is **$12.00** plus **$163.50** — **$175.50**.
**$58.50 on one bill for water alone**, and until now no one could ask for it.

A plan with the box left empty charges the same everywhere and never even looks
at whether an address is in or out of town, so a utility that does not do this
carries on exactly as before.

The sample utility now carries its four standing charges — water at **$8.00**
for households and **$15.00** for businesses, sewer at **$0.00** and refuse at
**$18.00** — so the plan builder has something to show.

And a utility that has tax authorities with no rates is now told so on its setup
checklist, with both numbers. **It is told, not stopped**: charging no tax is a
perfectly ordinary thing to do, and we cannot tell that apart from having
forgotten to type the rates in — so a person decides.

### What did not change

**Not one figure on any existing bill.** Every price above is a new box a
utility may now fill in; leave them alone and nothing moves. The frozen
finance figures were re-checked and are untouched — 33 of 33.

## [2.79.10] — 2026-08-28 · Three whole workflows had no way in. Now they do.

### The gap

Three jobs a utility does every week were fully built, fully tested, and
impossible to start.

**Moving a customer to a new address.** The screen existed. A clerk could open
it, fill in all five steps and press *Complete transfer* — and the button went
nowhere, because the address it posted to did not exist on the server.

**Disconnecting for non-payment, and reconnecting afterwards.** A clerk could
see the list of accounts on the collections ladder and could not act on a single
row of it. Opening a case, sending a notice, recording the signed receipt for a
certified letter, scheduling the cut, performing it, putting a medical or
weather hold on an account, lifting one, stopping the whole thing by hand,
marking a customer for reconnection and turning their supply back on — eleven
separate acts, every one written and tested, and not one of them reachable
except by someone typing Python at a server.

**Approving or cancelling a refund.** A refund could be asked for and then
neither approved nor voided, and there was no screen anywhere in the product
that could even show you a refund's reference number to act on.

Together that was about 1,800 lines of finished work that nobody could use.

### What changed

Twenty of these actions now have an address the product can call. A clerk can
complete a transfer, walk a collections case from first reminder to cut to
reconnection, and an administrator can approve or cancel a refund from a list
that finally shows them.

**The transfer and the disconnection got deliberately opposite treatments, and
the reason matters.** A transfer is one person at one screen for about ninety
seconds, so the whole thing is now a single all-or-nothing save: if any part of
it fails — most likely because a colleague claimed the same unit a moment
earlier — nothing at all is written and the clerk simply tries again. Before
this, a failure half way through would have left an invisible half-finished
transfer against that account, and because no screen lists transfers in
progress, **that account could never have been transferred again** without
somebody editing the database by hand.

A disconnection is the opposite. It runs over about three weeks and one of its
steps waits on a signed postal receipt coming back through the mail. Collapsing
that into a single save would have meant the product inventing a receipt for a
certified letter nobody sent, which is precisely the safeguard that stands
between a household and losing their water. So each step stays its own act, on
its own day, recorded by the person who did it.

**Nothing about how any of this is decided has changed.** No price, no fee, no
rounding and no rule moved. Where the product could not answer something before
— what a reconnection costs when that fee has not been set up, whether an
account is protected when only three of the ten protections exist — it still
says so in words instead of showing a number it made up.

### Fixed

Three faults were found by calling the new addresses rather than by reading the
code, and all three are fixed:

- Both refund controls would have refused **every** administrator who used them.
- Asking about an account belonging to a different utility returned an answer
  instead of "not found". Nothing leaked, but the product answered a question it
  should have declined.
- The reconnection fee is left blank until a utility sets that charge up, and
  the screen code did not expect a blank — the first screen to show it would
  have broken.

## [2.79.9] — 2026-08-28 · The import template you download is now one a person can fill in, and a failed import gives you something to quote

### The gap

A utility opened the meters template SMARTBillHub told them to start from and
found a column headed `unit_ref`. Their own words: *"when we add assets we have
to tie them to units; and in CSV file that we download there is not unit ID or
unit name that we can provide - what about this"*. The column was there. It was
headed in our internal field name, the three things it will accept were written
only in our source code, and the example cell was empty — which was the product
telling them "you have no units on file yet" in the one way nobody can read.

Separately: when an import failed on the live system, the screen said *"Something
went wrong. Nothing was saved — try again."* and nothing else. The same failure
was reported twice and neither report could be traced, because there was nothing
on the screen to quote and nothing in the log to look up.

### What changed

**The template speaks English.** Every downloadable import file — meters,
sub-meters, devices, premises, units and accounts — is now headed the way the
column is named on screen: `Unit`, `Address line 1`, `Meter type`. Upload it
back unedited and every column still recognises itself, which is what makes the
sample worth shipping at all.

**The screen says what the Unit column takes, on the page that hands you the
file** — the unit's number, or the premises and the unit together, or just the
unit label when only one unit in the utility carries it. Those sentences already
existed one step later, on the mapping screen, which is after the file has been
filled in.

**A utility with no units yet is told so, and told the order.** Premises first,
then Units, then this import. Previously that fact arrived as an empty cell, and
an empty cell is legal here — it loads the meter into inventory — so nothing
looked wrong.

**The accounts template stopped inventing a unit number.** It shipped `U-00001`,
which is not a unit any particular utility has, on the one template where the
column is required.

**A failed import now carries a short reference** — something like `5F2B-9C1D` —
on the screen and in the server log, written the moment the request arrives.
Read it down the phone and support can find the request, including the case that
defeated us before: the server being killed mid-import and never answering at
all.

### Nothing bills differently

No money rule, no rate, no invoice and no ledger entry is touched by any of this.

## [2.79.8] — 2026-08-28 · A connection size nobody priced is refused, not billed at another size's rate

### The gap

A water connection that is 3 inches across — a size this utility had never put a
price against — was billed **$8.00**, which is the price of a 5/8-inch
connection. Nothing looked wrong on the bill. The engine had a refusal written
for exactly this case, in these words: *"the bill refuses rather than charging
$0.00 for a size the utility has never priced."* It could never fire, because
the part of the code that decides which sizes a rate schedule serves was being
handed the customer's own size and told to serve it. The answer was always yes.

### What changed

The sizes a rate schedule serves are now read from the rate schedule. A meter
whose size is not on it is **refused by name** — the message says which size it
could not price — and it is never quietly given another size's rate. The
5/8-inch customer is unchanged and still pays $8.00.

Three things deliberately did not change:

* **Sewer** is not priced by pipe size at all — it is a share of the water bill —
  so a sewer line with a blank size is correct and still bills.
* **Battery storage and steam heat** still stop and say nobody has set their size
  bands yet. That is a different fact from having no sizes, and it stays that way.
* **Nothing bills differently today.** This engine has no caller in the live bill
  run; the only thing that exercises it watches from the side and prices nothing.
  The sizes are being loaded onto meters first, and this is switched on after.

Also fixed: a size that had been typed in but given no usage rates of its own was
telling the engine *"this size has no usage rates at all"* rather than *"use the
schedule's normal rates"* — which would have billed **$0.00 for every gallon**
that customer used.

## [2.79.7] — 2026-08-28 · You can finally tell us how big a meter's connection is

### The gap

Rate schedules have been able to price by connection size for weeks: type a
ladder for a 5/8" tap and a different one for a 2" tap, and the bill follows the
size. Only there was nowhere to say which size a meter was on. The field existed
in the database, and every way into it went through a programmer — no box on any
screen, no column in the meter upload.

So a utility that carefully typed a per-size ladder got the same prices on every
meter anyway. On our own water example that is **3.20 / 4.80 / 7.20** where a 2"
connection should read **3.45 / 5.10 / 7.70** — and on a migration of 1,847
meters, that is every bill on the account base, in the direction nobody checks.

### Added

- **A Connection size box when you add a meter**, and another on the form you
  reach from the pencil on the meters list, so a meter already on file can be
  corrected. Both are pick-lists drawn from your own Reference data sizes — you
  choose, you never type, because a typo here is a price nothing can quote.
- **A Connection size column in the meters upload file.** The sample file you
  download already has it, filled in with a size from your own list, so a
  spreadsheet built on it loads with the sizes attached.
- **The meter's detail screen now shows its connection size**, and says so in
  words when there is none: *"Not recorded — a rate ladder that prices by size
  cannot price this meter."*

### Notes

- **Leaving it blank is fine and always will be.** A migration where you do not
  yet know every size still loads; nothing is guessed and nothing is defaulted.
- **A size we do not recognise stops the row at the rehearsal**, by row number,
  with the size quoted — before anything is written — rather than loading a
  meter that then bills off the wrong price.
- **Sub-meters and behind-the-meter devices are unchanged.** A connection size
  describes the service connection a meter sits on, and those sit behind one.

## [2.79.6] — 2026-08-27 · An account that cannot be billed yet stops saying it owes you nothing

### The gap

An account still waiting to be switched on showed a balance of **$0.00**. That
is not a lie about the arithmetic — nothing has been posted against it — but it
is the wrong answer to the question the column is asking. *"You owe nothing"*
and *"nothing can be owed on this yet"* are different facts about a customer,
and the list spelled them the same way, so a brand-new account was
indistinguishable from a settled one at a glance.

### Fixed

- **A pending-activation account now reads `Awaiting` in the Balance column**, on
  the accounts list and on the account's own header, with the reason on hover:
  *"This account cannot be billed yet, so nothing can be owed on it. It is not a
  settled balance."*
- **A disconnected account still shows its debt, in full.** This was the trap
  worth naming: a cut account is also non-billable, and one of them was sitting
  on **$612.75** owed. Only a real, derived zero on an account that has never
  been billed reads `Awaiting`; any figure at all is shown as money, always.
- **The identifier on a service request is called one thing.** The form asked for
  a *Social Security Number* and the request's own detail screen called the same
  box *ID*. It is *Social Security Number* on both, which is what the design
  drew.

### Housekeeping

- Seven high-severity defects in the accounts and service-request area were found
  to be **already fixed** in the shipped product while the defect register still
  listed them as open. The rows are corrected, and a new check refuses a source
  file that claims a defect is closed while its register row says otherwise.

## [2.79.5] — 2026-08-27 · A meter can finally say what size it is, and the ruled price for that size reaches the bill

### The gap

Rate schedules have been able to price differently per connection size for a
week: a 2-inch water connection was meant to bill **3.45 / 5.10 / 7.70** where
every other size bills **3.20 / 4.80 / 7.20**. **Nothing in the product could
record what size a meter actually is** — not the meter record, not the service
point, not the unit — so every one of those customers was billed on the
every-size ladder, and the fallback was *correct*, which is why no test could go
red on it. The Size column on the route-meter picker had drawn an empty cell
since the day it was built, for the same reason.

### Fixed

- **A meter now carries its connection size** (`assets.size_class`), holding the
  utility service size classes ratified on 27 August — water 5/8" through 6",
  electric 1φ 100A through CT-metered, and the rest of the forty. Where a size is
  recorded and the schedule prices that size, the customer gets the ladder the
  utility typed.
- **Where a schedule prices per size and the meter's size was never filled in,
  the bill run stops that account by name** on the run screen instead of quietly
  charging the cheaper ladder. A bill that is twelve dollars a month short looks
  entirely normal, and nobody finds it.
- **The route-meter picker's Size column shows a size** instead of a dash.
- **The bill run's read seam now publishes the meter multiplier** beside the
  consumption it was computed from. Nothing on a bill changes: the same figure is
  priced the same way. It is published so a second reader can check the first.

### Not changed, deliberately

**No existing bill moves by a cent.** Every meter already in every database keeps
an empty size, and an empty size prices exactly as it did before this release.

### Still owed

**There is no box on any screen and no column in any upload file for a person to
type a size into yet** — only the system can set one, and the demo tenant is
seeded with one so the feature can be walked end to end. A real utility cannot
record its own sizes until that control ships.

## [2.79.4] — 2026-08-27 · A clerk stops reading our defect numbers, and the close-out finally says why it refused

### Execution sequence step 3b — the gates that are red on something a customer can see

Four gates were triaged by what a utility actually reads. **Two are fixed. Two
turned out not to be what their headline said, and are recorded rather than
"fixed" into looking green.**

### Fixed

- **Six strings printed an internal register id to a utility user, in all
  eleven languages** (a seventh carried one and is drawn on no screen — a
  retired sentence a test pins as absent; it was cleaned up with them). A German-speaking clerk opening an import read *"…der
  Zuordnungsdatensatz enthält keine Spaltenzuordnung (DEF-512)"* — our defect
  number, after a sentence describing a database row. It now reads *"Gespeicherte
  Zuordnungsvorlagen sind noch nicht verfügbar; ordnen Sie die Spalten im
  nächsten Schritt von Hand zu."* Three of the seven needed only the id taken
  out; four said nothing a clerk could act on once it was gone and were
  rewritten. The ids moved into the code comments beside the strings, where

- **The account close-out's six refusals had no words in any language and
  rendered as silence.** A clerk closing out an account that was still occupied,
  or dating the close-out before the cut, saw nothing at all happen. All six now

- The **Work** module reads **Interventions** in French, as it already read

- `G15`'s ten *"parity failures"* are **two unrelated things in one shape**

- `G28` stays red on its raise-site ratchet alone — 555 against 498 (`DEF-1860`),
