## [2.79.3] — 2026-08-27 · The defect register can be counted again, and the gate suite can start again

### Execution sequence step 2 — one severity vocabulary, and G46 wired

`severity` had held **nine values across two vocabularies** since 2026-08-10, so
every count ever taken from it was wrong — 173 `major` rows were read as though
they did not exist. 270 rows are collapsed onto `critical`/`high`/`medium`/`low`
by a rule that preserves order and **never demotes a row**, and `DEF-358`'s
shifted field (a severity sitting in `module`) is repaired by hand. `G46` now
enforces it, so the tenth value cannot arrive the way the first nine did.

### Fixed

- **The whole gate suite had been refusing to start for every lane on this
  branch** (`DEF-1785`). `G46` shipped unregistered with its reason written in a
  docstring; `run_gates._assert_registry_sane` reads the registry, not prose, and
  refuses to run *any* gate when a module has no row. `G42` then caught a second
  fault the moment it was registered — the gate defined `main()` and no `run()`.
  Both fixed, and `G46` now self-tests all four of its clauses on every run.
- The execution-sequence file's measurement line mixed both vocabularies, so it
  added up to 354 while three of its four cells were wrong (`DEF-1786`). It now
  carries both readings of "open" and names the state it was measured at.
- Two lanes allocated the same two defect ids minutes apart (`DEF-1787`). An
  allocated id is now re-derived from the pinned tip at push time, like a blob.

Nothing a utility sees changes in this build.

## [2.79.2] — 2026-08-27 · Five worklists had a filter that ignored every click. Now they have one that works

### CR-045 wave G — Disconnects, Move-ins, Move-outs, New connects and Transfers

The five lists behind the Accounts page can now be narrowed, and the narrowing
happens on the server — so the count beside the list is the real count, not the
part of it that happened to be on the page you were looking at.

* **Disconnects** — by case state.
* **New connects** — by the state of the build.
* **Move-ins** — by state: scheduled, due, or waiting on the customer.
* **Move-outs** — by when the account closed: last 7, 30 or 90 days.
* **Transfers** — by state.

**Four of these five already had something that looked like a filter, and that
was the problem.** Each carried a row of tabs — All, In progress, Waiting, and
so on — where the filter belongs on the toolbar. Every one of those tabs but
the first was greyed out, and the first was always the one already selected, so
the row could not be used for anything. It was there because the design draws
those tabs and we have not yet been able to answer a question about them: when
a job is *both* part-way done *and* waiting on somebody, which single tab is it
in? Nobody has decided, and guessing would hide jobs rather than fail loudly.

**Filtering turned out to be a different question, and one we can answer today.**
A tab has to put every row in exactly one place. A filter just asks "is this row
in this state?" — it says nothing about the rows it leaves out, so it needs no
such decision. So the dead tabs are gone and a real filter is in their place;
the tabs will come back when the question is settled, working.

**Two of the five could never have had those tabs turned into a filter anyway.**
Move-outs is the clearest: this product only records a move-out once it has
happened, so three of the four tabs it drew describe something we do not store
at all. Its filter asks about the closing date instead, which is a fact we
really do hold.

**Where a state cannot honestly be offered, it is not offered at all** — rather
than shown greyed. A greyed tab can explain itself; a filter option cannot, and
an option that always comes back empty reads as "there are none", which would
be untrue.

The two remaining lists in the product with no filter — Settings › Users and
Settings › Reference data — are recorded so they are not lost again.

## [2.79.1] — 2026-08-27 · Two lists could always be exported; nobody had drawn the button

### CR-045 wave E — routes and cycles get their download control

Settings › Routes and Settings › Cycles can now be downloaded as a spreadsheet,
like every other list that offers it.

**Almost none of this was new work, and that is the point worth recording.** The
export for both lists had been built, registered and tested to the byte —
there is a test that writes the file, reads it back and checks the column
headings and the values — and it had been that way since the export was
written. What was missing was the button. So the feature existed, was known to
work, and could not be reached by anyone using the product.

The download honours whatever the list is currently showing, so a filtered list
downloads filtered — including the new frequency filter on cycles, which
narrows the file as well as the screen.

**The change request said five lists could not be exported. Two of them could.**
That number came from looking at screens for a missing button rather than from
reading the list of exports the server actually offers — the same way the
filter wave was under-counted earlier. The remaining three — service requests,
reference data and the chart of accounts — genuinely have no export yet, so
that work is three items rather than five.

## [2.79.0] — 2026-08-27 · Four more lists can be narrowed, and the narrowing happens on the server

### CR-045 waves B and D — filters that actually filter, and prompts that tell the truth

**Four screens gained a filter they never had.** Assets › Imports, Accounts ›
Imports, Premises › Imports and Settings › Routes & cycles (which draws two
tables) each had a toolbar with a search box and nothing else. They now carry
the same removable-chip filters every other list uses — run status and upload
target on the import histories, cycle and status on routes, frequency and
status on cycles.

**The important part is where the narrowing happens.** These lists ask the
server for a page at a time, so a filter applied in the browser would narrow
the page you were already looking at — a subset of a subset — and quietly hide
rows that were never sent. Every one of these filters is sent to the server,
which is also how the import histories got a real fix along the way: the
Accounts › Imports tab used to ask for the most recent 200 imports of *any*
kind and then keep the account ones. A utility importing premises and meters
heavily could push its account imports out of that 200 and be told it had never
imported an account, while those imports sat in rows the server had declined to
send. It now asks for account imports specifically.

**Five search boxes now say what they actually match.** Routes, cycles, the
template catalogue and the chart of accounts had prompts like *"Search
routes…"*, which names nothing. Two others were under-promising in a way that
hid a working feature: the premises list has always searched by **city** and
the units list by **address**, and neither prompt admitted it — so nobody
tried. Both now say so.

**One task could not be done and is written down instead.** The change request
asked for the rate-schedule search to name a *code*, on the grounds that the
server already matched one. It does not — rate schedules have no code at all;
the neighbouring plans and charge codes do, which is very likely how the note
got written. Giving them one is a database change, not a wording change, so the
prompt is left alone rather than made to promise something the search cannot
do. That is exactly the fault this change request exists to remove, and it is
recorded rather than repeated.

**Still outstanding, and named rather than implied:** five more lists —
disconnects, move-ins, move-outs, new connects and transfers — still cannot be
filtered. Four of them draw a row of segment buttons that look like a filter
and do nothing when clicked. The server side for all five was built earlier
this month; only the screens are missing.

## [2.78.0] — 2026-08-27 · The written rules stop contradicting the working product

### CR-046 wave H — the record catching up with the code

Nothing a customer sees changes in this build. What changes is the paperwork the
next person builds from, and three pieces of it were wrong.

**A signed rule said the opposite of the ruling it carried.** The rule for account
numbers opened with *"an account number is issued from the tenant's series, never
taken from an uploaded file"* — and the Product Owner had reversed exactly that
eleven hours earlier: *"we use utility provdied account number here - we dont create
our own number"*. The product was built correctly; only the heading was wrong. But a
heading is what a search returns and where a reader stops, and the procedure this
project follows tells people to search the rules before asking anything. It now says
what the ruling says, with the old wording kept and marked superseded.

**Three rule numbers had been given out twice.** The duplicate-ID check was failing
on the branch, and all three duplicates came from this same change. Two were
deliberate amendments written the way this project writes them — repeat the row so
the original stays readable — and they simply needed numbers of their own. The third
was a genuine collision: one number naming both the account-identifier rule and the
rule that links a tenant's account to its landlord's. They are now separate numbers,
with every reference moved in the same commit.

**A design diagram was missing its first question.** The picture of what happens to
each row of a meter upload started at *"does this row name a unit?"* — leaving out
the question the Product Owner had drawn themselves: *does this row name a meter we
already hold?* It is stamped, and the four standalone upload pages carry the right
flow.

**Also recorded:** the change request said four upload files; the product has six.
Sub-meters and devices follow the same rule and are not built yet, and the one real
hazard there is written down — once we issue a master meter's number, a first
migration's sub-meter file cannot name its master by a number it has never seen.

## [2.77.0] — 2026-08-27 · A solar utility can finally say it sells solar

### CR-039 wave A task 2 — signup offered six of the ten services

The platform has sold **ten** services since the first migration — electric,
water, gas, sewer, trash, storm water, solar, broadband, thermal/heat and
battery. The signup page offered **six**. A storm-water, solar, thermal or
battery utility could complete signup, see a green tick, and land in a product
where every service it actually bills was switched off — with nothing on any
screen saying why.

**The ruling was ten days old when this shipped.** The Product Owner settled it
on 2026-08-17 — *"we will provdie full list for all services - they can always
select what they want out of it; more is better ; less is contraint"* — and the
server was rewritten the next day to match: it validates a chosen service
against the live catalogue, and gives all ten a row at provisioning with the
chosen ones enabled. **Only the list of chips on the page stayed at six.**

**What changed:** four more chips, in the order the platform seeds its services,
with names in all eleven languages.

**Why nothing caught it.** Every check in this repo that could see a missing
service compares one part of the app to another part of the app. This one was a
list in the browser disagreeing with a list in the database, and no check
crossed that line. There is now one that does — it reads the platform's own seed
and asserts the chips are exactly it, in that order. The screen test that was
supposed to cover this had also been green the whole time, because it checked
that six named services were present and never that no others were missing.

### Also in this build

* The lockfile's version had drifted a release behind `package.json` again
  (2.76.3 against 2.76.4) — the same drift the version check was extended for in
  DEF-347. Both copies now read the shipped version.

## [2.76.4] — 2026-08-27 · The big migration can actually be committed

### DEF-1108 (high) — every deferred import over the approval bar died in the worker

A utility migrating meters is the case this product was built for, and above
**5,000 rows** it could not commit at all if its file had more than a handful of
rejects. The operator uploaded, reviewed the dry run, saw *"63 rejected of
12,400"*, ticked the approval and pressed commit. The call answered **202
Accepted** — and then the background job died with
`BIZ-APPROVAL (metering.import.approver_role)`, a demand for a *role*. **Not one
of the 12,337 good rows was written, and there was no action the operator could
take**, because the thing being asked for was something the background worker
structurally cannot have.

**Why.** BR-MET-098 says a load with too many rejects needs an Owner or Admin to
approve it, and the product asks that person on the request that starts the run.
Over the async bar the commit is handed to a worker to finish — and the worker
deliberately carries an actor **id and no role**, because the role was already
checked at the door. The approval check ran a second time inside the worker,
where the answer could only ever be "no".

**The fix.** The approver is decided at the door, once, and the answer travels
with the job:

* `load()` now performs BR-MET-098's approver check itself, **before** handing
  the work to a worker, so anyone who may not approve is refused on the call
  they actually made — the same refusal, at the moment it makes sense.
* On success it records **who** approved, and the worker asks *"was this approval
  given by a role-checked approver?"* rather than re-asking for a role.
* That record cannot be faked: the service strips any caller-supplied approver
  id before reading anything, and writes its own only after its check passes.

**Nothing else moved.** Imports under 5,000 rows behave exactly as before, and a
Billing Clerk still cannot be their own second pair of eyes — that refusal now
happens on their own call instead of by accident in a worker.

**No rule changed and no figure moved.** CR-026's 5,000-row bar and
BR-MET-098's 5% / 10-row bars are untouched, and a new test asserts all three so
they cannot be quietly lowered to make a slow test faster.

**What should have caught it:** nothing exercised a deferred load *across* the
approval bar. The one test that did is marked slow inside a file that takes 3-5
minutes, so the habit is to skip it. `tests/test_def1108_deferred_load_approver.py`
now covers the same seam with no slow marker, in under a second per case.

## [2.76.3] — 2026-08-27 · The asset import stops paying for the customer base

### DEF-1549 (CRITICAL) — a one-column lookup was costing a whole screen, once per import row

The Product Owner's twenty-row asset import timed out on the deployed build a
**second** time, hours after `DEF-1075` shipped. That fix was real — it removed
the `ensure_reference_catalogs` N+1, 1,920 queries down to 32 — and it uncovered
a larger one standing behind it. Gunicorn logged `[CRITICAL] WORKER TIMEOUT
(pid:44)`, killed the worker mid-row, and the transaction rolled back: nothing
was saved, and the operator was told only *"Something went wrong."*

**What it cost, measured on the PO's own file (20 rows, `unit_ref` blank on all
twenty):**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the commit, tenant with **no** customers | 1,092 queries | **292** |
| the commit, same tenant, **12 service points** | **5,892** queries | **292** |
| extra queries **per row**, bought by the customer base | **+240** | **+0.0** |
| `service_default_uom("water")` | 281 | **1** |
| `active_account_count("water")`, 12 points | 25 | **3** |
| `services_overview()` — the S8 screen — 12 points | 281 | **61** |

The `+240 per row` is the whole defect. It is multiplicative in
`rows × services × points`, so it is **exactly zero on an empty tenant** and
grows without bound on a real one. At a remote database's 15–20 ms round trip,
5,892 queries is roughly 90 seconds — past the 60-second gunicorn timeout, which
is what the PO watched happen.

**The mechanism.** `assets._create_asset_inner` asked
`seams.service_default_uom(service)` **once per row**. That walked
`service_catalog()` → `tenancy.services_overview()` — the **S8 SCREEN read** —
which builds a row for every active catalog service, each calling
`customers.active_account_count`, which issued **two queries per service point**.

**The knowledge was already in the repo.** `DEF-324` diagnosed this same
mechanism one function along in August — 47 seconds of a single provisioning
request — and built the batched cure `service_default_uoms()`, whose own
docstring names the cost. What was never published was the **singular**
equivalent, so every per-row caller kept reaching through the screen.

### What changed

* **`tenancy.selectors.service_default_uom`** — the missing singular, one
  indexed query. Deliberately **not** `service_default_uoms().get(code)`: the
  plural filters `enabled=True` and the walk it replaces did not, so that
  one-line version would have turned every meter of a **switched-off** service
  into a silent `unit_missing` refusal. A test pins that case.
* **`customers.active_account_count`** batches its point lookups through a new
  `metering.selectors.service_codes_for_points`. Fixed at the source, not routed
  around — its other callers are the **S8 services screen**, the BR-TEN-026
  disable guard and `reports.queries`, all of which were paying it on every
  render for any tenant with customers.
* **No per-request memo**, and that is a recorded trade rather than an omission:
  after the first fix it would save ~19 queries out of **292**, and
  `tenant_services.primary_uom` — unlike the catalogue `DEF-1075` memoised — is
  written **during provisioning, in the same context that then seeds meters**.
  Four invalidation sites for 6% is how the next defect gets made.
* **`GUNICORN_TIMEOUT` was not raised.** `docker-entrypoint.sh` says in its own
  comment that raising it hides the symptom.

### The check that comes with it

`test_def1080_assets_commit_path.py` already carried a query-count guard, and it
**passed throughout both outages** — its ceiling was the *previous* defect's
arithmetic (96/row; this cost 55), and every tenant in the suite has **no service
points**, so the quadratic term was multiplied by zero. The new guard is
**differential and has no ceiling at all**: same twenty rows, two estate sizes,
and the two must cost the same. Proved RED against the previous build first.

### DEF-1690 (low) — filed, not fixed

`reports.queries.filter_options()` reads the same S8 screen payload to answer
*"enabled services: code and name"*. Not a loop, so it never blew up; the row
names the cheap read that replaces it, and the prevention both `DEF-324` and
`DEF-1549` have now asked for twice — **something in this repo that can assert
the query count of a read.** Nothing does.

## [2.76.2] — 2026-08-27 · The Social Security number is captured, encrypted, and proved

### DEF-632 (CRITICAL) — the screen's promise becomes true

PO ruling, verbatim: *"We tell customers their Social Security number is stored
encrypted - Verify and keep the promise ... We need to capture SSN and encript it;
we have to ensure it is working"*.

**Until today the product stored no Social Security number at all.** The
application form drew the field and told the applicant *"Stored encrypted and
shown to staff as the last four digits only"*, and the capture path **refused
fourteen identifier field names outright** rather than keep a promise it could not
keep. That was the right interim state; this ruling replaces it with the thing
itself.

**What a customer gets.** An applicant types **123-45-6789**. The database row
holds about sixty characters of ciphertext and — read back directly, through a
second connection — contains no `123`, no `456789` and no `123456789`. Staff see
**••• ••• • 6789**. The audit record of who changed what holds **•••••6789**. The
number is in no list response, no export, no log line and no error message.

**How.** `service_requests.ssn` is an app-layer encrypted column (AES-256-GCM, a
fresh nonce per write, bound cryptographically to that one column so a value
lifted into another column will not decrypt). The mechanism was already built and
signed under `OQ-016`; this connects it to the screen that was asking for it.
`BR-CUS-092` is the rule and no new rule was minted.

### What deliberately did NOT change

* **The driving licence is still not captured.** `BR-CUS-092`(a) names two
  identifiers and this ruling named one. Twelve identifier field names still
  refuse by name, and the screen still says so rather than going quiet.
* **You still cannot search for a customer BY their Social Security number.**
  Scrambling it differently every time is what keeps it safe; the price is that it
  cannot be looked up. The identity matcher is separate work and is not built.

## [2.76.1] — 2026-08-27 · The premises owner becomes a real master account

### DEF-650 (CRITICAL) — a charge cannot be posted to free text

PO ruling, verbatim: *"so premises owner is master accountin system. you ahve to
showall details form account - Bascially Premises -> owner = Master account - it
can be existing master account also so at the time of premises creation we should
check - how you will handle this"*.

`BR-MET-105` (PO 2026-08-24) sends the empty-unit base charge — worked at
**$30.50/month** — to *"the owner / landlord"*, and the owner was a **string on a
premise row**. The move-out wizard printed the limitation in its own shipped copy:
*"Owner is free text on the premise record, not an account. That limits where a
shortfall can be sent."* A signed rule with no posting target is the worst state a
signed rule can sit in, and it sat in it for three days.

**The one missing link.** `premises_owners.master_account_id` (`metering 0041`)
completes a chain that was otherwise already built:
`Premises.owner → PremisesOwner → accounts`.

**The check the PO asked for.** At premises creation the owner name resolves three
ways and no fourth:

| answer | what happens | why |
|---|---|---|
| **exact** | the party is REUSED whole, with its account | the key is the database's own `uq_premises_owners_tenant_name_ci` — a lookup, not a heuristic |
| **near** | OFFERED; the clerk decides | PO decision 3 — *"two landlords with similar names are two parties, and merging them bills the wrong one"* |
| **none** | the caller creates one, with a category it supplies | no category is ever read off a name (BR-MET-151 clause 3) |

**Geometry is retired.** `BR-CUS-171` found a master by walking the premises'
common areas and taking whoever pays for the hallway. PO decision 4 replaces it
outright — *not* as a fallback, because *"a fallback that disagrees with the
declared owner would silently bill a different party"*. Its two failures are gone
by construction: a premises with **no common area** now has a master, and **two
masters over one premises** no longer make the answer `None`.

**The owner's details come from the ACCOUNT** — number, kind, payer, outstanding
balance, read through the seam at the moment of asking. Nothing is copied onto a
metering row, so there is no second writable copy to drift.

### DEF-1088 · DEF-1247 (HIGH) — the first bulk upload no longer creates the problem at scale

The importer mapped `owner` to the FREE-TEXT column, so a utility's first upload —
the one that creates every premises it has — produced a tenant where not one
premises had a typed owner. Since CR-039 wave C the model-derived offered set
shipped **both** headers, so the alias loop also left `owner_manager` unclaimed and
fed the free-text field from the typed column's own header.

`Owner` now reaches the **typed** owner and `Owner name (legacy)` the free text.
**Re-pointing a header utilities already ship is safe because nothing is lost:**
the load writes both — the typed link when the party exists, and the operator's own
string into `owner_manager` as BR-MET-151 provenance. A file that used to fill one
column now fills that same column *and* resolves a party.

Two stage-3 rules, asymmetric on purpose: a **near** match is an ERROR that rejects
the row (an import has no clerk, and both ways of resolving an ambiguity on the
operator's behalf are forbidden); an **unknown** name is a WARNING that loads,
because an error would refuse every row of every first upload — the PO's own
concern: *"we will need to careful what we do when we upload presmies in the system
first time"*.

### Existing data — kept, never dropped and never invented

`metering 0041` writes **no data**. A premises already carrying a free-text owner
keeps it, stays listed by `unmatched_premises_qs()`, and is matched by a person.
Dropping the text would lose a utility's own record of who owns an address;
manufacturing parties from strings would invent customers, which BR-MET-151
clause 3 already forbids. The mandatory owner is on **create only** — a required
field on PATCH would make a ten-year-old address unsaveable.

### Not shipped, and minted rather than guessed

**`OQ-790`** — when the owner's ACCOUNT comes into existence and whether it is
`master` or `regular`. The PO ruled both halves and they do not meet: decision 2
says create one, and closing `OQ-500` the same day made master-ness *"derived from
whether anyone else occupies the premises"* and *"never chosen at creation"* — and
at premises creation nobody occupies anything. `ensure_owner_master_account` raises
`NotImplementedError("OQ-790")` at its own door; `link_owner_master_account` is the
door that works today, and it covers the PO's headline case of an account that
already exists.

## [2.76.0] — 2026-08-27 · Two billing rulings: a service with no meter bills, and the reconnection fee becomes money

### DEF-161 (CRITICAL) — a service with no meter BY DESIGN bills from its base charge

PO ruling: *"the bill refuses because trash has no meter - this is correct - (a)
Teach it that a service with no meter by design is normal — bill it from its
base charge or percentage and never ask for a read."*

A plan carrying trash could not be billed **at all**: metering answered
`no_meter` for a service point with no asset, billing treated every absence as
BR-BIL-015's missing read, and the whole account was refused. The only decision
that released it — `bill_without_service` — DELETED the service from the bill,
so **$18.00 a month per trash account reached no customer**.

**The deliverable is the DISTINCTION, not the release.** `tenant_services.metered`
(BR-RAT-081) is the signal and gets its first reader in the product (closing
DEF-495):

| the service point | the declaration | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| no asset | declared **unmetered** | bills its **base charge**, never asked for a read |
| no asset | not declared (the default) | still **refuses** — a setup fault a human sees |
| has an asset, no read | — | still **refuses** — BR-BIL-015, untouched |

Both directions are asserted. A tenant that never touched the column has an
empty unmetered set, so every existing bill prices byte-identically and no ❄️
FROZEN B4/B5 figure moves — golden-verify stays **33 PASS / 0 FAIL**.

The S31.2 Reads tab now shows a designed absence as *"Not metered"* rather than
*"No reading (service_not_metered)"*, because no reading was ever wanted.

### DEF-708 — the $75.00 reconnection fee becomes a real charge

PO ruling: *"Make the fee a real charge — It becomes a line that can be billed
and paid, so the gate has something to check."*

The fee was recorded on the disconnect case and posted nowhere, so
`mark_reconnecting` — which reads AR — admitted `A-11340` at **$8,240.00** where
BR-CUS-104 says **$8,315.00** is owed.

* `BILL_TYPES` gains **`fee`**: an invoice whose whole content is charge-code
  lines. No plan, no tariff, no usage, no proration and no tax pass.
* `apps/billing/fee_bill.py` is the ad-hoc charge service `customers` recorded
  as missing on 2026-08-25. It drafts, issues and posts a fee from the tenant's
  OWN charge code (BR-BIL-007 — never a literal) and refuses by name when the
  code is unknown, retired, percent-priced or unmapped to a GL account.
* `commit_cut` raises and issues it inside the cut's own transaction, so a cut
  whose fee cannot be charged does not happen.
* **`mark_reconnecting` is unchanged** — that is the point. The gate always read
  AR; what was missing was the fee being in AR.

⚠ The rejected one-line fix (folding the case's recorded figure into the gate)
is now pinned by a test: it would refuse every cut customer **forever**, because
the cached figure never clears when money posts.

## [2.75.0] — 2026-08-27 · CR-045 wave A: the shared toolbar frame, and an action row that holds actions

**⛔ FOUR PRODUCT-OWNER REPORTS IN ONE DAY WERE ONE DEFECT WEARING FOUR COSTUMES:
a row of controls over capacity, with every individual control correct.**
*"tool bar also not correct on this screen"* · *"buttons are still at wring places -
do you ahve rules for button"* · *"UI is broken at Park"* · a search placeholder cut
at *"Search asset #, serial, r"*.

* **The search box on all 27 lists had NO CSS RULE AT ALL** (`DEF-1150`).
  `.table-search input` carried `min-width: 220px` *and* the whole field kit, and
  nothing had rendered `.table-search` since the Route B migration — so with
  Tailwind's preflight in front the box was an unstyled ~170px browser default,
  cutting 20 of 27 prompts. It is now `flex-[1_1_20rem] min-w-[15rem]
  max-w-[32rem]` on the wrapper, wearing the declared `.input` field kit. **The
  floor is 240px and not 320px on purpose:** the toolbar was already over budget,
  and a hard 320px floor would push the filters onto a second row.
* **The reads toolbar gets a capacity answer, not another nudge** (`DEF-1085`).
  ~1,360px of controls in the ~1,150px a 1,440px laptop leaves. Row one is now B14
  rule 12's set plus the export — a BOUNDED set — and dimension controls get a
  **designed** second row. Swept across Premises, Units and Reads, all three of
  which had written the same workaround comment.
* **The column picker no longer opens off the edge of the screen** (`DEF-1085`).
  It was `right-0` unconditionally; the PO screenshotted its heading reading
  *"OW / HIDE"*. Anchoring is arithmetic now, and it flips rather than clipping —
  in both directions, so the fix does not simply mirror the bug.
* **A status pill is not an action** (`DEF-966`). It leaves the page header's
  action row and joins the identity — r10 draws it that way on every screen, and
  ~20 detail screens are corrected with no call-site edits.
* **A disabled control's reason is not a button** (`DEF-1083`). The bill run's
  footer no longer has a paragraph sharing a line with `Save & exit` and `Park`.
* **`Download CSV` becomes a `↓` glyph**, both variants, 36px square — the width
  that pays for the wider search box. The sentence survives as the accessible name
  and the tooltip.

**Held by three new checks**, each proved RED first: G43 clause (c) refuses a
dimension control in the download slot (it named all three offenders on the
pre-fix tree), the toolbar's slot order is pinned, and the popover's anchoring is
unit-tested in both directions. **None of them can see a wrapped row** — no gate in
this repo reads rendered output, and all four defects existed only there.

## [2.62.2] — 2026-08-27 · a quantity reads like a quantity

**Fixed (DEF-894).** Every quantity in the product printed at its STORAGE
precision — `8.000000 kgal`, `1008.000000`, and `1016.000000 · 8.000000 kgal`
on all 41 stops of a printed route sheet. The Product Owner ruled the display
rule after finding it live: **at most two decimals, trailing zeros trimmed.**

* One composer, `apps/metering/quantity_display.py`, reached by every surface —
  the reads list, the reading detail headline, its working, the read history,
  the route sheet and the correction modal's prefill. Six surfaces formatting
  independently is how three of them drift.
* **The trim is the half a two-decimal fix would miss.** `$8.00` is right and
  `8.00 kgal` is noise: a currency's precision belongs to the currency, a
  quantity's is what the meter measured. The suite asserts `"8"` and explicitly
  not `"8.00"`.
* Storage is untouched — six places is still what is stored and computed with.

**Why no gate caught it:** the money rule fixes display at 2dp for money and
percentages and is silent on consumption, so there was no figure to check
against. The prototype had been drawing `684 kWh` and `3.72 kgal` the whole
time. Written down now as **BR-MET-144**.

## [2.62.1] — 2026-08-27 · the read-validation settings page, as the PO asked for it

**Fixed (DEF-900), three things on one screen.**

* **Descriptions cap at 80%** — B14 rule 18's own `--desc-measure` token, which
  has existed since 2026-08-16 and this page never used. Six descriptions were
  capped by `max-w-prose` instead: a real utility, the wrong cap.
* **One collapsible panel per service.** A ten-service tenant opened on ten full
  threshold forms, fourteen inputs each. The first service now lands open and
  the rest are one click — through the EXISTING `Disclosure`, which already
  pairs `aria-expanded` with `aria-controls` off one id.
* **The two columns line up.** A plain two-column grid let each field stack at
  its own height, so wherever one side carried a help line and the other did
  not the inputs sat at different heights. `grid-rows-subgrid` aligns the label,
  help and input rows across both columns without inventing help text for the
  empty side and without touching the shared `TextField` — no other form moves.

**Answered, and filed rather than changed (DEF-901):** *are these settings
applicable to sewer?* **No.** Sewer is priced as a percentage of the water usage
charge and reads no register at all; trash is a flat per-cart charge with no
meters. The page renders a section per *enabled* service rather than per
*metered* one, so it offers thresholds that can never fire.

## [2.62.0] — 2026-08-27 · the demo tenant bills TWO months, and the money happens in between

**CR-040 wave C.** The seeded utility finished one billing cycle and staged two.
It now finishes **two** and stages the third — and, more to the point, the
payments block runs **between** the two runs, so the second cycle bills an estate
that already carries June's collections and (once wave D lands) a refund and a
corrected overcharge.

* The billing block is **two blocks**: `seed_sample_records` (cycle one) and
  `seed_sample_second_cycle` (cycle two). The billing engine is untouched — the
  seeder already drove all five phases through the doors the bill-run screen
  uses, so this is a question of *when*, not *what*.
* July is a billed period, issued 2 August, and **left uncollected on purpose**:
  a bill days old against a mid-August "today" is a bill nobody has paid, which
  gives the ageing report a live current bucket beside June's aged one.
* **August is still unbilled.** That has survived three rulings about how many
  months a demo carries, and the acceptance test now asserts the invariant —
  *the last declared period is never billed* — instead of naming a month.

**No cron and no second worker** (PO 2026-08-27: *"if you can run jobs using
celery and complete 2 billing cycle -im good with it"*). The seeding job is
already a background job; it now runs both cycles inside it.

**Corrected on the way past:** three docstrings and a panel label that described
a one-month fixture, one of which had been wrong for ten days on a published
seam name.

* `TC-15` asserts the three figures and the engine's own worth for them

* `TC-16` asserts the refusal path: the quantity still shows, the refusal names
