## [2.36.0] — 2026-08-22 · CR-028 · Assets: the registry to r10, and the imports are real

- The Assets registry matches the design: KPI cards, per-tab columns, master/sub
  tags, sub-meter last reads, tab-named import buttons — and no credit money on
  the Behind-the-meter tab, by ruling.
- Importing assets is the five-stage workflow, up to 100,000 rows: meters,
  sub-meters and devices each with their own field map, rules, sample file and
  a seeded default mapping template ("recognised: Meters default").
- A blank unit on an import row is accepted into inventory, never an error —
  one asset, one unit, exactly as ruled.
- The demo tenant finally carries trash carts (3 × $15.00 = $45.00 now walks),
  a real master with sub-meters, all five device kinds and aged inventory.
- Assets can now record what they cost, who supplied them, expected life and —
  at retirement — book value with the operator's recorded treatment. None of it
  touches Finance, by ruling.

## [2.30.2] — 2026-08-22 · CR-009 · The notification rule page can finally be edited

### Added
- **Every card on a notification rule's page is now something you can change, not just read.** Open Settings → Notifications and pick an event: who it goes to (every contact or just the main one, which services, households or businesses, whether accounts on a payment plan are skipped), which channels it goes out on — each with a template chosen from your real Templates catalog and a language setting — and when it goes (straight away, a number of days later, or at a fixed time of day), what happens in quiet hours, and what to do if it fails. One Save writes it all, tells you it saved, and takes you back to the list. Until now these cards showed the settings and offered no way to change them, even though the system underneath accepted every one of these changes (DEF-286).
- **The page will not let you save something incoherent.** "A number of days later" without the number, a time-of-day send without the time, or a save with nothing changed — each is refused on the page, in words, before anything is sent.

### Changed
- **The Services setting on a rule now reads in plain words** ("All services", or your own service names) instead of the internal code `all`.

### Known limitation
- **You pick which template a channel uses, not which variant of it.** Choosing between a template's own variants (Spanish, large print) per event needs a decision about how that is stored, which is back with the product owner.

## [2.30.0] — 2026-08-22 · CR-021 · Staff can attach taxes and fees to a plan

### Added
- **The plan wizard's Taxes step now lets you attach individual taxes and fees from your catalogue**, beyond the ones an authority you bound already brings. Pick a tax on the left, it appears under "On this plan" on the right, and it reaches the bill exactly the way an authority's own taxes do — same conditions, same dates, same arithmetic. Nothing about how a tax is calculated changed; only which taxes a plan can carry.
- **What you cannot do is remove a mandated tax.** A tax an authority you bound levies stays on the bill whether or not anyone ticked it — the step marks those "brought by jurisdiction" and gives them no remove control, and the server refuses a detach attempt on one, by name. Removing something you attached yourself is always allowed; that undoes your own choice and nothing else.
- **The same tax reached both ways is charged once.** Bind Texas (6.25%) and also attach the state tax by hand, and a $100.00 bill carries $6.25 — never $12.50.

### Fixed
- **Taxes with no service restriction were invisible on the Taxes step.** A tax that applies to every service was read by the step's filter as applying to none, so it never appeared in the catalogue. It does now, and its row says "every service" (DEF-534).

## [2.29.9] — 2026-08-20 · The buttons are drawn by one piece of code now, and it says what a button IS

### Changed
- **Every button on eight screens is drawn from a single description instead of a name pointing at a stylesheet.** Nothing you can see has changed — the buttons were measured in four states (resting, hovered, being pressed, and unavailable) against the ones they replace, 16,608 measurements, and not one came out different. What changed is underneath: a button now says *what it is* ("the primary action", "the small size") rather than naming a style that may or may not exist. Naming a style that does not exist is the fault that has left screens looking broken six times in five months, and it is not possible to make in the new form.
- **The one control that was silently doing nothing was found this way.** On Settings → Reference data → Templates, the category chips at the top were meant to look selected when you click one. The mark they carry was never drawn by anything, so the selected chip has always looked exactly like the unselected ones. It is recorded as a defect and left alone here, because this release deliberately moves no pixels.

### Added
- **The two button sizes the design agreed can now actually be counted.** Each button records its own size and role in the page, so "how many button sizes does this screen use?" is now a question that can be asked and answered automatically. It could not be before — and the product turns out to be drawing four different small-button shapes under a single agreed size, which is recorded and not yet fixed.

### Known limitation
- **Eight screens of the product use the new form; the rest still use the old one.** Both work, they render identically, and they will co-exist until the migration finishes. This release is a measured trial of the approach, not the finish of it.

## [2.29.8] — 2026-08-20 · A check that was quietly reading the code by two different rulebooks now reads it by one

### Fixed
- **Two of our automated checks were reading your screens by slightly different rules, and neither could tell.** Both of them exist to catch the same bad thing: a piece of the interface that asks for a style nobody ever wrote, which renders as nothing and looks broken to you while every test we own reports success. That mistake reached customers six times in five months. The two checks had grown up in different halves of the build system, which cannot talk to each other, so each carried its own copy of the rule — and every one of the three corrections we have ever made to that rule was applied to one copy and not the other.
- **There is now one copy, plus a set of ten worked examples both checks must get right.** Each example is a mistake that has genuinely happened, including the one that lost two real styles while appearing to improve. If either check ever drifts again, it fails on the example that names the old bug, on the same day, instead of silently reading your screens by weaker rules.
- **Nothing on any screen changed.** This is a change to how we check the product, not to the product. The check reports exactly the same numbers before and after.

## [2.29.7] — 2026-08-20 · Three panel titles are the right size, and four more services have a colour

### Changed
- **Three headings changed size, and they are the only things on any screen that moved.** The title at the top of a pop-up form (for example "Add to Areas & sub-areas") and the title at the top of the route and cycle wizards are both **bigger — 22 pixels to 25**. The step heading inside the Run bills wizard is **smaller — 22 pixels to 20**. Every element of the surfaces they sit on was measured before and after; the complete list of differences is those three headings and nothing else.
- **Why they moved at all:** the product's agreed size list has a heading step at 20 and one at 25, and nothing at 22 — so these three titles had been borrowing the name meant for a *figure* (the big numbers on the dashboard). A title wearing a figure's name looks harmless and stops being harmless the moment those figures are set to shrink on smaller screens, which is the next thing planned. They were moved onto real heading names before that happens rather than after.
- **The wizard title was smaller than the heading below it, and now it is not.** "New route" was drawn at 22 pixels above a step heading at 24. It is now 25.

### Added
- **The four services that had no colour now have one.** SMARTBillHub bills ten services and only six had a colour of their own — Storm water, Solar, Thermal/Heat and Battery all drew the same grey dot, so three of them were indistinguishable from each other anywhere a service is shown as a tag. Storm water is now dark blue, Solar olive, Thermal/Heat magenta and Battery teal, on both the Plans & Rates dots and the service tags on the Premises and Reads screens.
- **Storm water's dot is a ring, not a filled circle**, and that is on purpose: it belongs to the same family as Water and the two blues are hard to tell apart at the size these dots are drawn. A different shape reads at any size and reads for a colourblind operator, where a different shade of blue does not.
- **Broadband keeps the purple it has always had.** The design proposal this came from wanted to rename it and give the name to something else; it was not applied. No service has two colours.

### Known limitation
- **Solar's colour is the weakest of the four and is recorded as such.** Solar reads amber to anyone who works with it, and amber is already Gas. Olive is the nearest free hue to the sun and is clearly apart from Trash's dark green, but it is a compromise forced by a palette that is already occupied, not a choice anyone would make from scratch.
- **Six hand-typed sizes still remain** — the sidebar wordmark, a pricing sentence, two 24-pixel headings, a column-chooser button and a reading comparison. The rule agreed here is that a size used at two or three places is not worth a new name on the list; these are left exactly as they are, marked in the code, and revisited if the count grows.

## [2.29.6] — 2026-08-19 · Two figures on screen got smaller, and the size list can no longer be got round

### Changed
- **The big figures on your dashboard are slightly smaller — 30 pixels to 26.** This is the one number the last release said was still hand-typed and being raised as a question. It has been answered: figures like these are their own kind of text, not headings, and 26 pixels is the size agreed for them. You will see it on the dashboard and on every screen with a strip of figures across the top — Finance, Deposits, Premises, Reads, Outstandings and the by-premises report.
- **The big "Today" total on Payments is smaller too — 40 pixels to 32**, for the same reason. It had been drawn at the size meant for a full-page wizard title, which it is not; it is a money figure.
- **Six more hand-typed sizes were replaced by a name, and none of them changed how anything looks.** A modal title, a wizard heading, a bill-run heading, a lookup figure, a reading figure and a stat figure now read from the agreed list instead of a number typed in place.
- **Those two figures above are the ONLY things on any screen that moved.** Every element of twenty-five screens was measured before and after: eleven thousand of them, and the complete list of differences is those two figures and nothing else. Four of the six full-page photographs are identical to the byte.

### Added
- **A check that refuses a text size that is not on the agreed list.** The last release said plainly that nothing yet stopped someone typing a new size. Something does now, it runs on every change, and it found seven sizes already written that way on its first run — all of them on the Rate schedules screen, all at sizes the list already contains, and all now written by name. Nothing about that screen changed.
- **The project's code checker now actually runs when changes are made.** It had been set up and wired to nothing, so for months it only ran if someone remembered to run it by hand.

### Known limitation
- **Six hand-typed sizes remain, and they are a different problem from the last fourteen.** Each is a size that is right for what it is but has no name on the list — the SMARTBillHub wordmark in the sidebar, a marketing sentence on the pricing page, a settings heading, a wizard heading, a column-chooser button and a reading comparison. Two of them are drawn exactly as the design does it, so changing them would move away from the design rather than toward it. They are marked in the code and raised as a question rather than guessed (OQ-279).
- **The new check counts sizes; it cannot tell a heading from a button.** A size that is on the list but used for the wrong kind of text still passes. That is the same question as above and it needs a person.

## [2.29.5] — 2026-08-19 · Text sizes across the product now come from one agreed list

### Changed
- **The product now uses one agreed set of text sizes, and almost every piece of text on every screen reads from it.** Three hundred and twenty-eight hand-typed sizes were replaced by a name from that list. **Nothing you look at moved**, with the exceptions below: a size written as "13 pixels" and a size written as "the panel-body size, which is 13 pixels" draw the same letters.
- **The pricing page headline is bigger — 42 pixels to 56.** It is the one place a size was meant to change: it is a marketing headline and it was being drawn at the size meant for a wizard title.
- **The smallest text in the product got slightly bigger.** Eight places drew text at 9 or 10 pixels, which is below the size the design system says is comfortably readable — a sort arrow in table headers, the version number on the sidebar, the notification-bell count, a few small labels and pills. All of them are now 11 pixels. Seventy-seven pieces of text in the whole product changed size, and this is seventy of them.
- **Three sizes that sat between two agreed ones were settled by looking at each in place** — a wizard preview panel moved up to match the controls above it, a card description moved down so it no longer matched its own title, and the sentence an approver signs before a bill run moved up, because it had been drawn no heavier than the text around it.

### Known limitation
- **Fourteen sizes are still hand-typed, and that is deliberate.** They are sizes the agreed list does not contain — a KPI figure, a few panel titles, the big "Today" total on payments — and choosing one for them would change how nine screens look without anyone deciding to. They are marked in the code and raised as a question rather than guessed (OQ-278).
- **Nothing yet stops someone typing a new size that is not on the list.** The list makes that checkable; it does not make it impossible. That arrives with the rest of the styling change, which is what the whole list was written for.

## [2.29.4] — 2026-08-19 · Groundwork for the styling change, on one screen

### Changed
- **One screen — Plans & Rates → Rate schedules — is now styled the new way**, as the trial the styling change asks for before the other 126 screens follow. **It looks exactly as it did**: measured element by element in a real browser, nothing on the page changed by so much as a pixel, and the full-page photograph before and after is identical byte for byte (CR-018 Phase 1).
- **The product now downloads about 7 kB more stylesheet.** Almost all of that is a one-off cost that is now paid; each further screen adds roughly a kilobyte while removing more hand-written styling than it adds. The whole change is expected to finish smaller than it started.

### Fixed
- **About 8 kB of a developer test page was being sent to you on every page load.** It had no effect on anything you see, and it is no longer included.

### Known limitation
- **The other 126 screens are unchanged** and this release does not begin them. Three questions have to be answered by a person first — what size a heading is meant to be, what sizes small text is allowed to be, and how one internal check should work — because guessing any of them would change how screens look without anyone deciding to (OQ-275, OQ-276, OQ-277).

## [2.28.0] — 2026-08-19 · What the product says when it has to say no

### Changed
- **Every message you see when the product refuses something is now written for you, not for us.** Four hundred and twenty-two refusals were written next to the rule they enforce and carried the rule's own code with them, so a clerk trying to put an account on budget billing read *"a per-account budget level override requires a REASON (BR-BIL-017 as OQ-068 closed it: allowed with reason + audit)"*. They now read *"A budget-level override needs a reason. Enter one and we'll record it against the account."* The engineering detail has not been thrown away — it goes to the audit trail and the server log, where support can still find it (DEF-322).
- **Refusal messages are shorter.** No sentence runs past twelve words and no message past two sentences. Fifty-eight were longer than that and have been cut back — by dropping the explanation of WHY, never the sentence that tells you what to do next.

### Fixed
- **Fifty-one refusals had no message at all.** They showed you their internal name — a clerk choosing a short password read `errors.identity.password_too_short` under the box, and someone trying to activate a discount with no start date got a blank refusal. Every one now says what is wrong and what to do about it, in all eleven languages.
- **A system error now says it is a system error, and gives you something to quote.** For the twelve failures you can never cause yourself, the product says *"Something went wrong on our side. Nothing was changed — quote 5F2B-9C1D to support."* That reference has existed on every refusal since March and was shown to nobody. It is short enough to read down a phone, and support can search for it (DEF-328).

### Known limitation
- **Support can look that reference up for some failures and not yet others.** The audit trail records a refused attempt when it is a rule refusal or a permission denial, and a programming error is neither — so for ten of the twelve, support finds the reference in the server log rather than in the audit screen. Whether the audit trail should cover system errors too is being raised rather than guessed at (OQ-271).

## [2.27.1] — 2026-08-19 · Eight screens were rendering as plain text

### Fixed
- **Eight screens in the product were showing as unformatted running text instead of as designed.** The bill-layout chooser on Settings → Configure → Templates ran its five options together into one paragraph — *"StandardUS Letter. …In use In use CompactUS Letter…"* — where it should be five cards you can pick between. On Settings → Notifications a label and its number collided into a single word, reading **"Waiting93"**. The upload-reads screen showed its three source options as flowing text with stray radio buttons beside them. The same fault affected fix-a-bill, one-time bill, budget bills, the change-plan wizard, the payment-plan wizard and account actions (DEF-314, DEF-315, DEF-327).
- **Thirty-seven database codes were being shown to you as if they were English.** Template names read `payment_plan_active` rather than "Payment plan active". They now read as sentences, and the ones with their own spelling are spelled properly — "SMS", not "Sms" (DEF-317).

### Added
- **A check that refuses a screen asking for a style that does not exist.** This is what the eight screens had in common: each named a style the product had never been given. Nothing could see it — the code compiled, the tests passed, and only a person looking at the screen could tell. The same fault had been found and fixed by hand six times since March, each time as a list of names rather than as the missing check. It is now counted, and the count can only go down.

### Known limitation
- **One screen still has a layout problem this release does not solve.** The left-hand column of Settings → Notifications runs far longer than the right, so most of it sits below the fold. Balancing the two columns, or letting them scroll separately, is a design decision and is being raised rather than guessed at (DEF-316).

## [2.27.0] — 2026-08-19 · Background work actually runs now

### Fixed
- **Work the product promised to do in the background was not being done at all, on the deployed build, in four places.** When you did something that takes a while, the product recorded the request, told you it had accepted it, and then nothing picked it up. Nothing failed and nothing said anything — the request simply sat there. Four things were affected: **a bulk price change** (you changed your prices, the product agreed, and no price changed), **the sample data for a brand-new utility** (a new customer's account opened empty), and **both of the audit-trail downloads** (DEF-320, DEF-326).
- The queue now has something reading it. All four were checked by actually running them — a real background worker, on a real database, in the configuration the deployed build uses — and all four completed.

### Changed
- **The application now runs three background pieces alongside the website**: a queue, a worker that does the work in it, and a scheduler. They are part of the standard installation.

### Known limitation
- **An existing installation does not pick this up on its own.** A running deployment needs the new pieces started and two settings changed on the host itself; nothing in this release reaches a machine that is already configured.
- **The scheduler has nothing scheduled yet.** It is installed and running, and the three recurring jobs it is meant for — old-record archiving, report clean-up and message pacing — are not built. It will sit idle until they are, and saying so is more useful than implying otherwise.

## [2.26.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-017 · Signing up no longer leaves you staring at nothing

### Added
- **A new screen tells you what is being built while you wait for it.** Signing up used to end with a button press and then nothing — no message, no progress, no indication that anything was happening — while the product spent the best part of a minute building your utility behind a blank browser. It now names the work as it goes: your utility and your owner login, your reference lists, your chart of accounts and number series and document templates, and the sample data. Each line says whether it is working, done or waiting, and when it finishes it tells you what it built for you — *"20 lists, 149 rows"*, *"All 10 blocks loaded"* — before taking you to your setup checklist.
- **It says the thing a person actually needs to hear**: *"Thank you for waiting. Your utility is being set up and your data is being seeded right now."* and *"You do not need to do anything. Nothing you typed is lost."*
- **Every figure on it is real.** The counts come from what the server actually wrote, and the sample-data line follows the real background job block by block. There is no invented progress bar and no timer pretending to be progress.
- **If part of the sample data does not load, the screen says so and does not whisk you away.** Your utility is still ready and still yours; the screen tells you your setup checklist names what is missing and where to load it again.

### Fixed
- **Creating a utility was taking 78 seconds and roughly half of that was one piece of housekeeping repeated 304 times.** Working out which services a utility sells was being answered by building the whole Settings → Services screen — ten rows, each with its own lookups — instead of by the single question that answers it. The same signup now takes 45 seconds end to end on the same machine, with nothing else changed (DEF-324).

### Known limitation
- **On the deployed build the sample data may never load at all, and nothing says so.** The background job is created and there is nothing running to pick it up. This is recorded as a defect and the fix is a deployment choice we have put to you with the cost of each option, rather than one we have made quietly (DEF-320).

## [2.25.1] — 2026-08-19 · CR-016 · The screens are made to match the design again

### Fixed
- **The small red label above every page title was rendering as ordinary body text.** The design calls for an 11-pixel uppercase accent line — "REPORT" above *Reports*, "ROUTES" above the routes table — and it was drawing as plain 15-pixel grey-black copy on six screens. Twenty-six screens ask for that label and no stylesheet in the application defined it, so it had never worked (DEF-308).
- **Lists were set in six different type sizes.** Table text rendered at 10, 11, 12, 13, 13.5 and 14 pixels depending on which screen you were on, and ten screens showed more than one of those at the same time. Every table in the product is now one size for its rows and one size for its column headings, and the column headings are uppercase over a rule, the way the design draws them (DEF-310).
- **Buttons were set in five different sizes**, including one that was simply whatever the browser felt like because no rule reached it. There are two now, as intended: standard, and small (DEF-311).
- **Form fields sat at four different heights** — 27, 33, 36 and 38 pixels — so a row of filters never lined up. They are all one height. Date boxes, which were the tallest, now match everything else (DEF-313).
- **Six dropdowns on the settings and list screens were still drawing the operating system's own control** rather than ours, because two shared components quietly erased the arrow the rest of the product draws (DEF-309).
- **Fifteen colour and spacing values referred to names that were never defined**, and eleven of those had no fallback — meaning the instruction was thrown away entirely. A table border that never drew, five margins that were never applied, two links that rendered in ordinary ink, and six greys that were not the design's grey (DEF-312).

### Changed
- **The style check that reads the running application now records what the design system looks like rather than how far the product is from it.** Every number in it is at its correct value, so the first screen that breaks any of them turns it red.

## [2.25.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-015 · The dashboard shows the period you ask it for

### Added
- **You can now choose which period the dashboard reports on**, and it opens on your **last completed billing cycle** — the run that has actually gone out — rather than on the calendar month. A utility that bills on the 25th used to open the dashboard on the 3rd and see almost nothing: revenue near zero, service mix nearly empty, for the first week of every month, with nothing actually wrong. Four windows are offered — your last completed cycle, the last 30 days, this accounting period and the one before it — and a utility with no cycle set up yet gets the last 30 days instead.
- **The dashboard says, in dates, which period it is showing you** — *"Showing Aug 12, 2026 – Aug 19, 2026"* — above the figures rather than hidden inside the picker. Once you can choose a window, your dashboard and your Finance page can show different numbers and both be right, and this is what lets you see why at a glance.
- **The period you are looking at is part of the web address**, so you can send someone the link and they will see the same figures you are looking at.
- **The dashboard now tells you how old the figures on screen are** — *"Read 4 minutes ago"* — because it keeps them for five minutes to save re-reading them on every visit, and it should say so rather than quietly disagree with Finance.

### Fixed
- **The dashboard was labelling itself with a date that had not happened yet.** On the 19th of August it said its figures were *"as of Aug 31"* — eleven days into the future — because it took the end of the accounting period rather than the moment the figures were read. It now says today's date mid-period, and the closing date once a period has closed, so a figure on the dashboard and the same figure in Finance can finally be compared by the dates they carry (DEF-299).
- **A utility with no financial year set up saw a dashboard of dashes.** Every money figure was blank because there was no accounting period to add up. It now shows the last completed cycle or the last 30 days, with the dates stated, and only the two accounting-period choices are withheld — with a line saying why.

### Known limitation
- **The demo tenant's sample data is still dated July**, so several tiles read zero for a current window. The period picker fixes this for real utilities; the sample data is a separate job and has not been done.

## [2.24.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-016 · The product stops explaining itself to you

### Changed
- **Screens no longer show you our internal rule numbers, story numbers, file names or web addresses.** A System Admin at a small utility was reading things like *"Rule BR-BIL-015 · column bill_run_decisions.case"*, *"Story US-BIL-002 · GET /billing/runs/{id}/findings"* and *"apps/notifications/bulk_summary.queue_bulk_summary"* — a database column name, an address inside our software, and the name of one of our source files. Two of our own internal rulings were on screen, quoted with their dates. All thirteen Settings screens were walked in a browser and every one of them is now clean; across the whole product, 219 such strings were rewritten.
- **Where the product cannot do something yet, it still says so — in your words instead of ours.** Nothing was hidden to tidy this up: every honest statement about a missing feature is still there. *"no SMTP adapter is built and no message leaves the building on any email path (BR-NOT-013)"* now reads **"Email sending is not switched on yet, so no email leaves the building. Filling this in now means email works the moment it is switched on."** Same fact, nothing about our internals.
- **Settings → Configure → Templates is readable.** The "Used by" column held whole paragraphs of engineering notes, which also pushed the "Last edited" and "Actions" columns off the right-hand edge of the screen. Each entry is now a sentence — *"Not in use yet — the bill run does not attach inserts."*, *"Disconnection notice — final stage, sent by certified mail."* — and the table fits.
- **Settings → Notifications explains the four automatic-message settings without citing a meeting.** *"All four start ON by Product Owner ruling (2026-08-17)"* is now *"All four start switched on."* A setting that is saved but not yet acted on says exactly that, in plain terms.
- **A note about our own requirements document has been removed from the Notification rules screen.** It reported that the written requirement names sixteen events and describes fifteen. That is true, and it is nothing a utility can act on.

### Fixed
- **Two disconnection-notice types showed their internal name instead of their real one** on Settings → Notifications — you saw `notifications.tones.class.disconnect_notice_10_day` where the words "Disconnection notice — 10 day" belong. All three notice stages now have proper names, in all eleven languages (DEF-318).
- **Rule references have been taken off the bill-layout and billing-run panels.** They were the bold opening of every bullet in the "what this screen cannot do yet" lists (DEF-319).

### Added
- **A check that stops this happening again.** The build now fails if any text destined for a screen contains one of our internal references — a rule or story number, a file name, a web address, a database column, or a quoted internal ruling. It was first proved to catch all 219 of the existing ones before being trusted (G28).

## [2.23.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-012 · The dashboard shows YOUR services

### Changed
- **The Service mix panel now lists the services your utility actually sells — all of them — instead of a fixed five.** A utility that sells broadband and water used to meet five rows headed Electric, Water, Sewer, Trash and Gas, three of which it could never fill, with its own broadband revenue tucked into a footnote. It now sees Water and Broadband, in the order the platform lists services. A service you have switched on but have not billed this month still gets its row, drawn as a dash — never as `$0.00`, which would read as "we sold none of this" rather than "nothing here yet". Revenue that belongs to no service at all — a late fee is charged to an account, not to a service — is still reported separately, so the panel can never add up to less than the month's revenue.
- **A dashboard figure the product cannot count now says "Not counted yet"** instead of explaining our own software architecture to you. The technical reason is still there, in the small print under the figure, for anyone who needs it.
- **A to-do row whose count could not be worked out shows no number at all** rather than a zero. A zero said "nothing needs your attention", which was untrue when nothing had been counted.
- **The Recent activity panel says how far back it is looking** — the last 24 hours. "Nothing has happened here yet" means something very different on a utility's first Monday than it does on its hundredth.
- **The cycle line no longer offers a set-up link.** It states where your billing cycles stand; setting them up lives on Settings → Routes & Cycles, which is in the sidebar of every screen.
- **The dashboard is re-read every five minutes rather than every thirty seconds**, so returning to it through the day costs the server far less work. Nothing you see is older than five minutes.

### Fixed
- A to-do row for closing the accounting period would have taken the whole To-do panel down with it the day that figure is published, because the panel expected a number and that item is a period, not a count (DEF-304).
- The four to-do links pointed at the right screens by coincidence rather than by wiring, so renaming a screen would have broken all four silently (DEF-305).

## [2.21.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-011 · The Phase-4 decision batch

### Added
- **A System Admin can change a teammate's email address, not just their name.** The Users screen's Edit panel now carries an Email field beside Full name, and it says what changing it means: the address is how that person signs in, and no verification message goes anywhere because nothing in this product sends mail. The server has validated, refused duplicates and audited an email change since the day it was written — there was simply no box to type one in (DEF-290).
- **A new utility is created with its security policy written down**, instead of the product falling back to values held in code for any utility that never opened the Security screen. Nobody's rules change: the row is written at exactly the figures that screen has always shown — minimum password length 8, upper/lower/number required, a symbol optional, passwords that never expire, a 60-minute idle timeout and no IP restriction. What changes is that those figures are now the utility's own data, so a future change to the platform's defaults cannot quietly re-set a utility's password rule with nobody's name on it. Utilities that already exist are repaired with `manage.py seed_demo --tenant <subdomain>`.

### Changed
- **Two questions the Product Owner was asked as code numbers have been asked again in plain English** — whether paper size is a setting or a second document to edit, and what to do about three switches on the Notifications screen that turn on something nothing fires — each with the figure attached and the options named (`12-governance/17-cr011-po-decision-batch.md`).

## [2.22.0] — 2026-08-19 · CR-010 · Seed data must be COMPLETE

> Assigned **2.20.0** and re-assigned. The bump never reached `package.json`: a
> concurrent lane's write took that line from 2.19.1 straight to 2.21.0 in the
> same minutes, so **2.20.0 was never a build anyone can look at** and is
> retired unused. Recorded rather than quietly renumbered.

### Fixed
- **A new utility's notification rules are written when the utility is created**, alongside its dispatch settings, instead of appearing the first time somebody opens the screen. Before this, "has this utility configured its notifications?" answered *no rows* for every tenant nobody had visited — indistinguishable from "never set up". Fifteen event rules and their twenty-six channel rows now land at sign-up, with the past-due reminder already skipping customers on a payment plan. Nothing is sent on any channel; this decides what *would* be. Tenants that already exist are repaired with `manage.py seed_demo --tenant <subdomain>`.

### Changed
- **The seed is measured, on screen and in a test.** A tenant is planted with **31 configure cards** on Settings → Configure — 20 seeded lists, 7 configuration panels and 4 Work lists not yet set up — and the seeded vocabulary is 26 units of measure · 23 charge codes · 12 asset types · 12 account sub-types · 9 meter size classes · 7 payment methods and thirteen more lists. The priced catalogue a bill is built from is **6 rate schedules · 23 charge codes · 5 plans · 5 Texas tax rates across 7 jurisdictions** for a tenant created today.

### Known
- The demo tenant on a deployment created before 2026-08-18 shows no district on its premises and no sub-type on its accounts: the sample plant learned to set both, and a change to the plant does not reach a tenant already planted. Load sample data again, or provision a fresh tenant, to see them.

## [2.5.0] — 2026-08-17 · CR-005 · SET-08 Numbering
### Added
- **Every system-generated number now has a format a System Admin can set.** Twenty-two series in five groups (Customers & premises · Billing & payments · Finance · Work · Assets & reads), up from the five a tenant was seeded with. Each row carries ready-made formats, a plain prefix-free option, an editable next counter, a "restart each year/month" choice, a live preview and a reset that confirms before it moves.
- **"How they appear together"** — the right rail shows an account, bill, payment and receipt number in a bill header, a work-order card and a finance trail, re-rendering as formats change so the effect is visible before saving.
- **The Work series ship as formats now** (work order · service template · dispatch batch), standalone in Settings per the PO's ruling. No work-order table is created and OQ-249 is untouched.

### Fixed
- **A manual journal entry posted with NO NUMBER on every tenant in existence.** `SERIES_DEFAULTS` seeded five series while nine were known, so `JE-` had no row and S56 showed a 36-character id where three ratified documents say **JE-104**. The map is now derived from one catalog, so the next series cannot go missing the same way. Deposit batches (`DEP-`), receipts (`RCT-`) and accounting exports (`EXP-`) had the same gap and are seeded too. Tenants that already exist are repaired with `manage.py seed_demo --tenant <subdomain>`.
- Premises, unit and read-batch numbers, which metering has asked the numbering kernel for since it was built and got `numbering_series_missing` for, now allocate.

### Changed
- `number_series` gains `restart_period` and `period_counted` (tenancy migration 0012). **Every existing row lands at `never`, which is exactly what it does today** — no live counter moves because a column arrived.
- Format validation now also enforces ≤24 characters and a counter pad of ≤8. The CR's pad MINIMUM of four is deliberately not enforced — it would make the shipped `ADJ-{000}` unsaveable (OQ-250).
